1.subtitle: The Great Indictment
1.intro:
Where we are. Chapter 1 is the door into the book. Placed first, though probably spoken late in Isaiah’s ministry (see the note on vv. 7–9), it sets out the whole case between God and his people: the charge, the evidence, the offer and the verdict.

The message. God’s people have rebelled against the Father who raised them, and he will not accept their religion in place of their lives: worship offered by hands that crush the helpless is hateful to him. Yet the God who brings the charge also offers to wash out the stain nothing else can remove, and he will purify his city by fire and redeem it by justice.

Why it was said. Judah was busy with temple worship while its courts were bought, its widows and orphans went unheard and its countryside was stripped by invasion (see the introduction). The people assumed that their sacrifices kept God on their side.

How the chapter makes its case. First the charge (vv. 1–9): heaven and earth are called as witnesses, the children know less than an ox, the nation is beaten from head to foot, and only God’s mercy has left any survivors. Then the worship (vv. 10–20): God refuses sacrifices, festivals and prayers, because the hands lifted to him are full of blood, and asks instead for justice for the fatherless and the widow; then, with the case proved, he says “come now”, and scarlet sins can be white as snow. Finally the fire (vv. 21–31): the faithful city has become unfaithful, so God will smelt out the dross, give back her name and redeem Zion by justice, while those who cling to their idols burn with them.

Where it leads. The chapter points to Christ chiefly by the need it exposes and the character of God it reveals, with the promise of v. 18 at its centre. A wounded body no one binds up, a stain no washing removes, a God who must be just and yet longs to forgive: Isaiah does not say here how these meet. Fifty-two chapters later the Servant is wounded so that “with his wounds we are healed” (53:5), and at the cross God shows himself “just and the justifier of the one who has faith in Jesus” (Romans 3:26). Zion redeemed by justice is the gospel in a sentence.

For us. This chapter will not let us hide behind religious activity or a tidy life: God wants our sin brought into the open, not covered with more offerings. Nor will it let us despair. The God who sees the blood on our hands is the one who says “come”, and those he washes he sets to learning good, beginning with people who can never repay them.

keyVerse.quote: “Come now, let us reason together, says the LORD: though your sins are like scarlet, they shall be as white as snow; though they are red like crimson, they shall become like wool.”
keyVerse.note: This verse comes straight after one of the most severe charges in Scripture, and that is what gives it its force: the invitation goes to the guilty before any improvement, and the change promised is total, scarlet to snow, crimson to wool. God does not say ‘reform first, then I will reason with you’; he says come, and his grace makes us able to come. How a just God can say it, the book shows in the Servant who was “pierced for our transgressions” (53:5).

1.theology:
Worship and the life behind it. Verses 10-17 are not an attack on ceremony; God designed every element being refused. They are about worship that has come loose from the worshipper’s life, and the test applied is justice for the fatherless and the widow, who have nobody to plead for them and no way of repaying help. Jesus brings the identical charge against men meticulous about tithing herbs and careless about justice and mercy (Matt. 23:23).

Judgment as smelting. Verse 25 sets the pattern for the whole book: God will smelt away your dross, as a refiner melts silver to remove the waste. His fire is aimed at what is worthless, for the sake of what is precious.

Redeemed by justice. Verse 27 is the hardest and best sentence in the chapter: Zion is redeemed by justice, not by justice being waived. If God simply overlooks what verses 15 and 23 describe he has abandoned righteousness; if he enforces it there is nobody left. Isaiah states both and does not explain how, because the explanation is a cross outside the same city, where God is shown to be just and the justifier (Rom. 3:26).
1.reflection:
Isaiah’s first charge is not immorality but forgetting whose we are: the ox knows its owner, “but Israel does not know” (v. 3). How can people who are busy with religion still not know the God who feeds them? Where are you most tempted to forget where your good things come from?

God refuses worship from people whose hands are full of blood (vv. 11–15) and asks instead for justice for the fatherless and the widow (v. 17). Who near you, or in your church, cannot repay you or defend themselves, and what would learning to do good look like towards them?

Verse 18 comes after seventeen verses of prosecution. Why does it matter that the offer is made to the guilty before they improve? Have you ever thought your sin too deep or too long-standing for this verse?

Zion is “redeemed by justice” (v. 27). Why would a forgiveness that simply ignored sin not be good news? How does the cross let God be both just and the one who forgives (Romans 3:26)?

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–9 — The Ox Knows Its Owner
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God’s children have forgotten whose they are, and their wounds are what that forgetting has cost them. The vision is dated across four kings of Judah (v. 1). Heaven and earth are summoned as witnesses, as when the covenant was made, to hear a Father’s charge: the children he raised have rebelled and know less than an ox knows of its owner (vv. 2–3). The nation is a body beaten from head to foot that will not be treated (vv. 4–6). The land is burned and occupied, and Jerusalem stands alone like a watchman’s hut in a stripped field (vv. 7–8). Only God’s mercy in leaving a few survivors has kept them from Sodom’s end (v. 9).
verseByVerse.theology: The chapter is shaped like a court case, but God is not a judge prosecuting strangers. He is bound by covenant to a people who swore loyalty to him, which is why at the key point he speaks as a father, not a lawyer. Rebellion here is a son’s, not a criminal’s. And verse 9 puts the remnant, the few whom God keeps, on the first page: that anyone survives at all is God’s restraint and not Israel’s merit. Paul quotes it to say just that (Rom. 9:29).
verseByVerse.examples: A dog runs to the door at the sound of its owner's car. A son who has been given everything can pass his father in the street and not stop. Verse 3 says Israel is the son.

verseByVerse.quote: The vision of Isaiah the son of Amoz, which he saw concerning Judah and Jerusalem in the days of Uzziah, Jotham, Ahaz, and Hezekiah, kings of Judah. Hear, O heavens, and give ear, O earth; for the LORD has spoken: "Children have I reared and brought up, but they have rebelled against me. The ox knows its owner, and the donkey its master's crib, but Israel does not know, my people do not understand."
verseByVerse.commentary:
God takes his people to court like a grieving father: the children he raised have turned against him and do not even know whose they are.

Hear, O heavens, and give ear, O earth. Any Israelite would recognise the opening. Heaven and earth were the witnesses called when God made his covenant with Israel (Deuteronomy 30:19; 32:1), and calling them again means a case is being brought. This is a courtroom, and the defendant is God’s own people.

Children have I reared. Yet the charge does not sound legal. Not “a nation has broken its treaty”, but children have I reared: a father who fed them and raised them, and has been thrown over. God speaks as accuser and as grieving parent in one sentence, and the grief is the louder half.

The ox knows its owner. An ox is not clever. It knows who feeds it and where the food is, and that is enough. Israel does not know even that. The first charge is not immorality, though plenty comes later, but not knowing whose they are and where their food comes from, and every other sin in the chapter grows out of that soil (compare Romans 1:21).

The ox, the donkey and the manger. The ox and donkey of nativity scenes are not in Luke; early Christians took them from this verse, whose “crib” is a feeding trough. The scene is legend, but the irony is real. When the Lord himself lay in a manger, “his own people did not receive him” (John 1:11), and he wept over the city that “did not know the time of your visitation” (Luke 19:44): the Father’s grief of v. 2 on a human face.
verseByVerse.note: Isaiah (“the LORD saves”) prophesied in Jerusalem for about forty years, from roughly 740 to 700 BC, under four kings of Judah. The New Testament quotes him more than any other prophet.

verseByVerse.quote: Ah, sinful nation, a people laden with iniquity, offspring of evildoers, children who deal corruptly! They have forsaken the LORD, they have despised the Holy One of Israel, they are utterly estranged. Why will you still be struck down? Why will you continue to rebel? The whole head is sick, and the whole heart faint. From the sole of the foot even to the head, there is no soundness in it, but bruises and sores and raw wounds; they are not pressed out or bound up or softened with oil.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Sin has left the whole nation beaten and sick from head to foot, and still they refuse the treatment that would heal them.

Ah, sinful nation. The Hebrew word behind “Ah” is the one Isaiah uses for “Woe”, closer to a groan than a shout. Laden with iniquity is a pack animal under a load it cannot put down: sin has not set them free, it has loaded them down. The Holy One of Israel appears here for the first time, Isaiah’s own name for God, used about twenty-five times through the book; what it means he learns in the temple (6:3–5).

From the sole of the foot even to the head. Why go on being struck down? The beating is God’s discipline, and they keep provoking more. Then an unsparing medical examination: three kinds of injury at three depths, the bruise under the skin, the open sore, the fresh wound, and no healthy tissue anywhere to start treating from. Nobody has done the three ordinary things you do for a wound: press it clean, bind it up, soothe it with oil. Help was available; nobody used it.

Softened with oil. Many Christians have heard an echo here of the Samaritan who poured on oil and wine and bound up a stranger’s wounds (Luke 10:34), and have seen in him a picture of Christ; that is an echo, not the parable’s point. The firmer link is in Isaiah himself. The same book describes a servant wounded for our transgressions and says that “with his wounds we are healed” (53:5), which Peter applies to Christ (1 Peter 2:24). The nation nobody would treat is healed at last by one who takes the wounds himself.

verseByVerse.quote: Your country lies desolate; your cities are burned with fire; in your very presence foreigners devour your land; it is desolate, as overthrown by foreigners. And the daughter of Zion is left like a booth in a vineyard, like a lodge in a cucumber field, like a besieged city. If the LORD of hosts had not left us a few survivors, we should have been like Sodom, and become like Gomorrah.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The land lies burned and Jerusalem stands alone, and the only reason anyone is left is that God himself left them.

Your country lies desolate. The charge is no longer a picture but a fact: burned towns, occupied fields, all of it in your very presence. Isaiah does not date this oracle, but it fits the Assyrian invasion of 701 BC best. Sennacherib boasted of taking forty-six walled towns of Judah and shutting Hezekiah up in Jerusalem “like a bird in a cage”. If so, the chapter was placed at the front of the book as a summary of the whole case, though spoken late in Isaiah’s ministry.

Like a booth in a vineyard. The daughter of Zion is Jerusalem pictured as a young woman. Through the growing season a watchman’s hut stood in the field, four poles and some branches, to guard the crop. When the harvest was over everyone left, and the hut stayed: a flimsy thing alone in a stripped field, waiting to fall over. That is Jerusalem: not destroyed, only left behind.

A few survivors. Here, on the first page, is a teaching that runs through the whole book: the remnant. The reason anybody is left is not that some of them were better, but that God left them. Sodom was wiped out completely, and only God’s holding back keeps Israel from the same end. Paul quotes this verse to explain why there is still a believing remnant in Israel in his own day (Romans 9:29). Anyone still standing is standing because God kept them. Later in the book the remnant is gathered up in one Servant, even called by Israel’s name (49:3), and everyone God has kept since is kept in him.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 10–20 — Your Hands Are Full of Blood
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God will not accept worship from hands that hurt the helpless, yet he offers to wash the very sins that make that worship hateful. He calls Jerusalem’s rulers Sodom and Gomorrah (v. 10) and refuses the whole worship he himself commanded, sacrifices, incense, new moons, Sabbaths and prayers, because the hands lifted to him are full of blood (vv. 11–15). What he asks for instead is nine commands, every one about other people: wash, stop doing evil, learn to do good, seek justice, defend the fatherless and the widow (vv. 16–17). Then the prosecutor opens a door nobody expected, scarlet sins made white as snow, and sets two roads before them (vv. 18–20).
verseByVerse.theology: The test God applies to worship here is not sincerity but justice, and the cure he offers is not more religion but cleansing (v. 18).
verseByVerse.examples: A man who sings loudly on Sunday and underpays his cleaner on Monday is the man of verse 15; the hymn does not cancel the wage.

verseByVerse.quote: Hear the word of the LORD, you rulers of Sodom! Give ear to the teaching of our God, you people of Gomorrah! "What to me is the multitude of your sacrifices? says the LORD; I have had enough of burnt offerings of rams and the fat of well-fed beasts; I do not delight in the blood of bulls, or of lambs, or of goats.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God calls the leaders of his holy city Sodom, and tells them their mountain of sacrifices means nothing to him while their lives defy him.

You rulers of Sodom! Verse 9 said they were nearly Sodom. Verse 10 calls them Sodom, to their faces, in the temple: the leaders of the city of David are given the name of the city God burned.

What to me is the multitude of your sacrifices? This is easily misused. God is not saying the sacrificial system was a mistake; he designed it and specified the animals he now lists. What he says is I have had enough: the system is working perfectly and he cannot bear it, because of who is bringing it. The sheer number is part of the problem. When something feels wrong, a religious person does more, answering a bad conscience with activity instead of dealing with what troubles it. The way through is the one v. 18 opens: bring the sin, not more offerings.

The blood of bulls. Even offered rightly, these sacrifices could never do what the worshippers wanted: “it is impossible for the blood of bulls and goats to take away sins” (Hebrews 10:4). They pointed to the one offering God does delight in, the body of his Son (Hebrews 10:5–10).

Hiding from God in church. We assume religion brings people close to God. These men are in the temple more than anyone, and they are using it to keep God at arm’s length. Flannery O’Connor saw the same from another angle in Wise Blood, whose young preacher of unbelief is convinced that the way to avoid Jesus is to avoid sin. A crowded religious calendar can work like that, or a tidy moral life, or a busy one with no religion at all: each handles God instead of meeting him, paying something so that he will not come closer. What God wants is not more payment but the sin itself, brought into the open and washed.

verseByVerse.quote: "When you come to appear before me, who has required of you this trampling of my courts? Bring no more vain offerings; incense is an abomination to me. New moon and Sabbath and the calling of convocations— I cannot endure iniquity and solemn assembly. Your new moons and your appointed feasts my soul hates; they have become a burden to me; I am weary of bearing them. When you spread out your hands, I will hide my eyes from you; even though you make many prayers, I will not listen; your hands are full of blood.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God refuses their worship, festivals and prayers alike, because the hands they lift to him are stained with the blood of people they have wronged.

This trampling of my courts. They came to the temple because he told them to, and he calls their arrival trampling, like cattle churning up the ground. The same feet in the same courtyard, but God no longer sees it as worship.

I cannot endure iniquity and solemn assembly. He rejects the whole calendar: incense, new moons, Sabbaths, festivals. What he cannot endure is iniquity and solemn assembly: not either one, but the two arriving together. Throughout the law they are my feasts, God’s appointed times; here they are your new moons and your appointed feasts. He has handed them back.

Your hands are full of blood. The reason is held back to the end. Hands spread out, palms lifted, is the posture of prayer, and God can see what is on them. He is not only describing murderers, though v. 21 names them, but respectable men who worship on the appointed day and whose money comes from people who cannot defend themselves. The blood is on the hands doing the praying, and that is why the praying is not heard. Only one man ever lifted truly clean hands to God (Psalm 24:4), and they were pierced for people whose hands are full of blood.

What it does not mean. Not that a struggling believer whose prayers feel unanswered is under this sentence. God refuses people who go on doing wrong and use worship to cover it: “If I had cherished iniquity in my heart, the Lord would not have listened” (Psalm 66:18). The one who comes confessing is exactly the one v. 18 invites.

verseByVerse.quote: Wash yourselves; make yourselves clean; remove the evil of your deeds from before my eyes; cease to do evil, learn to do good; seek justice, correct oppression; bring justice to the fatherless, plead the widow's cause.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Repentance is not more religion but a changed life, and God measures it by how we treat people who can do nothing for us.

Wash yourselves; make yourselves clean. Nine commands follow one after another. After four verses rejecting the entire calendar of worship, God’s list of what he wants contains no sacrifice, festival, prayer or incense. Every item is about somebody else.

Learn to do good. Stopping evil is a decision; goodness has to be learned, slowly, the way you learn a trade. Seek justice, correct oppression: both verbs are active, and both cost something. Oppression is not corrected by disapproving of it.

Bring justice to the fatherless. In that society a child with no father and a woman with no husband had little legal protection and often nobody to speak for them. God chooses them as the test precisely because there is nothing to gain by helping them. What a person does for someone who cannot repay him or complain about him is the truest measure of what he is.

What this looks like. Learning to do good starts near at hand. Find the widow and the fatherless where you are: the widow at church who eats alone on Sundays, the single mother at the school gate, the family fostering a child who would welcome a meal or a lift. True religion, James says, is “to visit orphans and widows in their affliction” (James 1:27). Look for oppression on your own patch. Are you paying the cleaner fairly and on time? Is the newest person at work blamed for everyone else’s mistakes? Correcting it may mean a hard conversation with someone more powerful than you. Invite people who cannot repay (Luke 14:13–14). Start small and keep going. A trade is learned by doing it badly at first. None of this earns the washing of v. 18. Christ gave himself “to purify for himself a people for his own possession who are zealous for good works” (Titus 2:14): the washing comes first, and the good works grow out of it.

Commands from a Father. These commands are spoken by the Father of v. 2 to children he reared, and the very next verse offers to wash them. None of us has kept this list; Christ kept it perfectly, gathering in the widow and the fatherless, and his obedience is counted to those who trust him. The Spirit he gives teaches the slow skill of doing good.

verseByVerse.quote: "Come now, let us reason together, says the LORD: though your sins are like scarlet, they shall be as white as snow; though they are red like crimson, they shall become like wool. If you are willing and obedient, you shall eat the good of the land; but if you refuse and rebel, you shall be eaten by the sword; for the mouth of the LORD has spoken."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Into the middle of the prosecution God puts a free offer: come to him, and sins that cannot be removed will be made completely clean; refuse, and judgment stands.

Come now, let us reason together. Seventeen verses of prosecution, and then this. The plaintiff, with the evidence on the table and the defendant’s hands visibly bloody, says come. The verb is a legal one, “let us argue the case out”, and what should follow is a sentence. What follows is an offer.

Though your sins are like scarlet. Scarlet and crimson were not stains but dyes. The scarlet of that world came from a small insect crushed for its pigment, and its whole value was that it did not come out: a dyer’s craft was making a colour that would survive washing, sunlight and years of wear. So God does not pick a mark that might scrub off with effort. He names the one colour guaranteed not to, and says it will be as white as snow.

As white as snow. The most permanent dye known to that world has been dealt with: not excused, not overlooked, not weighed against better years, but made white. What that would cost, and who would pay it, this chapter does not say. Fifty-two chapters later the same book describes a man pierced for transgressions and crushed for iniquities, and then it is plain how v. 18 can be true (compare Revelation 7:14).

If you are willing and obedient. Two roads follow, stated without softening, with a play on one Hebrew verb: you shall eat the good of the land, or you shall be eaten by the sword. The offer is free, but it can be refused, and refusing it is the one thing that cannot be undone. This does not make the washing a reward for obedience: to be willing is to take the gift, and obedience is the life of those who have.

Uncertain wording. The Hebrew is compressed, literally ‘if your sins are like scarlet, like snow they shall be white’, with nothing to mark a question. A few interpreters read an indignant question (‘can they be white?’). Most, with the ESV, read a promise, and vv. 19–20 support it: the offer stands, and the only question is whether they will take it.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 21–31 — The Smelting, and the Faithful City
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God will not give up his city: he will purify her by fire and redeem her by justice, while those who cling to their idols burn with them. He laments the faithful city turned unfaithful, her silver become dross, her wine watered down, her rulers bribed and the widow unheard (vv. 21–23). He counts his own people among his enemies, yet his vengeance turns out to be a refiner’s fire that smelts away the dross and gives the city back its judges and its old name (vv. 24–26). Zion will be redeemed by justice, and those who repent by righteousness, but those who forsake the LORD will be consumed (vv. 27–28), shamed by the sacred oaks and gardens they chose and set alight by their own work (vv. 29–31).
verseByVerse.theology: Judgment in Isaiah is a refiner's fire, and the end of it is a city called faithful again.
verseByVerse.examples: An old saying has it that the refiner keeps the silver in the fire until he can see his own face in it. That is the purpose of verse 25: not to destroy, but to make the city reflect her God again.

verseByVerse.quote: How the faithful city has become a whore, she who was full of justice! Righteousness lodged in her, but now murderers. Your silver has become dross, your best wine mixed with water. Your princes are rebels and companions of thieves. Everyone loves a bribe and runs after gifts. They do not bring justice to the fatherless, and the widow's cause does not come to them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The city once at home with justice has been unfaithful to God like an adulterous wife, its goodness watered down until bribes rule and the helpless go unheard.

How the faithful city has become a whore. “How” opens a funeral lament in Hebrew; it is the first word of Lamentations. God is not scolding but grieving aloud over a city, as you would over a person, and the prophets often picture the covenant as a marriage (Hosea 2; Jeremiah 3). The memory in the middle is tender: righteousness once lodged in her, stayed the night, had a room. There was a time when doing right was at home in that city.

Your silver has become dross. Two frauds, and both work the same way: the good is thinned with something cheap, and nobody outside can see it. Nobody sells dross as dross; it passes because it looks like silver. Nobody sells water as wine; you cut the wine until the profit is good and the customer cannot quite tell. There was never a day when Jerusalem decided to stop being faithful. It was watered down a little at a time, in steps small enough that nobody had to object to any one of them.

The widow’s cause does not come to them. The two groups from v. 17 return, to show where the watering down can be seen. The widow’s case never reaches the judge: not refused, just never arriving, because there is no fee attached to it and the calendar is full of cases that pay.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore the Lord declares, the LORD of hosts, the Mighty One of Israel: "Ah, I will get relief from my enemies and avenge myself on my foes. I will turn my hand against you and will smelt away your dross as with lye and remove all your alloy. And I will restore your judges as at the first, and your counselors as at the beginning. Afterward you shall be called the city of righteousness, the faithful city."
verseByVerse.commentary:
God counts his own corrupt people among his enemies, yet his judgment on them is a refiner’s fire, meant to burn out the dross and give back a faithful city.

Avenge myself on my foes. Three titles of God are stacked up, and then a sentence that should stop the reader: God will avenge himself on his enemies, and the people he means are Judah. His own covenant people have ended up among his enemies. Vengeance here is not spite but the Judge of all the earth putting wrong right, which only he is entitled to do (Deuteronomy 32:35; Romans 12:19), and the next verse shows what he means to do with it.

Smelt away your dross. A refiner brings silver to a heat that would ruin most things because there is silver in it, mixed with rubbish, and this is the only way to get it out. The fire is aimed at the dross; the silver is the reason for the fire. The heat is no cooler for the people inside it, but God is not disposing of Jerusalem. He is standing over it with a purpose, waiting for something to come clear.

The faithful city. There is the finished silver. Verse 21 mourned how the faithful city became a whore; v. 26 gives her back that very name. The judgment that would consume sinners fell on Christ, so the fires his people now pass through only refine (1 Peter 1:6–7), and the faithful city is finally the new Jerusalem, “prepared as a bride adorned for her husband” (Revelation 21:2).

Uncertain wording. “As with lye” (v. 25) names an alkali, potash, that could serve as a flux in smelting; some scholars, changing one letter, read ‘as in a furnace’. Either way, everything that is not silver is burned out.

verseByVerse.quote: Zion shall be redeemed by justice, and those in her who repent, by righteousness. But rebels and sinners shall be broken together, and those who forsake the LORD shall be consumed.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God will rescue Zion in a way that upholds his justice instead of setting it aside: those who turn back to him are saved, and those who forsake him perish.

Zion shall be redeemed by justice. Verse 27 holds in one sentence what the whole Bible works out, and the small word by carries the weight. Not despite justice, nor by justice set aside for people God is fond of: the rescue comes through the very thing that condemned her. Isaiah means first the purging justice of vv. 24–26, and those in her who repent are literally “her returning ones”.

The problem the chapter raises. If God simply forgives the blood, the bribes and the unheard widow, he has abandoned justice, and a God who waives justice for people he likes is not good; he merely has favourites. If he enforces it, there is nobody left to redeem. Isaiah says both happen: justice is done, and Zion is redeemed by it.

Just and the justifier. He does not explain how here, and he could not yet have. The explanation is a cross outside the same city, where God showed his righteousness “so that he might be just and the justifier of the one who has faith in Jesus” (Romans 3:26). Paul’s sentence and Isaiah’s are the same sentence, seven centuries apart.

Those who forsake the LORD shall be consumed. Verse 28 keeps the alternative in view without apology. The difference between the two outcomes is not the amount of guilt, which everyone in the city has, but whether the invitation of v. 18 was taken.

verseByVerse.quote: For they shall be ashamed of the oaks that you desired; and you shall blush for the gardens that you have chosen. For you shall be like an oak whose leaf withers, and like a garden without water. And the strong shall become tinder, and his work a spark, and both of them shall burn together, with none to quench them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Those who chose idols will be shamed by them and destroyed with them, set alight by their own work.

The oaks that you desired. The oaks and gardens are not scenery. They were sacred groves and garden shrines where respectable people in Judah went for the things they wanted and were not getting from the temple. They desired and chose them; nobody drifted into it.

Like an oak whose leaf withers. The reversal is exact. They went to the oaks; they will be a dying oak. They went to the watered gardens; they will be a garden with the water cut off. What a person gives himself to, he comes to resemble (Psalm 115:8), and if the thing has no life in it, neither will he. A garden without water does not look wrong for a while. Then it does.

The strong shall become tinder. The last image is a man and his life’s work catching fire from each other. The strong man is the dry kindling; the thing he built is the spark that lands on him. Nothing from outside is needed. What he made ignites what he is.

From courtroom to fire. So the book opens with a courtroom and closes its first chapter with a fire, and between them stands one sentence with an open door in it: come now, let us reason together, says the LORD: though your sins are like scarlet, they shall be as white as snow. Everything else in these sixty-six chapters is God making that sentence good, until the one wounded for us (53:5) invites everyone who thirsts to the waters no sacred garden could give (55:1).

2.subtitle: The Mountain of the LORD and the Day Against Pride
2.intro:
Where we are. Chapter 1 laid out the whole case against Jerusalem and ended with a city purified by fire. Chapter 2 opens a new collection (chapters 2–4) with a fresh heading, and it begins not with the charge but with the destination: what Zion will one day be.

The message. God’s purpose is that the whole world will come to learn from him and live at peace under his rule, and everything proud that stands in the way will be brought low on his day. So his people must stop trusting wealth, weapons, idols and other people, and walk in his light now. In the end there are only two responses to God’s glory: climb towards it, or hide from it.

Why it was said. Under Uzziah and Jotham Judah had grown rich and strong, with silver, horses and trade, and with the prosperity came foreign fortune-tellers and idols (see the introduction). A secure, successful people had quietly stopped needing God.

How the chapter makes its case. First the vision (vv. 1–4): in the latter days the LORD’s mountain is raised above all others, the nations stream up it to be taught, and God settles their quarrels until swords become ploughshares. At once it becomes an invitation: “come, let us walk in the light of the LORD” (v. 5). Then the present (vv. 6–8): a land filled with diviners, treasure, chariots and idols. So a day is coming against everything high, from cedars and mountains to towers and ships, and the refrain sounds twice: “the LORD alone will be exalted in that day” (vv. 9–17). Men will fling their idols to the moles and bats and run for the rocks (vv. 18–21). The last verse draws the lesson: stop trusting man (v. 22).

Where it leads. The chapter leads to Christ by promise and by the character of God. The nations began streaming to the LORD when the risen Jesus sent his word out “beginning from Jerusalem” (Luke 24:47), and believers “have come to Mount Zion” (Hebrews 12:22). And the God who alone will be exalted has shown his height in the one who humbled himself to the cross, whom “God has highly exalted” (Philippians 2:9). Revelation borrows this chapter’s caves and rocks for those who hide “from the wrath of the Lamb” (Revelation 6:16).

For us. Every reputation, portfolio and achievement we look up to is scheduled to be levelled, so it is foolish to lean on any of them, or to put on any person the weight only God can carry. The God who brings down the proud has come down himself to make peace, and the invitation of v. 5 is still open: come, walk in his light today.

keyVerse.quote: “The haughty looks of man shall be brought low, and the lofty pride of men shall be humbled, and the LORD alone will be exalted in that day.”
keyVerse.note: The sentence comes twice as the chapter’s refrain (vv. 11 and 17). Isaiah is not predicting that God will win a close contest at last; he is declaring that the exaltation of the LORD is the fixed destination of history, so every attempt at self-exaltation is moving against the grain of the universe. The New Testament shows where it ends: every knee bowing to Jesus, the Lord who humbled himself (Philippians 2:9–11).

2.theology:
Peace as a consequence, not a policy. The order in verse 4 decides its meaning: God judges between the nations and settles their disputes, and then the weapons are recycled. Nations do not disarm and thereby find peace; they disarm because their quarrels are being resolved at a throne whose verdicts hold. Remove the judge and the ploughshares go back to being swords.

The day against height. The catalogue in vv. 12-16 runs deliberately from what God grew to what men built, and nothing on it is sinful in itself. What the cedars, towers and ships have in common is that people look up at them, and the refrain states the principle twice: the LORD alone will be exalted in that day.

Two responses to one glory. The same splendour draws the nations up a mountain (v. 3) and drives men into caves (v. 19).
2.reflection:
In vv. 2–4 the nations come to God asking to be taught his ways, and peace follows his judgment. What would it look like for your church to be the kind of place where people come wanting to learn how to live? What quarrel in your own life needs to be brought to God’s verdict?

Isaiah moves straight from the vision of the future to “come, let us walk in the light of the LORD” (v. 5). How should the certainty of where history is going change the way you live this week?

The land was “filled” with treasure, horses and idols, things good in themselves until they became trusted (vv. 7–8). What things that you have made or earned are most likely to become what you look up to? How can you tell when a gift has become an idol?

“Stop regarding man in whose nostrils is breath” (v. 22). Whom are you tempted to lean on more heavily than a person can bear? How does Jesus, the one Man who can carry the whole weight, free you to love such people instead of needing them?

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–5 — The Mountain All Nations Climb
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God’s purpose is a world that comes to him to be taught and lives at peace under his rule, and that hope calls his people to walk in his light now. In the latter days the mountain of the LORD’s house is raised above every other, and the nations stream up to it, urging one another to come and learn his ways, while his word goes out from Jerusalem (vv. 1–3). He judges their disputes, so that weapons are beaten into farm tools and war is no longer learned (v. 4). At once the vision becomes an invitation to Israel: come, let us walk in the light of the LORD (v. 5).
verseByVerse.theology: This is a promise about God's rule before it is a promise about human peace: the peace follows the throne.
verseByVerse.examples: A family who know a long-lost son is coming home start laying the table before he arrives. Verse 5 asks God's people to live like that.

verseByVerse.quote: The word that Isaiah the son of Amoz saw concerning Judah and Jerusalem. It shall come to pass in the latter days that the mountain of the house of the LORD shall be established as the highest of the mountains, and shall be lifted up above the hills; and all the nations shall flow to it, and many peoples shall come, and say: "Come, let us go up to the mountain of the LORD, to the house of the God of Jacob, that he may teach us his ways and that we may walk in his paths." For out of Zion shall go forth the law, and the word of the LORD from Jerusalem.
verseByVerse.commentary:
In the last days God will lift his rule above every other power, and the nations will come to him of their own accord, wanting to learn how to live, while his word goes out from Jerusalem.

The mountain of the house of the LORD. Zion is not a high mountain; the hills around it overlook it, and any Israelite knew it. So this is not a claim about geology but about which authority will finally be visibly on top.

All the nations shall flow to it. The verb is the surprise. Water does not flow uphill. Isaiah pictures peoples pouring upward to God, as if gravity had been reversed. Nor is it Israel inviting the nations: the nations urge each other to go and be taught by a God who was not theirs. What they want is not prosperity or protection but that he may teach us his ways: they are hungry to know how to live. The house of the God of Jacob was always meant to be, as Jesus said, “a house of prayer for all the nations” (Mark 11:17).

Out of Zion shall go forth the law. The traffic runs both ways in the same verse: they come up, and the word goes out. That is what happened when the apostles, taught by Jesus in Jerusalem, were sent from that city to the ends of the earth, “beginning from Jerusalem” (Luke 24:47; Acts 1:8).

Where Christians differ: when are the “latter days”, and how is the mountain raised? Dispensationalists and other premillennial Christians look for a future earthly reign of Christ centred on Jerusalem, with literal world peace. This commentary’s view: the New Testament says the latter days began with Christ: “in these last days he has spoken to us by his Son” (Hebrews 1:2; compare Acts 2:17). The mountain of the LORD is being raised now, as the nations stream to Christ and the word goes out from Jerusalem, and believers “have come to Mount Zion” (Hebrews 12:22). The peace of v. 4 is begun in the gospel and completed when Christ returns and makes all things new.
verseByVerse.note: Micah 4:1–3 gives almost the same oracle.

verseByVerse.quote: He shall judge between the nations, and shall decide disputes for many peoples; and they shall beat their swords into plowshares, and their spears into pruning hooks; nation shall not lift up sword against nation, neither shall they learn war anymore. O house of Jacob, come, let us walk in the light of the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When God settles the nations’ quarrels, they will turn their weapons into tools for growing food, and that coming peace is a call to walk in his light now.

He shall judge between the nations. The most famous sentence in the chapter, and its order is usually missed. The disarmament comes second. First God arbitrates, and only then are the weapons melted down. This is not naive pacifism, nor a policy proposal: nations disarm because their quarrels are settled by a judge whose verdict holds.

Swords into plowshares. The metalwork is exact: the same iron, reheated, hammered into a tool for growing food. The materials of killing become the materials of feeding. War is a discipline, studied, taught, funded and rehearsed in every generation; Isaiah promises a world where nobody learns it any more.

Let us walk in the light of the LORD. Then, without a pause, the vision becomes an instruction for this afternoon. The nations said come, let us go up; Isaiah says come, let us walk. The light is God’s, not ours: he teaches his ways, and for the Christian it is his Spirit who leads us in them. If that is where history is going, start living in that direction now, which is the proper use of any promise about the future.

The peace already made. The judge of v. 4 has already settled the deepest quarrel, ours with God, at the cross: “he himself is our peace” (Ephesians 2:14), and in him enemies who were divided become one people. And “if we walk in the light, as he is in the light, we have fellowship with one another, and the blood of Jesus his Son cleanses us from all sin” (1 John 1:7).

What this looks like. Bring your quarrels to his verdict. Before you fight your brother over the inheritance or a colleague over the credit, ask what God says about it, and accept it even when it goes against you. Beat a sword into a plowshare. The sharp tongue that wins arguments can be retrained to encourage; the hours spent rehearsing a grievance can be spent praying for the person. Stop learning war. Do not keep a file of wrongs, or practise the speech you will make next time. Make the first move. “If possible, so far as it depends on you, live peaceably with all” (Romans 12:18). None of this is mere niceness; it is living now by the peace Christ has made.

What it does not mean. Not that all force is now forbidden. The verse describes the peace God brings when he judges, not a policy for states before that day; Scripture still allows the lawful force of government and the defence of the vulnerable (Romans 13:4), though Christian pacifists, who read it otherwise, deserve respect. But Christ’s kingdom is never advanced by the sword.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 6–22 — The Day Against Everything Tall
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Where the nations climb towards God, his own people hide from him, because everything proud will be brought low and the LORD alone exalted. The land is full of fortune-tellers, foreign deals, treasure, chariots and idols, and the people bow to what their own fingers made (vv. 6–8). So a day is coming against everything high, cedars, mountains, towers, walls and ships, and the refrain sounds twice that the LORD alone will be exalted (vv. 9–17). The idols vanish, flung to the moles and bats by men running for the rocks from the splendour of his majesty (vv. 18–21). Verse 22 draws the practical lesson: stop trusting mere man.
verseByVerse.theology: The judgment falls on height as such, because pride is the sin that makes a creature into a rival of God. What God grew and what men built come down under the same sentence, which says that the problem was never the thing but the trust placed in it.
verseByVerse.examples: When a house is on fire, nobody runs back for the television. Verse 20 is that night for the idolaters, when they discover what their gods were worth.

verseByVerse.quote: For you have rejected your people, the house of Jacob, because they are full of things from the east and of fortune-tellers like the Philistines, and they strike hands with the children of foreigners. Their land is filled with silver and gold, and there is no end to their treasures; their land is filled with horses, and there is no end to their chariots. Their land is filled with idols; they bow down to the work of their hands, to what their own fingers have made.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God has given his people up to what they chose, because a land that once looked to him has filled itself with fortune-tellers, foreign deals, money, weapons and idols.

You have rejected your people. The vision breaks off and the present arrives. Full or filled comes four times in three verses, each time naming something that has taken up the space God should occupy.

Fortune-tellers like the Philistines. First, imported divination, the omen-readers of the east and the fortune-tellers of the Philistines. A people who have God’s own word are buying their future from anyone who will sell it.

No end to their treasures. Then silver, gold, horses, chariots. These are not sins but blessings, and Isaiah is writing in a time of real prosperity. What he flags is no end, twice. An accumulation with no stopping point is the surest sign that something has stopped being useful and started being trusted. Any Israelite would hear the law of the king behind the list: he was not to acquire many horses, or excessive silver and gold, lest his heart turn away (Deuteronomy 17:16–17). The long prosperity of Uzziah’s reign (2 Chronicles 26) had brought exactly what that law warned against.

The work of their hands. The fourth filling names where the others were leading: a man makes a thing and then kneels to it. Most idolatries since have kept that shape: we build the thing, then we need it, then we serve it.

The idols in our pockets. We think of idols as statues, and so assume a modern person has none. But this is how a made thing gets power over its maker. We design devices to serve us and then reach for them before we have said good morning to the people we love. We build careers to provide for a family, and the family ends up serving the career. Nobody decides to bow; the thing simply becomes the first thing we look at, the last we put down, and the one we feel lost without. The answer is not to smash everything we make, for work and tools are good gifts, but to put them back beneath the God who made us. And he is the one Maker who, instead of asking to be served by what he made, came to serve it: “the Son of Man came not to be served but to serve” (Mark 10:45).

Uncertain wording. Two phrases in v. 6 are compressed in Hebrew. “Full of things from the east” is literally ‘full from the east’; the ESV supplies “things”, while many scholars think a word for diviners has dropped out, which suits the fortune-tellers that follow. “Strike hands with the children of foreigners” most likely means making deals or alliances with foreigners, though it could mean they abound in foreign children. Either way the charge is the same: Judah has filled itself from every source but God.

verseByVerse.quote: So man is humbled, and each one is brought low— do not forgive them! Enter into the rock and hide in the dust from before the terror of the LORD, and from the splendor of his majesty. The haughty looks of man shall be brought low, and the lofty pride of men shall be humbled, and the LORD alone will be exalted in that day.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God’s own people will run and hide from his glory, because the day is coming when all human pride is brought low and the LORD alone is exalted.

Do not forgive them! Verse 9 ends with a hard line, most naturally the prophet speaking rather than God. Leave it uncomfortable: a man who has watched his own people kneel to what their fingers made does not always find the gracious sentence first. But it is not a private curse. It is the prophet agreeing with God’s sentence on a people bowing to idols, and Isaiah has already proclaimed forgiveness (1:18) and will soon cry out over his own sin (6:5). The verse shows how seriously God takes idolatry; it does not shut the door on any who repent.

Enter into the rock and hide in the dust. Here is the reversal that governs the rest of the chapter. In v. 3 the nations went up the mountain. Here God’s own people go down, into rock crevices and dust, looking for somewhere low enough to be missed. It is the same God in both scenes. The difference lies entirely in whether his arrival is what you have been waiting for or what you have been avoiding.

The LORD alone will be exalted. The chapter’s refrain, which returns in v. 17. Read it as a statement of fact rather than a threat and it becomes something to rest on: there is exactly one throne, and the competition for it is imaginary. Every reputation, empire, portfolio and self-assessment now standing tall is due to be levelled, because only one thing in the universe is truly high, and on that day it will be obvious.

Uncertain wording. The Hebrew of “do not forgive them” is literally ‘and do not lift up to them’. “Lift up” often means to forgive (lifting away guilt), which the ESV follows; others read ‘you cannot raise them up’, or ‘do not lift them up’, continuing the theme of bringing low. The sense is not in doubt: their pride has brought them down, and there is no excusing it.

verseByVerse.quote: For the LORD of hosts has a day against all that is proud and lofty, against all that is lifted up—and it shall be brought low; against all the cedars of Lebanon, lofty and lifted up; and against all the oaks of Bashan; against all the lofty mountains, and against all the uplifted hills; against every high tower, and against every fortified wall; against all the ships of Tarshish, and against all the beautiful craft.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God’s day will come against everything people look up to instead of him, whether he grew it or they built it.

Against all the cedars of Lebanon. The catalogue is one of the great lists in the prophets, and its order matters. It begins with what God grew: the cedars of Lebanon, the timber kings sent ships for, the most magnificent living thing in that world; the oaks of Bashan; the mountains and hills.

Against every high tower. Then it moves to what men built: towers and fortified walls, the security a city puts up so it can sleep; the ships of Tarshish, great ocean-going merchant ships, the visible symbol of a trading economy (where Tarshish lay is uncertain, perhaps in Spain); and the beautiful craft.

All that is proud and lofty. Nature and culture, the military and the commercial, and the same verdict falls on all of it, though there is nothing wrong with a cedar, a wall or a ship. What they have in common is height. Every item is something a person looks up at, and a creature has only so much looking up in him; every bit spent on a cedar or a share price is taken from God. So God’s day here is not against wickedness in general but against tallness, everything people look up to instead of him.

The one who came down. Only one person was ever truly high, and he did not grasp at it, but “humbled himself by becoming obedient to the point of death, even death on a cross. Therefore God has highly exalted him” (Philippians 2:8–9). That is the way up in God’s world: “Humble yourselves before the Lord, and he will exalt you” (James 4:10).

Uncertain wording. The word behind “beautiful craft” (v. 16) is rare and its meaning uncertain. It may mean ships, matching the ships of Tarshish, or more generally prized objects or showpieces. Either way it names the luxuries a wealthy people admired.

verseByVerse.quote: And the haughtiness of man shall be humbled, and the lofty pride of men shall be brought low, and the LORD alone will be exalted in that day. And the idols shall utterly pass away. And people shall enter the caves of the rocks and the holes of the ground, from before the terror of the LORD, and from the splendor of his majesty, when he rises to terrify the earth.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When God appears, human pride has nothing left to stand on, the idols simply vanish, and proud people hide in the ground from the beauty of his majesty.

The haughtiness of man shall be humbled. The refrain returns, word for word, and now the reason for the whole catalogue is plain. The cedars, towers and ships were never the point; they were what the haughtiness was standing on. Cut down the platform and the pride has nowhere to be.

The idols shall utterly pass away. In half a line the idols are disposed of. Not defeated, not argued with; they simply stop existing, as a shadow does when the thing casting it is moved. Isaiah gives the gods of the nations no more than that, and does not look back at them.

The splendor of his majesty. The men who were looking up at cedars are now underground looking for a hole. What drives them there is not fire, armies or plague, but the splendour of his majesty: the sheer beauty and weight of God, which they cannot stand in front of. The same glory that draws the nations up a mountain in v. 3 sends these men into the rocks in v. 19, and nothing about the glory has changed between the two verses.

Climb, or hide. What a person does when God finally becomes unmistakable is the most revealing thing about him, and this chapter has only two options: climb, or hide. Revelation takes up these very caves and rocks for the last day, when the great of the earth beg the mountains to hide them “from the wrath of the Lamb” (Revelation 6:16). The glory people flee is the glory of the Lamb who was slain for them, and the only safe hiding place is in him.

verseByVerse.quote: In that day mankind will cast away their idols of silver and their idols of gold, which they made for themselves to worship, to the moles and to the bats, to enter the caverns of the rocks and the clefts of the cliffs, from before the terror of the LORD, and from the splendor of his majesty, when he rises to terrify the earth.
verseByVerse.commentary:
On that day people will fling away the expensive gods they made, because what cannot help on the worst day was never worth trusting.

Cast away their idols. Almost comic and entirely serious: men running for the caves, throwing away their gods as they run.

Which they made for themselves. Isaiah keeps every detail that makes it bite. Their idols of silver and their idols of gold cost a great deal. They were made for themselves to worship, not inherited or imposed: each man commissioned his own. Now they are flung aside as dead weight by the very people who paid for them, because when you are running for a hole in the ground you do not carry anything that cannot help you. That is the whole argument against idolatry in one gesture: the test of what a thing is worth is what you do with it on the worst day.

To the moles and to the bats. The gods end up with the creatures of the dark, blind things that live under the ground and in the roof space. It is a contemptuous line, and also a placing: they have finally been put where they belong.

From before the terror of the LORD. The verse ends with the words of v. 19. Everything the chapter has listed, silver, gold, cedars, towers, ships and idols, is being abandoned by men looking for a rock to get behind. Only one thing is standing.

verseByVerse.quote: Stop regarding man in whose nostrils is breath, for of what account is he?
verseByVerse.commentary:
Since every human being lives on borrowed breath, stop resting your life on people and rest it on the LORD.

Stop regarding man. One verse, the practical landing of everything above it, and short enough to act on: stop.

In whose nostrils is breath. The phrase is deliberately physical. Not man who is weak or foolish, but man who is currently breathing, which describes everybody. It goes back to Genesis 2:7, where God breathed into a man’s nostrils the breath of life. A human being is dust with borrowed air in it, and nobody is told in advance when the loan will be called in.

Of what account is he? The answer expected is none, and that needs care, because this book insists everywhere that people matter enormously to God. What is denied is not human worth but human weight: the reliability of a creature as something to build a life on.

Too much weight on people. This is a mercy as much as a warning. Much disappointment comes from putting more onto a person than a person can carry: a leader, a spouse, a parent, oneself. Only the LORD is not borrowing his next breath.

How do I take the weight off people? Notice where the weight is. The person whose silence ruins your day, whose approval you keep checking for, whose failure feels like the end of the world, is probably carrying more than a creature can. Tell God what you were expecting. Name it in prayer: I needed him to make me feel safe; I needed her to make me feel I matter. Move that weight to the LORD. “Put not your trust in princes, in a son of man, in whom there is no salvation” (Psalm 146:3); the one who says “I will never leave you nor forsake you” (Hebrews 13:5) can carry it. Then love them more freely. Timothy Keller often pointed out that when we look to a spouse to give us what only God can give, we crush them, and then resent them for failing. Taking the weight off people does not mean caring less. It lets them be human again, and lets you forgive them for it.

Is trusting Jesus leaning on breath? Christians are told to trust a man, Jesus, and Jeremiah says a curse rests on the man who trusts in man and makes flesh his strength (Jeremiah 17:5). Yet the New Testament calls everyone to trust Jesus, because he is not only a man. He is the eternal Word through whom all things were made and in whom was life (John 1:3–4), who took flesh, died, and now always lives (Hebrews 7:25). Verse 22 forbids leaning on any creature. It leaves one Man on whom all the weight may rest, because in him the LORD who alone will be exalted has come near, and he has already carried the heaviest weight of all, our sin, on the cross.

3.subtitle: Judgment on Jerusalem's Leaders
3.intro:
Where we are. Chapter 2 ended with a day against everything proud and a warning to stop trusting mere man. Chapter 3 shows what that looks like in Jerusalem, from the judges at the gate to the women parading in the street.

The message. When a people turns its back on God, one of his judgments is simply to take away what it took for granted: bread, water, and wise and capable leaders. Society then turns on itself, and those who used their power to grind the poor will answer to God himself, while their stolen finery is stripped away. Yet in the middle of the ruin God promises that it will be well with the righteous, and he still calls the nation “my people”.

Why it was said. Judah’s prosperity had made its leaders rich at the expense of the poor, and the wealth was openly displayed (see the introduction). A people that trusted its leaders and wealth needed to hear that all of it was on loan from God.

How the chapter makes its case. First the withdrawal (vv. 1–7): God takes away supply and every kind of competent person, boys rule, neighbours turn on each other, and no one will accept the leadership of a heap of ruins. Then the reason (vv. 8–12): they defy God’s glory and parade their sin without shame; yet it will be well with the righteous, and God still says “my people”. Then the court (vv. 13–15): the LORD stands to judge the leaders who have ground the faces of the poor. Finally the inventory (vv. 16–26): the haughty daughters of Zion lose their finery item by item, beauty is exchanged for shame, and the city sits empty on the ground.

Where it leads. The chapter points to Christ chiefly by the need it exposes: a people without true leaders, the poor crushed by those meant to protect them, and a city stripped and shamed. Isaiah soon answers it by promise. In place of boys as princes God will give a child who is “Wonderful Counselor” (9:6), on whom rests “the Spirit of counsel and might” (11:2), and who will judge the poor with righteousness (11:4). And the next verses after this ruin speak of “the branch of the LORD” (4:2), the one who was himself stripped and shamed so that the shamed might be clothed.

For us. Thank God for every good leader, honest judge and daily meal, since all of them are on loan. Ask whether anything in your house came from people who could not stop you taking it. And when everything is falling apart, hold on to God’s promise that it will be well with the righteous, who are righteous only in Christ.

keyVerse.quote: “Tell the righteous that it shall be well with them, for they shall eat the fruit of their deeds. Woe to the wicked! It shall be ill with him, for what his hands have dealt out shall be done to him.”
keyVerse.note: These two verses stand in the middle of unrelenting judgment as a reminder that Isaiah’s God is not arbitrary: the moral universe holds, and whatever the righteous suffer in a corrupt society, the final word over their lives is well. This is not optimism but certainty about how God will settle things, and it makes perseverance possible. Only in Christ is anyone counted righteous, and at the cross the one whose hands had dealt out only good took what ours deserved.

3.reflection:
God judges Jerusalem by taking away its bread, its soldiers, judges, elders and skilled workers (vv. 1–3). Which of the ordinary gifts of good order and capable people do you most take for granted? How might you thank God, and pray, for them this week?

The people “proclaim their sin like Sodom; they do not hide it” (v. 9). How is the loss of shame different from being freed from false shame? How does Christ, who bore our shame, make it possible to own up without being crushed?

In the middle of judgment God says, “Tell the righteous that it shall be well with them” (v. 10). When doing right seems to be a losing strategy, what helps you keep going? Who is righteous in God’s sight, and how?

God locates the stolen goods: “the spoil of the poor is in your houses” (v. 14), and in vv. 16–23 the finery is on display in the street. Where might our comfort or our way of dressing and spending depend on others’ hardship, and what would change if we took this seriously?
