verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–15 — When God Removes the Grown-Ups
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God judges a proud people by taking away the leaders and the order they took for granted, and calls its rulers to account for crushing the poor. He removes bread and water and every kind of competent person, and leaves boys to rule (vv. 1–4). Neighbours turn on each other, and no one will take charge of the ruins (vv. 5–7), because the people defy God’s glory and flaunt their sin without shame (vv. 8–9). Yet two steady sentences promise that it will be well with the righteous and ill with the wicked, and God still calls the nation his people (vv. 10–12). Then he stands up in court against the elders and princes who have devoured his vineyard and ground the faces of the poor (vv. 13–15).
verseByVerse.theology: What God gives a society, he can take away; and a people who have lost their shame have lost the road back.
verseByVerse.examples: A firm whose founders have retired and whose new managers are out of their depth is a small picture of verse 4. Nobody attacked it; the wise simply left, and nobody noticed until the decisions started going wrong.

verseByVerse.quote: For behold, the Lord GOD of hosts is taking away from Jerusalem and from Judah support and supply, all support of bread, and all support of water; the mighty man and the soldier, the judge and the prophet, the diviner and the elder, the captain of fifty and the man of rank, the counselor and the skillful magician and the expert in charms. And I will make boys their princes, and infants shall rule over them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God judges Jerusalem by taking away what it leans on, its food and water and all its capable people, until only boys are left to rule.

Taking away. The whole chapter turns on one verb. Not sending but taking away: the judgment is a subtraction, and it begins with bread and water, the two things a city cannot do without for a week.

The mighty man and the soldier. Then the people, and the list is a working society dismantled by category: the men who fight, decide cases, advise, know a trade. Even the fraudulent professions go; a nation losing its charm-sellers has still lost people it was relying on. These are not villains being punished but competences being removed, and every one is a gift held on loan, which nobody notices until it is gone.

I will make boys their princes. The result is not tyranny but immaturity in charge. Isaiah is not insulting the young; he describes leadership without the weight that years and the fear of God are meant to produce. Not an invader at the gate, but a room full of people who are not up to it, and no one else available.

The counsellor God will give. Isaiah does not leave the throne empty. Where God here removes the counsellor, he will soon promise a child called “Wonderful Counselor” (9:6), on whom rests “the Spirit of counsel and might” (11:2). The leadership Judah lost is given back, perfected, in Christ.

verseByVerse.quote: And the people will oppress one another, every one his fellow and every one his neighbor; the youth will be insolent to the elder, and the despised to the honorable. For a man will take hold of his brother in the house of his father, saying: "You have a cloak; you shall be our leader, and this heap of ruins shall be under your rule"; in that day he will speak out, saying: "I will not be a healer; in my house there is neither bread nor cloak; you shall not make me leader of the people." For Jerusalem has stumbled, and Judah has fallen, because their speech and their deeds are against the LORD, defying his glorious presence. For the look on their faces bears witness against them; they proclaim their sin like Sodom; they do not hide it. Woe to them! For they have brought evil on themselves.
verseByVerse.commentary:
With no one fit to lead, society turns on itself, and Jerusalem falls because it openly defies God and has lost even the capacity for shame.

The people will oppress one another. With nobody holding the structures, the pressure turns sideways, onto his fellow and his neighbour. When a society stops working, people do not become cruel to strangers first. They become cruel to whoever is nearest.

You have a cloak; you shall be our leader. The scene is almost comic and entirely desperate. The qualification for high office has become owning a coat, and the man seized refuses it: I will not be a healer. When people stop competing for office and start refusing it, everyone can see there is nothing left to lead.

They do not hide it. Their words and deeds defy, literally, the eyes of God’s glory (v. 8), and the diagnosis in v. 9 is not how great the sin is but that they no longer try to hide it. Shame is unattractive, but it is also a signal that somebody still knows the standard. When the hiding stops, the standard has gone, and with it the words a person needs in order to repent. It is the descent Paul traces in Romans 1, where people not only do such things but approve those who practise them (Romans 1:32).

Isn’t shame always bad for us? Our culture has good reasons to distrust shame, for much of it is cruel: the shame heaped on the poor, the abused, the different. The researcher Brené Brown has distinguished guilt, “I did something bad”, from shame, “I am bad”, and argued that guilt can help us change while shame usually crushes. That is wise, and Scripture would add that much of the shame people carry was never theirs to carry. But v. 9 shows the other danger, the one a therapeutic age forgets: a people can lose the capacity to blush, and then it has lost the alarm that tells it something is wrong. So the Bible refuses both our usual options. It will not heap shame on people, and it will not pretend there is nothing to be ashamed of. It takes the shame seriously enough to move it. Christ bore it in public, stripped and mocked, so that the person who owns up need not be crushed. Only a forgiven person can afford to blush.

verseByVerse.quote: Tell the righteous that it shall be well with them, for they shall eat the fruit of their deeds. Woe to the wicked! It shall be ill with him, for what his hands have dealt out shall be done to him. My people— infants are their oppressors, and women rule over them. O my people, your guides mislead you and they have swallowed up the course of your paths.
verseByVerse.commentary:
However things look, God keeps the accounts: it will be well with the righteous and ill with the wicked, and he still calls his failing nation “my people”.

Tell the righteous that it shall be well with them. Two verses of daylight in a collapsing chapter, and the most useful thing in it. They do not promise the righteous an exemption: the boys are still in charge, the bread is still gone, and the righteous live in the same city as everyone else. What is promised is an outcome. When the worst people prosper, the evidence says that integrity is a losing strategy and nobody is keeping accounts. These verses say the accounts are kept, and a person will in the end eat the fruit of what he actually did. That is not wages earned by the righteous; it is the Father keeping faith with those he has made his own.

What his hands have dealt out. Verse 11 is exact justice: what the wicked did to others will be done to them. Only one man ever dealt out nothing but good, and at the cross what our hands had dealt out was done to him, so that sinners clothed in his righteousness might hear v. 10 spoken over them.

O my people. Then back to the ruin, with the tenderest possible address: my people, twice in one verse, of a nation described as ungovernable. He has not stopped calling them his. And the guides have not merely given bad directions but swallowed up the course of your paths, consumed the road itself.

Does “women rule over them” forbid women in leadership? The line is a lament over weak and oppressive rule, set beside “infants” (v. 4): the men who should lead have failed. It is not itself a rule about women in office; the New Testament’s teaching on elders is given elsewhere (1 Timothy 2:12; 3:1–7).

Uncertain wording. The Greek Old Testament reads creditors instead of women, from almost the same Hebrew letters. Either way, the line laments rulers who exploit and mislead.

verseByVerse.quote: The LORD has taken his place to contend; he stands to judge peoples. The LORD will enter into judgment with the elders and princes of his people: "It is you who have devoured the vineyard, the spoil of the poor is in your houses. What do you mean by crushing my people, by grinding the face of the poor?" declares the Lord GOD of hosts.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God himself stands up in court against the leaders of his people, who have plundered his vineyard and crushed the poor to fill their own houses.

The LORD has taken his place to contend. The courtroom of chapter 1 reconvenes, and the posture is described twice: he has taken his place, he stands. A judge sitting is deliberating; a judge standing is about to give his verdict.

With the elders and princes of his people. He goes for the leadership. Not the nation in general, nor the young men insulting their elders in v. 5, but the elders and princes, who had the power to prevent what happened and used it to profit instead.

You who have devoured the vineyard. Chapter 5 is coming, where the vineyard turns out to be Israel itself, and these men have eaten it. Then the sentence that needs no interpretation: the spoil of the poor is in your houses. Not in your policies; in your houses. God names the location of the stolen goods, and it is where these men eat dinner. Every comfortable object in the room came from somebody who could not stop them taking it.

What do you mean? A question, worse than a verdict: the incredulity of someone who cannot make sense of what he sees.

Grinding the face of the poor. The image is a millstone: a face pressed into the grinding surface and turned. It is one of the most violent pictures in the prophets, and it describes what these men would have called ordinary business: foreclosures, wages withheld, cases quietly not heard. God watches respectable commerce and describes it as a face under a stone.

The Lord of the vineyard. Jesus brought the same charge against leaders who “devour widows’ houses” (Mark 12:40), and told of tenants who seized the vineyard and killed the owner’s son (Mark 12:1–12). The Son they killed is the King who will judge the poor with righteousness (11:4).

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The pride and plunder of Jerusalem are on display in the finery of its wealthy women, and God will strip it all away until the city sits empty in the dust. The daughters of Zion walk with outstretched necks to be seen, and the Lord will shame them by exposing them (vv. 16–17). A long inventory of twenty-one articles of finery, jewellery, charms, perfume and fine clothes, is taken away item by item (vv. 18–23). Five exchanges reverse it exactly, perfume to rottenness and beauty to branding (v. 24), and with the men fallen in battle the city sits in mourning on the ground (vv. 25–26).
verseByVerse.theology: This is not disapproval of ornament. It is judgment on people who show off their worth by what they wear while the poor pay for it.
verseByVerse.examples: A designer handbag bought on wages withheld from a cleaner is the inventory of verses 18-23 in modern dress.

verseByVerse.quote: The LORD said: Because the daughters of Zion are haughty and walk with outstretched necks, glancing wantonly with their eyes, mincing along as they go, tinkling with their feet, therefore the Lord will strike with a scab the heads of the daughters of Zion, and the LORD will lay bare their secret parts.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The proud women of Jerusalem parade their wealth to be admired, and God will shame the display by stripping it away.

The daughters of Zion are haughty. Isaiah moves from the courts to the street, and what he describes is a walk: necks stretched to gain height, eyes working the crowd, short deliberate steps, and ankle ornaments made to be heard, so that people look before they can see who is coming. Every detail is about being noticed. This is a performance, not women enjoying themselves.

Where the finery came from. Read it in its place and the connection is unmistakable. Two verses ago the spoil of the poor was in these houses; now it is walking down the street on display. The finery is the proceeds. Isaiah objects not that these women look good but that worth is now measured by looking good, and the poor, their faces under a millstone, are paying for it.

The LORD will lay bare. The judgment is aimed at the display. What was elevated is made repellent; what was arranged to be seen is exposed. It is harsh, and it is the exact shape of the offence: a life organised around being looked at is judged by being looked at. What is described is the shame conquered cities suffered when captives were stripped and led away. Scripture records it as judgment on a proud city; it never approves the stripping or abuse of anyone.

Uncertain wording. The word translated “secret parts” in v. 17 is rare. The ESV takes it as nakedness; others, comparing related languages, read ‘foreheads’ or ‘scalps’, matching the scab on their heads. Either way, what they displayed becomes their disgrace.

verseByVerse.quote: In that day the Lord will take away the finery of the anklets, the headbands, and the crescents; the pendants, the bracelets, and the scarves; the headdresses, the armlets, the sashes, the perfume boxes, and the amulets; the signet rings and nose rings; the festal robes, the mantles, the cloaks, and the handbags; the mirrors, the linen garments, the turbans, and the veils.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God will take away every piece of jewellery and fine clothing the proud trusted to make them somebody, item by item.

The finery of the anklets. Twenty-one items, named one after another with no comment attached, and the effect of the list is the argument. Isaiah inventories the jewellery like a bailiff going through a house.

The crescents and the amulets. Some of it is unexpectedly specific. Crescents and amulets are moon charms and things worn to ward off harm: the idolatry of chapter 2 worn as an accessory. Perfume boxes, signet rings, handbags, mirrors: imported luxuries.

The Lord will take away. The verb governing all twenty-one is the one the chapter opened with. God removes the bread, the judges and the ornaments with the same hand, which puts them, disconcertingly, in one category. Read at length the list stops sounding like wealth and starts sounding like weight: small things each acquired to say something about the wearer, none able to say anything on the day God lists them for removal.

What it does not mean. Not that jewellery or beautiful clothes are sinful; in Ezekiel 16:11–13 God himself adorns Jerusalem with jewellery. But the adorning that matters is “the imperishable beauty of a gentle and quiet spirit” (1 Peter 3:4). The question is what the finery is for, and who paid for it.

Uncertain wording. Several of these Hebrew words occur only here, so many items are uncertain and translations differ widely. The general sense is clear: the whole wardrobe of a wealthy woman of the day.

verseByVerse.quote: Instead of perfume there will be rottenness; and instead of a belt, a rope; and instead of well-set hair, baldness; and instead of a rich robe, a skirt of sackcloth; and branding instead of beauty. Your men shall fall by the sword and your mighty men in battle. And her gates shall lament and mourn; empty, she shall sit on the ground.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Everything the proud put on will be replaced by its opposite, and the city that paraded itself will sit stripped, bereaved and empty in the dust.

Instead of perfume there will be rottenness. Five exchanges, each the exact opposite of what it replaces: perfume for rot, a worked belt for a length of rope, arranged hair for a shaved head, a fine robe for sackcloth (see mourning customs), and beauty for a brand, probably the mark burned into a slave or captive. The symmetry is the message. The judgment is shaped precisely to the thing judged: what was put on comes off, and what replaces it is what was underneath all along.

Empty, she shall sit on the ground. The chapter ends with a single figure. The city, pictured as a woman, the one who walked with outstretched neck and tinkling anklets, now sits in the dirt, her men fallen and her gates mourning. It is the posture of a mourner, and what is left when everything has been taken: no jewellery, no performance, nobody watching.

Where substitutes for God lead. That is where every substitute for God eventually puts a person, and the chapter is honest enough to stop there rather than hurry to the comfort. But the next word of comfort Isaiah gives is “in that day the branch of the LORD shall be beautiful and glorious” (4:2), and that beauty is not something anyone puts on. That Branch is Christ, and the shame of this chapter is the kind he carried: he was stripped, and “endured the cross, despising the shame” (Hebrews 12:2), so that people left empty on the ground might be clothed “with the garments of salvation” (61:10).

Uncertain wording. The word rendered “branding” in v. 24 is uncertain. It can be read as a rare noun for a burn mark, as the ESV does, or as the common word “for”, with something like “shame” understood (“shame instead of beauty”). Either way, beauty gives place to disgrace.

3.theology:
Judgment as subtraction. Nothing invades in this chapter. God takes away, and the premise is that leadership, wisdom, skill and even ordinary maturity are gifts held on loan rather than achievements. A nation rarely loses them dramatically; it discovers one day that the serious people have gone.

The end of shame. Verse 9 marks the point after which a people can no longer correct itself: they proclaim their sin like Sodom; they do not hide it. When the hiding stops, the standard has gone, and with it the words repentance needs.

Two verses that hold. Verses 10 and 11 sit inside the ruin and promise the righteous no exemption from it. What they promise is that outcomes are still real, which is precisely what collapse makes people doubt. And the inventory of vv. 18-23 belongs to the same argument: it is not prudishness about jewellery but God taking away what pride had put on.

4.subtitle: The Branch of the LORD
4.intro:
Where we are. Chapter 4 is only six verses, and it closes the collection that began at 2:1. Its first verse finishes the ruin of chapter 3, where the men fell in battle and Jerusalem sat empty on the ground; then the light breaks in, and the section that opened with the mountain of the LORD (2:2–4) ends with his glory over Mount Zion.

The message. Judgment is not God’s last word to his people. After the stripping, he will raise up a beautiful and glorious Branch, wash away the filth and bloodstains of his city, make holy everyone he has written down for life, and spread his own presence over them as shelter. What judgment removes, grace restores, and more than restores.

Why it was said. Chapters 1–3 have stripped away every human hope from Judah (see the introduction). A people told that their leaders, wealth and finery will all be taken needed to know whether anything would be left, and whether God was finished with them.

How the chapter makes its case. First the bottom of the ruin (v. 1): so many men have died that seven women plead with one man for his name, to take away their disgrace. Then, with the same words “in that day”, the turn (v. 2): the Branch of the LORD is beautiful and glorious, and the land bears fruit for the survivors. Those who remain are called holy, recorded for life (v. 3), because the Lord himself has washed them by a spirit of judgment and burning (v. 4). Finally God spreads over the whole of Zion the cloud and fire that once led Israel out of Egypt, a canopy and a shelter from heat and storm (vv. 5–6).

Where it leads. The chapter leads to Christ by direct promise. The Branch of the LORD is the first sprouting of a title the prophets give the coming King (11:1; Jeremiah 23:5; Zechariah 6:12), fulfilled in Jesus, the shoot from the stump of Jesse. John the Baptist promised that he would baptise “with the Holy Spirit and fire” (Matthew 3:11), the washing by judgment and burning of v. 4. And the cloud of glory over a whole people comes true as the Word who “dwelt among us” (John 1:14) makes his church God’s dwelling, until “the dwelling place of God is with man” (Revelation 21:3).

For us. No one is too far gone for this chapter: God brings beauty out of ruin, and his people are made holy by his washing, not their own. If you are looking for someone whose name will take away your disgrace, Christ gives his, and with it a shelter no storm can tear down.

keyVerse.quote: “In that day the branch of the LORD shall be beautiful and glorious, and the fruit of the land shall be the pride and honor of the survivors of Israel.”
keyVerse.note: The title “Branch”, introduced here, becomes one of the richest descriptions of the Messiah in the Old Testament. It speaks of growth from existing roots rather than an alien intrusion: Jesus is not an afterthought to Israel’s story but grows from it, like a shoot from a felled tree (11:1). And in him what was laid waste becomes beautiful again.

4.theology:
The Branch. Verse 2 introduces the first title of the Messiah in the book, and later prophets build on it. Here he is beautiful and glorious; in 53:2 the same book will say he had “no form or majesty”. Both are said of one person.

A remnant that was written down and washed. The survivors, the remnant God keeps through the judgment, are recorded for life, each name entered in advance, and they are called holy on the strength of what was done to them: the Lord washed the filth and cleansed the bloodstains. Every verb belongs to God.

The canopy. The cloud and fire that settled over one tent now cover the whole of Mount Zion and all her assemblies: the presence spread from a building and a priesthood to a people.
4.reflection:
The seven women of v. 1 ask for nothing but a man’s name, to take away their reproach. Where do people today look for someone whose approval will make them somebody? What difference does it make that God says, “I have called you by name, you are mine” (43:1)?

The Branch is “beautiful and glorious” (v. 2), yet in 53:2 the Servant has “no form or majesty that we should look at him.” How do these two pictures of Christ belong together, and why do we need both?

The survivors are called holy because the Lord has washed them, by a spirit of judgment and of burning (vv. 3–4). How does it help to know that holiness is first something God does to us? How have you seen God use hard things to make his people clean?

God promises his presence over “the whole site of Mount Zion and over her assemblies” as shade and shelter (vv. 5–6). How should it change our view of our church’s ordinary gatherings to know that God has promised to dwell among his people?
4.text: <sup>1</sup>And seven women shall take hold of one man in that day, saying, "We will eat our own bread and wear our own clothes, only let us be called by your name; take away our reproach."<sup>2</sup>In that day the branch of the LORD shall be beautiful and glorious, and the fruit of the land shall be the pride and honor of the survivors of Israel.<sup>3</sup>And he who is left in Zion and remains in Jerusalem will be called holy, everyone who has been recorded for life in Jerusalem,<sup>4</sup>when the Lord shall have washed away the filth of the daughters of Zion and cleansed the bloodstains of Jerusalem from its midst by a spirit of judgment and by a spirit of burning.<sup>5</sup>Then the LORD will create over the whole site of Mount Zion and over her assemblies a cloud by day, and smoke and the shining of a flaming fire by night; for over all the glory there will be a canopy.<sup>6</sup>There will be a booth for shade by day from the heat, and for a refuge and a shelter from the storm and rain.

verseByVerse.ref: v. 1 — Seven Women and One Man
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The ruin of Jerusalem is so complete that its women will beg for a husband’s name simply to escape disgrace. This single verse finishes chapter 3: the men have fallen by the sword (3:25), and so few are left that seven women take hold of one man. They will supply their own food and clothing, the very things a husband owed, and ask only to be called by his name to take away their reproach. It is the lowest point of the section, and the ground from which the Branch of the LORD will grow.
verseByVerse.theology: Scripture does not hurry past grief: the promise of verse 2 is spoken to people like these women.
verseByVerse.examples: Many a widow has found that the bills could be managed, and that what hurt was the empty chair and the sense of being looked at differently. Isaiah 54:4 is written for her.

verseByVerse.quote: And seven women shall take hold of one man in that day, saying, "We will eat our own bread and wear our own clothes, only let us be called by your name; take away our reproach."
verseByVerse.commentary:
So many men have fallen that seven women will beg one man for his name, wanting nothing from him but to be rid of their disgrace. The chapter division is unhelpful here: this verse finishes chapter 3, where the men of Jerusalem fell by the sword, and shows what that looks like afterwards.

Seven women shall take hold of one man. Seven is probably a round number for many, so this is not an unusual case being reported but a condition being described: a generation of men is gone, and the ordinary workings of family life have stopped.

Only let us be called by your name. What they offer and what they ask are telling. They will provide their own food and clothing, the two things a husband was obliged to supply (Exodus 21:10). They ask for nothing that costs him anything. What they want is his name, and one other thing: take away our reproach. In that society a woman without husband or children carried a public shame, and it is the shame rather than the poverty that these women cannot bear.

Who gives you your name? We are told today that identity is something you create: decide who you are and let nobody tell you otherwise. These women know something our slogans hide. You cannot simply name yourself; worth has to be given by someone whose verdict counts. Free to define ourselves, we spend our lives looking for the partner, employer, audience or parent whose approval will finally make our self-definition stick, and the verdict is never final, because any of them can take it back. Isaiah’s God speaks into exactly that hunger: “I have called you by name, you are mine” (43:1), and his people “shall be called by a new name that the mouth of the LORD will give” (62:2). In Christ that naming is done. A Christian’s identity rests not on a spouse, a role or a following but on belonging to him, and the name cannot be revoked, because it was paid for.

Does the verse approve of one man taking seven wives? No. It describes the desperation of a ruined society, not an ideal. From the beginning marriage was one man and one woman (Genesis 2:24; Matthew 19:4–6), and Scripture reports polygamy without approving it. The reproach of the childless and the widowed is answered later in this same book, tenderly: the barren woman is told to sing and the widow that she will remember her reproach no more (54:1–4), and those with no children are promised “a name better than sons and daughters” (56:5).

Comfort spoken into darkness. Isaiah put this verse here deliberately, before the glory of the next. His comfort is always spoken into a particular darkness, never past it, and this ruined city is the ground the Branch grows out of.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 2–6 — The Branch and the Canopy
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: After the ruin, God himself will make his people beautiful, holy and safe under his presence. In that day the Branch of the LORD will be beautiful and glorious, and the land will bear fruit for the survivors (v. 2). Everyone left in Zion, recorded for life, will be called holy (v. 3), because the Lord will have washed away the city’s filth and bloodstains by a spirit of judgment and of burning (v. 4). Then over the whole of Mount Zion and its assemblies he will spread the cloud by day and fire by night that once led Israel, a canopy over the glory and a shelter from heat and storm (vv. 5–6).
verseByVerse.theology: Holiness here is a gift before it is a task: God writes the names, and God washes the people.
verseByVerse.examples: A family caught by a storm on an open hillside, who find a shepherd's hut that holds, know what verse 6 promises.

verseByVerse.quote: In that day the branch of the LORD shall be beautiful and glorious, and the fruit of the land shall be the pride and honor of the survivors of Israel. And he who is left in Zion and remains in Jerusalem will be called holy, everyone who has been recorded for life in Jerusalem,
verseByVerse.commentary:
After the judgment God will raise up a beautiful and glorious Branch, the coming King, and everyone he has written down for life in Zion will be called holy.

In that day. Three words in and the whole book changes direction. The words in that day, which have introduced disasters since chapter 2, now introduce a person.

The branch of the LORD. The word is tsemach, a sprout or growth, and this is its first use as a title. Isaiah develops it into the shoot from the stump of Jesse (11:1); Jeremiah speaks of a righteous Branch who will execute justice (Jeremiah 23:5); Zechariah uses it of a king who is also a priest and builds the temple (Zechariah 6:12–13). It starts here, in one line, at the bottom of a ruined chapter.

Beautiful and glorious. Forty-nine chapters later the same book describes a servant with no beauty that we should desire him (53:2). It is the same person, despised in his suffering and glorious in his reign, and the New Testament keeps both: the one who emptied himself (Philippians 2:7), and the one whose “face was like the sun shining in full strength” (Revelation 1:16). The fruit of the land is the blessing that flows from his reign: a ruined countryside fruitful again.

Recorded for life. The picture comes from a city’s register of citizens: to be written in it was to belong and to have the right to live there, and false prophets are warned that they will not be “enrolled in the register of the house of Israel” (Ezekiel 13:9). Scripture speaks of such a book from Moses (Exodus 32:32) to its last pages, where only those “written in the Lamb’s book of life” enter the city (Revelation 21:27). These survivors are left not because they were better but because their names were written. They are called holy, which is not a description of how they behaved; the next verse explains where the holiness came from.

Where Christians differ: is “the branch of the LORD” the Messiah, or the renewed growth of the land, set in parallel with the fruit of the land? Some careful interpreters take it as the land’s fruitfulness given by God after judgment. This commentary’s view: the Branch elsewhere is the coming King (Jeremiah 23:5; Zechariah 3:8; 6:12), and here it is beautiful and glorious, the LORD’s own. The likeliest reading is the Messiah, with the land’s fruitfulness as the blessing of his reign.
verseByVerse.note: “The branch of the LORD” becomes a title of the coming King.

verseByVerse.quote: when the Lord shall have washed away the filth of the daughters of Zion and cleansed the bloodstains of Jerusalem from its midst by a spirit of judgment and by a spirit of burning. Then the LORD will create over the whole site of Mount Zion and over her assemblies a cloud by day, and smoke and the shining of a flaming fire by night; for over all the glory there will be a canopy. There will be a booth for shade by day from the heat, and for a refuge and a shelter from the storm and rain.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Lord himself will wash his people clean by a purifying judgment, and then spread his own glorious presence over all of them as a shelter.

Washed away the filth. Here is why they are called holy in v. 3, and it is entirely done to them. The Lord washes; the Lord cleanses. The two things removed are the two things chapter 3 was about: the filth of the daughters of Zion, the proud display and the oppression that paid for it, and the bloodstains, which were on the hands lifted in prayer back in 1:15.

By a spirit of judgment and by a spirit of burning. The cleansing is not gentle, and it is not a passing over. It is the refiner’s fire of 1:25 applied to people, and what comes out the other side is a community that can be called holy. John the Baptist used the same pairing of Christ: “He will baptize you with the Holy Spirit and fire” (Matthew 3:11). The washing Isaiah promised is what Christ gives by his Spirit, having borne the burning judgment himself.

A cloud by day. Every Israelite knew this picture. The pillar of cloud and fire had gone before them out of Egypt (Exodus 13:21) and had settled over the tabernacle (Exodus 40:34–38): one cloud, over one tent, where the priests went in and everyone else stayed outside. What is promised here is the same presence over the whole site of Mount Zion and over her assemblies, the entire community, not one building and not only the priests.

Over all the glory there will be a canopy. The word for canopy is used of a wedding chamber (Joel 2:16), and the booth is the same word as the flimsy booth in the stripped vineyard at 1:8, but now it is God’s, and it holds. Shade in the heat, cover in the storm: the two things a person outdoors most needs.

From an empty city to a canopy. Where chapter 3 left a city sitting empty on the ground, chapter 4 leaves a people under a canopy with the glory of God overhead. The Word “dwelt among us” (John 1:14), and his people are now built together into “a dwelling place for God by the Spirit” (Ephesians 2:22). The last word comes at the end of the Bible, in the same imagery: “Behold, the dwelling place of God is with man. He will dwell with them” (Revelation 21:3).

Uncertain wording. The last line of v. 5 is compressed, literally ‘for over all glory a canopy’. It may mean that God’s glory itself will be a canopy over his people, or that a covering will be spread over all the glory, as the cloud shielded Israel from seeing God’s glory directly. Either way, his people live under his protecting presence. In v. 4 the word for “spirit” can also mean wind or blast, a scorching wind of judgment; the ESV’s “spirit” fits the inward cleansing being described.

5.subtitle: The Song of the Vineyard and the Six Woes
5.intro:
Where we are. Chapter 5 closes the opening movement of the book (chapters 1–5). After the cleansed Zion of chapter 4, it returns to the Jerusalem of Isaiah’s day and sums up the case against it, before chapter 6 tells how the prophet was called.

The message. God has done for his people everything love could do, and what he has received back is injustice dressed up as success. Because they have rejected his word, he will take away the protection they took for granted and summon a foreign army with a whistle. When everything human falls, the holy God still stands, “exalted in justice” (v. 16).

Why it was said. Under Uzziah and Jotham Judah was prosperous and secure (see the introduction). The rich were buying out their neighbours, the courts could be bought, and people took their comfort as proof that God was pleased with them, while some mocked the prophet’s warnings (v. 19).

How the chapter makes its case. First a song (vv. 1–7): Isaiah sings of a friend’s vineyard planted with every care that yields only wild grapes, lets the crowd pass judgment, and then names the vineyard: it is them, and God looked for justice and found bloodshed. Then six woes (vv. 8–23) show what the wild grapes look like, from land-grabbing and drunken feasting to relabelling evil and selling verdicts. Finally the sentence (vv. 24–30): because they rejected the law of the LORD, his hand is stretched out still, and he whistles for a tireless army from the ends of the earth, until the land lies in darkness.

Where it leads. The chapter leads to Christ by pattern and by the need it exposes. Jesus retold this song against the leaders of the same city, adding what the song never imagined: last of all the owner sent his own son, and they killed him (Matthew 21:33–41). Israel was the vine that failed; Jesus calls himself “the true vine” (John 15:1), the one in whom the fruit God looked for at last grows. And the God who is “exalted in justice” (v. 16) shows that justice most fully at the cross, where he is both just and the one who forgives (Romans 3:26).

For us. This chapter will not let us measure ourselves by prosperity, busyness or the approval of the people around us; God looks for justice and righteousness. Nor can we produce that fruit by trying harder. It grows only in those who are joined to the true vine, and it shows in how we treat neighbours who are weaker than we are.

keyVerse.quote: “Woe to those who call evil good and good evil, who put darkness for light and light for darkness, who put bitter for sweet and sweet for bitter!”
keyVerse.note: This woe describes a society that has not merely forgotten God’s standards but turned them upside down, deliberately and completely: evil and good, darkness and light, bitter and sweet. Once a people has renamed evil, it has lost the words it would need to repent, and correction can no longer come from within. Only a word from outside, from God, can break through, and the gospel is that word: it calls sin by its name because it can forgive it.

5.theology:
The song that convicts the audience. Isaiah lets the crowd pass a verdict before he names the defendant, and the question of verse 4 closes every exit in advance. Jesus made this song his own against the same city (Matt. 21:33-46).

The six woes as a diagnosis. Their order is deliberate: wealth and pleasure dull the eyes, self-confidence grows in that ground, and self-confidence makes the renaming of good and evil possible. These are charges that Israel has broken her covenant with God, not merely social comment: Israel was called to be a society that looked like its God.

Judgment as withdrawal, and as an army. The sentence in vv. 5-6 is mostly subtraction, the same shape as chapter 3; in vv. 26-30 God summons an empire with a whistle. Either way, the darkness at the end is not outside his hand.
5.reflection:
God asks, “What more was there to do for my vineyard, that I have not done in it?” (v. 4). List some of the things God has given you. What fruit is he looking for in return, and what excuses do you hear yourself making when it is missing?

The six woes (vv. 8–23) describe sins that look respectable: buying up property, enjoying good things, being confident in our own judgment. Which of them is most easily mistaken for success where you live? Which comes closest to you?

Verse 12 condemns people who enjoy music and feasting but “do not regard the deeds of the LORD”. What good things fill your days so fully that you stop noticing what God is doing?

Jesus retold this song and added the son whom the tenants killed (Matthew 21:33–41), and he calls himself the true vine (John 15:1–5). How does that change the way we answer the question of verse 4, and where does the fruit God looks for actually come from?

When I looked for it to yield grapes, why did it yield wild grapes?<sup>5</sup>And now I will tell you what I will do to my vineyard. I will remove its hedge, and it shall be devoured; I will break down its wall, and it shall be trampled down.<sup>6</sup>I will make it a waste; it shall not be pruned or hoed, and briers and thorns shall grow up; for righteousness, but behold, an outcry!<sup>8</sup>Woe to those who join house to house, who add field to field, until there is no more room, and you are made to dwell alone in the midst of the land.<sup>9</sup>The LORD of hosts has sworn in my hearing: "Surely many houses shall be desolate, large and beautiful houses, without inhabitant.<sup>10</sup>For ten acres of vineyard shall yield but one bath, and a homer of seed shall yield but an ephah."<sup>11</sup>Woe to those who rise early in the morning, that they may run after strong drink, who tarry late into the evening as wine inflames them!<sup>12</sup>They have lyre and harp, tambourine and flute and wine at their feasts, but they do not regard the deeds of the LORD, or see the work of his hands.<sup>13</sup>Therefore my people go into exile for lack of knowledge; their honored men go hungry, and their multitude is parched with thirst.<sup>14</sup>Therefore Sheol has enlarged its appetite and opened its mouth beyond measure, and the nobility of Jerusalem and her multitude will go down, her revelers and he who exults in her.<sup>15</sup>Man is humbled, and each one is brought low, and the eyes of the haughty are brought low.<sup>16</sup>But the LORD of hosts is exalted in justice, and the Holy God shows himself holy in righteousness.<sup>17</sup>Then shall the lambs graze as in their pasture, and nomads shall eat among the ruins of the rich.<sup>18</sup>Woe to those who draw iniquity with cords of falsehood, who draw sin as with cart ropes,<sup>19</sup>who say: "Let him be quick, let him speed his work that we may see it; let the counsel of the Holy One of Israel draw near, and let it come, that we may know it!"<sup>20</sup>Woe to those who call evil good and good evil, who put darkness for light and light for darkness, who put bitter for sweet and sweet for bitter!<sup>21</sup>Woe to those who are wise in their own eyes, and shrewd in their own sight!<sup>22</sup>Woe to those who are heroes at drinking wine, and valiant men in mixing strong drink,<sup>23</sup>who acquit the guilty for a bribe, and deprive the innocent of his right!<sup>24</sup>Therefore, as the tongue of fire devours the stubble, and as dry grass sinks down in the flame, so their root will be as rottenness, and their blossom go up like dust; for they have rejected the law of the LORD of hosts, and have despised the word of the Holy One of Israel.<sup>25</sup>Therefore the anger of the LORD was kindled against his people, and he stretched out his hand against them and struck them, and the mountains quaked; For all this his anger has not turned away, and his hand is stretched out still.<sup>26</sup>He will raise a signal for nations far away, and whistle for them from the ends of the earth; and behold, quickly, speedily they come!<sup>27</sup>None is weary, none stumbles, none slumbers or sleeps, not a waistband is loose, not a sandal strap broken;<sup>28</sup>their arrows are sharp, all their bows bent, their horses' hoofs seem like flint, and their wheels like the whirlwind.<sup>29</sup>Their roaring is like a lion, like young lions they roar; they growl and seize their prey; they carry it off, and none can rescue.<sup>30</sup>They will growl over it on that day, like the growling of the sea. And if one looks to the land, behold, darkness and distress; and the light is darkened by its clouds.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God has given his people everything, and they have given him back injustice. Isaiah sings a love song about a friend who planted a vineyard on the best ground and spared no effort, yet reaped only wild grapes (vv. 1–2). Then the singer speaks as the owner and asks the people of Jerusalem to judge between him and his vineyard: what more could he have done (vv. 3–4)? He announces that he will take down the hedge, stop tending it and hold back the rain (vv. 5–6). Only then does verse 7 name the vineyard: it is Israel and Judah, and where God looked for justice and righteousness he found bloodshed and the cry of the oppressed.
verseByVerse.theology: The question of verse 4 is not cruelty but grief: God had given everything.
verseByVerse.examples: A father who paid for the best school and the music lessons, and hears his grown son say "You never gave me anything", knows something of the ache in verse 4.

verseByVerse.quote: Let me sing for my beloved my love song concerning his vineyard: My beloved had a vineyard on a very fertile hill. He dug it and cleared it of stones, and planted it with choice vines; he built a watchtower in the midst of it, and hewed out a wine vat in it; and he looked for it to yield grapes, but it yielded wild grapes.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God planted his people with every care a farmer could give, and they produced nothing but sour, useless grapes.

Let me sing for my beloved. Isaiah opens by performing. This is a ballad about a friend and his vineyard, the kind of song heard at a harvest festival, and the crowd settles in to enjoy it.

On a very fertile hill. Every line raises the expectation: the best ground available. Dug it and cleared it of stones is the back-breaking part, as anyone who has worked stony hill country knows. Choice vines, not ordinary stock. A watchtower, which you build when you expect a crop worth guarding. A wine vat cut into the rock, a permanent installation made in advance for a harvest he was sure of. Nothing has been withheld and nothing done cheaply, and by now the audience is entirely on the farmer’s side, which is why the song spends five clauses on the preparation.

But it yielded wild grapes. The song stops. The word is small and sour: the fruit of an uncultivated vine, hard, bitter and no good for wine. Every advantage, and the crop is what you would have got from ground nobody touched.
verseByVerse.note: The vineyard returns, with a happier ending, in 27:2-6.

verseByVerse.quote: And now, O inhabitants of Jerusalem and men of Judah, judge between me and my vineyard. What more was there to do for my vineyard, that I have not done in it? When I looked for it to yield grapes, why did it yield wild grapes?
verseByVerse.commentary:
God himself steps out of the song and asks his people to judge: what more could he have done? The honest answer is nothing, and the failure belongs entirely to the vineyard.

Judge between me and my vineyard. The singer turns to the crowd, and the pronouns have quietly changed. It was my beloved’s vineyard in verse 1; now it is my vineyard. Someone else has begun speaking through the singer, and the audience is being asked for a verdict.

Nathan’s method. This is what Nathan did with David (2 Samuel 12:1–7): tell a man a story about somebody else, let him pass judgment, then tell him whose story it was. It works because we see right and wrong clearly in someone else’s case.

What more was there to do for my vineyard? Not more sunlight, not better vines, not another year. The investment was complete and the failure is the vineyard’s. Most excuses for a fruitless life are versions of “I was not given enough”: enough teaching, advantage, grace or time. Verse 4 asks what exactly was missing, and waits.

God did more than the song imagined. Jesus answered the question in his retelling of this song. The owner sent servant after servant to the tenants, and last of all his own son, and they threw him out of the vineyard and killed him (Matthew 21:33–39). God did more than the song imagined: he gave his Son. And where Israel the vine yielded wild grapes, Jesus calls himself the true vine (John 15:1), the vine that bore all the fruit God looked for. Those joined to him bear it too, by his Spirit and not by their own sap, and where their fruit is still poor, his is counted as theirs.

verseByVerse.quote: And now I will tell you what I will do to my vineyard. I will remove its hedge, and it shall be devoured; I will break down its wall, and it shall be trampled down. I will make it a waste; it shall not be pruned or hoed, and briers and thorns shall grow up; I will also command the clouds that they rain no rain upon it. For the vineyard of the LORD of hosts is the house of Israel, and the men of Judah are his pleasant planting; and he looked for justice, but behold, bloodshed; for righteousness, but behold, an outcry!
verseByVerse.commentary:
Because the vineyard bore no fruit, God will take away his protection and his care; then the song names the vineyard, and it is his own people, who gave him bloodshed where he looked for justice.

I will remove its hedge. The vineyard is not uprooted or burned. The protection comes off: the hedge and the wall that kept out animals and passers-by are taken away, and whatever happens is allowed to happen. Then the care stops. No pruning, no hoeing, and briers and thorns come up, as they do on any ground left alone. The last clause gives away who is speaking: I will also command the clouds. No farmer can do that. Judgment here is largely God withdrawing his care, as in chapter 3, where he took things away rather than sending anything.

The vineyard of the LORD of hosts. Now verse 7 names the vineyard: the house of Israel, the men of Judah. The crowd that has just delivered a verdict discovers it was about them.

He looked for justice, but behold, bloodshed. In Hebrew the last line is two puns (see the note), and it is unforgettable. The words for justice and bloodshed sound almost alike, and so do the words for righteousness and outcry. That is the whole indictment: what came up sounds almost exactly like what was planted, and it is the opposite of it. The last word is the heaviest: an outcry, the noise the oppressed make, the word used of Israel crying out under the slave-masters of Egypt (Exodus 3:7). God went into his vineyard listening for righteousness and heard people screaming.
verseByVerse.note: In Hebrew v. 7 is a double pun: justice (mishpat) / bloodshed (mispach); righteousness (tsedaqah) / an outcry (tse‘aqah).

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: These six woes show what the wild grapes of verse 7 look like in daily life, and every one of them is respectable. Some men buy up their neighbours’ land until they live alone in an empty countryside (vv. 8–10). Others give the whole day to drink and music and never notice what God is doing, so the nation goes into exile and the grave opens wide, while God alone is exalted in justice (vv. 11–17). Some haul their sin along and dare God to act (vv. 18–19); some call evil good (v. 20); some trust their own wisdom (v. 21); and the judges are heroes at drinking who sell verdicts (vv. 22–23).
verseByVerse.theology: "Woe" was the cry of a funeral; Isaiah speaks it over people who are still alive.
verseByVerse.examples: When cruelty is called honesty and lust is called being true to yourself, verse 20 is being fulfilled in ordinary speech.

verseByVerse.quote: Woe to those who join house to house, who add field to field, until there is no more room, and you are made to dwell alone in the midst of the land. The LORD of hosts has sworn in my hearing: "Surely many houses shall be desolate, large and beautiful houses, without inhabitant. For ten acres of vineyard shall yield but one bath, and a homer of seed shall yield but an ephah."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Woe to those who buy out their neighbours until they own everything: they will end up alone, and the land they seized will not feed them.

Woe. The word was the cry mourners raised over the dead (1 Kings 13:30). Isaiah speaks it six times over people who are still alive and doing well.

Woe to those who join house to house. The first woe is about property, and what makes it bite is that it was legal. Under the law each family held its land as a gift from God; it could not be sold away for good, and in the Year of Jubilee it came back to the family (Leviticus 25:23–28). These men buy up struggling neighbours one at a time until whole villages belong to one estate. Micah, preaching in the same years, saw the same thing: “They covet fields and seize them, and houses, and take them away” (Micah 2:2).

You are made to dwell alone. Isaiah names where it ends: until there is no more room. The successful accumulator finishes in an empty landscape, because he has bought everyone out. The loneliness is not a punishment added to the sin; it is the sin, arrived at its destination.

Many houses shall be desolate. The great houses will stand empty, and then comes a farming sum that would have made the audience wince. Ten acres (literally ten yokes, the land ten teams of oxen could plough in a day) will yield one bath of wine, a few gallons, and a homer of seed will yield an ephah, a tenth of what was sown. The land itself stops cooperating. A man can acquire ground; he cannot make it yield.

What it does not mean. Not that owning property, building a business or prospering is wrong. The sin is getting more by pushing others out, using the law against people too weak to resist.
verseByVerse.note: A bath was about 6 gallons; a homer about 6 bushels.

verseByVerse.quote: Woe to those who rise early in the morning, that they may run after strong drink, who tarry late into the evening as wine inflames them! They have lyre and harp, tambourine and flute and wine at their feasts, but they do not regard the deeds of the LORD, or see the work of his hands.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Woe to those who give their whole lives to pleasure: they enjoy God’s gifts and never notice God.

Woe to those who rise early in the morning. The second woe covers a whole day. Rise early and tarry late: this is not people with full lives occasionally drinking too much, but the whole waking day given over to drink. Isaiah is describing dedication.

Lyre and harp, tambourine and flute. Four instruments are named and none of them is the problem; feasting, wine and music appear elsewhere in Scripture as God’s gifts (Psalm 104:15).

They do not regard the deeds of the LORD. The charge is what all this costs them: they do not notice. God is at work in their own century, and Isaiah has been announcing it at the top of his voice for four chapters, but these people have a calendar too full to look up.

In everyday life. This reaches far beyond a drinking culture. It is possible to be surrounded by good things, enjoying them competently, and to be blind to the one thing happening in the room: not because the good things are evil, but because attention is limited, and they have taken all of it.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore my people go into exile for lack of knowledge; their honored men go hungry, and their multitude is parched with thirst. Therefore Sheol has enlarged its appetite and opened its mouth beyond measure, and the nobility of Jerusalem and her multitude will go down, her revelers and he who exults in her. Man is humbled, and each one is brought low, and the eyes of the haughty are brought low. But the LORD of hosts is exalted in justice, and the Holy God shows himself holy in righteousness. Then shall the lambs graze as in their pasture, and nomads shall eat among the ruins of the rich.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Because they did not know their God, the people will go into exile and the grave will swallow great and small alike; but in the ruins God stands, holy and exalted in justice.

For lack of knowledge. The reason given for the exile is not idolatry or injustice, though both are in the chapter, but lack of knowledge: the failure Isaiah opened the book with, where the ox knew its owner and Israel did not (1:3). It is not ignorance of facts. They no longer know whose they are.

Their honored men go hungry. The reversal is exact. Men who rose early to drink are parched; the honoured go hungry. The appetite that ran their days in verse 11 is the appetite left empty here.

Sheol has enlarged its appetite. Isaiah pictures the grave as the one thing in the chapter with a bigger appetite than theirs. They stretched their capacity for consumption; death stretches wider, and the nobility and the crowd go down together. Pride is brought low (v. 15), and where the rich had their estates, lambs graze among the ruins (v. 17).

The LORD of hosts is exalted in justice. Then, in the middle of the wreckage, verse 16 lifts the eyes. Everything so far has been people failing at justice and righteousness. Here are the two words again, and this time they belong to God, and they are not failing. He is exalted in justice: not in spite of it, and not by setting it aside. When everything human collapses, what stands in the ruins is the holiness of God, and Isaiah puts the line here so that the reader has something to look at besides the damage. How a God exalted in justice can also save the guilty, the book will show in the Servant who bears their sins (53:5–6).

Uncertain wording. The second half of verse 17 is hard to translate. The word the ESV renders nomads usually means strangers or sojourners, and translations differ over who eats in the ruins of the rich: wandering herdsmen, strangers, or (on another reading) young goats. The sense is clear either way: the great estates will become open pasture.

verseByVerse.quote: Woe to those who draw iniquity with cords of falsehood, who draw sin as with cart ropes, who say: "Let him be quick, let him speed his work that we may see it; let the counsel of the Holy One of Israel draw near, and let it come, that we may know it!" Woe to those who call evil good and good evil, who put darkness for light and light for darkness, who put bitter for sweet and sweet for bitter! Woe to those who are wise in their own eyes, and shrewd in their own sight!
verseByVerse.commentary:
Some people work hard at their sin and dare God to act; others swap the labels on good and evil; beneath both lies a settled confidence in their own wisdom.

Who draw sin as with cart ropes. These people are not dragged into sin; they haul it, in harness, like a man pulling a loaded cart uphill. Sin is worked at and towed behind a life at great cost. And they tow it with a taunt, daring the Holy One to get on with the judgment he keeps announcing (v. 19). That nothing has happened yet is taken as proof that nothing will, the same scoffing Peter expects in the last days: “Where is the promise of his coming?” (2 Peter 3:4).

Who call evil good and good evil. The fourth woe does not describe confusion. Confused people are uncertain; these people are confident. They have simply swapped the labels, deliberately, in all three pairs: good and evil, light and darkness, sweet and bitter. A society that has renamed evil has destroyed the words its own repentance would need. You cannot turn from something you have agreed to call good.

Wise in their own eyes. The fifth woe explains the fourth. Nobody relabels good and evil by accident. It takes a settled confidence in one’s own judgment, and that confidence is the root from which the swapping grows.

Who decides what is good? Many now assume that each of us writes the labels for ourselves, yet we are as quick to condemn as any generation; we simply put the labels on different things, often on whatever threatens the life we want. Why? Because a fixed standard means a fixed verdict, and a verdict against us is unbearable unless there is some way back from it, so we move the standard instead. The gospel offers the one thing that makes honesty safe. If the Judge has taken the verdict himself, if “for our sake he made him to be sin who knew no sin” (2 Corinthians 5:21), we no longer need to rename our evil in order to survive it. We can call it by its real name, because it has been forgiven.

verseByVerse.quote: Woe to those who are heroes at drinking wine, and valiant men in mixing strong drink, who acquit the guilty for a bribe, and deprive the innocent of his right!
verseByVerse.commentary:
Woe to the leaders who are brave only at drinking and who sell justice: they let the guilty go and rob the innocent.

Heroes at drinking wine. The last woe pairs two things that look unrelated and are not, and the joke in the first half is bitter. Heroes and valiant men are war words, the vocabulary of soldiers who hold the line. This is what the courage of the ruling class has been spent on: an impressive capacity for drink.

Who acquit the guilty for a bribe. These same men sit as judges, and both halves of a court go wrong at once. The second is the worse: letting a guilty man off is a failure; taking an innocent man’s right away is theft, with the law as the instrument.

The six woes together. Read together, the woes are a diagnosis rather than a list, and not one of these is spectacular wickedness. Every one is respectable, and most of them are what success looks like from the outside, which is why Isaiah aimed them at a nation that thought it was doing rather well.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 24–30 — He Whistles, and They Come
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Because the people rejected the law of the LORD, judgment will come like fire through stubble, and it will not stop until it has done its work. Their root is rotten and their blossom goes up like dust (v. 24). God has already struck them, and a refrain sounds for the first time that will return four times in chapters 9 and 10: “his hand is stretched out still” (v. 25). Now he raises a banner and whistles for a nation from the ends of the earth, an army that never tires, stumbles or sleeps, and roars like a lion over its prey (vv. 26–29). The chapter ends with the land in darkness (v. 30).
verseByVerse.theology: God commands the empires he judges his people with. He does not improvise or scramble; he whistles, and a superpower arrives on schedule. That is a hard comfort, and it is a comfort: what is coming is not chaos, and it is not outside his hand.
verseByVerse.examples: When the Assyrian army came, it was as Isaiah described; Sennacherib’s own annals boast of forty-six walled towns of Judah he took.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore, as the tongue of fire devours the stubble, and as dry grass sinks down in the flame, so their root will be as rottenness, and their blossom go up like dust; for they have rejected the law of the LORD of hosts, and have despised the word of the Holy One of Israel. Therefore the anger of the LORD was kindled against his people, and he stretched out his hand against them and struck them, and the mountains quaked; and their corpses were as refuse in the midst of the streets. For all this his anger has not turned away, and his hand is stretched out still.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Because they have rejected God’s word, judgment will burn them like stubble, and God’s hand, already raised against them, is not yet lowered.

Their root will be as rottenness. What looked alive at the surface was rotten underneath, and the blossom goes up as dust at the first heat.

They have rejected the law of the LORD of hosts. The cause is stated plainly: they rejected the law and despised the word. Under all six woes lies one act. The land-grabbing, the drinking, the relabelling and the bribes all come from one decision: to reject what God has said.

His hand is stretched out still. Here the refrain sounds for the first time; it returns three times in chapter 9 and once in chapter 10 (9:12, 17, 21; 10:4), always meaning the same thing: this is not finished. The hand has struck and has not gone back down, because the striking has not yet produced what it was sent for. As chapter 9 will say outright, “the people did not turn to him who struck them” (9:13), and that turning is what the hand was reaching for the whole time.

verseByVerse.quote: He will raise a signal for nations far away, and whistle for them from the ends of the earth; and behold, quickly, speedily they come! None is weary, none stumbles, none slumbers or sleeps, not a waistband is loose, not a sandal strap broken; their arrows are sharp, all their bows bent, their horses' hoofs seem like flint, and their wheels like the whirlwind. Their roaring is like a lion, like young lions they roar; they growl and seize their prey; they carry it off, and none can rescue. They will growl over it on that day, like the growling of the sea. And if one looks to the land, behold, darkness and distress; and the light is darkened by its clouds.
verseByVerse.commentary:
At God’s whistle a tireless army comes from far away, and the land is left in darkness; yet Isaiah will show that the darkness is not the end.

He will raise a signal for nations far away. God whistles, and an empire comes. He makes the same gesture in chapter 7, whistling for the fly and the bee (7:18), and the casualness is the point: superpowers come when he calls them. The signal is a banner on a pole set up on a bare hill to rally troops from far away. The nation from afar is Assyria, God’s rod against his people (10:5), and after it Babylon. Isaiah will raise the same banner again for the root of Jesse, to whom the nations come not to plunder but to seek him (11:10).

None is weary, none stumbles. The list is of what is not wrong: nobody tired, nobody tripping, nobody asleep, no belt working loose, not one sandal strap broken. Anyone who has watched an organisation try to move knows how unlikely that is. They roar like a lion over prey that no one can rescue. It is set deliberately against the vineyard: there everything was given and nothing grew; here nothing is out of place and everything works.

The light is darkened by its clouds. The chapter ends in the dark: when everything has been given and the fruit is still wild, this is what is left.

Light after the darkness. But Isaiah has arranged his book with care, and a few chapters on the same voice says: “The people who walked in darkness have seen a great light” (9:2). Matthew hears that promise fulfilled when Jesus began to preach in Galilee (Matthew 4:15–16). The night at the end of the vineyard song is real, but it is not final, and the light that ends it is not grown out of the vineyard. It is given, as everything on that hillside was given from the start.

Uncertain wording. The last word of verse 30, translated clouds, is a rare word found nowhere else in the Old Testament. It probably means clouds or heavy mist, and the picture is clear: the light is swallowed up.

50.subtitle: The Servant’s Obedience
50.intro:
Where we are. Chapter 49 ended with God promising to take the prey back from the tyrant and to save Zion’s children. Chapter 50 answers the exiles’ feeling that God had divorced them, gives the third Servant Song (vv. 4–9), the first to show the servant suffering, and closes with two ways of walking in the dark.

The message. God has not divorced his people or sold them to pay a debt; their own sins sent them away, and his hand is not too short to bring them back. The way back is opened by a servant who listens to God every morning, freely gives his back to those who beat him, and sets his face like flint because God will vindicate him. So whoever walks in darkness should trust in the LORD’s name and lean on him, not light a fire of his own.

Why it was said. The exiles thought God had sent them away for good, or that some stronger power now owned them (see the introduction). They also faced long darkness with no visible sign of rescue, and the temptation to make their own way by their own light.

How the chapter makes its case. No certificate, no creditor (vv. 1–3): Israel was sent away for her own sins, and when God called no one answered, though his hand still dries up seas. The taught servant (vv. 4–9): he is wakened morning by morning to hear, gives his back to the smiters and his face to spitting, sets his face like flint, and dares any accuser to step forward. Two ways in the dark (vv. 10–11): the one who fears the LORD but has no light is told to trust the name; those who kindle their own fires are left to walk by them and lie down in torment.

Where it leads. This song leads to Christ by direct promise, and the Gospels show it fulfilled in detail. Jesus “set his face to go to Jerusalem” (Luke 9:51); he was struck and spat upon in the high priest’s court and in the Roman guardroom (Matthew 26:67; 27:30); Paul gives his courtroom to every believer: “It is God who justifies. Who is to condemn?” (Romans 8:33–34). The servant who trusted in the dark is the Son who committed his spirit to the Father (Luke 23:46).

For us. Begin each day as the servant did, with an open ear before an open mouth, so that you have a word for the weary. When you walk in darkness, do not take that as proof that God has gone, and do not grab a homemade torch: lean your weight on the name of the LORD, trusting the one who stood in the dock for you.

keyVerse.quote: “But the Lord GOD helps me; therefore I have not been disgraced; therefore I have set my face like a flint, and I know that I shall not be put to shame.”
keyVerse.note: The servant’s confidence is entirely borrowed: it flows from God’s help, not from his own constitution. Luke says that Jesus “set his face to go to Jerusalem” (Luke 9:51), and the deliberateness is the point. He was not swept toward the cross by events but walked toward it with resolve, sure that the Father was with him and that the end would not be shame.

50.reflection:
The servant is wakened “morning by morning” to listen before he speaks, so that he may “sustain with a word him who is weary” (v. 4). What helps you hear God through his word each day? Who around you is weary, and what kind of word actually helps a tired person?

The servant says, “I gave my back to those who strike” and “I hid not my face” (v. 6). Why does it matter that Jesus went to the cross willingly, not as a victim of events (John 10:18)?

Paul applies verses 8 and 9 to every believer: “Who shall bring any charge against God’s elect? It is God who justifies” (Romans 8:33). Which accusations, from others or from your own conscience, most need to hear that verdict?

Verse 10 describes someone who fears the LORD and obeys, yet “walks in darkness and has no light”. What fires of your own (v. 11) are you tempted to light in such times, and what would it look like instead to “trust in the name of the LORD and rely on his God”?

Behold, for your iniquities you were sold, and for your transgressions your mother was sent away.<sup>2</sup>Why, when I came, was there no man; why, when I called, was there no one to answer? Is my hand shortened, that it cannot redeem? Or have I no power to deliver? Behold, by my rebuke I dry up the sea, I make the rivers a desert; their fish stink for lack of water and die of thirst.<sup>3</sup>I clothe the heavens with blackness and make sackcloth their covering."<sup>4</sup>The Lord GOD has given me the tongue of those who are taught, that I may know how to sustain with a word him who is weary. Morning by morning he awakens; he awakens my ear to hear as those who are taught.<sup>5</sup>The Lord GOD has opened my ear, and I was not rebellious; I turned not backward.<sup>6</sup>I gave my back to those who strike, and my cheeks to those who pull out the beard; I hid not my face from disgrace and spitting.<sup>7</sup>But the Lord GOD helps me; therefore I have not been disgraced; therefore I have set my face like a flint, and I know that I shall not be put to shame.<sup>8</sup>He who vindicates me is near.
