Walk by the light of your fire, and by the torches that you have kindled! This you have from my hand: you shall lie down in torment.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God has not divorced his people or sold them to a creditor; they were sent away for their own sins, and he is still able to save. He asks for a certificate of divorce and a creditor’s name, and neither exists: there is no final break and no rival claim, only sin, which he can deal with (v. 1). Then he turns their complaint round: when he came, no one was there, and when he called, no one answered. His hand is not too short to redeem; at his rebuke seas dry up and the sky is dressed in black (vv. 2–3).
verseByVerse.theology: The door was never legally shut. By denying both a certificate and a creditor, God leaves the exile in the one category from which a kinsman with the price can always bring someone home, and he is that kinsman.
verseByVerse.examples: Verse 2 names a pattern that runs through the book and through much Christian experience of God's supposed silence: the people complain that God was absent, God answers that they were absent when he came, and only one of the two had actually gone missing.

verseByVerse.quote: Thus says the LORD: "Where is your mother's certificate of divorce, with which I sent her away? Or which of my creditors is it to whom I have sold you? Behold, for your iniquities you were sold, and for your transgressions your mother was sent away. Why, when I came, was there no man; why, when I called, was there no one to answer? Is my hand shortened, that it cannot redeem? Or have I no power to deliver? Behold, by my rebuke I dry up the sea, I make the rivers a desert; their fish stink for lack of water and die of thirst. I clothe the heavens with blackness and make sackcloth their covering."
verseByVerse.commentary:
God has not divorced his people or sold them to a creditor: their own sins sent them away, and his hand is still strong enough to bring them back. The silence they blamed on God was their own.

Your mother’s certificate of divorce. Two legal questions, and to each the answer is that the document does not exist. The mercy lies in which questions God chooses. Under the law, a divorced wife who had married another could never be taken back (Deut. 24:1–4); a debtor sold into slavery could always be bought out by a kinsman with the price in his hand. God denies both. There was no certificate, so she is not permanently dismissed; there was no creditor, so nobody holds a claim on her that must be honoured. What is left is the one situation from which return is possible.

Does Jeremiah not say that God gave faithless Israel a decree of divorce (Jeremiah 3:8)? He does, of the northern kingdom, and in the same chapter he begs her to return (3:12–14), which the law of divorce would forbid. The prophets use the picture to make different points: Jeremiah to show how far the unfaithfulness went, Isaiah to show that no final divorce has shut the way home.

For your iniquities you were sold. The cause is named without cruelty and without evasion: nobody sold Israel; Israel sold herself. That is worse in one way and much better in another, because a problem you created is one God can undo without anybody else’s permission.

Why, when I came, was there no man? Then the charge is reversed. The exiles said God had gone. God replies that he came and the house was empty; he called and nothing came back.

Is my hand shortened, that it cannot redeem? The answer is given in creation: by a rebuke he dries up the sea and clothes the heavens in black. The hand that parted the water at the exodus has not shrunk. What has changed is who is at home when he calls.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 4–9 — The Taught Tongue and the Set Face
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: In the third Servant Song the servant speaks of the cost of obedience and of the God who will vindicate him. His first claim is that he is taught: God wakens his ear morning by morning, so that he can sustain the weary with a word (v. 4). He does not rebel or turn back, but freely gives his back to the smiters and his face to spitting (vv. 5–6). Because the Lord GOD helps him, he sets his face like flint, sure he will not be shamed (v. 7), and he dares any accuser to step forward, for his vindicator is near and his opponents will wear out like moth-eaten cloth (vv. 8–9).
verseByVerse.theology: This song brings the servant's suffering into the open for the first time, and it insists on two things: the suffering is chosen (v. 6), and the confidence that carries him through it comes from outside himself: not I am strong but the Lord GOD helps me (v. 7). That is why we can follow him and not only admire him.
verseByVerse.examples: The order of verse 4 is the order of every good pastor and friend: those who can sustain the weary with a word are those who have first been sustained themselves, morning by morning, by what God has said.

verseByVerse.quote: The Lord GOD has given me the tongue of those who are taught, that I may know how to sustain with a word him who is weary. Morning by morning he awakens; he awakens my ear to hear as those who are taught.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The servant’s first credential is that he is a pupil: God opens his ear every morning, so that he has the right word for the weary.

The tongue of those who are taught. The servant claims not authority or power but that he has been taught, the word Isaiah used of his own disciples in 8:16.

To sustain with a word him who is weary. The purpose is specific: not to win arguments, but to hold up somebody tired with a word placed exactly where the weight is. Most speech aimed at an exhausted person makes things worse: advice, cheer, comparison, the wrong verse at the wrong moment. Knowing how to sustain the weary is a taught skill.

Morning by morning he awakens. It is learned morning by morning, which means most of those mornings were unremarkable and none was skipped. What is wakened is the ear: God’s first act each day is to open the servant’s hearing, and everything he says later comes out of what he took in first. The servant who sustains the weary of the whole world sat still every morning and let God speak to him first. The Gospels show him rising very early to pray (Mark 1:35) and saying that he spoke only what the Father had taught him (John 8:28).

Who is speaking? The song does not name him until verse 10, and some hear the prophet, who knew mockery himself, or Israel. But this servant is obedient where Israel was not (48:8; 50:5), gives his back to the smiters willingly, and is vindicated by God (vv. 6–9). Following the New Testament, Christians read the speaker as the Messiah, whose path a faithful prophet’s sufferings could only foreshadow.
verseByVerse.note: The third Servant Song (vv. 4–9).

verseByVerse.quote: The Lord GOD has opened my ear, and I was not rebellious; I turned not backward. I gave my back to those who strike, and my cheeks to those who pull out the beard; I hid not my face from disgrace and spitting.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The servant obeyed without turning back, and freely handed himself over to beating, humiliation and spitting.

I was not rebellious. The opened ear produces obedience, shown in two refusals: not rebellious, not turning back. Isaiah does not say the servant was enthusiastic; he did not refuse and he did not retreat, which is what obedience looks like from inside when the thing asked is hard. It is exactly what Israel, whose ear has not been opened (48:8), never did, and what none of us has done wholeheartedly for a single day. He did it in our place, and his obedience is counted to those who belong to him (Rom. 5:19).

I gave my back to those who strike. Read the verbs before the injuries: I gave, I hid not. This is a man describing what he handed over, and the New Testament keeps the distinction. Jesus says of his life, “No one takes it from me, but I lay it down of my own accord” (John 10:18).

My cheeks to those who pull out the beard. The injuries are specific. The back given to flogging. The beard pulled out, in that world the deliberate stripping of a man’s dignity, a humiliation that lasted as long as the beard took to grow back. And spitting, the most contemptuous thing one person can do to another, needing no weapon. Matthew records them as events: they spat in his face and struck him (Matt. 26:67); they scourged him and spat on him again (Matt. 27:26, 30). Isaiah wrote the list centuries earlier, and a high priest’s court and a Roman guardroom filled it in.

Decided in advance. Nobody prised his face round; he did not turn it away. Every blow landed on someone who had decided in advance not to move, and he had decided it in the light of what it was for.

verseByVerse.quote: But the Lord GOD helps me; therefore I have not been disgraced; therefore I have set my face like a flint, and I know that I shall not be put to shame.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Because God helps him, the servant sets his face like flint toward his suffering, certain that it will not end in shame.

But the Lord GOD helps me. Everything hangs on the first clause. The servant is resolute not because he is a resolute sort of person but because the Lord GOD helps him. Take the help away and the flint face goes with it. That matters for anyone trying to imitate him: this endurance is not a temperament some people have but strength drawn from elsewhere, and the believer draws on the same source, the Spirit of the Lord GOD who rested on the servant (61:1) and now lives in his people (Rom. 8:11).

I have set my face like a flint. Flint is used precisely because it does not give. The face shows what a person intends, and this one has been set, a deliberate act rather than a mood that happened to hold. Luke uses the phrase: “he set his face to go to Jerusalem” (Luke 9:51). He was not swept there by events or cornered by a plot. He turned his head and walked.

I shall not be put to shame. Not that it will not hurt, or be brief, but that the end will not be humiliation, which is exactly what it looked like to everyone watching on the day, and exactly what it turned out not to be.

verseByVerse.quote: He who vindicates me is near. Who will contend with me? Let us stand up together. Who is my adversary? Let him come near to me. Behold, the Lord GOD helps me; who will declare me guilty? Behold, all of them will wear out like a garment; the moth will eat them up.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The servant dares anyone to accuse him, because God, who declares him in the right, stands beside him, and every accuser will wear away.

Let us stand up together. The scene becomes a courtroom, and the servant is on his feet inviting prosecution. He is not defending himself; he is asking whether anybody wants to try.

He who vindicates me is near. To vindicate is to declare someone in the right, what the New Testament calls justification, and the point is how close he is. The Judge is not distant or undecided; he is standing next to the defendant.

The moth will eat them up. The prosecution is not defeated in argument but outlasted, like an old coat in a cupboard quietly eaten through. Every charge in the room will wear out, and the moth is already in the cloth.

Who will declare me guilty? Paul hands this courtroom to ordinary Christians: “Who shall bring any charge against God’s elect? It is God who justifies. Who is to condemn?” (Rom. 8:33–34), on the ground that the one who first stood in that dock stood there for us. So the accusations a believer knows best about himself, the true ones with dates attached, are in a room where the Judge has already spoken and the prosecutor is being eaten by moths.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 10–11 — Two Ways of Walking in the Dark
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The chapter ends with two people in the same darkness, and only one of them is being led. The one who fears the LORD and obeys his servant, yet walks in darkness with no light, is told to trust in the name of the LORD and lean on his God (v. 10). Those who kindle their own fires and walk by their own torches are left to the light they made, and it ends in torment (v. 11). The servant has just shown the first way; the chapter invites the reader to walk it.
verseByVerse.theology: The man in verse 10 has not drifted from God, and that is why the verse matters so much pastorally. What is asked of him is not a feeling but a decision to lean.
verseByVerse.examples: The two verses describe a choice everybody faces in a season of unanswered prayer: wait in the dark holding a name, or manufacture some light of your own and walk by that.

verseByVerse.quote: Who among you fears the LORD and obeys the voice of his servant? Let him who walks in darkness and has no light trust in the name of the LORD and rely on his God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A believer who fears God and obeys can still walk in total darkness, and is told not to find a light but to lean his whole weight on the LORD’s name.

Walks in darkness and has no light. Everything depends on who is described. This man fears the LORD and obeys the voice of his servant: by every measure the book has offered, he is where he should be. And he has no light. Not dim light; none.

When a believer cannot see. That dismantles an assumption that does enormous damage: that if a Christian cannot see, something must have gone wrong, some sin unconfessed or faith insufficiently exercised. Isaiah puts an obedient, God-fearing man in total darkness and does not suggest he has made a mistake.

Trust in the name of the LORD. What is asked is not a feeling or an explanation. Rely on his God is the word for leaning, putting your weight on something. He is not told to find the light or to generate an assurance he does not have, but to put his weight on a name in the dark.

The servant’s path. The servant has just walked through blows and spitting with no visible vindication, trusting a God who did not intervene. Verse 10 invites the believer onto the same path, and it is offered to people who will walk it less steadily than he did, and who lean on him when they cannot lean well.

How do I trust in the dark? The verse names two things to do, and both can be done without seeing anything. Say the name. When the diagnosis is unclear, or the prayer for a wandering child has gone unanswered for years, do not wait for an explanation; tell God what you know of him, the name he proclaimed to Moses: The LORD, the LORD, a God merciful and gracious (Exod. 34:6). Put your weight down. Rely means lean, so do the next obedient thing as if he were holding you up: go to work, gather with his people on the Lord’s Day, answer the email kindly. Refuse the homemade torch. Verse 11 warns against lighting your own fire: the quick fix, the drink at 2 a.m., the decision forced just to end the uncertainty. Hold on to the one who held on. In the deepest dark there has ever been, Jesus still said, Father, into your hands I commit my spirit! (Luke 23:46), and the Father raised him. Because he trusted for you, your darkness is not proof that God has gone: even the darkness is not dark to you (Psalm 139:12).

verseByVerse.quote: Behold, all you who kindle a fire, who equip yourselves with burning torches! Walk by the light of your fire, and by the torches that you have kindled! This you have from my hand: you shall lie down in torment.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Those who refuse to wait on God and make their own light are left to walk by it, and it ends in torment.

All you who kindle a fire. The other man in the same darkness is not a villain. It is dark, and rather than standing still he strikes a spark and makes a light. Anyone would. That is why the warning is needed: the fire is not gross wickedness but self-reliance, the understandable refusal to wait holding nothing but a name. It looks like initiative, and it works for a while.

Walk by the light of your fire. The invitation is bitter. God does not put the fire out. He lets the man have exactly what he made and lets it take him where it goes.

You shall lie down in torment. The last word of the chapter is a bed, where you end up when you finally stop walking. The torches got him through the night and did not get him anywhere he wanted to be. One man holds a name he cannot see; the other holds a light he made. Only one is being led, and it is the one who looks, from outside, to have nothing at all.

Making your own light. Verse 11 could describe the modern West. Having decided that the universe gives no light of its own, our culture has made a virtue of kindling it: no given meaning, so create your own; no given self, so invent one; no given path, so follow whatever burns brightest in you. It is presented as courage, and sometimes it is. But a light you make yourself shows you only as far as your own small fire reaches, and it has to be fed all the time, by success, by romance, by the next project, or it goes out. Many find in middle age that the fire they fed so carefully has lit a very small circle. Isaiah offers something stranger: to walk in the dark holding a name. That sounds like less, until you learn whose name it is. The one who said, I am the light of the world. Whoever follows me will not walk in darkness (John 8:12), walked into the deepest darkness himself, so that those who trust him would never be left in it.

Uncertain wording. The word behind burning torches is rare; it appears to mean firebrands or flaming arrows (compare Proverbs 26:18), and the verb is literally gird yourselves. Whether the picture is of torches for walking or of weapons for fighting, the point is the same: people arming themselves with fire of their own making.

50.theology:
Chosen suffering, not endured misfortune. This song insists on who does the acting: I gave my back, I hid not my face. The servant is a volunteer, not a victim, and his confidence comes just as plainly from the help of the Lord GOD.

The courtroom, handed over. Verses 8 and 9 have the servant on his feet inviting prosecution because his vindicator is near, and the accusers are not argued down; they wear out like moth-eaten cloth. Paul gives the same courtroom to every believer, on the ground that the one who first stood in that dock stood there for us.

Darkness is not always evidence. The man in verse 10 fears the LORD and obeys the servant and has no light, and Isaiah does not treat that as a symptom of sin or of deficient faith; neither should anyone using this chapter pastorally. Verse 11 shows the alternative without caricature: a self-made light is the reasonable response to darkness, it genuinely works for a while, and it ends in torment.

51.subtitle: Look to the Rock from Which You Were Cut
51.intro:
Where we are. Chapter 50 ended with the servant who gave his back to the smiters and the call to trust the LORD in the dark. Chapter 51 speaks to the fear of the faithful in Israel: three calls to listen, three calls to wake, and a cup taken out of Jerusalem’s hand.

The message. Do not be afraid, because the God who made a nation out of one old man is the God who comforts you now. Everything that looks permanent, the sky, the earth and the people who threaten you, will wear out, but his salvation lasts for ever. He has not been asleep; you have forgotten him. And the cup of his wrath that Jerusalem has drunk to the dregs, he now takes from her hand.

Why it was said. The faithful remnant were few, their city in ruins, and their oppressors loud (see the introduction). They felt too small to rebuild anything, they lived in fear of men who seemed to hold their future, and they wondered why God’s arm was not moving.

How the chapter makes its case. Look (vv. 1–8): back to Abraham and Sarah, from whom God made many out of one; out to the nations, who will receive his justice; up to the heavens, which will vanish while his salvation lasts; and at the critics, whom the moth will eat. Wake (vv. 9–16): the people cry to the arm of the LORD to awake as at the exodus; God promises a singing return and asks why they fear mortal man and forget their Maker. Stand up (vv. 17–23): Jerusalem, staggering from the cup of wrath with no son to help her, is told that her Lord, who pleads her cause, has taken the cup from her hand and will give it to her tormentors.

Where it leads. The chapter leads to Christ by covenant and by pattern. The promise to Abraham pointed to one offspring, “who is Christ” (Galatians 3:16), in whom the one becomes a multitude. The arm of the LORD that the people beg to wake is revealed in the servant (53:1; John 12:38). And the cup of wrath, taken from Jerusalem but not poured away, is the cup Jesus prayed over in Gethsemane and then drank (Matthew 26:39; John 18:11), so that it would never be handed to his people again.

For us. When you feel small, remember how little God began with and how much he made of it. When people frighten you, set their passing lives beside God’s everlasting salvation. And when your conscience reminds you what you deserve, look at the cup: Christ has drunk it, and you will drink it no more.

keyVerse.quote: “Lift up your eyes to the heavens, and look at the earth beneath; for the heavens vanish like smoke, the earth will wear out like a garment, and they who dwell in it will die in like manner; but my salvation will be forever, and my righteousness will never be dismayed.”
keyVerse.note: The permanence of God’s salvation is set against the impermanence of everything else. Sky and earth, the most stable things anyone can name, are shown to be temporary, and what stands is what God has promised. This is not escapism but realism: the solid-looking things will pass, and the fragile-looking promise will not, because it rests on the Son who remains (Hebrews 1:11–12).

51.reflection:
God tells discouraged people to “look to Abraham your father and to Sarah who bore you; for he was but one when I called him” (v. 2). Where do you feel too small or too few for what God has called you to? How does God’s record of beginnings, from Abraham to twelve ordinary disciples, encourage you?

Verse 6 says the heavens will vanish like smoke but God’s salvation will be for ever. What in your life feels most solid and permanent? How should God’s everlasting salvation change the weight you give it?

God asks, “who are you that you are afraid of man who dies … and have forgotten the LORD, your Maker” (vv. 12–13). Whose opinion or power do you fear most? What practical habits help you remember God when fear rises?

God takes the cup of wrath from Jerusalem’s hand (v. 22), and Jesus later drank the cup the Father gave him (John 18:11). How does knowing who drank the cup change the way you face guilt and God’s judgment?

And where is the wrath of the oppressor?<sup>14</sup>He who is bowed down shall speedily be released; he shall not die and go down to the pit, neither shall his bread be lacking.<sup>15</sup>I am the LORD your God, who stirs up the sea so that its waves roar— the LORD of hosts is his name.<sup>16</sup>And I have put my words in your mouth and covered you in the shadow of my hand, establishing the heavens and laying the foundations of the earth, and saying to Zion, 'You are my people.'"<sup>17</sup>Wake yourself, wake yourself, stand up, O Jerusalem, you who have drunk from the hand of the LORD the cup of his wrath, who have drunk to the dregs the bowl, the cup of staggering.<sup>18</sup>There is none to guide her among all the sons she has borne; there is none to take her by the hand among all the sons she has brought up.<sup>19</sup>These two things have happened to you— who will console you?— devastation and destruction, famine and sword; who will comfort you?<sup>20</sup>Your sons have fainted; they lie at the head of every street like an antelope in a net; they are full of the wrath of the LORD, the rebuke of your God.<sup>21</sup>Therefore hear this, you who are afflicted, who are drunk, but not with wine:<sup>22</sup>Thus says your Lord, the LORD, your God who pleads the cause of his people: "Behold, I have taken from your hand the cup of staggering; the bowl of my wrath you shall drink no more;<sup>23</sup>and I will put it into the hand of your tormentors, who have said to you, 'Bow down, that we may pass over'; and you have made your back like the ground and like the street for them to pass over."

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God tells his frightened faithful people to look in three directions, and each look gives them courage. Look back to the quarry they were cut from: Abraham was one man and Sarah was barren, yet God made a nation of them, and he will turn Zion’s wilderness into Eden (vv. 1–3). Look out: his law and justice are going out as a light to the peoples, and the coastlands wait for him (vv. 4–5). Look up: the heavens will vanish like smoke and the earth wear out like a garment, but his salvation is for ever (v. 6). So do not fear the insults of mortal men, whom the moth will eat (vv. 7–8).
verseByVerse.theology: Each of the three looks moves the eye away from present circumstances to something God has already done or has promised. Courage in this chapter is built out of memory and promise, not mood.
verseByVerse.examples: A congregation that has dwindled to a handful can hear verses 1-2 as addressed to it: God has never needed large numbers to begin with, and he once began a nation with a childless old couple.

verseByVerse.quote: "Listen to me, you who pursue righteousness, you who seek the LORD: look to the rock from which you were hewn, and to the quarry from which you were dug. Look to Abraham your father and to Sarah who bore you; for he was but one when I called him, that I might bless him and multiply him. For the LORD comforts Zion; he comforts all her waste places and makes her wilderness like Eden, her desert like the garden of the LORD; joy and gladness will be found in her, thanksgiving and the voice of song.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When God’s people feel too few to have a future, he tells them to remember how he made a nation out of one old man and a barren woman, and promises to turn their ruins into Eden.

Look to the rock from which you were hewn. Before any promise is made, the people are sent to look at a hole in the ground. A quarry is where stone is cut out, and the shape left behind tells you the size of what was taken. God tells a demoralised community to go and stand at their own quarry.

Look to Abraham your father and to Sarah who bore you. Then he names it, and its smallness is the argument: one elderly man and one woman who could not have children. Every Israelite alive was cut out of that. Paul describes it plainly: Abraham was about a hundred years old and his body as good as dead, and Sarah’s womb likewise (Rom. 4:19).

He was but one when I called him. The reasoning is arithmetic. You are worried that there is not enough left of you to rebuild a nation. Count what he started with last time.

Makes her wilderness like Eden. The promise does not stop at recovery. The wilderness becomes Eden, the highest comparison available: the end is not a return to the way things were before the trouble, but to the way things were before anything went wrong at all.

How do I look to the rock? This is a command for discouraged people, and it is carried out with the memory. Go back to your own quarry. Recall where you were when God called you, and how little you brought. Remember how he began. When your church is thirty people in a rented hall, or you are the only believer in your family, read again what he started with: one old man, one childless woman, and later twelve ordinary men in Galilee. For whoever has despised the day of small things shall rejoice (Zech. 4:10). Look to the true offspring. Paul says the promise to Abraham pointed to one offspring, who is Christ (Gal. 3:16). Jesus became the single grain that falls into the earth and dies, and so bears much fruit (John 12:24); and if you are Christ’s, then you are Abraham’s offspring (Gal. 3:29). Then do the small thing. Pray for the one neighbour, teach the four children in Sunday school, and leave the multiplying to the God who has done it before.

verseByVerse.quote: "Give attention to me, my people, and give ear to me, my nation; for a law will go out from me, and I will set my justice for a light to the peoples. My righteousness draws near, my salvation has gone out, and my arms will judge the peoples; the coastlands hope for me, and for my arm they wait. Lift up your eyes to the heavens, and look at the earth beneath; for the heavens vanish like smoke, the earth will wear out like a garment, and they who dwell in it will die in like manner; but my salvation will be forever, and my righteousness will never be dismayed.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God’s saving justice is going out to all nations, and it will outlast the sky and the earth themselves.

I will set my justice for a light to the peoples. The horizon widens without warning. A people concerned only with getting home are told that something is going out from God to the whole world, and the far islands are waiting for it.

The earth will wear out like a garment. The second look is upward, at the most permanent things anyone can name, the sky and the ground under our feet, and Isaiah says both will wear out. The sky goes like smoke off a fire; the earth wears out the way a coat does, not dramatically but thin at the elbows, one season at a time until it is not worth mending. Hebrews uses the same picture of the world and sets against it the Son, who remains (Heb. 1:11–12).

What God’s righteousness is. Most of us hear “God’s righteousness” and brace ourselves, as if it meant only the standard we fall short of. But Isaiah keeps pairing it with salvation: “My righteousness draws near, my salvation has gone out” (v. 5). God’s righteousness here is his action as well as his standard: God doing what is right, keeping his promises and putting wrong things right, which for his people means putting them right with him. He is “a righteous God and a Savior” (45:21), and the two are not rivals. That is good news because of the cross, where sin was not overlooked but paid for, so that God is “just and the justifier of the one who has faith in Jesus” (Romans 3:26). So when your conscience accuses you, do not try to slip past God’s righteousness to reach his mercy. In Christ his righteousness is on your side, and it will outlast the sky. See Justification.

Uncertain wording. The phrase translated will die in like manner can also be read will die like gnats, since the Hebrew word is spelled like the word for gnats. Either way the dwellers on the earth are as passing as the earth itself.

verseByVerse.quote: "Listen to me, you who know righteousness, the people in whose heart is my law; fear not the reproach of man, nor be dismayed at their revilings. For the moth will eat them up like a garment, and the worm will eat them like wool, but my righteousness will be forever, and my salvation to all generations."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Those who carry God’s law in their hearts need not fear people’s insults, because the critics will pass away like moth-eaten wool, while God’s salvation lasts for ever.

Fear not the reproach of man. The fear addressed here is being talked about. Reproach and reviling are what people say, and fear of it is one of the most controlling forces there is: it decides careers, silences convictions, and reorganises whole lives around a conversation that may never happen.

The people in whose heart is my law. God addresses the people in whose heart is my law, a law he himself promised to write there (Jer. 31:33). The courage asked of them rests on what he has done in them, not on their nerve. And his answer to the critics is a moth. He does not say they are wrong; he says they will not last. The image from verse 6 returns, applied to the people whose opinion is running your life.

A test of proportion. Hold the two timescales side by side, as the verse asks. The remark repeating in your head for days, and the man who made it, will both be gone inside a century; the moth is unhurried and entirely reliable. God’s righteousness will still be in force. None of this says reproach does not hurt. It says a person can be genuinely frightened of something that is quietly being eaten.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 9–16 — Awake, Arm of the LORD
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The people cry to God to wake up, and God answers that they are the ones who have forgotten. They call the arm of the LORD to awake as when he crushed Rahab and made a road through the sea (vv. 9–10), and the promise of a singing return to Zion, first given at the close of chapter 35, stands as the answer (v. 11). God then asks why they fear mortal man and forget their Maker, and where the oppressor’s fury has gone (vv. 12–13). The man bowed down will soon be freed, and the God who stirs the sea has put his words in Zion’s mouth and calls her his people (vv. 14–16).
verseByVerse.theology: The prayer and the answer are aimed in opposite directions and both are right: they tell God to wake up, and God tells them they have fallen asleep to who he is.
verseByVerse.examples: The fear of verse 12 is familiar in any workplace or family where one person's displeasure governs everyone else's day. The cure offered is not bravado but remembering who stretched out the heavens.

verseByVerse.quote: Awake, awake, put on strength, O arm of the LORD; awake, as in days of old, the generations of long ago. Was it not you who cut Rahab in pieces, who pierced the dragon? Was it not you who dried up the sea, the waters of the great deep, who made the depths of the sea a way for the redeemed to pass over? And the ransomed of the LORD shall return and come to Zion with singing; everlasting joy shall be upon their heads; they shall obtain gladness and joy, and sorrow and sighing shall flee away.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The people boldly call on God to act as he did at the exodus, and his answer is the promise of a joyful homecoming where sorrow will flee.

Awake, awake, put on strength, O arm of the LORD. The people answer back, and it is a bold prayer. They tell God to wake up and roll up his sleeve, which is what the arm means here, and they build their case out of his own history.

Who cut Rahab in pieces. Rahab here is not the woman of Jericho but a poetic name for Egypt and for the sea monster of ancient story (compare 30:7). Pagan stories told of a god fighting a dragon of chaos; Isaiah borrows that language for a real event on a real morning at the edge of a real sea: the LORD’s defeat of Egypt and the road through the water for the redeemed. The prayer is an argument, not nostalgia: the arm that did this is still his arm. The New Testament names that arm: to whom has the arm of the Lord been revealed? (John 12:38, quoting 53:1).

Sorrow and sighing shall flee away. Verse 11 is the last verse of chapter 35, repeated almost word for word. The promise that closed the first half of the book is produced again as the answer to a prayer, like a document brought out of a drawer and laid on the table. It did not need rewriting.
verseByVerse.note: Rahab is a poetic name for Egypt or the sea monster of chaos.

verseByVerse.quote: "I, I am he who comforts you; who are you that you are afraid of man who dies, of the son of man who is made like grass, and have forgotten the LORD, your Maker, who stretched out the heavens and laid the foundations of the earth, and you fear continually all the day because of the wrath of the oppressor, when he sets himself to destroy? And where is the wrath of the oppressor?
verseByVerse.commentary:
God, who comforts his people, asks why they fear mortal men and forget their Maker: fear grows as the memory of God shrinks.

I, I am he who comforts you. They told God to wake up; he answers by asking what they have been sleeping through.

Afraid of man who dies. The question is pointed: not who is the man you fear, but who are you to be afraid: a person who has the Maker of the heavens and is frightened of grass.

Have forgotten the LORD, your Maker. The diagnosis in the middle is the part to keep. Fear is traced not to weakness or temperament but to forgetting. As the memory of God shrinks, the man who threatens you grows, because the two cannot both fill the mind. Jesus gave the same cure: do not fear those who can kill the body, but remember the Father who counts the hairs of your head (Matthew 10:28–31).

Where is the wrath of the oppressor? The last question is asked as if the oppressor had already gone. Fear ran all day because of a fury that was coming, and the question is where it has got to. Chapter 41 made the same promise about enemies who are searched for and not found (41:12).

verseByVerse.quote: He who is bowed down shall speedily be released; he shall not die and go down to the pit, neither shall his bread be lacking. I am the LORD your God, who stirs up the sea so that its waves roar— the LORD of hosts is his name. And I have put my words in your mouth and covered you in the shadow of my hand, establishing the heavens and laying the foundations of the earth, and saying to Zion, 'You are my people.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The God who rules the roaring sea promises release and bread to the man bowed down, and with the same hand that founded the world he calls Zion his people.

He who is bowed down shall speedily be released. See how small and physical the promise is. The man bent double under a load will be let go; he will not die in the pit; there will be bread. Nothing about empires: release, survival and dinner.

Who stirs up the sea so that its waves roar. In the very next line stands the God who stirs the sea until it roars. The same verse holds the ocean and the loaf, and the God who does the one guarantees the other.

I have put my words in your mouth. Three things are done with the same hand: it fills a mouth with words, covers a head like shade at noon, and lays the foundations of the world. Then the sentence ends where nobody would predict: and saying to Zion, ‘You are my people.’ The founding of the universe and the naming of one battered community stand in a single line, with no change of tone. The hand that spread out the heavens shades one head, and is not stretched by holding both.

Uncertain wording. Establishing the heavens is literally planting the heavens, as if the sky were a tree God set in the ground. The sense is the same: he founded it.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 17–23 — The Cup Taken Out of Her Hand
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Jerusalem, who has drunk God’s wrath to the bottom of the cup, is told to wake, because God is taking the cup away. She staggers in the street with none of her children to take her hand, struck by devastation, famine and sword, and no one to comfort her (vv. 17–20). Then her Lord, who pleads his people’s cause, announces that he has taken the cup of staggering from her hand: she will drink it no more, and it will go to the tormentors who made her lie down like a street for them to walk over (vv. 21–23).
verseByVerse.theology: The cup is not emptied and it is not cancelled. It is moved, and the next two chapters show into whose hand it finally goes.
verseByVerse.examples: A mother with no child to take her arm (v. 18) is a picture many a lonely widow or neglected parent could draw of her own life. The chapter does not answer it with advice but with an advocate who comes himself (v. 22).

verseByVerse.quote: Wake yourself, wake yourself, stand up, O Jerusalem, you who have drunk from the hand of the LORD the cup of his wrath, who have drunk to the dregs the bowl, the cup of staggering. There is none to guide her among all the sons she has borne; there is none to take her by the hand among all the sons she has brought up. These two things have happened to you— who will console you?— devastation and destruction, famine and sword; who will comfort you? Your sons have fainted; they lie at the head of every street like an antelope in a net; they are full of the wrath of the LORD, the rebuke of your God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jerusalem has drunk God’s wrath to the bitter dregs and lies helpless, with none of her children to lift her up and no one to comfort her.

Wake yourself, wake yourself. The word comes back the other way round. They said awake, awake to the arm of the LORD; now the LORD says wake yourself, wake yourself to Jerusalem. The one accused of sleeping tells the accuser to get up off the floor.

The cup of his wrath. The cup is one of the Bible’s great images: the wrath of God, measured out and handed over to be drunk (Jeremiah 25:15; Psalm 75:8). Jerusalem has had it, and drunk it to the dregs, the bitter sediment a person reaches only when nothing is left in the cup.

There is none to take her by the hand. Then the most desolate sentence in the chapter, and it is a domestic one. A woman staggers in the street and not one of her children is there to take her arm. She raised them all. The city is pictured not as a fortress that fell but as a mother nobody came for.

Who will comfort you? The question is asked twice in one verse and left hanging; Isaiah does not rush to answer it. Her sons lie like an antelope in a net, an animal that has run its heart out and now lies still and tangled, with nothing left, at the corner where everyone walks past.

Textual note. In verse 19 the traditional Hebrew text reads how shall I comfort you?; some ancient copies and versions read who will comfort you?, which the ESV follows. Either way, no human comforter is found.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore hear this, you who are afflicted, who are drunk, but not with wine: Thus says your Lord, the LORD, your God who pleads the cause of his people: "Behold, I have taken from your hand the cup of staggering; the bowl of my wrath you shall drink no more; and I will put it into the hand of your tormentors, who have said to you, 'Bow down, that we may pass over'; and you have made your back like the ground and like the street for them to pass over."
verseByVerse.commentary:
God, the advocate of his people, takes the cup of wrath out of Jerusalem’s hand for ever and gives it to her tormentors.

Drunk, but not with wine. She staggers like someone drunk, but there is no wine in this; what makes her stagger is what she has suffered. God addresses her in that condition rather than waiting for her to recover.

Your God who pleads the cause of his people. This is a courtroom title. He is not the distant judge in this scene but the advocate at their side, and the advocate’s first act is to reach out and take the cup away.

I will put it into the hand of your tormentors. Watch what happens to the cup, because it is the hinge of the chapter. It is not emptied onto the ground. It is transferred. Wrath in this book is always real, always measured, and always drunk by somebody; the only open question is who is holding the cup.

You have made your back like the ground. The last image is of a people ordered to lie face down so that soldiers could walk across them. One chapter earlier the servant said that he gave his back to those who strike (50:6). Jerusalem’s back was taken. His was given.

The cup in his own hand. Isaiah does not yet say how a holy God can take the cup from his people without simply pouring it away; chapter 53 begins the answer. Centuries later a man knelt in a garden at night, looked at the cup, and asked whether it could pass from him; then he stood up and said that the cup the Father had given him was his to drink (Matt. 26:39; John 18:11). Every drop Jerusalem had staggered under, and more, went down the throat of the Servant. He took the cup out of their hand by putting it in his own.

51.theology:
Argue from the quarry. The chapter’s cure for despair is not encouragement but evidence, and the evidence is the reader’s own existence. When the remaining material looks too small to build anything with, God points to what he began with last time.

What is actually permanent. The heavens and the earth, the most stable things anyone can name, are compared to clothing that wears out, and so are the people whose opinions govern a life (vv. 6, 8). This is not escapism; it is seeing what truly lasts. The things that feel most solid are passing, and the promise made to a defeated people is not.

Fear as forgetting. The people tell the arm of the LORD to awake (v. 9); God tells Jerusalem to wake herself (v. 17). Between the two commands fear is diagnosed as a failure of memory rather than of nerve (vv. 12-13).

The cup is moved, not cancelled. Wrath in Isaiah is never waved away. Jerusalem drinks it to the dregs, and then her advocate takes it from her hand. Mercy that costs nobody anything is not the mercy Isaiah is describing; in Gethsemane the cost was counted, and paid (Matt. 26:39).

52.subtitle: How Beautiful Are the Feet
52.intro:
Where we are. Chapter 51 called on the arm of the LORD to awake and ended with the cup of wrath taken from Jerusalem’s hand. Chapter 52 turns the call back on Zion, announces God’s reign, sends the exiles out of Babylon, and begins the fourth Servant Song (52:13 to 53:12), the heart of the book.

The message. Wake up and get dressed for freedom, because God has already redeemed you, freely, for the sake of his own name. The runner on the mountains brings the news every captive longs for: your God reigns. And the way God will bare his arm before the nations is through a servant whose face is marred beyond recognition, and who will be lifted high and sprinkle many nations.

Why it was said. The exiles in Babylon were humiliated, their temple vessels in a foreign treasury and God’s name mocked every day by their captors (see the introduction). They needed to hear that God had not lost, that their release was certain, and that he would bring them out in peace.

How the chapter makes its case. Wake and dress (vv. 1–6): Zion is told to put on strength and untie her own neck, because she was sold for nothing and will be redeemed without money; God acts for his name. Beautiful feet (vv. 7–12): a herald brings good news, the watchmen and the ruins sing, God bares his holy arm before the nations, and the people leave Babylon clean and unhurried, with God before them and behind. The servant (vv. 13–15): he will act wisely and be high and lifted up, though his appearance is so marred that many are appalled, and he will sprinkle many nations while kings fall silent.

Where it leads. The chapter leads to Christ by direct promise. Jesus came into Galilee proclaiming the gospel of God and the kingdom at hand (Mark 1:14–15), the herald and the reigning God in one person, and Paul quotes verse 7 for every preacher who carries the news (Romans 10:15). The holy arm God bares turns out, one verse into chapter 53, to be a servant no one would look at twice. The marred one who is lifted up is the crucified and exalted Christ, whose blood cleanses people from every nation (1 Peter 1:2).

For us. In Christ you have been redeemed, so stand up and take off the ropes you still wear; obedience is the first act of a freed person, not the price of freedom. Carry the news that your God reigns with beautiful feet. And look at the marred servant until, like the kings, you have nothing left to say but worship.

keyVerse.quote: “How beautiful upon the mountains are the feet of him who brings good news, who publishes peace, who brings good news of happiness, who publishes salvation, who says to Zion, ‘Your God reigns.’”
keyVerse.note: Paul quotes this verse in Romans 10:15 to show why preachers are sent, extending the herald’s task to every Christian witness. The feet are beautiful not because the messenger is, but because of the news they carry. Every announcement of the gospel echoes this verse: “Your God reigns” is the core of Christian proclamation, because in Christ God has won the battle and come back to his people.

52.reflection:
Zion is told to “loose the bonds from your neck” (v. 2) because she will be “redeemed without money” (v. 3). Why does it matter that God’s command to live free comes after his act of redemption, not before? What “rope” do you still wear that Christ has already paid to remove?

God acts because “my name is despised” (v. 5). How does it steady your faith to know that God’s rescue of his people is bound up with his own honour, not only with his feelings?

“How beautiful upon the mountains are the feet of him who brings good news” (v. 7). Why might sharing the gospel feel intrusive today, and how does the picture of a herald with news of a won battle change that? Who is one person you could tell?

The servant will be “high and lifted up” (v. 13), yet his appearance is “so marred, beyond human semblance” (v. 14). How do the cross and the exaltation of Jesus belong together, and what does it mean for you that his suffering makes others clean (v. 15)?

Their rulers wail," declares the LORD, "and continually all the day my name is despised.<sup>6</sup>Therefore my people shall know my name. Therefore in that day they shall know that it is I who speak; here I am."<sup>7</sup>How beautiful upon the mountains are the feet of him who brings good news, who publishes peace, who brings good news of happiness, who publishes salvation, who says to Zion, "Your God reigns."<sup>8</sup>The voice of your watchmen—they lift up their voice; together they sing for joy; for eye to eye they see the return of the LORD to Zion.<sup>9</sup>Break forth together into singing, you waste places of Jerusalem, for the LORD has comforted his people; he has redeemed Jerusalem.<sup>10</sup>The LORD has bared his holy arm before the eyes of all the nations, and all the ends of the earth shall see the salvation of our God.<sup>11</sup>Depart, depart, go out from there; touch no unclean thing; go out from the midst of her; purify yourselves, you who bear the vessels of the LORD.<sup>12</sup>For you shall not go out in haste, and you shall not go in flight, for the LORD will go before you, and the God of Israel will be your rear guard.<sup>13</sup>Behold, my servant shall act wisely; he shall be high and lifted up, and shall be exalted.<sup>14</sup>As many were astonished at you— his appearance was so marred, beyond human semblance, and his form beyond that of the children of mankind—<sup>15</sup>so shall he sprinkle many nations. Kings shall shut their mouths because of him, for that which has not been told them they see, and that which they have not heard they understand.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–6 — Wake Up and Get Dressed
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Zion is told to wake and dress for freedom, because God has already redeemed her for the sake of his name. The cry the people raised to God’s arm comes back to them: put on strength and beautiful garments, rise from the dust and untie your own neck (vv. 1–2). She was sold for nothing and will be redeemed without money, as when God brought his people out from Egypt and from Assyria’s oppression (vv. 3–4). God acts because his name is mocked all day long; his people will know his name, and he answers them, “here I am” (vv. 5–6).
verseByVerse.theology: The commands rest on a fact already accomplished: Zion is told to rise because she has been redeemed, not in order to be (vv. 1-3). And the ground of it all is God's own name (v. 5).
verseByVerse.examples: "Redeemed without money" (v. 3) has a deeper echo in the New Testament: you were ransomed not with silver or gold but with the precious blood of Christ (1 Pet. 1:18-19). No price was owed to the captor; the cost of bringing sinners home was borne by God himself.

verseByVerse.quote: Awake, awake, put on your strength, O Zion; put on your beautiful garments, O Jerusalem, the holy city; for there shall no more come into you the uncircumcised and the unclean. Shake yourself from the dust and arise; be seated, O Jerusalem; loose the bonds from your neck, O captive daughter of Zion.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Zion must wake up, dress for celebration and untie her own chains, not to earn her freedom but because God has already set her free.

Awake, awake, put on your strength, O Zion. In 51:9 the people prayed, “Awake, awake, put on strength, O arm of the LORD,” believing the problem was a sleeping God. Here the words come back aimed the other way. God does not argue with the prayer; he repeats it to the people who prayed it. The arm was never asleep; the city was.

Put on your beautiful garments. She is told not to work or to prepare a defence but to dress for a festival, while nothing in her circumstances has yet changed.

Shake yourself from the dust and arise. Sitting in dust was what mourners and prisoners did (see mourning customs); getting up is what a person does who has stopped mourning. And loose the bonds from your neck: she is told to untie herself, which she could not have done a moment earlier and can do now, because verse 3 is about to say the price has been settled.

Redeemed, then commanded. That is the order of every command God gives his people. He does not say free yourself and then I will redeem you. He says: you have been redeemed, now take the rope off. The instruction is not the condition of the rescue; it is the first act of a rescued person. So a Christian who feels bound is usually not being asked to try harder at being free. He is being asked to believe an announcement already made about him, and to stand up in the strength of the Spirit God gives those he has set free (Rom. 8:2).

How do I take the rope off? Start with the announcement, not the effort. Name the rope. It may be a habit you have stopped fighting, an old shame that answers back whenever someone praises you, or a grudge you keep tying tighter. Say it plainly to God. Hear what is already true. Christ has paid the price that verse 3 says is settled, so speak Paul’s words over it: consider yourselves dead to sin and alive to God in Christ Jesus (Rom. 6:11). Stand up and get dressed. Zion is told to put on her beautiful garments, and Paul says, put on the Lord Jesus Christ, and make no provision for the flesh (Rom. 13:14): pour the bottle away, block the website, write the letter of apology. Do one free thing today. Pray in the morning as his child, not as a prisoner on probation, and tell a trusted friend, so the knot is not retied in secret. For freedom Christ has set us free; stand firm therefore (Gal. 5:1).

The uncircumcised and the unclean. Those who will no longer enter are invaders who profaned the city, not every foreigner. Isaiah welcomes foreigners who join themselves to the LORD (56:6–7), and the true circumcision is of the heart (Rom. 2:28–29).

verseByVerse.quote: For thus says the LORD: "You were sold for nothing, and you shall be redeemed without money." For thus says the Lord GOD: "My people went down at the first into Egypt to sojourn there, and the Assyrian oppressed them for nothing.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God received no price when his people were taken, so he owes no price to get them back: they will be redeemed freely.

You were sold for nothing. Two halves of one transaction, and both are free. God received nothing when Israel went into exile; chapter 50 was blunter still: for your iniquities you were sold (50:1). And Babylon will get no price when she comes out. No ransom is negotiated, no compensation paid.

Why no price is due. The reason is legal rather than sentimental. If Babylon had bought Israel fairly, a redemption price would be due; because she simply took what was not hers, God can walk in and take it back without a transaction. A captor with no valid claim is owed nothing.

My people went down at the first into Egypt. Then the history, given as a pattern rather than a list: Egypt at the beginning, Assyria in the middle, Babylon now. Three times the same shape, a people taken by someone with no right to them and a God who comes and gets them out. The exiles are not living through something unprecedented but through the third act of a play whose ending they already know.

Redeemed without money. The phrase that keeps recurring is for nothing: taken for nothing, oppressed for nothing, redeemed without money. Everything here is unpaid on one side and unearned on the other, which is a fair description of how anyone comes home to God. The New Testament adds what Isaiah leaves for chapter 53: no money changed hands, but a price was paid, “not with perishable things such as silver or gold, but with the precious blood of Christ” (1 Peter 1:18–19), paid not to the captor but to God’s own justice.

verseByVerse.quote: Now therefore what have I here," declares the LORD, "seeing that my people are taken away for nothing? Their rulers wail," declares the LORD, "and continually all the day my name is despised. Therefore my people shall know my name. Therefore in that day they shall know that it is I who speak; here I am."
verseByVerse.commentary:
God will act because his name is being mocked, and his people will come to know that he is present and speaking: “here I am.”

My name is despised. God’s reason for acting is not the one most readers would predict: not first their suffering, though he has spoken of it at length, but his name. All day long in Babylon people are drawing the obvious conclusion from a defeated people, that their God was too weak to hold his own city, and they are saying it aloud where he can hear.

A solid comfort. That is a strange comfort, and a very solid one. If God rescued only when moved by pity, the rescue would rest on the strength of a feeling. Because his own reputation is staked on it, it rests on something that cannot waver. Israel’s safety is welded to God’s honour, and he will not have his name despised.

Here I am. The passage moves from the nations mocking the name to the people knowing it, and ends on here I am. Those are the words a servant says when a master calls: what Abraham said on the mountain, what Moses said at the bush, what Isaiah said when God asked whom he should send (6:8). Here God says it: the master answering, present and available, to people who had spent seventy years convinced he was not listening.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 7–12 — Beautiful Feet, and an Unhurried Exodus
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The good news of God’s reign reaches Zion, and his people go home in peace under his protection. A herald on the mountains brings news of peace and salvation, “Your God reigns”, and the watchmen sing as they see the LORD return (vv. 7–8). Even Jerusalem’s ruins are told to sing, for God has comforted and redeemed his people, baring his holy arm so that all the ends of the earth will see his salvation (vv. 9–10). Then the call to leave Babylon: touch nothing unclean, carry the LORD’s vessels in purity, and go without haste, for the LORD goes before them and guards the rear (vv. 11–12).
verseByVerse.theology: Verse 7 is the Old Testament's clearest statement of what a gospel announcement is: a single claim about who is on the throne. And verse 10's bared arm sets up the question chapter 53 opens with: to whom has the arm of the LORD been revealed?
verseByVerse.examples: The vessels of verse 11 did come home. When Cyrus let the exiles go, he brought out the temple vessels Nebuchadnezzar had taken, 5,400 of gold and silver, and they were carried back to Jerusalem (Ezra 1:7-11).

verseByVerse.quote: How beautiful upon the mountains are the feet of him who brings good news, who publishes peace, who brings good news of happiness, who publishes salvation, who says to Zion, "Your God reigns." The voice of your watchmen—they lift up their voice; together they sing for joy; for eye to eye they see the return of the LORD to Zion.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The best news a captive city can hear arrives: God has won and reigns, and he is coming back to Zion.

How beautiful upon the mountains are the feet. A city under occupation, a battle fought out of sight, everybody waiting to hear which way it went. The first anyone will know is a runner on the skyline, and long before his words can be heard his feet can be seen. That is why the beauty lands on the feet, the least lovely part of a man who has run for miles over rock. They are beautiful because of what arrives with them.

Your God reigns. Four announcements build, good news, peace, happiness, salvation, and then compress into three words. Not that the situation has improved, but that God is on the throne and the outcome follows.

The herald on the ridge. When Jesus came into Galilee proclaiming the gospel of God, his message was this verse brought near: the time is fulfilled, the kingdom of God is at hand (Mark 1:14–15). He was the herald on the ridge, and also the God whose reign the herald announces.

Why preachers are sent. Paul quotes the verse to answer how anyone comes to faith: how are they to hear without someone preaching? “As it is written, ‘How beautiful are the feet of those who preach the good news!’” (Rom. 10:14–15). The runner on the ridge became Paul’s reason for sending preachers everywhere.

Isn’t it rude to share your faith? Many now feel that religion belongs in private, like a medical history, and that trying to persuade someone is trespass. Behind that is a fair instinct: nobody wants to be pressured, and Christians have sometimes been crass. But notice what the runner carries. Not an opinion about how to live, which we might reasonably keep to ourselves, but news of an event: the battle is over, the city is free, your God reigns. We would think a herald from the battlefield cruel, not polite, if he kept the news to himself while the city lay awake in fear. The same holds for the gospel, if it is true at all: it is a report of what God has done in Christ, and it concerns everyone. That gives no licence for pushiness; the feet are beautiful partly because they belong to one who publishes peace. But the most loving thing a Christian can do for a neighbour may be the very thing our culture finds least polite: to tell them.

Eye to eye they see the return of the LORD to Zion. The watchmen were posted to see trouble coming. What they see is God coming back, eye to eye, at close range, with nothing between.

verseByVerse.quote: Break forth together into singing, you waste places of Jerusalem, for the LORD has comforted his people; he has redeemed Jerusalem. The LORD has bared his holy arm before the eyes of all the nations, and all the ends of the earth shall see the salvation of our God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Even the ruins are told to sing, because God has already redeemed his people and is showing his saving power before the whole world.

You waste places of Jerusalem. The instruction is given to rubble: not to the returning exiles or the priests, but to the burnt districts nobody had rebuilt, the parts of the city that were only evidence of what had happened. They are told to sing.

He has redeemed Jerusalem. The tenses are the point. He has comforted; he has redeemed. Isaiah writes it as finished while the ruins are still ruins, which is what makes the command to sing possible. The rubble is not singing in hope of something; it is singing about something done.

The LORD has bared his holy arm. Baring the arm is what a man does before hard work or a fight: sleeve pushed back, muscle out where everyone can see it. God does it publicly, before every nation, and the whole earth will watch the result.

Where the bared arm leads. Hold that image for one chapter. The next thing said about the arm of the LORD is a question, “to whom has the arm of the LORD been revealed?” (53:1), and the answer is almost nobody. God bares his arm before the world in 52:10, and in 53:2 what the world sees is a man with no form or majesty that anyone should look at him. The arm was bared exactly as promised. It simply did not look like an arm.

verseByVerse.quote: Depart, depart, go out from there; touch no unclean thing; go out from the midst of her; purify yourselves, you who bear the vessels of the LORD. For you shall not go out in haste, and you shall not go in flight, for the LORD will go before you, and the God of Israel will be your rear guard.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God’s people are to leave Babylon clean, as priests carrying his holy things, and without panic, because God himself guards them front and rear.

Depart, depart, go out from there. The order to leave is doubled like the order to wake, and the instructions are priestly rather than practical: no packing list, no route, no rations. Touch nothing unclean. Purify yourselves. Carry the vessels properly.

You who bear the vessels of the LORD. The temple articles that Nebuchadnezzar had carried off are going home (Ezra 1:7–11), and those carrying them are treated as though they were Levites. A column of freed slaves becomes a religious procession. Paul quotes the verse to the church at Corinth (2 Cor. 6:17) to say the same to people rescued by Christ: those brought out do not carry the idols of the old place with them, and the call to be clean comes after the redemption, not as its price.

You shall not go out in haste. Every reader would think of the first exodus. That night the Passover was eaten standing, belts fastened, sandals on and staff in hand, in haste (Exod. 12:11), and then the people were pursued to the edge of the sea by chariots. It was an escape. This is not. Nobody is chasing them, so nobody needs to run.

The God of Israel will be your rear guard. The reason is given at both ends of the column: God in front, God behind, so that no danger can reach them from either direction. A rescue that has to be hurried could still fail. This one is secured front and rear before the first foot moves, which is why the people can walk out of Babylon at the pace of the slowest among them.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 13–15 — Behold My Servant — the Song Begins
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The fourth Servant Song begins with its ending: the servant who will be horribly disfigured will be lifted high and will cleanse the nations. God announces first that the servant will act wisely and be high and lifted up, in words used of God’s own throne (v. 13). Then he explains why so many were appalled: the servant’s appearance was marred beyond human likeness (v. 14). Yet he will sprinkle many nations, and kings will fall silent before him, seeing and understanding what they had never been told (v. 15).
verseByVerse.theology: God gives away the ending first, so that the darkest passage in the Old Testament is read inside a verdict already delivered (52:13; 53:12), and the servant is priest as well as victim before the song has properly begun (v. 15).
verseByVerse.examples: The astonishment of verse 14 and the shut mouths of verse 15 are the same reaction at two stages: first at what was done to him, then at who he turned out to be.

verseByVerse.quote: Behold, my servant shall act wisely; he shall be high and lifted up, and shall be exalted.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God begins the song of his suffering servant with its ending: the servant will succeed and be exalted to the height that belongs to God himself.

Behold, my servant shall act wisely. The greatest of the Servant Songs gives away the ending first. Before a syllable about the marred face, the sorrows, the piercing and the grave, the servant comes out on top. Shall act wisely can also be rendered shall prosper: he will do it well and it will work. Then three verbs piled up, each meaning to be raised: high, lifted up, exalted.

How the ending frames it. The horror of chapter 53 is enclosed at both ends by a verdict, high and lifted up here, a portion with the many at 53:12, so the reader enters the darkest passage in the Old Testament already knowing how it ends.

He shall be high and lifted up. The words have been heard before. In chapter 6 Isaiah saw the Lord “sitting upon a throne, high and lifted up” (6:1), with the seraphim covering their faces and the building shaking, and the phrase is used again of God in 57:15. Isaiah takes the vocabulary of God enthroned and lays it on a servant whose appearance, one verse later, will be beyond human semblance. He does not explain it. He lets the reader stand between the two sentences and work out what he is being told. John did: he quotes chapter 53 and chapter 6 side by side and says that Isaiah “saw his glory and spoke of him” (John 12:38–41).

Who is the servant? Older Jewish interpretation, including the Aramaic paraphrase called the Targum, applied 52:13 to the Messiah, though it turned the suffering onto others. The standard Jewish reading since the Middle Ages is Israel, suffering in exile for the nations; God does call Israel my servant (41:8; 49:3), and some say the prophet himself. But this servant is sinless (53:9), suffers willingly and silently (53:7), and dies for the sins of “my people” (53:8), which Israel, suffering for its own sins (40:2), cannot do for itself. The New Testament identifies him as Jesus (Acts 8:32–35; 1 Pet. 2:22–25), and Jesus applied the song to himself (Luke 22:37). This commentary reads the servant as an individual, Christ, suffering for the people and distinct from them (see the note on Isaiah 53).
verseByVerse.note: The fourth Servant Song (52:13–53:12): the suffering, atoning, exalted Servant.

verseByVerse.quote: As many were astonished at you— his appearance was so marred, beyond human semblance, and his form beyond that of the children of mankind— so shall he sprinkle many nations. Kings shall shut their mouths because of him, for that which has not been told them they see, and that which they have not heard they understand.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The servant will be disfigured beyond recognition, and through that suffering he will cleanse many nations, leaving kings speechless.

His appearance was so marred. Marred is disfigurement, the ruin of a thing’s shape; beyond human semblance means past the point where the eye registers a person. Not badly beaten, but no longer recognisably one of us. And the reaction is astonishment, being appalled into stillness, the way traffic stops at an accident.

So shall he sprinkle many nations. The verb is the priestly one. Sprinkling is what a priest did with blood, on the altar, on the mercy seat (the cover of the ark) and on the people, to make the unclean fit to approach God (Lev. 4; 16). So the disfigured man of verse 14 is the priest, not only the victim: his suffering is not only something done to him; by it he makes others clean. Peter writes to believers scattered among the nations, chosen “for sprinkling with his blood” (1 Peter 1:2).

Kings shall shut their mouths because of him. In verse 14 people stare in horror; in verse 15 kings shut their mouths, men who have run out of anything to say. The same figure produces both reactions, at different points in the story.

Paul’s working rule. Paul made the last line his working rule, preaching where Christ had not been named: “Those who have never been told of him will see, and those who have never heard will understand” (Rom. 15:20–21). The song was, from its first appearance, aimed at people with no reason to expect it.

Uncertain wording. The verb translated sprinkle is disputed. Elsewhere it means sprinkling blood, oil or water, but here no liquid is named and the nations are its direct object, so some translators render it startle (the ESV gives this in its note), and the ancient Greek translation reads many nations will marvel at him, which matches the astonishment of verse 14. This commentary keeps sprinkle, the word as it stands in the sacrificial system. Also in verse 14 the Hebrew switches abruptly from you to his; the sense is clear either way: people were appalled at the servant.

52.theology:
The command rests on the fact. Zion is told to loose her own bonds (v. 2) after she is told you shall be redeemed (v. 3). That is the structure of every command God gives his people, and her redemption is free for a legal reason, not a sentimental one: the captor paid nothing for her, so he is owed nothing for her.

God’s name as the ground of rescue. The motive for the exodus from Babylon is God’s own honour, publicly despised while his people sit in captivity (v. 5). That is a more solid foundation than divine sympathy, because a reputation staked cannot waver as a feeling might.

The song opens with the verdict. Before any suffering is mentioned, the servant is high and lifted up, in the vocabulary used of God on the throne at 6:1, and the disfigured man sprinkles many nations, on the reading the ESV text adopts (its note gives "startle"). The atrocity of chapter 53 is framed at both ends by an outcome already announced.

53.subtitle: The Suffering Servant
53.intro:
Where we are. Chapter 52 ended with a herald running over the mountains to tell Zion that her God reigns, and with the opening of the fourth Servant Song (52:13–15), which gives away the ending first: the servant “shall be high and lifted up” (52:13), the words used of the Lord on his throne (6:1). Chapter 53 is the body of that song: the speakers look back in astonishment on what was done to the servant, and why.

The message. The man everyone wrote off as cursed by God was indeed bearing God’s judgment, but for our sins, not his own. The LORD laid our iniquity on his innocent servant and crushed him as a guilt offering, and then raised him to see his offspring and to make many to be accounted righteous. The suffering was not a tragedy God salvaged; it was the plan by which he saves.

Why it was said. The exiles were waiting for release from Babylon (see the introduction), but chapters 40 to 52 have made plain that their deeper trouble was sin, which no Cyrus could remove (43:24–25; 50:1). This song answers the question the book has carried since 1:18: how a holy God can make scarlet sins as white as snow.

How the chapter makes its case. First the report almost nobody believed, about a man despised and rejected (vv. 1–3). Then the confession at the centre: he bore our griefs, was pierced for our transgressions, and the LORD laid on him the iniquity of us all (vv. 4–6). Then his silent trial, unjust death and strange burial, though he was innocent (vv. 7–9). Last, God’s purpose: the crushing was the LORD’s will, a guilt offering, and the dead servant will see offspring, justify many and intercede for transgressors (vv. 10–12).

Where it leads. This is direct promise, and the New Testament applies it to one person. Jesus quotes verse 12 of himself (Luke 22:37); Matthew sees verse 4 in his healings (Matt. 8:17); John explains unbelief by verse 1 (John 12:38); Philip starts from verses 7–8 and tells the good news about Jesus (Acts 8:32–35); and Peter builds his picture of the cross from verses 5, 6 and 9 (1 Pet. 2:22–25). The silent trial, the death among criminals and the rich man’s tomb fit one man. And the past tense of the song is where every believer stands, looking back at the cross.

For us. Anyone can say the first half of verse 6 of himself; the second half has to be believed: the LORD has laid your iniquity on him. Come with nothing in your hands. And when you suffer unjustly, his silence is your pattern and his intercession your security (1 Pet. 2:21–23; v. 12).

keyVerse.quote: “But he was pierced for our transgressions; he was crushed for our iniquities; upon him was the chastisement that brought us peace, and with his wounds we are healed.”
keyVerse.note: This is one of the clearest statements in the Bible of penal substitution, Christ bearing in our place the penalty our sins deserved. The prepositions carry the weight: for our transgressions, for our iniquities. The chastisement, God’s judicial punishment, fell on him so that peace could come to us. This is not one theory of the atonement among others; it is the grammar Isaiah uses to describe what God planned.

53.theology:
Penal substitution. This is the Old Testament’s fullest account of what later theology calls penal substitution: Christ bearing the penalty of our sins in our place. What settles it as substitution rather than mere sympathy is the wording of verse 5: four clauses, each setting what fell on him against what comes to us, and nothing shared.

The Father is the agent, not the spectator. Verse 6 says the LORD laid the iniquity on him and verse 10 says it was the LORD’s will to crush him. This rules out the picture of a kind Son winning round a reluctant Father. Mercy is not wrung out of an unwilling God; his justice, carried out on the servant, is the means his mercy uses.

Justification, and resurrection. Verse 11 holds both halves of justification in one line: the verdict, and its ground, which lies outside the sinner in the servant who bears his sin (see on v. 11), and the promises made to a man already cut off out of the land of the living require a resurrection that Isaiah states without explaining. On the extent of the “many,” godly readers differ; beyond dispute is that his death achieves its purpose. The servant does not merely make righteousness available. He makes many righteous.
53.reflection:
Verse 3 says “we esteemed him not,” and verse 4 that we thought him “stricken, smitten by God.” Why do people still find it hard to see God’s power in a crucified man, and what made the difference for you?

Verse 5 sets what fell on him against what comes to us, four times over. Which of those four clauses do you most need to hear this week, and why?

“All we like sheep have gone astray” is easy to agree with; “the LORD has laid on him the iniquity of us all” has to be believed (v. 6). What keeps Christians from believing the second half about their own sin, and how would you help a friend who struggles with it?

Peter makes the silent servant the pattern for believers who suffer unjustly (1 Pet. 2:21–23), and verse 12 says he still “makes intercession for the transgressors.” How should those two truths shape the way you respond when you are wronged?

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The world looked at God’s servant and saw nothing worth having, because God’s power came in a form nobody expected. The confessing community, looking back on what they once thought, laments how few believed the report (v. 1). Then they give the reason: he grew up like a shoot out of dry ground, with nothing in his looks or standing to earn a second glance (v. 2). So the verdict was reached: despised, rejected, a man of sorrows from whom people turned their faces, and reckoned worth nothing (v. 3). The stanza exposes our habit of judging by appearances and prepares for the great correction that follows.
verseByVerse.theology: The stumbling-block here is the incarnation itself, before ever the cross. The Word became flesh in a form that gave the eye nothing to admire, so that faith could never rest on appearance. God showed himself in this servant and, in the same act, hid himself.
verseByVerse.examples: John quotes verse 1 at the close of Jesus' public ministry (John 12:38) to explain why the signs did not produce faith. The problem was never a shortage of evidence.

verseByVerse.quote: Who has believed what he has heard from us? And to whom has the arm of the LORD been revealed? For he grew up before him like a young plant, and like a root out of dry ground; he had no form or majesty that we should look at him, and no beauty that we should desire him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Almost nobody believed the news about the servant, because God’s mighty arm came as an unremarkable man with nothing to draw the eye.

Who has believed what he has heard from us? The song opens not with the servant but with a complaint about how badly the news has gone down. The herald of 52:7 has run with a report, and almost nobody has believed it.

To whom has the arm of the LORD been revealed?
