The arm of the LORD is God’s power in action: the arm that cut Rahab in pieces (here not the woman of Jericho but the sea monster that stood for Egypt) and dried up the sea (51:9–10), bared in the sight of all the nations (52:10). Every reader of Isaiah expected it to look like the Red Sea standing up in two walls. Here it is revealed, and it looks like a man nobody wanted to look at. People did not believe because they could not see almighty power in that form.

He grew up before him like a young plant. Before him: before God, who was watching when nobody else was. A shoot out of dry ground has no reason to be there: Nazareth, a carpenter’s shop, thirty years of nothing a historian would record. Isaiah has used the picture before, of a shoot from the stump of Jesse (11:1): new life from a royal line that looked dead.

He had no form or majesty that we should look at him. Verse 2 does not say he was ugly. It says there was nothing about him that would make you want him, and the four Gospels never once describe what he looked like. What usually draws us to a person, looks, possessions, admirers, is exactly what led a generation to walk past God in the flesh.

Where Christians differ. Who is the servant? Jewish interpreters have long read him as Israel, which Isaiah itself calls my servant (41:8; 49:3) and pictures suffering among the nations; the reading deserves a respectful hearing. Others suggest the prophet himself, or a faithful remnant.

This commentary’s view. With the New Testament, this commentary reads the servant as an individual, Christ, distinct from the people he suffers for: he is stricken for the transgression of my people (v. 8); he is without violence or deceit (v. 9), while Isaiah’s Israel is a sinful nation (1:4); and he has a mission to Israel itself (49:5–6). Asked whom the prophet meant, Philip answered with Jesus (see on vv. 7–8).

verseByVerse.quote: He was despised and rejected by men, a man of sorrows and acquainted with grief; and as one from whom men hide their faces he was despised, and we esteemed him not.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The servant was a man marked by sorrow, and the world, the speakers included, looked away from him and reckoned him worth nothing.

A man of sorrows and acquainted with grief. The ESV notes give the plainer sense of the nouns: sorrows can be rendered pains, grief can be rendered sickness, and acquainted with can be rendered knowing. He knew grief the way a man knows his trade. It was not an episode in his life; it was his address.

As one from whom men hide their faces. This is not hostility but a reflex, the look away from someone weeping on a pavement. We turn from concentrated pain because we cannot hold it, and that is why it indicts us. And esteemed is a reckoning word, the language of the account book: we reckoned up his worth and put it at nothing.

He was despised and rejected by men. John says it in one line: “his own people did not receive him” (John 1:11). The one through whom the world was made stood in it and was passed over. Every eye that turned away was an eye he had designed. He went on holding together the atoms of the men who despised him, and did not stop.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: This is the centre of the poem, and of the Old Testament’s teaching on the cross: the servant suffered God’s punishment, but for our sins. Verse 4 turns the confession round: the griefs were ours, though we read his suffering as God’s verdict on him. Verse 5 states the exchange in four clauses, his wounds set against our transgressions and iniquities, our peace and our healing. Verse 6 gives the reason and names the one who acted: we all went our own way, and the LORD himself laid our iniquity on him. Nothing here is accident or mere sympathy; it is substitution, planned by God.
verseByVerse.theology: The guilt is real, the punishment is real, and it is borne by another at God's own initiative: in verse 6 it is the LORD who lays the iniquity on him.
verseByVerse.examples: Verse 6 is the one sentence in Scripture that almost anyone can say of himself without argument. Its second half is the one that has to be believed.

verseByVerse.quote: Surely he has borne our griefs and carried our sorrows; yet we esteemed him stricken, smitten by God, and afflicted. But he was pierced for our transgressions; he was crushed for our iniquities; upon him was the chastisement that brought us peace, and with his wounds we are healed.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The servant was indeed under God’s judgment, but for our sins, borne in our place so that we have peace and healing.

Surely he has borne our griefs. Surely is a word of correction: no, actually. Griefs and sorrows are the same two Hebrew words that made him a man of sorrows in verse 3: the grief he was known by was never his own; he was carrying ours. Matthew quotes the line over an evening of healings (Matt. 8:16–17): the bearing began long before Calvary, in every case he touched. And griefs are griefs: he carries the sorrow of the bereaved as well as the sickness of the ill, so those who mourn have a Saviour who has borne what they bear.

Yet we esteemed him stricken, smitten by God. The crowd at the cross was not wrong to think that God was judging. They were wrong about who was being judged.

He was pierced for our transgressions; he was crushed for our iniquities. The gospel is in the grammar of verse 5: four clauses, and in each what falls on him is set against what belongs to us, our transgressions and iniquities, our peace and our healing. The suffering is all his and the benefit all ours. Pierced and crushed are violent, final words (the King James Version’s wounded and bruised render the same Hebrew), and he did not lift a hand to stop them: the crushing was not a defeat but the price he came to pay.

Upon him was the chastisement that brought us peace. Chastisement is a father’s discipline, here carried to its full penalty. It fell on him and the peace came to us: not a calm feeling but the end of a war (Rom. 5:1). And wounds is the raised welt a blow leaves on skin. With those we are healed.

Does “with his wounds we are healed” mean the atonement guarantees physical healing now? Matthew sees it begun in Jesus’ healings, and the resurrection body will be whole. But Peter applies the verse to sin: that we might die to sin and live to righteousness. By his wounds you have been healed (1 Pet. 2:24). Believers are not promised healing on demand in this life; Paul left Trophimus ill (2 Tim. 4:20). So pray for healing, and use doctors and medicine gladly; neither is a failure of faith. The healing bought at the cross is certain, and the body’s share in it comes at the resurrection.

verseByVerse.quote: All we like sheep have gone astray; we have turned—every one—to his own way; and the LORD has laid on him the iniquity of us all.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Every one of us has wandered off our own way, and the LORD himself has laid the guilt of us all on his servant.

All we like sheep have gone astray. The verse begins with all and ends with all, and between them each individual has his own direction: the condition is universal and the wandering personal. The picture is sheep, not wolves, the animal that drifts off one mouthful at a time. That is how most people are lost: not by deciding against God on a particular day, but by grazing steadily in a direction nobody chose.

The LORD has laid on him the iniquity of us all. Then the one who acts: the LORD has laid it on him, made it fall upon him. God did not merely permit this. And the chapter closes by reversing the verb: the one on whom our sin was laid makes intercession, laying our case before God (v. 12).

Where faith happens. Most people grant the first half of the verse easily. The second half asks you to believe that the iniquity you know to be yours is no longer where you left it. If you find it hard to say, it is still true for everyone who trusts him: the LORD has laid it on him, and it is not coming back to you. Peter puts the two halves together: “you were straying like sheep, but have now returned to the Shepherd and Overseer of your souls” (1 Pet. 2:25). The one on whom the iniquity was laid is the Shepherd it was laid for.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 7–9 — Silent, Cut Off, and Buried
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The third stanza follows the servant through trial, death and burial, and shows a substitute who is both willing and innocent. He is silent like a lamb led to the slaughter, though he could have spoken (v. 7). An unjust process takes him away and cuts him off from the land of the living with no descendants, struck down for the transgression of God’s people (v. 8). He is given a grave with the wicked and with a rich man, though he had done no violence and spoken no deceit (v. 9). His silence shows that he went willingly; his innocence shows that he was fit to stand in our place.
verseByVerse.theology: The sinlessness of verse 9 is what qualifies the servant to be a substitute, and the silence of verse 7 shows that the substitute was willing.
verseByVerse.examples: Peter holds up the servant's silence as the pattern for believers who suffer unjustly: when he was reviled, he did not revile in return, but entrusted himself to the one who judges justly (1 Pet. 2:23).

verseByVerse.quote: He was oppressed, and he was afflicted, yet he opened not his mouth; like a lamb that is led to the slaughter, and like a sheep that before its shearers is silent, so he opened not his mouth. By oppression and judgment he was taken away; and as for his generation, who considered that he was cut off out of the land of the living, stricken for the transgression of my people?
verseByVerse.commentary:
The servant went silently and willingly to an unjust death, and was cut off with no future, struck down for the transgression of God’s people.

He opened not his mouth. Said twice in one verse, this is not a man too broken to speak but a man declining to. He is silent before the high priest until put on oath (Matt. 26:62–63); he gives Pilate no answer, “not even to a single charge, so that the governor was greatly amazed” (Matt. 27:14); and before Herod, who questioned him at length hoping for a miracle, he says nothing at all (Luke 23:9). Any one of those silences could have been broken. Like the servant who gave his back to those who strike (50:6–7), he is not passive but resolved, holding still.

Like a lamb that is led to the slaughter. an Ethiopian official was reading this sentence aloud on the Gaza road when Philip drew alongside, and his question is the right one: “About whom, I ask you, does the prophet say this, about himself or about someone else?” Philip began with that passage and told him the good news about Jesus (Acts 8:32–35).

By oppression and judgment he was taken away. The courts and the rulers, using all the forms of law, remove him. To be cut off with no descendant was the bleakest thing that could be said of a man in Israel, a name ending in the middle of a sentence. Keep it in view: Isaiah is about to promise this childless dead man a family (v. 10).

Stricken for the transgression of my people. The voice changes. The confessing crowd has been saying our since verse 4; now a single voice speaks, and calls them my people: God’s own claim on those for whom the servant was struck.

Uncertain wording. Verse 8 is difficult Hebrew. The word rendered generation can mean a man’s contemporaries, his descendants, or his fate, so the line may ask who among his contemporaries cared, or (as the King James Version has it) who shall declare his generation?, who will speak of descendants he does not have. The main clauses are not in doubt: an unjust process, a life cut off, a death for the people’s transgression.
verseByVerse.note: Acts 8:32-33 quotes vv. 7-8 from the Greek Old Testament, which differs in places from the Hebrew.

verseByVerse.quote: And they made his grave with the wicked and with a rich man in his death, although he had done no violence, and there was no deceit in his mouth.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The innocent servant was given a criminal’s grave and yet laid in a rich man’s tomb, and his sinlessness is what fitted him to die for others.

They made his grave with the wicked and with a rich man in his death. Two burials in one line that do not belong together: executed criminals were buried without honour among the condemned, and a rich man’s tomb is the opposite. The contradiction sat unexplained for centuries until a wealthy man, Joseph of Arimathea, asked Pilate for the body and laid it in his own new tomb (Matt. 27:57–60). The burial seals the death: a body shut behind a stone is a body everyone agrees is dead. Yet it is also the first movement upward in the poem: at the very bottom, something is done for him rather than to him.

Although he had done no violence, and there was no deceit in his mouth. Isaiah tests him in the two places where every human life fails, the hands and the tongue, and finds no fault in either. Peter quotes the clause of Jesus (1 Pet. 2:22). It does more than praise him. A substitute with sin of his own has a debt of his own, and a debtor cannot pay another man’s debt. The innocence of verse 9 is what makes the exchange of verse 5 lawful rather than merely moving.

Uncertain wording. The Hebrew reads literally in his deaths, a plural that may stress the violence of the death, and a rich man stands where the parallel might lead us to expect another word for the wicked, so some take the rich as oppressors or propose a different word. The ESV keeps the Hebrew as it stands, and the Gospels show both halves coming true.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 10–12 — He Shall See and Be Satisfied
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The final stanza lifts the curtain on God’s purpose and on what lies beyond the grave. The crushing was the LORD’s will, the servant’s life a guilt offering, and the dead man is promised offspring, long life and success (v. 10). He sees the fruit of his anguish and is satisfied, and by bearing their iniquities he makes many to be accounted righteous (v. 11). So God gives him a victor’s portion, because he poured out his soul to death, was numbered with the transgressors, bore the sin of many, and still intercedes for them (v. 12). The song that began with an unbelieved report ends with a risen, praying Saviour.
verseByVerse.theology: Justification is stated here in its two halves (see on v. 11). And the future tenses in a poem about a grave are one of the Old Testament's clearest pointers to resurrection: a soul poured out to death is promised offspring, length of days and satisfaction.
verseByVerse.examples: The family promised to a dead man in verse 10 is still being born. Every person who comes to faith in Christ is one of the offspring the servant was told he would see.

verseByVerse.quote: Yet it was the will of the LORD to crush him; he has put him to grief; when his soul makes an offering for guilt, he shall see his offspring; he shall prolong his days; the will of the LORD shall prosper in his hand. Out of the anguish of his soul he shall see and be satisfied; by his knowledge shall the righteous one, my servant, make many to be accounted righteous, and he shall bear their iniquities.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The servant’s suffering was God’s saving purpose: offered as a guilt offering, he will live again to see his offspring, and by bearing their sins make many righteous.

Yet it was the will of the LORD to crush him. One of the hardest sentences in the Old Testament, and softening it helps nobody. The verb behind the will of means to delight in. The Father was not a bystander to the cross. Nor did he watch his Son’s agony with enjoyment: this is the settled pleasure of a purpose achieved, and the same verse ends the will of the LORD shall prosper in his hand, and what prospers is the rescue of the people of verse 6. What God willed was not the pain for its own sake but what the pain was buying. Peter preached the same in Jerusalem: Jesus was “delivered up according to the definite plan and foreknowledge of God” (Acts 2:23).

When his soul makes an offering for guilt. The word is asham, the guilt offering of Leviticus 5:14–6:7, the one sacrifice with a repayment attached: the worshipper brought the ram and restitution plus a fifth. The servant does not buy a love God did not have; he turns away God’s just wrath by bearing the penalty, and pays back what our sin had taken.

He shall see his offspring; he shall prolong his days. Impossible clauses in the middle of a funeral: two verses ago this man was cut off with no future. Only resurrection makes both true of one person, and Isaiah states it centuries early without explaining it.

Out of the anguish of his soul he shall see and be satisfied. He looks at what the anguish bought and is satisfied, which is what Hebrews means by “who for the joy that was set before him endured the cross” (Heb. 12:2). If you have ever wondered whether you personally are worth that price, the answer is not yours to calculate. He has done the sum, and he is satisfied.

Make many to be accounted righteous. Both halves of justification stand in one line. Accounted righteous is courtroom language, to declare in the right, not to make gradually better, and the ground of the verdict is the clause beside it: he shall bear their iniquities. Our sin was reckoned to him in verse 6; his standing is reckoned to us here (Rom. 5:19).

Isn’t this a father punishing his innocent son? Some have recoiled from this verse as cosmic cruelty: an angry Father venting wrath on a victim who did nothing wrong. If that were the picture, the recoil would be right. But it misses who is on the cross. The servant is not a third party dragged in to absorb someone else’s anger: in Christ God was reconciling the world to himself (2 Cor. 5:19). The Son goes willingly, giving his back to those who strike (50:6), and he is himself the arm of the LORD (53:1). John Stott, in The Cross of Christ (1986), called it the self-substitution of God: the Judge, in the person of his Son, bearing the sentence he had passed. Abuse is the strong making the weak pay; at the cross the one with every right to make us pay paid instead. The justice is real, because sin is real; and the love is greater, because the one who bore the penalty was God himself.

Where Christians differ. Who are the “many” he makes righteous? Many Christians hold that Christ died equally for all people, pointing to All we like sheep have gone astray (v. 6) and to 1 John 2:2.

This commentary’s view. The servant here does not merely make righteousness possible: he shall make many to be accounted righteous and shall bear their iniquities. So this commentary reads his death as aimed at the many it actually saves, while its offer goes to all without reservation. Those who read it otherwise trust the same Saviour, and are honoured here. If you come to him, you are among the many.

Uncertain wording. When his soul makes an offering for guilt can also be translated when you make his soul an offering, spoken to God; either way his own life is the offering. And by his knowledge may mean by what the servant knows and makes known, or by people coming to know him; both fit the chapter.
verseByVerse.note: A Dead Sea Scroll reads “he shall see light” (ESV note).

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore I will divide him a portion with the many, and he shall divide the spoil with the strong, because he poured out his soul to death and was numbered with the transgressors; yet he bore the sin of many, and makes intercession for the transgressors.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Because he died for sinners, bore their sin and still prays for them, God gives the servant a conqueror’s reward.

Therefore I will divide him a portion with the many. The imagery turns military at the last moment: the commander’s share of the spoil. And it begins with therefore. The exaltation is not compensation to console him; it is the reward of an achievement, grounded in the four clauses that follow. Paul traces the same therefore from the cross to the throne (Phil. 2:8–9).

Numbered with the transgressors. Jesus quoted these words of himself on the last night of his life: “For I tell you that this Scripture must be fulfilled in me” (Luke 22:37). Within hours he was crucified between two criminals, and one of them asked to be remembered and was promised paradise.

And makes intercession for the transgressors. The last verb in the poem is present: he makes intercession. Not made. The Hebrew verb is the one in verse 6, with the direction reversed: what was laid on him was our guilt; what he lays before God is our case. He prayed for the men who crucified him while they did it (Luke 23:34), and he goes on: “he always lives to make intercession for them” (Heb. 7:25; Rom. 8:34).

Where the poem closes. The poem that opened with a report nobody believed closes with the man in the report praying for the people who did not believe it. He does not beg; he asks on the ground of a finished work. The wounds are the argument, the verdict is already in, and the intercession has not paused. He was despised and we esteemed him not, and he is at this moment naming us before the throne of God.

Uncertain wording. The word translated the many can also mean the great, and the strong can mean the numerous, so the lines may give him a place among the great, or make the many themselves his portion. Either way it is a victor’s reward.

6.subtitle: Holy, Holy, Holy: Isaiah's Vision and Call
6.intro:
Where we are. After five chapters of charges and woes, Isaiah tells how he became a prophet, in the year King Uzziah died, about 740 BC. The call comes here rather than in chapter 1 so that, having heard what God requires, we now see who God is, and how a man of unclean lips came to speak for him.

The message. The LORD is holy beyond all comparison, and the whole earth is full of his glory. No sinner can stand before him, yet he himself provides cleansing from his altar and then sends the cleansed to speak for him. His word will harden a people who have refused it, until judgment empties the land; but a holy seed survives in the stump of the felled tree.

Why it was said. A long and prosperous reign was ending, Assyria was rising, and Judah had already shown in chapters 1–5 that it would not listen (see the introduction). Isaiah needed to know before he began that the King of Judah had not died with Uzziah, and that his preaching would not turn the nation.

How the chapter makes its case. First the throne (vv. 1–4): the Lord high and lifted up, the seraphim crying “Holy, holy, holy”, the temple shaking and filling with smoke. Then the man (vv. 5–7): Isaiah pronounces woe on himself, and a burning coal from the altar takes his guilt away. Then the mission (vv. 8–13): he overhears God asking whom he shall send and volunteers, and is sent with a word that will harden, until the cities are empty and even a remaining tenth is burned, leaving only a stump that is holy seed.

Where it leads. Here the New Testament speaks directly. John says that Isaiah “saw his glory and spoke of him” (John 12:41): the Lord on the throne was the Son. The cleansing comes by pattern: guilt is taken away by fire from an altar of sacrifice, as ours is by Christ’s death. The hardening of verses 9–10 is applied by Jesus himself to those who heard his parables and would not understand (Mark 4:11–12). And the holy stump is a promise: from it grows the shoot of Jesse (11:1), the Messiah.

For us. This chapter cures small views of God and of sin together. Only those who have seen his holiness know their need, and only those who have been cleansed by his sacrifice are free to say, “Here I am! Send me”, and to keep going when the response is hard.

keyVerse.quote: “Holy, holy, holy is the LORD of hosts; the whole earth is full of his glory.”
keyVerse.note: The threefold “holy” is the heart of Isaiah’s vision and, in a sense, of the whole book. Everything Isaiah says flows from it: judgment is what holiness does when people keep refusing to repent, and comfort is what holiness does for the broken and contrite (57:15). The second line sends the vision outward: if the whole earth is full of his glory, the whole earth needs to hear of him, and that is where the call of verse 8 leads.

6.theology:
Holiness. This is the Old Testament’s defining text on holiness, and it presents it as more than moral purity. Of every attribute of God, holiness alone is tripled.

Atonement and access. Verses 5-7 run in the gospel’s own order and it is never reversed: the sight of holiness produces the knowledge of guilt, and the confession of guilt is met by an atonement that comes from the altar, where something has died. Isaiah contributes nothing and is asked for nothing.

Judicial hardening, and its limit. In verses 9-10 God confirms in blindness those who have already refused to see. Two things stand together: God hardens (Isaiah 6:10) and they harden themselves (Matt. 13:15). Neither cancels the other. And verse 13 sets the limit: the hardening is real and it is not the last word, because the stump left in the ash is holy seed.
6.reflection:
Isaiah saw the Lord on his throne “in the year that King Uzziah died” (v. 1), when an earthly security had just been taken away. When has a loss or change shown you more of who God is? What earthly “throne” are you most tempted to lean on?

Isaiah’s response to God’s holiness was “Woe is me!” (v. 5). Why do people who have truly seen God become more aware of their sin, not less? What does that suggest about Christians who feel little need of forgiveness?

The cleansing came from the altar, before Isaiah offered to serve (vv. 6–8). How does the order of being cleansed first and sent second change the way we think about serving God? Where are you hanging back because you have not really believed you are forgiven?

Isaiah was sent to people who would not listen, and asked, “How long, O Lord?” (v. 11). How does this chapter help you when sharing the gospel seems to change nothing? What does the holy stump of verse 13 add?
6.text: <sup>1</sup>In the year that King Uzziah died I saw the Lord sitting upon a throne, high and lifted up; and the train of his robe filled the temple.<sup>2</sup>Above him stood the seraphim. Each had six wings: with two he covered his face, and with two he covered his feet, and with two he flew.<sup>3</sup>And one called to another and said: "Holy, holy, holy is the LORD of hosts; the whole earth is full of his glory!"<sup>4</sup>And the foundations of the thresholds shook at the voice of him who called, and the house was filled with smoke.<sup>5</sup>And I said: "Woe is me! For I am lost; for I am a man of unclean lips, and I dwell in the midst of a people of unclean lips; for my eyes have seen the King, the LORD of hosts!"<sup>6</sup>Then one of the seraphim flew to me, having in his hand a burning coal that he had taken with tongs from the altar.<sup>7</sup>And he touched my mouth and said: "Behold, this has touched your lips; your guilt is taken away, and your sin atoned for."<sup>8</sup>And I heard the voice of the Lord saying, "Whom shall I send, and who will go for us?" Then I said, "Here I am! Send me."<sup>9</sup>And he said, "Go, and say to this people: "'Keep on hearing, but do not understand; keep on seeing, but do not perceive.'<sup>10</sup>Make the heart of this people dull, and their ears heavy, and blind their eyes; lest they see with their eyes, and hear with their ears, and understand with their hearts, and turn and be healed."<sup>11</sup>Then I said, "How long, O Lord?" And he said: "Until cities lie waste without inhabitant, and houses without people, and the land is a desolate waste,<sup>12</sup>and the LORD removes people far away, and the forsaken places are many in the midst of the land.<sup>13</sup>And though a tenth remain in it, it will be burned again, like a terebinth or an oak, whose stump remains when it is felled." The holy seed is its stump.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–4 — The Throne That Was Never Vacant
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: In the year an earthly throne fell empty, Isaiah is shown the throne that never does. King Uzziah’s long reign is over, and Isaiah sees the Lord sitting on a throne, high and lifted up, with only the hem of his robe filling the temple (v. 1). Burning creatures, the seraphim, stand above him, covering their faces and feet with four of their six wings (v. 2), and call to one another that the LORD of hosts is holy, holy, holy, and that his glory fills the whole earth (v. 3). At their voice the doorposts shake and the house fills with smoke (v. 4).
verseByVerse.theology: An earthly throne falls empty, and the throne of heaven is shown to have been occupied all along.
verseByVerse.examples: The threefold Holy of verse 3 (the church calls it the trisagion, "thrice holy") became one of its oldest songs of praise, sung in the liturgies of East and West and heard again around the throne in Revelation 4:8. Every congregation that sings Holy, holy, holy is quoting the seraphim.

verseByVerse.quote: In the year that King Uzziah died I saw the Lord sitting upon a throne, high and lifted up; and the train of his robe filled the temple. Above him stood the seraphim. Each had six wings: with two he covered his face, and with two he covered his feet, and with two he flew.
verseByVerse.commentary:
In the year a proud king died, Isaiah was shown the throne that never falls empty: the Lord, exalted beyond measure, attended by burning creatures who hide their faces before him.

In the year that King Uzziah died. Uzziah had reigned fifty-two years, long enough that few could remember another king, and the nation had been prosperous and secure for most of it. In about 740 BC that ended, and the throne in Jerusalem was empty. In that year Isaiah sees another throne, occupied.

How Uzziah died. Uzziah did not die well. When he was strong he grew proud and walked into the temple to burn incense, work that belonged to the priests, and when eighty priests told him to leave, he raged at them with the censer in his hand. Leprosy broke out on his forehead as he stood there, and he lived shut out from the house of the LORD until he died (2 Chronicles 26:16–21). So the chapter opens in the year a king died for pushing into the holy place, and then takes a man much further in, to the throne itself (see verses 6–7).

The train of his robe filled the temple. Only the hem is mentioned: not the Lord, not his face, but the trailing edge of his clothing, and it fills the whole building. Isaiah describes what he could take in, and he could take in the hem.

Above him stood the seraphim. The seraphim are burning ones, from the verb to burn. Four of their six wings are for covering. Creatures with no sin to hide, standing closest to the throne, give two thirds of their equipment to not looking and not being seen.

High and lifted up. Isaiah uses this phrase again of God (57:15), and once of a human being: of a Servant whose appearance was “marred, beyond human semblance” (52:13–14). The same words describe the enthroned Lord and the disfigured man, and the book lays the two pictures side by side and lets the reader work out who he has been looking at.

Did Isaiah see God? No one can see God’s face and live (Exodus 33:20). Isaiah saw a vision of the Lord’s glory, not God’s unveiled being, and John says that “Isaiah said these things because he saw his glory and spoke of him” (John 12:41), meaning Christ. The one Isaiah saw was the Son.
verseByVerse.note: King Uzziah died about 740 BC. As heavenly beings, seraphim (“burning ones”) appear only here in the Bible.

verseByVerse.quote: And one called to another and said: "Holy, holy, holy is the LORD of hosts; the whole earth is full of his glory!" And the foundations of the thresholds shook at the voice of him who called, and the house was filled with smoke.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God is holy as nothing else is, set apart from everything he has made, and his glory fills not only the temple but the whole earth.

Holy, holy, holy is the LORD of hosts. Hebrew repeats a word for emphasis, and the seraphim say this one three times. Not powerful, powerful, powerful, nor faithful, faithful, faithful, though God is both. Of everything that could be said about him, they say holy.

What holiness is. Holiness here is not chiefly moral, though it includes the moral. It is the fact that God is in a category with nobody else in it. Everything we have ever met was made; he was not. That is why creatures without sin still cover their faces: not out of guilt, but because a creature is standing before the One who was never made. There is no second of him, nothing to set beside him for scale, and the seraphim have looked at him for as long as they have existed and never once grown used to it.

The whole earth is full of his glory! The second line swings the door outward: not the temple, the whole earth. What Isaiah sees in one room is the true condition of the fields outside, of Assyria, of the sea; the vision is simply the moment the curtain came off.

The foundations of the thresholds shook. The stonework moves at the voice of a created being; God himself has not yet spoken. Then smoke, the veiling cloud of Sinai and the tabernacle (Exodus 19:18; 40:34): God hiding himself in the very moment he shows himself, because unveiled glory would not leave a man alive to write the chapter.

Does the threefold “holy” teach the Trinity? The repetition is Hebrew emphasis: supremely holy. It does not prove the Trinity by itself, but Christians have rightly heard it in the light of the whole Bible: the same cry rises before the throne in Revelation 4:8, and John says the glory Isaiah saw was Christ’s (John 12:41).

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The holy God undoes the sinner and then, from his own altar, makes him clean. Chapter 5 pronounced six woes on others; here Isaiah pronounces the seventh on himself. Having seen the King, he knows he is lost, a man of unclean lips living among a people of unclean lips (v. 5). He is not left there. One of the seraphim flies to him with a burning coal taken from the altar, touches his mouth with it, and declares that his guilt is taken away and his sin atoned for (vv. 6–7).
verseByVerse.theology: Access to God is always the result of a sacrifice applied, never of a moral improvement achieved.
verseByVerse.examples: A cleansing that comes from an altar rather than from effort is precisely what makes assurance possible. Anyone who has tried to feel forgiven by resolving to do better knows the difference. The coal in verse 6 touches the one part of Isaiah he had just named as unclean, and the word in verse 7 is spoken over him before he has done anything at all with his cleaned mouth.

verseByVerse.quote: And I said: "Woe is me! For I am lost; for I am a man of unclean lips, and I dwell in the midst of a people of unclean lips; for my eyes have seen the King, the LORD of hosts!"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Seeing the holy King, Isaiah pronounces the seventh woe on himself: he is undone, a man of unclean lips among a people of unclean lips.

Woe is me! Count the woes. Chapter 5 has six, and Isaiah was right every time. Here is the seventh, the first he has pronounced on himself.

For I am lost. The word means undone, ruined, brought to silence. He does not say he feels unworthy or needs more time; those are things a man says when he is comparing himself with other men. Isaiah has stopped comparing.

A man of unclean lips. He has just heard lips that exist to say holy, and the contrast has found him at the point of his own calling. A prophet is a mouth, and the one faculty his life depends on is the one he now knows is filthy. Nor does he use his vision to climb out of his nation: he is one of a people of unclean lips, and says so.

The same response to Jesus. When Peter saw what Jesus had done with the nets, he fell at his knees and said, “Depart from me, for I am a sinful man, O Lord” (Luke 5:8). The holiness that undid Isaiah in the temple met Peter in a fishing boat, in the person of Christ.

A test for us. Most of us assess ourselves against the people nearest us, which is why we come out around average and can live with it. Try the other measure: the one the seraphim cannot look at. Everyone who has done that honestly has arrived at Isaiah’s word, and nobody has ever arrived at it by trying harder.

verseByVerse.quote: Then one of the seraphim flew to me, having in his hand a burning coal that he had taken with tongs from the altar. And he touched my mouth and said: "Behold, this has touched your lips; your guilt is taken away, and your sin atoned for."
verseByVerse.commentary:
God answers Isaiah’s confession at once, from the altar of sacrifice: the coal touches his lips, and his guilt is taken away and his sin atoned for.

A burning coal from the altar. Isaiah is not left in his ruin to see what he will do about it. The remedy comes from the altar, the one place in the building where something has died. The coal is hot because of a sacrifice, and the seraph carries it with tongs.

He touched my mouth. The last man we heard of who came into contact with God’s holiness was Uzziah, of whom Scripture says “the LORD touched the king, so that he was a leper to the day of his death” (2 Kings 15:5). The word is the same. Uzziah was touched and it destroyed him; Isaiah is touched, in a holier place, and it cleans him. The difference is not the men, nor the degree of exposure, since Isaiah’s is greater. It is the altar. Holiness came at Uzziah with nothing in between. What comes to Isaiah has passed through the fire of a sacrifice first.

Your guilt is taken away, and your sin atoned for. Guilt, the liability, is taken away. Sin, the offence, is atoned for, covered, the verb that gives the Day of Atonement its name. And it is announced as done: not shall be, not may be if he perseveres, but done, over the man while he is still standing there with the smoke in the room.

An altar outside a city wall. The coal came from the altar, and the altar had a victim on it. Every believer since has been cleansed the same way, at an altar outside a city wall: Jesus “suffered outside the gate in order to sanctify the people through his own blood” (Hebrews 13:12), and the fire fell on him instead of on us.

Neither self-esteem nor self-hatred. We were long told that most of our troubles come from thinking too little of ourselves, though a large review of the research in 2003 found that raising self-esteem had delivered far less than promised. Isaiah cuts across both our usual cures. In verse 5 he sees himself truly, worse than he had imagined; in verse 7 he is declared clean, more fully than he could have hoped. Self-esteem tells us to stop confessing; self-hatred tells us that confession is all there is. Isaiah confesses fully and is cleansed fully, and the cleansing does not come from inside him. It comes from the altar. A Christian’s confidence is not a high opinion of himself but a high opinion of the sacrifice, and nothing he discovers about himself can shake it.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 8–13 — Send Me, and the Message That Hardens
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The cleansed man is sent, and the message he is given will confirm a stubborn people in their refusal until judgment has run its course. Isaiah overhears the Lord asking whom he shall send and volunteers at once (v. 8). He is sent to tell the people to keep hearing without understanding, and his preaching will dull their hearts so that they do not turn and be healed (vv. 9–10). When he asks how long, the answer is: until the cities are empty and the people removed far away (vv. 11–12). Even a remaining tenth will be burned, yet the felled tree keeps a stump, and the stump is holy seed (v. 13).
verseByVerse.theology: Verses 9-10 are the classic Old Testament statement of judicial hardening: God, as judge, confirming people in the blindness they have chosen. The word that should have saved becomes the instrument of judgment, not because God is arbitrary but because a rejected offer of grace does not stay indefinitely on the table. The tree comes down; the stump is holy seed.
verseByVerse.examples: Missionaries have laboured for decades with few converts, and seen a later generation come to Christ through the Bible they translated. Isaiah's commission had that shape: little fruit in his lifetime, and a book that has never stopped bearing it.

verseByVerse.quote: And I heard the voice of the Lord saying, "Whom shall I send, and who will go for us?" Then I said, "Here I am! Send me."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The cleansed man overhears God asking for a messenger, and offers himself before he knows what the task will cost.

Whom shall I send? Isaiah is not addressed. He overhears. The question goes out into the council of heaven without naming him, and his answer is a man with the taste of a hot coal still in his mouth saying, before anyone asks him, that he will go.

Who will go for us? The plural stands beside the singular shall I send. Some hear God speaking with his heavenly court, as in the vision of 1 Kings 22:19–20. The church has also long heard in it a hint, not a proof, of the Trinity: there is one God, and yet he can say us (compare Genesis 1:26).

Cleansing before commission. The order matters. The cleansing came in verse 7, the commission in verse 8. The man of verse 5 was undone and had nothing to offer anybody. What made him usable was not a recovery of confidence but a coal from an altar, and his readiness is the overflow of being forgiven, not the price of it.

Here I am! Send me. He volunteers before the job description arrives, and the job description, when it comes, is the hardest in the Bible.

In everyday life. When you hang back from something God has plainly put in front of you, is it humility, or is it that you have not believed verse 7 about yourself? A great deal of Christian reluctance is guilt never dealt with, passing itself off as modesty. The cure is not a firmer resolution, but to hear the sentence spoken over the cleaned mouth, and then to answer.

verseByVerse.quote: And he said, "Go, and say to this people: "'Keep on hearing, but do not understand; keep on seeing, but do not perceive.' Make the heart of this people dull, and their ears heavy, and blind their eyes; lest they see with their eyes, and hear with their ears, and understand with their hearts, and turn and be healed."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Isaiah is sent to a people who will not listen, and his preaching will confirm them in the refusal they have already chosen: a judgment from God, yet never an excuse for them.

Make the heart of this people dull. Every preacher’s instinct is to soften this, and it should be resisted. The stated effect of Isaiah’s preaching is that the people will be less able to repent afterwards than before: lest they turn and be healed.

A judicial hardening. Two things must be held together. First, this is a judge’s sentence, not an arbitrary act. Chapters 1 to 5 have shown a people with every advantage, a vineyard planted and fenced by God himself (5:1–7), who produced wild grapes. The hardening confirms a verdict the nation has spent five chapters pronouncing on itself. There is a point at which a refused offer is withdrawn, and Isaiah is sent to be the instrument of the withdrawal.

Human responsibility remains. Second, it never dissolves human responsibility. Matthew quotes this passage from the Greek Old Testament (the Septuagint, the translation Jews made before Christ), which words it differently: “For this people’s heart has grown dull, and with their ears they can barely hear, and their eyes they have closed” (Matthew 13:15). The closing is now something they did to themselves. God hardens; they harden themselves; and no one at the last day will be able to say he wanted to see and was prevented.

In the New Testament. This passage is quoted or applied in all four Gospels and in Acts (Matthew 13:14–15; Mark 4:12; Luke 8:10; John 12:40; Acts 28:26–27). Jesus used it of those who heard his parables without understanding; John and Paul used it of those who saw his signs and heard his gospel and still did not believe. It is the answer the New Testament reaches for when the problem is not a shortage of light.

Not pointless. There is a mercy hidden in the commission. Isaiah is told that his ministry will not produce national repentance, not that it will be pointless. He goes, for decades, writing the book an Ethiopian official would be reading aloud in his chariot seven centuries later when Philip ran up beside him and told him about Jesus from it (Acts 8:30–35). Faithfulness was never measured by the response in the room.

For the tender conscience. A person who fears he has been hardened, and grieves over it, is showing the very softness this verse says the hardened lack. The invitation of 1:18 still stands open to him.
verseByVerse.note: “Make the heart of this people dull” states the commission by its result: Isaiah’s preaching will fix the people in the course they have already chosen.

verseByVerse.quote: Then I said, "How long, O Lord?" And he said: "Until cities lie waste without inhabitant, and houses without people, and the land is a desolate waste, and the LORD removes people far away, and the forsaken places are many in the midst of the land.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Isaiah asks how long he must preach to deaf ears, and is told: until the land lies empty.

How long, O Lord? Isaiah does not object or bargain, but neither does he accept the commission comfortably. The bearer of the hardening word finds it unbearable and says so, the mark of a true prophet as against a man who enjoys announcing judgment. The psalms ask it often (Psalm 13:1), and the martyrs under the altar are still asking it in Revelation 6:10.

Until cities lie waste without inhabitant. The answer is worse than the question. Not until they listen, not for a generation: until the cities are empty, houses stand with nobody in them, and fields go back to scrub. It is what the Assyrian invasions began and the Babylonian deportations, a century and a half later, completed.

No optimistic estimates. God does not negotiate here, and there is a comfort in that which is rarely noticed: he does not manage his servants with optimistic estimates. He tells them what it will actually cost, and then sends them.

verseByVerse.quote: And though a tenth remain in it, it will be burned again, like a terebinth or an oak, whose stump remains when it is felled." The holy seed is its stump.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Judgment will go on until even the survivors are burned, yet the felled tree keeps a living stump, and that stump is the holy seed from which God’s promise will grow.

Though a tenth remain in it. Suppose a tenth survives, the remnant everyone hopes for. That tenth will be burned too. The exile came in waves, and each wave took the survivors of the last.

Whose stump remains when it is felled. Then the picture changes. Anyone who has felled a large tree knows the sight: trunk, branches, shade and fruit gone, and an ugly disc of cut wood in the ground that looks like the end of the matter. It is not. A stump is a living root system with its top taken off.

The holy seed is its stump. These last six words come with no explanation whatever. Follow the seed forward, because Isaiah does. In chapter 11 the felled royal line puts out “a shoot from the stump of Jesse” (11:1). In chapter 53 the shoot is a person, who “grew up before him like a young plant, and like a root out of dry ground” (53:2), with nothing about him to attract a second look. Paul reads the root of Jesse as Christ (Romans 15:12).

The stump was holy. So the chapter that begins with a dead king and ends with a burnt field points, in its last clause, to Jesus of Nazareth: everything visible taken away, and the promise still in the ground. God said he would judge, and he judged, and there was never a moment when the fire was outside his hand or the seed outside his keeping. The tree came down. The stump was holy. And out of that stump, in the fullness of time, came the one whose glory Isaiah had seen at the beginning of the chapter.

Uncertain wording. The Hebrew of verse 13 is difficult. The word translated burned may also mean grazed bare, and the words translated stump and felled are rare, so translations vary in the details. The overall picture is not in doubt: a tree cut down to the ground, with life still in what remains.

Textual note. The Greek Old Testament leaves out the final clause, but the Hebrew text has it, and so does the Great Isaiah Scroll found at Qumran (see the Dead Sea Scrolls).

7.subtitle: The Sign of Immanuel
7.intro:
Where we are. The scene moves from the temple to the road. A few years after his call, Isaiah meets King Ahaz, Uzziah’s grandson, in his first recorded encounter with a king. Chapters 7–12 belong together, and the child named here runs through them to the King of 9:6–7 and the shoot of Jesse in chapter 11.

The message. In a crisis, God’s people stand only by trusting his word: “If you are not firm in faith, you will not be firm at all” (v. 9). God’s promise to David cannot be overthrown by two petty kings, and when the king of Judah refuses even to ask for a sign, God gives one anyway: a son called Immanuel, God with us. But the protection the faithless king has bought instead will become the very disaster he feared.

Why it was said. About 734 BC Syria and the northern kingdom of Israel marched on Jerusalem to replace Ahaz with a king who would join their stand against Assyria (see the introduction). Ahaz, terrified, was turning for help to Assyria itself, and paid for it with the temple’s silver and gold (2 Kings 16:7–9).

How the chapter makes its case. First the threat (vv. 1–9): the house of David shakes like a forest, and God sends Isaiah to tell Ahaz that the two invaders are smouldering stumps, their plan will fail, and only faith will stand. Then the sign (vv. 10–17): God offers Ahaz any sign he likes, Ahaz refuses in pious words, and the sign is given over his head to the house of David: the virgin’s son, Immanuel; before he is old enough to choose good, the two enemy kings will be gone, but the king of Assyria will come. Finally the cost (vv. 18–25): four pictures of what Assyria will do, from flies and bees to a hired razor and vineyards gone to thorns.

Where it leads. Here Isaiah points to Christ by direct promise. A child born in those years was the near sign, but the promise reaches beyond him, and Matthew says it is fulfilled in Jesus, born of the virgin Mary: “they shall call his name Immanuel” (Matthew 1:23). The faithless son of David refused to trust; the true Son of David trusted perfectly, and is himself God with us.

For us. Fear drives us, as it drove Ahaz, to buy security from something other than God, and what we hire to save us ends up ruling us. The answer is to trust the God who has come to be with us in his Son, and to take him at his word before we can see how things will turn out.

keyVerse.quote: “Therefore the Lord himself will give you a sign. Behold, the virgin shall conceive and bear a son, and shall call his name Immanuel.”
keyVerse.note: The sign is given not to Ahaz but in spite of him, to “the house of David” (v. 13), the dynasty that would one day produce the one the sign points to. A child born in Ahaz’s day was the near sign, but Matthew’s use of the verse is not forced on it: only in Mary’s son is every word fulfilled, a virgin conceiving and a child who is God with us in person.

7.theology:
Faith is not an addition to security; it is the floor. The wordplay in verse 9, firm in faith and firm at all, both from the root behind amen, says that to believe God is to stand firm, and there is no standing firm without it. The threat Ahaz would not trust God about was nearly spent, and the empire he hired to avoid it destroyed him.

The sign, near and far. Verse 16 needs something to happen in Ahaz’s own lifetime, and Matthew says a birth in Bethlehem seven centuries later fulfilled the same words (Matt. 1:22-23). How the two fit, and what the Hebrew word almah means, are taken up at verse 14.

Immanuel. The answer given to a terrified dynasty is not a battle plan but a name, and the weight of the name falls on one small word: God with us.
7.reflection:
When the news came, “the heart of Ahaz and the heart of his people shook as the trees of the forest shake before the wind” (v. 2). What news makes you shake? How does God’s description of the enemy as “two smoldering stumps of firebrands” (v. 4) help you see your fears in proportion?

Ahaz refused a sign with pious words: “I will not put the LORD to the test” (v. 12). How can religious language become a cover for not trusting God? Where might you be doing that?

Ahaz paid Assyria to rescue him, and Assyria became the razor that shaved Judah (v. 20). What do people today “hire” to keep them safe, and how does it end up ruling them?

The sign God gave was a child called Immanuel, “God with us” (v. 14), and Matthew says it is fulfilled in Jesus. What difference does it make that God’s answer to fear is not a plan but a person who is with us?
7.text: <sup>1</sup>In the days of Ahaz the son of Jotham, son of Uzziah, king of Judah, Rezin the king of Syria and Pekah the son of Remaliah the king of Israel came up to Jerusalem to wage war against it, but could not yet mount an attack against it.<sup>2</sup>When the house of David was told, "Syria is in league with Ephraim," the heart of Ahaz and the heart of his people shook as the trees of the forest shake before the wind.<sup>3</sup>And the LORD said to Isaiah, "Go out to meet Ahaz, you and Shear-jashub your son, at the end of the conduit of the upper pool on the highway to the Washer's Field.<sup>4</sup>And say to him, 'Be careful, be quiet, do not fear, and do not let your heart be faint because of these two smoldering stumps of firebrands, at the fierce anger of Rezin and Syria and the son of Remaliah.<sup>5</sup>Because Syria, with Ephraim and the son of Remaliah, has devised evil against you, saying,<sup>6</sup>"Let us go up against Judah and terrify it, and let us conquer it for ourselves, and set up the son of Tabeel as king in the midst of it,"<sup>7</sup>thus says the Lord GOD: "'It shall not stand, and it shall not come to pass.<sup>8</sup>For the head of Syria is Damascus, and the head of Damascus is Rezin. And within sixty-five years Ephraim will be shattered from being a people.<sup>9</sup>And the head of Ephraim is Samaria, and the head of Samaria is the son of Remaliah. If you are not firm in faith, you will not be firm at all.'"<sup>10</sup>Again the LORD spoke to Ahaz:<sup>11</sup>"Ask a sign of the LORD your God; let it be deep as Sheol or high as heaven."<sup>12</sup>But Ahaz said, "I will not ask, and I will not put the LORD to the test."<sup>13</sup>And he said, "Hear then, O house of David! Is it too little for you to weary men, that you weary my God also?<sup>14</sup>Therefore the Lord himself will give you a sign. Behold, the virgin shall conceive and bear a son, and shall call his name Immanuel.<sup>15</sup>He shall eat curds and honey when he knows how to refuse the evil and choose the good.<sup>16</sup>For before the boy knows how to refuse the evil and choose the good, the land whose two kings you dread will be deserted.<sup>17</sup>The LORD will bring upon you and upon your people and upon your father's house such days as have not come since the day that Ephraim departed from Judah—the king of Assyria!"<sup>18</sup>In that day the LORD will whistle for the fly that is at the end of the streams of Egypt, and for the bee that is in the land of Assyria.<sup>19</sup>And they will all come and settle in the steep ravines, and in the clefts of the rocks, and on all the thornbushes, and on all the pastures.<sup>20</sup>In that day the Lord will shave with a razor that is hired beyond the River —with the king of Assyria—the head and the hair of the feet, and it will sweep away the beard also.<sup>21</sup>In that day a man will keep alive a young cow and two sheep,<sup>22</sup>and because of the abundance of milk that they give, he will eat curds, for everyone who is left in the land will eat curds and honey.<sup>23</sup>In that day every place where there used to be a thousand vines, worth a thousand shekels of silver, will become briers and thorns.<sup>24</sup>With bow and arrows a man will come there, for all the land will be briers and thorns.<sup>25</sup>And as for all the hills that used to be hoed with a hoe, you will not come there for fear of briers and thorns, but they will become a place where cattle are let loose and where sheep tread.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: When two kings march on Jerusalem, God tells Judah’s king that the threat is nearly spent, and that he will stand only if he trusts God’s word. Syria and the northern kingdom of Israel come up against Jerusalem, and the king and his people shake like trees in a wind (vv. 1–2). God sends Isaiah with his son, whose name means “A remnant shall return”, to meet Ahaz at the city’s water supply and tell him not to fear these two smouldering stumps (vv. 3–4). Their plan to put their own man on David’s throne (vv. 5–6) will not stand; their kingdoms are only cities ruled by men. Then comes the condition: “If you are not firm in faith, you will not be firm at all” (vv. 7–9).
verseByVerse.theology: What is really under attack is God's promise to David, and the promise is what holds.
verseByVerse.examples: When the news is frightening, verse 4 asks us to borrow God's estimate of the threat rather than the one arriving on our phones.

verseByVerse.quote: In the days of Ahaz the son of Jotham, son of Uzziah, king of Judah, Rezin the king of Syria and Pekah the son of Remaliah the king of Israel came up to Jerusalem to wage war against it, but could not yet mount an attack against it. When the house of David was told, "Syria is in league with Ephraim," the heart of Ahaz and the heart of his people shook as the trees of the forest shake before the wind.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When two neighbouring kings march on Jerusalem, the king and his people shake with fear, though God has already set a limit on the threat.

In the days of Ahaz. Assyria was expanding westward and swallowing small states. Syria (Aram) and the northern kingdom of Israel had joined forces to resist it, and wanted Judah in the alliance. Judah declined, so the two marched on Jerusalem to remove Ahaz and put in a king who would join (see the note).

But could not yet mount an attack against it. Isaiah tells you the outcome before he tells you the fear. The siege never succeeds. God’s restraint is already in place, holding the thing at arm’s length, before a word of prophecy has been spoken.

As the trees of the forest shake before the wind. One of the best pictures in the book. Not a tree in a wind but a whole forest, every trunk moving at once: that is what the news does to Jerusalem, king and people shaking together because somebody has come in with a report.

The house of David was told. Two details do quiet work. Isaiah does not say Ahaz was told but the house of David: the promise God made to David is what is really under threat, and the chapter will not let it out of sight. And the trembling is shared, the heart of Ahaz and the heart of his people. A frightened leader does not keep his fear to himself; it is the most contagious thing a man in authority carries, and it spreads at the speed of conversation.
verseByVerse.note: Syria (Aram) and Israel (Ephraim) attacked Judah to force it into their alliance against Assyria, about 734 BC.

verseByVerse.quote: And the LORD said to Isaiah, "Go out to meet Ahaz, you and Shear-jashub your son, at the end of the conduit of the upper pool on the highway to the Washer's Field. And say to him, 'Be careful, be quiet, do not fear, and do not let your heart be faint because of these two smoldering stumps of firebrands, at the fierce anger of Rezin and Syria and the son of Remaliah.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God sends Isaiah to meet the frightened king in the middle of his emergency plans, with a son whose name is a message and with God’s verdict on the enemy: two burnt-out sticks.

The conduit of the upper pool. Isaiah records the address with care. The upper pool was part of Jerusalem’s water supply, and the conduit the channel running from it. Ahaz is probably there because a besieged city dies of thirst before it dies of anything else, and he has gone to see whether the water can be secured. God meets him in the middle of his planning.

The same spot later. Twenty-nine chapters later the Assyrian field commander comes to taunt King Hezekiah, and he stands “by the conduit of the upper pool on the highway to the Washer’s Field” (36:2): the same words, the same patch of ground. Two kings of Judah, at one spot, each facing an army. Ahaz is offered a sign, turns it down and buys Assyrian protection. Hezekiah takes the enemy’s letter into the house of the LORD and spreads it out before God (37:14). One reign ends in ruin and the other in deliverance, and the book quietly puts both decisions at the same address.

You and Shear-jashub your son. The boy comes because his name is the message: “A remnant shall return” (see the note). It cuts both ways, which is the point: only a remnant, a surviving few, but a remnant. Isaiah stands before a terrified king holding the hand of a child whose name says the nation will be cut down and not finished.

Two smoldering stumps of firebrands. Four commands (be careful, be quiet, do not fear, do not lose heart), and then God’s estimate of the crisis. Not two kings or two armies, but two sticks pulled from a fire, smoking because the flame has gone. They look alarming from a distance; there is no heat left in either. Within a few years both kings were dead, and within twelve years both their kingdoms had fallen to Assyria.
verseByVerse.note: “Shear-jashub” means “A remnant shall return” (ESV note).

verseByVerse.quote: Because Syria, with Ephraim and the son of Remaliah, has devised evil against you, saying, "Let us go up against Judah and terrify it, and let us conquer it for ourselves, and set up the son of Tabeel as king in the midst of it,"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The enemy plans to terrify Judah and put a puppet king on David’s throne, which makes the attack an assault on God’s promise to David.

Syria has devised evil against you. God quotes the enemy’s war council back to Ahaz. Whatever was said in a room in Damascus, God heard it, and that is itself part of the comfort.

Let us go up against Judah and terrify it. Their first aim is to terrify: to win the war by fear before they win it on the ground. When the forest shook in verse 2, the campaign was already partly successful, and not a soldier had arrived.

The son of Tabeel. The real target is in the last clause: an outsider, named only as the son of Tabeel, to sit on the throne of David. That makes this a crisis of faith and not only of war. God had promised David a house and a throne for ever (2 Samuel 7:16). Whether the coalition knows it or not, they are attacking a promise, and everything in the chapter follows from the fact that the promise cannot fail. It is the promise Gabriel announced to Mary: “the Lord God will give to him the throne of his father David” (Luke 1:32).

Uncertain wording. Who the son of Tabeel was is unknown; he was probably a Syrian, or a Judean noble friendly to Syria. The name seems to mean “God is good”, and some think the Hebrew spelling twists it slightly into “good for nothing”, a scornful pun on the man the enemy wanted as king.

verseByVerse.quote: thus says the Lord GOD: "'It shall not stand, and it shall not come to pass. For the head of Syria is Damascus, and the head of Damascus is Rezin. And within sixty-five years Ephraim will be shattered from being a people. And the head of Ephraim is Samaria, and the head of Samaria is the son of Remaliah. If you are not firm in faith, you will not be firm at all.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
God declares that the plot will fail, cuts the enemy down to size, and sets one condition before the king: only those who stand on God’s word will stand at all.

It shall not stand. The verdict comes before the argument: it will not happen. Everything after it is explanation.

The head of Damascus is Rezin. Then God cuts the threat down to size. What is Syria? A city. What is the city? A man. What is Israel? A city, and its head not even named, just the son of Remaliah, as you refer to someone you do not think worth naming. Fear makes things bigger; God counts them out and they shrink. Most fears do not survive being listed one by one, and the ones that do are worth taking to God rather than to a scheme of our own.

If you are not firm in faith. Both Hebrew verbs come from the root behind amen, meaning firm or reliable (see the note). If you will not hold on, you will not be held up. Ahaz is told that trust in God is the only firm ground, and warned that he is standing somewhere else.

Faith as God’s gift. The call to faith comes wrapped in God’s promise to David, and the faith it asks for is itself God’s gift. No son of David trusted as he should, Ahaz least of all; the true Son of David did, saying “I will put my trust in him” (Hebrews 2:13), and his faithfulness covers ours. The Spirit he gives is the one who makes frightened hearts firm.

Why sixty-five years? Samaria fell twelve years later, but within the sixty-five years Assyria deported Israel and resettled the land with foreigners (2 Kings 17:24), so that Ephraim ceased to exist as a people. Ezra 4:2 names Esarhaddon of Assyria as one who brought settlers, and his reign falls about sixty-five years after 734 BC.
verseByVerse.note: A wordplay on the Hebrew root aman (the root of “amen”): “If you are not firm (ta’aminu) in faith, you will not be firm (te’amenu) at all.”

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 10–17 — The Sign He Would Not Ask For
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: When Ahaz will not trust God, God gives the house of David a sign anyway, and it is far greater than anything the king would have asked. God offers Ahaz any sign he likes, from the depths to the heights (vv. 10–11). Ahaz refuses in pious words (v. 12), and Isaiah answers that the Lord himself will give a sign to the house of David: the virgin will conceive and bear a son, and call his name Immanuel, God with us (vv. 13–14). Before the boy can tell right from wrong, the two kings Ahaz dreads will be gone, though he will eat the food of a stripped land (vv. 15–16). And worse is coming: the king of Assyria (v. 17).
verseByVerse.theology: God's answer to unbelief is not to withdraw his promise but to give a greater sign than anyone had asked for.
verseByVerse.examples: Someone who says "I don't want to bother God with this" while quietly making their own arrangements is closer to Ahaz than to humility.

verseByVerse.quote: Again the LORD spoke to Ahaz: "Ask a sign of the LORD your God; let it be deep as Sheol or high as heaven."
verseByVerse.commentary:
God comes back to the faithless king and offers him any sign he cares to name.

Again the LORD spoke to Ahaz. Ahaz has already been given a word from God and has not responded, and God comes back. That one word, again, says as much about God’s character as the rest of the offer.

Ask a sign of the LORD your God. God uses a possessive: your God. After the trembling, with Ahaz’s mind already turning to Assyria, God is still claiming the relationship out loud. It will matter at verse 13.

Let it be deep as Sheol or high as heaven. Elsewhere people who demand signs are rebuked; here God volunteers one, unasked, and lets the king set the terms. Between the depths of the grave and the height of the sky is everything there is. Whatever Ahaz’s problem is, it is not a shortage of evidence: he was not asked to trust in the dark, but to name what would convince him, with a blank cheque in his hand.

verseByVerse.quote: But Ahaz said, "I will not ask, and I will not put the LORD to the test." And he said, "Hear then, O house of David! Is it too little for you to weary men, that you weary my God also?
verseByVerse.commentary:
Ahaz refuses the sign in pious words, because he has already chosen to trust Assyria; so Isaiah turns from the king to the whole house of David.

I will not put the LORD to the test. It is the most religious sentence in the chapter, and it is a lie. Ahaz quotes Deuteronomy 6:16 accurately, and sounds like the only reverent man in the room. But God has just commanded him to ask. A text about not demanding proof cannot be used to refuse proof God has offered; that is Scripture used as a cover.

Ahaz’s secret deal. We know what is being covered. Ahaz sent to Tiglath-pileser of Assyria saying, “I am your servant and your son. Come up and rescue me”, and stripped the silver and gold from the house of the LORD to pay for it (2 Kings 16:7–8). His refusal here suggests the decision was already made, perhaps the messengers already on the road, and a sign from God would only have complicated it.

Quiet unbelief. This is the unbelief the chapter exists to expose, and it is not the noisy kind. It is the man who will not ask God for anything because he has quietly arranged matters and does not want the arrangement disturbed, and who dresses the refusal as humility.

That you weary my God also? Isaiah’s patience goes, and the pronoun changes. God said your God; Isaiah now says my God. He will not leave the possessive in the king’s mouth after what has just come out of it. And he addresses the house of David (the “you” is plural, see the note). The man has disqualified himself; what follows is spoken over his head, to a dynasty with a promise attached.
verseByVerse.note: “My God” is Isaiah’s God (ESV note). The “you” of vv. 13–14 is plural (ESV note): the sign is for the whole house of David.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore the Lord himself will give you a sign. Behold, the virgin shall conceive and bear a son, and shall call his name Immanuel.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Because Ahaz will not ask, God himself gives the house of David a sign: the virgin will bear a son whose name declares that God is with his people. A child of Ahaz’s day was the first, partial sign; only in Jesus is every word fulfilled.

Therefore the Lord himself will give you a sign. Because you would not ask, not in spite of it. The refusal does not cancel the sign; it provokes it, and the sign turns out to be immeasurably larger than anything Ahaz would have thought to request. Ahaz would not choose, so the Lord himself will.

The virgin shall conceive and bear a son. Isaiah speaks of a particular young woman, the virgin, without naming her. The Hebrew word has been argued over for centuries (see the box below on the wording), but the sign is meant to be remarkable: God offered one “deep as Sheol or high as heaven” (v. 11), and a young woman having a baby in the usual way is not a sign of that order; it happens every week.

Then and later. Something happened in Ahaz’s own lifetime, or verse 16 would be meaningless, and it was never the whole of what the sign was for. Matthew, writing of a birth in Bethlehem seven centuries later, says plainly: “All this took place to fulfill what the Lord had spoken by the prophet” (Matthew 1:22–23). The near event was the shadow; Matthew names the one who cast it. Isaiah himself points the same way: the land is called Immanuel’s (8:8), and the child of 9:6–7 is called “Mighty God” and sits on David’s throne for ever.

Immanuel. The name is the thing. Not God for us, or above us, or watching, but with us (see the note). To a king shaking like a forest, that is the whole answer, and it is not a strategy but a person. Matthew opens his Gospel with this verse and closes it with the last words Jesus speaks: “behold, I am with you always, to the end of the age” (Matthew 28:20). The name given to a frightened dynasty is the promise the risen Christ leaves with his church, and between those two sentences stands everything he did.

Where Christians differ: who was the child in Ahaz’s day? Some say a son of the royal house, even Hezekiah; others a son of Isaiah himself (8:3–4), since the sign was to be fulfilled before the two kings were gone (v. 16). Some hold that the verse speaks of Christ alone, and that the boy’s age in verse 16 simply measures the time. Critical scholars see only a child of Isaiah’s day. This commentary’s view: a child born in those years was the near sign, and the prophecy reached beyond him to Immanuel himself, as 8:8 and 9:6–7 show and as Matthew says. Those who hold this view and those who see Christ alone agree with Matthew on what matters most: only in Mary’s son is every word fulfilled, a virgin conceiving and a child who is God with us in person.

Uncertain wording. The Hebrew word here is almah. It means a young woman of marriageable age, and it is not the technical word for a virgin; another word (betulah) usually carries that sense more precisely. Jewish readers have long argued from this that Isaiah meant an ordinary young woman, and Christians should feel the force of it rather than talk past it. It is why some modern translations, such as the RSV and NRSV, read young woman, while the KJV, NKJV and ESV read virgin. Three things stand on the other side. First, in none of its few appearances does almah clearly describe a married woman, and where the context is plain it is used of an unmarried girl (Rebekah in Genesis 24:43; probably Miriam in Exodus 2:8), so virgin is a fair rendering even if it is not the word’s strict definition. Second, the Jewish scholars who translated the Scriptures into Greek, probably two centuries or so before Christ, with no Christian argument to make, rendered it parthenos, which plainly means virgin. Third, the setting calls for a sign of extraordinary weight (v. 11). The likely meaning is a young unmarried woman, a virgin, and Matthew’s reading follows the word’s natural sense.
verseByVerse.note: “Immanuel” means “God is with us” (ESV note).

verseByVerse.quote: He shall eat curds and honey when he knows how to refuse the evil and choose the good. For before the boy knows how to refuse the evil and choose the good, the land whose two kings you dread will be deserted.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Before the child is old enough to know right from wrong, the two kings Ahaz fears will be gone; yet the child’s food, curds and honey, warns that Judah too will be stripped bare.

Before the boy knows how to refuse the evil. The sign now has a clock. A small child takes a few years to reach the age when he can tell right from wrong, and before he gets there the two kingdoms terrifying Ahaz will be empty ground. It happened. Damascus fell to Assyria in 732 BC and Rezin was killed; Samaria fell in 722 and the northern kingdom ended. Ahaz was shaking like a forest before two states with a handful of years left in them.

He shall eat curds and honey. This reads like a delicacy and it is nothing of the kind. Verse 22 explains: when the fields are trampled and the vineyards gone, what is left is what a surviving cow gives and what wild bees make. It is the food of a land gone back to the wild.

A double-edged sign. So the sign is double-edged all the way through, and Isaiah does not soften it. The child’s name is God-with-us; the child’s food is the food of a ruined country. Anyone tempted to take the promise as a guarantee that nothing hard will happen has to reckon with the menu. God with us has never meant God instead of trouble. It means God present in the middle of it, a smaller thing to say and a far larger thing to have, and the one who fulfilled this name was himself born into a poor home in an occupied land.

Uncertain wording. The little Hebrew word joining the two halves of verse 15 can mean when, by the time that or so that, so the verse may say that the child will eat curds and honey when he reaches the age of choosing, or until he does, or that he will be raised on it to learn to choose. The ESV’s when fits verse 16, and the point is the same on any reading: he grows up in a stripped land.

verseByVerse.quote: The LORD will bring upon you and upon your people and upon your father's house such days as have not come since the day that Ephraim departed from Judah—the king of Assyria!"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Lord will bring on Judah the worst days since the kingdom split, and the bringer of them will be the very king Ahaz has paid to protect him: the king of Assyria.

Such days as have not come. The sentence is built to explode at the end. It rolls across three targets (you, your people, your father’s house) and reaches for the worst memory in the nation: the day the kingdom split after Solomon, when ten tribes walked away (1 Kings 12). Nothing that bad has happened since; something that bad is coming. Then, held to the very end: the king of Assyria.

The ally is the catastrophe. That is the man Ahaz has just paid. He emptied the temple treasury to hire this protection, and Isaiah announces him as the disaster. The very thing bought at such cost to keep trouble out is the door trouble walks through. Ahaz was frightened of two smouldering stumps, and to escape them he invited a fire. The threat he would not trust God about was small and nearly spent; the one he created by not trusting was an empire.

The saviours we hire. Ahaz did what nearly everybody does when frightened: he found something big enough to make him feel safe and paid for it. We do the same in subtler currencies. Afraid of insignificance, we hire a career. Afraid of being alone, we hire a relationship and load our whole life onto it. Afraid of the future, we hire money and keep paying. Each choice is reasonable, and each quietly turns from servant into master, because whatever you trust to save you can also demand anything of you. The damage in most lives is rarely done by the thing that frightened us; it is done by what we reached for to avoid it. Isaiah’s point is not that planning, saving or loving are wrong, but that what we turn to instead of God always costs more than the thing we feared.

A different kind of rescuer. The gospel offers a rescuer of another kind. Ahaz paid Assyria with the temple’s treasure; the Son of David paid for us with himself, and a Saviour who has already given everything for you has nothing left to extort.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Four pictures, each beginning “in that day”, show what Ahaz’s choice will cost: the power he hired to save him will strip his land bare. God will whistle for Egypt and Assyria, and they will settle over the land like flies and bees until there is nowhere left to hide (vv. 18–19). The king of Assyria, the razor Ahaz paid for, will shave Judah from head to foot (v. 20). A farmer will be left with a heifer and two sheep, and the few survivors will live on curds and honey (vv. 21–22). Valuable vineyards will go back to briers and thorns, fit only for hunters and grazing cattle (vv. 23–25).
verseByVerse.theology: Ahaz hired Assyria, and God says the razor is his. The power a frightened man buys to protect himself becomes the instrument of his ruin. Refusing to trust God costs more than the danger it was meant to avoid.
verseByVerse.examples: A shopkeeper who pays a protection racket to keep out one gang, and then watches the racketeers take the shop, has done what Ahaz did.
