verseByVerse.quote: In that day the LORD will whistle for the fly that is at the end of the streams of Egypt, and for the bee that is in the land of Assyria. And they will all come and settle in the steep ravines, and in the clefts of the rocks, and on all the thornbushes, and on all the pastures.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God will whistle for Egypt and Assyria, and their armies will settle over the whole land like flies and bees, leaving nowhere to hide.

The LORD will whistle. Four oracles follow, each opening in that day, and together they describe the country Ahaz’s decision produces. In the first, a man whistles for his animals, and what comes is Egypt and Assyria, the two great powers between which Judah was pinned throughout its history. God calls them, and they come. That is the sovereignty the chapter has been quietly asserting from verse 1: not merely that God permits the great powers to move, but that they move when he makes a sound.

The fly and the bee. The insects are chosen with care. A fly from the streams of the Nile, where standing water breeds them in clouds; a bee from Assyria, which stings. Neither can be fought. No border keeps out flies and no formation keeps out bees; they arrive in numbers, through every gap, and settle.

They will all come and settle. Isaiah lists the terrain until none is left: ravines, clefts in the rocks, thornbushes, pastures, the wild places and the farmed. The clefts of the rocks are where people hide when an army comes. The hiding places are occupied too.

verseByVerse.quote: In that day the Lord will shave with a razor that is hired beyond the River —with the king of Assyria—the head and the hair of the feet, and it will sweep away the beard also.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The king of Assyria, whom Ahaz hired, is God’s razor, and he will shave Judah bare in shame.

A razor that is hired. One word carries the verse: hired. Ahaz sent the money and made the arrangement. The razor is hired all right, but God is holding the handle. The king thinks he is the customer; he is the one being shaved. The River is the Euphrates (see the note), Assyria’s home.

It will sweep away the beard also. In that world a man’s beard was his dignity. When David’s envoys had half their beards shaved off, they were too ashamed to come home and stayed in Jericho until it grew back (2 Samuel 10:4–5). This shaving is total, head, body and beard, and the nation is left as exposed as a man stripped of every hair in public: the price of a contract signed in panic by a man who had been offered a sign as deep as Sheol and would not take it.
verseByVerse.note: “The River” is the Euphrates (ESV note): Assyria.

verseByVerse.quote: In that day a man will keep alive a young cow and two sheep, and because of the abundance of milk that they give, he will eat curds, for everyone who is left in the land will eat curds and honey.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The few survivors will live on what a heifer and two sheep can give, because there will be almost no one left to feed.

A young cow and two sheep. The camera comes down from empires to one farmer, and what he has left is a heifer and two sheep. Isaiah does not say he owns them; he says he will keep them alive, the language of a man getting animals through a bad season.

Because of the abundance of milk. Then the strangest phrase in the chapter: abundance, from one cow. It is not prosperity but arithmetic. There is milk to spare because there is almost nobody left to drink it: a full jug in an empty village. And here is the phrase from verse 15 again, now explained. The food of Immanuel’s childhood is the food of the survivors, what an animal gives and what wild bees make, because nothing is being sown.

Milk and honey again. The promised land was to be “a land flowing with milk and honey” (Exodus 3:8), a picture of abundance. Here are milk and honey again, and they mean the opposite: not a land so rich that it overflows, but a land so empty that there is nothing else to eat. The same two words, turned inside out.

verseByVerse.quote: In that day every place where there used to be a thousand vines, worth a thousand shekels of silver, will become briers and thorns. With bow and arrows a man will come there, for all the land will be briers and thorns. And as for all the hills that used to be hoed with a hoe, you will not come there for fear of briers and thorns, but they will become a place where cattle are let loose and where sheep tread.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Land that was carefully farmed for generations will go back to briers and thorns, fit only for hunters and stray cattle: the vineyard of chapter 5, abandoned.

A thousand vines, worth a thousand shekels of silver. A thousand vines at a shekel each was a serious vineyard, the kind of asset a family builds over generations: terraced, walled, pruned and passed down. Vines take years to yield anything; whoever plants one plants it for his children. All of it goes back to briers and thorns: not burned or seized, simply abandoned.

With bow and arrows a man will come there. A man walks onto what used to be the vineyard carrying hunting weapons, because there is game in it now. That single detail shows how far it has gone: cultivated land has become country you enter armed.

The hills that used to be hoed. The terraced hillsides are the saddest item on the list. Every terrace was built by hand, stone by stone, to hold soil on a slope, the labour of generations. Now nobody will even walk up there for the thorns, and cattle wander where vines stood.

The same vineyard. Read this beside chapter 5 and it is the same vineyard. There God dug it, cleared it, planted choice vines, looked for grapes and found wild ones, and said he would let it be overgrown with briers and thorns (5:6). Chapter 5 passed the sentence; chapter 7 shows it carried out. And it began with a king who was offered a sign as deep as the grave and as high as heaven, and said he would rather not.

8.subtitle: Fear God Alone
8.intro:
Where we are. Chapter 8 runs straight on from chapter 7. Ahaz has refused the sign and turned to Assyria; now, perhaps a year later, Isaiah’s second son is born with a name that sets the clock running, and the prophet turns from the king to the small circle who will listen.

The message. God’s word cannot fail: Damascus and Samaria will be plundered within a child’s first years, and Judah, which despised God’s quiet care for the might of Assyria, will be flooded to the neck. In such a time God’s people must not fear what everyone fears, but fear the LORD himself, who is a refuge to those who trust him and a stone that trips those who refuse him. They are to hold on to his word and wait for him, and turn from every other voice.

Why it was said. Judah was in a panic, with rumours of plots everywhere, the court leaning on Assyria and people turning to mediums (see the introduction). The few who still trusted the LORD needed to know how to live in a nation that had rejected his word.

How the chapter makes its case. First the sign (vv. 1–4): a witnessed notice and a baby named “quick spoil, swift plunder”. Then the flood (vv. 5–8): the people refused the gentle waters of Shiloah, so the River will sweep over them to the neck, though the land is still Immanuel’s, and the nations’ plans will come to nothing, “for God is with us” (vv. 9–10). Then the call (vv. 11–18): let the LORD be your fear, a sanctuary and a stone of stumbling; seal the testimony among the disciples and wait for him. Finally the darkness (vv. 19–22) that swallows those who consult the dead.

Where it leads. The New Testament takes up this chapter directly. Peter applies verses 12–13 to Christians and puts Christ where Isaiah put the LORD of hosts (1 Peter 3:14–15). Paul and Peter both say that Jesus is the stone of stumbling of verse 14 (Romans 9:33; 1 Peter 2:8). Hebrews hears Christ himself speaking the words of verses 17–18 (Hebrews 2:13). And the darkness at the end gives way at once to the promise of a great light, which Matthew sees dawn in Jesus’ ministry in Galilee (9:1–2; Matthew 4:15–16).

For us. We live surrounded by a culture’s fears and voices. This chapter calls us to fear God more than anything else, which is what sets us free from every lesser fear, to keep to his word when others go looking elsewhere, and to wait for him in hope when he seems hidden.

keyVerse.quote: “But the LORD of hosts, him you shall honor as holy. Let him be your fear, and let him be your dread.”
keyVerse.note: This verse does not tell us to stop fearing but to fear the right thing. The person who fears the LORD of hosts is freed from the paralysing fear of everything else. Peter applies it to Christians facing hostility (1 Peter 3:14–15) and puts Christ in the LORD’s place: in a threatening world the answer to anxiety is not stoic courage but a heart taken up with the holiness of the one who, in Christ, has made us his own.

8.reflection:
The people of Judah were swept along by talk of conspiracy and by what everyone feared (v. 12). What fears dominate the conversation around you, at work, online or at home? How can you stay informed without catching the mood?

Isaiah is told, “Let him be your fear, and let him be your dread” (v. 13). How does fearing God differ from being afraid of him, and why does it free us from lesser fears? How does knowing him in Christ shape that fear (Romans 8:15)?

The same LORD is “a sanctuary and a stone of offense” (v. 14), and the New Testament says this of Jesus (1 Peter 2:6–8). Why does Jesus divide people in this way? Have you known him as both?

Isaiah says, “I will wait for the LORD, who is hiding his face” (v. 17), while others turned to mediums (v. 19). Where are you tempted to look for guidance or comfort apart from God’s word? What helps you keep waiting when God seems hidden?

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–10 — A Name on a Placard
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God fixes his word in writing and in a child’s name, and then warns Judah that despising his quiet care will bring a flood, though the land still belongs to Immanuel. Isaiah writes a dated, witnessed notice and names his newborn son Maher-shalal-hash-baz: before the boy can say “My father”, Damascus and Samaria will be plundered (vv. 1–4). Because Judah refused the gently flowing waters of Shiloah, God will send the mighty River, the king of Assyria, to flood the land up to the neck (vv. 5–8). Yet the nations who plot against God’s people will be shattered, for God is with us (vv. 9–10).
verseByVerse.theology: The sign is dated and public, and Isaiah stakes his credibility on a timetable a toddler can measure.
verseByVerse.examples: It is easy to treat the ordinary means God uses (his word read and preached, prayer, the Lord's Supper, a faithful local church) the way Judah treated Shiloah: small, slow and unremarkable beside whatever impressive alternative is on offer. Verse 6 warns that the quiet supply is the one that does not fail.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the LORD said to me, "Take a large tablet and write on it in common characters, 'Belonging to Maher-shalal-hash-baz.' And I will get reliable witnesses, Uriah the priest and Zechariah the son of Jeberechiah, to attest for me." And I went to the prophetess, and she conceived and bore a son. Then the LORD said to me, "Call his name Maher-shalal-hash-baz; for before the boy knows how to cry 'My father' or 'My mother,' the wealth of Damascus and the spoil of Samaria will be carried away before the king of Assyria."
verseByVerse.commentary:
God has Isaiah publish a dated, witnessed notice and give his newborn son its message for a name: Damascus and Samaria will be plundered before the child can say “My father”.

Take a large tablet. The instruction is to make a placard: a large writing surface, in common characters, ordinary script that anyone walking past can read. This is a public notice.

Reliable witnesses. Two named public figures witness it, which is how you proved a document’s date in a world without newspapers. When Assyria strips Damascus and Samaria, nobody will be able to say the prophecy was written afterwards. Uriah the priest is probably the Uriah who soon afterwards built Ahaz a copy of the altar the king had seen in Damascus (2 Kings 16:10–16), so one witness was a man close to the king, whose word nobody at court could dismiss.

Call his name Maher-shalal-hash-baz. Then Isaiah’s wife conceives (see the note), and the words of the placard become a child’s name. It means, roughly, “quick spoil, swift plunder”: words about looting, hung on a baby, to be called across a courtyard every day for years.

Before the boy knows how to cry “My father”. Verse 4 gives the timetable in the only unit at hand: how long before a child can say dada. Perhaps a year or two. Within that time the two capitals whose alliance has Jerusalem shaking will be stripped, and so they were: Damascus fell in 732 BC, and Samaria lost much of its territory and people in the same campaigns.

A family that is the message. Isaiah had already taken one son to meet Ahaz, Shear-jashub, “A remnant shall return” (7:3); now a second carries plunder in his name. The prophet’s children go through their childhood as walking sermons (v. 18), a harder calling than it sounds.

Uncertain wording. The word for tablet is rare, and the phrase translated in common characters is literally “with a man’s stylus”. It probably means ordinary writing that anyone could read, though some take it as the ordinary pen of a common man. The purpose is plain either way: a notice for the public.
verseByVerse.note: Isaiah's wife is called the prophetess (v. 3), either because she shared his calling or simply as the prophet's wife; the text does not say which.

verseByVerse.quote: The LORD spoke to me again: "Because this people has refused the waters of Shiloah that flow gently, and rejoice over Rezin and the son of Remaliah, therefore, behold, the Lord is bringing up against them the waters of the River, mighty and many, the king of Assyria and all his glory. And it will rise over all its channels and go over all its banks, and it will sweep on into Judah, it will overflow and pass on, reaching even to the neck, and its outspread wings will fill the breadth of your land, O Immanuel."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Because the people despised God’s quiet provision and admired the powers around them, God will send the might of Assyria over them like a river in flood, though the land still belongs to Immanuel.

The waters of Shiloah that flow gently. Shiloah was the channel that brought water to Jerusalem from the Gihon spring, a small conduit running quietly along the valley beside the city. It was not impressive, but it was dependable, running gently every day for centuries. It stands for God’s quiet care of his people, with his promise to David, and they refused it: not because it failed, but because it was small.

The waters of the River, mighty and many. So they will get a river instead. The River is the Euphrates, Assyria’s great river, and it is everything Shiloah is not: vast, powerful, impressive, the artery of the empire they have been admiring. And rivers flood. This one comes over its banks, across the border, up through the country, and stops at the neck, the height at which a man is still alive, but only just. The impressive alternative always looks like an upgrade until it is at your throat. In verse 8 the flood becomes a bird of prey spreading its wings over the land (see the note).

O Immanuel. Then, at the end of the flood, the name from chapter 7. It is still his land. The water reaches the neck and not over the head, and the reason is that name, the last word of the verse: God with us. The child of the promise is spoken of as the owner of the land, a hint that he is more than any ordinary child of Ahaz’s day (compare 9:6–7).

Uncertain wording. The words rejoice over Rezin and the son of Remaliah are hard to pin down. They probably point to people in Judah who were glad of the northern alliance and its plan for a new king (7:5–6); some read the Hebrew differently, as melting in fear before those kings. Either way, the people looked to men and not to the LORD.
verseByVerse.note: In verse 8 the flood becomes a bird of prey whose outspread wings cover the land, mixing two pictures of the same overwhelming army.

verseByVerse.quote: Be broken, you peoples, and be shattered; give ear, all you far countries; strap on your armor and be shattered; strap on your armor and be shattered. Take counsel together, but it will come to nothing; speak a word, but it will not stand, for God is with us.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Let the nations arm and plot as they will: their plans will come to nothing, because God is with his people.

Be broken, you peoples. Isaiah turns to the nations with a challenge that is almost a taunt. Twice he tells them to strap on their armour, and twice, in the same breath, tells them what will happen: be shattered. He announces the defeat inside the invitation to try.

Take counsel together, but it will come to nothing. Nations that mean business hold a council and issue a declaration; both are named, and both dismissed. It is a remarkable thing to say from a small hill-country kingdom whose leaders are shaking.

For God is with us. The whole argument rests on the last words, which in Hebrew are Immanuel. The name given as a sign to a frightened king in chapter 7 has become a battle cry. It is not a claim that Judah is strong, or right, or likely to win. It is a claim about who is present. Every plan the nations make is made in a room where God is already standing.

In the New Testament. The New Testament never lets the name become sentimental. It is the name over a cradle in Bethlehem (Matthew 1:23), and it is why Paul can ask what shall separate us from the love of Christ, and answer: nothing (Romans 8:31–39). If God is for us, and with us, the size of the opposition stops mattering.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 11–22 — Let Him Be Your Fear
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: In a land gripped by panic, God’s people are to fear him alone, hold on to his word and wait for him. God warns Isaiah not to walk in the people’s way or fear what they fear, but to honour the LORD of hosts as holy and let him be their fear (vv. 11–13). The LORD will be a sanctuary to some and a stone that trips many (vv. 14–15). The testimony is bound up among the disciples, and Isaiah waits in hope for a God who is hiding his face, he and his children standing as signs (vv. 16–18). Those who consult the dead instead of God’s word have no dawn, and are driven into thick darkness (vv. 19–22).
verseByVerse.theology: The section asks where a believer's fear should point, and answers with the LORD himself. Verse 14 then explains why the same God is safety to some and ruin to others, and the rest of the chapter shows what happens to a people who will not have him.
verseByVerse.examples: A household can live on alarming news until the talk of plots and threats becomes its own way of speaking. Verses 11 to 13 do not ask for indifference to real dangers; they ask that the LORD be set before the mind first, so that everything else is seen at its true size.

verseByVerse.quote: For the LORD spoke thus to me with his strong hand upon me, and warned me not to walk in the way of this people, saying: "Do not call conspiracy all that this people calls conspiracy, and do not fear what they fear, nor be in dread. But the LORD of hosts, him you shall honor as holy. Let him be your fear, and let him be your dread.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God warns Isaiah not to catch the panic of the people around him, but to fear the LORD himself, and that greater fear frees him from every lesser one.

With his strong hand upon me. God takes hold of his prophet about the mood of the country: the danger that Isaiah will start thinking like everyone around him.

Do not call conspiracy all that this people calls conspiracy. The country is in a panic and has developed a vocabulary for it: everything is a plot, every event somebody’s scheme. God’s instruction is to stop using the words. That is a striking command, because a shared vocabulary of fear is almost impossible to resist; joining in feels like realism rather than a choice. Isaiah is to opt out of the national conversation while still living in the nation.

Let him be your fear. God does not tell Isaiah to be less afraid. He tells him to be afraid of something else. Fear is not treated here as a fault to be removed but as something to be aimed. A person who fears God rightly has spent his fear, and has none left over for Assyria. The cure for fearing the wrong thing is not calm; it is a larger and better fear, which makes a man immovable before everything smaller. That fear is not a feat of nerve. The LORD of hosts is the God who has made his people his own, and for the Christian it is his Spirit, given to us as sons, who turns slavish dread into the reverent trust that can stand (Romans 8:15).

In the New Testament. Peter quotes these verses to Christians facing real hostility: “Have no fear of them, nor be troubled, but in your hearts honor Christ the Lord as holy” (1 Peter 3:14–15). Where Isaiah wrote the LORD of hosts, Peter writes Christ the Lord: the one Isaiah was told to fear and honour as holy is Jesus.

What this looks like. Fear is aimed by what fills the mind, so aiming it is a matter of ordinary habits. Watch the vocabulary: when the office or the group chat talks in panic about the economy, the election or the redundancies, you can stay informed without taking up the language of dread. Turn the news into prayer: read the headline, then bring it before the LORD of hosts, the commander of every army there is. Ask the larger question: before a hard decision, ask not first “What will they think?” or “What if it goes wrong?” but “What would please him?” Jesus put it plainly: “do not fear those who kill the body but cannot kill the soul” (Matthew 10:28). And remember whose you are. The one we fear is the one who in Christ bore the judgment we feared, so this fear draws us near instead of driving us away: “There is therefore now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus” (Romans 8:1). A heart settled there has nothing left to spend on Assyria.

verseByVerse.quote: And he will become a sanctuary and a stone of offense and a rock of stumbling to both houses of Israel, a trap and a snare to the inhabitants of Jerusalem. And many shall stumble on it. They shall fall and be broken; they shall be snared and taken." Bind up the testimony; seal the teaching among my disciples. I will wait for the LORD, who is hiding his face from the house of Jacob, and I will hope in him. Behold, I and the children whom the LORD has given me are signs and portents in Israel from the LORD of hosts, who dwells on Mount Zion.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The LORD himself is a refuge to those who fear him and a stone that trips those who refuse him; so Isaiah entrusts God’s word to his disciples and waits in hope, while he and his children stand as living signs.

A sanctuary and a stone of offense. A sanctuary is a place you run to and are safe. A stone of stumbling is the thing in the path that puts you on your face. God is both, not by changing but by being what he is. An immovable rock in your road is either your refuge or your obstacle, depending on which way you are travelling.

The same stone in both halves. Paul applies this verse to Christ (Romans 9:33), and so does Peter (1 Peter 2:8), setting it beside the stone the builders rejected: precious to those who believe, a rock of offence to those who do not. It is the same stone in both halves of the verse, and the same Christ to every hearer.

Bind up the testimony. When the word is refused, it is not withdrawn; it is entrusted. It is bound up and sealed among a small group who will keep it. That is the pattern in every generation where truth is unwelcome: not a louder public campaign but a faithful handing-over to whoever will hold it.

I will wait for the LORD. Verse 17 is the most honest sentence in the chapter. Isaiah does not claim to see what God is doing. He says God is hiding his face, and in the same breath says he will wait and hope. Faith does not mean that God is no longer hidden; it is what a man does while he is.

I and the children whom the LORD has given me. Isaiah and his sons, with their message-names, are signs to the nation. Hebrews takes these words, with the trust of verse 17, and puts them in the mouth of Christ, speaking of the people God has given him: “I will put my trust in him. … Behold, I and the children God has given me” (Hebrews 2:13).

What it means to wait for the LORD. We usually hear waiting as wasted time. In the Old Testament it is the opposite: putting your whole weight on God before you can see him move, and turning down every quicker rescue on offer. Ahaz would not wait; he hired Assyria. Isaiah waits, because what he leans on is not his reading of events but the word God has given (v. 16). No one ever waited as Christ did. He took no shortcut in Gethsemane, and on the cross, with the Father’s face hidden from him, he still cried, “My God, my God” (Mark 15:34). He “continued entrusting himself to him who judges justly” (1 Peter 2:23), and on the third day the Father answered. Because he waited and was not put to shame, your waiting is not wasted. When an answer to prayer is slow this week, keep praying and keep doing the next right thing, rather than reaching for the quick fix you know is wrong.

Uncertain wording. Verse 16 does not say who is speaking. It may be the LORD, so that the disciples are his, or Isaiah, speaking of his own followers. The sense is the same either way: God’s word is kept safe among those who receive it.

verseByVerse.quote: And when they say to you, "Inquire of the mediums and the necromancers who chirp and mutter," should not a people inquire of their God? Should they inquire of the dead on behalf of the living? To the teaching and to the testimony! If they will not speak according to this word, it is because they have no dawn. They will pass through the land, greatly distressed and hungry. And when they are hungry, they will be enraged and will speak contemptuously against their king and their God, and turn their faces upward. And they will look to the earth, but behold, distress and darkness, the gloom of anguish. And they will be thrust into thick darkness.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A people who reject God’s word do not stop seeking guidance; they turn to the dead, and end in thick darkness. The test of every voice is God’s own word.

Inquire of the mediums. Having refused the word of God, the country does not become unbelieving; it becomes superstitious. The appetite for guidance does not disappear when the true source is rejected; it goes shopping. Saul, when God would no longer answer him, went to the medium at Endor (1 Samuel 28).

Who chirp and mutter. Isaiah describes the mediums with contempt: they chirp and mutter, the noises of birds and insects, sound without content. Then the question that dismantles the whole trade: should they inquire of the dead on behalf of the living? The living have a problem and are taking it to corpses.

To the teaching and to the testimony! Verse 20 is the test, and it is simple. Measure every claimed word from God against the word already given. If it does not agree with that, the reason is not that the speaker has fresh light. It is that he has none: no dawn.

Speak contemptuously against their king and their God. The end of the road is a hungry man cursing upward: not an argument against God but a grievance shouted at him, which is what unanswered appetite turns into. Look up: nothing but rage. Look down: distress and gloom. The chapter shuts in thick darkness.

No gloom for her who was in anguish. But the very next sentence in the book, which the chapter division has separated from this one, begins: “But there will be no gloom for her who was in anguish” (9:1). Isaiah wrote the darkness and the dawn as one movement. The people who walked in this darkness are the people who will see a great light, and Matthew sees that light rise when Jesus begins to preach in Galilee (Matthew 4:15–16).

For those who grieve. Those who grieve may long to hear once more from someone they have lost, and that longing is human and is not mocked here. But Scripture forbids seeking the dead (Deuteronomy 18:10–12), and the comfort it offers instead is better: the living God, and a risen Christ who holds the keys of death (Revelation 1:18).

When a culture stops believing, it starts consulting. Many expected that societies leaving Christianity behind would become coolly rational. What has happened is closer to Isaiah 8: horoscopes, tarot, “manifesting” and a whole industry of spiritual advice have flourished as church attendance has fallen. Notice what the mediums offer: guidance with no Lord attached, a spirituality that asks nothing of you. Isaiah’s test still works: does it agree with the word God has already given? The Christian answer to the hunger is not to mock it but to point it home. The God who speaks is not a murmur from the dead. He is the God who “in these last days … has spoken to us by his Son” (Hebrews 1:2), and that Son came back from the dead to say so.

Uncertain wording. The end of verse 20 is difficult. They have no dawn may mean that those who do not speak by God’s word have no light in them, or that there is no morning, no future, for those who follow them. In verse 21 the Hebrew says only that they will pass through “it”, which the ESV takes to mean the land. The direction of the passage is clear: away from God’s word lies only deepening darkness.

8.theology:
Shiloah and the Euphrates. God's quiet, dependable provision was refused because it was small, and the empire's river was preferred; the quiet gift is the one that does not flood.

Fear redirected, not removed. God does not tell Isaiah to be less afraid but to be afraid of something else. We will still catch the national panic and fear the wrong things. Christ feared his Father perfectly in our place and was heard because of his reverence (Heb. 5:7); his trust is counted as ours, so the way back from our fears is to confess them and turn again to the God who is with us.

Sanctuary and stumbling stone. Verse 14 makes God both without any change in him, and the New Testament finds that stone in Christ: the one we either run to or fall over.

9.subtitle: A Great Light — The Child Born to Us
9.intro:
Where we are. Chapters 7 and 8 told how King Ahaz, threatened by Syria and the northern kingdom of Israel, refused the sign God offered and sent to Assyria for help instead. Chapter 8 ended with a people consulting the dead and looking into “distress and darkness, the gloom of anguish” (8:22). Chapter 9 opens with but.

The message. God answers the darkness with a child. Light will dawn first on the lands that were ruined first, because a son of David’s line will be born who is called Mighty God, and his reign of peace will grow without end; the LORD’s own zeal guarantees it. But a people that will not turn to the God who strikes them, and only rebuilds in better materials, will find that his hand is stretched out still.

Why it was said. Isaiah spoke into the Assyrian crisis of about 734 to 732 BC (see the introduction). Tiglath-pileser had already stripped Galilee and carried off its people (2 Kings 15:29), and the northern kingdom, rather than repent, boasted that it would rebuild. Judah needed to know whether David’s house had a future, and Israel why its troubles kept coming.

How the chapter makes its case. First the promise (vv. 1–7): light on Zebulun and Naphtali (vv. 1–2), joy, a broken yoke and burned battle gear (vv. 3–5), all because of the child with four names whose kingdom grows without end (vv. 6–7). Then, with no bridge, three rounds of judgment on the northern kingdom, each closing with the same refrain: a proud boast of rebuilding answered by enemies on both sides (vv. 8–12); leaders and led cut off together, head and tail (vv. 13–17); and wickedness burning like a forest fire until brothers devour one another (vv. 18–21). The refrain runs on into 10:4.

Where it leads. The chapter leads to Christ by direct promise. Matthew says the light dawned when Jesus made his home in Capernaum, in the territory of Zebulun and Naphtali, and began to preach (Matthew 4:13–16), and the angel told Mary that her son would have the throne of his father David and a kingdom without end (Luke 1:32–33). The child born and the son given is Jesus, truly man and truly God, whose government rests on the shoulder that carried his cross. The second half exposes the need he meets: a people who will not turn.

For us. No darkness is too deep or too settled for this light. The hand stretched out still is a warning against meeting trouble with better bricks instead of repentance, and an invitation: the child given is the Prince of Peace, and the way back to God through him is open.

keyVerse.quote: “For to us a child is born, to us a son is given; and the government shall be upon his shoulder, and his name shall be called Wonderful Counselor, Mighty God, Everlasting Father, Prince of Peace.”
keyVerse.note: The name Mighty God (El Gibbor) is the same phrase used of God himself in Isaiah 10:21. Isaiah is not hedging when he calls this coming child God; he is asserting it. The church’s confession that the Son is truly God has its Old Testament foundation here. Matthew, Luke, and John each draw on Isaiah 9 in their portraits of Jesus.

9.theology:
The four names. Few verses say so much about the coming Christ in so little space. The child is born into our race and given from outside it, and he is called what God is called.

The outstretched hand. The refrain, “his hand is stretched out still”, pictures a hand raised to strike and also held out to reach, and the judgment continues because it has not yet done what it was sent to do: turn a people back to the God who still holds out his hand. That hand is still out to us. We do not turn as we should, and Christ, the child of verse 6, turned to his Father perfectly in our place; his righteousness is counted as ours, so the way back is open to anyone who will take the hand and confess (1 John 1:9).

Sin as a fire that feeds itself. In vv. 18-21 wickedness burns, and it is the wrath of the LORD: God hands a people over to what they chose. Isaiah placed the child before all of this, so the answer is already on the page when the reader reaches the worst of it.
9.reflection:
The people “walked in darkness” and then “dwelt” in it (v. 2), and the light shone first on despised Galilee. Where have you seen darkness become a settled address, in your own life or someone else’s? What does it mean that the light came to them rather than waiting for them to find it?

Which of the four names in verse 6 do you most need to know Jesus by at the moment, and why? What difference does it make that “the zeal of the LORD of hosts will do this” (v. 7)?

Israel met disaster by planning to rebuild with dressed stones and cedars (v. 10), without asking why the bricks fell. How do we do the same after a setback, as individuals or as churches? What would it look like to turn “to him who struck them” (v. 13)?

Verse 21 shows brother tribes united only against a common enemy. Where do you see that counterfeit unity today, in politics, online or in the church? How does Christ, who “himself is our peace” (Ephesians 2:14), build a different kind?
9.text: <sup>1</sup>But there will be no gloom for her who was in anguish. In the former time he brought into contempt the land of Zebulun and the land of Naphtali, but in the latter time he has made glorious the way of the sea, the land beyond the Jordan, Galilee of the nations.<sup>2</sup>The people who walked in darkness have seen a great light; those who dwelt in a land of deep darkness, on them has light shone.<sup>3</sup>You have multiplied the nation; you have increased its joy; they rejoice before you as with joy at the harvest, as they are glad when they divide the spoil.<sup>4</sup>For the yoke of his burden, and the staff for his shoulder, the rod of his oppressor, you have broken as on the day of Midian.<sup>5</sup>For every boot of the tramping warrior in battle tumult and every garment rolled in blood will be burned as fuel for the fire.<sup>6</sup>For to us a child is born, to us a son is given; and the government shall be upon his shoulder, and his name shall be called Wonderful Counselor, Mighty God, Everlasting Father, Prince of Peace.<sup>7</sup>Of the increase of his government and of peace there will be no end, on the throne of David and over his kingdom, to establish it and to uphold it with justice and with righteousness from this time forth and forevermore. The zeal of the LORD of hosts will do this.<sup>8</sup>The Lord has sent a word against Jacob, and it will fall on Israel;<sup>9</sup>and all the people will know, Ephraim and the inhabitants of Samaria, who say in pride and in arrogance of heart:<sup>10</sup>"The bricks have fallen, but we will build with dressed stones; the sycamores have been cut down, but we will put cedars in their place."<sup>11</sup>But the LORD raises the adversaries of Rezin against him, and stirs up his enemies.<sup>12</sup>The Syrians on the east and the Philistines on the west devour Israel with open mouth. verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–7 — A Great Light, and the Child
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Into the darkness God speaks a promise of light, and the reason for it is a child. The lands Assyria ruined first, Zebulun and Naphtali in Galilee, will be the first to see a great light (vv. 1–2). The people will grow and rejoice like farmers at harvest or soldiers dividing spoil, because God has broken the oppressor’s yoke as he once routed Midian through Gideon, and the boots and bloodied cloaks of war are burned (vv. 3–5). All of it rests on one birth: a child who carries the government and bears names that belong to God, whose kingdom on David’s throne grows without end, guaranteed by the LORD’s own zeal (vv. 6–7).
verseByVerse.theology: The whole section is God's answer to the dark: the light, the joy and the broken yoke all hang on the birth of verse 6, and verse 7 makes the outcome depend on God alone.
verseByVerse.examples: The names of verse 6 are worth praying with. When guidance runs out, he is Wonderful Counselor; when strength fails, Mighty God; when death has taken someone, an Everlasting Father who will not leave his people to a successor; when there is strife, the Prince of Peace.

verseByVerse.quote: But there will be no gloom for her who was in anguish. In the former time he brought into contempt the land of Zebulun and the land of Naphtali, but in the latter time he has made glorious the way of the sea, the land beyond the Jordan, Galilee of the nations. The people who walked in darkness have seen a great light; those who dwelt in a land of deep darkness, on them has light shone.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The darkness that ended chapter 8 will give way to light, and it will dawn first on the northern lands that suffered first, Galilee of the nations.

But there will be no gloom. Chapter 8 ended in the dark, with people consulting mediums, distressed and hungry, looking to the earth and seeing only “distress and darkness, the gloom of anguish” (8:22). The first word here is but, and it turns the whole book.

The land of Zebulun and the land of Naphtali. Then Isaiah names a particular district. These two tribal territories were the far north, up against the frontier, and the first ground Assyria took: Tiglath-pileser stripped them and deported the people around 733 BC, years before Samaria fell (2 Kings 15:29). They were also the most mixed region in the country, which is what Galilee of the nations means: too many foreigners, too far from the temple, the part of Israel a Jerusalem man would mention with a hint of scorn. First to be ruined, they are first to be made glorious. The light does not start at the centre and work outward. It starts at the edge.

The people who walked in darkness. They walked in darkness, getting on with things, living whole lives in it; and they dwelt in it, a word for settling and making a home. Darkness had stopped being a crisis and become an address. The phrase behind deep darkness is the one Psalm 23:4 uses for the valley of the shadow of death.

On them has light shone. They did not find the light, kindle it or walk toward it. It shone on them. Isaiah writes in the past tense, the prophetic perfect: a thing so certain it is reported as done.

The light in Galilee. Seven centuries later a carpenter from Nazareth made his home in Capernaum, by the sea, in the territory of Zebulun and Naphtali, and Matthew reached for this verse to say why (Matthew 4:13–16). Jesus said, “I am the light of the world” (John 8:12), and no one is too far from the centre, or too long settled in the dark, for that light. It is not found by effort but received.

Uncertain wording. The two verbs of verse 1 can each be taken more than one way: the first means to make light of, the second to make heavy or to make glorious. Most translations, like the ESV, read humiliation then honour. A few take the second as a further blow, but the opening but and the light of verse 2 favour the ESV.
verseByVerse.note: Isaiah 9:1 is 8:23 in the Hebrew numbering, and 9:2 is 9:1 (ESV notes).

verseByVerse.quote: You have multiplied the nation; you have increased its joy; they rejoice before you as with joy at the harvest, as they are glad when they divide the spoil. For the yoke of his burden, and the staff for his shoulder, the rod of his oppressor, you have broken as on the day of Midian. For every boot of the tramping warrior in battle tumult and every garment rolled in blood will be burned as fuel for the fire.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God will multiply his people, fill them with joy and break the oppressor’s yoke as completely as he did in Gideon’s day, until the very gear of war is burned.

As with joy at the harvest. Two pictures of gladness. Harvest joy is the relief at the end of a year’s work when the crop is actually in. Victory joy is the noise of soldiers dividing plunder after a battle they expected to lose. One is the joy of provision, the other of deliverance, and Isaiah wants both.

The yoke of his burden. Three things that press on a shoulder: the yoke of a draught animal, the staff used to drive it, the rod of the man in charge. That is what occupation felt like: not dramatic, just a permanent weight in the same place.

As on the day of Midian. Gideon had thirty-two thousand men, and God cut him down to three hundred, then won the battle with trumpets, jars and torches (Judges 7). It is the standard biblical instance of a victory nobody could take credit for, and the coming deliverance will be that kind: disproportionate, unearned and plainly God’s.

Burned as fuel for the fire. The last image is a bonfire of military kit: the boot of a soldier tramping in step, the noise an occupied people hear in their streets, and a cloak stiff with dried blood. Not captured or stored for next time, but burned. That is not a ceasefire, which keeps the equipment, but an end to the need for it, the same promise as swords beaten into ploughshares (2:4).

The victory behind the joy. The next verse gives the reason, and it is not an army but a child. The decisive battle was won when Christ disarmed the powers at the cross (Colossians 2:15); the bonfire of every weapon waits for his return.

Textual note. In verse 3 the Hebrew as written reads not increased the joy, as in the King James Version; the scribes’ marginal reading, which sounds the same, gives increased its joy, and modern translations rightly follow it.

verseByVerse.quote: For to us a child is born, to us a son is given; and the government shall be upon his shoulder, and his name shall be called Wonderful Counselor, Mighty God, Everlasting Father, Prince of Peace.
verseByVerse.commentary:
All this light and freedom comes through a child, born into our race and given from God, who will carry the weight of rule and whose names declare him wise beyond wonder, God himself, a father for ever and the bringer of peace.

For to us a child is born. Everything in the previous verses hangs on this for: the darkness lifts, the yoke breaks and the boots burn because of a birth. The two verbs do not say the same thing twice. A child is born: the ordinary way a human being arrives, so this one is genuinely ours, from inside the race, with a mother. A son is given: that is not how babies come. Gifts come from somewhere else, from someone who had them first. Isaiah sets both in one line without explaining, and in the eighth century BC the two halves of the sentence state what the church would later confess: Christ is truly man and truly God.

The government shall be upon his shoulder. The shoulder was where a burden went, the same shoulder that carried the oppressor’s yoke two verses ago. What is laid on this one is the whole weight of rule. He went out of Jerusalem “bearing his own cross” (John 19:17), and that is how his rule was won: the shoulder that holds up the world first carried our sins.

Wonderful Counselor. Not a counsellor who merely happens to be wonderful: the first word means a wonder, the term used for God’s miraculous acts. His counsel is itself a miracle. Set that against chapter 7, where a king was offered counsel from God and took Assyria’s instead.

Mighty God. In Hebrew it is El Gibbor. Some have reached for softer renderings, such as divine hero, and the text does not allow it. Isaiah uses the identical phrase a chapter later of God himself: “A remnant will return, the remnant of Jacob, to the mighty God” (10:21). If it means God there, it means God here.

Everlasting Father. This does not confuse the Son with God the Father; Isaiah is not speaking here of the persons of the Trinity. It is a title of care and permanence: a king who fathers his people rather than using them, and never dies and leaves them to a successor. Every royal line is a sequence of funerals. This one is not.

Prince of Peace. Shalom is not merely the absence of fighting but wholeness: everything in its place, nothing broken. Under him things are right, and Paul can say of him, “he himself is our peace” (Ephesians 2:14).

Is this child Hezekiah? Some Jewish readers have held so. Hezekiah was a good king born in this era, but no son of Ahaz could be called Mighty God, and of no human king could it be said that of the increase of his government and of peace there will be no end. The New Testament applies the passage to Jesus (Matthew 4:15–16; Luke 1:32–33), which is why it is read at Christmas.

How Jewish readers take it. Jewish interpreters often read the names differently: the long title belongs to God, who gives the child his name, so that the one who is Wonderful Counselor, Mighty God and Everlasting Father calls him Prince of Peace (so Rashi). The older Aramaic Targum reads the verse of the Messiah, in whose days peace will increase. That grammar is possible, but the plainest reading, followed by the ESV and most translations, gives all four names to the child. This commentary, with Luke 1:32–33, hears in them the child born at Bethlehem.

Uncertain wording. Each name is a pair of Hebrew words, and the pairing is not quite certain: the King James Version prints Wonderful, Counsellor as two names, making five, where most modern translations read four. Everlasting Father is literally father of eternity. Neither point changes what the names claim.

Textual note. The Greek Old Testament renders the names quite differently, calling the child the messenger of great counsel; English Bibles follow the Hebrew, which has all four names (in its verse 5).

verseByVerse.quote: Of the increase of his government and of peace there will be no end, on the throne of David and over his kingdom, to establish it and to uphold it with justice and with righteousness from this time forth and forevermore. The zeal of the LORD of hosts will do this.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The child’s reign will grow without end on David’s throne, upheld by justice and righteousness for ever, and God’s own zeal guarantees it.

Of the increase of his government. Two phrases carry the verse: increase and no end. Isaiah is not promising a golden age, the thing empires have before they decline, but a kingdom always growing, never at its height, because there is no height to reach. Syria and Ephraim are smouldering stumps (7:4); Assyria is a hired razor (7:20) that will itself be broken. Every power in these chapters rises to fall, and the only exception has a child on the throne.

On the throne of David. The promise is anchored to a specific dynasty and covenant (2 Samuel 7:12–16), the one under attack in chapter 7, when a coalition tried to put the son of Tabeel on that seat (7:6). It could not be broken, and this verse is why.

With justice and with righteousness. The kingdom is upheld not by force, nor merely by the right family line, but by justice and righteousness, the two things every king in Isaiah’s Judah was supposed to provide and did not (5:7). It stands because it is right, which no human government has managed for a generation.

The zeal of the LORD of hosts will do this. The guarantee comes last for a reason. Everything promised in verses 6 and 7 is enormous, and none of it depends on Israel, the house of David, politics or anybody responding well. It rests on God’s zeal, his burning, jealous determination to get it done. The failure catalogued next changes nothing: he is not waiting for better material. So when the church seems to shrink where you live, the verse still stands: the increase of his government does not depend on us.

Where Christians differ: now, or in a future earthly reign? Dispensationalists and other premillennial Christians look for a thousand-year reign of Christ from Jerusalem in which this verse is fulfilled, and faithful believers differ here.

This commentary’s view. The angel promised Mary that her son would receive “the throne of his father David” (Luke 1:32), and Peter says God fulfilled his oath to David in raising Christ to his right hand (Acts 2:30–36). Christ reigns on that throne now, and the kingdom will be complete when he returns.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The first round of judgment exposes a proud refusal to learn from disaster. God has sent his word against the northern kingdom, and its people answer the collapse of their buildings with a boast: they will rebuild in dressed stone and cedar (vv. 8–10). They never ask why the bricks fell. So the LORD presses harder, raising enemies on both sides, Syrians in the east and Philistines in the west, to devour Israel (vv. 11–12). Then the refrain sounds for the first time in this chapter: his anger has not turned away, and his hand is stretched out still.
verseByVerse.theology: Verse 10 is the picture of a people who will not repent, and it sounds like courage.
verseByVerse.examples: The refrain at verses 12, 17 and 21 divides the rest of the chapter into three rounds, each ending with the same unanswered hand.

verseByVerse.quote: The Lord has sent a word against Jacob, and it will fall on Israel; and all the people will know, Ephraim and the inhabitants of Samaria, who say in pride and in arrogance of heart: "The bricks have fallen, but we will build with dressed stones; the sycamores have been cut down, but we will put cedars in their place."
verseByVerse.commentary:
God’s word of judgment falls on the northern kingdom, because it met disaster with a proud boast of rebuilding and never asked why its buildings fell.

The Lord has sent a word against Jacob. The turn is abrupt, and it is meant to be. One verse ago the government was on the child’s shoulder and there was no end to peace. Now a word has been sent, like something thrown, and it will fall on Israel, a nation already struck once that has decided what it thinks about that. Jacob and Israel here mean the northern kingdom, Ephraim, with its capital Samaria.

The bricks have fallen, but we will build with dressed stones. The boast of verse 10 is the most quotable sentence in the chapter and the most chilling, because it sounds magnificent: the language of resilience. The upgrade is real. Mud brick was what ordinary houses were made of, cheap and quick; dressed stone was quarried, cut square and expensive. Sycamore-fig was the common tree of the lowlands, useful and unimpressive; cedar came from Lebanon by ship and ox-cart and was what kings panelled palaces with (see Cedars of Lebanon). They answer a disaster by trading up.

Not one word about why the bricks fell. That is the whole indictment, and it is why the sentence is so unnerving. There is no open defiance of God here, no denial, just a people who have taken a blow, absorbed it as a setback and moved straight to the rebuild. Isaiah calls it pride and arrogance of heart. The event was meant to produce a question. It produced a building plan.

When something falls down. The instinct to repair, improve and press on is a virtue nearly everywhere else. Here it damns them, because they used it to avoid the one question the collapse was sent to raise. When something in a life falls down, the better reflex is not grim self-improvement either, but to go back to the God who sent the blow, who has not stopped calling these people his own.

verseByVerse.quote: But the LORD raises the adversaries of Rezin against him, and stirs up his enemies. The Syrians on the east and the Philistines on the west devour Israel with open mouth. For all this his anger has not turned away, and his hand is stretched out still.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God answers the boast with more pressure, enemies on every side, and his hand stays raised because his people have still not turned.

The LORD raises the adversaries of Rezin. The answer to the building programme is not a lecture but more pressure. God raises and stirs up: both verbs have him as the subject, moving nations the way chapter 7 had him whistling for flies and bees (7:18).

Devour Israel with open mouth. Syrians from the east and Philistines from the west: a nation squeezed rather than invaded, by an animal that does not need to hurry.

His hand is stretched out still. A hand stretched out is the posture of a man about to strike and also of a man reaching for someone. It stays out because the turning has not happened (v. 13): judgment continues because it has not yet done what it is sent to do. It is a strange kind of mercy: a God who will not let the consequences stop while there is still a chance they might work.

The hand still held out. Paul hears the same God in Isaiah’s last chapters, speaking of Israel: “All day long I have held out my hands to a disobedient and contrary people” (Romans 10:21, from Isaiah 65:2). In Christ that hand is still held out to anyone who will take it.

Uncertain wording. The adversaries of Rezin is puzzling, because in 734 BC Rezin of Syria was Israel’s ally. Probably the power God raises against Rezin, Assyria, which took Damascus in 732 BC, strips Israel of its ally, and old neighbours then turn on it. Some suggest a small change in the Hebrew to read his adversaries, meaning Israel’s; the sense is unaffected.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 13–17 — Head and Tail Cut Off
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The second round names the root of the trouble and strikes at those who led the people astray. Israel did not turn to the God who struck them, or even seek him (v. 13). So in one day the LORD cuts off head and tail, the honoured elder and the lying prophet, the whole social order from top to bottom (vv. 14–15). The guides misled and the guided were swallowed up with them, and corruption is so universal that even the young men, the fatherless and the widows are no longer spared (vv. 16–17). The refrain sounds again, the hand still out.
verseByVerse.theology: The judgment falls on leadership first and hardest, and the followers go down with them rather than instead of them.
verseByVerse.examples: The section warns anyone who teaches others, and anyone who chooses whom to listen to: a people tends to get the teachers it wants to hear (2 Tim. 4:3).

verseByVerse.quote: The people did not turn to him who struck them, nor inquire of the LORD of hosts. So the LORD cut off from Israel head and tail, palm branch and reed in one day— the elder and honored man is the head, and the prophet who teaches lies is the tail;
verseByVerse.commentary:
The root of the trouble is that the people would not turn to the God who struck them, so he removes their whole leadership in a day, from honoured elders to lying prophets.

The people did not turn to him who struck them. Here is the diagnosis for the whole chapter: not that they were struck, but that they did not turn to him who struck them, nor inquire of the LORD of hosts. When something falls in on a person, the options are to blame, to rebuild, to endure, or to turn to God about it. This nation rebuilt, and did not even ask.

Head and tail, palm branch and reed. Isaiah uses a merism, a way of saying “everything” by naming the two ends: head and tail, the tall palm and the low reed. The whole social order from top to bottom is removed in one day.

The elder and honored man is the head. Then he interprets his own image, and that is where it bites. The head is the establishment, the respected figures whose judgment a nation relies on (see Elders).

The prophet who teaches lies is the tail. Putting the false prophet at the tail is a deliberate insult; the tail is the least dignified end of an animal. But it is also exactly right about the damage he does. He speaks in God’s name, so people follow where he points, and he points the wrong way. A nation can survive bad politicians. It has much more trouble surviving men who tell it, religiously and reassuringly, that nothing is wrong.

Why go to the hand that struck you? Verse 13 assumes something many of us resist: that the hand causing the pain is the right place to go with it. Surely the healthy response is to walk away from anyone who hurts us? But Israel walked away into a building programme (v. 10), not freedom. C. S. Lewis wrote in The Problem of Pain that God whispers to us in our pleasures but shouts in our pains: pain is his megaphone to rouse a deaf world. A megaphone is not an act of hostility. It is what you use when someone is walking towards a cliff and cannot hear you. And the hand stretched out over Israel is the hand that would one day be stretched out on a cross, taking the heaviest blow itself. That is why Christians can turn to God in suffering rather than away from him (on suffering itself, see the note on Job 1:20–22). The one who wounds is the one who was wounded for us, and he still says, Come to me (Matthew 11:28).

verseByVerse.quote: for those who guide this people have been leading them astray, and those who are guided by them are swallowed up. Therefore the Lord does not rejoice over their young men, and has no compassion on their fatherless and widows; for everyone is godless and an evildoer, and every mouth speaks folly. For all this his anger has not turned away, and his hand is stretched out still.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Misleading leaders and the people who followed them perish together, and the corruption is so complete that not even the young, the fatherless and the widows are spared.

Those who guide this people have been leading them astray. The verbs are set against each other. The guides lead astray, an active thing, done by people whose whole task was the opposite. The guided are swallowed up: passive, consumed, disappearing.

Both groups go. Isaiah does not give the followers the exemption a modern reader expects. Being badly led is a real misfortune, but in this chapter it is not an excuse. These people had the law, the prophets and the covenant, and took their directions from men who found it convenient to lie. Somebody chose the guides.

No compassion on their fatherless and widows. This is the hardest sentence in the chapter, and it should not be smoothed over. The fatherless and the widow are the people God commands Israel to protect on almost every page of the law (Exodus 22:22–24), and here they fall outside his compassion. Isaiah gives the reason: everyone is godless and an evildoer. God has not changed his mind about the vulnerable; the corruption has gone everywhere, so there is no longer an innocent class to plead for.

What it does not mean. This is a sentence on one generation in which everyone had joined the rot, not a statement that God has stopped caring for the weak. The same book promises a king who will judge the poor with righteousness (11:4), and God remains “Father of the fatherless and protector of widows” (Psalm 68:5).

His hand is stretched out still. The refrain sounds a second time, and the reach is still unanswered.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 18–21 — The Fire That Eats Itself
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The third round shows sin as a fire that feeds on the people who kindle it. Wickedness burns like a forest fire, and that burning is also the wrath of the LORD, handing the people over to what they chose; they become the fuel, and no one spares another (vv. 18–19). The picture turns to a hunger that eats and is never satisfied, until each devours his own arm: Manasseh and Ephraim, brother tribes, tear at each other, united only in their hostility to Judah (vv. 20–21). The chapter ends on the refrain, with the hand still stretched out and no one taking it.
verseByVerse.theology: Isaiah describes judgment here less as a fire God brings in than as wickedness burning on its own.
verseByVerse.examples: Churches and families can fall into the unity of verse 21, held together by a common opponent rather than by love. It feels like agreement, and it lasts only as long as the enemy does.

verseByVerse.quote: For wickedness burns like a fire; it consumes briers and thorns; it kindles the thickets of the forest, and they roll upward in a column of smoke. Through the wrath of the LORD of hosts the land is scorched, and the people are like fuel for the fire; no one spares another.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Sin is a fire that spreads by itself through a whole people, and that burning is also the wrath of God, handing them over to what they chose.

Wickedness burns like a fire. It is not God who burns here; it is wickedness. Sin is not merely an offence that gets punished, it is a fire, and fires need no one to keep them going.

It consumes briers and thorns. It spreads in stages. First the briers and thorns, the dry scrub at the edge of a field that nobody values (see Thorns and Thistles); then the thickets; then the forest, rolling upward in a column of smoke. That is where it always starts: in the parts of a life or a nation that seem too minor to matter.

Through the wrath of the LORD of hosts. Now both are said at once, and that is what makes the passage honest. The fire is wickedness burning on its own, and it is the wrath of the LORD. There is no contradiction: God’s judgment here largely consists in handing a people over to what they have chosen and declining to put it out (compare Romans 1:24). What burns them is their own.

Like fuel for the fire. Not victims of the fire but its fuel, every person both fuel and flame. And the first sign of a society properly alight is not atrocity but this: no one spares another. Patience quietly runs out everywhere, and nobody lets anybody off anything any more.

The fire that only God can put out. A fire like this cannot be argued with or managed. God put it out at the root when the wrath our sin had kindled fell on his Son, and he gives his Spirit to make a new heart where the old one burned (Ezekiel 36:26).

verseByVerse.quote: They slice meat on the right, but are still hungry, and they devour on the left, but are not satisfied; each devours the flesh of his own arm, Manasseh devours Ephraim, and Ephraim devours Manasseh; together they are against Judah. For all this his anger has not turned away, and his hand is stretched out still.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Sin is a hunger that is never satisfied, until a people devours itself, and brother tribes find unity only in hatred of a common enemy.

They slice meat on the right, but are still hungry. The picture is a man eating in both directions at once and getting no fuller. From fire Isaiah moves to appetite: a fire can be starved, but a hunger like this cannot be fed. The more it consumes, the emptier it is.

Each devours the flesh of his own arm. A man so hungry that he eats himself, starting with the limb he would need to feed himself. It is grotesque on purpose. Isaiah wants the reader to flinch, because nations do exactly this without noticing.

Manasseh devours Ephraim. Here is the arm, named. Manasseh and Ephraim were the two sons of Joseph, and their tribes were the twin heartland of the northern kingdom. They were not neighbours but brothers, one household, the flesh of the same arm, and they are eating each other. The northern kingdom’s last decades were a run of assassinations and coups (2 Kings 15:8–30).

Together they are against Judah. The last and bitterest clause. Two peoples tearing at one another can still agree on one thing, a shared enemy. That is the only unity left to them, the counterfeit kind, produced by hostility rather than love, which holds only as long as the common enemy is there.

The unity of a common enemy. A great deal of modern life runs on this verse. Political movements that agree on little hold together by loathing the other side. Online crowds gather around a shared object of contempt. Even churches can find a warmth in agreeing about who is wrong that they never found in agreeing about who Christ is. It feels like belonging, but it needs an enemy, and when one is gone it finds another, often in its own ranks. That is Manasseh eating Ephraim.

A different kind of unity. Christ did not unite his people against a common enemy; he united them by dying for his enemies, and we were among them. “For he himself is our peace, who has made us both one and has broken down in his flesh the dividing wall of hostility” (Ephesians 2:14). A community built on that needs no one to blame. At its centre is the one who was made the outcast for it.

Why the child comes first. The refrain sounds a third time, and the chapter stops on it: the hand is still out and nobody has taken it. That is why Isaiah put the child and the four names before a word of this ruin. When the reader reaches brothers eating each other under an outstretched hand, the answer has already been given, fourteen verses back. A child is born. The government is on his shoulder. The zeal of the LORD of hosts will do this.

Uncertain wording. The flesh of his own arm is what the Hebrew says. Some translations, following ancient renderings, read his neighbour’s flesh or his own kindred; the meaning is the same, a people turning on its own.

10.subtitle: Woe to Unjust Laws — Assyria the Rod of God
10.intro:
Where we are. Chapter 10 runs straight on from 9:8–21. Its first four verses are the last of the judgments that end with the refrain “his hand is stretched out still” (from 5:25). Then Isaiah turns from the people being struck to the empire God strikes them with: Assyria.

The message. God rules even the empires that do not know him. He sends Assyria as the rod of his anger against his godless people, yet Assyria’s pride and cruelty are its own, and when God has finished his work he will break the rod. So his people need not fear it: a remnant will return to the mighty God, and the proud forest will fall under his axe.

Why it was said. King Ahaz had leaned on Assyria for help (2 Kings 16:7), and Assyria soon became the threat itself: Samaria fell in 722 BC, and in 701 BC Sennacherib’s army stood before Jerusalem (see the introduction). Judah needed to know who was really in charge of history, and whether anything of God’s people would be left.

How the chapter makes its case. A last woe falls on lawmakers who write oppression into statute (vv. 1–4). Assyria is the rod in God’s hand, though it has no idea of it (vv. 5–7). The emperor boasts (vv. 8–14), and God answers that an axe cannot boast over the one who swings it, and will burn the proud forest (vv. 15–19). A remnant will lean on the LORD in truth (vv. 20–23); Zion is told not to fear, for the yoke will break as at Midian and the sea (vv. 24–27). The invader marches to within sight of Jerusalem (vv. 28–32), and the Lord fells the forest (vv. 33–34), clearing the ground for the shoot of 11:1.

Where it leads. The chapter leads to Christ chiefly through the character of God it reveals, and through its promise of a remnant. The God who used Assyria’s free and wicked choices for his just purpose did so supremely at the cross, where Jesus was “delivered up according to the definite plan and foreknowledge of God” and killed “by the hands of lawless men” (Acts 2:23). The remnant returns to “the mighty God”, the very name given to the child in 9:6, and Paul sees that remnant, saved by grace, in the Jews who believed in Jesus (Romans 9:27; 11:5).

For us. No power that frightens us is more than an axe in God’s hand, and none will escape account for its pride. That frees us from both fear and flattery of the powerful, and humbles us, because success is never proof of our own greatness. Lean on the Holy One in truth.

keyVerse.quote: “Woe to Assyria, the rod of my anger; the staff in their hands is my fury!”
keyVerse.note: God is not merely making use of Assyria’s power after the event; he is directing it. The world’s dominant military power is a stick in the hand of the LORD. That does not make Assyria innocent, for verses 12–19 judge it for its pride, but it does make God sovereign over the most frightening human powers of every age.

10.theology:
Sovereignty and responsibility, both asserted. God calls Assyria the rod of my anger and says I send him and I command him (vv. 5-6). Two verses later: but he does not so intend, and his heart does not so think (v. 7). The emperor is acting out of his own ambition, every decision genuinely his, and he is judged for it. Isaiah states both and reconciles neither. This commentary holds, with the Westminster Confession of Faith and the 1689 London Baptist Confession (3.1), that God ordains whatever comes to pass, yet so that he is not the author of sin and the creature's will is not overridden. The New Testament says the same about the cross (Acts 2:23).

The axe. Assyria’s sin was to assume that it had produced its own success. Every power makes that mistake when God is using it and it thinks it is in charge.

Leaning, and the two names in verse 21. The remnant will lean no longer on the one who struck them but on the LORD, in truth, and what it returns to is the mighty God, the name given to the child in 9:6. Paul applies the promise to his own generation (Rom. 9:27-28).
10.reflection:
Verses 1–2 condemn people who “keep writing oppression” through the proper channels. Where might rules you help to make or keep, at work, in church or at home, quietly turn the needy away? What would fairer rules look like?

God calls Assyria “the rod of my anger” (v. 5), yet Assyria “does not so intend” (v. 7) and is judged for its pride. How does holding both truths together help you face evil done to you or to people you love? How does the cross (Acts 2:23) show them together?

“Shall the axe boast over him who hews with it?” (v. 15). Where are you tempted to take credit for what God has done through you, and what would it look like to give it back to him?

The remnant “will no more lean on him who struck them, but will lean on the LORD” (v. 20). What are you tempted to lean on in place of God, and what would leaning on him “in truth” look like this week?
