verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–4 — Woe to Those Who Write the Laws
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The last woe of the series exposes injustice written into law. Woe to those who draft decrees that turn the needy away from justice and make widows and orphans their prey: they are robbing God’s own poor with the paperwork in order (vv. 1–2). Three questions follow that no legal skill can answer: what will they do on the day of punishment, where will they flee, and where will they leave their wealth (v. 3)? Nothing is left but captivity or death, and the refrain sounds for the last time: his hand is stretched out still (v. 4).
verseByVerse.theology: The last woe in this run is aimed at the law itself: injustice done through the proper channels, with the paperwork in order.
verseByVerse.examples: Anyone who writes rules for others, in a business, a school, a church or a home, can ask of each one whom it protects and whom it quietly turns away. A rule can be correctly made and still be a way of robbing the poor of their right.

verseByVerse.quote: Woe to those who decree iniquitous decrees, and the writers who keep writing oppression, to turn aside the needy from justice and to rob the poor of my people of their right, that widows may be their spoil, and that they may make the fatherless their prey! What will you do on the day of punishment, in the ruin that will come from afar? To whom will you flee for help, and where will you leave your wealth? Nothing remains but to crouch among the prisoners or fall among the slain. For all this his anger has not turned away, and his hand is stretched out still.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God pronounces woe on those who use the law itself to rob the poor, and no statute will shelter them on the day of account.

Woe to those who decree iniquitous decrees. Chapter 5 pronounced six woes, and Isaiah then pronounced one on himself (6:5). This one is aimed at those who draft the laws. They are not taking bribes in dark corners; they are writing. There is a process, there are clerks, and the output is oppression with a seal on it. The writers who keep writing has the sound of an industry: a steady output of statutes, each narrowing somebody’s rights a little further.

To rob the poor of my people of their right. The aim is stated with no euphemism: to turn the needy away from justice, to rob the poor of their right, not their charity, and to make widows and orphans into plunder. And they are my people: God takes the theft personally.

Injustice by statute. That is harder to repent of than ordinary theft, because everyone involved can point to a statute. The judge is following the law. The clerk is filing correctly. The system is working as designed, and the design is the crime.

What will you do on the day of punishment? The questions of verse 3 have no answer. Legal skill is worth nothing before a judge who is not bound by their laws; nothing drafted in Jerusalem has jurisdiction in that court.

His hand is stretched out still. The refrain sounds for the fifth and final time (5:25; three times in chapter 9; here). The hand has been reaching since the vineyard song of chapter 5, and nobody has taken it.

Where the woe reaches. It reaches anyone who holds power over others, in an office, a church or a home, and none of us has used it without fault. Christ, who had all authority, used it wholly for the poor and was condemned under a lawful-looking process in our place. His righteousness is counted as ours, and his Spirit now makes his people just where they once used the rules for themselves.

When the system is the sin. Some say injustice lives mainly in structures, laws and institutions that grind people down whoever runs them; others, mainly in individual hearts, and that talk of systems excuses personal responsibility. Isaiah lets neither side off. The oppression of verse 1 is structural, written into statute. But the woe is addressed to people, to those who decree and those who keep writing. Systems are made by hearts and kept running by hearts. So those who blame only the system must ask what part their own comfort plays in it, and those who blame only individuals must admit that a decent person can serve an unjust arrangement for years without noticing. The gospel lets us look at both without flinching. Someone forgiven at the cross has no reputation left to protect, and no need to prove his righteousness by denouncing others. He can simply begin, in his office, his vote or his household, to write fairer rules.

Uncertain wording. The start of verse 4 is compressed in Hebrew, literally something like except one crouches under the prisoners. The ESV gives the likely sense: the wealthy lawmakers will end either as captives or among the dead.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 5–19 — The Axe and the Man Who Swings It
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God rules the empire that does not know him, and he will judge it for its pride. Assyria is the rod of his anger, sent against his godless people, though the emperor means only to destroy and conquer (vv. 5–7). He boasts that his commanders are kings, that every city falls alike, and that Jerusalem’s God is one more idol (vv. 8–11). When God has finished his work on Zion he will punish that arrogant heart, which claims to have gathered the earth like eggs from a nest (vv. 12–14). But an axe cannot boast over the one who swings it (v. 15), so the Light of Israel will become a fire and burn Assyria’s forest until a child could count the trees (vv. 16–19).
verseByVerse.theology: This passage states one of the hardest things in theology and refuses to soften either half: God is directing Assyria, and Assyria is responsible for the pride and cruelty with which it does what God uses it to do.
verseByVerse.examples: Success tempts anyone to read it as proof of their own greatness: the business that grew, the ministry that filled a building, the career that went well. Verse 15 is the corrective. The work may be real; the hand that held the tool was God's.

verseByVerse.quote: Woe to Assyria, the rod of my anger; the staff in their hands is my fury! Against a godless nation I send him, and against the people of my wrath I command him, to take spoil and seize plunder, and to tread them down like the mire of the streets. But he does not so intend, and his heart does not so think; but it is in his heart to destroy, and to cut off nations not a few;
verseByVerse.commentary:
God sends Assyria as the rod of his anger against his godless people, while Assyria, knowing nothing of it, acts from its own lust to destroy.

Woe to Assyria, the rod of my anger. The most powerful empire on earth is a stick, and the woe falls on it before its work has begun.

The staff in their hands is my fury! God does not say he permits Assyria, or that he will make the best of what it does. He calls it my rod, and the fury in the Assyrian hand is mine. Two more verbs follow, I send him and I command him. The orders are specific, and the target is God’s own people, a godless nation.

But he does not so intend. Verse 7 is one of the most important in the Bible for how God governs the world. The emperor does not believe in God and has never received an instruction. He is doing what emperors do, expanding, destroying and annexing, entirely out of his own ambition and appetite, and every decision is genuinely his.

Both true at once. God sent him; he does not so intend. Isaiah puts the two sentences two verses apart and does not explain how they fit together, and neither does the rest of Scripture. The clearest parallel is the cross. In one sentence Peter says that Jesus was delivered up “according to the definite plan and foreknowledge of God”, and that “you crucified and killed by the hands of lawless men” (Acts 2:23). The worst act in history was both the wicked choice of men and the plan by which God saved the world.

Evil never has the last word. No power that oppresses God’s people is outside his hand, and none escapes answering for what it did. Joseph could say, “you meant evil against me, but God meant it for good” (Genesis 50:20). That neither makes evil good nor excuses it; it means evil never has the last word.

verseByVerse.quote: for he says: "Are not my commanders all kings? Is not Calno like Carchemish? Is not Hamath like Arpad? Is not Samaria like Damascus? As my hand has reached to the kingdoms of the idols, whose carved images were greater than those of Jerusalem and Samaria, shall I not do to Jerusalem and her idols as I have done to Samaria and her images?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Assyrian king boasts that no city and no god has ever stopped him, so Jerusalem and its God will go the way of the rest.

For he says. Isaiah lets the emperor speak for himself, a masterpiece of self-portraiture. Nobody had to caricature this man; he only had to be quoted.

Are not my commanders all kings? My officers outrank other nations’ rulers: the brag of an organisation so large that its middle management is more powerful than the neighbours.

Is not Calno like Carchemish? Then six cities set out as equations: Calno like Carchemish, Hamath like Arpad, Samaria like Damascus. Each pair names two cities Assyria had already taken, and the list moves south, nearer and nearer to Jerusalem. The point is the pattern: however large or well defended a place is, they all end the same way.

The kingdoms of the idols. Here the boast becomes theology and gets it exactly wrong. The emperor has noticed that gods do not stop him. He has ranked the temples of the nations he has taken by the quality of their statuary, and concluded that Jerusalem’s God is simply one more, and judging by the workmanship, not a leading example. His officer will make the same speech outside Jerusalem’s walls (36:18–20).

The conqueror’s mistake. He reasons that because he has never been stopped, no god can stop him. But he has never been stopped only because God has been holding the handle. And by counting the living God among the idols he has made the one mistake no power survives (37:23).

verseByVerse.quote: When the Lord has finished all his work on Mount Zion and on Jerusalem, he will punish the speech of the arrogant heart of the king of Assyria and the boastful look in his eyes. For he says: "By the strength of my hand I have done it, and by my wisdom, for I have understanding; I remove the boundaries of peoples, and plunder their treasures; like a bull I bring down those who sit on thrones. My hand has found like a nest the wealth of the peoples; and as one gathers eggs that have been forsaken, so I have gathered all the earth; and there was none that moved a wing or opened the mouth or chirped."
verseByVerse.commentary:
When God has finished disciplining Zion, he will punish the Assyrian king’s boast that his own strength and wisdom gathered the earth like eggs from a nest.

When the Lord has finished all his work. The judgment on Judah runs its full course first; only then does God turn to the instrument. Assyria’s day comes second, and it comes.

The speech of the arrogant heart. What is punished is the speech and the boastful look: the arrogance with which Assyria did what God used it to do. That arrogance is the emperor’s own, which is why he answers for it.

By the strength of my hand I have done it. Three times in one verse: my hand, my wisdom, I have understanding. He is not merely proud of the results; he is certain that he himself is their cause. How different the Son of God, who could have said it with truth, and said instead, “I can do nothing on my own” (John 5:30).

As one gathers eggs that have been forsaken. The image he chooses is chilling because it is so casual. Taking the wealth of nations was like reaching into an abandoned nest: no resistance, no noise, none that moved a wing or opened the mouth or chirped. He describes conquering the known world as an errand a boy could run, and he is not exaggerating.

How it was fulfilled. The Assyrian army was struck down before Jerusalem in 701 BC (37:36), and Nineveh itself fell in 612 BC, as Nahum foretold.

verseByVerse.quote: Shall the axe boast over him who hews with it, or the saw magnify itself against him who wields it? As if a rod should wield him who lifts it, or as if a staff should lift him who is not wood! Therefore the Lord GOD of hosts will send wasting sickness among his stout warriors, and under his glory a burning will be kindled, like the burning of fire. The light of Israel will become a fire, and his Holy One a flame, and it will burn and devour his thorns and briers in one day. The glory of his forest and of his fruitful land the LORD will destroy, both soul and body, and it will be as when a sick man wastes away. The remnant of the trees of his forest will be so few that a child can write them down.
verseByVerse.commentary:
An axe cannot boast against the one who swings it, so God will burn Assyria’s proud army like a forest until a child could count what is left.

Shall the axe boast over him who hews with it? The whole empire is answered with a question about carpentry, and it is unanswerable. An axe does real work, as Assyria’s conquests were real. What it cannot do is take the credit, because it did nothing that a man’s arm did not make it do, and no amount of felled timber changes which of the two is holding the other.

As if a rod should wield him who lifts it. Isaiah pushes it to absurdity: a rod that wields the man, a stick that picks up a person. Once stated plainly, the empire’s view of itself is not frightening. It is ridiculous.

The light of Israel will become a fire. The God who is light to his people is fire to those who set themselves against him: the same holiness, met from opposite sides. Wasting sickness among his stout warriors, and a fire that devours in one day, point ahead to the night the angel of the LORD struck the Assyrian camp (37:36).

So few that a child can write them down. The perfect ending for a passage about a boast. The army that gathered the earth like eggs is reduced to a number a child could write down, and the counting is the humiliation.

Uncertain wording. The last phrase of verse 18 rests on a rare Hebrew word. The King James Version renders it as when a standardbearer fainteth; most modern translations take it, as the ESV does, of a sick man wasting away, which fits the wasting sickness of verse 16.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 20–34 — The Remnant Leans, and the Forest Falls
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God’s people need not fear the empire, because a remnant will lean on him and the invader’s forest will fall. In that day the survivors will stop leaning on the power that struck them and lean on the LORD in truth; a remnant will return to the mighty God, though destruction is decreed (vv. 20–23). So Zion is told not to be afraid: as at Midian and the Red Sea, God will turn his anger on the oppressor and break the yoke (vv. 24–27). The invader marches village by village until he shakes his fist at Jerusalem (vv. 28–32), and the Lord lops the boughs and fells the forest (vv. 33–34).
verseByVerse.theology: The section turns from the empire to the people it struck. A remnant comes back to God, Zion is told not to fear, and the invader's last approach ends under God's axe.
verseByVerse.examples: The march of verses 28 to 32 is how fear often comes: one place at a time, each a little nearer, until it stands in sight of home. God's word in verse 24 was given before the march began: do not be afraid.

verseByVerse.quote: In that day the remnant of Israel and the survivors of the house of Jacob will no more lean on him who struck them, but will lean on the LORD, the Holy One of Israel, in truth. A remnant will return, the remnant of Jacob, to the mighty God. For though your people Israel be as the sand of the sea, only a remnant of them will return. Destruction is decreed, overflowing with righteousness. For the Lord GOD of hosts will make a full end, as decreed, in the midst of all the earth.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A remnant of Israel will stop leaning on the power that struck it and return to the mighty God in truth, while his decreed judgment runs its righteous course.

Will lean on the LORD. The verb is lean, used twice in one sentence to make the contrast exact. They had been leaning on Assyria, which was Ahaz’s whole policy (2 Kings 16:7), and Assyria is the one that struck them. Now they lean on God.

In truth. Isaiah has described religion careful in its forms and empty within, festivals God could not bear and prayers he would not hear (1:13–15). This leaning is real, and the phrase is there because the difference is not visible from outside.

A remnant will return. Two names are hidden in verse 21, and together they tie three chapters into one. A remnant will return is, in Hebrew, Shear-jashub, the name of the boy Isaiah took with him to meet Ahaz (7:3). The name of the child who walked beside his father as a living sign turns out to be a line of this promise.

To the mighty God. In Hebrew, El Gibbor, the second of the four throne-names given to the child in 9:6. Here it is unmistakably God himself, and the one the remnant returns to bears the child’s name.

Only a remnant of them will return. The promise has an edge. Israel is as the sand of the sea (Genesis 22:17), yet only a remnant returns; the destruction overflowing with righteousness is just. Paul quotes these verses of his own generation: “Though the number of the sons of Israel be as the sand of the sea, only a remnant of them will be saved” (Romans 9:27). Belonging to the nation never saved anyone; in Paul’s day the remnant was “a remnant, chosen by grace” (Romans 11:5).

What do you lean on? Everyone leans on something: a salary, a relationship, a reputation. Verse 20 asks whether it is something that may one day strike us, or the Holy One who cannot fail.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore thus says the Lord GOD of hosts: "O my people, who dwell in Zion, be not afraid of the Assyrians when they strike with the rod and lift up their staff against you as the Egyptians did. For in a very little while my fury will come to an end, and my anger will be directed to their destruction. And the LORD of hosts will wield against them a whip, as when he struck Midian at the rock of Oreb. And his staff will be over the sea, and he will lift it as he did in Egypt. And in that day his burden will depart from your shoulder, and his yoke from your neck; and the yoke will be broken because of the fat."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Zion need not fear Assyria, because God’s anger will soon turn from his people to the oppressor, and he will break the yoke as at Midian and the Red Sea.

O my people, who dwell in Zion. The address is tender in the middle of an invasion. The command not to fear rests on that possessive: the striking will happen, but they are his, and they are not to be afraid of it.

As the Egyptians did. The comparison is deliberate. Everyone hearing it knew how Egypt’s oppression ended: at the sea, with Israel free.

In a very little while my fury will come to an end. The anger has a time limit. It has been stretched out through five chapters, but it is not permanent, and it turns, not on them, but on the instrument.

As when he struck Midian at the rock of Oreb. Two rescues are named, both of the kind where numbers made no difference: Gideon’s victory, when the Midianite prince Oreb was killed at the rock that bears his name (Judges 7:25), and the staff of Moses lifted over the Red Sea (Exodus 14:16). Isaiah keeps reaching for these two because they are the times when Israel contributed nothing and the result was total.

His yoke from your neck. The picture at the end is a farm animal unharnessed, the weight lifted off the shoulder and the yoke off the neck. It is the same yoke that is broken in 9:4, as on the day of Midian, in the passage about the child. Isaiah’s promises keep converging on the same gesture: someone taking a load off a neck that could not remove it. Christ does it for good: “Come to me, all who labor and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest” (Matthew 11:28).

Uncertain wording. The last words, because of the fat, are obscure in Hebrew. One likely picture is an ox grown so well fed that its neck bursts the yoke; some translations change the Hebrew slightly and read a place name, making the words the start of the invader’s march in verse 28. Either way the yoke breaks from God’s side, not by any effort of the one wearing it.

verseByVerse.quote: He has come to Aiath; he has passed through Migron; at Michmash he stores his baggage; they have crossed over the pass; at Geba they lodge for the night; Ramah trembles; Gibeah of Saul has fled. Cry aloud, O daughter of Gallim! Give attention, O Laishah! O poor Anathoth! Madmenah is in flight; the inhabitants of Gebim flee for safety. This very day he will halt at Nob; he will shake his fist at the mount of the daughter of Zion, the hill of Jerusalem.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The invader marches village by village down the northern road until he halts in sight of Jerusalem and shakes his fist at it.

He has come to Aiath. These are villages on the northern approach to Jerusalem, in the order an invading army would reach them, closer with every clause.

At Michmash he stores his baggage. The army strips down for the final push. They have crossed over the pass, the steep gorge between Michmash and Geba where Jonathan once climbed out to attack the Philistines (1 Samuel 14:4–5), and at Geba they lodge for the night, which means people in the next village lay awake knowing where the camp fires were.

O poor Anathoth! Now the villages are named as they panic: Ramah trembles, and Gibeah of Saul, the first king’s home town, has fled. Anathoth is an hour or so’s walk from the city and would one day be Jeremiah’s home town (Jeremiah 1:1). Ordinary places on a familiar road fall one by one.

This very day he will halt at Nob. There he stops, on the last ridge, within sight of the city: close enough to make a gesture, and that is what he does. Not an assault, but a raised fist at a hill. The next verse answers the fist.

Which invasion? Sennacherib’s main army in 701 BC came from the coast and Lachish, so many think this is a poetic picture of the threat, or another Assyrian advance. Either way, the fear was real.
verseByVerse.note: Several of these places, such as Madmenah and Gebim, can no longer be located with certainty; Aiath is probably Ai.

verseByVerse.quote: Behold, the Lord GOD of hosts will lop the boughs with terrifying power; the great in height will be hewn down, and the lofty will be brought low. He will cut down the thickets of the forest with an axe, and Lebanon will fall by the Majestic One.
verseByVerse.commentary:
As the invader reaches the city, the Lord cuts him down like a forest, and everything lofty is brought low.

The Lord GOD of hosts will lop the boughs. The answer to the raised fist is a woodsman. Assyria has been a forest through this chapter, its glory consumed and its trees so few a child could count them, and now God comes into it with an axe. Lop, hewn down, brought low: three verbs, all of them downward.

The great in height will be hewn down. The phrase reaches back to chapter 2, where the day of the LORD was against all the cedars of Lebanon and everything lofty (2:12–13). The principle has not changed: there is one who is high, and everything else is timber.

Lebanon will fall by the Majestic One. The chapter ends in a clearing: trunks on the ground, the man with the axe still standing. It is the end of the Assyrian question in this part of the book, and it came true when the angel of the LORD struck Sennacherib’s camp (37:36).

Not the end of the sentence. Isaiah wrote the next line without a break, and a chapter division hides the join: there shall come forth a shoot from the stump of Jesse (11:1). Out of the same felled ground, something green. The axe that ends the empire clears the way, and the shoot is not an afterthought to the felling but the reason a stump was left standing at all. God’s judgments on the proud always make room for his King.

11.subtitle: The Root of Jesse and the Peaceable Kingdom
11.intro:
Where we are. Chapter 10 ended with God felling the Assyrian forest; chapter 11 begins in the clearing, with a green shoot from a cut stump. It is the summit of the promises of a coming King in chapters 7 to 11, after Immanuel (7:14) and the child with four names (9:6–7).

The message. From the cut-down family of David, God will raise a King on whom his Spirit rests, who gives the poor true justice and defeats the wicked by his word. Under him even creation will be at peace, because the earth will be full of the knowledge of the LORD, and he will be a banner to which the nations come, as God gathers his scattered people in a second exodus.

Why it was said. Judah’s king had refused to trust God, its leaders were corrupt, and Assyria was scattering Israel across the world (see the introduction). Isaiah’s hearers needed to know that judgment would not be the end of David’s line, or of God’s people.

How the chapter makes its case. First the King (vv. 1–5): a shoot from the stump of Jesse (v. 1), the Spirit resting on him (v. 2), judging the poor rightly and striking the wicked with the breath of his lips (vv. 3–4), bound with righteousness and faithfulness (v. 5). Then his kingdom (vv. 6–9): wolf with lamb, the lion eating straw, a child at the cobra’s hole, because the earth is full of the knowledge of the LORD (v. 9). Then his people (vv. 10–16): the root of Jesse as a banner for the nations (v. 10), a second gathering from every land (vv. 11–12), Ephraim and Judah reconciled (vv. 13–14), and a highway home as at the exodus (vv. 15–16).

Where it leads. The chapter leads to Christ by direct promise. Jesus is the shoot from Jesse’s line, born in Bethlehem when David’s house had been out of power for centuries. The Spirit came down on him and remained (John 1:32–33); Paul applies verse 4 to his return (2 Thessalonians 2:8) and verse 10 to his gathering of the Gentiles (Romans 15:12). The peace he began at the cross will be complete in the new creation (65:25; Romans 8:21).

For us. Nothing God has promised is finished while the stump remains, so there is hope for lives and churches that look cut down. The King we follow judges the poor rightly, and his people must do the same. And the peace of verse 9 grows wherever the knowledge of the LORD spreads, beginning wherever former enemies are reconciled at his table.

keyVerse.quote: “And the Spirit of the LORD shall rest upon him, the Spirit of wisdom and understanding, the Spirit of counsel and might, the Spirit of knowledge and the fear of the LORD.”
keyVerse.note: The Spirit does not come and go on this King: he rests on him. At Jesus’ baptism the Spirit descended and remained on him (John 1:32–33). Every gift the Messiah’s work requires, wisdom to teach, counsel to govern, might to deliver, knowledge and the fear of God to judge rightly, is present in him at once and without measure (John 3:34).

11.theology:
The stump. The image is humiliating before it is glorious, and that is the lesson. That David’s line had been cut down to a stump never stood in the way of the promise; it was how the promise said the king would come. No king of Isaiah's own day, not Hezekiah nor Josiah, ever came near this portrait; the New Testament names the one who does. Isaiah lays the thread deliberately: the holy seed in the stump at 6:13, the shoot here, and a root out of dry ground with no form or majesty at 53:2.

The Spirit who rests. The sixfold description supplies precisely what every leader in chapters 1 to 10 lacked. The Spirit does not add anything to the Son as God; he equips him as man for the work. And the Spirit who rests on the Son is the Spirit he has poured out on his people (Acts 2:33), so the fear of the LORD and the delight in it that we cannot produce are his gift to us.

A textual note. The Hebrew lists six qualities. The Greek Old Testament (the Septuagint, the ancient Jewish translation into Greek) and the Latin render the fear of the LORD twice, once as godliness, which is how the church came to speak of the seven gifts of the Spirit. And when Paul quotes verse 10 he follows the Greek, in him will the Gentiles hope, where the Hebrew has the nations seeking him; the sense is the same.

Peace by saturation, not by restraint. The lion is not fenced from the ox — it eats straw, which is a change in what a lion is. And verse 9 makes the cause explicit: they do not hurt or destroy for the earth is full of the knowledge of the LORD as the waters cover the sea. The new creation is not kept peaceful by force; it is peaceful because the knowledge of God fills it. Isaiah returns to the whole vision at 65:25, set in the new heavens and new earth, and Habakkuk borrows verse 9 whole (Hab. 2:14).
11.reflection:
The shoot grows from a stump that looked finished (v. 1). Where in your life, family or church does something God promised seem cut down? How does the way God kept this promise, through a birth in Bethlehem, give you hope?

The King “shall not judge by what his eyes see” but judges the poor with righteousness (vv. 3–4). Whose cases tend to be lost where you live, work or worship, and how should following this King change the way we treat them?

The peace of verses 6–9 comes because “the earth shall be full of the knowledge of the LORD” (v. 9). Why can force, education or policy never produce this peace? Where have you seen the knowledge of God begin to reconcile former enemies?

Ephraim’s jealousy and Judah’s harassment will be taken away (v. 13). Is there an old grievance in your family or church that seems as immovable as a sea? What would it mean to bring it to the God who divides seas?
11.text: <sup>1</sup>There shall come forth a shoot from the stump of Jesse, and a branch from his roots shall bear fruit.<sup>2</sup>And the Spirit of the LORD shall rest upon him, the Spirit of wisdom and understanding, the Spirit of counsel and might, the Spirit of knowledge and the fear of the LORD.<sup>3</sup>And his delight shall be in the fear of the LORD. He shall not judge by what his eyes see, or decide disputes by what his ears hear,<sup>4</sup>but with righteousness he shall judge the poor, and decide with equity for the meek of the earth; and he shall strike the earth with the rod of his mouth, and with the breath of his lips he shall kill the wicked.<sup>5</sup>Righteousness shall be the belt of his waist, and faithfulness the belt of his loins.<sup>6</sup>The wolf shall dwell with the lamb, and the leopard shall lie down with the young goat, and the calf and the lion and the fattened calf together; and a little child shall lead them.<sup>7</sup>The cow and the bear shall graze; their young shall lie down together; and the lion shall eat straw like the ox.<sup>8</sup>The nursing child shall play over the hole of the cobra, and the weaned child shall put his hand on the adder's den.<sup>9</sup>They shall not hurt or destroy in all my holy mountain; for the earth shall be full of the knowledge of the LORD as the waters cover the sea.<sup>10</sup>In that day the root of Jesse, who shall stand as a signal for the peoples—of him shall the nations inquire, and his resting place shall be glorious.<sup>11</sup>In that day the Lord will extend his hand yet a second time to recover the remnant that remains of his people, from Assyria, from Egypt, from Pathros, from Cush, from Elam, from Shinar, from Hamath, and from the coastlands of the sea.<sup>12</sup>He will raise a signal for the nations and will assemble the banished of Israel, and gather the dispersed of Judah from the four corners of the earth.<sup>13</sup>The jealousy of Ephraim shall depart, and those who harass Judah shall be cut off; Ephraim shall not be jealous of Judah, and Judah shall not harass Ephraim.<sup>14</sup>But they shall swoop down on the shoulder of the Philistines in the west, and together they shall plunder the people of the east. They shall put out their hand against Edom and Moab, and the Ammonites shall obey them.<sup>15</sup>And the LORD will utterly destroy the tongue of the Sea of Egypt, and will wave his hand over the River with his scorching breath, and strike it into seven channels, and he will lead people across in sandals.<sup>16</sup>And there will be a highway from Assyria for the remnant that remains of his people, as there was for Israel when they came up from the land of Egypt.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–5 — A Shoot from the Stump
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God will raise from the cut-down family of David a King who has everything Israel’s rulers lacked. He grows as a shoot from the stump of Jesse, out of a dynasty everyone had written off (v. 1). The Spirit of the LORD rests on him, with wisdom and understanding, counsel and might, knowledge and the fear of the LORD (v. 2). He delights in that fear, sees past appearances, gives the poor and meek true justice, and overcomes the wicked by his word alone (vv. 3–4). Righteousness and faithfulness are the belt that holds him ready for action (v. 5).
verseByVerse.theology: The section is a portrait of the coming king: where he comes from, what rests on him, how he judges, and what holds him together.
verseByVerse.examples: Verse 4 answers every generation that assumes righteousness needs an army. This king wins with a word, and his people's confidence rests there too.

verseByVerse.quote: There shall come forth a shoot from the stump of Jesse, and a branch from his roots shall bear fruit.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Out of the cut-down stump of David’s family God will bring a new shoot, a King who grows from what everyone had written off.

One picture cut in half. The last two verses of chapter 10 belong with this one. God has just gone through Assyria’s army like a woodsman: “Lebanon will fall by the Majestic One” (10:34). Great trees on the ground, the axe still in his hand. Then, in the silence after the felling, a green shoot.

A branch from his roots. The parallel word, branch, is netser: a sprout, the thin growth that comes off a stump nobody expected anything from. Not a bough of a standing tree, but growth out of the cut, at ground level.

The same stump. Isaiah has used this image before. At his call, when he asked how long the judgment would last, he was told until cities lie waste without inhabitant, and the answer ended with a felled tree and a promise: “The holy seed is its stump” (6:13). That was the seed. This is what came up.

The stump of Jesse. Isaiah could have said David, and did not. He says Jesse: David’s father, a farmer in Bethlehem with a lot of sons, a man of no importance until a prophet came to his door (1 Samuel 16:1–13). To name Jesse is to reach back past the whole monarchy, as if the royal line had been cut down so completely that it had to start again from the family it came from.

A stump was never the obstacle. This is why the New Testament makes so much of a birth in Bethlehem to people of no standing, when Herod, an Idumean (a descendant of Edom, not of David), sat on the throne, and the house of David had been out of power for nearly six hundred years. Matthew probably hears this very word, netser, when he says Jesus would be called a Nazarene (Matthew 2:23). The dynasty had long been a stump. That was never the obstacle. It was the point.

Hope for what has been cut down. God often lets what people trusted be cut down, so that what grows is plainly his. Nothing is finished while he holds the stump.

How Jewish readers take it. Jewish interpreters have long read this chapter of the Messiah: the Targum renders the shoot as a king from the sons of Jesse, the Messiah from his sons’ sons. Maimonides, describing the messianic age, takes the wolf and lamb of verse 6 as a figure for Israel living safely among the nations. The difference is timing: a common Jewish objection is that the world is not yet at peace, so the Messiah cannot have come. This commentary answers that the shoot has appeared and his peace has begun, while its fullness waits for his return (Romans 15:12; Revelation 5:5).
verseByVerse.note: Job 14:7-9 uses the same picture: there is hope for a tree that is cut down, for at the scent of water its stump will sprout again.

verseByVerse.quote: And the Spirit of the LORD shall rest upon him, the Spirit of wisdom and understanding, the Spirit of counsel and might, the Spirit of knowledge and the fear of the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Spirit of the LORD will rest on this King for good, giving him every gift of wisdom, power and godliness that Israel’s leaders lacked.

The Spirit of the LORD shall rest upon him. The first thing said about the shoot is who is on him. The Spirit rushed on Samson, on Gideon and on Saul, and could leave again (1 Samuel 16:14). Here the word is rest: settle, alight, stay, the difference between a bird landing on a branch and one passing overhead. That was the sign John the Baptist was given: the Spirit descended and remained on him (John 1:32–33). Others had the descending. The mark was that it stayed.

The three pairs. Christian tradition has long counted seven gifts here (see the textual note in this chapter’s theology); in the Hebrew there are six, or seven with the Spirit of the LORD at the head. Wisdom and understanding: knowing what is true and seeing how it fits together. Counsel and might: knowing what to do and being able to do it, rarely found in the same person. Knowledge and the fear of the LORD: and it ends there deliberately, because in this book the fear of the LORD is where knowledge begins, not a pious extra added at the end.

Unlike the leaders before him. Set the list against the leaders Isaiah has described for ten chapters: rulers who could not judge, elders who took bribes, prophets who lied, a king who would not ask God for a sign. Every item is something they lacked, and the shoot arrives with all of it.

The Spirit on one Man. The Spirit of the LORD is not a force or a feeling but God himself, present and at work, hovering over the waters at creation and giving skill, courage and words for a task. Here he rests on one Man. In the synagogue at Nazareth Jesus read, “The Spirit of the Lord is upon me” (Luke 4:18), and every wise word he spoke and every healing he gave was the life of a Man filled with the Spirit.

The same Spirit for us. He did not keep the Spirit to himself. Raised and exalted, he “received from the Father the promise of the Holy Spirit” and poured him out (Acts 2:33). So the gifts listed here are not a standard you must reach alone; they are the work of the Spirit who rested on Christ, now given to everyone joined to him. When you face a decision this week and do not know what to do, ask: your heavenly Father will “give the Holy Spirit to those who ask him” (Luke 11:13). See God the Holy Spirit in the Theological Dictionary.

verseByVerse.quote: And his delight shall be in the fear of the LORD. He shall not judge by what his eyes see, or decide disputes by what his ears hear, but with righteousness he shall judge the poor, and decide with equity for the meek of the earth; and he shall strike the earth with the rod of his mouth, and with the breath of his lips he shall kill the wicked.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Delighting in the fear of God, this King will see past appearances to the truth, give the poor and meek real justice, and overthrow the wicked by his word alone.

His delight shall be in the fear of the LORD. Not his duty: his delight. Everything that follows about his justice comes out of that, which is the right order. A judge is only as good as what he loves.

He shall not judge by what his eyes see. These are the two ways every human court goes wrong: misled by how things look and by what people say, the only evidence it has. Samuel could not, until at Jesse’s house, where the shoot of verse 1 comes from, God told him as he looked at Eliab that man looks on the outward appearance but the LORD looks on the heart (1 Samuel 16:7). This King sees the thing itself.

The poor and the meek of the earth. Not justice in general, but the poor and the meek, whose cases go wrong in every court in history because nobody speaks for them. In chapter 10 Isaiah denounced men who wrote laws “to turn aside the needy from justice and to rob the poor of my people of their right” (10:2). Here is the reversal, for the very same people.

With the rod of his mouth. No army, no sword. He speaks, and it is done, which is how the world was made and how it will be judged. Paul applies the clause to the return of Christ, who will kill the lawless one “with the breath of his mouth” (2 Thessalonians 2:8). The strongest thing in the universe turns out to be his word.

For his people. Those who follow this King cannot be content with justice that favours the well connected. In a church, a workplace or a family, his people learn to ask whose case is being lost because no one speaks for it (James 2:1–4).

Uncertain wording. His delight shall be translates a Hebrew phrase that means literally his smelling, breathing in something with pleasure; the same verb is used when God says he takes no delight in Israel’s assemblies (Amos 5:21). Most take it, as the ESV does, as delight; some as keen perception, a nose for what is true. Both suit a judge who is not fooled by appearances.

verseByVerse.quote: Righteousness shall be the belt of his waist, and faithfulness the belt of his loins.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Righteousness and faithfulness are what hold this King together and keep him ready to act, so he is always right and always reliable.

The belt of his waist. Everything before this verse described what he does; this describes what holds him together. The belt in that world was not decoration. A man wore a long robe, and to fight, run or work he had to gather it up and bind it at the waist (see Clothing). The belt turned a loose garment into something you could move in; gird up your loins means get ready to act. So righteousness is not the King’s ornament but the thing that gathers him and makes him able to move at all.

Righteousness and faithfulness. The two words are chosen as a pair. Righteousness is being right, doing what matches God’s own character. Faithfulness comes from the root of amen, on which chapter 7 built its great pun (7:9): reliability, being something you can put your weight on, the very thing chapter 7 asked of Ahaz. He is right, and he is dependable, and the second is what makes the first useful to anyone else.

Unlike Ahaz. What held Ahaz together was an Assyrian treaty; what held the elders of chapter 3 together was what they could take. The coming King is bound by his own righteousness, which cannot be bought off, frightened or loosened, and it is this righteousness that is counted to those who trust him (2 Corinthians 5:21). Paul tells believers to fasten on the belt of truth and the breastplate of righteousness (Ephesians 6:14): what the King wore, he gives his people to wear.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Under this King creation itself will be at peace, because the earth will be full of the knowledge of God. Predators and prey live together, the lion eats straw like the ox, and a little child leads them (vv. 6–7). Infants play safely at the snake’s hole, where the ancient enmity of Genesis 3 is over (v. 8). Verse 9 gives the cause: nothing will hurt or destroy in all God’s holy mountain, for the knowledge of the LORD will fill the earth as the waters cover the sea. This is a creation remade, not merely restrained.
verseByVerse.theology: What is described is creatures changed, not creatures held back, and the cause is the knowledge of God filling everything.
verseByVerse.examples: The peace of these verses is not yet complete, but it has begun. Wherever the knowledge of the LORD spreads, in a home, a church or a neighbourhood, old enemies can already sit at one table.

verseByVerse.quote: The wolf shall dwell with the lamb, and the leopard shall lie down with the young goat, and the calf and the lion and the fattened calf together; and a little child shall lead them. The cow and the bear shall graze; their young shall lie down together; and the lion shall eat straw like the ox. The nursing child shall play over the hole of the cobra, and the weaned child shall put his hand on the adder's den.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Under the coming King even the animal world will be remade, so that predators and prey live together and the youngest child is safe beside the deadliest snake.

The wolf shall dwell with the lamb. Familiarity has flattened these verses, so read what is claimed. Not that the wolf is restrained from the lamb, penned separately or fed elsewhere, but that it dwells with it, the word for settling, living at the same address.

The lion shall eat straw like the ox. This makes the point unmistakable. A lion cannot digest straw; its teeth, gut and instinct are built around killing. To say it eats straw is not to say it has been tamed but that it has been remade. What is promised is not better behaviour in a fallen creation but a different creation.

A little child shall lead them. The herdsman is a toddler. A boy from Jesse’s house once had to fight a lion for his flock (1 Samuel 17:34–35); this child simply walks in front. Then the two most helpless humans, a nursing child and a weaned child, are put at the two most lethal spots in the landscape.

Back to the beginning. In the third chapter of the Bible the enmity was set between the serpent and the woman, and between his offspring and hers: “he shall bruise your head, and you shall bruise his heel” (Genesis 3:15). A heel is what a snake strikes at a hole in the ground. Here the ancient hostility is over, not because the child is protected from the serpent, but because the war has already been won by Christ, the promised offspring of the woman.

Every revolution has promised this. Many political movements of the modern age promised some version of these verses, and several killed millions trying to build it. The trouble was not the dream, which was Isaiah’s before it was anyone else’s, but the method. They tried to make the lion eat straw by force or education, and the lion was still a lion. This peace needs a new creation, not a new policy, and a King on whom the Spirit rests. The American Quaker painter Edward Hicks painted his Peaceable Kingdom some sixty times while his own religious community tore itself apart in a bitter schism: even people who love the vision cannot produce it. The Christian hope is not that we will finally build it, but that the one who has crushed the serpent will bring it with him, and has already begun it wherever former enemies kneel side by side at his table.

Where Christians differ: when is this peace? Premillennial readers see a literal millennial kingdom between Christ’s return and the final state; others take the passage purely as a picture of gospel peace among former enemies (Ephesians 2:14).

This commentary’s view. The peace is begun in the reconciling work of Christ and fully realised in the new creation, when “the creation itself will be set free from its bondage to corruption” (Romans 8:21; compare 65:25). This commentary takes that amillennial view because the New Testament ties creation’s release to Christ’s return and the resurrection (Romans 8:23), not to an age between; faithful Christians who read the passage differently are brothers in the same hope. Will there be animals then? The renewed creation will not be empty of the creatures God made; beyond that Scripture does not say, and we should not claim more.

Uncertain wording. In verse 6, and the fattened calf together is the Hebrew as it stands. Some translations, following ancient renderings, read shall feed together, a very similar word, which matches the grazing of verse 7. The picture is the same either way.

verseByVerse.quote: They shall not hurt or destroy in all my holy mountain; for the earth shall be full of the knowledge of the LORD as the waters cover the sea.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Nothing will harm or destroy in God’s holy mountain, because the knowledge of the LORD will fill the earth as completely as water fills the sea.

They shall not hurt or destroy. To hurt is to damage what is there; to destroy is to end it. Take both out of a marriage, a workplace or a nation, and almost nothing is left of what we mean by trouble.

In all my holy mountain. The scope grows within the line. It begins at my holy mountain, Zion, one hill, and by the end of the sentence it is the earth. The peace does not stay in the sanctuary; it spreads from it until it covers everything.

The earth shall be full of the knowledge of the LORD. Then the cause, the sentence to keep. The peaceable kingdom is not produced by law, by force or by removing the dangerous animals. Wolves lie down with lambs because the earth is full of the knowledge of the LORD; that is what the word for says. And it means every hurt and every destruction now happening comes from a place where that knowledge is thin.

As the waters cover the sea. The measure is the sea: not rain on it or a tide across it, but water all the way down and all the way across, with no dry spot anywhere. Habakkuk found the line and used it again (Habakkuk 2:14). That is the promised saturation: not that many people will know God, but that the world will be full of the knowledge of him as the ocean is full of water.

Knowledge that spreads now. This knowledge is not mere information but knowing God as he has made himself known, and that comes through Christ, in whose face shines “the light of the knowledge of the glory of God” (2 Corinthians 4:6). Every time the gospel is told and believed, the waters rise a little. That is why mission matters, and why the peace begins in a church before it fills the world.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 10–16 — The Signal, and the Second Exodus
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The King becomes a banner for the nations and the gatherer of his scattered people in a second exodus. The root of Jesse stands as a signal, and the nations come to seek him (v. 10). God stretches out his hand a second time to gather the remnant from every land and from the four corners of the earth (vv. 11–12). The old jealousy between Ephraim and Judah departs, and united they overcome their former enemies (vv. 13–14). God divides the sea and splits the river, and a highway runs home from Assyria as there once was from Egypt (vv. 15–16).
verseByVerse.theology: The second time in verse 11 is the key to the section: God's later rescues are built on the pattern of the exodus so that his people can recognise them.
verseByVerse.examples: The healing of verse 13 is put beside the drying of a sea. Anyone carrying an old family or church grievance can take heart from that: what feels impossible to remove is exactly the kind of thing this God removes.

verseByVerse.quote: In that day the root of Jesse, who shall stand as a signal for the peoples—of him shall the nations inquire, and his resting place shall be glorious.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The King from Jesse’s line will stand like a banner on a hill, the nations will come to seek him, and his resting place will be glorious.

The root of Jesse. The shoot of verse 1 has become the root, a quiet change and a large one. In verse 1 he grew out of Jesse’s stump; here he is what Jesse’s family grew out of. Both are true, and the New Testament says so in one breath: “I am the root and the descendant of David” (Revelation 22:16).

A signal for the peoples. A signal is a standard raised on a hill, a rallying point you can see from far away and walk toward. And the traffic is the surprise. The nations have been the problem for ten chapters; now they come to inquire. Not to attack, trade or demand tribute, but to ask. The banner goes up and the enemy comes over to find out what it means.

In the New Testament. Paul quotes this verse at the end of his argument in Romans, the last of four Scriptures showing that the Gentiles were always in the plan: “The root of Jesse will come, even he who arises to rule the Gentiles; in him will the Gentiles hope” (Romans 15:12). What Isaiah saw as a banner on a hill, Paul spent his life lifting up before the nations, and Jesus said that when he was lifted up from the earth he would draw all people to himself (John 12:32).

His resting place shall be glorious. The glory is located not in his throne or battlefield but in his resting place, where he stops. Everything in this chapter has been moving toward something settled: the Spirit who rests on him, the animals lying down, and finally the King himself, glorious in his rest, which he shares with all who come to him (Hebrews 4:9–10).

verseByVerse.quote: In that day the Lord will extend his hand yet a second time to recover the remnant that remains of his people, from Assyria, from Egypt, from Pathros, from Cush, from Elam, from Shinar, from Hamath, and from the coastlands of the sea. He will raise a signal for the nations and will assemble the banished of Israel, and gather the dispersed of Judah from the four corners of the earth.
verseByVerse.commentary:
As he once brought Israel out of Egypt, God will reach out a second time to gather his scattered people from every corner of the earth to the banner he has raised.

Yet a second time. The rest of the chapter turns on these words. There was a first: God stretched out his hand over Egypt and brought a people out of slavery through a sea, and every Israelite knew the story by heart. By calling this the second, Isaiah tells his readers what kind of event to expect, and gives them the pattern to recognise it by.

From Assyria, from Egypt, from Pathros. Eight places, less a list than a compass: Assyria, Elam and Shinar (Babylonia) to the east; Egypt, Pathros (Upper Egypt) and Cush, running up the Nile into Africa, to the south; Hamath to the north; and the coastlands, Isaiah’s word for everywhere across the water. The first exodus came out of one country; this one comes out of everywhere, because the scattering has gone everywhere. God’s rescue is shaped to the size of the loss.

The banished and the dispersed. Two words for the lost. The banished were driven out, removed by judgment. The dispersed were simply scattered, ending up far away without any single moment of expulsion. Both are gathered. It makes no difference whether a person left under judgment or merely drifted: the same banner is raised and the same hand collects them.

Where Christians differ: who is gathered “a second time”? Some see the return from Babylon; dispensationalists see a future regathering of ethnic Israel to the land.

This commentary’s view. The lands named reach far beyond Babylon, and Paul quotes this chapter of Christ gathering the nations (Romans 15:12). The best reading is that it is fulfilled as Christ gathers his people, Jews and Gentiles, from every land into one people. Faithful interpreters differ on Israel’s future: many Reformed readers, from Romans 11:25–26, also expect a great turning of Jewish people to Christ before the end, which fits this reading rather than contradicting it. The old enemies of verses 13–14, Ephraim and Judah, Philistia, Edom and Moab, are drawn from Isaiah’s world to describe the gospel overcoming every hostility (Ephesians 2:14), not a future land war.
verseByVerse.note: Cush is probably Nubia (ESV note).

verseByVerse.quote: The jealousy of Ephraim shall depart, and those who harass Judah shall be cut off; Ephraim shall not be jealous of Judah, and Judah shall not harass Ephraim. But they shall swoop down on the shoulder of the Philistines in the west, and together they shall plunder the people of the east. They shall put out their hand against Edom and Moab, and the Ammonites shall obey them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The old rivalry between Ephraim and Judah will be taken away, and the reunited people will overcome the enemies around them.

The jealousy of Ephraim shall depart. One of the most striking verses, because of where Isaiah puts it: among dried-up seas and gathered nations, as though it belonged in the same category of difficulty.

An old wound. The kingdom split after Solomon, and for two centuries the two halves had been rivals, the north jealous of the south’s temple and dynasty, the south contemptuous of the north’s shrines and coups. Only a few years earlier that rivalry had put an army from Ephraim outside Jerusalem’s walls, trying to pull down the house of David (7:1). This is the specific quarrel that shaped everything in chapters 7 to 10.

Judah shall not harass Ephraim. Both sides are named, each with its own fault. Ephraim’s is jealousy, the resentment of the one who feels overlooked. Judah’s is harassment, the needling of the one who feels superior. Neither is let off.

Not negotiated, but removed. Isaiah does not say they negotiate. The jealousy departs, taken away by the same hand that splits a river, which is a fair estimate of how hard it is to remove an old grievance. The church knows such grudges too, and God does this work now by his Spirit, whose fruit is love and peace where envy was (Galatians 5:22–26). United, they turn together against their old enemies (v. 14; on how to read this, see this commentary’s view on vv. 11–12).

verseByVerse.quote: And the LORD will utterly destroy the tongue of the Sea of Egypt, and will wave his hand over the River with his scorching breath, and strike it into seven channels, and he will lead people across in sandals. And there will be a highway from Assyria for the remnant that remains of his people, as there was for Israel when they came up from the land of Egypt.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God will repeat the exodus on a greater scale, dividing the waters and building a highway so that his people can walk home from exile in peace.

The tongue of the Sea of Egypt. The exodus is staged again with the same props. A sea destroyed: the tongue of the Sea of Egypt is probably the Gulf of Suez, the northern arm of the Red Sea, near the waters of the exodus. A river struck: the River, the ESV notes, is the Euphrates, the far boundary and the road home from Assyria. God waves his hand over it, as Moses lifted his staff, and it splits into seven channels.

He will lead people across in sandals. The first crossing was in haste, at night, with chariots behind. This time they walk over dry-shod at an ordinary pace: the same miracle, with the panic taken out.

A highway from Assyria. That is the road the deportations went out on, the route by which Zebulun and Naphtali were emptied (9:1), the long march east that families disappeared down and did not come back. The same road will carry them home. God does not build a new route to avoid the memory; he turns the road of exile into the road of return, so that nobody walking it can mistake who arranged it.

The true exodus. Isaiah will return to this highway (35:8; 40:3), and the Gospels open with John the Baptist preparing it for the Lord (Mark 1:2–3). On the mountain of transfiguration Moses and Elijah spoke with Jesus about his departure, in Greek his exodus, which he was about to accomplish at Jerusalem (Luke 9:31). The road home from every exile runs through him (John 14:6).

From an axe to a highway. The chapter that began with an axe ends with a highway full of people. Out of it came a shoot with the Spirit resting on him, who judged the poor rightly and slew the wicked with a word, under whom the lion eats straw and a baby plays at the snake’s hole, whose banner the nations walk toward, and whose road runs home from the place of exile. The holy seed was in the stump the whole time, and the woodsman knew.

Uncertain wording. Two words in verse 15 are uncertain. Utterly destroy is a Hebrew verb normally used of devoting something to destruction; some translations read dry up, a verb differing by one letter, which suits the crossing. Scorching breath renders a word found only here, probably a hot, mighty wind, like the east wind that drove back the sea (Exodus 14:21). The sense is clear either way.
verseByVerse.note: “The River” is the Euphrates (ESV note).

12.subtitle: A Song of Salvation
12.intro:
Where we are. Chapter 12 is the short hymn that closes the first part of the book (chapters 1 to 12). After the indictment, the vision of the Holy One and the promises of Immanuel, the child and the shoot of Jesse, the people God has rescued break into song “in that day”, the day of the second exodus just promised (11:10–16).

The message. Judgment is not God’s last word to his people; this song is. They will thank him that his anger has turned away and he has comforted them, and confess that God himself has become their salvation, so they trust and are not afraid. And they will tell the whole earth what he has done, because the Holy One of Israel is great in their midst.

Why it was said. Isaiah’s hearers faced Assyrian invasion, and their children would face exile in Babylon (see the introduction). They had heard much of God’s anger, and needed to know where his ways with them would end.

How the chapter makes its case. Two short stanzas, each opening “You will say in that day”. The first is personal (vv. 1–3): thanks that God’s anger has turned to comfort (v. 1), trust in the words of the song Israel sang at the Red Sea (v. 2), and joy in drawing water from the wells of salvation (v. 3). The second turns outward (vv. 4–6): give thanks, call on his name and make his deeds known among the peoples (v. 4); sing, for he has done gloriously (v. 5); shout for joy, for the Holy One of Israel is great in your midst (v. 6).

Where it leads. The chapter leads to Christ by promise and pattern: it is the song of the new exodus, sung by those he redeems. The anger turns away because it fell on the Servant who was wounded for our transgressions (53:5), Christ our propitiation (Romans 3:25). The word for salvation, yeshuah, echoes the name Jesus, given because he would save his people from their sins (Matthew 1:21); at the Feast of Tabernacles he offered himself as the water (John 7:37–38); and the Holy One came to live in the midst of his people when the Word became flesh (John 1:14). The redeemed will sing it in full as “the song of Moses, the servant of God, and the song of the Lamb” (Revelation 15:3).

For us. Christian praise begins with honest thanks that we deserved God’s anger and have received his comfort instead. Keep drawing from the wells with joy, in his word, in prayer and at his table, and let what he has done for you spill over into telling others.

keyVerse.quote: “Behold, God is my salvation; I will trust, and will not be afraid; for the LORD GOD is my strength and my song, and he has become my salvation.”
keyVerse.note: The salvation this song celebrates turns out, in the fullness of time, to have a name: the child was to be called Jesus, for he will save his people from their sins (Matt. 1:21). The song that brings the first section of Isaiah to a close is a song about the one who will bring all of God’s purposes to their close.

12.reflection:
The song begins, “though you were angry with me, your anger turned away, that you might comfort me” (v. 1). Why does praise that admits we deserved God’s anger ring truer than praise that pretends nothing was wrong? How did God’s anger turn away from us?

“I will trust, and will not be afraid” (v. 2). What fear are you facing at present, and what difference does it make that God himself has become your salvation, not merely your helper?

Jesus offered himself as the source of living water (John 7:37–38). What helps you keep coming back to him “with joy” (v. 3), and what tends to turn it into mere duty?

Verse 4 joins thanking God and telling others in one breath. Who in your life might you tell, simply and gently, what God has done for you? What would make it easier to begin?
12.text: <sup>1</sup>You will say in that day: "I will give thanks to you, O LORD, for though you were angry with me, your anger turned away, that you might comfort me.<sup>2</sup>"Behold, God is my salvation; I will trust, and will not be afraid; for the LORD GOD is my strength and my song, and he has become my salvation."<sup>3</sup>With joy you will draw water from the wells of salvation.<sup>4</sup>And you will say in that day: "Give thanks to the LORD, call upon his name, make known his deeds among the peoples, proclaim that his name is exalted.<sup>5</sup>"Sing praises to the LORD, for he has done gloriously; let this be made known in all the earth.<sup>6</sup>Shout, and sing for joy, O inhabitant of Zion, for great in your midst is the Holy One of Israel."

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–3 — You Were Angry, and You Comforted Me
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The rescued begin their song with honest thanks: God’s anger was real, and it has turned to comfort. One forgiven person speaks to God, admitting the anger and rejoicing that it turned away so that God could comfort (v. 1). Then, in the words Israel sang at the Red Sea, he confesses that God himself is his salvation, his strength and his song, so he will trust and not be afraid (v. 2). And the whole people are pictured drawing water with joy from wells of salvation that never run dry (v. 3).
verseByVerse.theology: The first stanza is personal: one forgiven person speaking to God, and then to himself about God.
verseByVerse.examples: A believer who sings an old psalm or hymn in a hard week is doing what this chapter describes: borrowing the words of those rescued before, and finding they fit.

verseByVerse.quote: You will say in that day: "I will give thanks to you, O LORD, for though you were angry with me, your anger turned away, that you might comfort me. "Behold, God is my salvation; I will trust, and will not be afraid; for the LORD GOD is my strength and my song, and he has become my salvation."
verseByVerse.commentary:
On the day of salvation God’s people will thank him that his anger has turned to comfort, and confess that he himself is their salvation, so they trust him without fear.

You will say in that day. After eleven chapters of vineyard, woes and Assyrian armies comes a song. That day is the day of 11:10–16, when the root of Jesse is raised as a banner and God brings his people home; this is what they will sing on the far side.

Though you were angry with me. The first thing said is not I was innocent or it was a misunderstanding. It is you were angry with me, stated plainly, in the past tense, as a fact about which there is now no argument. Praise that has to pretend nothing was wrong is always thin, because everyone knows better. This song knows exactly what it was rescued from, which is why it can be glad without reserve.

That you might comfort me. The loveliest words in the verse give the purpose: the anger turned away that you might comfort me. God turned his anger away in order to get to the comforting. It is the note on which the second half of the book will open: “Comfort, comfort my people” (40:1).

Behold, God is my salvation. Not only the one who gives salvation, but the salvation itself: he has become my salvation. Verse 2 repeats what Israel sang on the far bank of the Red Sea: “The LORD is my strength and my song, and he has become my salvation” (Exodus 15:2). Isaiah puts the old song in the mouth of a new generation because the rescue is the same rescue and the Redeemer the same Redeemer, which is why the church has always been able to sing songs written by people it never met.

I will trust, and will not be afraid. The trusting comes first and the fearlessness follows. Nobody here is told to stop being afraid by sheer willpower; the God who has become their salvation is the reason they need not be.

How can God’s anger turn away? The song does not say, but the rest of the book does: the Servant of chapter 53 is wounded for our transgressions, and the chastisement that brought us peace is laid on him (53:5). The New Testament calls Christ the propitiation for our sins, the one in whom God’s anger was not ignored but borne (Romans 3:25; 5:9). The comfort of this verse is that the anger, once real, has nowhere left to fall on those who are his.

Uncertain wording. The LORD GOD in verse 2 is unusual Hebrew: the short divine name Yah followed by the full name, a doubling for emphasis. And the word for my song may also mean my might or my protection, both here and in Exodus 15:2. Most translations keep song, which suits a chapter that is itself a hymn.

verseByVerse.quote: With joy you will draw water from the wells of salvation.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Salvation is like water from wells that never run dry, and God’s people will keep drawing from them with joy.

The wells of salvation. In a country where water is the daily problem, a well is where a household walks every morning, and the difference between a village with one and a village without is the difference between staying alive and having to leave (see Wells and Cisterns). To be told there are wells, plural, is to be told the supply is not going to run out.

Salvation. The word Isaiah chooses is yeshuah, close to Yeshua, the Hebrew form of the name that would one day be given to a boy in Nazareth, because he would save his people from their sins (Matthew 1:21).

At the Feast of Tabernacles. Centuries later, at the Feast of Tabernacles, priests carried water in a golden pitcher from the pool of Siloam up to the temple and poured it out at the altar, and later Jewish writings connect this verse with that rite. On the last day of the feast, with the water ceremony fresh in everyone’s memory, Jesus stood up in the temple courts and cried out, “If anyone thirsts, let him come to me and drink” (John 7:37–38). He was standing in front of people who had just sung about wells of salvation and telling them where the well was.

With joy you will draw water. The word to keep is joy. Not duty, not mere relief: drawing water here is glad, the way a homecoming is glad. Whatever else the Christian life is, it is meant to involve going back to the same source again and again, in his word, in prayer and at his table, and being pleased about it.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 4–6 — Make Known His Deeds Among the Peoples
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Salvation received becomes salvation announced, as the song turns outward to the whole earth. The people urge one another to give thanks, call on God’s name, make known his deeds among the peoples and proclaim that his name is exalted (v. 4). They sing because he has done gloriously, and that must be known in all the earth (v. 5). The song ends with a shout of joy from Zion: the Holy One of Israel, whose holiness once undid Isaiah, is great in their midst (v. 6).
verseByVerse.theology: Those who have received salvation go on to announce it, not as a reluctant duty but as an overflow: a report this good does not stay in a room. For the church the telling is the Spirit's work as much as ours; he was given so that ordinary forgiven people would be witnesses (Acts 1:8).
verseByVerse.examples: Verse 4 does not ask every believer to become a preacher. It asks that what God has done be told, at a kitchen table or over a fence as readily as from a pulpit, because he has done gloriously.

verseByVerse.quote: And you will say in that day: "Give thanks to the LORD, call upon his name, make known his deeds among the peoples, proclaim that his name is exalted. "Sing praises to the LORD, for he has done gloriously; let this be made known in all the earth. Shout, and sing for joy, O inhabitant of Zion, for great in your midst is the Holy One of Israel."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Those whom God has saved will praise him and tell the whole world what he has done, shouting for joy because the Holy One of Israel lives among them.

And you will say in that day. Now everything faces outward. Count the verbs: give thanks, call, make known, proclaim. The first two are directed to God and the second two at everybody else, and Isaiah puts them in one sentence without a seam. There is no moment in this song when the community finishes worshipping and starts evangelising. The same breath does both.

For he has done gloriously. The reason for the singing is not the experience of the singers but the quality of what God did, and a thing done that well cannot reasonably be kept in one country: let this be made known in all the earth.

Great in your midst is the Holy One of Israel. The last line takes the book back to its beginning. In chapter 6 Isaiah stood in the temple while the seraphim called to one another, Holy, holy, holy is the LORD of hosts; the building shook, and he said, Woe is me! For I am lost. That is what the holiness of God did to the best man in Jerusalem. Here the same title is on the lips of ordinary people, and it is the reason they are shouting with joy. Nothing has changed about the holiness. What has changed is that a coal came from the altar, the guilt was taken away, and the anger turned aside so that comfort could get through.

The gospel in one line. He is holy, and in the middle of them, and they are singing about it. The holiness that ought to undo a sinner becomes the thing he cannot stop celebrating. It came true when the Word became flesh and dwelt among us (John 1:14), and it will be complete when the redeemed sing “the song of Moses, the servant of God, and the song of the Lamb” (Revelation 15:3).

How do I make known his deeds? The song does not ask for a speech; it asks people to tell what God has done. Start with what he did for you. Jesus sent a healed man home with this charge: Go home to your friends and tell them how much the Lord has done for you, and how he has had mercy on you (Mark 5:19). When a neighbour asks how you got through the redundancy or the diagnosis, the door is open; say plainly that God held you, and how. Point past yourself. The deed to tell in the end is the cross and the empty tomb, not your own improvement: your story is the way in, and his is the thing to tell. Thank him aloud at home first. People who give thanks and call on his name at the table and with their children find words for him in public. Be ready, and gentle. Peter describes Christians as always being prepared to make a defense to anyone who asks you for a reason for the hope that is in you; yet do it with gentleness and respect (1 Peter 3:15). You are not selling anything. The one who has done gloriously is great in your midst, and you are simply saying so.

12.theology:
Praise that names what it was rescued from. True praise admits that the anger was real and has turned, and it turned that you might comfort me.

The same song as the sea. The rescue and the Redeemer are the same as at the Red Sea, and the trust comes first and the fearlessness follows.

The wells, and the circle closed. The wells of salvation point to the one who stood in the temple and said where the well was (John 7:37-38), and the song ends with the Holy One of chapter 6 in the midst of a people who are no longer undone by him but glad.

13.subtitle: The Oracle Against Babylon
13.intro:
Where we are. Chapters 1–12 have set out Judah’s sin and its coming King, closing in a song of salvation. Now a new block begins, the oracles against the nations (chapters 13–23), and it opens not with Assyria, the danger at the door, but with Babylon, in Isaiah’s day still a restless province of the Assyrian empire.

The message. God rules the empires as surely as he rules Judah, and he has fixed a day to bring down human pride wherever it sets itself up in his place. Babylon, “the glory of kingdoms” (v. 19), will fall to an army God himself musters and its fall is a window on the last day of the LORD, when he will “punish the world for its evil” (v. 11). No power is permanent but his.

Why it was said. Judah lived between giants: Assyria pressing on its borders, and later Babylon, which courted Judah as an ally (39:1–7) before destroying Jerusalem (see the introduction). A small people needed to know that the empires are not the last word, and that the God of Zion is the Judge of all the earth.

How the chapter makes its case. God raises a banner and summons his “consecrated ones”, a pagan army that does not know whose work it is doing (vv. 1–5). The day of the LORD breaks, and hands go limp and hearts melt (vv. 6–8). Then the language outgrows one city: sun, moon and stars go dark, heaven and earth shake, and the world is punished for its pride (vv. 9–13). The sack is told without softening (vv. 14–16). Last, God names the Medes, who cannot be bought off, and Babylon goes the way of Sodom, its palaces left to hyenas and jackals (vv. 17–22).

Where it leads. The chapter leads to Christ through the day of the LORD it describes and the holiness of God it reveals against all pride. Jesus took up the words of verse 10 for his own coming (Matthew 24:29), and Revelation takes Babylon as the name of every proud world power that will fall before him (Revelation 18:2). Yet the darkness of that day fell first on Christ himself, when darkness covered the land as he bore his people’s sin (Mark 15:33). The Judge of the last day has already stood under its wrath, so that it need not fall on those who trust him.

For us. No empire, ideology or market that looks permanent will outlast the day God has set, so we need neither fear it nor envy it. And the same day that will bring down every proud heart calls us to humble ourselves now and run to Christ, who took its darkness for us.

keyVerse.quote: “I will punish the world for its evil, and the wicked for their iniquity; I will put an end to the pomp of the arrogant, and lay low the pompous pride of the ruthless.”
keyVerse.note: The oracle against one historical empire has this universal horizon: “I will punish the world.” Babylon is the example; the arrogance of the whole world is what God charges. Every empire that mistakes its power for permanence is, in Isaiah’s vision, standing where Babylon stood, and heading where Babylon went.

13.reflection:
God calls a pagan army “my consecrated ones” (v. 3), soldiers who had no idea they were serving him. Where is it hardest for you to believe that God rules over powers that do not acknowledge him? How does this chapter help?

Of all the world’s sins, verse 11 singles out “the pomp of the arrogant”. Why is pride the sin this chapter names? What forms does it take in our culture, and in your own heart?

Jesus used the language of verse 10 for his own return (Matthew 24:29), and darkness covered the land when he died (Mark 15:33). How does knowing that Christ bore God’s judgment change the way a believer looks towards the day of the LORD?

Babylon looked permanent and became a ruin (vv. 19–22). What power or system seems permanent to you today? How can Christians live under it without fear and without envy?
