The sound of an uproar of kingdoms, of nations gathering together! The LORD of hosts is mustering a host for battle.<sup>5</sup>They come from a distant land, from the end of the heavens, the LORD and the weapons of his indignation, to destroy the whole land.<sup>6</sup>Wail, for the day of the LORD is near; as destruction from the Almighty it will come!<sup>7</sup>Therefore all hands will be feeble, and every human heart will melt.<sup>8</sup>They will be dismayed: pangs and agony will seize them; they will be in anguish like a woman in labor. They will look aghast at one another; their faces will be aflame.<sup>9</sup>Behold, the day of the LORD comes, cruel, with wrath and fierce anger, to make the land a desolation and to destroy its sinners from it.<sup>10</sup>For the stars of the heavens and their constellations will not give their light; the sun will be dark at its rising, and the moon will not shed its light.<sup>11</sup>I will punish the world for its evil, and the wicked for their iniquity; I will put an end to the pomp of the arrogant, and lay low the pompous pride of the ruthless.<sup>12</sup>I will make people more rare than fine gold, and mankind than the gold of Ophir.<sup>13</sup>Therefore I will make the heavens tremble, and the earth will be shaken out of its place, at the wrath of the LORD of hosts in the day of his fierce anger.<sup>14</sup>And like a hunted gazelle, or like sheep with none to gather them, each will turn to his own people, and each will flee to his own land.<sup>15</sup>Whoever is found will be thrust through, and whoever is caught will fall by the sword.<sup>16</sup>Their infants will be dashed in pieces before their eyes; their houses will be plundered and their wives ravished.<sup>17</sup>Behold, I am stirring up the Medes against them, who have no regard for silver and do not delight in gold.<sup>18</sup>Their bows will slaughter the young men; they will have no mercy on the fruit of the womb; their eyes will not pity children.<sup>19</sup>And Babylon, the glory of kingdoms, the splendor and pomp of the Chaldeans, will be like Sodom and Gomorrah when God overthrew them.<sup>20</sup>It will never be inhabited or lived in for all generations; no Arab will pitch his tent there; no shepherds will make their flocks lie down there.<sup>21</sup>But wild animals will lie down there, and their houses will be full of howling creatures; there ostriches will dwell, and there wild goats will dance.<sup>22</sup>Hyenas will cry in its towers, and jackals in the pleasant palaces; its time is close at hand and its days will not be prolonged.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–16 — Why There Are Eleven of These
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God musters the armies of the world, and the day he brings on proud Babylon is a preview of the last day for the whole world. He raises a banner and summons his “consecrated ones”, a pagan army that does not know it serves him, and the roar of the nations gathering is his roll call (vv. 1–5). The day of the LORD breaks, and hands go limp and hearts melt as in labour (vv. 6–8). Then the vision widens past one city: the lights of heaven go out, heaven and earth shake, and the world is punished for its pride (vv. 9–13). Verses 14–16 then show, without softening, what the fall of a city meant for those inside it.
verseByVerse.theology: These oracles are not foreign policy. They say that the God of a small hill kingdom governs every empire on the map, that no power is outside his jurisdiction, and that his people never have to treat history as though he were absent from it. Each oracle also turns toward mercy somewhere.
verseByVerse.examples: Babylon is placed first although Assyria was the present danger (in Isaiah's day Babylon was a restless province courting Judah as an ally, 39:1–7), because Babylon is more than a country in this book: it is the standing name for human empire that puts itself in God’s place.

verseByVerse.quote: The oracle concerning Babylon which Isaiah the son of Amoz saw.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Here begin the oracles in which God claims every nation as his to judge, and the first is against Babylon, shown to Isaiah long before Babylon became a world power.

Which Isaiah the son of Amoz saw. The block runs to chapter 23. The signature is the same as 1:1 and 2:1: what follows is not political commentary but something the prophet was shown, more than a century before Babylon destroyed Jerusalem, while it was still a restless province under Assyria.
verseByVerse.note: Oracle translates a Hebrew word that can also mean a burden: a weighty message laid on the prophet to carry.

verseByVerse.quote: On a bare hill raise a signal; cry aloud to them; wave the hand for them to enter the gates of the nobles. I myself have commanded my consecrated ones, and have summoned my mighty men to execute my anger, my proudly exulting ones.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God himself summons a distant army against Babylon, and though its soldiers fight for their own glory, he calls them his own, set apart for his purpose.

On a bare hill raise a signal. A banner on a treeless hill could be seen for miles, and with shouts and waving arms it summoned troops from far away. The army is called to enter the gates of the nobles, probably the gates of proud Babylon itself, though the city is not named again until verse 19. The voice giving the orders is God’s: I myself have commanded.

My consecrated ones. The striking phrase is temple vocabulary, used of people set apart for a holy purpose, and here it describes a pagan army. They have no idea they are consecrated. God calls them his anyway, as he called Assyria his rod three chapters earlier (10:5).

My proudly exulting ones. The soldiers think their victories are their own; God calls them my mighty men all the same. Their pride is real and they will answer for it, as Assyria did (10:12–15), but it does not take them one step outside his purpose.

verseByVerse.quote: The sound of a tumult is on the mountains as of a great multitude! The sound of an uproar of kingdoms, of nations gathering together! The LORD of hosts is mustering a host for battle. They come from a distant land, from the end of the heavens, the LORD and the weapons of his indignation, to destroy the whole land.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The roar of nations gathering for war is the LORD of hosts calling his army to the roll, and he comes with it as the one who wields every weapon.

The LORD of hosts is mustering a host. First a roar on the mountains as nation after nation gathers; then the explanation, with a play on words. LORD of hosts means the LORD of armies, of heaven and earth, and here he is literally mustering a host. What sounds to the listeners like the politics of empire is a roll call he is taking.

From the end of the heavens. The army comes from a distant land; verse 17 will name the Medes, from the mountains east of Babylon. Isaiah puts the LORD and his soldiers in one phrase: the LORD and the weapons of his indignation. The armies are the weapons; he is the one who wields them, and the target is the whole land.

verseByVerse.quote: Wail, for the day of the LORD is near; as destruction from the Almighty it will come! Therefore all hands will be feeble, and every human heart will melt. They will be dismayed: pangs and agony will seize them; they will be in anguish like a woman in labor. They will look aghast at one another; their faces will be aflame.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The day of the LORD is near, and when it breaks on Babylon no strength or courage will stand: terror will seize every body like the pains of labour.

Wail, for the day of the LORD is near. The call to the people under attack is to lament, not to fight. The Hebrew has a sound play English cannot keep: destruction (shod) comes from the Almighty (Shaddai). The ruin will come from the God whose name it echoes.

Every human heart will melt. Isaiah does not describe fear as a feeling. He describes what it does to a body when the news arrives: hands drop, hearts melt, faces burn.

Like a woman in labor. The picture is chosen for two things: the pain cannot be escaped once it begins, and it comes suddenly, at a time no one has fixed. Paul uses the same picture for the last day: sudden destruction “as labor pains come upon a pregnant woman, and they will not escape” (1 Thessalonians 5:3). The faces aflame are probably flushed with terror and shame as people stare at one another and find no help there.

verseByVerse.quote: Behold, the day of the LORD comes, cruel, with wrath and fierce anger, to make the land a desolation and to destroy its sinners from it. For the stars of the heavens and their constellations will not give their light; the sun will be dark at its rising, and the moon will not shed its light.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The day of the LORD is God’s judgment falling on sin, and here the fall of Babylon opens into a picture of the last day, when creation itself goes dark.

The day of the LORD comes. Everything so far could describe the sack of a city; what follows could not. Israel had long spoken of the day of the LORD as the day God would step in and defeat his enemies, and Amos had already warned his hearers that for them it would be darkness, not light (Amos 5:18–20). The prophets use the phrase for each great act of God’s judgment, and above all for the last one.

Cruel, with wrath and fierce anger. “Cruel” does not mean that God delights in pain; it means the day brings no reprieve to those it comes against, as mercy in a courtroom ends when the sentence is read. And it is aimed, not random: to destroy its sinners from it.

The sun will be dark at its rising. Not clouds, but the sun dark at its rising, the one moment it can always be relied on. Isaiah moves from a military campaign to the end of the world without a break, because the prophet sees the fall of Babylon and the last day together, like a near hill and a far mountain in one view (see the introduction): the one is a rehearsal for the other, and both are the day of the LORD.

In the New Testament. Jesus uses this vocabulary of his own return, the sun darkened, the moon not giving its light, the stars falling (Matthew 24:29), and John uses it again in Revelation; Isaiah is one of its chief sources. The Judge of that day first stood under judgment himself: when darkness covered the land at noon on Good Friday (Mark 15:33), many Christians have seen the day of the LORD falling, for once, on the one who did not deserve it.

verseByVerse.quote: I will punish the world for its evil, and the wicked for their iniquity; I will put an end to the pomp of the arrogant, and lay low the pompous pride of the ruthless. I will make people more rare than fine gold, and mankind than the gold of Ophir. Therefore I will make the heavens tremble, and the earth will be shaken out of its place, at the wrath of the LORD of hosts in the day of his fierce anger.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God will judge the whole world for its evil, and above all for the pride that puts people in his place; heaven and earth will shake at his anger.

I will punish the world for its evil. God himself speaks, and the scope is the world. One sin is singled out: the pomp of the arrogant and the pompous pride of the ruthless. This is the day against everything lofty of chapter 2 (2:11–17), now aimed at the proudest city of all. Pride is named because it is the sin that puts a human being in God’s place, and Babylon is its capital (see the section introduction above).

More rare than fine gold. Verse 12 is a terrible way of counting. In a sacked city gold is what becomes scarce; Isaiah says people will be scarcer. Ophir, wherever it lay (probably in Arabia or East Africa), was proverbial for the finest gold (1 Kings 9:28; Job 28:16).

I will make the heavens tremble. Verse 13 shakes both heaven and earth, and the reason is given twice: the wrath of the LORD of hosts, the day of his fierce anger. The New Testament takes up the same language: God will once more shake “not only the earth but also the heavens”, so that only what cannot be shaken remains, and believers are given “a kingdom that cannot be shaken” (Hebrews 12:26–28).

verseByVerse.quote: And like a hunted gazelle, or like sheep with none to gather them, each will turn to his own people, and each will flee to his own land. Whoever is found will be thrust through, and whoever is caught will fall by the sword. Their infants will be dashed in pieces before their eyes; their houses will be plundered and their wives ravished.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When Babylon falls its foreign crowds scatter for home, and those caught in the city suffer every horror of ancient war; Scripture does not soften the cost of the judgment it announces.

Like a hunted gazelle. Babylon was a great trading city full of foreigners: merchants, hired soldiers and peoples deported there from every corner of the empire. When it falls, the crowd breaks up and each runs for home, as panicked as a gazelle with the hunters behind it. The second picture is sadder: sheep with none to gather them, people without a shepherd. The empire that gathered the nations to itself cannot hold them for a day.

Whoever is found will be thrust through. Verses 15 and 16 describe what conquest did to civilians in that world, and the Bible does not pretend war is clean.

Does God approve of such atrocities? This is a prophecy of what the invading armies will do when God gives proud Babylon over to judgment, as Assyria had been his rod (10:5–7). It is no command to Israel and no model for war; God is not the author of the cruelty (Habakkuk 1:13), and the armies remain guilty for it. Psalm 137:9 voices the same grief from the other side; it is the cry of the wronged handing vengeance to God, not a licence to take it.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 17–22 — Owls Where the Palaces Were
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Babylon’s fall is certain, because God has named both its conqueror and its end. He stirs up the Medes, an enemy that cannot be bribed and will not spare (vv. 17–18). Babylon, “the glory of kingdoms”, will be overthrown like Sodom and Gomorrah (v. 19), and left so empty that not even a passing shepherd will camp there (v. 20). Wild animals will howl in its palaces (vv. 21–22). The last line sets the clock: “its time is close at hand.” Spoken while Babylon was still rising, the word came true in stages over the centuries that followed, and Babylon became the Bible’s name for every proud power that will fall.
verseByVerse.theology: The section names a city, an enemy and an outcome, made while Babylon was still rising. How it came true, in stages over centuries, is traced below.
verseByVerse.examples: Every generation has its own Babylon, a power or system that seems permanent. Believers do not need to fear it or envy it; its expiry date is already set.

verseByVerse.quote: Behold, I am stirring up the Medes against them, who have no regard for silver and do not delight in gold. Their bows will slaughter the young men; they will have no mercy on the fruit of the womb; their eyes will not pity children. And Babylon, the glory of kingdoms, the splendor and pomp of the Chaldeans, will be like Sodom and Gomorrah when God overthrew them. It will never be inhabited or lived in for all generations; no Arab will pitch his tent there; no shepherds will make their flocks lie down there. But wild animals will lie down there, and their houses will be full of howling creatures; there ostriches will dwell, and there wild goats will dance. Hyenas will cry in its towers, and jackals in the pleasant palaces; its time is close at hand and its days will not be prolonged.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God names the people who will conquer Babylon and declares that the proudest city on earth will end as an empty ruin, home only to wild animals.

I am stirring up the Medes. God names the executioner a century and a half ahead, and picks out the detail that matters: the Medes cannot be bought. Babylon’s wealth, its usual way of buying safety, is useless against an enemy that does not want money.

Babylon, the glory of kingdoms. Isaiah gives Babylon its full titles before he demolishes it. The city had walls said to be wide enough to drive chariots along, and gardens that ancient writers counted among the wonders of the world. He is not underestimating it.

It will never be inhabited. Verse 20 promises more than destruction: disuse. Ruins usually have some afterlife, a traveller’s camp or a shepherd’s fold in a broken courtyard. Not this one: nobody will find it worth stopping at.

Hyenas will cry in its towers. Animals in the throne rooms are the standing answer to every empire that believes it is the exception. God told a small nation, in advance, what would one day be living in the greatest of them.

How it was fulfilled. Babylon fell to Cyrus of Persia and his Median allies in 539 BC with little fighting, and stayed inhabited for centuries. The fulfilment came in stages: conquest by Persia, damage after a revolt against Xerxes, then a long decline into the empty ruin it had become by the early centuries after Christ. Revelation takes up Babylon as the name for every proud world system that God will bring down (Revelation 18:2).

Was this written after the event? Many modern scholars date the oracle to the exile because it names Babylon and the Medes. This commentary takes the heading in verse 1 at its word: the God who declares the end from the beginning (46:10) can name a coming conqueror, and the Medes were already a known people in Isaiah’s day (2 Kings 17:6). The question is still debated, but nothing in the oracle requires a later author.

Uncertain wording. The Hebrew words behind howling creatures, ostriches, hyenas and jackals are rare, and older versions render them differently (the King James Version has “doleful creatures”, “owls” and “dragons”). The word for wild goats means “hairy ones”, and some take it of goat-demons thought to haunt ruins, as at Leviticus 17:7. Whichever creatures are meant, the palaces become a haunt of the desert.
verseByVerse.note: The Medes joined Persia to take Babylon in 539 BC.

13.theology:
Why eleven chapters about other nations. The oracles of chapters 13-23 say that God does not merely take an interest in the empires but rules them, appoints their dates and holds them to account. Each oracle also turns toward mercy somewhere in it; that is the pattern rather than the exception.

Babylon first, and why. In this book Babylon is the name for human empire that puts itself in God’s place, and Revelation takes these chapters as its pattern for Babylon the great (Rev. 17-18).

The Day of the LORD. At verse 10 the language outgrows any sack of any city. The prophet sees the fall of Babylon and the end of the world together, the near judgment as a rehearsal for the last, and the Judge of that day is the one who first bore its darkness himself.

14.subtitle: The Taunt Against the King of Babylon
14.intro:
Where we are. Chapter 14 continues the oracle against Babylon begun in chapter 13. Having seen the city fall, Isaiah now gives God’s people the song they will sing over its king, and then adds two short oracles against powers nearer home, Assyria and Philistia.

The message. The ruler who said in his heart, “I will make myself like the Most High” (v. 14), ends in the pit, unburied and mocked by the dead kings he despised, while God has compassion on his people and gives them rest. Pride that climbs to heaven is brought down to Sheol. God’s purpose for the whole earth cannot be turned back, and the one safe place in the world is the Zion he has founded for the afflicted.

Why it was said. Judah lived under rulers who would not let their prisoners go home (v. 17): Assyria in Isaiah’s day, Babylon later (see the introduction), and its neighbours were looking for alliances to break free. God’s people needed to know that every tyrant has an end set by God, and that their safety lay not in treaties but in him.

How the chapter makes its case. First God promises compassion, homecoming and rest, with foreigners joining his people (vv. 1–3); only then comes the taunt. The earth falls quiet and sings (vv. 4–8); the dead kings rise to greet the tyrant (vv. 9–11); his five boasts of “I will” are answered by one line, the pit (vv. 12–15); his corpse lies unburied (vv. 16–20); and his city is swept away (vv. 21–23). Then God swears to break Assyria on his own mountains, a purpose nobody can annul (vv. 24–27), and warns Philistia not to rejoice too soon, answering its envoys with Zion (vv. 28–32).

Where it leads. The chapter leads to Christ by contrast and by promise. The king of Babylon grasped at equality with the Most High and fell to the pit; Christ, who was in the form of God, did not count equality with God a thing to be grasped, but came down to the cross and was highly exalted (Philippians 2:6–9). And the Zion that God founded as a refuge for the afflicted (v. 32) rests on the stone he lays there, which the New Testament names as Christ (28:16; 1 Peter 2:6).

For us. The ladder of the five “I wills” runs through every human heart, and it has no top. The gospel does not tell us to climb harder; it gives rest from the climbing in the one who came down for us. And under every tyrant and every fear, the hand stretched out over the world (v. 27) belongs to the God who shelters the afflicted.

keyVerse.quote: “You said in your heart, ‘I will ascend to heaven; above the stars of God I will set my throne on high; I will sit on the mount of assembly in the far reaches of the north; I will ascend above the heights of the clouds; I will make myself like the Most High.’”
keyVerse.note: The five “I will” statements show pride with nothing left to hide it. Behind every act of human arrogance lies this claim: I will be my own ultimate authority. The king of Babylon is the extreme form of what is present in every sinful heart. This is why pride is not just a character flaw but rebellion against God: it puts the self in God’s place.

14.reflection:
The taunt is sung only after the LORD has given his people rest (v. 3). How should Christians respond when a cruel or corrupt power falls? Where is the line between rejoicing in justice and gloating?

The king said in his heart, “I will make myself like the Most High” (v. 14). Where do you see this ladder of self-making in our culture, and in your own ambitions? Why is it so exhausting?

Read verses 13–15 beside Philippians 2:6–9. What does Christ’s coming down show about the way to true greatness, and how does it give rest to people who are tired of climbing?

When envoys asked where Judah stood, the answer was “The LORD has founded Zion” (v. 32). What do you lean on when you feel threatened, and what would it mean to take refuge in Christ instead?

"The LORD has founded Zion, and in her the afflicted of his people find refuge."

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–3 — The Song Belongs to People Who Got Home
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Before the taunt is sung, God says who will sing it: a people he has had compassion on, chosen again and brought home. Their return reverses the exile, and foreigners attach themselves to the house of Jacob, a first glimpse of the nations being gathered in (vv. 1–2). The song belongs to the day the LORD gives them rest from their pain and hard service (v. 3). That order matters. The fall of the oppressor is sung by the freed, as the relief of people God has rescued, not the spite of people still in chains.
verseByVerse.theology: The section sets the scene for the taunt: it is sung by people already given rest, and so it is the relief of the freed rather than the spite of the chained.
verseByVerse.examples: Christians who rejoice at the fall of a cruel power can learn from the order here: first God's compassion on his own, then the song. Joy at the end of oppression is right; gloating over a person is not ours to do.

verseByVerse.quote: For the LORD will have compassion on Jacob and will again choose Israel, and will set them in their own land, and sojourners will join them and will attach themselves to the house of Jacob. And the peoples will take them and bring them to their place, and the house of Israel will possess them in the LORD's land as male and female slaves. They will take captive those who were their captors, and rule over those who oppressed them. When the LORD has given you rest from your pain and turmoil and the hard service with which you were made to serve,
verseByVerse.commentary:
God will have compassion on his people, bring them home with foreigners joining them, and give them rest; only then is the taunt sung.

The LORD will have compassion on Jacob. Before the song begins, Isaiah says who sings it. Not prisoners spitting at a wall, but people God has already had compassion on, chosen again and brought home; verse 3 dates the song to the day the LORD gives them rest. That keeps it from being gloating: the freeing of the captive and the fall of the captor are one event, and only the freed sing about it.

Sojourners will join them. In an oracle about the destruction of a foreign empire, foreigners are being brought in, as Isaiah keeps saying they will be. The reversal of verse 2, captors becoming servants, is that world’s language for fortunes turned round; Isaiah later shows what it comes to: foreigners who join themselves to the LORD, to love his name and be his servants, welcomed into his house of prayer (56:6–7).

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The tyrant who tried to climb above the stars ends in the pit, and the whole earth breathes again. The song opens with the oppressor stopped and the world at rest, even the cedars of Lebanon glad that the woodcutters have gone (vv. 4–8). Below, the dead kings rise to greet him: he has become as weak as they are (vv. 9–11). At the centre stand his five boasts, ending in “I will make myself like the Most High”, and God’s one-line answer: the pit (vv. 12–15). Onlookers stare at his unburied corpse (vv. 16–20), and God sweeps his city away (vv. 21–23).
verseByVerse.theology: The section moves in a single arc, from the earth at rest to the pit and back to a ruined city, and at its centre is the heart that said I will.
verseByVerse.examples: Jesus' words that he saw Satan fall like lightning from heaven (Luke 10:18) sound like an echo of this passage, though they are not a quotation of it.

verseByVerse.quote: you will take up this taunt against the king of Babylon: "How the oppressor has ceased, the insolent fury ceased! The LORD has broken the staff of the wicked, the scepter of rulers, that struck the peoples in wrath with unceasing blows, that ruled the nations in anger with unrelenting persecution.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The song celebrates that the tyrant who never stopped striking has been stopped for good, and that it was the LORD who broke his sceptre.

This taunt against the king of Babylon. A taunt was a recognised form: a mocking funeral song, sung with the rhythm of a lament and the content of a celebration.

How the oppressor has ceased. The first word of the song is the verb for stopping and resting (shavat), the verb behind “Sabbath”. It answers the rest God has just promised his people (v. 3) and leads to the earth’s rest (v. 7). The oppressor never stopped, and the song says so twice: unceasing blows, unrelenting persecution. Now he has stopped, for good.

The LORD has broken the staff of the wicked. Not a rival empire, as a historian would say, but the LORD ended it. Staff and sceptre were the signs of a ruler’s power, and the same picture was used of Assyria, the rod in God’s hand (10:5, 15). A sceptre used only to strike is broken by the one who lent it.

Were these oracles fulfilled? Assyria’s army was broken before Jerusalem in 701 BC and Nineveh fell in 612; Babylon fell to Persia in 539 and became a ruin; Moab, Egypt and the Philistines were crushed by Assyria and Babylon. Specific prophecy, fulfilled as given, is part of Isaiah’s own argument that the LORD alone declares the end from the beginning (46:9–10).

verseByVerse.quote: The whole earth is at rest and quiet; they break forth into singing. The cypresses rejoice at you, the cedars of Lebanon, saying, 'Since you were laid low, no woodcutter comes up against us.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
With the tyrant gone, the whole earth, even its forests, breathes again and breaks into song.

The whole earth is at rest and quiet. First silence, then song. The nations he oppressed break forth into singing, a phrase Isaiah later uses for the joy of redemption (44:23; 49:13; 55:12).

The cypresses rejoice at you. Even the trees are glad. The great cedar forests of Lebanon, stripped for generations to build imperial palaces and warships, breathe out because the logging has stopped: the landscape was a victim too, and is relieved too. Kings of both Assyria and Babylon boasted in their inscriptions of the cedars they cut in Lebanon, and Isaiah puts the same boast in the mouth of Sennacherib (37:24).

verseByVerse.quote: Sheol beneath is stirred up to meet you when you come; it rouses the shades to greet you, all who were leaders of the earth; it raises from their thrones all who were kings of the nations. All of them will answer and say to you: 'You too have become as weak as we! You have become like us!' Your pomp is brought down to Sheol, the sound of your harps; maggots are laid as a bed beneath you, and worms are your covers.
verseByVerse.commentary:
In the realm of the dead, the kings he despised rise to greet him with the news that he is now as weak as they are, his splendour exchanged for maggots and worms.

Sheol beneath is stirred up to meet you. The scene shifts underground, where the dead kings get up from their shadowy thrones. “The shades” (rephaim) are the dead pictured as faint, strengthless shadows of what they were, and that is the point of what they say.

You too have become as weak as we! It is the greeting of a club nobody wants to join, delivered with grim satisfaction by members who were once told they were nothing beside him.

Maggots are laid as a bed beneath you. The man who slept in the finest room in the world gets a mattress of maggots and a blanket of worms. Isaiah sets the king’s end against the king’s splendour, item for item, down to the sound of your harps.

What Sheol is. Sheol is the Old Testament’s name for the realm of the dead. The scene of dead kings rising to greet the tyrant is poetry, a taunt, not a map of the afterlife; the New Testament gives clearer teaching on the state of the dead (Luke 16:22–23; Philippians 1:23).

verseByVerse.quote: "How you are fallen from heaven, O Day Star, son of Dawn! How you are cut down to the ground, you who laid the nations low! You said in your heart, 'I will ascend to heaven; above the stars of God I will set my throne on high; I will sit on the mount of assembly in the far reaches of the north; I will ascend above the heights of the clouds; I will make myself like the Most High.' But you are brought down to Sheol, to the far reaches of the pit.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The king who set out in his heart to climb above the stars and make himself like God is flung down to the depths, and his fall is as deep as his pride was high.

O Day Star, son of Dawn! The title names the morning star, the last light in the sky before the sun puts it out: a fitting title for a king who thought he outshone everything.

You said in your heart. Five sentences, each built on I will, show how pride climbs, step by step. Ascend. Set my throne. Sit. Ascend again. And then the last, where every one of the others was always heading: I will make myself like the Most High. All of it happens in his heart, not in a speech or a decree. Nobody heard it, and it is the sentence God answers.

But you are brought down to Sheol. God’s answer takes one line (v. 15), deliberately shaped like the boast: the far reaches of the north are answered by the far reaches of the pit. The length of the fall matches the height of the ambition. What the passage exposes is the pride behind every throne that puts itself in God’s place, a pride far older than Babylon.

The one who came down. Set these five boasts beside Philippians 2:6–8. The king of Babylon grasped at equality with the Most High and fell to the pit. Christ was in the form of God and did not count equality with God a thing to be grasped, but came down, took the form of a servant and went to the cross. The one climbed and was cast down; the other descended and is highly exalted, given the name above every name (Philippians 2:9). Every human pride is a small copy of Babylon’s ladder, and the gospel is the news of the one who came down it to fetch us.

The exhausting ladder. Strip away the royal setting and the five boasts sound like the creed of modern self-making: you can be anything you want, and the only limit is your will. It sounds like freedom, but it is a ladder with no top: if your worth is what you make of yourself, you can never stop making, and the people around you become rungs or rivals. That is why it matters that the chapter began with people to whom the LORD has given rest from your pain and turmoil and the hard service with which you were made to serve (v. 3). The opposite of the climber is not the failure; it is the one who has been given rest. The gospel ends the climbing not by telling us to aim lower but by telling us that the one who came down has already raised us up and seated us with him (Ephesians 2:6), where there is nothing left to grasp.

Where Christians differ. Is the Day Star Satan or the king of Babylon? The taunt names the king of Babylon (v. 4), and verse 16 calls him the man who made the earth tremble. Yet many since the early church have read verses 12–15 as the fall of Satan, because of fallen from heaven and the boast I will make myself like the Most High.

This commentary’s view. The passage is about the king, and his pride mirrors the pride of the devil who stands behind such rulers (compare Ezekiel 28; 1 Timothy 3:6). “Lucifer” is simply the Latin for Day Star, which the King James Version kept from the Latin Bible; in Hebrew it is a title, not Satan’s proper name, and the verse is not an account of the devil’s origin. Scripture tells us little about that, and this passage should not be made to say more. Tellingly, the New Testament gives the title morning star to Christ (2 Peter 1:19; Revelation 22:16).

Uncertain wording. The Hebrew helel occurs only here. Most take it from a root meaning to shine, the morning star (probably the planet Venus), as the ancient Greek and Latin translations did; a few connect it with a verb meaning to wail. Some scholars hear in the Day Star and the mount of assembly an echo of a Canaanite story of a star that tried to climb to the high god’s throne and was thrown down; if so, Isaiah borrows it as a taunt, not as belief.
verseByVerse.note: “The far reaches of the north” may be rendered “the remote parts of Zaphon” (ESV note), a mountain north of Israel where Canaanite myth placed the assembly of the gods.

verseByVerse.quote: Those who see you will stare at you and ponder over you: 'Is this the man who made the earth tremble, who shook kingdoms, who made the world like a desert and overthrew its cities, who did not let his prisoners go home?'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Onlookers stare at the body of the man who shook the world and can hardly believe it is him; the last thing they remember is that he never let his prisoners go home.

Is this the man who made the earth tremble? Back at ground level, a crowd stands round a body. They stare and ponder, the slow double-take of people trying to match what is in front of them with what they remember. Four achievements are listed; all true, and none of them helps.

Who did not let his prisoners go home. The last charge is the human one. Deporting conquered peoples and keeping them far from home was the settled policy of Assyria and Babylon, and it is the very policy the LORD reverses when Cyrus lets the exiles go home (44:28; Ezra 1:1–4).

verseByVerse.quote: All the kings of the nations lie in glory, each in his own tomb; but you are cast out, away from your grave, like a loathed branch, clothed with the slain, those pierced by the sword, who go down to the stones of the pit, like a dead body trampled underfoot. You will not be joined with them in burial, because you have destroyed your land, you have slain your people. "May the offspring of evildoers nevermore be named!
verseByVerse.commentary:
Other kings lie in honoured tombs, but this one is thrown out unburied, because his ambition destroyed even his own land and people.

You are cast out, away from your grave. Other kings got tombs; this one is thrown out like a lopped branch, trampled underfoot, not joined with them in burial. In a world where a proper grave was the last dignity a great man could count on, the king who wanted to sit above the stars ends without a plot of ground.

Because you have destroyed your land. The reason, given in verse 20, is a surprise: not only what he did to other nations but what he did to his own. You have destroyed your land, you have slain your people. Pride that will climb over the nations will climb over its own people as well, and God counts that against it.

Which king was this? Isaiah does not name him, and the taunt fits a kind of ruler as much as one man. Some think of Sargon II of Assyria, who also ruled Babylon and whose body was lost on a battlefield in 705 BC; others of a later Babylonian king. The point does not depend on the identification.

verseByVerse.quote: Prepare slaughter for his sons because of the guilt of their fathers, lest they rise and possess the earth, and fill the face of the world with cities." "I will rise up against them," declares the LORD of hosts, "and will cut off from Babylon name and remnant, descendants and posterity," declares the LORD. "And I will make it a possession of the hedgehog, and pools of water, and I will sweep it with the broom of destruction," declares the LORD of hosts.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God himself signs the sentence: the tyrant’s dynasty will not rise again, and Babylon will be swept away into a marsh.

Prepare slaughter for his sons. Verse 21 is hard, and it belongs to the world of dynasties, where a surviving son meant a restored regime: lest they rise and possess the earth. God will cut off from Babylon name and remnant.

Declares the LORD of hosts. The song is over, and God signs the sentence himself. Three times in two verses declares the LORD is set against the king’s five boasts (vv. 13–14): now it is God who says I will rise up, I will make, I will sweep. Babylon did not fall in a day: Cyrus took it in 539 BC almost without a fight, and it declined over centuries until it was largely abandoned (see the note on 13:17–22).

The broom of destruction. The greatest city on earth becomes a swamp with wild creatures in it. That is the end of the I will of verse 13.

Does God punish children for their fathers’ sins? Each person answers for his own sin (Deuteronomy 24:16; Ezekiel 18:20). This is the sentence on a tyrant’s dynasty, so that its evil will not rise again; the sons who would carry on their father’s tyranny share his judgment.

Uncertain wording. The creature of verse 23 (qippod) is uncertain. Most modern versions have hedgehog or porcupine; older ones a marsh bird (the King James Version has “bittern”). Either way, a creature of the wasteland.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: What God has purposed for the whole earth will stand, and the one safe place in it is the Zion he has founded. God swears that Assyria will be broken on his own mountains and its yoke lifted from his people, then widens the oath to all nations: who will annul his purpose, or turn back his hand? (vv. 24–27). He warns Philistia not to celebrate the death of an oppressor, for a worse one is coming (vv. 28–31). And when envoys come looking for allies, Judah’s answer is not a treaty but a refuge: the LORD has founded Zion for the afflicted of his people (v. 32).
verseByVerse.theology: Verse 27 carries the whole run of oracles against the nations in chapters 13 to 23. It asks who can annul what the LORD has purposed or turn back his hand, and the expected answer for every nation is nobody.
verseByVerse.examples: In a chapter full of thrones and corpses, the final word is a shelter for people with nothing. That is still the church's answer when the world asks where it stands.

verseByVerse.quote: The LORD of hosts has sworn: "As I have planned, so shall it be, and as I have purposed, so shall it stand, that I will break the Assyrian in my land, and on my mountains trample him underfoot; and his yoke shall depart from them, and his burden from their shoulder." This is the purpose that is purposed concerning the whole earth, and this is the hand that is stretched out over all the nations. For the LORD of hosts has purposed, and who will annul it? His hand is stretched out, and who will turn it back?
verseByVerse.commentary:
God has sworn to break Assyria in his own land, and that oath is one instance of a single purpose for the whole earth that nobody can annul.

The LORD of hosts has sworn. The chapter turns from Babylon, still rising, to Assyria, at the door, with an oath whose structure is the point: as I have planned, so shall it be, and as I have purposed, so shall it stand. What God intends happens. That is the difference between his plans and the king’s, who said five things in his heart and saw none of them happen.

I will break the Assyrian in my land. Assyria will be broken not far away but on my mountains, in the land it invaded. It happened in 701 BC, when Sennacherib’s army surrounded Jerusalem and was struck down in a night (37:36), and the yoke of verse 25 was lifted.

Concerning the whole earth. A promise about one invasion becomes a statement about the whole earth and all the nations, because the oracles of chapters 13 to 23 are not separate policies, one for each nation, but one hand over one world. Verse 27 is the sentence they all rest on. It asks two questions, and the expected answer to each is nobody.

In everyday life. It is also the answer to a fear older than Assyria. Whatever is stretched out over a life, a diagnosis, a government, a decline that seems unstoppable, there is one hand in the universe that cannot be turned back, and it belongs to someone who is for his people.

verseByVerse.quote: In the year that King Ahaz died came this oracle: Rejoice not, O Philistia, all of you, that the rod that struck you is broken, for from the serpent's root will come forth an adder, and its fruit will be a flying fiery serpent. And the firstborn of the poor will graze, and the needy lie down in safety; but I will kill your root with famine, and your remnant it will slay. Wail, O gate; cry out, O city; melt in fear, O Philistia, all of you! For smoke comes out of the north, and there is no straggler in his ranks. What will one answer the messengers of the nation? "The LORD has founded Zion, and in her the afflicted of his people find refuge."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Philistia must not celebrate the fall of its oppressor, because a worse one is coming; the one safe place is the Zion God has founded, where his afflicted people find refuge.

Rejoice not, O Philistia. Philistia is celebrating a death as the end of the pressure, and Isaiah tells them to stop. The heading dates the oracle by a king’s death, as 6:1 dated Isaiah’s call. With Ahaz gone, his son Hezekiah would soon be courted by neighbours planning revolt against Assyria, which is probably why the chapter ends with envoys at the door (v. 32), and why Isaiah answers them with Zion, not a treaty.

From the serpent’s root will come forth an adder. The image is a family tree of snakes, each generation worse than the last. The relief is temporary, and the successor is more dangerous than the one who died. Anyone who has watched a bad situation improve slightly and concluded it is over knows the shape of Philistia’s mistake.

The needy lie down in safety. Two futures stand side by side in verse 30: the poorest of the poor graze and lie down in safety, while the proud lose even their root. It is the pattern of the whole book in a sentence. The smoke from the north (v. 31) is an army on the march, burning as it comes, with no straggler in its ranks.

What will one answer the messengers of the nation? Envoys arrive, presumably seeking an alliance, and ask where Judah stands. The reply says nothing about armies or treaties: The LORD has founded Zion, and in her the afflicted of his people find refuge.

The afflicted of his people find refuge. That is the last word of the chapter: a founded city, and in it a shelter for the afflicted. What the king of Babylon tried to build for himself, God simply provides, to people who have nothing to bring. The New Testament names the stone laid in that Zion as Christ himself (28:16; 1 Peter 2:6), and tells believers they have already come to the city of the living God (Hebrews 12:22).

Uncertain wording. Whose death Philistia celebrates is not certain. The rod that struck you may be an Assyrian king (Tiglath-pileser III died about 727 BC) or Ahaz himself, and the year of Ahaz’s death is itself disputed (about 727 or 715 BC). The flying fiery serpent (also 30:6) uses the word for the “fiery serpents” of Numbers 21:6; it is probably a poetic picture of a deadly, darting snake rather than a winged creature.

14.theology:
Who is allowed to sing it. The taunt belongs to the day God gives his people rest (v. 3), which keeps a mocking funeral song from being mere gloating.

The five "I wills". The pride that climbs is in every human heart, ours included, and the gospel does not answer it by helping us climb higher. Christ came down in our place, humbled to the cross, and it is his lowliness, not ours, that is counted to us (Philippians 2:6–8); the way back for the proud is to confess it and be lifted by him.

The purpose nobody annuls. Verse 27 is widened from one invasion to the whole earth. The chapter then ends, after all its thrones and corpses, on a founded city and a refuge for the afflicted (v. 32).

15.subtitle: The Oracle Against Moab
15.intro:
Where we are. After Babylon, Assyria and Philistia (chapters 13–14), the oracles against the nations turn to Moab, Judah’s neighbour east of the Dead Sea, descended from Lot (Genesis 19:37). Chapters 15 and 16 form a single oracle, and this chapter is its first half.

The message. Moab will be laid waste suddenly, town after town, and its people will flee with whatever they can carry. Yet the oracle is not a victory song. In the middle of the judgment a voice cries, “My heart cries out for Moab” (v. 5): the God who judges a proud enemy justly also grieves over it. His judgment is real, and it is never cold.

Why it was said. Moab was a blood relative and an old enemy, and in Isaiah’s lifetime Assyrian armies marched through it again and again (see the introduction). Judah might well have been glad to see it suffer. God’s people needed to learn that the nations are in his hand, and that his justice is not their spite.

How the chapter makes its case. Two cities fall in a night, and the whole land goes into mourning, town after named town, with shaved heads, sackcloth and wailing on the rooftops (vv. 1–4). Then comes the cry of grief, as fugitives flee south (v. 5). The water fails, families carry their savings across a stream, and the wailing fills the land to its borders (vv. 6–8). The chapter ends with no relief: the waters run with blood, and God promises even more (v. 9).

Where it leads. The chapter points to Christ through the character of God it reveals. The God who grieves over a people he must judge is seen in Jesus, who wept over Jerusalem as it was about to reject him (Luke 19:41–44). At the cross justice and grief meet fully: God does not lower his justice to spare sinners, but bears its cost himself in his Son. And the next chapter offers Moab’s refugees shelter under the throne of David (16:5), the throne Christ now holds.

For us. We may not watch the judgment of others with triumph or indifference, whether a hostile nation’s or that of someone who has wronged us. Christ’s people are to share his heart: to grieve over the ruin sin brings, to pray for enemies, and to point them to the refuge he offers.

keyVerse.quote: “My heart cries out for Moab.”
keyVerse.note: The brevity of this line is part of its power. In the middle of an oracle announcing destruction, a heart cries out, and as 16:9–11 shows, it is finally God’s own. Judgment and compassion do not cancel each other in God; both are present at once. That is why the cross shows God’s justice at its most severe and his love at its deepest together.

15.reflection:
Moab was an old enemy, yet the oracle says, “My heart cries out for Moab” (v. 5). How do you usually react when people you dislike, or a nation you distrust, meet disaster? What would it look like to share God’s heart instead?

Verse 7 pictures families carrying “the abundance they have gained” across a stream as they flee. What would you try to carry? What does this verse teach about where to put our security (Matthew 6:19–21)?

Jesus wept over Jerusalem even as he announced its judgment (Luke 19:41–44). How does seeing justice and grief together in God help you understand the cross?

The chapter ends with no comfort in its last line. Why might it be important to face the seriousness of judgment honestly before hearing the offer of refuge in chapter 16?
15.text: <sup>1</sup>An oracle concerning Moab. Because Ar of Moab is laid waste in a night, Moab is undone; because Kir of Moab is laid waste in a night, Moab is undone.<sup>2</sup>He has gone up to the temple, and to Dibon, to the high places to weep; over Nebo and over Medeba Moab wails. On every head is baldness; every beard is shorn;<sup>3</sup>in the streets they wear sackcloth; on the housetops and in the squares everyone wails and melts in tears.<sup>4</sup>Heshbon and Elealeh cry out; their voice is heard as far as Jahaz; therefore the armed men of Moab cry aloud; his soul trembles.<sup>5</sup>My heart cries out for Moab; her fugitives flee to Zoar, to Eglath-shelishiyah. For at the ascent of Luhith they go up weeping; on the road to Horonaim they raise a cry of destruction;<sup>6</sup>the waters of Nimrim are a desolation; the grass is withered, the vegetation fails, the greenery is no more.<sup>7</sup>Therefore the abundance they have gained and what they have laid up they carry away over the Brook of the Willows.<sup>8</sup>For a cry has gone around the land of Moab; her wailing reaches to Eglaim; her wailing reaches to Beer-elim.<sup>9</sup>For the waters of Dibon are full of blood; for I will bring upon Dibon even more, a lion for those of Moab who escape, for the remnant of the land.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–9 — The Prophet Weeps for the Enemy
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Moab’s fall is told as a lament, and the grief at its centre is finally God’s. Two cities fall in a night, and the whole land goes into mourning, town by named town, with shaved heads, sackcloth and wailing on the rooftops (vv. 1–4). Then a voice cries out for Moab as its fugitives flee south (v. 5). The water fails and families carry their savings across a stream (vv. 6–7); the cry fills the land to its borders (v. 8), and the chapter ends in blood, with worse still to come (v. 9). It never lets the reader forget that the names on the list were towns full of people.
verseByVerse.theology: The section is a lament, not a victory announcement, and it never lets the reader forget that the names on the list were towns full of people.
verseByVerse.examples: The chapter refuses a division most religious people find comfortable: our nation whom God loves, their nation whom he does not. The God who deals with sin in justice also grieves over those who go down under it, which is why the same book can end with all flesh coming to worship (66:23).

verseByVerse.quote: An oracle concerning Moab. Because Ar of Moab is laid waste in a night, Moab is undone; because Kir of Moab is laid waste in a night, Moab is undone. He has gone up to the temple, and to Dibon, to the high places to weep; over Nebo and over Medeba Moab wails. On every head is baldness; every beard is shorn; in the streets they wear sackcloth; on the housetops and in the squares everyone wails and melts in tears. Heshbon and Elealeh cry out; their voice is heard as far as Jahaz; therefore the armed men of Moab cry aloud; his soul trembles. My heart cries out for Moab; her fugitives flee to Zoar, to Eglath-shelishiyah. For at the ascent of Luhith they go up weeping; on the road to Horonaim they raise a cry of destruction;
verseByVerse.commentary:
Moab is ruined overnight and the whole land goes into mourning, and in the middle of the judgment a voice, finally God’s own, cries out in grief for the enemy.

Laid waste in a night. Two cities, both gone in a night, and the sentence repeats itself in almost the same words, which is how people talk when they cannot take something in.

The place names. There is no need to look up the place names; the effect is what matters: Dibon, Nebo, Medeba, Heshbon, Elealeh, Jahaz, ordinary towns named one after another the way a local would name them, each now a place where somebody is weeping. The temple and high places of verse 2 belong to Chemosh, Moab’s god (Numbers 21:29; 1 Kings 11:7). Moab’s first move in the disaster is to go up and weep before him, which is where the next chapter will leave it (16:12).

On every head is baldness. Shaved heads and cut beards were the visible signs of grief in that world (see mourning customs): a man did to his own body what the disaster had done to his life. The grief fills the two places where a town is most itself: the flat roofs where families slept and talked in the evening, and the squares where they did business.

My heart cries out for Moab. Without warning, in an oracle against a hostile neighbour, somebody is grieving. It may be the prophet, but in 16:9–11 the one who weeps is the one who has silenced Moab’s harvest, and so many hear God’s own grief in the prophet’s.

Judgment and grief together. God has judged Moab justly and he is heartbroken about it, and Scripture never treats those two as needing to be reconciled. It is the same heart we see in Jesus, who stood on a hill outside Jerusalem, looked at the city that was arranging his death, and wept over it (Luke 19:41).

Uncertain wording. Several names here are obscure. Eglath-shelishiyah may mean “the third Eglath”, to tell it apart from other places of that name; older versions took it as “a heifer three years old”. The word for temple in verse 2 is simply “the house”, and some take it as a place name. The sites of Ar, Luhith and several other towns are uncertain.
verseByVerse.note: Kir of Moab is probably Kir-hareseth (16:7), the modern Kerak; the site of Ar is uncertain.

verseByVerse.quote: the waters of Nimrim are a desolation; the grass is withered, the vegetation fails, the greenery is no more. Therefore the abundance they have gained and what they have laid up they carry away over the Brook of the Willows. For a cry has gone around the land of Moab; her wailing reaches to Eglaim; her wailing reaches to Beer-elim. For the waters of Dibon are full of blood; for I will bring upon Dibon even more, a lion for those of Moab who escape, for the remnant of the land.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Moab’s water fails, its people flee carrying what they can, and the chapter ends without relief, with more judgment still to come.

The waters of Nimrim are a desolation. In that dry country, when the water goes, everything goes: grass, vegetation, everything green.

What they have laid up. Verse 7 is one of the saddest sentences in the prophets, and it is about luggage. Everything a family had built up and put by, the whole slow accumulation of a life, is now what they can carry across a stream while running away. It measures possessions by the test that finally applies: what happens to them on the day you have to leave. And the cry has filled the country to its borders (v. 8).

Even more. The last words are God’s: I will bring upon Dibon even more. The waters of Dibon are full of blood, and the lion is most likely a figure for a further invader, falling on the few who escape.

Why Isaiah does not hurry. The next chapter will tell Moab’s refugees where to run and offer them shelter under a throne in Judah, but Isaiah does not hurry to it. He lets a chapter end in blood and weeping, because that is honest, and because the offer of refuge means nothing to anyone who has not first been allowed to see what is being fled from.

Uncertain wording. The standard Hebrew text spells the town Dimon, which sounds like dam, “blood”, and is probably a wordplay; some ancient copies read Dibon, as the ESV does. The Brook of the Willows was probably a stream on Moab’s southern border, but it cannot be identified with certainty, nor can Eglaim and Beer-elim.

15.theology:
The prophet weeps for the enemy. Moab was an old adversary and a blood relative, descended from Lot (Gen. 19:37), with a long record of hostility toward Israel. What makes this oracle remarkable is its tone: it is a lament, and the grief in verse 5, my heart cries out for Moab, is most naturally God’s own.

Justice and grief together. God judges Moab and mourns Moab, and Scripture never treats those as needing reconciliation. The same heart is seen in Jesus, who wept over the city that was arranging his death (Luke 19:41).

What possessions weigh on the day you leave. Verse 7 measures a lifetime's gains by what can be carried across a stream, and the chapter is allowed to end with no comfort in the last line.

16.subtitle: Moab's Pride and the Promise of the Throne
16.intro:
Where we are. Chapter 16 completes the oracle against Moab begun in chapter 15. That chapter ended in blood and flight; this one opens with advice for the refugees about where to run.

The message. God offers Moab’s fugitives shelter in Zion and tells his own people to hide them. A refuge is only as good as the one at its centre, and this one rests on a throne established in steadfast love, held by a king who judges justly (v. 5). But Moab is too proud to come (v. 6). So the lament returns, God grieves again, and Moab wears himself out praying at his own high place to no avail, with three years left (vv. 12–14).

Why it was said. As Assyria pressed on the region, Moab’s refugees really did stream across the fords of the Arnon (see the introduction), and Judah had to decide what to do with old enemies at its door. Moab’s pride was proverbial (Jeremiah 48:29; Zephaniah 2:8–10), and the oracle shows what it cost.

How the chapter makes its case. The refugees are told to send tribute to the ruler in Zion (vv. 1–2), and Judah is told to shelter them, like shade at noon (vv. 3–4). The offer rests on a throne in the tent of David (v. 5). Then pride refuses (v. 6); the lament returns for Moab’s ruined vineyards, and God’s own inner parts moan like a lyre (vv. 7–11). Moab wearies himself at the high place and does not prevail (v. 12), and a fixed term of three years is set (vv. 13–14).

Where it leads. Verse 5 is a promise of the King. No king of David’s line fitted it; the throne established in steadfast love is the throne of 9:7, promised to Mary’s son (Luke 1:32–33). A Moabite woman once came for refuge under the wings of Israel’s God, and from her line came David and Jesus (Ruth 2:12; Matthew 1:5). The shelter proud Moab refused is offered still in Christ, who never casts out anyone who comes to him (John 6:37).

For us. What keeps people outside the refuge is not a lack of welcome but pride, and sincere religion at the wrong address cannot save. Come to Christ as a supplicant; then, like Judah, be shade at noon for the outcasts and the frightened at your own door.

keyVerse.quote: “Then a throne will be established in steadfast love, and on it will sit in faithfulness in the tent of David one who judges and seeks justice and is swift to do righteousness.”
keyVerse.note: The four qualities named, steadfast love, faithfulness, justice and righteousness, are qualities of God himself, the God who keeps covenant, here given to the coming king. Every good king in Israel’s history showed them in part; the Messiah shows them fully. This is the throne that will have no end (9:7), and the refuge it offers is open to outsiders.

16.reflection:
Judah is told to shelter Moab’s refugees, “Make your shade like night at the height of noon” (v. 3). Who are the outcasts and frightened people near you, and what would it look like for your church to be that kind of shade?

Verse 5 describes a throne established in steadfast love and faithfulness. How does Jesus fulfil this, and why does the character of the King matter for anyone looking for refuge?

Moab refused the shelter out of pride (v. 6). In what ways does pride keep people, including you, from receiving grace? What does coming as a supplicant involve?

Moab “wearies himself on the high place” and does not prevail (v. 12). Why is sincerity not enough? How does the gospel comfort someone whose faith feels weak (Mark 9:24)?
16.text: <sup>1</sup>Send the lamb to the ruler of the land, from Sela, by way of the desert, to the mount of the daughter of Zion.<sup>2</sup>Like fleeing birds, like a scattered nest, so are the daughters of Moab at the fords of the Arnon.<sup>3</sup>"Give counsel; grant justice; make your shade like night at the height of noon; shelter the outcasts; do not reveal the fugitive;<sup>4</sup>let the outcasts of Moab sojourn among you; be a shelter to them from the destroyer. When the oppressor is no more, and destruction has ceased, and he who tramples underfoot has vanished from the land,<sup>5</sup>then a throne will be established in steadfast love, and on it will sit in faithfulness in the tent of David one who judges and seeks justice and is swift to do righteousness."<sup>6</sup>We have heard of the pride of Moab— how proud he is!— of his arrogance, his pride, and his insolence; in his idle boasting he is not right.<sup>7</sup>Therefore let Moab wail for Moab, let everyone wail. Mourn, utterly stricken, for the raisin cakes of Kir-hareseth.<sup>8</sup>For the fields of Heshbon languish, and the vine of Sibmah; the lords of the nations have struck down its branches, which reached to Jazer and strayed to the desert; its shoots spread abroad and passed over the sea.<sup>9</sup>Therefore I weep with the weeping of Jazer for the vine of Sibmah; I drench you with my tears, O Heshbon and Elealeh; for over your summer fruit and your harvest the shout has ceased.<sup>10</sup>And joy and gladness are taken away from the fruitful field, and in the vineyards no songs are sung, no cheers are raised; no treader treads out wine in the presses; I have put an end to the shouting.<sup>11</sup>Therefore my inner parts moan like a lyre for Moab, and my inmost self for Kir-hareseth.<sup>12</sup>And when Moab presents himself, when he wearies himself on the high place, when he comes to his sanctuary to pray, he will not prevail.<sup>13</sup>This is the word that the LORD spoke concerning Moab in the past.<sup>14</sup>But now the LORD has spoken, saying, "In three years, like the years of a hired worker, the glory of Moab will be brought into contempt, in spite of all his great multitude, and those who remain will be very few and feeble."

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Moab’s refugees are offered a refuge in Zion, and it rests on a throne established in steadfast love. They are told to send tribute to Judah’s ruler, as Moab once sent lambs to Israel’s king, for they are scattered like birds at the fords of the Arnon (vv. 1–2). Judah is told to take them in and hide them, making its shade like night at noon (vv. 3–4). The whole offer rests on the coming King: a throne in the tent of David, where one sits in faithfulness who seeks justice and is swift to do righteousness (v. 5). Refugees from a nation under judgment are told to run towards God’s people.
verseByVerse.theology: The direction of the counsel is the surprise: refugees from a nation under judgment are told to run toward God's people.
verseByVerse.examples: Verse 4 gives the church a picture of what it can be for the frightened, whether refugees, the newly bereaved, or anyone whose day has turned harsh: shade like night at the height of noon.

verseByVerse.quote: Send the lamb to the ruler of the land, from Sela, by way of the desert, to the mount of the daughter of Zion. Like fleeing birds, like a scattered nest, so are the daughters of Moab at the fords of the Arnon. "Give counsel; grant justice; make your shade like night at the height of noon; shelter the outcasts; do not reveal the fugitive; let the outcasts of Moab sojourn among you; be a shelter to them from the destroyer. When the oppressor is no more, and destruction has ceased, and he who tramples underfoot has vanished from the land, then a throne will be established in steadfast love, and on it will sit in faithfulness in the tent of David one who judges and seeks justice and is swift to do righteousness."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Moab’s refugees are told to seek shelter in Zion, Judah is told to hide them, and the offer rests on a coming King whose throne is established in steadfast love.

Send the lamb to the ruler of the land. The chapter opens with advice to the fugitives of chapter 15: send tribute, go to Jerusalem, put yourselves under Judah’s king. Lambs were Moab’s old currency of tribute: its king once paid Israel a hundred thousand of them a year (2 Kings 3:4).

Like fleeing birds. Birds knocked out of a nest, still in the air with nowhere to land: a column of refugees with nowhere to stop.

Do not reveal the fugitive. Now Judah is addressed, and none of the instructions sounds optional; this one assumes somebody is hunting the fugitives. Judah is asked to give only what it had received: a people once strangers in Egypt, sheltered by the God who brought them out, are to shelter the stranger in turn (see hospitality).

Make your shade like night at the height of noon. In that climate the middle of the day is dangerous, and the only mercy is shadow. God asks his people to be, for the frightened, what a wall of shade is at noon: a patch of night in the worst part of the day.

Then a throne will be established in steadfast love. The offer rests on a throne. Which king of Judah fits it, a throne established in steadfast love, held by one who is swift to do righteousness? None of them. It is the throne of the promised King in 9:7, and Isaiah reaches for it here because a refuge is only as good as the character of whoever sits at its centre.

A Moabite who came. Moab as a nation would not stoop, but one Moabite once did. Ruth left her country and her gods, took refuge under the wings of the God of Israel (Ruth 2:12), and became the great-grandmother of David; Matthew names her in the genealogy of Jesus (Matthew 1:5). The tent of David that Moab’s refugees are invited to had already sheltered a Moabite, and from her line came its true King. When Amos promised that God would raise up the fallen tent of David, James heard in it the gathering of Gentiles into the church (Amos 9:11; Acts 15:16–17). The shelter refused by proud Moab is open still, under Christ.

Uncertain wording. Verse 1 is compressed and hard to read. It is not certain who is speaking or who sends the lamb, and Sela, meaning “rock”, may be a particular town in Edom or simply the rocky country to the south where the fugitives had fled. Most take it, as here, as advice to renew Moab’s old tribute to Zion.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Moab’s pride refuses the refuge, and what remains is grief and a religion that cannot help. Moab is too proud to stoop (v. 6). So the lament returns, for the raisin cakes of Kir-hareseth and the famous vines of Sibmah cut down by foreign lords, and God himself weeps, his inner parts moaning like a lyre (vv. 7–11). Moab wears himself out at his high place and does not prevail (v. 12). Then a date is attached to the old word: within three years, counted as exactly as a hired worker counts his days, Moab’s glory will be brought low (vv. 13–14).
verseByVerse.theology: The section shows what happens when grace is refused: the lament returns, and the religion that remains gets nothing.
verseByVerse.examples: It is possible to be busy with religion and still refuse the one door God has opened. The remedy is not more effort at the high place but the humility to come to Christ as a supplicant, which he never turns away (John 6:37).

verseByVerse.quote: We have heard of the pride of Moab— how proud he is!— of his arrogance, his pride, and his insolence; in his idle boasting he is not right. Therefore let Moab wail for Moab, let everyone wail. Mourn, utterly stricken, for the raisin cakes of Kir-hareseth. For the fields of Heshbon languish, and the vine of Sibmah; the lords of the nations have struck down its branches, which reached to Jazer and strayed to the desert; its shoots spread abroad and passed over the sea. Therefore I weep with the weeping of Jazer for the vine of Sibmah; I drench you with my tears, O Heshbon and Elealeh; for over your summer fruit and your harvest the shout has ceased. And joy and gladness are taken away from the fruitful field, and in the vineyards no songs are sung, no cheers are raised; no treader treads out wine in the presses; I have put an end to the shouting. Therefore my inner parts moan like a lyre for Moab, and my inmost self for Kir-hareseth.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Moab is too proud to accept the refuge, so the lament returns, and God himself grieves over the ruin of its famous vineyards.

We have heard of the pride of Moab. The offer of verses 3 and 4 is not taken, and verse 6 is the whole explanation. Isaiah says the same thing five times over in one line: arrogance, pride, insolence, idle boasting. There was nothing else to say.

Why Moab refused. Moab did not refuse because the shelter was inadequate, or the terms truly humiliating, or Judah untrustworthy. It refused because going would have meant arriving as a supplicant at the door of a smaller neighbour and admitting it needed help. Pride is more than an unattractive trait; it is what makes grace impossible to accept. Everything in verses 3 to 5 was free, and the one qualification for receiving it was the willingness to stoop.

The vine of Sibmah. The grief returns, and it is agricultural. The vines of Sibmah were famous (see vine and vineyard); Isaiah describes them reaching all the way to Jazer and wandering out into the desert, a picture of extravagant growth, now cut down by foreign lords.

My inner parts moan like a lyre for Moab. The one who says I have put an end to the shouting also says I weep. His inner parts moan like a lyre, a low vibration in the body, the way a struck string goes on sounding. He offered the refuge, it was refused out of pride, the judgment fell, and he is not detached about any of it.

Uncertain wording. The raisin cakes of Kir-hareseth (v. 7) translate a word that elsewhere means raisin cakes, often eaten at festivals (Hosea 3:1), but some take it here as “foundations” or “men” of the city, as the parallel in Jeremiah 48:31 has. The sea of verse 8 is probably the Dead Sea.

verseByVerse.quote: And when Moab presents himself, when he wearies himself on the high place, when he comes to his sanctuary to pray, he will not prevail. This is the word that the LORD spoke concerning Moab in the past. But now the LORD has spoken, saying, "In three years, like the years of a hired worker, the glory of Moab will be brought into contempt, in spite of all his great multitude, and those who remain will be very few and feeble."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Moab wears himself out in prayer at his own shrine and gets nothing, and God sets a fixed term of three years before its glory is brought low.

He wearies himself on the high place. Moab is not irreligious. He presents himself, goes up to the high place, the hilltop shrine of his god, and wearies himself there, the word suggesting real effort, prolonged and exhausting. He comes to his sanctuary to pray, and nothing happens.

Religion at the wrong address. There was no shortage of devotion in Moab. There was a shortage of the one thing that would have made devotion useful: the humility to walk to Zion when the door was open. A man can spend enormous energy on religion at the wrong address, and Isaiah has just shown what that costs.

Isn’t sincerity what really counts? Most people today would give Moab full marks: he prayed until he was exhausted, and surely a God worth the name would honour the effort, whatever address was on the envelope. It is a generous instinct, and in the rest of life we know it is false. A man who sincerely takes the wrong medicine is not cured by his sincerity, and a woman who sincerely trusts a fraudster still loses her savings. Sincerity measures how hard we hold on; it says nothing about whether the thing we hold can hold us. Chemosh could not answer, however earnestly he was asked. That is the hard edge of this verse, and the gospel is its gentle centre. Faith does not have to be strong or impressive when its object is. A father once came to Jesus with half a faith and said so, “I believe; help my unbelief!” (Mark 9:24), and his son was healed. A trembling prayer to the true God goes further than a lifetime of devotion at the wrong high place, because what saves is not the grip but the One gripped.

Like the years of a hired worker. Then a date: three years, like the years of a hired worker, a labourer on a fixed contract who counts the days exactly and will not work one more. Verse 13 marks the change: what has gone before is a word the LORD had spoken about Moab in the past, possibly given earlier to Isaiah or to another prophet, and now he attaches a date to it.

A date that can be checked. Isaiah stakes the oracle on a verifiable timetable, as he did with the child in chapter 8. He names a country, a cause and a number of years, and invites his hearers to check. We cannot now date the oracle precisely enough to name the campaign that fulfilled it, though the marches of Sargon II or Sennacherib through the region are likely candidates.

16.theology:
Refuge offered to the enemy. God’s people are told to take in the refugees of a hostile nation, as a duty, not an optional kindness. For the church this is not a load to be carried by willpower: we were the outcasts Christ sheltered, and his Spirit makes his people a shade for others.

A throne that no king of Judah fitted. Verse 5 grounds the whole offer in a throne established in steadfast love; no king of David’s line in Israel’s history fits that description, and the New Testament shows whose throne it is.

Pride as the thing that cannot receive. Moab did not decline because the shelter was inadequate but because accepting it meant arriving as a supplicant, and verse 12 shows the alternative: a nation wearying itself in prayer at the wrong address.

17.subtitle: The Oracle Against Damascus — and a Remnant Who Returns
17.intro:
Where we are. After Babylon, Philistia and Moab, the oracles against the nations turn to Damascus, the capital of Syria, and its ally Ephraim, the northern kingdom of Israel. Their march on Jerusalem had made the heart of Ahaz shake “as the trees of the forest shake before the wind” (7:2).

The message. The powers that frightened God’s people will themselves be brought almost to nothing, and Israel, which joined Damascus instead of trusting the LORD, will share its fall. Yet the judgment has a purpose: when everything else has been stripped away, the few who are left will look to their Maker. The ruin came from forgetting the God of their salvation, and however loudly the nations roar, he has only to rebuke them, and by morning they are gone.

Why it was said. About 734 BC Rezin of Damascus and Pekah of Israel marched on Jerusalem, and Ahaz sent to Assyria for help instead of trusting God (see the introduction; 7:1–9). This oracle tells Judah that the coalition it feared had little time left: Damascus fell to Assyria in 732 BC and Samaria in 722. It also warns Judah against the same forgetting.

How the chapter makes its case. Damascus becomes a heap of ruins and Ephraim grows lean, left like a gleaned field or a beaten olive tree with a few berries at the top (vv. 1–6). Then the purpose: in that day man will look to his Maker, not to the altars his own hands have made (vv. 7–8). The cause follows: they forgot the God of their salvation and planted pleasant gardens for other gods, and the harvest fled away in a day of grief (vv. 9–11). Finally the nations roar like the sea, but God rebukes them and they blow away like chaff: terror at evening, gone before morning (vv. 12–14).

Where it leads. Chiefly by the character of God, revealed fully in Christ. The handful of berries kept by grace is the remnant Paul sees in his own day, “chosen by grace” (Romans 11:5), gathered now in Christ, the true vine (John 15:1). The Rock Israel forgot did not forget them, and in Christ he came looking for the forgetful. The rebuke that scatters the roaring nations is heard again on the lake of Galilee, when Jesus rebukes the wind and the sea and there is a great calm (Mark 4:39).

For us. People seldom abandon God by argument; they forget him while their gardens flourish. When God strips away what we leaned on, it is mercy meant to turn our eyes back to him. And whatever fills the night with fear, the morning belongs to him.

keyVerse.quote: “In that day man will look to his Maker, and his eyes will look on the Holy One of Israel.”
keyVerse.note: This is the goal of all of Isaiah’s prophecy compressed into one verse. The point of every judgment oracle is not to destroy but to turn eyes that have been fixed on everything else back to the only one worth looking at. All true recovery begins and ends with the Holy One of Israel.

17.reflection:
Verse 6 pictures the survivors as two or three berries left at the top of a beaten olive tree: kept, not better than the rest. How does it change the way you see yourself to know that you stand by grace and not by your own strength (Romans 11:5–6)?

Israel did not reject God; they forgot him (v. 10) while their gardens flourished (v. 11). What are the “pleasant plants” in your life that crowd God out of your planning, and what would remembering him look like this week?

Verses 7–8 describe a loss that turns a person’s eyes from what his hands have made to his Maker. Have you known a loss like that? How can you stand beside someone going through one now without making light of their pain?

“At evening time, behold, terror! Before morning, they are no more!” (v. 14). What fears fill your nights, and how does Jesus’ rebuke of the wind and the sea (Mark 4:39) help you face them?
