verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–6 — Two or Three Berries on the Highest Bough
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The two powers that terrified Judah are brought almost to nothing, and only a gleaning of Israel is left. Damascus will cease to be a city, its towns given over to grazing flocks, and Ephraim, which joined Syria against Judah, will lose its fortress and share Syria’s fate (vv. 1–3). Then harvest pictures show what remains of Jacob: a well-fed body grown lean, a field after the reapers and gleaners have been through it, and an olive tree beaten with poles, with two or three berries left at the top of the highest bough (vv. 4–6). The few who survive are not the best of Israel. They are simply the ones God kept.
verseByVerse.theology: The section answers the terror of chapter 7: the two powers that frightened Ahaz are themselves brought to almost nothing.
verseByVerse.examples: A believer who feels part of a small, unimpressive remnant, in a shrinking church or a hostile place, can take heart from verse 6. The few berries are not there by accident; they were kept.

verseByVerse.quote: An oracle concerning Damascus. Behold, Damascus will cease to be a city and will become a heap of ruins. The cities of Aroer are deserted; they will be for flocks, which will lie down, and none will make them afraid. The fortress will disappear from Ephraim, and the kingdom from Damascus; and the remnant of Syria will be like the glory of the children of Israel, declares the LORD of hosts. And in that day the glory of Jacob will be brought low, and the fat of his flesh will grow lean. And it shall be as when the reaper gathers standing grain and his arm harvests the ears, and as when one gleans the ears of grain in the Valley of Rephaim. Gleanings will be left in it, as when an olive tree is beaten— two or three berries in the top of the highest bough, four or five on the branches of a fruit tree, declares the LORD God of Israel.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The two allies that frightened Judah will be brought almost to nothing, and only a few will be left, like berries out of reach on a beaten olive tree.

Damascus will cease to be a city. Not merely defeated, but gone as a city. Its towns will be given over to flocks, which will lie down there with none to frighten them: a picture of sheep dozing in the streets of a capital.

When it happened. The coalition that sent Ahaz emptying the temple treasury in panic (2 Kings 16:8) had about a decade left. In 732 BC Assyria took Damascus, killed its king and ended the kingdom of Syria (2 Kings 16:9); Samaria fell in 722. The city later recovered, but as a power it ceased; a heap of ruins is prophecy’s strong language for the end of a nation.

The fat of his flesh will grow lean. Ephraim chose the alliance, and shares the fate. The image is a well-fed body wasting away: not killed, but reduced. Verse 3 ties the two allies to one fate with grim irony: what remains of Syria will be like the glory of the children of Israel, that is, as faded as Ephraim’s.

As when an olive tree is beaten. Verse 6 gives the remnant, described more honestly than anywhere else in the book. Olives were harvested by beating the tree with poles (Deuteronomy 24:20), and what survived a beating was whatever the poles could not reach: a few berries at the very top, a handful on the outer branches. That is what is left of the northern kingdom: not a faithful core that stood firm, but two or three berries that happened to be out of reach. Isaiah does not flatter the remnant. It survives because of where it was kept, not because of what it was.

A remnant chosen by grace. Paul says the same of his own day: there is a remnant, chosen by grace, and if by grace then not on the basis of works (Romans 11:5–6). The few berries at the top of the tree are kept by God’s choosing, and Christ, the true Israel and the true vine (John 15:1), is the one in whom that remnant is held; no one can snatch his sheep out of his Father’s hand (John 10:29).

Uncertain wording. The cities of Aroer (v. 2) is puzzling in an oracle about Damascus, since the best-known Aroer lay far south, on the Arnon. Perhaps another Aroer is meant, or land east of the Jordan that Damascus had ruled. The ancient Greek translation reads instead that the cities will be deserted for ever. Either way, the land is emptied.
verseByVerse.note: The Valley of Rephaim (v. 5) lay just south-west of Jerusalem, fertile land Isaiah's hearers would have known well.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 7–11 — In That Day a Man Will Look
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The disaster has a purpose: to turn a people’s eyes back to the God who made them. In that day a man will look to the Holy One of Israel and no longer to the altars and Asherim his own hands have made (vv. 7–8). Then the cause of the ruin is named. Israel’s strong cities will be deserted as the Canaanites once deserted theirs, because Israel has forgotten the God of its salvation and the Rock of its refuge (vv. 9–10). In his place they planted pleasant gardens and a foreign vine, which sprang up in a day and blossomed by morning, but on the day of grief there was no harvest (vv. 10–11).
verseByVerse.theology: The section turns from what is lost to what the loss was for: a people looking again at their Maker.
verseByVerse.examples: Forgetting God rarely feels like rebellion. It looks like a full diary and a prayerless week; the remedy is to come back to him, and he is still the God of your salvation.

verseByVerse.quote: In that day man will look to his Maker, and his eyes will look on the Holy One of Israel. He will not look to the altars, the work of his hands, and he will not look on what his own fingers have made, either the Asherim or the altars of incense. In that day their strong cities will be like the deserted places of the wooded heights and the hilltops, which they deserted because of the children of Israel, and there will be desolation. For you have forgotten the God of your salvation and have not remembered the Rock of your refuge; therefore, though you plant pleasant plants and sow the vine-branch of a stranger, though you make them grow on the day that you plant them, and make them blossom in the morning that you sow, yet the harvest will flee away in a day of grief and incurable pain.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When everything else is gone, people will turn from the gods they made to the God who made them; their ruin came because they forgot him and planted quick gardens in his place.

Man will look to his Maker. One word is used four times in verses 7 and 8: look. The man in this verse does not acquire new information; he turns his head. He had looked at altars and objects his own fingers made; now he looks at the one who made him. That contrast is the whole point. (The Asherim were wooden poles set up beside altars for the goddess Asherah.)

What the disaster was for. Judgment in this book is often simply the removal of everything else worth looking at, until our eyes rest where they belonged all along. The gospel keeps the same verb: Isaiah will later write, “Turn to me and be saved, all the ends of the earth!” (45:22), and the New Testament tells the Christian to run looking to Jesus (Hebrews 12:2).

Their strong cities will be like the deserted places. Verse 9 draws the consequence from Israel’s own history. Their strong cities will be like the places the Canaanites abandoned when Israel came in under Joshua: the people who once moved into deserted cities will leave theirs deserted.

You have forgotten the God of your salvation. The cause is not rebellion but forgetting. Nobody in Israel had concluded that God did not exist. They had simply stopped remembering him, with the quiet neglect that befalls anything that is always there. And it is still the God of your salvation they forgot: the cure is not a resolve to remember harder but a return to the Rock who has not forgotten them, through the word and prayer by which his Spirit keeps us mindful of him.

Pleasant plants. The substitute is a garden: fashionable imported stock that comes up beautifully, growing the same day and blossoming the same morning. Many think of a pagan custom: small gardens of quick-sprouting plants tended for a fertility god (later linked with Adonis), which sprang up fast and withered as fast. The vine-branch of a stranger points the same way, to foreign religion as well as foreign stock.

The harvest will flee away. On the day of grief there is no harvest. That is the test every substitute for God eventually fails: not whether it flourishes, but whether it is still there on the worst morning of your life.

How a culture forgets God. We imagine that societies lose their faith through argument: a famous book, a discovery, a debate lost. Isaiah’s picture is closer to how it usually happens. The new gardens simply flourish. Life fills up with things that work, and God, who does not need replanting every season, drops out of the planning. Many people now are less unbelievers than people for whom the question seldom comes up. Sociologists can describe that drift; Isaiah adds what they cannot, the day of grief when the garden has nothing to give.

The forgetting runs one way. Augustine confessed that God had been with him the whole time while he was not with God. So here: Israel forgot the God of your salvation, but he never forgot them, and the rest of the book is his refusal to: “Even these may forget, yet I will not forget you” (49:15). In Christ that refusal came looking for us: the shepherd goes after the lost sheep until he finds it (Luke 15:4–6).

Uncertain wording. Verse 9 is compressed. Where the Hebrew has the wooded heights and the hilltops, the ancient Greek translation names two Canaanite peoples, the Hivites and the Amorites. Either way the cities are those the Canaanites abandoned before Israel. The link of pleasant plants (v. 10) with Adonis is possible but not certain.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 12–14 — At Evening, Terror; Before Morning, Gone
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: However loudly the nations roar, God has only to rebuke them. The armies of many peoples thunder like the sea (v. 12), but at his word they flee like chaff on the mountains and whirling dust before a storm (v. 13). Terror at evening, gone before morning: that is the end of those who plunder God’s people, and the chapter calls it their portion and their lot, the settled rule rather than a single incident (v. 14). Twenty chapters later an Assyrian army camps around Jerusalem at night and is dead by morning (37:36).
verseByVerse.theology: In three verses the threat of all the nations turns out to be a storm that passes, and the last line states the lesson: so it always ends for those who plunder God’s people.
verseByVerse.examples: Verse 14 is the most usable sentence in the chapter for anyone going to bed frightened: what fills the night has an appointment with the morning.

verseByVerse.quote: Ah, the thunder of many peoples; they thunder like the thundering of the sea! Ah, the roar of nations; they roar like the roaring of mighty waters! The nations roar like the roaring of many waters, but he will rebuke them, and they will flee far away, chased like chaff on the mountains before the wind and whirling dust before the storm. At evening time, behold, terror! Before morning, they are no more! This is the portion of those who loot us, and the lot of those who plunder us.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The nations that roar like the sea are rebuked by a word and blown away like chaff: what terrifies at evening is gone by morning.

The thunder of many peoples. The chapter ends with noise. Isaiah describes not the armies but the sound they make, and compares it twice to the sea, which for an inland people was the standing image of a force that could not be reasoned with or stopped.

He will rebuke them. No battle, no army. God speaks sharply and the sea turns out to have been chaff all along: the light husk left on the threshing floor, which a hillside wind takes without effort.

At evening time, behold, terror! Verse 14 repays memorising for the right kind of night. Isaiah puts the two times side by side with nothing in between. Evening: terror, immediate, with behold in front of it because it is right there in the room. Morning: gone. Not defeated after a long campaign, simply not there when the light comes. Twenty chapters later that is exactly what happens outside Jerusalem, where an Assyrian army lies encamped at night and by morning is all dead bodies (37:36).

The portion of those who loot us. This is no single incident but the settled rule, the portion and lot of all who plunder God’s people. What has terrified them through the night has an appointment with the morning.

The one who rebukes the sea. The same verb returns in the Gospels. When a storm on the lake terrified the disciples, Jesus “rebuked the wind and said to the sea, ‘Peace! Be still!’” and there was a great calm (Mark 4:39). The disciples asked who this could be; Isaiah and the psalms had already answered (Psalm 65:7). And the darkest night of all ended at dawn on the first day of the week, with the tomb empty.

What it does not mean. Not that God’s people never face a long night: Judah’s fortified cities fell before Jerusalem was spared (36:1). The promise is not that the night will be short, but that it will not have the last word.

17.theology:
Two or three berries. Isaiah does not flatter the survivors: they are not a faithful core that stood firm but a handful kept by grace, out of reach of the poles.

Judgment as the clearing of the view. The conversion of verses 7 and 8 consists entirely of a change of direction, away from the work of his hands and toward his Maker, and the cause of the ruin is named as forgetting (v. 10), the ordinary neglect that befalls anything that is always there.

Evening and morning. The roaring of the nations is answered by a rebuke and becomes chaff, and the chapter calls that the settled rule, not a single incident.

18.subtitle: The Oracle Against Cush
18.intro:
Where we are. Between the oracle on Damascus and the long oracle on Egypt comes a short word to Cush, the land far up the Nile whose kings had taken Egypt and now ruled both. Its envoys have come by sea and by papyrus boat, and they are waiting in Jerusalem for an answer.

The message. While the nations hurry to build alliances, God watches quietly, and he will act at exactly the right moment. Judah does not need Cush to save it from Assyria: the LORD himself will cut the threatening power down just before its harvest. And the distant nation that came to talk politics will one day come to Zion with a gift for the LORD.

Why it was said. In the years before 701 BC, Hezekiah’s court was tempted to join a revolt against Assyria backed by Egypt and its Cushite rulers (see the introduction; 20:5–6; 30:1–2). Isaiah sends the envoys home with a word from God instead of a treaty.

How the chapter makes its case. Isaiah addresses the land of whirring wings, describes its tall and feared people with respect, and sends its messengers home (vv. 1–2). The whole world is told to watch for God’s signal and listen for his trumpet (v. 3). Then the heart of the chapter: God watches quietly from his dwelling, like the heat and dew that ripen a crop (v. 4), and just before harvest he cuts the vine back and leaves its branches to the birds and beasts (vv. 5–6). At that time the same people bring tribute to Mount Zion (v. 7).

Where it leads. By promise. Verse 7 belongs with the promises that the nations will stream to Zion (2:2–4; Psalm 68:31). Its first fruits came on a desert road, when an Ethiopian official, returning from worship in Jerusalem, heard Philip explain Isaiah 53 and was baptised into Christ (Acts 8:26–39). The Zion to which the nations now come is “the city of the living God”, where Jesus is the mediator of a new covenant (Hebrews 12:22–24).

For us. God’s quiet is not his absence. In a crisis we rush for whatever alliance or fix is on offer; this chapter calls us to wait for the God who watches before he acts and whose timing is never late. And it reminds us that he is gathering people from the ends of the earth, perhaps even from the nations we fear.

keyVerse.quote: “For thus the LORD said to me: I will quietly look from my dwelling like clear heat in sunshine, like a cloud of dew in the heat of harvest.”
keyVerse.note: The image of God watching quietly from his dwelling is one of the most calming pictures of his sovereignty in Scripture. It is not passivity: the harvest is coming and the pruning hooks are ready (v. 5). It is the quiet confidence of one who is never caught off guard, never reactive, always working towards his own purposes at exactly the right pace.

18.reflection:
Envoys from Cush came offering an alliance against Assyria (vv. 1–2). When you face a threat, what alliances or quick fixes are you most tempted to run to before you have prayed?

God says, “I will quietly look from my dwelling” (v. 4). How can you tell the difference between God’s quiet and God’s absence? When has his timing proved better than yours?

The nation that came to talk politics ends up bringing tribute to the LORD on Mount Zion (v. 7), and an Ethiopian official was among the first Gentiles to be baptised (Acts 8:26–39). Which people do you find it hardest to imagine coming to Christ, and how might you pray for them?
18.text: <sup>1</sup>Ah, land of whirring wings that is beyond the rivers of Cush,<sup>2</sup>which sends ambassadors by the sea, in vessels of papyrus on the waters! Go, you swift messengers, to a nation tall and smooth, to a people feared near and far, a nation mighty and conquering, whose land the rivers divide.<sup>3</sup>All you inhabitants of the world, you who dwell on the earth, when a signal is raised on the mountains, look! When a trumpet is blown, hear!<sup>4</sup>For thus the LORD said to me: "I will quietly look from my dwelling like clear heat in sunshine, like a cloud of dew in the heat of harvest."<sup>5</sup>For before the harvest, when the blossom is over, and the flower becomes a ripening grape, he cuts off the shoots with pruning hooks, and the spreading branches he lops off and clears away.<sup>6</sup>They shall all of them be left to the birds of prey of the mountains and to the beasts of the earth. And the birds of prey will summer on them, and all the beasts of the earth will winter on them.<sup>7</sup>At that time tribute will be brought to the LORD of hosts from a people tall and smooth, from a people feared near and far, a nation mighty and conquering, whose land the rivers divide, to Mount Zion, the place of the name of the LORD of hosts.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God’s quiet watchfulness puts the busy diplomacy of the nations in its place, and the chapter ends with a distant people worshipping him. Envoys from Cush, a tall and feared nation far up the Nile, have come in papyrus boats; Isaiah sends them home and tells the whole world to watch for God’s signal (vv. 1–3). God does not hurry. He watches from his dwelling like the steady heat and dew that ripen a crop (v. 4), and just before harvest he cuts the vine back, leaving its branches to the birds and beasts (vv. 5–6). Then the same people come to Mount Zion, bringing tribute to the LORD of hosts (v. 7).
verseByVerse.theology: The section sets God's stillness against the bustle of diplomats, and ends with the diplomats' own nation as worshippers.
verseByVerse.examples: When a crisis tempts us to rush for whatever alliance or fix is on offer, verse 4 is worth holding on to. God's quiet is not absence, and his timing is set by him, not by the urgency of the people around us.

verseByVerse.quote: Ah, land of whirring wings that is beyond the rivers of Cush, which sends ambassadors by the sea, in vessels of papyrus on the waters! Go, you swift messengers, to a nation tall and smooth, to a people feared near and far, a nation mighty and conquering, whose land the rivers divide. All you inhabitants of the world, you who dwell on the earth, when a signal is raised on the mountains, look! When a trumpet is blown, hear!
verseByVerse.commentary:
Isaiah sends home the envoys of a great, distant nation and tells the world to watch for what God will do.

Beyond the rivers of Cush. Cush is roughly modern Sudan, and in Isaiah’s day its kings had taken Egypt and ruled both. Its envoys have come down the Nile in papyrus boats and on by sea to see whether Judah will join a coalition against Assyria. A Cushite king, Tirhakah, did march out against Sennacherib in 701 BC (37:9), and it did not save Judah.

A nation tall and smooth. The description is respectful rather than mocking: a tall people, feared near and far, whose land the rivers divide. Isaiah is not belittling them. He is sending them home without the answer they came for, which is a different thing.

All you inhabitants of the world. The audience widens from one embassy to everybody alive. A signal is coming that all will see and a trumpet all will hear, and when they come, the question this delegation travelled so far to ask will have answered itself.

Uncertain wording. Whirring wings translates a rare word that imitates buzzing: most think of the insects of the Nile valley, some of the sails of many boats. Smooth probably means smooth-skinned or clean-shaven. The opening Ah is often translated “woe”, but nothing here condemns Cush, so it is probably a call for attention.
verseByVerse.note: Cush is probably Nubia (ESV note); its kings ruled Egypt for much of the late eighth and seventh centuries BC.

verseByVerse.quote: For thus the LORD said to me: "I will quietly look from my dwelling like clear heat in sunshine, like a cloud of dew in the heat of harvest." For before the harvest, when the blossom is over, and the flower becomes a ripening grape, he cuts off the shoots with pruning hooks, and the spreading branches he lops off and clears away. They shall all of them be left to the birds of prey of the mountains and to the beasts of the earth. And the birds of prey will summer on them, and all the beasts of the earth will winter on them. At that time tribute will be brought to the LORD of hosts from a people tall and smooth, from a people feared near and far, a nation mighty and conquering, whose land the rivers divide, to Mount Zion, the place of the name of the LORD of hosts.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God watches quietly until the right moment, cuts down the threatening power just before its harvest, and will one day receive worship from the people who came seeking an alliance.

I will quietly look from my dwelling. Verse 4 is the sentence the chapter exists for, and everything turns on one word: quietly. Ambassadors are travelling, coalitions forming, the great question of the decade urgently negotiated, and God says he is watching from home without raising his voice.

Clear heat in sunshine. Both pictures are agricultural. Clear heat in sunshine is the steady warmth that ripens a crop: no storm, just the conditions doing their work day after day. A cloud of dew in the heat of harvest is the moisture that settles overnight in the hottest weeks. Neither makes any noise. Both are irresistible. God is not indifferent and he is not scrambling; he is watching the way a farmer watches a ripening field, waiting for the exact day.

He cuts off the shoots. Then he moves. The picture is a vine cut back just before its grapes ripen: the threatening power, most likely Assyria, is cut down when its plans are almost complete. The cutting is thorough: what is left on the ground feeds the birds for a summer and the beasts for a winter. So it was in 701 BC, when Sennacherib’s army was struck down outside Jerusalem (37:36).

Tribute will be brought to the LORD of hosts. The chapter began with Cush sending ambassadors to Judah to talk politics. It ends with the same people arriving at Zion with a gift for God. That is what these oracles keep doing: the nations appear first as a threat or a temptation, and at last as worshippers.

The nations come to Zion. Cush bringing gifts to Zion belongs with the promise that the nations will come to the LORD (2:2–4; Psalm 68:31). Its first fruits came when an Ethiopian official went home from Jerusalem baptised into Christ (Acts 8:27–39), and it continues as the gospel reaches Africa and every nation.

18.theology:
Quietly. The chapter turns on a single word in verse 4, quietly: God is watching a ripening field and waiting for the exact day.

The timing of the cut. For a nation tempted to solve its problem by treaty, the diplomacy is beside the point: the decisive act has a date, and the date is not being set in any of the capitals involved.

Threat, then worshipper. The same people who came to talk politics arrive at Mount Zion with a gift, which is why these oracles against the nations are not merely a list of judgments.

19.subtitle: The Oracle Against Egypt — and Egypt's Redemption
19.intro:
Where we are. After the short word to Cush, Isaiah turns to Egypt, the great power Judah was most tempted to lean on against Assyria (30:1–2; 31:1). It is the most surprising of all the oracles against the nations.

The message. God takes Egypt apart, its gods, its unity, its river and its famous wisdom, to show that Egypt cannot save even itself. But he strikes in order to heal. The chapter that begins with the LORD riding on a cloud against Egypt ends with Egyptians crying to him, receiving a saviour and being called, with Assyria, his own people. God’s last word over Israel’s oldest enemies is a blessing.

Why it was said. In Isaiah’s day Egypt was divided and weak, and fell first to Cushite and later to Assyrian kings, yet Judah’s politicians kept looking to it for rescue (see the introduction; 20:5–6; 30:1–7). The oracle exposes that hope as empty, and opens a far larger one: that the nations Israel feared would one day worship Israel’s God.

How the chapter makes its case. The LORD comes on a swift cloud; the idols tremble, and Egypt falls into civil war and panic, consults the dead, and is handed to a hard master (vv. 1–4). The Nile fails, and every trade that lived by it collapses (vv. 5–10). Egypt’s celebrated counsellors cannot say what the LORD has planned, and the nation staggers like a drunk (vv. 11–15). Then six sayings beginning “in that day” turn the chapter round: Egypt trembles (vv. 16–17), five cities swear allegiance to the LORD (v. 18), an altar stands in Egypt and God sends a saviour when they cry (vv. 19–20), Egypt knows the LORD, who strikes and heals (vv. 21–22), and a highway joins Egypt and Assyria in worship, with Israel as the third, a blessing in the midst of the earth (vv. 23–25).

Where it leads. By promise and by pattern. Verse 20 retells the exodus with Egypt in Israel’s place: they cry out, and God sends a saviour. That Saviour is Christ, who was himself carried into Egypt as a child and called out of it (Matthew 2:13–15), and in whom Gentiles who were far off have been brought near, with the dividing wall broken down (Ephesians 2:13–14). The promise that all the families of the earth would be blessed in Abraham comes true in Abraham’s offspring, Christ (Galatians 3:8, 16).

For us. No nation, family or past lies beyond the reach of this God. When he strikes, he means to heal; and the people we find hardest to imagine as brothers and sisters may be the very ones he will call “my people”.

keyVerse.quote: “Blessed be Egypt my people, and Assyria the work of my hands, and Israel my inheritance.”
keyVerse.note: The terms “my people” and “my inheritance” are names for God’s covenant people, used elsewhere in the Old Testament of Israel alone. Here “my people” is given to Egypt, and Assyria is called the work of God’s hands. This does not cancel God’s choice of Israel but widens it: the covenant blessing flows outward to the nations, as God promised Abraham: “in you all the families of the earth shall be blessed” (Genesis 12:3).

19.theology:
Judgment aimed at what a nation trusts. God does not attack Egypt’s army. He dries the Nile and confuses the counsellors, which is how a civilisation is dismantled rather than merely defeated.

The exodus, performed for Egypt. The rescue that was carried out against Egypt is to be carried out for Egypt: the same mercy, extended to the old enemy, with an altar in the middle of the land of bondage.

The three titles of verse 25. Egypt and Assyria are given Israel’s covenant names, and Israel is not displaced but stands as one of three. It is the promise to Abraham coming true, and it leads on to the church, where Christ has broken down the dividing wall between Jew and Gentile (Ephesians 2:14).
19.reflection:
Egypt trusted its gods, its river and its wise men, and God took each apart (vv. 1–15). What is your “Nile”, the thing that seems too reliable to fail? What would it mean to hold it as a gift rather than stand on it?

Verse 12 asks, “Where then are your wise men?” Where do people around you look for guidance about the future, and how does the gospel answer that hunger (Hebrews 1:1–2)?

The LORD strikes Egypt, “striking and healing” (v. 22). Have you known God’s discipline that turned out to be aimed at healing? How might that shape the way you pray for someone who is suffering now?

God calls Egypt “my people” and Assyria “the work of my hands” (v. 25), the very nations that enslaved and crushed Israel. Who do you find it hardest to imagine as a brother or sister in Christ, and what does Ephesians 2:14 say to that?

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–15 — The Wisdom of Egypt Fails
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God dismantles everything Egypt trusted, to show that Egypt cannot save even itself. The LORD rides into Egypt on a swift cloud and its idols tremble; the nation turns on itself in civil war, loses its nerve, consults mediums and the dead, and falls to a hard master (vv. 1–4). Then the Nile, the source of all Egypt’s life, fails, and fishermen, flax workers and weavers despair one trade at a time (vv. 5–10). Finally Egypt’s famous wisdom collapses: the princes of Zoan and Memphis cannot tell what the LORD has purposed, and the nation staggers like a drunk (vv. 11–15).
verseByVerse.theology: The first half of the chapter takes Egypt apart piece by piece: its gods, its unity, its river and its wisdom.
verseByVerse.examples: Every culture has its Nile, the thing that seems too reliable to fail, whether a pension, an economy or a health service. These verses do not despise such gifts, but they warn against making any of them the ground we stand on.

verseByVerse.quote: An oracle concerning Egypt. Behold, the LORD is riding on a swift cloud and comes to Egypt; and the idols of Egypt will tremble at his presence, and the heart of the Egyptians will melt within them. And I will stir up Egyptians against Egyptians, and they will fight, each against another and each against his neighbor, city against city, kingdom against kingdom; and the spirit of the Egyptians within them will be emptied out, and I will confound their counsel; and they will inquire of the idols and the sorcerers, and the mediums and the necromancers; and I will give over the Egyptians into the hand of a hard master, and a fierce king will rule over them, declares the Lord GOD of hosts.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The LORD himself comes against Egypt: its gods tremble, its people turn on one another and run to mediums, and it falls under a harsh ruler.

Riding on a swift cloud. The image is a war-chariot, and the chariot is a cloud. God comes into Egypt personally, and the first things to react are the statues.

The idols of Egypt will tremble. Egypt had more gods than any nation in the region, held for millennia. Isaiah gives them one verb: they tremble. Nothing is argued; the LORD arrives, and they cannot stand still, as on the night of the exodus, when he executed judgments on all the gods of Egypt (Exodus 12:12).

Egyptians against Egyptians. The judgment begins as civil war, the hardest disaster to blame on anyone outside: a nation coming apart along its own seams. Then its spirit, its confidence and sense of itself, is emptied out, and its counsel confounded.

They will inquire of the idols. The reflex is the one Isaiah has already described in Judah (8:19). When real guidance fails, the appetite for guidance does not go away; it turns to whatever is on offer. The most sophisticated civilisation on earth ends up asking questions of the dead.

The hard master. Isaiah does not name the fierce king. In his lifetime Egypt was split among rival rulers until the Cushite king Piye took the whole country, about 728 BC; in the next century the Assyrian Esarhaddon captured Memphis (671 BC) and Ashurbanipal sacked Thebes (663 BC). Any of them fits. For Judah, whose leaders kept looking to Egypt for rescue, the point was plain: the nation they hoped would save them could not save itself.

Why does a sceptical age read its horoscope? As science advanced and churches emptied, the old superstitions were meant to fade with the old faith. Instead astrology apps, tarot cards and talk of what the universe is telling us are thriving, often among the most educated. Isaiah would not be surprised. The Belgian writer Émile Cammaerts, summing up Chesterton, observed that the first effect of not believing in God is to believe in anything. The hunger for guidance and for someone who knows the future is no leftover from a primitive past; it belongs to creatures made by a God who speaks. Cut off from him, it feeds on whatever is at hand. The gospel does not mock that hunger. It satisfies it. The One who actually holds the future has spoken to us by his Son (Hebrews 1:2), and the Son says to the anxious, “Let not your hearts be troubled” (John 14:1).

verseByVerse.quote: And the waters of the sea will be dried up, and the river will be dry and parched, and its canals will become foul, and the branches of Egypt's Nile will diminish and dry up, reeds and rushes will rot away. There will be bare places by the Nile, on the brink of the Nile, and all that is sown by the Nile will be parched, will be driven away, and will be no more. The fishermen will mourn and lament, all who cast a hook in the Nile; and they will languish who spread nets on the water. The workers in combed flax will be in despair, and the weavers of white cotton. Those who are the pillars of the land will be crushed, and all who work for pay will be grieved.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Nile, Egypt’s life, will fail, and every trade that lives by it will collapse.

The river will be dry and parched. To feel this you have to know that Egypt was the Nile. The country is a green ribbon a few miles wide with desert on both sides; food, trade, calendar and religion all ran off one river that flooded on schedule every year, a flood itself worshipped as a god. It was the most reliable thing in the ancient world, and Isaiah says it will fail.

Reeds and rushes will rot away. He follows the drying down through the land: the reed beds rot, the sown ground by the river goes bare, the crops blow away.

The fishermen will mourn. Then the trades, one by one: line fishermen, net fishermen, flax workers, weavers. Isaiah takes the disaster out of the palace and puts it in the hands of men who get up early, because that is where a failed river is felt.

The river that does not fail. Every culture has its Nile, the thing too reliable to fail, and every Nile eventually does. Jesus offers what no river can: water that becomes in the one who drinks “a spring of water welling up to eternal life” (John 4:14).

Uncertain wording. The sea (v. 5) is almost certainly the Nile itself, broad enough to be called a sea. In verse 10, pillars may instead mean weavers, continuing the list of trades, and all who work for pay has also been read as makers of dams or fishponds. Either way, everyone who lived by the river is broken.

verseByVerse.quote: The princes of Zoan are utterly foolish; the wisest counselors of Pharaoh give stupid counsel. How can you say to Pharaoh, "I am a son of the wise, a son of ancient kings"? Where then are your wise men? Let them tell you that they might know what the LORD of hosts has purposed against Egypt. The princes of Zoan have become fools, and the princes of Memphis are deluded; those who are the cornerstones of her tribes have made Egypt stagger. The LORD has mingled within her a spirit of confusion, and they will make Egypt stagger in all its deeds, as a drunken man staggers in his vomit. And there will be nothing for Egypt that head or tail, palm branch or reed, may do.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Egypt’s famous wise men are exposed as fools, because no human wisdom can tell what the LORD has planned, and the nation staggers like a drunk.

The princes of Zoan are utterly foolish. After the river, the wisdom. Egyptian counsel was proverbial, and its wisdom literature was old before Israel existed. When Solomon is praised, he is said to have surpassed the wisdom of Egypt (1 Kings 4:30). Zoan in the delta and Memphis, the ancient capital, were seats of Pharaoh’s court.

I am a son of the wise. Isaiah’s charge is not that these men are unintelligent but that they are trading on an inheritance. A son of the wise, a son of ancient kings is a boast about ancestry, not wisdom, and ancestry is exactly what fails when something truly new arrives.

Where then are your wise men? Verse 12 is the test, and no adviser can pass it. The question is not whether they are clever but whether any of them can tell what God intends, which no human wisdom can work out; it has to be told to us.

As a drunken man staggers. The final picture is undignified on purpose: the most sophisticated state in the world lurching about like a drunk who has fallen in his own mess. And verse 15 says there is nothing left for anyone in Egypt to do, great or small (head or tail, palm branch or reed, as in 9:14–15).

The wisdom of God. Paul echoes Isaiah’s taunt: “Where is the one who is wise? … Has not God made foolish the wisdom of the world?” (1 Corinthians 1:20). The purpose God has purposed, which Egypt’s sages could not tell, is now revealed in a crucified Messiah, “the power of God and the wisdom of God” (1 Corinthians 1:24).

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Six sayings beginning “in that day” turn judgment into mercy, until God calls Egypt and Assyria his own. Egypt first trembles before the LORD’s hand and before Judah (vv. 16–17). Then five Egyptian cities speak the language of Canaan and swear allegiance to the LORD (v. 18); an altar and a pillar stand as a witness in the land, and when Egyptians cry out under oppressors God sends them a saviour, as he once did for Israel (vv. 19–20). Egypt comes to know the LORD, who strikes and heals (vv. 21–22). Finally a highway joins Egypt and Assyria in worship, and Israel stands with them as the third, a blessing in the midst of the earth (vv. 23–25).
verseByVerse.theology: The second half of the chapter is mercy to the old enemy, rising step by step to the blessing of verse 25.
verseByVerse.examples: No one is too far gone for this chapter. If God could call Egypt my people, there is no family history, nation or past that puts a person beyond his reach.

verseByVerse.quote: In that day the Egyptians will be like women, and tremble with fear before the hand that the LORD of hosts shakes over them. And the land of Judah will become a terror to the Egyptians. Everyone to whom it is mentioned will fear because of the purpose that the LORD of hosts has purposed against them. In that day there will be five cities in the land of Egypt that speak the language of Canaan and swear allegiance to the LORD of hosts. One of these will be called the City of Destruction. In that day there will be an altar to the LORD in the midst of the land of Egypt, and a pillar to the LORD at its border. It will be a sign and a witness to the LORD of hosts in the land of Egypt. When they cry to the LORD because of oppressors, he will send them a savior and defender, and deliver them. And the LORD will make himself known to the Egyptians, and the Egyptians will know the LORD in that day and worship with sacrifice and offering, and they will make vows to the LORD and perform them. And the LORD will strike Egypt, striking and healing, and they will return to the LORD, and he will listen to their pleas for mercy and heal them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Egypt, once terrified, will turn to the LORD, cry to him and be given a saviour, as Israel once was, for he strikes Egypt in order to heal it.

In that day. Six paragraphs now begin with in that day, and between the first and the last the chapter turns completely round. It begins with Egypt trembling before the hand of the LORD, and even before little Judah, not because of Judah’s army but because of what the LORD has purposed (vv. 16–17).

Five cities in the land of Egypt. Then five Egyptian cities speak the language of Canaan, that is, Hebrew, and swear loyalty to Israel’s God. Not conquered, but converted.

An altar to the LORD. An altar in the middle of Egypt, and a pillar at its border claiming the land for the LORD. For a people who remembered Egypt as slavery and brick quotas, this is close to unthinkable: the place of bondage becomes a place of sacrifice.

He will send them a savior. Verse 20 deliberately echoes Exodus 2–3. Israel cried out under oppression, and God heard and sent a deliverer; here the Egyptians cry out, and God sends them a saviour. It is the same rescue, with the old enemy in Israel’s place. The exodus was performed against Egypt; God intends to perform it for Egypt.

Striking and healing. The book opened by saying Israel did not know its owner as well as an ox knows its master (1:3). Here Egypt knows him. And verse 22 puts the whole chapter in one line: the LORD strikes Egypt, striking and healing, and when they return he will listen to their pleas for mercy and heal them. The blow was aimed at the healing all along.

The Saviour Egypt is given. Isaiah does not name the savior and defender, but the promise finds its answer in Christ, who was carried into Egypt as a child and called out of it (Matthew 2:13–15).

Has anything like it happened? Egyptians heard the apostles at Pentecost (Acts 2:10), and Egypt became one of the earliest strongholds of the church, with a Christian community that survives to this day. Some Jews in the second century before Christ even built a temple in Egypt and cited this verse to justify it: the promise was taken seriously, though that building is not its fulfilment.

Where Christians differ: how will this be fulfilled, given that sacrifice was limited to the one place God chose (Deuteronomy 12)? Dispensational readers expect a literal future Egypt and Assyria worshipping in a millennial age. Others read Isaiah as describing the nations’ future worship in the language of his own day, as Malachi speaks of incense offered among the nations (Malachi 1:11), fulfilled not in a literal altar but in Egyptians worshipping the true God through Christ.

This commentary’s view: the second, amillennial reading, because the New Testament treats the gathering of the nations as happening now, through the gospel (Acts 15:14–17), and the joining of old enemies into one people of God is what the gospel does (Ephesians 2:14; Galatians 3:28). Faithful Christians who see more still to come are brothers in the same hope.
verseByVerse.note: “City of Destruction” may read “City of the Sun” (ESV note) — Heliopolis. The two Hebrew words differ by one letter; the Dead Sea Isaiah scroll and some Hebrew manuscripts read “sun”.

verseByVerse.quote: In that day there will be a highway from Egypt to Assyria, and Assyria will come into Egypt, and Egypt into Assyria, and the Egyptians will worship with the Assyrians. In that day Israel will be the third with Egypt and Assyria, a blessing in the midst of the earth, whom the LORD of hosts has blessed, saying, "Blessed be Egypt my people, and Assyria the work of my hands, and Israel my inheritance."
verseByVerse.commentary:
A highway will join Egypt and Assyria in worship, and Israel will stand with them as a blessing, as God gives his own titles to the nations that had been Israel’s worst enemies.

A highway from Egypt to Assyria. A road runs between the two superpowers, and the traffic on it is not military. For centuries armies had marched along that corridor, and Judah was the small country between them, the ground they marched over. Isaiah sees the same road with worshippers on it, going both ways.

Israel will be the third. Not the centre with two lesser nations around it, but one of three, in the middle of the earth, as a blessing. That is the promise to Abraham coming true: “in you all the families of the earth shall be blessed” (Genesis 12:3).

Egypt my people. My people is Israel’s phrase throughout the Bible, and it is given to Egypt, the house of slavery, the nation of the brick pits and the drowned chariots. The work of my hands is the language of creation and craftsmanship, and it is given to Assyria, the empire that destroyed the northern kingdom and stood outside Jerusalem’s walls. And Israel keeps its own title, my inheritance, alongside them.

By grace, not by merit. Nothing is taken from Israel. Something is given to everybody else, by grace and not by merit, and the two nations that between them account for most of Israel’s suffering are named with the love God has for his own.

Where the oracles have been going. The oracles against the nations begin as judgments on empires and end with God calling his oldest enemies his people. The same road leads on to the church of Ephesians 2, Jew and Gentile with the dividing wall broken down.

What it does not mean. Not that every nation’s gods lead to the same place: Egypt and Assyria are blessed because they worship the LORD (v. 23), their idols left trembling (v. 1).
verseByVerse.note: The highway of verse 23 echoes the highway home from Assyria in 11:16; here it carries worshippers between the nations.

20.subtitle: The Sign of Isaiah's Nakedness
20.intro:
Where we are. Chapter 20 is a short prose interlude among the oracles against the nations, dated to the year Assyria captured the Philistine city of Ashdod, about 711 BC. It drives home the words to Cush (chapter 18) and Egypt (chapter 19) with a sign no one in Jerusalem could ignore.

The message. Do not trust Egypt and Cush to save you from Assyria: they will be led away as naked captives themselves. God makes the point not with a sermon but with his prophet’s body, as Isaiah walks naked and barefoot for three years. Everyone who leaned on Egypt will be left asking, “how shall we escape?”, and the only answer is the LORD.

Why it was said. Ashdod rebelled against Assyria counting on Egyptian help, and the help never came. Judah was being drawn into the same rebellion and the same hope (see the introduction; 30:1–5; 31:1).

How the chapter makes its case. The date sets the sign in a crisis everyone could see (v. 1). God tells Isaiah to loose his sackcloth and take off his sandals, and he does so (v. 2). Then God explains: as Isaiah has walked for three years, so Assyria will lead away the captives of Egypt and Cush, young and old, stripped and shamed (vv. 3–4). Those who hoped in them will be dismayed, and the people of the coast will ask how they can escape now (vv. 5–6).

Where it leads. By pattern, and by the need it exposes. God calls Isaiah my servant, the title later given to the suffering Servant (42:1; 52:13). Isaiah bore public shame as a sign of judgment coming on others; Jesus was stripped in earnest, outside the city, while soldiers divided his clothes (John 19:23–24), and bore the judgment itself in the place of others. The chapter’s last question returns in the New Testament: “how shall we escape if we neglect such a great salvation?” (Hebrews 2:3). There is no escape through Egypt; there is through Christ, who “endured the cross, despising the shame” (Hebrews 12:2).

For us. Whatever we lean on instead of God, whether money, a relationship, a reputation or a powerful friend, will one day need rescuing itself. And faithfulness sometimes costs our dignity: Isaiah’s four words, “and he did so”, set the pattern, and Christ’s shame borne for us gives the strength.

keyVerse.quote: “And the inhabitants of this coastland will say in that day, ‘Behold, this is what has happened to those in whom we hoped and to whom we fled for help to be delivered from the king of Assyria! And we, how shall we escape?’”
keyVerse.note: The question “how shall we escape?” is where every misplaced trust ends. When the thing we trusted, whether Egypt, an alliance, a financial plan or a relationship, fails, we are left with the question Isaiah has been asking since chapter 1: to whom are you actually looking? The book’s answer is always the same, “look to the rock from which you were hewn” (51:1), and Hebrews turns the question towards the salvation God has given in Christ (Hebrews 2:3).

20.reflection:
Isaiah’s response to a humiliating command is four words: “and he did so” (v. 2). Where might faithfulness to Christ cost you dignity or reputation, and what makes obedience hard there?

Judah was tempted to lean on Egypt and Cush, the impressive powers of the day (vv. 5–6). What impressive-looking securities are you tempted to trust, and what would it look like for them to fail?

“And we, how shall we escape?” (v. 6). How does Hebrews 2:3 turn that question towards the gospel, and how would you answer it for a friend?

Isaiah bore shame as a sign; Christ “endured the cross, despising the shame” (Hebrews 12:2) in our place. How does his shame borne for you help you face shame, whether from your own sin or from other people’s contempt?
20.text: <sup>1</sup>In the year that the commander in chief, who was sent by Sargon the king of Assyria, came to Ashdod and fought against it and captured it—<sup>2</sup>at that time the LORD spoke by Isaiah the son of Amoz, saying, "Go, and loose the sackcloth from your waist and take off your sandals from your feet," and he did so, walking naked and barefoot.<sup>3</sup>Then the LORD said, "As my servant Isaiah has walked naked and barefoot for three years as a sign and a portent against Egypt and Cush,<sup>4</sup>so shall the king of Assyria lead away the Egyptian captives and the Cushite exiles, both the young and the old, naked and barefoot, with buttocks uncovered, the nakedness of Egypt.<sup>5</sup>Then they shall be dismayed and ashamed because of Cush their hope and of Egypt their boast.<sup>6</sup>And the inhabitants of this coastland will say in that day, 'Behold, this is what has happened to those in whom we hoped and to whom we fled for help to be delivered from the king of Assyria! And we, how shall we escape?'"

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–6 — The Prophet's Body Becomes the Sermon
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God turns his prophet into a living picture of Egypt’s defeat, so that no one in Jerusalem can miss the warning. The date is Sargon’s capture of Ashdod, a city that rebelled trusting in Egypt and was not rescued (v. 1). God tells Isaiah to strip off his sackcloth and sandals, and he obeys (v. 2). For three years he walks naked and barefoot, and then God explains the sign: Assyria will lead away the captives of Egypt and Cush in just that shame (vv. 3–4). All who hoped in Egypt will be dismayed, left asking how they can possibly escape (vv. 5–6).
verseByVerse.theology: This is a sign-act, a message acted out rather than spoken, and here the cost is part of the message.
verseByVerse.examples: Few Christians are asked for anything like this, but faithfulness sometimes costs dignity: being the one at work who will not join in, or the relative who keeps speaking of Christ. Isaiah's four words, and he did so, are the pattern, and Christ's shame borne for us is the strength for it.

verseByVerse.quote: In the year that the commander in chief, who was sent by Sargon the king of Assyria, came to Ashdod and fought against it and captured it— at that time the LORD spoke by Isaiah the son of Amoz, saying, "Go, and loose the sackcloth from your waist and take off your sandals from your feet," and he did so, walking naked and barefoot.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God told Isaiah to strip off his sackcloth and sandals and go about like a prisoner of war, and Isaiah obeyed.

In the year that the commander in chief came to Ashdod. The date is unusually specific: Sargon II’s campaign against the Philistine city of Ashdod, led by his commander in chief (an Assyrian title), about 711 BC. Ashdod had rebelled against Assyria, counting on Egyptian support, and the support did not come. Sargon’s own inscriptions record the campaign and say that the rebel leader fled to the border of Egypt and Cush and was handed back in chains by the Cushite king. Since verse 3 looks back over three years, the sign probably began with the revolt and ran through the whole crisis.

Loose the sackcloth from your waist. Sackcloth was rough, dark cloth, the clothing of mourning and penitence, and Isaiah evidently wore it as a prophet. Without it and his sandals he looks like a prisoner of war being marched away, in public, in Jerusalem.

He did so. The response is four words: and he did so. No argument is recorded, no request for an alternative.

What it does not mean. Not that God makes light of modesty, or that we should seek shame for its own sake. This was a unique sign given to a prophet; what carries over is the obedience, not the costume.

Uncertain wording. Naked can mean completely unclothed or stripped to a loincloth, and it is disputed which is meant here. Either way Isaiah looked like a captive led into exile.
verseByVerse.note: Sargon II is named only here in the Bible, and for centuries he was known from no other source, until his palace at Khorsabad was excavated in the 1840s.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the LORD said, "As my servant Isaiah has walked naked and barefoot for three years as a sign and a portent against Egypt and Cush, so shall the king of Assyria lead away the Egyptian captives and the Cushite exiles, both the young and the old, naked and barefoot, with buttocks uncovered, the nakedness of Egypt. Then they shall be dismayed and ashamed because of Cush their hope and of Egypt their boast. And the inhabitants of this coastland will say in that day, 'Behold, this is what has happened to those in whom we hoped and to whom we fled for help to be delivered from the king of Assyria! And we, how shall we escape?'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Isaiah’s three years of shame picture Egypt and Cush led away captive, leaving all who trusted them asking how they can escape.

For three years. That detail changes what kind of story this is. Prophets were sometimes told to do arresting things, such as burying a loincloth or breaking a jar (Jeremiah 13; 19). Those are gestures; they take an afternoon. This ran for three years, in the capital, in front of neighbours and children. There was no moment when it was over and he could go back to being a respected man.

Worn, not preached. The message could have been preached in one sentence: Egypt will not save you. God did not want it preached. He wanted it worn.

So shall the king of Assyria lead away. Verse 4 is what the costume meant. Egypt and Cush, the powers everyone was banking on, would themselves be led away captive by Assyria in exactly that condition, old and young together. Isaiah was not dressed as a madman. He was dressed as the future. Assyria took Memphis in 671 BC and Thebes in 663.

Who the sign was for. The sign was never aimed at Egypt. It was aimed at everyone watching Egypt, including Judah, which was being urged into exactly that alliance. This coastland means the small states of the coast caught between the empires.

My servant Isaiah. God calls Isaiah my servant, the title that chapters 42 to 53 will give to another, the suffering Servant. Many Christians have seen in this servant’s public humiliation a small rehearsal of the one who was stripped in earnest, outside a city wall, while soldiers divided what he had been wearing (John 19:23–24). The likeness is one of pattern, not prediction: Isaiah bore shame as a sign of judgment on others; Christ bore it as the judgment itself, in their place, so that those who trust in him will never be put to shame.

And we, how shall we escape? The last line is the one to keep. It is the sound of someone whose support turns out to need rescuing itself. Hebrews asks the same question and answers it: “how shall we escape if we neglect such a great salvation?” (Hebrews 2:3). There is a way of escape, but it does not run through Egypt.

20.theology:
The message God would not let be spoken. The content of this sign is one sentence long, and God required three years of public humiliation to deliver it. The cost showed everyone how weighty the message was.

Aimed at the watchers, not the subject. The sign is about Egypt and Cush but is performed in Jerusalem, because it was meant for everyone banking on Egypt.

My servant Isaiah. The title in verse 3 is the one this book will later give to the Servant who bore shame not as a sign but in our place.

21.subtitle: Oracles Against Babylon, Edom, and Arabia
21.intro:
Where we are. Isaiah’s oracles against the nations (chapters 13–23) began with Babylon (chapters 13–14), and after Egypt and Cush (chapters 18–20) they come back to Babylon under a riddling title, then add two short words to Edom and Arabia. Chapter 20 has just shown Judah that Egypt cannot save it; here the other great hope of the age goes down too.

The message. Every power people lean on instead of God will fall, from the great city to the desert trader. “Fallen, fallen is Babylon” (v. 9) is good news for God’s crushed people, yet the prophet receives it with anguish, not glee. And to those who ask in the dark how long the night will last, God gives an honest answer and an open door: morning is coming, the night is not yet over, keep asking.

Why it was said. In Isaiah’s day Babylon was Assyria’s most stubborn rebel and a tempting ally for Judah (39:1–2), and the desert peoples of Edom and Arabia lived on trade routes that the wars kept cutting (see the introduction). Judah was tempted to pin its hopes on such partners. God tells his people in advance that every one of them will fail.

How the chapter makes its case. A vision of Babylon’s besiegers, Elam and Media, overwhelms the prophet, while in the city a banquet is broken up by the call to arms (vv. 1–5). A watchman waits day and night until riders bring the news, which is announced to God’s threshed people (vv. 6–10). From Edom a voice asks how much of the night remains, and is answered honestly and invited back (vv. 11–12). Arabia’s caravans hide in the scrub, Tema is told to feed the fugitives, and within a year Kedar’s glory is gone (vv. 13–17).

Where it leads. The chapter leads to Christ chiefly by pattern and by the need it exposes. Babylon’s fall is the first sounding of a cry that Revelation takes up over the last proud city (Revelation 18:2), whose end comes with Christ’s return. Edom’s question about the night is answered more fully in him: he rose at dawn, “the night is far gone; the day is at hand” (Romans 13:12), and his coming brings a day with no night after it (Revelation 22:5). And the bread and water for fugitives return in his own words: “I was thirsty and you gave me drink” (Matthew 25:35).

For us. Nothing we lean on instead of God will hold, however strong it looks. So we keep faithful watch, bring our questions to God in the dark and keep coming back, grieve rather than gloat when the proud fall, and meet the fugitive with bread, as Christ came out to meet us.

keyVerse.quote: “Watchman, what time of the night? Watchman, what time of the night? The watchman says: ‘Morning comes, and also the night.’”
keyVerse.note: The exchange is one of the strangest moments in the prophets, and its strangeness is the point: history does not move in a straight line from darkness to light. The right response is not to give up but to keep asking and to come back. Christians ask knowing that Christ’s rising has already begun the morning that will have no night after it.

21.reflection:
Isaiah was doubled over by a vision of his oppressor’s fall (vv. 3–4). Why do you think he reacted with anguish rather than celebration? How do you respond when people or powers you dislike are brought down?

The watchman’s work was mostly waiting at his post (v. 8). Where is God asking you to stay faithfully at a post while nothing visible seems to happen?

“Morning comes, and also the night” (v. 12). Which half of that answer do you find harder to accept, and how does Christ’s resurrection change the way Christians wait through the night?

Tema was told to meet fugitives with water and bread (v. 14). Who are the strangers near you, and what is one ordinary step your group could take toward them, as people Christ first came out to meet?

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–10 — The Watchman, and the Cost of Seeing
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The fall of the world’s great city is certain, and it is good news for God’s crushed people, but the prophet receives it with anguish rather than glee. A stern vision shows Elam and Media summoned against the city, here given the riddling name “the wilderness of the sea” (vv. 1–2). The vision doubles Isaiah over like a woman in labour (vv. 3–4), while in Babylon a banquet runs on until the order to oil the shields (v. 5). Then a watchman is posted and waits day and night until riders arrive with the news: Babylon has fallen, and her idols lie shattered (vv. 6–9). The prophet passes it on to his threshed and winnowed people (v. 10).
verseByVerse.theology: The section is as much about the prophet as about Babylon: the news of an oppressor's fall is received not as a detached report but with anguish.
verseByVerse.examples: The banquet of verse 5 is a warning about the feast that carries on while the enemy reaches the gate. A life can be absorbed in comfort while every warning sounds, and the time to listen is before the order to arm is shouted across the table.

verseByVerse.quote: The oracle concerning the wilderness of the sea. As whirlwinds in the Negeb sweep on, it comes from the wilderness, from a terrible land. A stern vision is told to me; the traitor betrays, and the destroyer destroys. Go up, O Elam; lay siege, O Media; all the sighing she has caused I bring to an end. Therefore my loins are filled with anguish; pangs have seized me, like the pangs of a woman in labor; I am bowed down so that I cannot hear; I am dismayed so that I cannot see. My heart staggers; horror has appalled me; the twilight I longed for has been turned for me into trembling. They prepare the table, they spread the rugs, they eat, they drink. Arise, O princes; oil the shield!
verseByVerse.commentary:
Babylon’s besiegers come like a desert storm, and God will end the groaning she has caused; yet the vision doubles the prophet over, while in the city the feast goes on until the call to arms.

The wilderness of the sea. The title is a riddle, and Babylon is meant (v. 9), sitting on its marshy plain between two rivers. What comes is described as desert whirlwinds, which arrive without warning and cannot be argued with.

All the sighing she has caused. God summons the attackers by name, and he is not merely toppling a power. He is ending the accumulated groaning of everybody Babylon has hurt; he has kept count of it, and his judgment answers it.

Pangs have seized me. Now Isaiah stops describing Babylon and describes himself, doubled over, unable to hear or see. The image is childbirth, the Bible’s usual picture for pain that cannot be postponed or escaped, and he is not the one being judged, only the one being shown it.

The twilight I longed for. Twilight is what a tired man waits for: the end of the day, the cool, the rest. He longed for evening, and it brought this.

They prepare the table. Then a banquet in six short clauses, and across it an order to grease the leather shields for battle. Daniel 5 describes such a night from inside the room, at the feast of Belshazzar, with writing appearing on the wall while the cups are still full.

Why Babylon again, after chapters 13 and 14? Babylon rebelled against Assyria more than once in Isaiah’s lifetime and was crushed in 710 and 689 BC, and some think this oracle first had those falls in view; the mention of Elam and Media points many others to 539 BC. Either way, the repetition makes the point of the whole block: the city that looked like the alternative to trusting God was going down, again and finally.

Uncertain wording. Why Babylon is called the wilderness of the sea is uncertain: perhaps for the marshes of southern Babylonia near the Gulf, perhaps as a hint that the proud city will become a desert (13:19–22).

verseByVerse.quote: For thus the Lord said to me: "Go, set a watchman; let him announce what he sees. When he sees riders, horsemen in pairs, riders on donkeys, riders on camels, let him listen diligently, very diligently." Then he who saw cried out: "Upon a watchtower I stand, O Lord, continually by day, and at my post I am stationed whole nights. And behold, here come riders, horsemen in pairs!" And he answered, "Fallen, fallen is Babylon; and all the carved images of her gods he has shattered to the ground." O my threshed and winnowed one, what I have heard from the LORD of hosts, the God of Israel, I announce to you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A watchman keeps his post day and night until riders bring the news, “Fallen, fallen is Babylon”, and the prophet passes it on to his crushed people as good news.

Go, set a watchman. The instruction is minimal: not interpret, not advise, but announce what he sees. And the watchman’s own report of the job is mostly waiting: continually by day and whole nights, watching an empty road with no way of knowing when or whether anything will come. That is a fair description of much faithful work: most of what God asks is not dramatic action but staying at a post while nothing visible happens.

Fallen, fallen is Babylon. After all the strain, the whole content of the vision is one sentence, said twice the way a breathless messenger speaks, and the gods that were meant to protect the city lie shattered to the ground. John hears the same double cry at the end of the Bible, over the last empire that thought it was permanent (Revelation 14:8; 18:2): every proud power set against God goes the same way, and the last falls when Christ comes.

O my threshed and winnowed one. The last line names the audience: Isaiah’s own people, who have been beaten like grain on a threshing floor and thrown into the air. For people crushed like that, the fall of the oppressor is good news.

Textual note. In verse 8 the standard Hebrew text reads a lion cried out; the ESV follows an ancient Hebrew copy that reads he who saw, a small difference in Hebrew letters.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 11–12 — Watchman, What Time of the Night?
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God gives an honest answer to a weary question, and leaves the door open. From Seir, the hill country of Edom, a voice calls twice to the watchman to ask how much of the night is left (v. 11). The answer refuses both easy replies: morning is coming, and so is more night. Then comes the mercy, an invitation to keep asking and to come back again (v. 12). In two of the most obscure verses in the book, Isaiah gives a word for every season of waiting: the darkness is real, the dawn is certain, and God does not tire of the same question.
verseByVerse.theology: The exchange is short and cryptic, but it is honest about the night and open about the morning.
verseByVerse.examples: Anyone in a long night of grief or uncertainty can take the watchman's last words as their own permission: keep asking, and come back again. God is not wearied by the same prayer brought twice.

verseByVerse.quote: The oracle concerning Dumah. One is calling to me from Seir, "Watchman, what time of the night? Watchman, what time of the night?" The watchman says: "Morning comes, and also the night. If you will inquire, inquire; come back again."
verseByVerse.commentary:
From Edom comes a weary question, how much of the night is left, and the watchman answers honestly: morning is coming, but so is more night; keep asking, and come back.

One is calling to me from Seir. Seir is the hill country of Edom, the people of Esau, no friend of Israel in Scripture. But the question is not hostile. It is exhausted, the most human sentence in all these oracles.

Watchman, what time of the night? Anyone who has been awake through a bad night knows why the question is asked twice. You do not ask the time for the information; you ask to be told it is nearly over. And the answer refuses to be simple, which is why it has puzzled readers for twenty-seven centuries.

Morning comes, and also the night. Morning comes is a real promise, and it is said first. And also the night is real too. Whoever wants a dawn with no darkness will not get one here, and whoever concludes that darkness is all there is has stopped reading halfway through the sentence.

If you will inquire, inquire; come back again. Here is the mercy: the door is not shut. The enquirer is not sent away but told to keep asking and to come back. For anyone who has put a question to God and received less than a full answer, this is what is on offer: not a timetable, but an open invitation to return with the same question to the one who actually knows what time it is.

The morning that has no night. Christians live in the same twilight, and they have been told more of the answer. “The night is far gone; the day is at hand,” Paul writes (Romans 13:12). Christ has already risen at dawn on the first day of the week, and his return will bring the morning that has no night after it (Revelation 22:5). Until then the watchman’s honesty holds: there is more night, and the morning is certain.

Uncertain wording. Dumah is also an oasis in northern Arabia, so some link this oracle with the next; the mention of Seir makes Edom more likely. The reply uses rare verbs, and its exact sense is debated (morning for some and night for others, or brief relief before fresh darkness); the ESV keeps the openness of the Hebrew.
verseByVerse.note: Dumah, meaning “silence,” may be a wordplay on Edom.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 13–17 — Bring Water to the Thirsty
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Judgment on the proud and mercy for the fugitive belong together in God’s word. War drives the trading caravans of Dedan off their routes to hide in the desert scrub (v. 13). The people of the oasis of Tema are told to go out to them with water and bread, for they have fled the sword and the bow (vv. 14–15). Then God sets a date: within a year, counted as exactly as a hired worker counts his term, the glory of Kedar, famous for its archers, will be gone and few of its fighters left (vv. 16–17). The LORD has spoken, and what a people was proudest of is what he takes away.
verseByVerse.theology: The last oracle pairs a command to show mercy with a sentence on pride.
verseByVerse.examples: When disaster drives people from their homes, believers are not first asked to explain it but to bring water and bread, and to go out to meet those who need it.

verseByVerse.quote: The oracle concerning Arabia. In the thickets in Arabia you will lodge, O caravans of Dedanites. To the thirsty bring water; meet the fugitive with bread, O inhabitants of the land of Tema. For they have fled from the swords, from the drawn sword, from the bent bow, and from the press of battle. For thus the Lord said to me, "Within a year, according to the years of a hired worker, all the glory of Kedar will come to an end. And the remainder of the archers of the mighty men of the sons of Kedar will be few, for the LORD, the God of Israel, has spoken."
verseByVerse.commentary:
War drives Arabia’s trading caravans into hiding, Tema is told to meet the fugitives with water and bread, and within a year Kedar’s famous glory will be gone.

O caravans of Dedanites. The last of the three oracles opens with people sleeping rough. The Dedanites were traders whose caravans normally camped at known stops with wells and shelter; these are in the scrub, off the route, hiding. Verse 15 gives four short phrases, and every one is a reason somebody left home in a hurry.

To the thirsty bring water. In the middle of a judgment oracle comes an instruction about hospitality. God announces a disaster and in the same breath tells the people next door what to do about its refugees: bring water, bring bread, and meet them, a verb that means going out toward them rather than waiting at your door. Prophecy in this book is never only information.

The cup reaches Christ. Jesus makes the same water and bread a test of the last day: “I was thirsty and you gave me drink, I was a stranger and you welcomed me” (Matthew 25:35). He speaks first of kindness to his needy brothers, but Scripture commands it towards every fugitive, and those who bring the cup were once thirsty themselves and given water without price (55:1).

What this looks like. Tema was told to go out to people it had never met, and the New Testament lays the same duty on every Christian: Do not neglect to show hospitality to strangers (Hebrews 13:2). Go toward them. Find out who the newcomers near you are (a refugee family in your street, overseas students far from home) rather than waiting for them to find your church. Start with bread and water. A meal, a lift to an appointment, help with a form in a language they cannot read: ordinary things, as the oracle’s were. Learn the name and the story. Each has fled from the swords of something; ask about home, and remember. Do it as people who were welcomed. We were strangers to God, alienated and hostile in mind (Colossians 1:21), and Christ came out to meet us and fed us at his own table. So the welcome is not a burden we carry but a kindness we pass on.

All the glory of Kedar will come to an end. The oracle ends with a date and a specific loss. Kedar, a desert people descended from Ishmael (Genesis 25:13), was famous for its archers, and it is precisely the famous thing that goes. According to the years of a hired worker is the same contract language used of Moab: a term counted exactly (see the note on 16:12–14).

The pattern of these chapters. That is the pattern of all eleven of these chapters: God takes away the particular thing it trusted in and was proud of, because the misplaced trust was the real problem.

Uncertain wording. In verse 13 in Arabia is spelled in Hebrew exactly like in the evening; the ESV’s reading suits the place names that follow.

21.theology:
The cost of seeing. The message of the first oracle is four words long, fallen, fallen is Babylon, and Isaiah spends much of it on what receiving the vision did to him.

Morning comes, and also the night. The reply to Edom’s twice-asked question refuses both simple answers, all morning or all night, and its last clause is the mercy: come back again.

Water and bread inside a judgment. Verse 14 interrupts an oracle of disaster to tell the neighbours what to do about its refugees, and verse 16 shows what all these oracles aim at: God brings to an end the thing a people trusted in.

22.subtitle: The Valley of Vision
22.intro:
Where we are. In the middle of the oracles against the nations (chapters 13–23), after Babylon, Edom and Arabia (chapter 21), comes a title that sounds like one more foreign place: “the valley of vision”. It is Jerusalem. The city that has watched God judge its neighbours now stands in the dock itself.

The message. God’s people are judged by the same standard as the nations, and their deepest sin is not weakness but self-reliance: in a crisis Jerusalem checked its weapons, walls and water, “but you did not look to him who did it” (v. 11). When God called for repentance, they threw a party of despair. Then God replaces a self-serving steward with a faithful one, and shows that even the best human steward cannot carry the whole weight of his house.

Why it was said. The setting is most likely Sennacherib’s invasion in 701 BC (see the introduction), when Hezekiah strengthened the walls and secured the water supply (2 Chronicles 32:2–5), and when Shebna and Eliakim served at his court (36:3). Jerusalem needed to learn that survival is not salvation, and that those who have heard most of God’s word are most accountable to it.

How the chapter makes its case. Jerusalem cheers on its rooftops over a disgrace while the prophet weeps (vv. 1–4). A day of siege comes, and the city prepares competently but never looks to the LORD (vv. 5–11). God calls for mourning and gets a feast whose motto is “Let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we die” (vv. 12–14). Then the oracle turns to one man: Shebna, carving himself a grand tomb, will be hurled away (vv. 15–19), and Eliakim will receive his robe and the key of the house of David (vv. 20–23); yet even this secure peg will give way under the weight hung on it (vv. 24–25).

Where it leads. Here the line to Christ is unusually direct, by promise and pattern. The risen Christ takes verse 22 for himself: he is the one “who has the key of David, who opens and no one will shut” (Revelation 3:7). Where Shebna served himself and Eliakim could not bear the load, Christ is faithful over God’s house as a son (Hebrews 3:6), the peg that does not give way, on whose shoulder the government rests (9:6). And the despairing slogan of verse 13 is answered by his resurrection (1 Corinthians 15:32).

For us. Competence is no substitute for prayer, and relief is no substitute for repentance. Those who hold any office are to serve, not build monuments to themselves. And no person, however good, can carry the whole weight of our lives; we may hang everything on Christ, who holds the key and will not fail.

keyVerse.quote: “I will place on his shoulder the key of the house of David. He shall open, and none shall shut; and he shall shut, and none shall open.”
keyVerse.note: What begins as a change of staff in Hezekiah’s court becomes one of the richest pictures of Christ in the Old Testament. The risen Christ takes these words for himself (Revelation 3:7): he alone decides who enters God’s house. No one comes to the Father except through him, and no one who comes through him is shut out.

22.reflection:
Jerusalem prepared carefully for the siege but “did not look to him who did it” (v. 11). In a crisis you are facing, what would it look like both to act wisely and to look first to God (compare Nehemiah 4:9)?

God called for weeping, and the city held a party (vv. 12–13). Has God ever been merciful to you, and you responded with relief rather than repentance? What would returning to him look like now?

Shebna carved himself a monument while the city was in danger (v. 16). In what ways are we tempted to secure our own name, and how does Luke 10:20 answer that longing?

Even Eliakim, the faithful steward, gave way under the weight hung on him (vv. 24–25). Whose weight are you trying to carry, or whom are you leaning on too heavily? What changes when Christ, who holds the key of David, carries it instead?
