verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Jerusalem stands under the same judgment as the nations, and its fault is self-reliance without repentance. The city is cheering on its rooftops over what is really a disgrace, for its leaders fled and were captured without a fight, and only the prophet weeps (vv. 1–4). In a day of siege the people check the armoury, count the breaches, pull down houses for the wall and secure the water, but never look to the LORD who planned it all (vv. 5–11). God calls for weeping and sackcloth and gets a feast with a motto of despair, and he pronounces a sentence of unatoned guilt on that hardened refusal (vv. 12–14).
verseByVerse.theology: Jerusalem is dropped into the list of nations under the same heading, without a word marking the change.
verseByVerse.examples: A family facing a diagnosis or a church facing a crisis can do everything sensible, and should. Verse 11 asks only whether, in all the planning, anyone has looked to the One who governs the crisis and prayed.

verseByVerse.quote: The oracle concerning the valley of vision. What do you mean that you have gone up, all of you, to the housetops, you who are full of shoutings, tumultuous city, exultant town? Your slain are not slain with the sword or dead in battle. All your leaders have fled together; without the bow they were captured. All of you who were found were captured, though they had fled far away. Therefore I said: "Look away from me; let me weep bitter tears; do not labor to comfort me concerning the destruction of the daughter of my people."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jerusalem, the city of God’s word, is now itself under God’s judgment: it celebrates on its rooftops over what is really a disgrace, while the prophet weeps alone.

The valley of vision. After oracles against Babylon, Moab, Damascus, Egypt and the rest comes one against the valley of vision: Jerusalem, where God gave his prophets their visions. The city that has been watching God judge its neighbours now finds itself on the list.

Gone up to the housetops. The city is on its flat roofs, shouting. Something has apparently gone well, a siege lifted, and the whole town is celebrating.

Your slain are not slain with the sword. Isaiah punctures it in one line. Look at your dead: they did not fall fighting. The leaders ran and were picked up on the road without the bow; nobody even had to shoot at them. The party is being held over a disgrace that the celebrants have decided to read as a deliverance.

Do not labor to comfort me. One man in a shouting city is crying, and he asks to be left alone: the comfort on offer would be false. He weeps for the daughter of my people, as one of them, not a spectator, and centuries later Jesus would weep over the same city (Luke 19:41).

The setting. This is most likely Jerusalem in 701 BC: the walls strengthened, the water secured (vv. 9–11; 2 Kings 20:20), and the city feasting instead of repenting when the siege lifted. Some see the fall of 586 BC as well, when the king and his soldiers fled by night and were captured (2 Kings 25:4–7), and Isaiah may be seeing the later disaster through the earlier.

verseByVerse.quote: For the Lord GOD of hosts has a day of tumult and trampling and confusion in the valley of vision, a battering down of walls and a shouting to the mountains. And Elam bore the quiver with chariots and horsemen, and Kir uncovered the shield. Your choicest valleys were full of chariots, and the horsemen took their stand at the gates. He has taken away the covering of Judah. In that day you looked to the weapons of the House of the Forest, and you saw that the breaches of the city of David were many. You collected the waters of the lower pool, and you counted the houses of Jerusalem, and you broke down the houses to fortify the wall. You made a reservoir between the two walls for the water of the old pool. But you did not look to him who did it, or see him who planned it long ago.
verseByVerse.commentary:
In a day of siege Jerusalem does everything sensible to defend itself, but never looks to the LORD who planned it all.

A day of tumult. The crisis is the Lord’s day: walls battered, the valleys full of chariots, and Elam and Kir at the gates, distant peoples probably serving in the Assyrian army (Kir was where Assyria had deported the people of Damascus, 2 Kings 16:9). The covering of Judah, its defences, is stripped away.

You collected the waters of the lower pool. The preparations are good ones. The armoury is checked: the House of the Forest, the cedar-pillared hall Solomon built, where his gold shields once hung (1 Kings 7:2; 10:17). The walls are surveyed and the breaches counted. Houses are demolished for stone to close the gaps, and a reservoir is built inside the defences. This is competent crisis management. The tunnel Hezekiah cut to bring the spring water inside the city can still be walked through today.

But you did not look to him who did it. Verse 11 is the charge, and it is not incompetence. The verb is the key: you looked to the weapons in verse 8, and you did not look to him in verse 11, the same action aimed two ways. They surveyed everything except the one who had arranged the crisis and had planned it, Isaiah says, long ago.

Competent and godless. It is possible to meet a disaster with total competence and complete godlessness: everything gets done, and nobody prays. The answer is not to do less, for the preparations were wise, but to look first to God and do it all in dependence on him, as Nehemiah’s builders did: “we prayed to our God and set a guard” (Nehemiah 4:9).

verseByVerse.quote: In that day the Lord GOD of hosts called for weeping and mourning, for baldness and wearing sackcloth; and behold, joy and gladness, killing oxen and slaughtering sheep, eating flesh and drinking wine. "Let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we die." The LORD of hosts has revealed himself in my ears: "Surely this iniquity will not be atoned for you until you die," says the Lord GOD of hosts.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God called his people to repent, and they feasted in despair instead; on that hardened refusal he pronounces guilt that will not be atoned for.

Called for weeping and mourning. God’s response to the crisis is a summons to grief and repentance: weeping, mourning, shaved heads, sackcloth, the visible signs of a nation that has understood something (see mourning customs). And what he gets is a barbecue.

And behold, joy and gladness. He called for one thing, and behold, here is the other. They are killing the animals that would have fed them through a siege and eating them tonight.

Let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we die. This is the sentence the chapter is remembered for: the motto of people who have looked at the situation, decided it is hopeless, and chosen to spend what is left on enjoyment. It is despair dressed up as a party, the exact opposite of what God asked for. Grief would have admitted that something could still be done.

The party at the end of the world. “You only live once” sounds like a celebration of life, and much of our culture runs on it: grab the experience, tick off the list, spend it while you can. Isaiah hears what is underneath: not joy, but despair with the music turned up. If tomorrow we die and that is all, the feast is a way of not thinking, and the guests keep glancing at the door. The Romans had a common epitaph that said it bleakly: I was not; I was; I am not; I do not care.

Eat and drink, for he died. Paul quotes the slogan as the only rational conclusion if the dead are not raised (1 Corinthians 15:32), and the resurrection turns the party round. Christians are not killjoys who refuse the feast; they have been told that every feast here is a first taste, not the last meal. Jesus gave his followers a supper to keep until he comes (1 Corinthians 11:26), and it is the opposite of Jerusalem’s banquet: not “eat and drink, for tomorrow we die”, but eat and drink, for he died, and tomorrow we live.

This iniquity will not be atoned for you. The verdict is the heaviest sentence in the chapter. It is not that the sin is too large to be atoned for: this book has said that sins like scarlet shall be as white as snow (1:18). It is that these people, called to mourn and throwing a feast instead, will carry this guilt until they die. Refusal can lose the moment when repentance was on offer. That moment is open now, and the grief God asks for is not ours to manufacture: his Spirit convicts and gives the godly sorrow that leads to repentance (2 Corinthians 7:10).

What if I fear I have done this? The sentence falls on people feasting in defiance, not on those who are troubled about their sin. A heart that grieves and wants to return is the opposite of the heart this verse describes, and the gospel’s door stands open to it: whoever comes to Christ he will never cast out (John 6:37), and the blood of Jesus cleanses from all sin (1 John 1:7).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 15–25 — Two Stewards and a Key
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God removes a steward who served himself and appoints one who will serve as a father, then shows that even the best human steward cannot carry all the weight. Shebna, chief official of the palace, is carving himself a splendid tomb while the city is in danger, and God will hurl him like a ball into a wide land (vv. 15–19). Eliakim receives his robe, sash and authority, becomes a father to Jerusalem, and is given the key of the house of David (vv. 20–23). But when his whole family hangs its weight on him, the secure peg gives way (vv. 24–25). The key waits for a shoulder strong enough, and the risen Christ claims it as his own.
verseByVerse.theology: The section sets two stewards side by side, one who served himself and one who was made a father to the city, and then admits that even the better one could not carry everything.
verseByVerse.examples: Parents, pastors and leaders all become pegs for others, and all of us give way somewhere. That is not the end of the story: the weight was never meant to rest finally on us, and Christ bears what we cannot.

verseByVerse.quote: Thus says the Lord GOD of hosts, "Come, go to this steward, to Shebna, who is over the household, and say to him: What have you to do here, and whom have you here, that you have cut out here a tomb for yourself, you who cut out a tomb on the height and carve a dwelling for yourself in the rock? Behold, the LORD will hurl you away violently, O you strong man. He will seize firm hold on you and whirl you around and around, and throw you like a ball into a wide land. There you shall die, and there shall be your glorious chariots, you shame of your master's house. I will thrust you from your office, and you will be pulled down from your station.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Shebna, the king’s chief official, is carving himself a grand tomb while the city is in danger, and God will hurl him away to die in a far country.

Shebna, who is over the household. To be over the household was to be the highest official under the king, the chief of staff of the palace. And Shebna is found cutting a tomb for himself in the rock, on the heights, in the good burial ground.

What have you to do here? God’s questions, what have you to do here, and whom have you here?, most naturally mean that Shebna is not even a native of Jerusalem. He has no family plot and no claim on that hillside, and he is quarrying himself a monument in it while an empire moves toward the city.

Throw you like a ball into a wide land. The judgment is almost comic in its physicality: God winds him up and throws him. A man obsessed with where his body will lie will be thrown into a wide land to die, far from the hillside he was carving, with his glorious chariots, the trappings of his rank, as the only reminder of what he was. The expensive tomb will wait, empty, for somebody else’s name.

A tomb in Silwan. A rock-cut tomb in the village of Silwan, across the valley from the City of David, bears an inscription for a royal steward whose name ends in -yahu; many think it was Shebna’s (Shebaniah). And by 36:3 he has been demoted to secretary, with Eliakim over the household, just as verses 20 and 21 said.

A warning for office holders. Shebna is the lasting picture of a public servant whose real project is his own fame: the city is in danger, and he is thinking about how he will be remembered. Anyone who holds office, in church or state, knows the temptation.

Why do we want so badly to be remembered? Shebna’s tomb has modern equivalents: the name on the building, the online presence curated for posterity. It is easy to sneer, but the longing is not foolish. It is the sense, built into creatures made in God’s image, that a life ought to count and ought to last. The trouble is where we try to secure it. In Shelley’s poem a traveller finds a broken statue in the desert, with the words “Look on my works, ye Mighty, and despair!” on its pedestal and nothing round it but sand. The gospel answers the longing instead of mocking it. A name carved in the rock of Jerusalem is fragile; a name known to God is not. Jesus told disciples delighted with their own success to “rejoice that your names are written in heaven” (Luke 10:20). And he himself was laid in a tomb cut in the rock for another man, and left it empty.

verseByVerse.quote: In that day I will call my servant Eliakim the son of Hilkiah, and I will clothe him with your robe, and will bind your sash on him, and will commit your authority to his hand. And he shall be a father to the inhabitants of Jerusalem and to the house of Judah. And I will place on his shoulder the key of the house of David. He shall open, and none shall shut; and he shall shut, and none shall open. And I will fasten him like a peg in a secure place, and he will become a throne of honor to his father's house. And they will hang on him the whole honor of his father's house, the offspring and issue, every small vessel, from the cups to all the flagons. In that day, declares the LORD of hosts, the peg that was fastened in a secure place will give way, and it will be cut down and fall, and the load that was on it will be cut off, for the LORD has spoken."
verseByVerse.commentary:
God gives Shebna’s office to Eliakim, a true father to the city, with the key of David’s house; but even this secure peg will give way, and the key waits for Christ, who holds it for ever.

My servant Eliakim. The replacement is named, and the transfer is done by God, not by the palace. He takes the robe off one man and puts it on another, ties the sash himself, and hands over the authority.

A father to the inhabitants of Jerusalem. The job description is the striking part: not administrator or chief officer, but a father to the inhabitants. That is what the office was always meant to be, and what Shebna had turned into a platform for himself.

The key of the house of David. The key of a great house was a substantial object, carried on the shoulder, and whoever carried it decided who came in and who stayed out. It was the visible sign of full authority in the king’s name.

Christ holds the key. On Patmos the risen Christ introduces himself to a struggling church as “the holy one, the true one, who has the key of David, who opens and no one will shut, who shuts and no one opens” (Revelation 3:7). He takes the words spoken over a palace steward in Jerusalem and applies them to himself: he alone decides who enters God’s house, and no one he lets in can be shut out.

The peg will give way. Then the chapter does something unexpected: it takes the promise back. Eliakim is a peg driven into a wall, and everything gets hung on him, the whole family, the honour, every cup and flagon, until the peg pulls out of the wall and the lot comes down.

Honesty about pegs. The best reading is that verses 24–25 describe Eliakim himself, made secure but loaded with the weight of his family until he and his house fall under the burden; some refer verse 25 back to Shebna instead. Either way, it is not cynicism about Eliakim but honesty about pegs. Load a whole household’s weight onto any human being, a leader, a father, a pastor, yourself, and eventually the fixing gives; this chapter records two men who could not carry the key of David. Christ is the peg that holds: the one on whose shoulder the government rests (9:6), who carries the whole weight of his Father’s house and every small vessel in it, and has never yet given way.

Is this the same as the keys given to Peter? Christ alone holds the key of David (Revelation 3:7). The binding and loosing Jesus gave Peter with the keys (Matthew 16:19) he then gives to the disciples gathered as the church (Matthew 18:18): authority to open the kingdom by preaching the gospel.

Where Christians differ. Roman Catholic writers have read the steward’s office here as one with successors, and so as a pattern for Peter and the popes after him.

This commentary’s view. With the Reformers, this commentary finds no such succession in either text: the keys are the authority of the gospel, given to the church, not to a line of popes. It honours the sincere faith of those who differ.

22.theology:
The oracle against us. Isaiah lets his readers in Jerusalem discover that they are not spectators at the trial of the nations; they are in the dock themselves. Whatever was enjoyable about watching God judge the neighbours stops being enjoyable here.

Competence without God. The charge is not incompetence but the same verb pointed two ways: you looked to the weapons, and you did not look to him who did it. When God then called for weeping (v. 12) he got a feast and a slogan of despair.

The key, and the peg. Shebna builds a monument to himself; Eliakim receives the key, words the risen Christ later takes for himself; and vv. 24-25 show that any human peg gives way. We have all leaned our weight on such pegs, and been such pegs for others; the gospel is that the weight now rests on Christ, who has carried it in our place and does not fail.

23.subtitle: The Oracle Against Tyre
23.intro:
Where we are. Chapter 23 is the last of the oracles against the nations that began with Babylon in chapter 13. The series ends as it began, with a great city, but this one is not an empire with an army: Tyre was the Phoenician port whose ships carried the trade of the Mediterranean world, from Spain to Egypt.

The message. The LORD of hosts rules the markets as surely as the armies. He brings Tyre down not because trade is wrong but to humble “the pompous pride of all glory” (v. 9), the pride of a city rich enough to make kings and sure it answered to nobody. Yet judgment is not his last word: after seventy years Tyre trades again, and its profits become “holy to the LORD” (v. 18), feeding and clothing his people.

Why it was said. Judah, small and threatened, was tempted to see wealth as the real security of the age (see the introduction), and Tyre seemed proof that money could do anything. God shows his people that the richest city on earth stands under his purpose, and that the wealth of the nations will in the end serve his kingdom.

How the chapter makes its case. Ships returning from Tarshish hear that their home port is gone, Sidon falls silent, and Egypt, whose grain Tyre carried, writhes at the news (vv. 1–7). Isaiah asks who planned this against “the bestower of crowns”, and answers that the LORD of hosts did, to humble pride; his hand over the sea breaks the trade of Canaan, as Babylonia was broken before it (vv. 8–14). After seventy years Tyre, like a forgotten prostitute singing for custom, returns to her trade, but now her wages are set apart for the LORD and supply those who live before him (vv. 15–18).

Where it leads. The chapter points to Christ by promise and by the character of God revealed in him. Its last verse is a seed of the vision in which the wealth of the nations comes to Zion (60:5) and the kings of the earth bring their glory into the new Jerusalem (Revelation 21:24), which Christ’s reign brings about. Jesus himself went to the region of Tyre and gave freely to a Gentile mother who asked only for crumbs (Mark 7:24–30). The King who could have bestowed every crown became poor so that we might become rich (2 Corinthians 8:9).

For us. Markets, careers and savings are not ultimate, and they are not the measure of our worth. God does not ask us to abandon honest work and trade but to hand them over to him: to hold wealth with open hands rather than hoarding it, and to let it serve his people and the world he loves, because Christ held nothing back for us.

keyVerse.quote: “The LORD of hosts has purposed it, to defile the pompous pride of all glory, to dishonor all the honored of the earth.”
keyVerse.note: The oracles against the nations are not spiteful; they make something clear. God is not against cities or commerce; he is against the pride that refuses to acknowledge him as the source of all prosperity. Every judgment in chapters 13–23 takes glory away from the proud and gives it back to God, to whom it belongs, and in the end it is the Lamb who was slain who is worthy to receive “power and wealth and wisdom and might and honor and glory and blessing” (Revelation 5:12).

23.reflection:
Tyre was “the bestower of crowns, whose merchants were princes” (v. 8). Where do you see people today treating money or markets as the power that answers to nobody? Where are you tempted to do the same?

Verse 9 says God’s target was not trade but pride. How can a Christian work hard in business or a career, and enjoy its rewards, without the pride that brought Tyre down?

Tyre’s profits “will not be stored or hoarded” but supplied the needs of God’s people (v. 18). What would it look like for your money and skills to pass through your hands like that?

Jesus later went to the region of Tyre and gave freely to a Gentile mother who had nothing to bring but her need (Mark 7:24–30). How does his generosity, and his becoming poor for us (2 Corinthians 8:9), change the way we hold what we have?
23.text: <sup>1</sup>The oracle concerning Tyre. Wail, O ships of Tarshish, for Tyre is laid waste, without house or harbor! verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–14 — The City That Made Kings
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Tyre is brought down by the LORD’s purpose, and what he humbles is not trade but pride. Ships coming home from Tarshish learn that there is no harbour left (v. 1); the merchants of Sidon, grown rich carrying Egypt’s grain, fall silent, and the sea itself mourns like a childless mother (vv. 2–4). Egypt writhes at the news, and Tyre’s people flee to distant colonies (vv. 5–7). Then Isaiah asks who has planned this against the bestower of crowns, and answers: the LORD of hosts, to dishonour the proud (vv. 8–9). His hand over the sea breaks the strongholds of Canaan, as Babylonia was broken before it (vv. 10–14).
verseByVerse.theology: Tyre is not judged for being commercial but for the pride that made trade the highest thing: a city rich enough to make kings, which assumed it answered to nobody.
verseByVerse.examples: Verse 8 asks who purposed it, and gets a name. Trade routes do not simply shift; behind the collapse of an economy everyone depended on stands a decision, and the decision is God's.

verseByVerse.quote: The oracle concerning Tyre. Wail, O ships of Tarshish, for Tyre is laid waste, without house or harbor! From the land of Cyprus it is revealed to them. Be still, O inhabitants of the coast; the merchants of Sidon, who cross the sea, have filled you. And on many waters your revenue was the grain of Shihor, the harvest of the Nile; you were the merchant of the nations. Be ashamed, O Sidon, for the sea has spoken, the stronghold of the sea, saying: "I have neither labored nor given birth, I have neither reared young men nor brought up young women." When the report comes to Egypt, they will be in anguish over the report about Tyre. Cross over to Tarshish; wail, O inhabitants of the coast! Is this your exultant city whose origin is from days of old, whose feet carried her to settle far away?
verseByVerse.commentary:
Tyre, the great trading port of the ancient world, is laid waste, and the whole commercial world mourns.

The oracle concerning Tyre. This time the target is a port with a fleet. Tyre was the commercial capital of the Mediterranean world: a Phoenician city on an island, very hard to besiege, whose ships ran from Spain to Egypt and whose colonies included Carthage. It made the purple dye that kings wore.

Wail, O ships of Tarshish. Ships of Tarshish were the big ocean-going vessels. Coming home from the far west, they hear at Cyprus that there is no harbour to come into.

Be still, O inhabitants of the coast. The business is described accurately: Phoenician ships buying Egyptian grain, the harvest of the Nile, and selling it round the sea, so that Tyre became the merchant of the nations. A trading shore told to be still is the sound of an economy stopping.

I have neither labored nor given birth. In verse 4 the sea itself speaks, like a mother who has lost every child. Sidon, the old Phoenician city whose name stands for the whole people, hears the sea say it has no sons or daughters left: the young men and women who crewed its ships and settled its colonies are gone. A seafaring nation had been the children of the sea, and now the sea is childless.

When the report comes to Egypt. Egypt’s anguish is not sympathy: when a trading partner of that size fails, everyone connected to it discovers how connected they were. And the people of this ancient city, who once sailed out to found colonies, now cross to Tarshish as refugees (vv. 6–7).

Uncertain wording. The Hebrew of verses 2–3 is compressed, and Shihor is a name for the Nile or one of its branches; the ESV gives the likely sense, that Tyre grew rich carrying Egypt’s grain.
verseByVerse.note: Tyre and Sidon were the great Phoenician sea-trading cities. Tarshish was probably in Spain; Kittim is Cyprus.

verseByVerse.quote: Who has purposed this against Tyre, the bestower of crowns, whose merchants were princes, whose traders were the honored of the earth? The LORD of hosts has purposed it, to defile the pompous pride of all glory, to dishonor all the honored of the earth. Cross over your land like the Nile, O daughter of Tarshish; there is no restraint anymore. He has stretched out his hand over the sea; he has shaken the kingdoms; the LORD has given command concerning Canaan to destroy its strongholds. And he said: "You will no more exult, O oppressed virgin daughter of Sidon; arise, cross over to Cyprus, even there you will have no rest." Behold the land of the Chaldeans! This is the people that was not; Assyria destined it for wild beasts. They erected their siege towers, they stripped her palaces bare, they made her a ruin. Wail, O ships of Tarshish, for your stronghold is laid waste.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The LORD of hosts planned Tyre’s fall to humble the pride of a city so rich it made kings.

The bestower of crowns. Tyre was rich enough to make kings, to fund or install a dynasty elsewhere. Whose merchants were princes: money had become the aristocracy. Armies mostly failed against its island walls, so the question of verse 8 is a real one.

The LORD of hosts has purposed it. God did it, and the target named is not trade but the pompous pride of all glory. Commerce is nowhere treated as evil, and Tyre will trade again in verse 18. What is judged is the assumption that a city which can buy anything answers to nobody. God has a day against everything tall (2:12–17), and wealth is among the tallest.

He has stretched out his hand over the sea. The phrase recalls the exodus (Exodus 14:21). The God who reached over water once for slaves reaches over it again, and this time what goes down is a market. Even in Cyprus Sidon’s people find no rest (v. 12).

Behold the land of the Chaldeans! The likeliest sense is: look at Babylonia, a people Assyria crushed and turned to ruins (as in 689 BC); if even they fell, so will Tyre.

When did Tyre fall? In stages. Its king fled before Sennacherib in 701 BC; Nebuchadnezzar besieged it for thirteen years in the sixth century and it submitted; and in 332 BC Alexander the Great built a causeway out to the island and took it. Jeremiah lists Tyre among the nations that would serve Babylon seventy years (Jeremiah 25:11, 22), which fits verse 15.

Too big to fail. In the financial crisis of 2008 some banks were called too big to fail, so woven into everything that the world could not let them go. Tyre was that kind of city. The modern assumption is close to Tyre’s own: markets are impersonal forces, like the weather, and a system that large answers to nobody. Isaiah’s question cuts across it: Who has purposed this? Behind the movement of money stands a Person, and he notices pride. That is sobering for an economy and freeing for a person: if the markets are not ultimate, then neither your portfolio nor your payslip is the measure of your worth. And the King who could have bestowed every crown chose instead to become poor, “so that you by his poverty might become rich” (2 Corinthians 8:9).

Uncertain wording. Verse 13 is one of the most difficult in Isaiah: who the people that was not are, and who raised the siege towers, is unclear. Verse 10 is obscure too: the word rendered restraint may mean a belt or a harbour, but either way Tyre’s hold over her colonies is broken.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 15–18 — Her Profit Will Be Holy
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Judgment is not God’s last word to Tyre: its wealth will be redirected to his people. Tyre lies forgotten for seventy years, the span of a long life (v. 15). Then it is pictured as an ageing prostitute walking the streets with a harp, singing to be noticed again, and it returns to trading with all the kingdoms (vv. 16–17). Nothing about the comeback is flattering. Yet verse 18 turns everything round: her merchandise and wages will be holy to the LORD, no longer hoarded but supplying food and fine clothing for those who live in his presence. It is a small seed of the end of the book, where the wealth of the nations comes to Zion.
verseByVerse.theology: The restoration is not a compliment: the city goes straight back to what it was. What changes is not the trade but where the profit ends up.
verseByVerse.examples: This is where the oracles against the nations have been going since chapter 13. The wealth of the nations, purged of its pride, is not destroyed but redirected to feed and clothe the people of God: a small seed of the vision at the end of the book, where the nations bring their glory in, and of the city whose gates never shut.

verseByVerse.quote: In that day Tyre will be forgotten for seventy years, like the days of one king. At the end of seventy years, it will happen to Tyre as in the song of the prostitute: "Take a harp; go about the city, O forgotten prostitute! Make sweet melody; sing many songs, that you may be remembered." At the end of seventy years, the LORD will visit Tyre, and she will return to her wages and will prostitute herself with all the kingdoms of the world on the face of the earth. Her merchandise and her wages will be holy to the LORD. It will not be stored or hoarded, but her merchandise will supply abundant food and fine clothing for those who dwell before the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
After seventy years Tyre returns to its trade, but now its profits are set apart for the LORD to feed and clothe his people.

Forgotten for seventy years. Seventy years, like the days of one king, is a round figure for a long subjection, long enough for those who remembered the city at its height to be gone. Tyre did recover its trade, under Persia.

The song of the prostitute. The image is deliberately unflattering: an ageing prostitute nobody calls for any more, walking the streets with a harp, singing well in the hope of being noticed. Nothing about the return is presented as redemption.

Holy to the LORD. The trade is not shut down; the money is redirected. What Tyre earns will be holy to the LORD, the technical term for something set apart for God’s use, and it buys food and clothing for the people who live in his presence. The difference between the city of verse 8 and the city of verse 18 is one clause: it will not be stored or hoarded. The commerce is identical; the accumulation has stopped, and what was piled up now passes through. That is still the shape of Christian giving.

Where the oracles end. So the run of oracles that opened with owls in Babylon’s palaces closes with a trading empire buying dinner for the people of God. The mercy promised to Jacob in 14:1 arrives in its most unexpected form: the profits of a merchant city. The nations arrive at Zion not only as worshippers but as suppliers, and everything they bring is holy (compare Revelation 21:24).

Christ in the region of Tyre. The Gospels carry this turn toward mercy into the life of Jesus. Crowds from around Tyre and Sidon came to hear him (Mark 3:8). He told the cities of Galilee that if his mighty works had been done in Tyre, it would have repented long ago (Matthew 11:21–22). And in the region of Tyre a Gentile mother, with nothing to bring but her need, asked for the crumbs from the children’s table and went home to find her daughter healed (Mark 7:24–30). The city that bestowed crowns on kings is visited at last by the King, and what he gives away there is free.

How can a prostitute’s wages be holy, when the law forbade them in God’s house (Deuteronomy 23:18)? The “prostitution” is Tyre’s trading with every kingdom for gain, not literal prostitution. The prophecy is of its wealth turned to the LORD’s service, as when the people of Tyre brought cedar for the second temple (Ezra 3:7) and later welcomed the gospel (Acts 21:3–4).

23.theology:
Not commerce, but the pride that made it ultimate. Tyre is described exactly, the bestower of crowns, whose merchants were princes. God does not judge its trade; he judges the assumption that a city which can buy anything answers to nobody.

Somebody purposed it. The LORD of hosts rules markets as surely as armies. The hand stretched over the sea (v. 11) is the hand that once opened the sea for slaves.

Redirected, not destroyed. Tyre returns to exactly what she was; what changes is the destination of the profit. It becomes holy to the LORD, and what was piled up now passes through to feed and clothe God’s people.

24.subtitle: The LORD’s Devastation of the Earth
24.intro:
Where we are. With chapter 24 the lens pulls back. Chapters 13–23 judged the nations one by one; chapters 24–27, often called the Isaiah apocalypse, speak of the whole earth judged and renewed. This chapter is the judgment, and the songs of salvation follow in chapters 25–27.

The message. The whole world is answerable to God, because humanity has broken the covenant on which it lives on his earth (v. 5). His judgment will level every distinction of rank and wealth, drain the joy from a world that sought joy apart from him, and shake the earth until it falls under the weight of its own sin. But devastation is not the last word: God will imprison the powers of heaven and earth, and the chapter ends with “the LORD of hosts reigns on Mount Zion” (v. 23).

Why it was said. Judah might have thought judgment was only for its neighbours, or that history was simply a contest of empires (see the introduction). Isaiah shows that every nation and every person stands before the same Judge, and that God’s people live in a world under the curse of broken covenant.

How the chapter makes its case. God empties the earth, and every distinction from priest to debtor counts for nothing (vv. 1–3), because the earth’s people have broken the everlasting covenant and a curse devours it (vv. 4–6). The world’s joy drains away, wine, music and the city’s life, leaving only gleanings (vv. 7–13). Songs rise from the ends of the earth, while the prophet wastes away at the treachery he sees (vv. 14–16). Terror, pit and snare close in, and the earth staggers and falls under its transgression (vv. 17–20). Then the LORD imprisons the powers of heaven and earth and reigns in glory on Zion, outshining sun and moon (vv. 21–23).

Where it leads. The chapter leads to Christ by the need it exposes and by promise. It shows a whole world under a curse it cannot lift, and “Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us” (Galatians 3:13). At the cross he disarmed the rulers and authorities (Colossians 2:15), and at his return the powers will be finally judged. The reign on Zion is the reign of God and the Lamb, in the city that needs no sun or moon, “for the glory of God gives it light, and its lamp is the Lamb” (Revelation 21:23).

For us. No rank, wealth or nation shelters anyone from God’s judgment, and no pleasure lasts in a world turned from its Maker. So we flee to Christ, who bore the curse; we hold worship and honest grief together while we wait; and we live now as people whose King already reigns.

keyVerse.quote: “The LORD of hosts reigns on Mount Zion and in Jerusalem, and his glory will be before his elders.”
keyVerse.note: After a chapter of comprehensive devastation, this sentence arrives like a foundation stone. The point of all the undoing is not destruction for its own sake but preparation: the earth is cleared for the reign that cannot be shaken. It is the same movement John sees in Revelation: the bowls of wrath followed by the marriage supper of the Lamb.

24.theology:
An earlier covenant than Sinai. The whole earth is answerable in these four chapters because the covenant it has broken is older than Israel: most likely the covenant with Noah, every living creature and the ground itself (v. 5), though some think more broadly of the order God set over humanity at creation.

Songs and grief, and then glory. Praise from the ends of the earth and a prophet wasting away stand side by side (vv. 14-16), unreconciled, as they are for anyone living between Christ’s first coming and his second. But the chapter does not end with either. It ends with the LORD of hosts reigning on Mount Zion.
24.reflection:
Verse 2 says the judgment falls alike on priest and people, master and slave, lender and borrower. Which distinctions do you rely on to feel secure, and why do they count for nothing before God?

Verse 5 says the earth “lies defiled under its inhabitants”. What difference does it make to believe that right and wrong are part of the world God made, not something we invent? How does Galatians 3:13 answer the curse of verse 6?

Isaiah hears songs from the ends of the earth and at the same moment cries, “I waste away” (v. 16). How do you hold together real worship and honest grief over the world? Which comes more naturally to you?

The chapter ends not with the ruin but with “the LORD of hosts reigns on Mount Zion” (v. 23). How might keeping that ending in view change the way you read the news this week?

For the windows of heaven are opened, and the foundations of the earth tremble.<sup>19</sup>The earth is utterly broken, the earth is split apart, the earth is violently shaken.<sup>20</sup>The earth staggers like a drunken man; it sways like a hut; its transgression lies heavy upon it, and it falls, and will not rise again.<sup>21</sup>On that day the LORD will punish the host of heaven, in heaven, and the kings of the earth, on the earth.<sup>22</sup>They will be gathered together as prisoners in a pit; they will be shut up in a prison, and after many days they will be punished.<sup>23</sup>Then the moon will be confounded and the sun ashamed, for the LORD of hosts reigns on Mount Zion and in Jerusalem, and his glory will be before his elders.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The whole earth stands under God’s judgment, and nothing people use to set themselves apart will shelter them. God empties the earth and twists its surface (v. 1), and verse 2 levels every social distinction, from priest and people to creditor and debtor. Verses 4 to 6 give the reason: the earth lies defiled under its inhabitants, who have broken the everlasting covenant, so a curse devours it. Verses 7 to 12 take the joy out of the world one item at a time: the wine fails, the music stops, the city is broken and every house is shut. Yet verse 13 leaves gleanings on a beaten olive tree, even here.
verseByVerse.theology: The judgment is universal in a way nothing before it in the book has been. Its grounds are older than Israel, a covenant made with all humanity, so no nation stands outside it.
verseByVerse.examples: The distinctions people spend their lives establishing, rank and wealth and who owes whom, count for nothing on the day being described. That is a warning to the strong, and a strange comfort to the weak.

verseByVerse.quote: Behold, the LORD will empty the earth and make it desolate, and he will twist its surface and scatter its inhabitants. And it shall be, as with the people, so with the priest; as with the slave, so with his master; as with the maid, so with her mistress; as with the buyer, so with the seller; as with the lender, so with the borrower; as with the creditor, so with the debtor. The earth shall be utterly empty and utterly plundered; for the LORD has spoken this word. The earth mourns and withers; the world languishes and withers; the highest people of the earth languish. The earth lies defiled under its inhabitants; for they have transgressed the laws, violated the statutes, broken the everlasting covenant. Therefore a curse devours the earth, and its inhabitants suffer for their guilt; therefore the inhabitants of the earth are scorched, and few men are left.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God will empty the whole earth in judgment, levelling every distinction, because humanity has broken his covenant.

The LORD will empty the earth. Eleven chapters have named nations one at a time. This one names none, because the subject is now the earth, and the four chapters that follow keep it there. The verb in he will twist its surface is unusual and physical: God will wring out the world like a cloth.

As with the people, so with the priest. Each of the six pairs names a relationship where somebody has the advantage: the priest over the layman, the master over the slave, the creditor over the debtor, which in that economy could mean owning a man’s future outright. In every case the verdict is the same: as with the one, so with the other. The gap both parties organised their lives around makes no difference on that day.

Broken the everlasting covenant. The last phrase of the charge widens it. This cannot be Sinai; most of the earth never received Sinai and could not break what it never had. The everlasting covenant is most likely the one God made after the flood with Noah, every living creature and the ground itself (Genesis 9:16), the terms on which human beings live on God’s earth. That is why the whole planet is answerable, and why a curse devours the earth (v. 6): a broken covenant brings its sanctions.

Is morality something we make up? Many people assume that right and wrong are human agreements, rules a society settles and revises. Isaiah assumes something stranger. The earth itself lies defiled under its inhabitants’ wrongdoing, as though the moral order were part of the world, like the grain in wood, so that cutting across it damages the material. C. S. Lewis argued in The Abolition of Man that the great civilisations have all recognised such an order, a moral law found rather than invented, and that a culture which debunks it does not become free, only unable to say why anything is wrong. In practice none of us can live as though morality were made up; we are outraged by injustice as though it broke something real. Scripture agrees: the work of the law is written on their hearts (Romans 2:15). That is bad news, because every one of us has broken it, and the setting for good news: the God whose order we broke kept faith when we did not, and in his Son he bore the curse of the law himself (Galatians 3:13).

What does chapter 24 describe? The Hebrew word can mean “land” or “earth”, and some read it of Judah and the exile. But the scope widens to the host of heaven and the kings of the earth (v. 21). The best reading is the final judgment of the whole world, with the exile as a foretaste.

Where Christians differ. Many modern scholars date chapters 24 to 27 centuries after Isaiah, mainly because of their worldwide, end-of-history scope.

This commentary’s view. The chapters share Isaiah’s vocabulary and themes (the beaten olive tree of 17:6, the hut of 1:8, the feast on Zion), and nothing in them requires a later author. This commentary reads them as Isaiah’s, while granting that the question is debated.
verseByVerse.note: Chapters 24–27 are often called the “Isaiah apocalypse”: judgment and salvation on a worldwide scale.

verseByVerse.quote: The wine mourns, the vine languishes, all the merry-hearted sigh. The mirth of the tambourines is stilled, the noise of the jubilant has ceased, the mirth of the lyre is stilled. No more do they drink wine with singing; strong drink is bitter to those who drink it. The wasted city is broken down; every house is shut up so that none can enter. There is an outcry in the streets for lack of wine; all joy has grown dark; the gladness of the earth is banished. Desolation is left in the city; the gates are battered into ruins. For thus it shall be in the midst of the earth among the nations, as when an olive tree is beaten, as at the gleaning when the grape harvest is done.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Every ordinary gladness is taken from a world that sought joy apart from God, yet even here a few gleanings are left.

The wine mourns. Isaiah takes seven verses to remove every source of ordinary gladness, because the losses pile up: the vine and its wine, then the tambourines, the crowd and the lyre, then the drinking songs.

Strong drink is bitter to those who drink it. The drink is still available; it has simply stopped working. That is more desolate than not having it, as anyone who has tried to enjoy something during a season of grief knows.

Every house is shut up. Then the town: every house shut and no life in the street. All joy has grown dark. This is not violence but a world with the pleasure taken out of it, which is its own kind of judgment.

As when an olive tree is beaten. The beaten olive tree of chapter 17 (17:6) closes the section, with a few olives left at the top. Even in the widest judgment in the book, Isaiah leaves gleanings.

The wine that ran out. Jesus began his signs at a wedding where the wine had run out (John 2:1–11). The gladness banished here is the gladness he came to restore, at the cost of the cup of judgment he drank himself.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 14–23 — Songs, and a Prophet Wasting Away
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Praise and grief stand side by side, and over both stands the reign of God. Voices from the west, the east and the coastlands give glory to the Righteous One (vv. 14–16a), and in the middle of the singing Isaiah cries that he is wasting away at the treachery around him (v. 16b). Terror, pit and snare close on the inhabitants of the earth, which staggers like a drunkard and falls under its transgression (vv. 17–20). Then the LORD punishes the powers of heaven and the kings of the earth, shutting them in a pit, and the chapter ends with sun and moon outshone as the LORD of hosts reigns on Mount Zion in glory before his elders (vv. 21–23).
verseByVerse.theology: The praise and the grief are both real, and Isaiah refuses to resolve them: people at the ends of the earth are already singing glory to the Righteous One while the prophet is undone by the treachery around him.
verseByVerse.examples: Read the terror of verses 17 to 20 with the ending in view. The pit and the snare are real, but the chapter that opened with the earth emptied closes with God enthroned and his glory before his elders.

verseByVerse.quote: They lift up their voices, they sing for joy; over the majesty of the LORD they shout from the west. Therefore in the east give glory to the LORD; in the coastlands of the sea, give glory to the name of the LORD, the God of Israel. From the ends of the earth we hear songs of praise, of glory to the Righteous One. But I say, "I waste away, I waste away. Woe is me! For the traitors have betrayed, with betrayal the traitors have betrayed."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Songs of praise rise from the ends of the earth while the prophet is undone by the treachery he sees, and both are true.

They sing for joy. In a chapter about the earth being emptied, some of the earth is already worshipping, and from the places furthest from Jerusalem: the west, the east, the coastlands of the sea. Judgment and praise are running at the same time, in the same world.

I waste away, I waste away. Then the prophet interrupts his own vision. He says twice that he is wasting away, then piles up the same word five times (traitors, betrayed, betrayal, traitors, betrayed), the sound of a man who cannot get past what he is looking at. The songs are deserved and his grief is warranted, and the two stand in adjacent sentences with no attempt to reconcile them.

Living between the comings. That is the honest position of anybody living between the first coming and the second. Christ has risen and the praise from the ends of the earth is genuine; the treachery is still going on, and it is right to be undone by it. Anyone who feels only one of those has stopped paying attention to half the evidence.

Uncertain wording. The word behind I waste away is rare; older translations took it as “my leanness” or even “my secret”, but wasting grief is the likely sense. In verse 15 in the east renders a word that usually means “lights”, probably the lands of the dawn.

verseByVerse.quote: Terror and the pit and the snare are upon you, O inhabitant of the earth! He who flees at the sound of the terror shall fall into the pit, and he who climbs out of the pit shall be caught in the snare. For the windows of heaven are opened, and the foundations of the earth tremble. The earth is utterly broken, the earth is split apart, the earth is violently shaken. The earth staggers like a drunken man; it sways like a hut; its transgression lies heavy upon it, and it falls, and will not rise again.
verseByVerse.commentary:
No one escapes the judgment, and the earth, shaken as in the flood, falls under the weight of its own transgression.

Terror and the pit and the snare. Three dangers come in sequence: the man runs from the first and lands in the second, climbs out of the second and is taken by the third. The ESV notes that the three Hebrew words sound alike, so the sentence sounds like what it describes.

The windows of heaven are opened. The windows of heaven were opened once before, at the flood (Genesis 7:11). Isaiah has grounded the judgment in the covenant made after that flood; now he reaches for the flood’s own vocabulary.

The earth staggers like a drunken man. Then two images that would be comic if they were not terrible: the planet lurching like a drunk and swaying like the flimsy watchman’s hut of chapter 1 (1:8). What brings it down is not the shaking. The earth falls because its own transgression is heavy upon it, a weight it can no longer hold up, and it will not rise again. Only one has ever carried the weight of the world’s transgression and risen again (53:6).

verseByVerse.quote: On that day the LORD will punish the host of heaven, in heaven, and the kings of the earth, on the earth. They will be gathered together as prisoners in a pit; they will be shut up in a prison, and after many days they will be punished. Then the moon will be confounded and the sun ashamed, for the LORD of hosts reigns on Mount Zion and in Jerusalem, and his glory will be before his elders.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God will imprison and judge the powers of heaven and earth, and reign on Zion in a glory that outshines sun and moon.

The host of heaven. The host of heaven is the spiritual powers; the kings of the earth the political ones. Scripture keeps them together, because earthly rulers so often draw on the unseen powers behind them, and God deals with both in one clause: a comfort to anyone who has felt that the trouble in the world has more behind it than the people visibly causing it.

After many days they will be punished. Then the interval: they are shut up, and after many days dealt with. The New Testament speaks of angels kept in chains until the judgment (2 Peter 2:4; Jude 6), and this time of holding explains why judgment is so long in coming.

The moon will be confounded and the sun ashamed. The sun and moon are not destroyed but ashamed, put in the shade the way a lamp is when a door opens onto daylight. Something brighter has arrived, and the two great lights that have measured every day since creation are simply outshone. John saw the end of it: a city with no need of sun or moon, because the glory of God gives it light and its lamp is the Lamb (Revelation 21:23).

His glory will be before his elders. The elders recall the seventy elders of Israel who saw the God of Israel on the mountain and ate and drank in his presence (Exodus 24:9–11), and John sees elders round the throne of God and of the Lamb (Revelation 4:4; 5:8).

Not the last word. The chapter that opened with a world wrung out like a cloth closes with God on his throne. The devastation was never the last word.

Where Christians differ. Premillennial readers link the pit and the many days to the thousand years of Revelation 20, when Satan is bound before the final judgment.

This commentary’s view. This commentary takes the amillennial view: the binding of the strong man began when Christ triumphed over the powers at the cross (Matthew 12:29; Colossians 2:15), the many days are the present age of the gospel, and the punishment comes at his return. Faithful Christians differ here, and all agree on what matters most: the powers behind the world’s evil are already prisoners, and their sentence is fixed.

25.subtitle: A Feast on the Mountain
25.intro:
Where we are. Chapters 24–27 widen Isaiah’s oracles against the nations into a vision of the whole earth judged and renewed. Chapter 24 ended with the world staggering like a drunkard and the LORD of hosts reigning “on Mount Zion and in Jerusalem” (24:23). Chapter 25 is the answer of the redeemed: a song, a feast and a promise.

The message. The God who brings down every proud city is the shelter of the poor, and his last word over a broken world is not ruin but a banquet. On his mountain he will spread a feast for all peoples, tear away the shroud that covers them, swallow up death for ever and wipe the tears from every face. Those who trusted him will say, “Behold, this is our God; we have waited for him.” Only pride stays outside, like Moab.

Why it was said. Isaiah’s hearers lived under the shadow of great empires and fortified cities, and of death itself (see the introduction). After chapter upon chapter of judgment, they needed to know where history ends and whether waiting for God is worth it.

How the chapter makes its case. First comes praise (vv. 1–5): God has kept his ancient plans, laid the proud city in ruins and been a stronghold and shade for the needy. Then the feast (vv. 6–9): on Mount Zion the LORD himself hosts all nations, removes the covering over them, destroys death, comforts the grieving and takes away his people’s shame, and they recognise him as the God they waited for. Last, a dark contrast (vv. 10–12): Moab, proud and skilful, flounders in a dung-pit, because pride refuses the seat at the table.

Where it leads. This chapter points to Christ by direct promise, and the New Testament says so. Jesus spoke of many coming from east and west to recline at this table (Matthew 8:11), and at the Last Supper he refused the cup until he drinks it new in his Father’s kingdom. He went into death and rose, the first instalment of “He will swallow up death forever” (v. 8), which Paul quotes of the resurrection (1 Corinthians 15:54), and Revelation 21:4 sets the wiping of tears at the heart of the new creation. The God the redeemed greet with “this is our God” has a face: the Lord Jesus.

For us. Death is an enemy, not a friend, and it will not have the last word. Grief may weep now, but every tear shed in faith is promised to God’s own hand. The way in is not skill or strength, which only keep Moab swimming, but taking the seat the host has paid for.

keyVerse.quote: “He will swallow up death forever; and the Lord GOD will wipe away tears from all faces, and the reproach of his people he will take away from all the earth.”
keyVerse.note: This is one of the clearest promises of resurrection in the whole Old Testament. “Swallow up death forever” is the language of total and permanent defeat: not death postponed but death ended. Paul places it at the climax of his argument for the resurrection (1 Corinthians 15:54), and John sets the wiping away of tears at the centre of the new creation (Revelation 21:4). The whole story of God’s saving work is heading towards this sentence.

25.theology:
Three things swallowed. Verses 7 and 8 name what is wrong with the world in order, and remove each one: the veil that stops people seeing; death, swallowed up forever; and the reproach that clings to God’s people. John hears the tear-wiping again at the very end of the Bible (Rev. 21:4).

For all peoples. The feast is not Israel’s with guests admitted but a table God himself spreads for everybody: the marriage supper John was told to write down (Rev. 19:9).

Two places to be. The chapter ends by naming somebody absent from a feast spread for all peoples: Moab, the nation offered shelter under David’s throne in chapters 15-16, which refused out of pride.
25.reflection:
The chapter opens with “O LORD, you are my God” after the most sweeping vision of judgment in the book (v. 1). Why does a clearer sight of God’s greatness lead to more personal praise, not less? Where has that been true for you?

God is “a shelter from the storm and a shade from the heat” (v. 4), yet he does not stop the storm. What storm are you in, and what would it mean to take shelter in him rather than ask only for the weather to change?

God’s answer to the ruin of chapter 24 is a feast for all peoples (vv. 6–8). How does the Lord’s Supper give us a foretaste of it, and how might that change the way we come to the table, or welcome others to it?

Moab is skilful and proud, and stays in the pit (vv. 10–11). In what ways are we tempted to rely on our own competence before God, and what does it mean instead to take a seat we did not earn?
