verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–5 — A Shelter in the Storm
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The prophet answers the judgment of the world with personal praise, because God has done exactly what he planned long ago. “O LORD, you are my God” (v. 1): the God of all the earth is the God of this one worshipper. He has made the proud, fortified city a heap that will never be rebuilt, and as a result strong nations come to fear and honour him (vv. 2–3). And he has been what the poor and needy most needed, a stronghold in distress, a shelter from the storm and a shade from the heat, silencing the noise and the song of the ruthless as a cloud quiets the heat of the day (vv. 4–5).
verseByVerse.theology: The chapter moves from the whole world to one person: the God who judges the whole earth is the one a poor man can call his stronghold.
verseByVerse.examples: For anyone caught in the storm of other people's cruelty (the ruthless of verse 4), this is the promise: not that the storm will never come, but that God himself will be something solid between you and it.

verseByVerse.quote: O LORD, you are my God; I will exalt you; I will praise your name, for you have done wonderful things, plans formed of old, faithful and sure. For you have made the city a heap, the fortified city a ruin; the foreigners' palace is a city no more; it will never be rebuilt. Therefore strong peoples will glorify you; cities of ruthless nations will fear you. For you have been a stronghold to the poor, a stronghold to the needy in his distress, a shelter from the storm and a shade from the heat; for the breath of the ruthless is like a storm against a wall, like heat in a dry place. You subdue the noise of the foreigners; as heat by the shade of a cloud, so the song of the ruthless is put down.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The prophet praises the God who has kept his ancient plans, brought down the proud city and sheltered the poor.

O LORD, you are my God. After eleven chapters of nations and one of the whole earth being wrung out, the chapter opens with a personal word. In this book, seeing how great God is does not push him further off; it makes people say my God.

Plans formed of old, faithful and sure. The praise has specific grounds. What has just been described was not improvised: it was decided long ago and has been kept. Both Hebrew words come from the root that gives us “amen”.

The fortified city a ruin. The unnamed city stands for every fortified city in the book, the human project of walls and self-security (24:10). Its fall does not destroy the nations; strong peoples will glorify you. They lose the walls and gain the God.

A stronghold to the poor. The praise is for what God has been to people with nothing: a shelter when the ruthless come like a storm against a wall, and a shade from the heat, in a country where shade is the difference between working and collapsing. God does not stop the weather in these verses. He is the wall and the shadow, and the song of the ruthless dies away like heat under a passing cloud (v. 5).

Uncertain wording. Which city is meant (v. 2)? Suggestions include Babylon, Nineveh and a Moabite city (v. 10). Most likely it is left unnamed on purpose, to stand for every proud city of chapters 13–24; the meaning does not depend on the name.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 6–9 — He Will Swallow Up Death Forever
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Here is the summit of chapters 24–27: on Mount Zion God himself hosts a feast for every nation and abolishes death. The LORD of hosts prepares the best food and finest wine for all peoples (v. 6). He swallows up the covering cast over the nations (v. 7), then swallows up death itself for ever, wipes away tears from all faces and removes his people’s reproach (v. 8). Verse 9 gives the words of the guests when it happens: “Behold, this is our God; we have waited for him.” Their long waiting is answered not with an explanation but with the presence of God himself.
verseByVerse.theology: Every verb in these verses belongs to God: he makes the feast, swallows the veil, swallows death, wipes the tears and takes away the reproach. The redeemed contribute only their waiting (v. 9).
verseByVerse.examples: For all peoples is said twice and all nations once, in four verses, and the menu is not survival rations but rich food and aged wine. It is the meal Jesus kept describing.

verseByVerse.quote: On this mountain the LORD of hosts will make for all peoples a feast of rich food, a feast of well-aged wine, of rich food full of marrow, of aged wine well refined. And he will swallow up on this mountain the covering that is cast over all peoples, the veil that is spread over all nations.
verseByVerse.commentary:
At the end of the story God himself will host a lavish feast for every nation on his mountain, and first remove the shroud that lies over them all.

On this mountain. It is one of the great sentences in the Old Testament, and almost every word is doing something. On this mountain: Mount Zion, where the LORD reigns before his elders (24:23), as Israel’s elders once saw God at Sinai and “ate and drank” (Exodus 24:11). The LORD of hosts: the commander of armies is the one cooking. Will make: he prepares it himself; nobody contributes a dish. For all peoples, in a book written for one nation: a table spread for everybody.

Rich food full of marrow. The best part of the animal, kept for honoured guests, and wine kept for years and strained clear: not merely adequate but lavish, and laid down in advance.

The veil that is spread over all nations. Before the eating, the covering over all nations has to go, most naturally a shroud, since the next verse names death. The trouble is not first that people refuse to look but that something is over their faces, like the veil Paul says lies over the heart until it turns to the Lord (2 Corinthians 3:14–16). And God does not lift it politely. He swallows it.

The host went without the wine. Jesus himself spoke of this table: many will come from east and west and recline at table with Abraham, Isaac and Jacob in the kingdom of heaven (Matthew 8:11). At the Last Supper he said he would not drink the fruit of the vine again until he drinks it new in his Father’s kingdom (Matthew 26:29). So the host first went without the wine, and went to the cross, before pouring it for his guests. Every Lord’s Supper is a foretaste of this table.

Where Christians differ: when is this feast? Dispensational readers see a millennial banquet in Jerusalem. Others see the marriage supper of the Lamb (Revelation 19:9) in the new creation, where God will wipe away every tear (Revelation 21:4), on the heavenly Zion (Hebrews 12:22). This commentary’s view: the second, amillennial reading, because the New Testament puts the swallowing of death at the resurrection when Christ returns (1 Corinthians 15:54), and after that there is no age in which death still operates. Faithful Christians who expect a millennial kingdom first share the same hope of the table.

Uncertain wording. The words for covering and veil are uncommon, and the picture is not certain: a mourner’s veil or burial shroud, blindness to God, or the nations’ disgrace. The shroud of death fits verse 8 best, but blindness belongs to the same curse.

verseByVerse.quote: He will swallow up death forever; and the Lord GOD will wipe away tears from all faces, and the reproach of his people he will take away from all the earth, for the LORD has spoken. It will be said on that day, "Behold, this is our God; we have waited for him, that he might save us. This is the LORD; we have waited for him; let us be glad and rejoice in his salvation."
verseByVerse.commentary:
God will destroy death for ever and wipe the tears from every face, and his people will know him as the God they waited for.

He will swallow up death forever. There is nothing like this sentence in the Old Testament before this point. The verb is the one used of the veil, and deliberately violent: not death managed or made less frightening, but swallowed, the way the earth swallowed the Egyptians (Exodus 15:12). And forever, so that it cannot come back. Most answers to death are strategies for coping with it; this verse says the thing itself will be removed from the world.

The Lord GOD will wipe away tears from all faces. Then something more intimate: God wipes away tears, a hand on a face, one person at a time. Whatever else the end of the world is, it includes God stooping to do that. And the reproach of his people, the long humiliation of having been on the losing side, goes too.

Behold, this is our God. The redeemed do not make a request; they recognise him, twice over. We have waited for him gathers all the waiting of this book (the watchman through whole nights, Edom asking what time it is, the prophet wasting away in chapter 24) and answers it with a face. The New Testament says whose: believers wait for the appearing of the glory of our great God and Saviour Jesus Christ (Titus 2:13), the one who was pierced for them.

The resurrection of the body. Paul quotes the line at the climax of his argument about the resurrection of the body (1 Corinthians 15:54), so Isaiah’s sentence has a set time: the day the dead are raised. And it already has a beginning, for Christ “abolished death and brought life and immortality to light through the gospel” (2 Timothy 1:10). He went down into death’s throat himself, and it could not hold him (Acts 2:24): the swallower was swallowed. His empty tomb is the first instalment of the promise.

Rage, or acceptance? Our culture holds two attitudes to death at once: it is natural, so make peace with it; and it is unmentionable, so spend fortunes trying to reverse ageing. Dylan Thomas, writing to his father as the old man declined, urged a third: “Do not go gentle into that good night,” and “Rage, rage against the dying of the light.” Isaiah stands nearer the rage than the calm. Death is not a friend, nor a part of life as God first made it; Paul calls it “the last enemy” (1 Corinthians 15:26). At the grave of Lazarus Jesus was “deeply moved in his spirit and greatly troubled” (John 11:33), words that carry indignation; then he did what rage cannot do. He went into death and swallowed it, and so set free those who through fear of death had been slaves all their lives (Hebrews 2:15).

For anyone grieving now. This does not forbid tears; Jesus wept at a friend’s grave minutes before raising him (John 11:35). Christians grieve, but not as those who have no hope (1 Thessalonians 4:13). Every tear shed in faith is one the Lord GOD has promised to wipe away with his own hand.

Textual note. Paul’s wording, “Death is swallowed up in victory” (1 Corinthians 15:54), follows a Greek rendering of the Hebrew word for forever, which in related usage can also mean victory. Both say the same thing: death is beaten, permanently.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The chapter ends abruptly with Moab, the proud nation that refused the shelter God offered (16:1–6), and shows what happens to pride beside the feast. The hand of the LORD rests on his mountain in blessing, but Moab is trampled down like straw in a dung-pit (v. 10). He strikes out with all his skill, like a swimmer, but the LORD brings low both his arrogance and his cleverness (v. 11), and his high walls go down to the dust (v. 12). The contrast is deliberate: a seat at the table for those who wait for God, and humiliation for those who trust themselves.
verseByVerse.theology: Isaiah places Moab here on purpose, and not out of spite: the feast is spread for all peoples, and Moab is kept from it by nothing but his own pride.
verseByVerse.examples: Pride does not always look like arrogance. Here it looks like competence: a man doing very well at keeping himself afloat, and refusing the hand that would lift him out.

verseByVerse.quote: For the hand of the LORD will rest on this mountain, and Moab shall be trampled down in his place, as straw is trampled down in a dunghill. And he will spread out his hands in the midst of it as a swimmer spreads his hands out to swim, but the LORD will lay low his pompous pride together with the skill of his hands. And the high fortifications of his walls he will bring down, lay low, and cast to the ground, to the dust.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Beside the feast lies Moab, the proud nation that refused God’s shelter, brought down with all its skill and walls.

Moab shall be trampled down. The abruptness is the point. Isaiah has just spread a table for all peoples, and in the next breath he names somebody who is not at it. Chapters 15 and 16 told why: Moab was offered shelter under David’s throne, tenderly, and refused it, and one line gave the reason with five words for pride (16:6).

In a dunghill. Straw was trodden into manure; the Hebrew word probably also plays on Madmen, a town of Moab (Jeremiah 48:2).

As a swimmer spreads his hands out to swim. The image is grotesque and exact: a man swimming in a dung-pit, and doing it well. Isaiah puts pompous pride and the skill of his hands in the same clause because they go down together. Moab is capable and expert, and all that skill is spent in filth that no skill can make clean.

Two places to be. There are two places to be at the end of this chapter: at a table on a mountain, eating food you did not provide, with the shroud taken off your face, or in the pit, swimming strongly. The difference is not that the guests swam better. They were given a seat by a host who paid for the meal himself.

What it does not mean. Not that God shuts out Moabites. Ruth the Moabite took refuge under his wings (Ruth 2:12) and became an ancestor of Christ (Matthew 1:5). Moab here is a nation in its pride; whoever comes humbly finds a place at the table.

Uncertain wording. Whose hands are spread out in verse 11? Most take the swimmer to be Moab; some take it to be the LORD, pushing Moab under as a swimmer pushes down the water. Either way Moab’s pride and skill go down together.

26.subtitle: The Song of the Strong City
26.intro:
Where we are. Chapter 26 continues the vision of the whole earth judged and renewed (chapters 24–27). After the feast of chapter 25 comes the song God’s people will sing “in that day” (v. 1), while they wait for him.

The message. Those who lean their whole weight on the LORD are kept in perfect peace, because he is an everlasting rock and everything good they have, he has done. Human effort, even at its most painful and sincere, cannot save the world or ourselves; we writhe and give birth to wind. But God will do what we cannot: “Your dead shall live; their bodies shall rise” (v. 19). Until then his people wait, sheltered, for a little while.

Why it was said. Judah knew proud cities, foreign masters and the failure of its own best efforts (see the introduction). Isaiah gives the faithful a song to sing before the victory, so they can wait in peace rather than panic.

How the chapter makes its case. The song begins with a city whose walls are salvation, and perfect peace for the mind stayed on God (vv. 1–4). The lofty city is laid low under the feet of the poor, and the singers wait for God in the night (vv. 5–9). Then the honest middle: favour does not reform the wicked, everything Israel has achieved God did, and the old masters are dead for good (vv. 10–15). In distress the people prayed and laboured, and produced nothing (vv. 16–18). Into that failure God promises resurrection (v. 19), then calls his people to shut their doors until his judgment has passed (vv. 20–21).

Where it leads. The chapter leads to Christ by direct promise. Its resurrection hope, echoed in Daniel 12:2, is fulfilled first in Jesus, “the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep” (1 Corinthians 15:20), who said that “an hour is coming when all who are in the tombs will hear his voice and come out” (John 5:28–29). The perfect peace of verse 3 is the peace he bought, for “upon him was the chastisement that brought us peace” (53:5). And the people hidden behind their doors while judgment passes recall Passover, fulfilled in Christ, “our Passover lamb” (1 Corinthians 5:7).

For us. Peace does not come from emptying the mind but from leaning it on God. When our best efforts have produced only wind, the gospel does not tell us to try harder; it tells us that God has done all our works for us and will raise our dead. We can wait in the dark “for a little while” (v. 20), because morning is coming.

keyVerse.quote: “You keep him in perfect peace whose mind is stayed on you, because he trusts in you.”
keyVerse.note: Perfect peace means complete peace: there is no part of a person’s life that this peace does not reach. And it comes from a relationship, not from circumstances: it belongs to the one whose mind rests on God. Philippians 4:7 is the New Testament counterpart: the peace of God that guards heart and mind in Christ Jesus.

26.reflection:
Verse 3 promises perfect peace to the one “whose mind is stayed on you”, that is, leaning its weight on God. What do you tend to lean on when you are anxious, and what would it look like this week to put your weight on him instead?

“My soul yearns for you in the night” (v. 9). What surfaces in your heart when you lie awake? How can the night become a time of seeking God rather than only of worry?

The people confess, “we have given birth to wind” (v. 18). Have you poured yourself into something that seemed to come to nothing? How do verse 12 and verse 19, and Paul’s words that “your labor is not in vain” (1 Corinthians 15:58), speak to that?

God tells his people to hide “for a little while until the fury has passed by” (v. 20). How does knowing that the Christian’s waiting is for a little while, sheltered by Christ, change the way we endure the present?
26.text: <sup>1</sup>In that day this song will be sung in the land of Judah: "We have a strong city; he sets up salvation as walls and bulwarks.<sup>2</sup>Open the gates, that the righteous nation that keeps faith may enter in.<sup>3</sup>You keep him in perfect peace whose mind is stayed on you, because he trusts in you.<sup>4</sup>Trust in the LORD forever, for the LORD GOD is an everlasting rock.<sup>5</sup>For he has humbled the inhabitants of the height, the lofty city. He lays it low, lays it low to the ground, casts it to the dust.<sup>6</sup>The foot tramples it, the feet of the poor, the steps of the needy."<sup>7</sup>The path of the righteous is level; you make level the way of the righteous.<sup>8</sup>In the path of your judgments, O LORD, we wait for you; your name and remembrance are the desire of our soul.<sup>9</sup>My soul yearns for you in the night; my spirit within me earnestly seeks you. For when your judgments are in the earth, the inhabitants of the world learn righteousness.<sup>10</sup>If favor is shown to the wicked, he does not learn righteousness; in the land of uprightness he deals corruptly and does not see the majesty of the LORD.<sup>11</sup>O LORD, your hand is lifted up, but they do not see it. Let them see your zeal for your people, and be ashamed. Let the fire for your adversaries consume them.<sup>12</sup>O LORD, you will ordain peace for us, for you have indeed done for us all our works.<sup>13</sup>O LORD our God, other lords besides you have ruled over us, but your name alone we bring to remembrance.<sup>14</sup>They are dead, they will not live; they are shades, they will not arise; to that end you have visited them with destruction and wiped out all remembrance of them.<sup>15</sup>But you have increased the nation, O LORD, you have increased the nation; you are glorified; you have enlarged all the borders of the land.<sup>16</sup>O LORD, in distress they sought you; they poured out a whispered prayer when your discipline was upon them.<sup>17</sup>Like a pregnant woman who writhes and cries out in her pangs when she is near to giving birth, so were we because of you, O LORD;<sup>18</sup>we were pregnant, we writhed, but we have given birth to wind. We have accomplished no deliverance in the earth, and the inhabitants of the world have not fallen.<sup>19</sup>Your dead shall live; their bodies shall rise. You who dwell in the dust, awake and sing for joy! For your dew is a dew of light, and the earth will give birth to the dead.<sup>20</sup>Come, my people, enter your chambers, and shut your doors behind you; hide yourselves for a little while until the fury has passed by.<sup>21</sup>For behold, the LORD is coming out from his place to punish the inhabitants of the earth for their iniquity, and the earth will disclose the blood shed on it, and will no more cover its slain.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Those who trust in the LORD are secure, because he himself is their wall and their rock. The song of Judah celebrates a strong city whose walls are salvation and whose gates stand open for a righteous, faithful people (vv. 1–2). Its most famous line follows: God keeps in perfect peace the one whose mind leans on him, because the LORD is an everlasting rock (vv. 3–4). The proud city is brought down to the dust and trampled by the feet of the poor (vv. 5–6). The singers walk a path God makes level and wait for him while his judgments are in the earth, longing for him in the night (vv. 7–9).
verseByVerse.theology: The strong city is set against the fortified city of chapter 25, and the difference is not masonry: God is its wall, and what its citizens do is trust.
verseByVerse.examples: This is a promise for the anxious, but not a technique for calming down. The peace of verse 3 comes to the person who keeps leaning on God when nothing else is steady, and it rests on what he is, an everlasting rock, not on how steady the leaning feels.

verseByVerse.quote: In that day this song will be sung in the land of Judah: "We have a strong city; he sets up salvation as walls and bulwarks. Open the gates, that the righteous nation that keeps faith may enter in. You keep him in perfect peace whose mind is stayed on you, because he trusts in you. Trust in the LORD forever, for the LORD GOD is an everlasting rock.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God’s people live in a city walled by his salvation, and whoever leans their whole weight on him is kept in perfect peace.

We have a strong city. One chapter ago a fortified city was made a heap. Here is another city, and the singers call it strong, but the strength is in the second half of the line: he sets up salvation as walls and bulwarks. What stands between this city and the world is not stone but salvation, and God put it there.

Open the gates. The gates are opened rather than defended. A city whose walls are God can afford open doors, which is where the Bible ends up: a city whose gates are never shut (Revelation 21:25).

You keep him in perfect peace. The Hebrew has no adjective; the phrase is simply shalom shalom, peace repeated, which is how that language says complete. And the second half of the verse is the key to the first.

Whose mind is stayed on you. Stayed means propped, leaning, resting weight against something, as a beam rests against a wall. The promise is not to the mind that thinks calm thoughts about God but to the mind that keeps putting its weight on him, and the reason it can is given at once: the LORD GOD is an everlasting rock, and he holds the weight.

What perfect peace is. We usually mean by peace a mind with nothing on it. Shalom is larger: wholeness, right with God, with others and within. Our deepest lack is not calm but being right with God, and Isaiah names how that comes: “upon him was the chastisement that brought us peace” (53:5). Christ took the blows that stood between us and God. And notice who does the keeping: You keep him. Paul says the same: “the peace of God, which surpasses all understanding, will guard your hearts and your minds in Christ Jesus” (Philippians 4:7). See Peace.

What is not promised. Not the absence of trouble: this chapter has a trampled city, a confession of total failure and a call to hide behind closed doors. It promises a stability the trouble cannot get at. So when worry wakes you at three in the morning, do not try to argue yourself calm. Name the thing to him, remember what your peace cost him, and lean there. Anxiety that will not lift is not simply a failure of faith; a biblical counsellor and a doctor’s check-up may be part of how God keeps you.

verseByVerse.quote: For he has humbled the inhabitants of the height, the lofty city. He lays it low, lays it low to the ground, casts it to the dust. The foot tramples it, the feet of the poor, the steps of the needy." The path of the righteous is level; you make level the way of the righteous. In the path of your judgments, O LORD, we wait for you; your name and remembrance are the desire of our soul. My soul yearns for you in the night; my spirit within me earnestly seeks you. For when your judgments are in the earth, the inhabitants of the world learn righteousness.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God brings the proud city down under the feet of the poor, while his people wait for him and long for him above everything.

The feet of the poor. God lays the lofty city low, and a third verb piles on: casts it to the dust. Then the detail that makes the verse: who walks on the ruins? Not an army, but the feet of the poor, the steps of the needy, the people whose labour built the lofty city and whose money paid for it. They are not conquering it, just walking over what is left, the quietest reversal in the book.

Your name and remembrance are the desire of our soul. God levels the path of the righteous, but they are not yet out of trouble: they wait for him in the path of your judgments. What they want is not first rescue but your name and remembrance, God himself, known and honoured: a striking thing for people in the middle of a judgment to say.

My soul yearns for you in the night. One of the most honest sentences about desire in the Old Testament. In the night, when there is nothing to distract, whatever a person actually wants surfaces without being asked, and what surfaces here is God himself. Nobody produces that longing by effort; it is the work of the God who first sought his people, and in the believer it is the Spirit who cries out to the Father (Romans 8:15).

The inhabitants of the world learn righteousness. God’s judgments are not simply destructive: they teach people who would not learn from kindness (v. 10).

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The middle of the song is unsparing about what human beings cannot do. Kindness shown to the wicked does not teach them righteousness, for they do not see the LORD’s majesty, and only his judgment will open their eyes (vv. 10–11). Whatever good Israel has known, God did it, and the foreign lords who once ruled them are dead and will not rise, while God has enlarged his people (vv. 12–15). Then comes the most honest confession in the chapter: in distress they prayed in whispers and laboured like a woman in childbirth, and gave birth only to wind, achieving no deliverance for the world (vv. 16–18).
verseByVerse.theology: This is the emptying that has to happen before verse 19 can be said, and it is why the deliverance that follows comes entirely from God.
verseByVerse.examples: Verse 10 corrects a hope many kind people hold: that enough kindness will make anyone good. Grace is never wasted, but what a hard heart lacks is not more favour but sight of the majesty of the LORD, and only God can give that.

verseByVerse.quote: If favor is shown to the wicked, he does not learn righteousness; in the land of uprightness he deals corruptly and does not see the majesty of the LORD. O LORD, your hand is lifted up, but they do not see it. Let them see your zeal for your people, and be ashamed. Let the fire for your adversaries consume them. O LORD, you will ordain peace for us, for you have indeed done for us all our works. O LORD our God, other lords besides you have ruled over us, but your name alone we bring to remembrance. They are dead, they will not live; they are shades, they will not arise; to that end you have visited them with destruction and wiped out all remembrance of them. But you have increased the nation, O LORD, you have increased the nation; you are glorified; you have enlarged all the borders of the land.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Kindness alone does not change the wicked; God has done every good thing his people have, and their old tyrants are gone for ever.

If favor is shown to the wicked. A sober observation that corrects a sentimental assumption: kindness does not automatically produce goodness. Show a man favour and he may simply take the advantage and go on as before, not because kindness is wasted but because the problem was never a shortage of it. The last clause names the root: he does not see the majesty of the LORD, and no improvement in circumstances repairs that.

Your hand is lifted up, but they do not see it. So the singers pray that the blind will see God’s zeal for your people and be ashamed: a prayer for his justice to become visible, not a private grudge.

You have indeed done for us all our works. Not that God helped with their works: everything Israel had accomplished turns out, when the accounts are opened, to have been done by God. That is humbling and, for anybody tired of carrying the weight of his own record, an enormous relief. (Compare Ephesians 2:10.)

Other lords besides you have ruled over us. Probably the foreign kings who had ruled God’s people, with the gods that came with them. Now they are shades, the powerless dead, and they will not arise. Five verses on (v. 19), the chapter will say the exact opposite about God’s own dead, and the contrast is deliberate. Meanwhile God has increased the nation (v. 15).

verseByVerse.quote: O LORD, in distress they sought you; they poured out a whispered prayer when your discipline was upon them. Like a pregnant woman who writhes and cries out in her pangs when she is near to giving birth, so were we because of you, O LORD; we were pregnant, we writhed, but we have given birth to wind. We have accomplished no deliverance in the earth, and the inhabitants of the world have not fallen.
verseByVerse.commentary:
In distress God’s people prayed and laboured with everything they had, and produced nothing: they cannot save themselves or the world.

A whispered prayer. Not eloquence or liturgy, but the sound a person makes under pressure when there is nothing left to say properly.

We have given birth to wind. One of the bleakest images in Scripture. Every part of the labour was real: they carried something, went into pains and cried out, and what came out was wind. All the pain of labour and no child.

We have accomplished no deliverance in the earth. What is confessed is not laziness but the failure of genuine, exhausting effort, a far harder thing to admit and a far more common experience.

When effort comes to nothing. Anyone who has poured years into something (a marriage, a ministry, a child, a work) and watched it come to nothing knows this verse from the inside. Isaiah lets the confession stand, because it has to stand before the next verse can be said. What follows is not an encouragement to try harder; it comes to people who have spent everything and produced air.

Uncertain wording. Verse 16 is very compressed Hebrew, and whispered prayer renders a word that elsewhere means a charm; the sense is a faint, desperate murmur. In verse 18 have not fallen may mean “have not been born”, continuing the childbirth picture. Either way, human labour brought no deliverance.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Into that confession of failure God speaks a promise only he can keep: his people’s dead will live and their bodies will rise. Those who sleep in the dust are told to wake and sing, for God’s dew will fall and the earth will give birth to the dead (v. 19), the very thing human labour could not produce. Meanwhile God’s people are to go indoors and shut the door for a little while, as on the night of Passover, until his fury has passed by (v. 20), for the LORD is coming to punish the earth, and the ground will give up the evidence of every murder it has hidden (v. 21).
verseByVerse.theology: The resurrection promise is placed where it is on purpose: it is spoken to people who have just admitted that all their effort produced nothing.
verseByVerse.examples: The instruction in verse 20 is unexpectedly domestic: go inside, shut the door, wait a little while.

verseByVerse.quote: Your dead shall live; their bodies shall rise. You who dwell in the dust, awake and sing for joy! For your dew is a dew of light, and the earth will give birth to the dead. Come, my people, enter your chambers, and shut your doors behind you; hide yourselves for a little while until the fury has passed by. For behold, the LORD is coming out from his place to punish the inhabitants of the earth for their iniquity, and the earth will disclose the blood shed on it, and will no more cover its slain.
verseByVerse.commentary:
What human labour could not do, God will: his people’s dead will rise bodily from the dust, and until then they shelter for a little while as his judgment passes.

Your dead shall live; their bodies shall rise. Into that confession God speaks, and this is the first unambiguous promise of bodily resurrection in the book. It is entirely physical. Your dead: particular people, belonging to somebody. Their bodies shall rise. You who dwell in the dust: the dead addressed directly and told not merely to get up but to sing for joy.

Whose they are. Five verses ago the other lords would not arise. Here the verdict is reversed for God’s own: the difference is not the quality of the dead but whose they are.

The earth will give birth to the dead. The picture answers verse 18. They gave birth to wind; the earth will give birth to the dead. The same labour, a different mother: what human labour could not produce, the ground will hand over when God’s dew falls on it. Dew was the morning moisture that revived parched ground, a picture of God’s life-giving power falling on the dust.

The rest of Scripture. Daniel says it plainly: “many of those who sleep in the dust of the earth shall awake” (Daniel 12:2). Paul builds a whole chapter on it: the body is sown perishable and raised imperishable (1 Corinthians 15:42).

Christ the firstfruits. Paul names the first to rise: “Christ has been raised from the dead, the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep” (1 Corinthians 15:20); he is “the firstborn from the dead” (Colossians 1:18). On the first Easter morning the earth gave birth to its first resurrection body, the pledge that it will give up the rest. So Paul’s chapter ends with an answer to those who gave birth to wind: “in the Lord your labor is not in vain” (1 Corinthians 15:58).

Enter your chambers. Many readers hear in verse 20 the night of the Passover, when no one was to go out of the door until morning (Exodus 12:22–23): stay indoors, sheltered by what God has provided, until judgment passes. Christians shelter in the same way, for “Christ, our Passover lamb, has been sacrificed” (1 Corinthians 5:7), and the wait is only for a little while (compare Hebrews 10:37).

The earth will disclose the blood shed on it. The last line answers every murder that was got away with. The ground has kept the record since Abel (Genesis 4:10); on that day it gives the evidence up. But there is “sprinkled blood that speaks a better word than the blood of Abel” (Hebrews 12:24): Abel’s cries for justice, Christ’s for mercy.

National revival or resurrection? Some read verse 19 as Israel’s national revival, like the dry bones of Ezekiel 37. But it says their bodies shall rise, and those who dwell in the dust awake, in contrast to the dead oppressors who will not arise (v. 14). With Daniel 12:2 it is one of the Old Testament’s clearest promises of bodily resurrection.

Uncertain wording. A dew of light is literally “of lights”; the same word means “herbs” in 2 Kings 4:39, so some translate “a dew of herbs”. Either way it pictures new life rising from the dust like grass after the night.
verseByVerse.note: Your dew is a dew of light: dew was the morning moisture that revived parched ground, here a picture of God’s life-giving power falling on the dust.

26.theology:
Peace as leaning. The peace of verse 3 is complete (shalom shalom), but it is not the absence of trouble. It belongs to the mind that keeps putting its weight on God, and it rests on what he is.

Giving birth to wind. The chapter will not let God’s people take credit for anything: all their works were his (v. 12), and their own best labour produced nothing (vv. 17-18). Only to people emptied like this can verse 19 be spoken.

Your dead shall live. The first unambiguous promise of bodily resurrection in Isaiah is spoken to the people who gave birth to wind. What human labour could not produce, God gives, and Christ’s rising is its firstfruits.

27.subtitle: The Great Harvest
27.intro:
Where we are. Chapter 27 closes the vision of the whole earth judged and renewed (chapters 24–27). After the feast of chapter 25 and the resurrection song of chapter 26, Isaiah shows how the story ends: the great enemy slain, God’s vineyard fruitful at last, and his scattered people gathered to worship.

The message. God will kill the dragon, every power of chaos and evil behind the empires, and he will turn his ruined vineyard into a garden that fills the world with fruit. His discipline of his people is measured and purposeful, aimed at removing their idols, not destroying them. And at the end he will gather them, one by one, to worship him on his holy mountain.

Why it was said. Judah lived among nations that seemed as unstoppable as sea monsters, and under the threat of exile for its own idolatry (see the introduction). Isaiah’s hearers had heard the vineyard song of chapter 5 end in briers; they needed to know whether God was finished with them.

How the chapter makes its case. First the LORD’s sword falls on Leviathan, the twisting serpent and dragon of the sea (v. 1). Then the vineyard song of 5:1–7 is sung again in reverse: the LORD now keeps and waters his vineyard, has no wrath, presses peace even on his enemies, and Jacob fills the world with fruit (vv. 2–6). God’s blows on his people were measured discipline to purge the idols, unlike his destruction of their oppressors, though the stubborn city still falls (vv. 7–11). Finally the LORD threshes his harvest from the Euphrates to Egypt, gleans his people one by one, and a great trumpet calls the scattered home to worship in Jerusalem (vv. 12–13).

Where it leads. The chapter reaches Christ by promise and pattern. The serpent first met in Eden (Genesis 3:15) is “that ancient serpent, who is called the devil and Satan” (Revelation 12:9), and Christ defeated him by dying, destroying “the one who has the power of death” (Hebrews 2:14). The vineyard that failed in chapter 5 finds its fruitfulness in the one who said, “I am the true vine” (John 15:1). And the great trumpet sounds again when he sends his angels to “gather his elect from the four winds” (Matthew 24:31).

For us. Evil is real and larger than any single villain, but it is not equal to God, and its end is fixed. God’s hard providences in a believer’s life are measured discipline, not destruction, because the destruction fell on Christ. And no one is lost in the crowd: he gathers his people one by one.

keyVerse.quote: “In days to come Jacob shall take root, Israel shall blossom and put forth shoots and fill the whole world with fruit.”
keyVerse.note: The vine that was stripped in chapter 5 becomes the vine that fills the earth. This is God’s way with his people all through Isaiah: judgment clears the way for new growth, and the new growth exceeds the old. The verse also points to Christ: Jesus declares himself the true vine (John 15:1), and his fruitfulness fills the world through those who abide in him.

27.reflection:
Verse 1 pictures evil as a dragon that only God can slay. Where do you see evil in the world, or in your own life, that feels too large to fight? How does Christ’s victory at the cross (Colossians 2:15) change the way you face it?

In chapter 5 God removed the hedge from his vineyard; here he says, “I, the LORD, am its keeper; every moment I water it” (v. 3), and “I have no wrath” (v. 4). What do these words show about God’s heart towards his people in Christ? Which do you find harder to believe?

God disciplined his people “measure by measure” to remove their idols (vv. 8–9). Can you look back on a hard season and see God’s purpose in it? What idols might he be clearing away now?

God’s people are gathered “one by one” (v. 12). How does it encourage you that God knows and gathers each person individually? Who might you pray for, or invite, to be gathered?
27.text: <sup>1</sup>In that day the LORD with his hard and great and strong sword will punish Leviathan the fleeing serpent, Leviathan the twisting serpent, and he will slay the dragon that is in the sea.<sup>2</sup>In that day, "A pleasant vineyard, sing of it!<sup>3</sup>I, the LORD, am its keeper; every moment I water it. Lest anyone punish it, I keep it night and day;<sup>4</sup>I have no wrath. Would that I had thorns and briers to battle! I would march against them, I would burn them up together.<sup>5</sup>Or let them lay hold of my protection, let them make peace with me, let them make peace with me."<sup>6</sup>In days to come Jacob shall take root, Israel shall blossom and put forth shoots and fill the whole world with fruit.<sup>7</sup>Has he struck them as he struck those who struck them? Or have they been slain as their slayers were slain?<sup>8</sup>Measure by measure, by exile you contended with them; he removed them with his fierce breath in the day of the east wind.<sup>9</sup>Therefore by this the guilt of Jacob will be atoned for, and this will be the full fruit of the removal of his sin: when he makes all the stones of the altars like chalkstones crushed to pieces, no Asherim or incense altars will remain standing.<sup>10</sup>For the fortified city is solitary, a habitation deserted and forsaken, like the wilderness; there the calf grazes; there it lies down and strips its branches.<sup>11</sup>When its boughs are dry, they are broken; women come and make a fire of them. For this is a people without discernment; therefore he who made them will not have compassion on them; he who formed them will show them no favor.<sup>12</sup>In that day from the river Euphrates to the Brook of Egypt the LORD will thresh out the grain, and you will be gleaned one by one, O people of Israel.<sup>13</sup>And in that day a great trumpet will be blown, and those who were lost in the land of Assyria and those who were driven out to the land of Egypt will come and worship the LORD on the holy mountain at Jerusalem.

verseByVerse.ref: v. 1 — The Sword and the Serpent
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: In a single verse Isaiah announces the end of the great enemy behind all the others. On that day the LORD, with his hard and great and strong sword, will punish Leviathan, the fleeing and twisting serpent, and slay the dragon in the sea. Isaiah takes the monster that his neighbours’ stories made the symbol of chaos and shows it slain by Israel’s God, the Creator, who has no rival. The serpent and the dragon point beyond any single empire to the power behind them, the ancient serpent of Eden, whose final defeat the New Testament traces to the cross and the return of Christ.
verseByVerse.theology: Isaiah names the monster three ways and kills it once. The God of Israel does not struggle with chaos as one power among others; he ends it.
verseByVerse.examples: Anyone who has felt evil as something larger and older than the people doing it can take this verse as a promise: the thing behind it all has a day appointed and a sword waiting.

verseByVerse.quote: In that day the LORD with his hard and great and strong sword will punish Leviathan the fleeing serpent, Leviathan the twisting serpent, and he will slay the dragon that is in the sea.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God will destroy the monster of chaos, the power behind every evil empire: the serpent Christ came to crush.

Leviathan the fleeing serpent. Every reader in that world knew Leviathan. In the stories of the region it is the sea monster of chaos, the thing that heaves under the water and that no one can hunt or bridle; the book of Job spends most of a chapter on the impossibility of catching it (Job 41). It stands for everything untamable and hostile to creation, and for the power behind the empires that behave the same way.

His hard and great and strong sword. The weapon has three adjectives before the target has its three names: a decisive victory over every version of the thing.

Does Isaiah believe the old myths, then? No. Texts from ancient Ugarit, north of Israel, describe a sea monster called Lotan with almost these words, the fleeing serpent and the twisting serpent. Isaiah borrows the picture his neighbours feared to say that the LORD is not one god struggling against chaos among others: he made the sea, and the monster is his to kill. Scripture uses the imagery of its world as a preacher uses a familiar picture, without endorsing the stories it came from.

The dragon that is in the sea. John saw who this was. In his vision the great dragon is thrown down, “that ancient serpent, who is called the devil and Satan, the deceiver of the whole world” (Revelation 12:9). The sword in this verse finishes what a serpent started in a garden.

The sword turns out to be a cross. The offspring of the woman promised in Genesis 3:15 crushed the serpent’s head by being bruised himself: through death he destroyed the one who has the power of death, that is, the devil (Hebrews 2:14), and at the cross he disarmed the rulers and authorities and triumphed over them (Colossians 2:15). The final blow is still to come: “The God of peace will soon crush Satan under your feet” (Romans 16:20). Set this verse beside 11:8, where a nursing child plays over the hole of a cobra and comes to no harm: that verse is only possible because of this one.

Why do our stories still need dragons? We have stopped believing in sea monsters, and many in the devil. Yet our best-loved stories are full of dark lords and evil larger than any villain, and when real horrors happen we reach for the old word: demonic. G. K. Chesterton argued in Tremendous Trifles that fairy tales do not teach children that dragons exist, since children know that already; what the tales give them is a St George who can kill the dragon. Everybody knows the dragon. The question is whether anyone can defeat it without becoming another tyrant. The gospel’s answer is a Champion who won by being wounded, and who uses his victory not to rule us by fear but to set us free.

Uncertain wording. Do the names describe one monster or three? Some see three empires, perhaps Assyria, Babylon and Egypt; most take them as one beast, as in the Ugaritic texts. Fleeing may also mean gliding. Either way, everything the monster stands for falls to one sword.
verseByVerse.note: Leviathan, the twisting serpent, stands for every power hostile to God.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 2–11 — The Vineyard Song, Sung Again
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The vineyard song of chapter 5 is sung again, and this time it ends in fruit, because God himself guards and waters his people. He is its keeper every moment, he has no wrath towards it, and he twice urges even its enemies to make peace with him (vv. 2–5); in days to come Jacob will take root and fill the whole world with fruit (v. 6). Verses 7 to 11 explain God’s dealings in the meantime: he has struck his people, but measuredly, unlike their oppressors, and the purpose of the exile is that the idols and altars be ground to chalk. The fortified city that will not understand is still left desolate.
verseByVerse.theology: Between the two vineyard songs stands everything the book has been promising. The vineyard has not improved itself; it has a keeper who will not let it go.
verseByVerse.examples: The order matters for anyone who has wandered: the offer of peace in verse 5 comes before the discipline of verses 7 to 11 is explained. God names his welcome first.

verseByVerse.quote: In that day, "A pleasant vineyard, sing of it! I, the LORD, am its keeper; every moment I water it. Lest anyone punish it, I keep it night and day; I have no wrath. Would that I had thorns and briers to battle! I would march against them, I would burn them up together. Or let them lay hold of my protection, let them make peace with me, let them make peace with me." In days to come Jacob shall take root, Israel shall blossom and put forth shoots and fill the whole world with fruit.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God sings his vineyard song again: now he guards his people himself, holds no wrath against them, urges peace even on his enemies, and makes them fill the world with fruit.

A pleasant vineyard, sing of it! Isaiah is starting the song of chapter 5 over. That vineyard song ended with wild grapes, a broken wall and briers. Here the first thing said about the vineyard is that it is pleasant.

Every moment I water it. What has changed is not the vineyard but the way its owner treats it. In chapter 5 he removed the hedge. Here he waters it every moment and keeps it night and day, lest anyone punish it. The disappointed owner has become the watchman over his own field.

I have no wrath. Then four words that should stop a reader who has come this far. The speaker is the God of the first vineyard song, the six woes, the hand stretched out in anger and the emptied earth. If thorns and briers came against the vineyard now, he would march out and burn them, for his anger is turned on whatever threatens it, not on the vineyard itself.

Let them make peace with me. The invitation is said twice. People repeat things when they badly want to be heard: this God is not weighing an approach but pressing the offer. The New Testament says what it cost him: God was pleased to reconcile all things to himself, “making peace by the blood of his cross” (Colossians 1:20).

Fill the whole world with fruit. The vineyard that produced wild grapes fills the whole world with fruit: the song that ended in briers ends in a harvest big enough for everybody.

The true vine. Jesus took up this vineyard language and applied it to himself: “I am the true vine, and my Father is the vinedresser” (John 15:1). Israel was the vine that failed to bear; Christ is the vine that did, and those joined to him by faith, from every nation, are the branches through whom the world is filled with fruit.

How does “I have no wrath” (v. 4) fit “he who made them will not have compassion on them” (v. 11)? Verse 4 is God’s word to his vineyard, his people, and his invitation to his enemies to make peace with him (v. 5). Verse 11 is for those who persist in refusing. Compassion is withheld only from those who reject it.

Uncertain wording. Verse 4 is very compressed, and the thorns and briers are uncertain: most likely enemies, or the weeds of sin, that God would burn to protect his vineyard. Verse 5 then offers them the alternative: let them lay hold of my protection.
verseByVerse.note: A new song of the vineyard, reversing 5:1–7.

verseByVerse.quote: Has he struck them as he struck those who struck them? Or have they been slain as their slayers were slain? Measure by measure, by exile you contended with them; he removed them with his fierce breath in the day of the east wind. Therefore by this the guilt of Jacob will be atoned for, and this will be the full fruit of the removal of his sin: when he makes all the stones of the altars like chalkstones crushed to pieces, no Asherim or incense altars will remain standing. For the fortified city is solitary, a habitation deserted and forsaken, like the wilderness; there the calf grazes; there it lies down and strips its branches. When its boughs are dry, they are broken; women come and make a fire of them. For this is a people without discernment; therefore he who made them will not have compassion on them; he who formed them will show them no favor.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God has struck his people in measured discipline to purge their idols, not to destroy them as he does their enemies; yet those who will not understand still fall.

Has he struck them as he struck those who struck them? Both questions expect the answer no: God has struck his people, but not as he struck their enemies. The difference between discipline and destruction is not the pain but the intention and the limit.

Measure by measure. The judgment was weighed out, not poured, rationed even at its worst: something to hold on to for anyone who has felt that the hard thing God sent had no bottom to it. Even the exile is the east wind, the scorching desert wind that withers a field, and even that lasts a day.

No Asherim or incense altars will remain standing. The aim was not to exact a penalty but to remove idols: the altar stones ground to chalk, the Asherah poles (wooden symbols of a Canaanite goddess) and incense stands gone. God was getting the rival gods out of the country. That is the full fruit of the removal of his sin.

Why the difference? For those who belong to Christ, every hard providence is discipline and never destruction, because the destruction has already fallen on him. “There is therefore now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus” (Romans 8:1), and “the Lord disciplines the one he loves” (Hebrews 12:6). The measuring hand is a Father’s.

The fortified city is solitary. The fortified city appears again, empty, a calf browsing in it and its dry boughs used for firewood. The hard sentence in verse 11 names the failure as a people without discernment, the same charge as 1:3, where the ox knew more than Israel did.

Does the exile atone for sin? No: atonement is by the blood of Christ alone. The exile was discipline that would purge the idols; forgiveness comes from God. Paul quotes these words in Romans 11:26–27 of the day God takes away the sins of Jacob.

Where Christians differ: what does Paul mean when he applies this verse to “all Israel” (Romans 11:26)? Many read a great future turning of Jewish people to Christ through the gospel; others, with Calvin, the whole people of God, Jew and Gentile; dispensational readers add a separate national plan. This commentary’s view: it does not press one reading, but holds with humility that Romans 11 most naturally looks for a future turning of many Jewish people to Christ, within the one people of God. All these readings put the forgiveness in Christ alone.

Uncertain wording. Measure by measure (v. 8) renders a rare expression, perhaps from a measure of grain, perhaps “by driving them out”. The fortified city (v. 10) is unnamed: Samaria, Jerusalem, or a hostile city like that of 25:2. The point stands in every reading.
verseByVerse.note: The Greek Old Testament reads “and this is the blessing when I take away his sin” (ESV note): the wording Paul quotes.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The four chapters end not in wreckage but in a harvest and a procession home. God threshes his grain across the whole land once promised, from the Euphrates to the Brook of Egypt, and gathers his people as a gleaner picks up grain, one by one (v. 12). Then a great trumpet is blown, and the lost in Assyria and the exiles in Egypt come and worship the LORD on the holy mountain at Jerusalem (v. 13). The devastation of chapter 24 was never the destination; it was the road to the mountain of the feast.
verseByVerse.theology: After four chapters of cosmic scale, the last picture is a harvest and a procession of people going up to worship.
verseByVerse.examples: The two countries named in verse 13 are the two that had swallowed God's people: Assyria, which deported the north, and Egypt, where refugees had fled. Both give their people back at the sound of a trumpet, the instrument Paul and John both reach for when they describe the last gathering of all.

verseByVerse.quote: In that day from the river Euphrates to the Brook of Egypt the LORD will thresh out the grain, and you will be gleaned one by one, O people of Israel. And in that day a great trumpet will be blown, and those who were lost in the land of Assyria and those who were driven out to the land of Egypt will come and worship the LORD on the holy mountain at Jerusalem.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The vision ends in a harvest: God gathers his scattered people one by one, and a great trumpet calls them home to worship.

The LORD will thresh out the grain. The two boundaries are the whole territory ever promised, from the great river to the wadi at the Egyptian border. Thresh is the beating that separates grain from husk on the threshing floor, so judgment is still in the picture, but what it produces is grain, and the grain is collected.

You will be gleaned one by one. Then the phrase that brings four chapters of worldwide scale down to the single person. After the earth emptied, death swallowed and the dragon killed, the gathering is done singly: each one seen, known and lifted. God is not too large for the individual. The same hand that wrings out a planet gleans a field one grain at a time.

A great trumpet will be blown. The summons is a trumpet, the instrument that called an assembly, announced the year of jubilee and gathered a scattered people. Paul reaches for it when he describes the last gathering, “at the last trumpet”, when the dead are raised imperishable (1 Corinthians 15:52).

Worship on the holy mountain. Four chapters that began with God emptying the earth end with people walking up a hill to worship. The devastation was never the destination. It was the road to a mountain with a feast on it.

Is this the return from exile, the church, or a future regathering? The return from Babylon was its beginning; but the great trumpet and the gathering from the ends of the earth point to Christ, who “will send out his angels with a loud trumpet call, and they will gather his elect” (Matthew 24:31). The gospel is gathering them now, from every nation, and that last trumpet will be loud and public, heard at his visible return, not a secret summons (1 Thessalonians 4:16).

27.theology:
The dragon dealt with. The ancient figure of chaos, and the power behind every empire that behaves like it, is named three ways and killed once. The gospel shows that the sword was a cross.

The vineyard song, sung again. The song that ended in briers in chapter 5 is sung again over the same vineyard, now watered every moment by a God who says I have no wrath and presses his offer of peace.

Discipline measured, and gathered one by one. God’s striking of his people was rationed and aimed at their idols, and the harvest at the end is gathered person by person.

28.subtitle: Woe to the Drunkards of Ephraim
28.intro:
Where we are. After the vision of the whole earth in chapters 24–27, Isaiah comes back to his own day. Chapter 28 opens a series of woes (chapters 28–33) aimed chiefly at Judah’s leaders, who sought an alliance with Egypt against Assyria instead of trusting the LORD. It begins with Samaria, capital of the northern kingdom, then turns on Jerusalem.

The message. Those who refuse God’s simple offer of rest and lean on their own clever arrangements are building on lies, and the storm will sweep them away. But God has already laid in Zion a tested and precious cornerstone, and whoever trusts in him will not need to run in panic. Even God’s judgments are measured like a wise farmer’s work, with harvest, not destruction, as their goal.

Why it was said. Samaria fell to Assyria in 722 BC, and Jerusalem’s rulers, facing the same empire, made a treaty with Egypt and thought themselves safe (see the introduction). Isaiah’s message to trust the LORD struck them as simplistic, and they mocked it as baby talk.

How the chapter makes its case. Samaria’s proud, drunken crown is fading and will be swallowed like an early fig, but the LORD will be a crown of glory to his remnant (vv. 1–6). Jerusalem’s priests and prophets are as drunk as Samaria’s, and they mock Isaiah’s teaching; so God will speak to them through foreign invaders, because they refused his offer of rest (vv. 7–13). Against their “covenant with death” God sets a sure foundation stone in Zion; the refuge of lies is swept away, and God does his strange work against his own people (vv. 14–22). A closing parable of the farmer shows that God ploughs and threshes with wisdom and restraint (vv. 23–29).

Where it leads. The cornerstone of verse 16 is one of the clearest promises of Christ in Isaiah, and the New Testament applies it to him three times (Romans 9:33; 10:11; 1 Peter 2:6): he is the stone God laid, rejected by the builders, chosen and precious. The rest the scoffers refused (v. 12) is the rest Jesus offers to “all who labor and are heavy laden” (Matthew 11:28). And the God of verse 29, “wonderful in counsel”, is the God whose Son bears the name Wonderful Counsellor (9:6).

For us. We are all tempted to trust visible arrangements more than an invisible God, and to find the gospel too simple. But every refuge except Christ is a bed too short to rest on. Build on the stone God has laid, and you need not be in haste, even when the hard seasons come, for the God who threshes is a careful farmer and knows when to stop.

keyVerse.quote: “Behold, I am the one who has laid as a foundation in Zion, a stone, a tested stone, a precious cornerstone, of a sure foundation. Whoever believes will not be in haste.”
keyVerse.note: The stone’s chief quality is that it has been tested, proven under pressure, and whoever builds on it will not need to run in panic. Peter and Paul both identify the stone as Christ (1 Peter 2:6; Romans 9:33), and the New Testament adds a warning: the same stone is “a rock of offense” to those who reject him. The stone is the same for everyone; what differs is whether a person builds on it or trips over it.

28.reflection:
Jerusalem’s leaders mocked God’s word as baby talk, yet it was an offer of rest (vv. 9–12). Why do capable, educated people sometimes find the gospel too simple? Where are you tempted to think you have outgrown it?

The rulers made “a covenant with death” and called it security (v. 15). What visible arrangements, plans or people are you tempted to trust instead of God? How would you know if one of them had become a “refuge of lies”?

“Whoever believes will not be in haste” (v. 16). What does it look like in your life to rest your weight on Christ, the tested cornerstone, rather than to rush about in panic?

The farmer does not plough or thresh for ever, and his God teaches him (vv. 23–29). How does this picture help you understand a hard season God has brought into your life, or someone else’s?
