No, he does not thresh it forever; when he drives his cart wheel over it with his horses, he does not crush it.<sup>29</sup>This also comes from the LORD of hosts; he is wonderful in counsel and excellent in wisdom.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Pride and drunkenness have blinded the leaders of God’s people, and because they mock his simple word they will hear him in a foreign tongue. The woe falls first on Samaria, whose proud garland is a fading flower that Assyria will swallow like the first ripe fig (vv. 1–4), while the LORD himself will be a crown of glory, justice and strength to his remnant (vv. 5–6). Then Isaiah turns to Judah, where priests and prophets reel with wine at tables covered in vomit (vv. 7–8). They mock his teaching as baby talk (vv. 9–10), so God will speak through foreign invaders to a people who refused his offer of rest (vv. 11–13).
verseByVerse.theology: The men whose office was to know God's mind are too drunk to hear it, and what they despise as childish is the very thing that would have saved them.
verseByVerse.examples: The church still attracts this charge. Plain teaching, repeated in small pieces, sounds simplistic to people who consider themselves past it, and Jesus thanked his Father for revealing these things to little children.

verseByVerse.quote: Ah, the proud crown of the drunkards of Ephraim, and the fading flower of its glorious beauty, which is on the head of the rich valley of those overcome with wine! Behold, the Lord has one who is mighty and strong; like a storm of hail, a destroying tempest, like a storm of mighty, overflowing waters, he casts down to the earth with his hand. The proud crown of the drunkards of Ephraim will be trodden underfoot; and the fading flower of its glorious beauty, which is on the head of the rich valley, will be like a first-ripe fig before the summer: when someone sees it, he swallows it as soon as it is in his hand.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Samaria’s proud, drunken leaders are like a wilting party garland, and Assyria will swallow the city as easily as a man eats the first fig of summer.

The proud crown of the drunkards of Ephraim. Samaria sat on a hill above a fertile valley, and Isaiah sees a wreath on a drunk man’s head, wilting while the party is still going. He begins with Samaria, probably before its fall in 722 BC, because Jerusalem’s leaders could watch a sister capital going down; then the oracle turns on them with these also (v. 7).

One who is mighty and strong. The instrument is Assyria, which took Samaria after a three-year siege (2 Kings 17:5–6); hail, tempest and flood are Isaiah’s pictures for its army (compare 8:7–8). The empire does the casting down, but the Lord “has” him: the storm belongs to God. The garland once worn high on the head ends trodden underfoot (v. 3), which is where every crown worn in pride ends.

Like a first-ripe fig before the summer. The first ripe fig of the season is irresistible; a man who spots one eats it standing there. That is what an empire will do with the northern kingdom: see it and swallow it.

verseByVerse.quote: In that day the LORD of hosts will be a crown of glory, and a diadem of beauty, to the remnant of his people, and a spirit of justice to him who sits in judgment, and strength to those who turn back the battle at the gate.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Where the leaders’ crown fades, the LORD himself will be his remnant’s glory, and give the justice and courage their leaders lacked.

A crown of glory. Here is the contrast the chapter is built on: the wilting wreath on a drunk head, and God himself as the unfading diadem of those who are left. Peter promises the same to those who serve Christ faithfully: “you will receive the unfading crown of glory” when the chief Shepherd appears (1 Peter 5:4).

A spirit of justice, and strength. What the drunk leaders lacked, the LORD will supply: a spirit of justice to the one who sits as judge, and strength to the soldiers who drive the enemy back from the city gate. Both fail in the next verse, where the judges stumble. Here they are gifts, not achievements, as with the King on whom “the Spirit of counsel and might” will rest (11:2).

verseByVerse.quote: These also reel with wine and stagger with strong drink; the priest and the prophet reel with strong drink, they are swallowed by wine, they stagger with strong drink, they reel in vision, they stumble in giving judgment. For all tables are full of filthy vomit, with no space left.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Judah’s priests and prophets are as drunk as Samaria’s, confused in the very visions and verdicts they exist to give.

The priest and the prophet reel with strong drink. Across the border in Judah the oracle finds the same condition in worse company: the priest and the prophet, the two offices responsible for knowing what God thinks and saying so. They reel in their visions and stagger in their verdicts, exactly where it matters, since a drunk prophet still prophesies and a drunk judge still decides. And Isaiah adds a detail he does not need: every table covered in vomit. He wants the reader in the room.

Swallowed by wine. The verb is the one used of the fig in verse 4: the empire will swallow Samaria, and Judah’s priests and prophets have already been swallowed, by wine. The leaders who should have seen the danger are consumed before any enemy arrives.

The leaders we need. Every failed priest and prophet made plainer the need for one who would not fail: a high priest “holy, innocent, unstained” (Hebrews 7:26), and a prophet whose words “are spirit and life” (John 6:63). Christ is both.

What it does not mean. Not that wine is forbidden; it is God’s gift (Psalm 104:15). Drunkenness is condemned, above all in leaders (1 Timothy 3:3). If your drinking is beyond your control, do not hide it: tell a pastor or trusted believer and see a doctor; seeking help is no failure of faith.

verseByVerse.quote: "To whom will he teach knowledge, and to whom will he explain the message? Those who are weaned from the milk, those taken from the breast? For it is precept upon precept, precept upon precept, line upon line, line upon line, here a little, there a little." For by people of strange lips and with a foreign tongue the LORD will speak to this people, to whom he has said, "This is rest; give rest to the weary; and this is repose"; yet they would not hear. And the word of the LORD will be to them precept upon precept, precept upon precept, line upon line, line upon line, here a little, there a little, that they may go, and fall backward, and be broken, and snared, and taken.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jerusalem’s leaders mock God’s plain word as baby talk, so God will speak to them through foreign invaders, because they refused his offer of rest.

To whom will he teach knowledge? This is one of the few places in Scripture where we hear a prophet’s opponents mimicking him. Their complaint is that Isaiah talks down to them, as though trained men with offices were babies just off the breast.

Precept upon precept. In Hebrew verse 10 is tsav latsav tsav latsav, qav laqav qav laqav, a sing-song of short words: adults doing an impression of the way a toddler is taught, aimed at a man preaching the word of God.

By people of strange lips. The answer fits the crime. You found my plain speech childish? Then you will hear from me in a language you genuinely cannot understand: Assyrian, shouted in your streets by soldiers. In verse 13 God hands their own syllables back: the word they mocked becomes the word that trips them.

This is rest. What they were mocking was not a complicated doctrine but an invitation to lie down. The word ridiculed as baby talk was the offer of rest to tired people.

Revealed to little children. Seven hundred years later another teacher said, “Come to me, all who labor and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest” (Matthew 11:28), and educated men found that simplistic too. He had just thanked his Father for hiding these things from the wise and revealing them to little children (Matthew 11:25): the toddler’s lesson the scoffers mocked turns out to be the way into the kingdom.

The snobbery of the sophisticated. Educated people have always found it hard to receive something simple; the modern version says faith may comfort the unschooled, but serious minds have moved on. Augustine tells in his Confessions that when he first opened the Scriptures as a gifted young student of rhetoric, they seemed unworthy to be compared with the dignity of Cicero; his pride shrank from their plain style. The problem is not a lack of intelligence. Rest has to be received, not mastered, so the gospel humbles the expert and the beginner alike. All come as children, to a Teacher who is “gentle and lowly in heart” (Matthew 11:29), and Augustine, the finest mind of his age, came at last.

A sign for unbelievers. Paul quotes verse 11 in his teaching on tongues (1 Corinthians 14:21). Foreign speech was God’s sign of judgment on a people who would not hear plain words, as when the Assyrians came; so tongues, Paul says, are “a sign not for believers but for unbelievers” (1 Corinthians 14:22).

Where Christians differ: does the gift of tongues continue today? Many godly Christians believe it does. This commentary’s view: the sign gift belonged to the apostolic era, confirming the apostles’ new message (Hebrews 2:3–4), and the church now hears God in the plain words of Scripture; a difference to hold with charity.

Uncertain wording. No one is sure what tsav and qav mean (v. 10): real words, “command” and “line”, as the ESV takes them; nonsense syllables of baby talk; or, since ts and q are neighbouring Hebrew letters, a child reciting the alphabet. On every reading Isaiah’s teaching is mocked as fit for infants.
verseByVerse.note: “Precept upon precept” is mocking baby-talk in Hebrew (tsav latsav, qav laqav). God will speak through foreign tongues instead.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 14–22 — A Covenant with Death, and a Stone
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Jerusalem’s rulers trust a treaty, and God sets against it the only foundation that will stand. He names their policy a covenant with death and a refuge of lies (vv. 14–15). Against it he lays in Zion a tested, precious cornerstone, a sure foundation for anyone who believes (v. 16). Then he measures the city with justice and righteousness, and the hail sweeps the false refuge away; the covenant with death is annulled, and the scourge comes morning by morning (vv. 17–19). Their security is a bed too short and a blanket too narrow (v. 20), for God will fight against his own people as he once fought for them, his strange and alien work (vv. 21–22).
verseByVerse.theology: Two refuges stand side by side: one made by men out of lies, one laid by God in Zion. Everything depends on which a person is standing on.
verseByVerse.examples: Every age makes its covenants with death. Nobody draws one up under that heading; it is always called security, or realism, or keeping our options open.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore hear the word of the LORD, you scoffers, who rule this people in Jerusalem! Because you have said, "We have made a covenant with death, and with Sheol we have an agreement, when the overwhelming whip passes through it will not come to us, for we have made lies our refuge, and in falsehood we have taken shelter"; therefore thus says the Lord GOD, "Behold, I am the one who has laid as a foundation in Zion, a stone, a tested stone, a precious cornerstone, of a sure foundation: 'Whoever believes will not be in haste.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
The rulers think a treaty has made them safe, but God has laid in Zion the one sure foundation, and whoever trusts it need never panic.

A covenant with death. No one said this in these words. The rulers had signed a treaty with Egypt to keep the Assyrians off, and Isaiah gives the policy its true name. A deal that buys safety from a power which cannot provide it, made in order to avoid trusting God, is a covenant with death, and the men who made it would have called it prudent foreign policy. This book calls practical arrangements by their names in God’s sight.

A tested stone, a precious cornerstone. Against the refuge of lies God sets a stone, and every word answers verse 15. Their shelter is falsehood; this is tested. Theirs is an arrangement; this is a foundation. Theirs will be swept away by the hail; this one is sure.

Christ the cornerstone. The New Testament takes this verse three times and always of one person: Peter, writing of a living stone rejected by men but chosen and precious in God’s sight (1 Peter 2:4–6), and Paul twice (Romans 9:33; 10:11). Peter and Paul join it to Psalm 118:22 and Isaiah 8:14: the same stone is a foundation to those who believe and a stumbling block to those who will not. Christ is not a support added to our arrangements but the one foundation God himself has laid (1 Corinthians 3:11), tested in the wilderness and at the cross, and found sure.

Whoever believes will not be in haste. The believer is not promised that he will be spared the storm; the next verses have hail sweeping away the refuge of lies. He will not be in haste: a man standing on rock does not have to run about. And the stone is laid before anyone believes: God says I am the one who has laid it. Faith does not build the foundation; it stands on one already there, which is why faith shows itself in not panicking.

Uncertain wording. Why death and Sheol? Most take it as Isaiah’s bitter name for the Egyptian alliance, which will bring the death it was meant to prevent; some hear a hint of the Canaanite death god, Mot, or of consulting the dead (8:19).

Textual note. Where the Hebrew says the believer will not be in haste, the Greek Old Testament reads “will not be put to shame”, and Peter and Paul quote that form. The two belong together: the one who has something sure underneath him neither panics now nor is disgraced at the end.
verseByVerse.note: A Dead Sea Scroll reads “I am laying” (ESV note).

verseByVerse.quote: And I will make justice the line, and righteousness the plumb line; and hail will sweep away the refuge of lies, and waters will overwhelm the shelter." Then your covenant with death will be annulled, and your agreement with Sheol will not stand; when the overwhelming scourge passes through, you will be beaten down by it. As often as it passes through it will take you; for morning by morning it will pass through, by day and by night; and it will be sheer terror to understand the message. For the bed is too short to stretch oneself on, and the covering too narrow to wrap oneself in. For the LORD will rise up as on Mount Perazim; as in the Valley of Gibeon he will be roused; to do his deed—strange is his deed! and to work his work—alien is his work! Now therefore do not scoff, lest your bonds be made strong; for I have heard a decree of destruction from the Lord GOD of hosts against the whole land.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God measures Jerusalem by his justice, sweeps away its false security, and does the strange work of fighting his own people.

Justice the line, and righteousness the plumb line. God comes to the building site with a builder’s tools. The measuring line and the plumb line find out whether a wall is straight, and the standards applied are justice and righteousness. The wall does not survive the measurement.

Your covenant with death will be annulled. The treaty is cancelled by the very thing it was signed to prevent, and the protection is not merely inadequate but annulled, as though the paper had never been valid.

The bed is too short. Then the best image in the chapter: a bed you cannot straighten out on, a blanket that will not cover you. Pull it up and your feet come out; cover your feet and your shoulders are cold. That is what trusting an inadequate refuge feels like from inside: not sudden catastrophe but a permanent, low-grade inability to rest, constant small adjustments and nothing ever quite right.

Strange is his deed! Two old victories are named: David’s at Perazim (2 Samuel 5:20), and at Gibeon either David’s or Joshua’s (Joshua 10:10–14). Then the unsettling phrase: God’s deed is strange, his work alien. He does at Jerusalem what he once did for Israel against her enemies. Judgment on his own people is work God himself calls alien to his character. He delights in steadfast love (Micah 7:18).

The strangest work of all. The strangest thing God ever did was to strike not merely his people but his own Son: “it was the will of the LORD to crush him” (53:10). At the cross the judgment due to people who make covenants with death fell on the cornerstone himself, so that it need never fall on those who trust him.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 23–29 — The Farmer Knows When to Stop
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The chapter ends with a gentle parable from the farm: God’s dealings with his people are as wise and measured as a good farmer’s work. A farmer does not plough for ever; he levels the ground and plants each crop in its proper place (vv. 23–25), and God himself taught him to do it (v. 26). He threshes each crop with the right tool, beating delicate dill and cumin with a stick, and does not crush the bread grain for ever (vv. 27–28). The God who gives the farmer such wisdom is “wonderful in counsel and excellent in wisdom” (v. 29), and his judgments aim at a harvest, not at destruction.
verseByVerse.theology: Twice the farmer's skill is traced to God (vv. 26, 29). The God who teaches a man when to stop threshing knows when to stop with his people.
verseByVerse.examples: This is the answer to the drunk mockery of verse 10 and to everyone since who has felt that a season of discipline had no reason behind it. There is a method, it varies with what is being handled, and it has a stopping point that was decided before it began.

verseByVerse.quote: Give ear, and hear my voice; give attention, and hear my speech. Does he who plows for sowing plow continually? Does he continually open and harrow his ground? When he has leveled its surface, does he not scatter dill, sow cumin, and put in wheat in rows and barley in its proper place, and emmer as the border? For he is rightly instructed; his God teaches him. Dill is not threshed with a threshing sledge, nor is a cart wheel rolled over cumin, but dill is beaten out with a stick, and cumin with a rod. Does one crush grain for bread? No, he does not thresh it forever; when he drives his cart wheel over it with his horses, he does not crush it. This also comes from the LORD of hosts; he is wonderful in counsel and excellent in wisdom.
verseByVerse.commentary:
As a wise farmer ploughs and threshes with care and knows when to stop, so God deals with his people in measure, aiming at a harvest.

Give ear, and hear my voice. The chapter that has had drunk priests, vomit on the tables and a covenant with death ends in a field, and the change of tone is deliberate.

Does he who plows for sowing plow continually? No farmer ploughs for ever. Ploughing is violent, the ground cut open and turned over, and it is also brief, because it is not the point: it is what you do before you sow. And the sowing is five actions, each crop in the place and manner that suits it. A farmer does not treat everything the same.

His God teaches him. Isaiah stops to say where the knowledge came from, and it is a striking claim: a farmer’s ordinary skill is something God taught him.

He does not thresh it forever. The harvest follows the same principle. Threshing uses heavy tools, a weighted sledge or a cart wheel, on the threshing floor, and you would ruin dill and cumin with either; those get a stick. Even the bread grain, which does need crushing, is not crushed forever: there is a point at which the man stops.

For a hard season. This is for everyone who has felt that a hard season had no reason in it. If God taught a farmer to match the tool to the crop, to use a stick where a sledge would destroy, and to know the moment the grain is ready and stop, will he be less careful with people? The ploughing in a life is not endless. The threshing is proportioned to what is being threshed. And neither ploughing nor threshing is the goal.

Wonderful in counsel. The goal is bread. And the God who taught the farmer is wonderful in counsel, the title Isaiah has already given to the child born for us (9:6). The hand that disciplines is the hand of the one who came to be bread for the world (John 6:51).

Uncertain wording. In rows and in its proper place (v. 25) render rare words of uncertain meaning; the point, that each crop has its own treatment, is unaffected.

28.theology:
Baby talk, and the offer inside it. What the leaders mocked as simplistic was an invitation to rest (v. 12). Refusing plain words, they would hear God speak in a language they could not understand.

Theological names for practical arrangements. Isaiah calls a treaty with Egypt a covenant with death. Against it God lays a tested stone in Zion, and the one who believes will not be in haste.

The farmer. The chapter ends by arguing from a farmer’s care for his crop to God’s care for his people: God’s discipline of his people is measured, varied and limited, and its object is bread.

29.subtitle: Ariel in Distress
29.intro:
Where we are. Chapters 28 to 33 are six woes on Jerusalem and its leaders, spoken while Hezekiah’s court was looking to Egypt for help against Assyria. Chapter 28 exposed rulers who mocked the prophet’s teaching as baby talk; chapter 29 turns on Jerusalem itself, under a riddling name, Ariel.

The message. God himself will besiege the city that thinks its festivals guarantee his presence, bring it down to whisper from the dust, and then blow its attackers away like a dream. The deeper trouble is not Assyria but a people who honour God with their lips while their hearts are far from him, so that his word is a sealed book to them. Yet the same God will open deaf ears and blind eyes and make grumblers teachable: what correct religion could not do, his grace will.

Why it was said. Jerusalem’s leaders kept the temple calendar running while settling their policy in secret, most likely the negotiations with Egypt that chapter 30 exposes (see the introduction). They assumed that a city with God’s altar in it could not fall, and that God did not see their plans.

How the chapter makes its case. First the siege (vv. 1–8): the altar city becomes an altar of fire, besieged by God until its voice comes from the ground; then the LORD of hosts scatters its enemies like chaff and a fading dream. Next the diagnosis (vv. 9–16): the people who blinded themselves are given over to blindness, and the vision is a sealed book, because worship has become lip-service and the fear of God “a commandment taught by men”, while the leaders plot in the dark as if the clay could deny its potter. Last the reversal (vv. 17–24): the deaf hear, the blind see, the humble rejoice, the ruthless vanish, and the God who redeemed Abraham makes Jacob’s children holy worshippers, the work of his hands.

Where it leads. Jesus quoted verse 13 to the Pharisees (Mark 7:6–7), and Paul quoted verse 14 of the cross, where God brought the wisdom of the wise to nothing (1 Corinthians 1:19). It leads to Christ chiefly by the need it exposes: lips near and hearts far describes every worshipper, and only the Son, whose heart was never far from his Father, has offered whole-hearted worship, and he gives his people a new heart by his Spirit. When he made the deaf hear and the blind see (Matthew 11:5), the reversal of verses 18 to 24 had begun.

For us. The danger here is not unbelief but well-run religion with the heart elsewhere. The answer is not trying harder to feel what we sing, but confessing the distance to the God who redeemed Abraham by grace and asking him to open our eyes.

keyVerse.quote: “This people draw near with their mouth and honor me with their lips, while their hearts are far from me, and their fear of me is a commandment taught by men.”
keyVerse.note: Jesus applied this verse to the Pharisees (Mark 7:6–7), the most religiously serious people of their generation, which shows that it describes a danger in every age. The danger is not having no religion but having one that keeps the right forms while holding the heart at a safe distance from God himself. It is the hinge of the chapter: the sealed book before it and the opened ears after it both turn on the state of the heart.

29.reflection:
Jerusalem kept every feast on time (v. 1) and still found God encamped against it. How can a settled religious routine become a way of keeping God at a distance, and what signs would show that it is happening to us?

Verse 13 describes lips near and hearts far, and a fear of God “taught by men”. Where do you most notice a gap between what you sing or say and where your heart is, and what does the chapter offer as the cure (vv. 18–24)?

The leaders hid their plans “deep from the LORD” (v. 15). What decisions are we tempted to make as if God were not in the room, and why does that turn the potter and the clay upside down (v. 16)?

God calls his restored people “the work of my hands” (v. 23). How does knowing that you are made, and in Christ made again, free you from the pressure to be self-made?

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God will besiege the city that trusts in its festivals, and then rescue it in an instant. Jerusalem is called Ariel, a name that probably means “altar hearth”, and told to let its feasts run their yearly round (v. 1). But God himself will distress the city and encamp against it, as David once did, until its voice whispers from the dust like a ghost’s (vv. 2–4). Then, without warning, the besieging horde becomes fine dust and chaff, as the LORD of hosts comes in storm and fire (vv. 5–6). The nations that fought against Zion prove to be like a hungry man’s dream of a meal: vivid, then gone, leaving nothing in the mouth (vv. 7–8).
verseByVerse.theology: The festivals were running on schedule, and Judah took that as proof that God was on its side. The passage dismantles that assumption before it offers any hope.
verseByVerse.examples: A religious calendar kept perfectly is no guarantee of God's favour. The question is whether anyone inside the walls is thinking about him.

verseByVerse.quote: Ah, Ariel, Ariel, the city where David encamped! Add year to year; let the feasts run their round. Yet I will distress Ariel, and there shall be moaning and lamentation, and she shall be to me like an Ariel.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jerusalem, proud to be the city of God’s altar, will itself become an altar, a place of fire and slaughter.

Ah, Ariel, Ariel. By verse 2 Isaiah is playing on the riddling name’s sense “altar hearth”, where the sacrifice burns: she shall be to me like an Ariel. The city proud of God’s altar will become what its altar is.

The city where David encamped. David once camped against this city and took it from the Jebusites (2 Samuel 5:6–9). Verse 3 uses the same verb with God as its subject: I will encamp against you. The city David besieged and made his own will be besieged again, by David’s God.

Let the feasts run their round. The command is ironic. Carry on: the calendar works perfectly, every feast on time, and that is precisely the problem, because the machinery is running and nobody is thinking about God.

Uncertain wording. Ariel can be read as “lion of God”, which would suit David’s royal city, or as “altar hearth”, its sense in Ezekiel 43:15–16. The second fits verse 2 best, though Isaiah may intend his hearers to catch both.
verseByVerse.note: Ariel (perhaps “altar hearth”) is a name for Jerusalem.

verseByVerse.quote: And I will encamp against you all around, and will besiege you with towers and I will raise siegeworks against you. And you will be brought low; from the earth you shall speak, and from the dust your speech will be bowed down; your voice shall come from the ground like the voice of a ghost, and from the dust your speech shall whisper.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God himself will besiege Jerusalem and bring it so low that its voice comes from the dust, which is where true prayer begins.

I will encamp against you. The shock is in who does it: not Assyria or Babylon but God, outside the walls, raising siegeworks. Judah’s whole assumption was that God was inside with them, guaranteed by the festivals.

From the dust your speech shall whisper. The purpose is not destruction. The city is brought down to whispering from the ground, like the voice of a ghost: Isaiah has watched a nation consult the dead (8:19), and now it sounds like the dead. That is a humiliation, and it is also where prayer begins. A city that shouts its festivals is not heard; a city whispering out of the dust can be, and for the first time it is talking to the right person.

verseByVerse.quote: But the multitude of your foreign foes shall be like small dust, and the multitude of the ruthless like passing chaff. And in an instant, suddenly, you will be visited by the LORD of hosts with thunder and with earthquake and great noise, with whirlwind and tempest, and the flame of a devouring fire. And the multitude of all the nations that fight against Ariel, all that fight against her and her stronghold and distress her, shall be like a dream, a vision of the night. As when a hungry man dreams, and behold, he is eating, and awakes with his hunger not satisfied, or as when a thirsty man dreams, and behold, he is drinking, and awakes faint, with his thirst not quenched, so shall the multitude of all the nations be that fight against Mount Zion.
verseByVerse.commentary:
In an instant the LORD himself will scatter the armies besieging Zion, and all their might will vanish like a dream.

Like small dust. The city was brought down to speak from the dust (v. 4); now its enemies become fine dust and passing chaff. The humbling of Zion and the scattering of its attackers are told in the same picture, one after the other.

Visited by the LORD of hosts. Thunder, earthquake, whirlwind and devouring fire are the signs of God’s own coming, as at Sinai (Exodus 19:16–18) and in David’s psalm of rescue (Psalm 18:7–15). Coming straight after verse 5, this visit is most likely a rescue: the storm breaks on the besiegers, not on the city. The God who encamped against Ariel is the God who comes to save it.

As when a hungry man dreams. The besieging horde blows away in an instant, suddenly. A starving man dreams a vivid meal and wakes emptier for having had it. That is what the armies against Zion amount to: a strong appetite, a convincing dream, and nothing in the mouth.

A first fulfilment. Many think the oracle was first fulfilled in 701 BC, when Sennacherib’s army lay round Jerusalem and was struck down in a single night (37:36). The pattern holds for Christ’s church, against which the gates of hell will not prevail (Matthew 16:18).

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The real problem is not the siege but worship that has become lip-service, so that God’s word no longer reaches his people. Having blinded themselves, they are now given over to blindness: God pours out a spirit of deep sleep and covers the eyes of the prophets and seers (vv. 9–10). The vision has become a sealed book to the literate and the illiterate alike (vv. 11–12). Verse 13 gives the reason: they honour God with their lips while their hearts are far from him, and their fear of him is a commandment taught by men; so he will act in ways that confound their wise (v. 14). Meanwhile their leaders plan in the dark, as if the clay could tell the potter that he did not make it (vv. 15–16).
verseByVerse.theology: What is described here is not a lack of religion but correct religion without a heart, and Jesus found it alive and well among the religious leaders of his own day.
verseByVerse.examples: This should sober anyone who assumes that better teaching or more study would solve a spiritual problem. Sometimes it would; in verses 11 and 12 the book is in their hands, and it does not get in.

verseByVerse.quote: Astonish yourselves and be astonished; blind yourselves and be blind! Be drunk, but not with wine; stagger, but not with strong drink! For the LORD has poured out upon you a spirit of deep sleep, and has closed your eyes (the prophets), and covered your heads (the seers). And the vision of all this has become to you like the words of a book that is sealed. When men give it to one who can read, saying, "Read this," he says, "I cannot, for it is sealed." And when they give the book to one who cannot read, saying, "Read this," he says, "I cannot read."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Because they have shut their own eyes, God now seals them shut: his word is in their hands, but it does not get in.

Astonish yourselves and be astonished. The commands are ironic: carry on doing what you have already done to yourselves. The drunkenness of chapter 28 is now diagnosed without the wine: they stagger, and there is nothing in the cup.

A spirit of deep sleep. The hardening of chapter 6, God’s judgment giving people over to the blindness they chose, returns and falls on the professionals, the prophets and seers whose whole task was to see and to say.

Like the words of a book that is sealed. The picture is fair to both kinds of people. The literate man is handed a sealed scroll and cannot get at it; the other cannot read. Neither is mocked as stupid. The barrier is not ability, and verse 13 says where it lies.

Who opens the book? Paul saw the same veil over his people when Moses was read, and added, “when one turns to the Lord, the veil is removed” (2 Corinthians 3:14–16). The risen Jesus “opened their minds to understand the Scriptures” (Luke 24:45): the sealed book is opened by its Author.

Is God unfair to close their eyes (v. 10)? It is judicial: a people that honoured him with their lips while their hearts were far from him (v. 13) is given over to the blindness it chose. Paul uses the verse of Israel’s hardening in his day (Romans 11:8). Yet the same God opens the book again (v. 18).

verseByVerse.quote: And the Lord said: "Because this people draw near with their mouth and honor me with their lips, while their hearts are far from me, and their fear of me is a commandment taught by men, therefore, behold, I will again do wonderful things with this people, with wonder upon wonder; and the wisdom of their wise men shall perish, and the discernment of their discerning men shall be hidden." Ah, you who hide deep from the LORD your counsel, whose deeds are in the dark, and who say, "Who sees us? Who knows us?" You turn things upside down! Shall the potter be regarded as the clay, that the thing made should say of its maker, "He did not make me"; or the thing formed say of him who formed it, "He has no understanding"?
verseByVerse.commentary:
God’s people can keep every form of worship while their hearts stay far away, and plan in secret as if the creature were the Creator.

Near with the mouth, far in the heart. This is not irreligion. These people draw near and honour God, and the services are correct and well attended. The failure is a distance, and the third clause names its cause: their fear of God has become a commandment taught by men, learned behaviour correctly performed, with nothing at the centre that came from God. It is religion that works perfectly with nobody home, the danger of the well-taught rather than the ignorant; better instruction cannot fix it, because good instruction produced it.

I will again do wonderful things. God’s answer (v. 14) leaves the experts helpless: the wisdom of their wise men shall perish. Paul hears the same pattern at the cross, where God made foolish the wisdom of the world (1 Corinthians 1:19–25).

Well did Isaiah prophesy. Jesus quotes verse 13 when Pharisees from Jerusalem ask why his disciples do not wash their hands according to the tradition of the elders: “Well did Isaiah prophesy of you hypocrites, as it is written, ‘This people honors me with their lips, but their heart is far from me; in vain do they worship me, teaching as doctrines the commandments of men’” (Mark 7:6–7; Matthew 15:8–9). He applies every clause and adds nothing.

The only cure. No honest reader can claim a heart that is never far while the lips are moving. The cure is not trying harder to feel what we sing but the repair the chapter ends with (v. 24): God gives a new heart and his Spirit (Ezekiel 36:26–27), and the Son, whose heart was never far from his Father, has offered in our place the whole-hearted worship we owe. The way back for the half-hearted is to confess it to the God who has promised to forgive (1 John 1:9).

Plans in the dark. The hidden counsel of verse 15 is most likely the negotiation with Egypt exposed in 30:1–2: a policy settled behind closed doors, without asking the prophet and, its makers imagined, out of God’s sight. Who sees us? is the question behind every plan made as if God were not in the room.

Shall the potter be regarded as the clay? The upside-down thinking behind it all: a pot saying that the potter did not make it. Paul takes up the image to answer the creature who argues with his Maker (Romans 9:20).

The pot that says it made itself. “He did not make me” is close to a modern creed: we admire the self-made person and are urged to create our own identity. Yet even Frederick Douglass, who rose from slavery by extraordinary effort and lectured on self-made men, insisted that strictly speaking there are no such people: everyone stands on gifts received from others. Isaiah goes further: the clay did not even supply itself. And the pot that insists on making itself becomes not freer but more anxious, because everything about it must now be justified by its own performance. The relief comes in verse 23, where God calls the same people the work of my hands. To be made is to be given yourself, and in Christ to be made again: “we are his workmanship, created in Christ Jesus for good works” (Ephesians 2:10). You do not have to author yourself; you can receive yourself from the One who designed you and loves what he made.

Textual note. Jesus’ wording follows the Septuagint (the Greek translation of the Old Testament that most first-century readers used), which renders the last clause “in vain do they worship me”; the Hebrew says their fear of God is a commandment taught by men. The two say one thing from two sides: worship built on human rules is empty.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: In a little while God will undo everything wrong in the chapter, and people who could not hear will become worshippers. The landscape turns over, forest into farmland (v. 17). The deaf hear the words of a book and the blind see, reversing the sealed book and closed eyes of verses 10 to 12 (v. 18). The meek and the poor rejoice in the Holy One, while the ruthless, the scoffers and those who twist justice in court disappear (vv. 19–21). The God who redeemed Abraham promises that Jacob will no longer be ashamed: his children, the work of God’s hands, will hallow his name, and the wandering and the grumblers will learn (vv. 22–24).
verseByVerse.theology: Isaiah undoes his own diagnosis clause by clause, which is his standard way of showing that judgment was never the destination.
verseByVerse.examples: For anyone who has been caught out in a careless word and made to pay for it out of all proportion, verse 21 is a promise: God sees the trap, and it has an end.

verseByVerse.quote: Is it not yet a very little while until Lebanon shall be turned into a fruitful field, and the fruitful field shall be regarded as a forest? In that day the deaf shall hear the words of a book, and out of their gloom and darkness the eyes of the blind shall see. The meek shall obtain fresh joy in the LORD, and the poor among mankind shall exult in the Holy One of Israel. For the ruthless shall come to nothing and the scoffer cease, and all who watch to do evil shall be cut off, who by a word make a man out to be an offender, and lay a snare for him who reproves in the gate, and with an empty plea turn aside him who is in the right.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Soon God will undo the chapter’s judgment: the deaf will hear his word, the blind see, the humble rejoice, and the unjust be gone.

Lebanon shall be turned into a fruitful field. The turn begins with a landscape rearranging itself: the forest of Lebanon becomes farmland and farmland forest. What looked fixed for ever can be changed.

The deaf shall hear the words of a book. Isaiah undoes his own diagnosis item by item. Verse 11 had a sealed book nobody could read; verse 18 has the deaf hearing the words of a book. Verse 10 had God closing the eyes of the prophets; verse 18 has the blind seeing out of gloom and darkness.

The meek shall obtain fresh joy in the LORD. This is the undoing of the specific judgment, and it comes to the least equipped: not the literate man who could not break the seal, but the deaf and the blind, the meek and the poor, whose cases never got a hearing (1:23).

The blind shall see. When John the Baptist asked from prison whether Jesus was the one to come, Jesus answered in the language of this chapter and its neighbours (35:5–6; 61:1): “the blind receive their sight … and the deaf hear … and the poor have good news preached to them” (Matthew 11:5). The promised reversal had begun, with the poor.

Who by a word make a man out to be an offender. Verse 21 names an evil precisely enough to be uncomfortable: catching someone in a phrase, taking it badly on purpose and using it to discredit him, and trapping the man who says the unpopular true thing in public. The gate was where the elders sat as a court (Ruth 4:1–2; Amos 5:10), so this is justice bent in the very place meant to secure it. The men to whom Jesus quoted verse 13 did exactly this, watching to catch him in his words (Luke 20:20). Christians should be the last to wield a phrase stripped of its context.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore thus says the LORD, who redeemed Abraham, concerning the house of Jacob: "Jacob shall no more be ashamed, no more shall his face grow pale. For when he sees his children, the work of my hands, in his midst, they will sanctify my name; they will sanctify the Holy One of Jacob and will stand in awe of the God of Israel. And those who go astray in spirit will come to understanding, and those who murmur will accept instruction."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The God who rescued Abraham by grace will take away Jacob’s shame and make his children true worshippers, even the wandering and the grumblers.

The LORD, who redeemed Abraham. An unusual and deliberate title. Before there was a nation, a law, a temple or a festival calendar, there was a man in Mesopotamia, Abraham, whom God went and got. The chapter that has spent sixteen verses on the failure of institutional religion reaches back past all of it to grace at the beginning.

No more shall his face grow pale. The promise is about shame: the face that blanches when a person is found out will not grow pale again.

His children, the work of my hands. This answers verse 16. There the clay denied that the potter made it; here the same people are named as his handiwork, and they do what their parents’ lips only pretended to do (v. 13): they sanctify the Holy One of Jacob, the first thing Jesus taught us to pray: “Hallowed be your name” (Matthew 6:9).

Those who go astray in spirit. The last verse names the two groups the chapter has described: those who go astray in spirit, the drunk without wine (vv. 9–10), and those who murmur, the plotters of verse 15. Neither is destroyed. The first comes to understanding, the very thing missing in 1:3, when the ox knew its owner and Israel did not; the second accepts instruction, the very thing mocked in chapter 28 as baby talk.

Not improved but mended. The chapter that began with a city whispering from the dust ends with people who have not merely had their situation improved, but have themselves been mended. This is the new covenant in miniature, God writing his law on the heart (Jeremiah 31:33), the covenant Jesus sealed in his blood (Luke 22:20).

Uncertain wording. Genesis never says that God “redeemed” Abraham. Most likely Isaiah means calling him out of an idolatrous family (Joshua 24:2–3); some think of his protection in Egypt and Gerar (Genesis 12; 20). Either way, Israel’s story began with God rescuing a man who had done nothing to deserve it.

29.theology:
God on the outside of the walls. Judah assumed God was inside the city, guaranteed by a festival calendar running on schedule. Isaiah puts him in the siege lines, bringing the city low until it whispers from the dust, which is where prayer starts.

Lips near, hearts far. Verse 13 describes the danger of the well-taught rather than the ignorant: the right words, with the fear of God turned into a commandment taught by men.

The diagnosis undone clause by clause. The sealed book is heard, the closed eyes are opened, and the far hearts come to understanding, and the reversals go to the least equipped. Jesus points to this very reversal. When John the Baptist sent from prison to ask whether he was the one who was to come, Jesus answered that the blind receive their sight and the deaf hear (Matthew 11:5), drawing on this chapter and on 35:5–6. The sealed book is opened, and the closed eyes are unclosed, by the Son in whom God has at last spoken plainly (Hebrews 1:1–2).

30.subtitle: The Rebellious Children
30.intro:
Where we are. The third woe of chapters 28 to 33 brings into the open what 29:15 hinted at: Hezekiah’s court has sent envoys and treasure to Egypt to buy protection against Assyria. Chapter 31 says it again in a few sharp lines.

The message. God’s people do not need a stronger ally; they need to come back to him and rest. “In returning and rest you shall be saved; in quietness and in trust shall be your strength” (v. 15), but they would not, preferring horses, treaties and prophets who spoke smooth things. Yet their refusal does not exhaust God. Because of it he “waits to be gracious”, and the chapter ends with a Teacher no longer hidden, a voice behind them, wounds bound up and the oppressor burned away.

Why it was said. Around 703 to 701 BC Judah joined a revolt against Assyria and looked to Egypt to back it (see the introduction). By worldly standards it was a sensible policy, and it was made without asking God.

How the chapter makes its case. The plan exposed (vv. 1–7): stubborn children make an alliance not of God’s Spirit and send their treasure through the Negeb to Egypt, “Rahab who sits still”. The refusal recorded (vv. 8–17): this people tells its prophets to speak smooth things and leave out the Holy One, so their sin will collapse like a bulging wall, and the quiet trust they refused gives way to headlong flight. The grace that waits (vv. 18–26): the LORD answers at the first cry, shows them their Teacher, guides their steps, and makes land and sky overflow as he binds up the wounds he struck. The enemy judged (vv. 27–33): the LORD comes in fire and storm against Assyria while his people sing as at a festival.

Where it leads. The chapter leads to Christ by the character of God it reveals and the rest it offers. The God who waits to be gracious is the father in Jesus’ parable who saw his son “while he was still a long way off” and ran (Luke 15:20). The rest of verse 15 is the rest Jesus offers the weary (Matthew 11:28), received by trust, not bought with treasure. And the God who wounded his people binds them up; in the end he took the blow himself, and “with his wounds we are healed” (53:5).

For us. Most of us have an Egypt, something we lean on because it feels like doing something. The chapter calls us to ask before we act, stop running and trust the God who is not reluctant but waiting. Those who have refused him before have not exhausted his patience.

keyVerse.quote: “In returning and rest you shall be saved; in quietness and in trust shall be your strength.”
keyVerse.note: The verse is both promise and rebuke, because it was refused. The strength on offer was the opposite of what anyone would expect: not cavalry but quietness, not diplomacy but trust. God’s way often looks inadequate until it is the only way left, and the tragedy of verse 16 is that Judah never found out whether it worked, because they would not try. It is the Old Testament shape of the gospel’s call to stop working for our safety and rest in another (Matthew 11:28).

30.reflection:
Judah’s plan was sensible, but it was made “without asking for my direction” (v. 2). What decisions have you made without really bringing them to God, and what would asking first look like in practice?

The people told their prophets, “speak to us smooth things” (v. 10). In what ways do we prefer a message that comforts without confronting, and how can a church guard against it?

“In returning and rest you shall be saved” (v. 15). What is your Egypt, the thing you lean on to feel secure, and why is resting in God often harder than working?

“The LORD waits to be gracious to you” (v. 18) comes straight after a story of refusal. How does this picture of God change the way you come back to him after failing?
