verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God’s people have chosen a sensible plan instead of him, and the section shows where that leads. The woe falls on stubborn children who make an alliance with Egypt without asking God (vv. 1–2); Pharaoh’s shelter will become their shame (vv. 3–5). Isaiah pictures their treasure carried on donkeys and camels through the dangerous Negeb to a nation he nicknames “Rahab who sits still” (vv. 6–7). The refusal is to be written down as a lasting witness, because the people want prophets who speak smooth things and say no more about the Holy One of Israel (vv. 8–11). Their sin will collapse like a bulging wall (vv. 12–14). God offered salvation in returning and rest, and they would not; so they will flee on the fast horses they chose (vv. 15–17).
verseByVerse.theology: Buying protection from an impressive thing that does not move is the folly this chapter exists to name, and every generation has its own Egypt.
verseByVerse.examples: The refusal in verse 15 is worth hearing as a question. When trouble comes, is the first move to ask God, or to load the camels?

verseByVerse.quote: "Ah, stubborn children," declares the LORD, "who carry out a plan, but not mine, and who make an alliance, but not of my Spirit, that they may add sin to sin; who set out to go down to Egypt, without asking for my direction, to take refuge in the protection of Pharaoh and to seek shelter in the shadow of Egypt! Therefore shall the protection of Pharaoh turn to your shame, and the shelter in the shadow of Egypt to your humiliation. For though his officials are at Zoan and his envoys reach Hanes, everyone comes to shame through a people that cannot profit them, that brings neither help nor profit, but shame and disgrace." An oracle on the beasts of the Negeb. Through a land of trouble and anguish, from where come the lioness and the lion, the adder and the flying fiery serpent, they carry their riches on the backs of donkeys, and their treasures on the humps of camels, to a people that cannot profit them. Egypt's help is worthless and empty; therefore I have called her "Rahab who sits still."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Judah’s alliance with Egypt is a competent plan made without God, and it will bring only shame, because the power they are paying is all reputation and no help.

Ah, stubborn children. The charge is not that they have no plan. They have a competent one: a defensive alliance with the only power in the region capable of standing up to Assyria. Isaiah’s objection is two words, not mine.

Without asking for my direction. That is the whole indictment, the same failure as chapter 22: not incompetence, not even disobedience to a stated command, but a decision of enormous consequence, to shelter under Pharaoh, taken without asking God.

An oracle on the beasts of the Negeb. Isaiah lets the reader watch the journey go past: a caravan crossing the Negeb, lion country and snake country, with everything the temple and the treasury could raise on donkeys and camels. The long sentence makes the reader feel the distance, risk and expense, and then the destination is dismissed in a single clause: a people that cannot profit them.

Rahab. The nickname makes the argument. Rahab was the name of the sea monster of chaos, raw mythic power, paired with Leviathan in Hebrew poetry (27:1; Job 26:12; Psalm 89:10), and it is what Egypt’s reputation amounted to. This Rahab is not the woman of Jericho; the two names are different words in Hebrew. And Scripture borrows the monster’s name as a poet’s image, the way we might call a bully a dragon, without believing in the monster.

Rahab who sits still. All the name, all the legend, all the terror, and no motion. Judah did not buy nothing; they bought something genuinely impressive that was never going to get up.

Uncertain wording. Zoan was a royal city in the Nile delta and Hanes probably Heracleopolis, further south, but whether his officials are Pharaoh’s or Judah’s envoys is unclear (v. 4); either way, great effort reaches deep into Egypt for nothing. “Rahab who sits still” renders a compressed Hebrew phrase (roughly “Rahab, they sit”) that translators reconstruct in different ways; the ESV’s reading is widely followed and fits the point.
verseByVerse.note: Zoan and Hanes were Egyptian cities. Rahab is a poetic name for Egypt.

verseByVerse.quote: And now, go, write it before them on a tablet and inscribe it in a book, that it may be for the time to come as a witness forever. For they are a rebellious people, lying children, children unwilling to hear the instruction of the LORD; who say to the seers, "Do not see," and to the prophets, "Do not prophesy to us what is right; speak to us smooth things, prophesy illusions, leave the way, turn aside from the path, let us hear no more about the Holy One of Israel." Therefore thus says the Holy One of Israel, "Because you despise this word and trust in oppression and perverseness and rely on them, therefore this iniquity shall be to you like a breach in a high wall, bulging out and about to collapse, whose breaking comes suddenly, in an instant; and its breaking is like that of a potter's vessel that is smashed so ruthlessly that among its fragments not a shard is found with which to take fire from the hearth, or to dip up water out of the cistern."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Because the people want comforting illusions instead of God’s word, and above all want to hear no more of the Holy One, their sin will bring a sudden and total collapse.

Write it before them on a tablet. The oracle is to be written down and kept for the time to come. Isaiah expects it to be needed again, which is why it is in the Bible and why it still reads like current affairs.

Speak to us smooth things. Here a nation states exactly what it wants from its clergy. Not silence: they want the prophets in business, saying pleasant, frictionless, comfortable things. Prophesy illusions: they are asking, knowingly, to be told what is not true. Every age has a market for this, and so does every heart; we would all rather be soothed than searched (2 Timothy 4:3).

Let us hear no more about the Holy One of Israel. The last clause is the most honest thing they say. Their trouble is not with the news but with God himself; they want him left out.

The God made to order. Sceptics have long argued that God is wishful thinking, a heavenly Father invented because we cannot face the universe alone. Verse 10 answers the charge, for here are people actually placing an order for the God they wish for, and he is nothing like the God of the Bible. Ask what people really wish for, and it is seldom a holy God; it is a God who agrees with us, or none at all. The God of this book is the one nobody would have invented: holy enough to say no to us, and so free to say what no projection would dare, that he waits to be gracious to the very people who asked him to leave (v. 18). A God made to order could flatter us. Only the Holy One could forgive us, and he did it at his own cost.

Like a breach in a high wall. Anyone who has seen an old wall beginning to lean knows the look. It does not fall for a long time; it sits there bulging, everyone gets used to it, and then one day it goes all at once.

Like that of a potter’s vessel. When it goes, the pieces are too small to be useful: not one fragment big enough to carry an ember from the hearth or scoop water from the cistern, the two most basic household tasks. Total loss, described by what can no longer be done with the wreckage.

verseByVerse.quote: For thus said the Lord GOD, the Holy One of Israel, "In returning and rest you shall be saved; in quietness and in trust shall be your strength." But you were unwilling, and you said, "No! We will flee upon horses"; therefore you shall flee away; and, "We will ride upon swift steeds"; therefore your pursuers shall be swift. A thousand shall flee at the threat of one; at the threat of five you shall flee, till you are left like a flagstaff on the top of a mountain, like a signal on a hill.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God offered rescue through turning back to him and trusting him quietly, but Judah refused, and so received the frantic flight it chose.

In returning and rest you shall be saved. God’s alternative to the Egyptian treaty is four words, and every one is passive. Returning: turning round and coming back, which requires no resources. Rest: stopping. Quietness: not speaking. Trust: leaning on somebody else. Nothing on the list is a strategy: no journey, no treasure on camels, no fast horses. It is the opposite of everything the nation had been doing since verse 1, and it is offered as the way to be saved.

But you were unwilling. The reply lands like a door closing. Not you could not, not “you misunderstood”, but you were unwilling, which locates the failure in the will, the honest diagnosis of most refusals of God’s help.

Therefore your pursuers shall be swift. The judgment is simply the request granted. You want speed? You shall have it: you will be the one running, and your pursuers will be quick. The last image is a bare pole on a summit, one thing left standing with nothing around it.

Why rest is hard. Rest and quietness sound easy and are not. They require a person to stop managing the situation, and the managing is where the sense of control lives. A caravan across the Negeb is exhausting, expensive and dangerous, and it feels like doing something; sitting still feels like negligence.

Lean your whole weight on him. The same offer stands at the centre of the gospel. Jesus says to the weary, “Come to me … and I will give you rest” (Matthew 11:28), and he asks for no caravan and no treasure, only that we stop running and lean our whole weight on him. Being saved in returning and rest is the Old Testament form of being put right with God by faith rather than by works. And because the failure lies in the will, so does the remedy: “it is God who works in you, both to will and to work for his good pleasure” (Philippians 2:13), by the Spirit this people never consulted (v. 1).

How do I return and rest? Returning and rest are not a technique, but they have a shape. Ask before you act. Judah went without asking for my direction (v. 2). Before the big decision (the move, the loan, the treatment, the reply to the angry email), bring it to God in prayer and to his Word, and if you can to a wise friend, before the caravan has left. Name your Egypt. What are you tempted to rely on instead of him: overwork, a useful contact, the savings account, your own cleverness? Use it if it is lawful, but do not lean on it. Do the next plain duty, then stop. Rest is not idleness; it is doing what is yours today and declining to carry tomorrow. Make the call, pay the bill, then go to bed. Keep quiet. Stop rehearsing every outcome in your head; tell God instead, and leave it with him. Rest on what is finished. Behind every restless scheme is the hope of securing ourselves, and Christ has already secured us: It is finished (John 19:30). Whoever rests in his work for salvation can learn to rest in his care for the week ahead.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Because his people refused him, the LORD waits to be gracious: this is mercy on the far side of judgment. He will answer at the first sound of their cry, and though hardship remains, their Teacher will no longer hide, and a voice behind them will say, “This is the way, walk in it” (vv. 18–21). They will throw away their idols as unclean (v. 22). Rain, harvest, pasture and streams follow, and even the sun and moon shine brighter on the day God binds up the wounds he struck (vv. 23–26). Then the LORD comes in burning anger against Assyria, while his people sing as on a festival night, and a pyre long prepared awaits its king (vv. 27–33).
verseByVerse.theology: The grace of verses 18 to 26 is given to the same people who refused it in verse 15. Nothing in between has made them deserve it; the therefore rests on God alone.
verseByVerse.examples: Before the voice of verse 21 comes the face of verse 20. For the believer the guidance is a person before it is a direction.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore the LORD waits to be gracious to you, and therefore he exalts himself to show mercy to you. For the LORD is a God of justice; blessed are all those who wait for him. For a people shall dwell in Zion, in Jerusalem; you shall weep no more. He will surely be gracious to you at the sound of your cry. As soon as he hears it, he answers you. And though the Lord give you the bread of adversity and the water of affliction, yet your Teacher will not hide himself anymore, but your eyes shall see your Teacher. And your ears shall hear a word behind you, saying, "This is the way, walk in it," when you turn to the right or when you turn to the left. Then you will defile your carved idols overlaid with silver and your gold-plated metal images. You will scatter them as unclean things. You will say to them, "Be gone!"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Because his people refused him, God waits to show them grace: he will answer their cry and teach and guide them himself, and they will throw away their idols.

Therefore the LORD waits to be gracious to you. The therefore is the most surprising word in the chapter. Everything before it is a nation refusing help, insisting on horses and asking its prophets for lies. Because of that, God waits to be gracious.

He exalts himself to show mercy. Not is delayed or withholds: God is like somebody at a window, watching for the moment when grace can be given, and the delay is not reluctance on his side. Then he exalts himself to show mercy: he rises like a king standing to act, and what he stands up to do is have compassion. Jesus drew the same God in the father who saw his son “while he was still a long way off” and ran to him (Luke 15:20).

Blessed are all those who wait for him. So both parties are waiting. The delay does not mean that God is absent while we are frustrated: he is waiting for us while we wait for him, and as soon as he hears the cry, he answers (v. 19).

The bread of adversity and the water of affliction. The adversity is not removed. Bread and water of affliction are still on the table, and in the middle of it the Teacher stops hiding. What is promised is not the end of hardship but the end of God’s apparent absence in it.

Your Teacher. Many Christians hear in this the day the Teacher came out of hiding altogether, when the Word became flesh and dwelt among us (John 1:14).

This is the way, walk in it. Verse 21 is often misread as a map. The voice is behind you, and it speaks when you turn to the right or … to the left: not an itinerary given in advance but correction given in the walking, by somebody following closely enough to see which way you drifted.

You will scatter them as unclean things. The response to seeing the Teacher is throwing the idols out as something filthy. Nothing argues an idol away like the arrival of the real thing.

How does God guide today? Not by new voices but by his word, which the Spirit applies to the heart (Psalm 119:105; 2 Timothy 3:16–17), with prayer, wisdom and the counsel of godly people. The Teacher of verse 20 is present to his people still, in Scripture.

Uncertain wording. Your Teacher can be read as singular or plural. The KJV’s “thy teachers” would mean the silenced prophets (v. 10) restored; the ESV takes it of God himself, and the singular verb (will not hide himself) favours that.

verseByVerse.quote: And he will give rain for the seed with which you sow the ground, and bread, the produce of the ground, which will be rich and plenteous. In that day your livestock will graze in large pastures, and the oxen and the donkeys that work the ground will eat seasoned fodder, which has been winnowed with shovel and fork. And on every lofty mountain and every high hill there will be brooks running with water, in the day of the great slaughter, when the towers fall. Moreover, the light of the moon will be as the light of the sun, and the light of the sun will be sevenfold, as the light of seven days, in the day when the LORD binds up the brokenness of his people, and heals the wounds inflicted by his blow.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When God restores his people, his generosity overflows into field, flock and sky, because the God who struck them is binding up their wounds.

He will give rain for the seed. After twenty-two verses of politics, what follows is a farm: the fruit of returning to God comes as weather, soil and livestock.

Seasoned fodder. Even the working animals get seasoned fodder, winnowed and cleaned, better than animals normally get. Isaiah’s picture of the restored world includes an ox eating well: God’s generosity reaches past the people to the beasts that pull their ploughs, a small detail that says a great deal about him.

Brooks running with water. There is water on the tops of hills, where water never is, and it comes in the day of the great slaughter, when the towers fall: the mercy and the judgment are the same day. Then the lights go up, the moon as bright as the sun and the sun seven times brighter.

The LORD binds up the brokenness of his people. The reason is the plainest language in the chapter: God heals the wounds inflicted by his blow. Isaiah does not soften it. The wounds being healed are the ones God inflicted; he does not pretend somebody else struck them. The same hand that struck binds up, and that healing is why the light grows seven times brighter.

The hand that struck. Isaiah will show how far this goes: the LORD laid the blow on his own Servant, “and with his wounds we are healed” (53:5). At the cross the blow fell on the Healer.

verseByVerse.quote: Behold, the name of the LORD comes from afar, burning with his anger, and in thick rising smoke; his lips are full of fury, and his tongue is like a devouring fire; his breath is like an overflowing stream that reaches up to the neck; to sift the nations with the sieve of destruction, and to place on the jaws of the peoples a bridle that leads astray. You shall have a song as in the night when a holy feast is kept, and gladness of heart, as when one sets out to the sound of the flute to go to the mountain of the LORD, to the Rock of Israel. And the LORD will cause his majestic voice to be heard and the descending blow of his arm to be seen, in furious anger and a flame of devouring fire, with a cloudburst and storm and hailstones. The Assyrians will be terror-stricken at the voice of the LORD, when he strikes with his rod. And every stroke of the appointed staff that the LORD lays on them will be to the sound of tambourines and lyres. Battling with brandished arm, he will fight with them. For a burning place has long been prepared; indeed, for the king it is made ready, its pyre made deep and wide, with fire and wood in abundance; the breath of the LORD, like a stream of sulfur, kindles it.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God himself will come in fire and storm to destroy Assyria, and his people will greet the rescue with festival songs.

The name of the LORD comes from afar. The chapter ends with a theophany, an appearance of God, and what comes is the name of the LORD, which in Hebrew usage means God himself in the character he has revealed. He is described entirely in terms of speech: lips, tongue, breath. The weapon is what he says.

You shall have a song. The sound of the redeemed is a festival night and a pilgrim walking up to the temple behind a flute (see pilgrim feasts). The chapter began with a caravan going the wrong way across a desert, carrying treasure to a monster that sits still. Both are journeys undertaken with everything the nation has. One goes south, in fear, at speed, and ends in shame. The other goes up a hill, at walking pace, to a flute.

To the sound of tambourines and lyres. The blows on Assyria fall to tambourines and lyres, festival instruments: judgment on the empire is set to music, a celebration by the people it had been crushing.

A burning place has long been prepared. The chapter closes on a burning ground, prepared, deep, wide, and lit by the breath of God. The word recalls Topheth, in the Valley of Hinnom outside Jerusalem, which gave its name to Gehenna, the word Jesus used for hell (Mark 9:43–48). The king it is made ready for is the king of Assyria, and there is probably a grim play on Molech, the god to whom children were burned at Topheth, whose name is built on the Hebrew word for king: the place of Judah’s darkest sin becomes the pyre of the empire’s king. It is a sober ending: the God who waits to be gracious is also a consuming fire, and Jesus, who warned of Gehenna more than anyone, came so that those who trust him need never go there.

Uncertain wording. The appointed staff (v. 32) renders a word whose sense is debated; some take it as the rod of punishment. A burning place (v. 33) is a rare word closely related to Topheth; the link is likely, not certain.
verseByVerse.note: Topheth was the place of child sacrifice in the Valley of Hinnom.

30.theology:
Rahab who sits still. The chapter’s argument is compressed into a nickname (v. 7): all the reputation of a monster and none of the motion. The charge against Judah is not incompetence but that they went without asking.

Four passive words, and an unwilling people. God offered returning, rest, quietness and trust (v. 15), not one of them a strategy, and the reply was but you were unwilling.

God waits. Verse 18 begins therefore and says the LORD waits to be gracious, and verse 26 ends with him healing the wounds inflicted by his blow. The God who heals the wounds of his own blow is the God who in Christ took the blow himself: by his wounds we are healed (53:5; 1 Peter 2:24).

31.subtitle: Woe to Those Who Go Down to Egypt
31.intro:
Where we are. The fourth of the six woes in chapters 28 to 33 returns to the Egyptian alliance of chapter 30, compresses the whole argument into a few lines, and closes with a promise.

The message. Do not trust what is strong; trust the One who is God. Egypt’s horses are many and mighty, but they are “flesh, and not spirit” (v. 3), and when the LORD stretches out his hand, helper and helped will fall together. Jerusalem’s real defender is God himself, as fierce as a lion that will not be scared off and as tender as birds hovering over their nest, and he will bring Assyria down by a sword no human hand wields. So turn back to him, and throw away your idols.

Why it was said. Faced with Sennacherib, Judah’s leaders were placing their hopes in Egyptian chariots (see the introduction and chapter 30). They kept the temple worship going, but in the decision that mattered most they did not look to the Holy One of Israel or ask him.

How the chapter makes its case. The woe (vv. 1–3): four clauses on what Judah relies on, two on what it neglects; yet God too is wise, his word stands, and Egypt is man and not God. The defender (vv. 4–5): a lion that will not be scared off its prey, and birds hovering over Jerusalem to protect, deliver, spare and rescue it. The call (vv. 6–7): turn back to the One you have deeply revolted against, for in that day the idols will be thrown away. The promise (vv. 8–9): Assyria will fall by a sword not of man, its officers fleeing in panic, at the word of the LORD whose fire is in Zion.

Where it leads. The chapter leads to Christ through the character of God it shows. Looking over Jerusalem, Jesus took up the picture of verse 5: “How often would I have gathered your children together as a hen gathers her brood under her wings, and you were not willing!” (Matthew 23:37), the same refusal as 30:15. The verb spare in verse 5 is the Passover word, and Christ is “our Passover lamb” (1 Corinthians 5:7). And as Assyria fell to a sword not of man, so the greater enemies, sin and death, fell when God in the flesh won by dying.

For us. Our horses are bank balances, contacts, technology and our own competence: good gifts and poor gods. The chapter asks a simple question. In the decisions that matter, do you look to the Holy One and ask him? And it gives the reason: the God who is fierce for his people gathers them under his wings.

keyVerse.quote: “The Egyptians are man, and not God, and their horses are flesh, and not spirit. When the LORD stretches out his hand, the helper will stumble, and he who is helped will fall, and they will all perish together.”
keyVerse.note: The verse does not disparage horses or military preparation as such, but exposes the mistake of treating flesh, mere created strength, as if it were spirit: giving to Egypt the trust that belongs only to God. That is idolatry in a practical form, not a carved image but an alliance trusted as the final security. The difference between man and God is one of kind, not of amount, and no number of horses crosses it.

31.reflection:
Verse 1 lists what Judah relied on, and then what it failed to do: “look to the Holy One of Israel or consult the LORD”. Where do you practise faith in one part of life while making the big decisions as though God were not involved?

“The Egyptians are man, and not God” (v. 3). What modern horses are we tempted to trust, and how can we use them gratefully without leaning our whole weight on them?

God is pictured both as a lion that will not be frightened off and as birds hovering over their young (vv. 4–5). Which picture do you most need just now, and how does Jesus’ lament over Jerusalem (Matthew 23:37) deepen it?

The call to “turn” comes after the promise of protection, not before it (vv. 5–6). What does that order teach about how God calls people back to himself?
31.text: <sup>1</sup>Woe to those who go down to Egypt for help and rely on horses, who trust in chariots because they are many and in horsemen because they are very strong, but do not look to the Holy One of Israel or consult the LORD!<sup>2</sup>And yet he is wise and brings disaster; he does not call back his words, but will arise against the house of the evildoers and against the helpers of those who work iniquity.<sup>3</sup>The Egyptians are man, and not God, and their horses are flesh, and not spirit. When the LORD stretches out his hand, the helper will stumble, and he who is helped will fall, and they will all perish together.<sup>4</sup>For thus the LORD said to me, "As a lion or a young lion growls over his prey, and when a band of shepherds is called out against him he is not terrified by their shouting or daunted at their noise, so the LORD of hosts will come down to fight on Mount Zion and on its hill.<sup>5</sup>Like birds hovering, so the LORD of hosts will protect Jerusalem; he will protect and deliver it; he will spare and rescue it."<sup>6</sup>Turn to him from whom people have deeply revolted, O children of Israel.<sup>7</sup>For in that day everyone shall cast away his idols of silver and his idols of gold, which your hands have sinfully made for you.<sup>8</sup>"And the Assyrian shall fall by a sword, not of man; and a sword, not of man, shall devour him; and he shall flee from the sword, and his young men shall be put to forced labor.<sup>9</sup>His rock shall pass away in terror, and his officers desert the standard in panic," declares the LORD, whose fire is in Zion, and whose furnace is in Jerusalem.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The whole chapter in miniature: trusting created strength instead of the Creator ends in a fall. Woe to those who go down to Egypt, relying on chariots because they are many and horsemen because they are strong, but do not look to the Holy One of Israel or consult the LORD (v. 1). Yet God too is wise: he brings disaster and does not call back his words (v. 2). Verse 3 states the point in one line: the Egyptians are man and not God, their horses flesh and not spirit, and when the LORD stretches out his hand, helper and helped fall together.
verseByVerse.theology: The argument is about what kind of thing Egypt is, not how good its army is: everything on the Egyptian side is flesh, mortal and created strength, and flesh cannot hold when God stretches out his hand.
verseByVerse.examples: Judah's leaders were not atheists. They simply made their biggest decision without asking God, a temptation most familiar to capable people with good options.

verseByVerse.quote: Woe to those who go down to Egypt for help and rely on horses, who trust in chariots because they are many and in horsemen because they are very strong, but do not look to the Holy One of Israel or consult the LORD! And yet he is wise and brings disaster; he does not call back his words, but will arise against the house of the evildoers and against the helpers of those who work iniquity. The Egyptians are man, and not God, and their horses are flesh, and not spirit. When the LORD stretches out his hand, the helper will stumble, and he who is helped will fall, and they will all perish together.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Trusting Egypt’s horses instead of asking God is folly, because Egypt is only created strength, and when God acts it will fall and take Judah with it.

Woe to those who go down to Egypt for help. The same policy as chapter 30, in a single sentence, and the structure of the verse is the argument: four clauses about what they rely on, then two about what they do not do, look and consult.

Two small omissions. Both missing actions are small. Looking is not a campaign and consulting is not a commitment. What Judah omitted was not obedience but a question, and the omission is the entire charge.

And yet he is wise. A dry remark in a chapter about a clever policy produced by capable men: God also has some competence in this area. And unlike theirs, his planning does not call back his words.

The Egyptians are man, and not God. Verse 3 is about what kind of thing Egypt is, not how good it is. Egypt’s chariots were famous, and Isaiah does not dispute it. But no amount of created strength adds up to the Creator’s: man is not God, flesh is not spirit, and no number of horses crosses that line.

Our horses and chariots. Egypt’s cavalry was the advanced technology of its day, and Judah trusted it the way we are tempted to trust ours. Many modern hopes are technical: the next medical breakthrough or generation of artificial intelligence will fix what is wrong with us. Isaiah does not despise horses, and Christians need not despise machines; both are gifts, and strong. But they are the wrong kind of thing to bear the weight of a life. Technology can make us faster, healthier and better informed; it cannot make us good, forgive us or love us, or stand between us and death. “Some trust in chariots and some in horses, but we trust in the name of the LORD our God” (Psalm 20:7). And the deliverance at the end of this chapter, by a sword, not of man, points on to a rescue no engineer could have designed: God himself, in the flesh, winning by dying.

They will all perish together. The last clause is the sober one. The nation that bought the protection goes down with the protection it bought, as always happens when a person ties himself to something that cannot stand.

Does this condemn using human means? No. The fault is trusting horses and allies instead of God, without consulting him. Using means wisely under God is not sin: “The horse is made ready for the day of battle, but the victory belongs to the LORD” (Proverbs 21:31).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 4–9 — The Lion and the Birds
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Jerusalem’s true defence is God himself, and he calls his people home. Two pictures could hardly be less alike: a lion growling over its prey, unmoved by the shouting shepherds, as the LORD comes down to fight on Mount Zion (v. 4); and birds hovering over the nest, as he protects, delivers, spares and rescues Jerusalem (v. 5). So turn back to him, however deep the revolt, for in that day everyone will throw away the idols his own hands made (vv. 6–7). Assyria will fall by a sword that is not man’s, its officers deserting the standard in panic, at the word of the LORD whose fire is in Zion (vv. 8–9).
verseByVerse.theology: The pair covers every direction from which danger can come. God is both the fierce defender and the tender protector, and his people need both.
verseByVerse.examples: For anyone frightened by the size of what is ranged against them, verse 4 is worth reading slowly: the shouting of the shepherds does not make the lion look up.

verseByVerse.quote: For thus the LORD said to me, "As a lion or a young lion growls over his prey, and when a band of shepherds is called out against him he is not terrified by their shouting or daunted at their noise, so the LORD of hosts will come down to fight on Mount Zion and on its hill. Like birds hovering, so the LORD of hosts will protect Jerusalem; he will protect and deliver it; he will spare and rescue it."
verseByVerse.commentary:
God will defend Jerusalem himself, as fearless as a lion over its prey and as tender as birds hovering over their nest.

As a lion or a young lion growls over his prey. The first picture is a lion standing over a kill. Shepherds have come out in a band, which is what you do about a lion, and they are shouting and banging. The lion does not look up, because numbers and noise do not frighten him. That is God defending Jerusalem: unimpressed by the size and volume of what is arrayed against him, and not moving off the hill.

Like birds hovering. The second picture could not be more different: a bird over the nest, wings out, hovering. A lion is what you want between you and the thing coming at you on the ground; a bird over the nest is what you want when the danger is above. Between them no direction is left from which anything can arrive.

He will protect and deliver it. The verbs are stacked: protect, protect, deliver, spare, rescue. That is not repetition but what an anxious person needs, the same reassurance said several ways.

He will spare and rescue it. Spare is the Passover verb, used when the LORD “passed over the houses of the people of Israel in Egypt” (Exodus 12:27). Behind this promise stands a night when the same God went through a country and stepped over the doors marked with blood; and “Christ, our Passover lamb, has been sacrificed” (1 Corinthians 5:7).

Under his wings. Jesus wept over the same city in the same picture: “How often would I have gathered your children together as a hen gathers her brood under her wings, and you were not willing!” (Matthew 23:37). The God who hovered over Jerusalem came to it in person.

Uncertain wording. The phrase translated fight on Mount Zion can also mean “fight against” it, and some read verse 4 as a warning: Jerusalem is the lion’s prey, held in God’s grip, and no Egyptian band will snatch it from him. The ESV reads it as defence, and verse 5 makes God’s purpose plain either way: to protect and rescue.

verseByVerse.quote: Turn to him from whom people have deeply revolted, O children of Israel. For in that day everyone shall cast away his idols of silver and his idols of gold, which your hands have sinfully made for you. "And the Assyrian shall fall by a sword, not of man; and a sword, not of man, shall devour him; and he shall flee from the sword, and his young men shall be put to forced labor. His rock shall pass away in terror, and his officers desert the standard in panic," declares the LORD, whose fire is in Zion, and whose furnace is in Jerusalem.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God calls his people to turn back to him and abandon their idols, because he will destroy Assyria by his own power, not by any human sword.

Turn to him. The application is one word: turn. Not build, not negotiate: come back. And it comes after the lion and the hovering wings, not before them. God does not wait to protect his people until they have returned; he tells them how he is covering them and then calls them home. The phrase from whom people have deeply revolted admits how far there is to come, and the call is issued anyway.

Everyone shall cast away his idols. The sign of the turning is a hand opening. The idols are the ones your hands have sinfully made for you, and the same hands throw them out. As with the Teacher in chapter 30, it is the arrival of the real thing that makes the images go.

A sword, not of man. The manner of the rescue is the point. There will be no heroic defence, no brilliant commander, no well-timed alliance. The empire no human force in the region could stop falls to something that is not a human force, which is why the horses in verse 1 were beside the point from the beginning.

Fulfilled outside Jerusalem. Six chapters later that is precisely what happens. An Assyrian army camps outside Jerusalem, and in the morning it is not there (37:36); no Judean sword is mentioned, because none was drawn.

His rock shall pass away in terror. Assyria’s rock passes away in terror, and its officers abandon the flag, the one thing a professional army does not do. Every side in this chapter has a rock. Judah has been trying to buy one in Egypt; Assyria’s dissolves; and the LORD, the one rock that cannot be moved, has been in Zion the whole time, his fire burning there, a furnace for his enemies.

Uncertain wording. Assyria’s rock (v. 9) may be its king, its fortress or its god (compare Deuteronomy 32:31). On any reading, whatever Assyria stood on gives way.

31.theology:
A statement about categories, not quality. Verse 3 sums up the chapter: man and not God, flesh and not spirit. And what Judah omitted was small: they did not look, and they did not consult.

The lion and the birds. The sparing of verse 5 recalls the Passover night, and that night pointed beyond itself: Christ, our Passover lamb, has been sacrificed (1 Corinthians 5:7), and those under his blood are passed over for good. And Jesus took the bird picture of verse 5 for himself as he wept over the same city: How often would I have gathered your children together as a hen gathers her brood under her wings (Matthew 23:37). The God who hovered over Jerusalem came and stood in its streets.

A sword, not of man. Verse 8 settles why the horses were beside the point: the rescue, when it came, needed no Judean sword at all.

32.subtitle: A King Who Reigns in Righteousness
32.intro:
Where we are. After four woes against Judah’s rulers and their Egyptian policy (chapters 28 to 31), chapter 32 lifts its eyes to what good rule looks like, warns the comfortable, and ends with the Spirit poured out. The last woe, on Assyria, follows in chapter 33.

The message. God will give his people a king who reigns in righteousness, under whom people shelter one another, eyes and ears are opened, and things are called by their true names. But first the complacent must learn to mourn, for the land will become a wilderness, until God pours out his Spirit from on high. Then justice will make its home in the wilderness, and righteousness will bear the fruit Judah could never produce by policy: peace, quietness and trust for ever.

Why it was said. Judah had scheming leaders, a court that trusted Egypt, and a comfortable class in Jerusalem who assumed the good years would go on (see the introduction). Assyria was about to strip the countryside (36:1), and the people needed both a warning and a hope that did not rest on any human government.

How the chapter makes its case. The king (vv. 1–8): a righteous king and just princes become shelter, water and shade for their people; the blindness and deafness of chapter 29 are healed; the fool and the scoundrel are no longer called noble. The complacent (vv. 9–14): women at ease are told to tremble and mourn now, for within a year the harvest will fail and the city will be left to wild donkeys. The Spirit (vv. 15–20): all this lasts “until the Spirit is poured upon us from on high”; then the wilderness becomes fruitful, righteousness yields peace, and God’s people live securely, sowing freely beside all waters.

Where it leads. The chapter leads to Christ by direct promise. Hezekiah may be the near horizon, but no king of Judah fulfilled verse 1; this is the King of 9:7 and 11:1–5, himself the hiding place from the storm. And verse 15 was fulfilled when the exalted Christ, having “received from the Father the promise of the Holy Spirit”, poured him out at Pentecost (Acts 2:33). The peace that righteousness produces is the peace with God we have through him (Romans 5:1).

For us. The fruit of righteousness cannot be produced by resolution or programme; it grows where the Spirit is poured out, and the Father gives the Spirit to those who ask him (Luke 11:13). And under this King we are to become for others what he is for us: a shelter from the wind, water in a dry place.

keyVerse.quote: “Until the Spirit is poured upon us from on high, and the wilderness becomes a fruitful field, and the fruitful field is deemed a forest.”
keyVerse.note: The word until carries the weight of chapters 28 to 32: all the woes, warnings and desolation last only until God acts. This is one of Isaiah’s clearest promises of the Spirit poured out, fulfilled at Pentecost, when the exalted Christ gave the Spirit and the wilderness began to bloom (Acts 2:33). What no policy could produce, the Spirit grows: justice, righteousness, peace and trust (vv. 16–17).

32.reflection:
Under the righteous king, “each will be like a hiding place from the wind” (v. 2). Who has been that kind of shelter for you, and where could you be one for someone else, at home, at work or in your church?

Verse 5 promises that the fool will no longer be called noble. What sins do we rename with softer words today, and why does the gospel make it possible to call them by their real names?

The women “at ease” are told to mourn before the loss arrives (vv. 9–11). Where might comfort have made us complacent, and what would it look like to take God’s warnings seriously?

Everything waits “until the Spirit is poured upon us from on high” (v. 15). Where do you rely on effort alone for fruit that only the Spirit can grow, and what would asking for him look like this week?

he plans wicked schemes to ruin the poor with lying words, even when the plea of the needy is right.<sup>8</sup>But he who is noble plans noble things, and on noble things he stands.<sup>9</sup>Rise up, you women who are at ease, hear my voice; you complacent daughters, give ear to my speech.<sup>10</sup>In little more than a year you will shudder, you complacent women; for the grape harvest fails, the fruit harvest will not come.<sup>11</sup>Tremble, you women who are at ease, shudder, you complacent ones; the hill and the watchtower will become dens forever, a joy of wild donkeys, a pasture of flocks;<sup>15</sup>until the Spirit is poured upon us from on high, and the wilderness becomes a fruitful field, and the fruitful field is deemed a forest.<sup>16</sup>Then justice will dwell in the wilderness, and righteousness abide in the fruitful field.<sup>17</sup>And the effect of righteousness will be peace, and the result of righteousness, quietness and trust forever.<sup>18</sup>My people will abide in a peaceful habitation, in secure dwellings, and in quiet resting places.<sup>19</sup>And it will hail when the forest falls down, and the city will be utterly laid low.<sup>20</sup>Happy are you who sow beside all waters, who let the feet of the ox and the donkey range free.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–8 — Each One a Hiding Place
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: A righteous king will make his people a shelter for one another and give things back their true names. A king will reign in righteousness and princes rule in justice (v. 1), and verse 2 shows what that does for ordinary people: each becomes a hiding place from the wind, streams in a dry place, the shade of a great rock. The closed eyes, deaf ears and confused hearts of chapter 29 are healed (vv. 3–4). The fool will no longer be called noble, nor the scoundrel honourable (v. 5), for the fool’s heart is busy with iniquity and the scoundrel ruins the poor with lies, while the noble man plans noble things and stands on them (vv. 6–8).
verseByVerse.theology: Good government in this chapter is measured by what it does for ordinary people, not by the splendour of the throne.
verseByVerse.examples: A society is in serious trouble when its words no longer match the facts, and part of what the coming king restores is accurate speech.

verseByVerse.quote: Behold, a king will reign in righteousness, and princes will rule in justice. Each will be like a hiding place from the wind, a shelter from the storm, like streams of water in a dry place, like the shade of a great rock in a weary land. Then the eyes of those who see will not be closed, and the ears of those who hear will give attention. The heart of the hasty will understand and know, and the tongue of the stammerers will hasten to speak distinctly.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God promises a king who rules in true righteousness, under whom his people become a shelter for one another and the blindness of the past is healed.

A king will reign in righteousness. After four chapters of woes against the rulers Judah actually had, here is one who governs properly, and the emphasis falls not on his power but on righteousness and justice, the two qualities every previous government in this book has lacked.

Each will be like a hiding place from the wind. The surprise is the subject of verse 2. It is not only the king who is the hiding place; it is each, each of the princes, each person under this reign. The effect of a righteous ruler is a society of people who shelter one another in bad weather.

Like the shade of a great rock in a weary land. All four images are useful rather than decorative. In that country a rock big enough to sit against is not scenery but survival. These are things you get behind, drink or sit under, and that is what a person becomes under a good king.

Then the eyes of those who see will not be closed. The diagnosis of chapter 29 is reversed item by item: closed eyes open, ears listen, the hasty heart understands, the stammering tongue speaks clearly. Isaiah announces the cure in the vocabulary of the disease, so that nobody can mistake which problem is being solved.

Is this king Hezekiah or the Messiah? Hezekiah is the near horizon, but the picture of perfect justice and a Spirit-filled age (v. 15) reaches beyond any king of Judah to the King of 9:7 and 11:1–5, Christ. He is the first hiding place, the rock in a weary land, and under his reign his people become shelters for one another.

Uncertain wording. Verse 2 begins simply “a man”, as in the KJV (a man shall be as an hiding place), and many older interpreters took that man to be the King himself, the Messiah sheltering his people. The ESV’s each takes it of every ruler under him. Both readings are possible, and they belong together.

verseByVerse.quote: The fool will no more be called noble, nor the scoundrel said to be honorable. For the fool speaks folly, and his heart is busy with iniquity, to practice ungodliness, to utter error concerning the LORD, to leave the craving of the hungry unsatisfied, and to deprive the thirsty of drink. As for the scoundrel— his devices are evil; he plans wicked schemes to ruin the poor with lying words, even when the plea of the needy is right. But he who is noble plans noble things, and on noble things he stands.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Under the righteous king, things are called by their true names again: the fool and the scoundrel are exposed, and the truly noble stand firm.

The fool will no more be called noble. This undoes one of the woes of chapter 5. In 5:20 the charge was against those who call evil good and good evil, the relabelling that destroys a society’s ability to repent, because you cannot turn from something you have agreed to call good. Here the names go back on the right things: under this king, words mean what they mean again.

The fool speaks folly. Isaiah defines his terms. The fool in Scripture is not unintelligent. His heart is busy, and his list runs straight from what he says about God to how he treats the hungry: he utters error about the LORD, and he leaves the hungry hungry and the thirsty dry. In this book those two are never separated; error about God and neglect of the poor are the same failure at two ends of a life.

As for the scoundrel. The scoundrel is more deliberate: he plans with lying words against people whose case is good, even when the plea of the needy is right. He knows.

He who is noble plans noble things. The contrast is not activity against passivity, for the noble man also plans. The difference is what he plans, and that he can stand on it, which the scoundrel cannot, because a scheme built on lies is no place to stand.

Why do we keep renaming things? Every age finds softer words for what it has decided to do: killing civilians becomes collateral damage, greed ambition, an affair finding yourself. George Orwell warned in his essay “Politics and the English Language” (1946) that political language “is designed to make lies sound truthful and murder respectable”. The heart does the same in miniature. We relabel our sins because we cannot bear to see them under their real names, having nowhere to take them. That is why the gospel restores language. Only someone who knows he can be forgiven can afford to call a sin a sin: “If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins” (1 John 1:9). The honest name is the first step to the cure.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Those who are comfortable and complacent must learn to mourn before the loss comes. Isaiah calls on the women who are at ease to listen (v. 9). In little more than a year they will shudder, for the grape harvest will fail (v. 10). They are to strip, put on sackcloth and beat their breasts for the pleasant fields and the fruitful vine (vv. 11–12), because thorns will cover the land and every joyful house in the exultant city; the palace will be forsaken, and the hill and the watchtower will become dens for wild donkeys (vv. 13–14).
verseByVerse.theology: The charge is not luxury but complacency. The word used of these women twice means secure and untroubled, sure that next year will be like this year.
verseByVerse.examples: The timescale is what makes it bite: in little more than a year, close enough to check and far enough away to ignore. Complacency is rarely argued out of a person; it is usually taken out by a season.

verseByVerse.quote: Rise up, you women who are at ease, hear my voice; you complacent daughters, give ear to my speech. In little more than a year you will shudder, you complacent women; for the grape harvest fails, the fruit harvest will not come. Tremble, you women who are at ease, shudder, you complacent ones; strip, and make yourselves bare, and tie sackcloth around your waist. Beat your breasts for the pleasant fields, for the fruitful vine, for the soil of my people growing up in thorns and briers, yes, for all the joyous houses in the exultant city. For the palace is forsaken, the populous city deserted; the hill and the watchtower will become dens forever, a joy of wild donkeys, a pasture of flocks;
verseByVerse.commentary:
The comfortable and secure are called to mourn now, before invasion strips the land, because ease that has forgotten God cannot last.

You women who are at ease. This is not a complaint about women. Isaiah picks out one group as an example, and the diagnosis is in two words: at ease and complacent, secure and confident that things will go on as they have. That is a condition, not a gender: the condition of people comfortable long enough to forget what their comfort rested on.

The grape harvest fails. The security is dismantled not by an army but by a failed harvest. The two were probably closer than they sound: if, as many think, the oracle comes from the years just before Sennacherib’s invasion of 701 BC, a failed vintage is what an army in the fields brings, and 37:30 speaks of two years in which Judah ate only what grew of itself.

Beat your breasts. The instruction is to strip, put on sackcloth and start mourning now, before the loss arrives: Isaiah’s way of asking people to feel a warning in advance. And the mourning is not left without an answer, for the same speech goes straight on to until the Spirit is poured upon us (v. 15). The call to grieve is a call back to the God who means to give what complacency had stopped asking for. “Blessed are those who mourn, for they shall be comforted” (Matthew 5:4).

Thorns and briers. The thorns and briers are the vineyard of chapter 5 again, and the ending is the one Isaiah keeps reaching for: not rubble, but wild donkeys enjoying themselves where the watchtower was.

Uncertain wording. In little more than a year (v. 10) renders a phrase, literally days upon a year, that may mean a year and a few days, or when the year comes round. Either way the warning is near and dated.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 15–20 — Until the Spirit Is Poured Out
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Everything hangs on one word: the desolation lasts until the Spirit is poured out from on high. Then the wilderness becomes a fruitful field, and justice and righteousness make their home there (vv. 15–16). Righteousness yields peace, and peace yields quietness and trust for ever, the very things Judah refused in 30:15 (v. 17). God’s people will live in secure and quiet homes even while the storm falls on the forest and the city (vv. 18–19), and blessed are those who sow beside all waters and let their animals range free (v. 20).
verseByVerse.theology: The turn does not come from better policy, a stronger alliance or reformed leadership, all of which the chapters before it have tried. It comes from on high.
verseByVerse.examples: For anyone who has tried to produce a settled heart by resolving to have one, verse 17 is good news: quietness and trust are a fruit before they are a task.

verseByVerse.quote: until the Spirit is poured upon us from on high, and the wilderness becomes a fruitful field, and the fruitful field is deemed a forest. Then justice will dwell in the wilderness, and righteousness abide in the fruitful field. And the effect of righteousness will be peace, and the result of righteousness, quietness and trust forever.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The desolation will last until God pours out his Spirit; then justice and righteousness will grow, and their fruit will be lasting peace, quietness and trust.

Until the Spirit is poured upon us from on high. Everything turns on a small word: until. The desolation of verses 13 and 14 has an end, and nothing before that point is going to work. Egyptian alliances, competent crisis management, walls surveyed and reservoirs cut have produced nothing. What will change the situation is not a policy, not even the better king just described, but the Spirit … poured upon us from on high.

The promise of the Spirit. This is the first time in the book that the transformation is credited to the Spirit poured out, and the promise runs on through Joel (Joel 2:28) and Ezekiel (Ezekiel 36:26) to a room in Jerusalem where it happened. At Pentecost Peter explained that the exalted Jesus had received the promised Spirit from the Father and poured him out (Acts 2:33): the gift of verse 15 comes from the hand of the King of verse 1.

Justice will dwell in the wilderness. The effect is agricultural, which in this book means real: wilderness becomes farmland and farmland forest. And justice and righteousness, the two things the vineyard failed to produce in 5:7, are described as living somewhere, which is what they do when the Spirit has been poured out rather than when a policy has been adopted.

The effect of righteousness will be peace. The order of verse 17 cannot be rearranged: righteousness produces peace, and peace produces quietness and trust. Those are exactly what God offered Judah in 30:15 as the way to be saved, and they were unwilling.

A fruit, not a policy. What could not be adopted as a policy turns out to be available as a fruit. Quietness and trust cannot be manufactured by deciding to have them; they grow at the end of a chain that begins with the Spirit poured out. For the Christian reader the chain begins with a righteousness given before it is lived: “since we have been justified by faith, we have peace with God through our Lord Jesus Christ” (Romans 5:1), and the Spirit then grows in us what we could never produce by resolving to (Galatians 5:22–23).

verseByVerse.quote: My people will abide in a peaceful habitation, in secure dwellings, and in quiet resting places. And it will hail when the forest falls down, and the city will be utterly laid low. Happy are you who sow beside all waters, who let the feet of the ox and the donkey range free.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God’s people will at last live in secure and quiet homes, sowing freely without fear, even while the storm of judgment falls elsewhere.

A peaceful habitation. Three phrases for the same thing, all domestic: a habitation, dwellings, resting places. After thirty-two chapters of walls, treaties, siegeworks and cavalry, what God finally gives his people is somewhere to live and the ability to sleep in it.

It will hail when the forest falls down. The hail and the falling forest are still there. Isaiah does not remove the weather in order to give rest; the storm goes on outside, as in 25:4, where God was the wall rather than the absence of the wind.

Happy are you who sow beside all waters. The last verse is a farm at peace, in two details a farmer would notice. Sow beside all waters: not in the one safe corner but everywhere, as a man does when he expects no one to take the crop. And the ox and donkey turned loose: in an unsafe country you keep livestock penned and watched, and letting them out is the most ordinary sign that the danger is over.

What the reign is for. The chapter that began with a righteous king ends with an untethered donkey wandering across a field somebody sowed without anxiety. That is what the reign in verse 1 is for, and a better picture of salvation than most grand ones: the peace Christ gives (John 14:27), worked out in ordinary life.

Uncertain wording. Verse 19 is obscure: which forest falls, and which city? Most likely it is judgment on the enemy (Assyria is a forest felled in 10:33–34) or on the proud city of this world, set beside the quiet homes of God’s people; some take it of Jerusalem humbled before its restoration. Either way, the storm falls while God’s people rest.

32.theology:
Each one a shelter. The King is the first hiding place, and under his rule his people become shelters for one another (v. 2).

Complacency, and a season. The women of vv. 9-14 stand for anyone comfortable long enough to forget what the comfort rests on, and the warning comes through a failed harvest.

Until the Spirit. Nothing before verse 15 will work; what changes the situation is the Spirit poured out from on high. The Spirit came when the King of verse 1 had been raised and enthroned: Peter says the exalted Jesus poured out the Spirit he had received from the Father (Acts 2:33).

33.subtitle: The LORD Is Our King
33.intro:
Where we are. Chapter 33 is the sixth and last of the woes that began in chapter 28, spoken while Assyria was closing in on Jerusalem and Judah’s hopes in Egypt were failing. The first five woes fell on Judah’s own leaders; this one falls on the destroyer himself, and it brings the long section of chapters 28 to 33 to its close.

The message. The destroyer who seems unstoppable will be destroyed when God rises, and the real question is not whether Assyria can stand before God but whether Zion can. God’s presence is a consuming fire, safe only for those he has made upright. Yet to them he promises the sight of the King in his beauty, a city that can never be moved, and a people with nothing wrong left in them, because their sin is forgiven. The LORD himself is judge, lawgiver and king, and he will save.

Why it was said. Hezekiah had paid Sennacherib a crushing tribute, even stripping the gold from the temple doors, and the Assyrian took it and marched on Jerusalem anyway (2 Kings 18:14–17; see the introduction). Treaties were worthless, the countryside was stripped, and those in Zion who had trusted alliances rather than God were terrified.

How the chapter makes its case. A woe and a prayer (vv. 1–6): the traitor will be betrayed, and the people ask God to be their arm every morning, for the fear of the LORD is Zion’s treasure. Collapse, and God rising (vv. 7–13): envoys weep, highways empty, the loveliest country withers, and the LORD says “now” three times. The question at the centre (vv. 14–16): sinners in Zion ask who can live with the consuming fire, and the answer is a portrait of integrity, kept safe and fed by God. The vision (vv. 17–24): the King in his beauty, the occupiers gone, Zion an immovable tent beside broad rivers, the LORD as judge, lawgiver and king, and a people forgiven.

Where it leads. The chapter leads to Christ first by the need it exposes: verse 15 describes a person no sinner is, and only Jesus has ever stood whole before the consuming fire; those who are in him stand there clothed in his righteousness. It leads by promise too. The King whom his people will see is the LORD himself (v. 22), and the New Testament shows us his face in Jesus, the judge, lawgiver and king who came to save. And the last verse puts forgiveness before healing, the very order Jesus followed with the paralysed man let down through a roof (Mark 2:5–11).

For us. When strength runs out, ask for it as this chapter does: every morning, for that day. And do not take God’s nearness for granted as Jerusalem did. The God who is a consuming fire is safe for sinners only in Christ, and in him the end of the road is not merely safety but seeing the King.

keyVerse.quote: “For the LORD is our judge; the LORD is our lawgiver; the LORD is our king; he will save us.”
keyVerse.note: The three offices of judge, lawgiver and king match the three branches of human government, but God holds them all himself. This is not a programme for a religious state now but a picture of the end, when all authority lent to human rulers returns to him. 1 Timothy 6:15 picks up the king language for Christ; James 4:12 the lawgiver-judge.

33.reflection:
The people pray, “Be our arm every morning” (v. 2). Why might God give strength one day at a time rather than storing it up for the future, and what would it look like to pray this way each morning this week?

The people who tremble in verse 14 are “in Zion”, living in the city of God’s presence. How can familiarity with church and worship make us careless of who God is, and why is the consuming fire good news for those who are in Christ?

Verse 15 describes integrity in money, in speech and in what we choose to hear and look at. Which of these lines is hardest for you to hold where you live and work, and what might holding it cost you?

The chapter’s reward is not only safety but a sight: “Your eyes will behold the king in his beauty” (v. 17). How does the hope of seeing Christ change the way you think about heaven, and about the troubles you face now?
