verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–13 — Be Our Arm Every Morning
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God will bring down the destroyer, and his people’s part is to wait for him and ask for his strength each day. The last woe falls on a traitor nobody has yet betrayed: his turn will come when he has finished (v. 1). The people answer with prayer, “Be our arm every morning,” and confess that the LORD on high is the stability of their times and the fear of him Zion’s treasure (vv. 2–6). Then the collapse: heroes cry, envoys weep, covenants are broken and the loveliest country withers (vv. 7–9). Into it the LORD says “now” three times and rises, and the nations’ schemes burn like stubble (vv. 10–13).
verseByVerse.theology: Verse 2 is the model prayer of this part of the book: strength asked for each day, not stored up in advance.
verseByVerse.examples: Praying every morning is not a sign of weak faith but of right faith. It assumes, correctly, that we will need God again today, and that he will be there.

verseByVerse.quote: Ah, you destroyer, who yourself have not been destroyed, you traitor, whom none has betrayed! When you have ceased to destroy, you will be destroyed; and when you have finished betraying, they will betray you. O LORD, be gracious to us; we wait for you. Be our arm every morning, our salvation in the time of trouble. At the tumultuous noise peoples flee; when you lift yourself up, nations are scattered, and your spoil is gathered as the caterpillar gathers; as locusts leap, it is leapt upon. The LORD is exalted, for he dwells on high; he will fill Zion with justice and righteousness, and he will be the stability of your times, abundance of salvation, wisdom, and knowledge; the fear of the LORD is Zion's treasure.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The destroyer who looks invincible will be destroyed in God’s time, and until then God’s people wait for him and ask for his strength one day at a time.

Ah, you destroyer. The last woe is aimed at Assyria without naming her, and it names what makes the wicked look invincible: not that they cannot fall, but that they have not yet. Isaiah’s answer is about timing: when you have ceased to destroy, you will be destroyed. The reckoning is not cancelled, only waiting its turn.

Be our arm every morning. The community answers not with a military plan but with the prayer everything since chapter 28 has been asking for: not once, for the emergency, but every morning, on the assumption that yesterday’s strength has been used up.

Daily supply. That is how the manna worked: gathered daily, and spoiled if stored (Exodus 16). It is also what Jesus taught us to ask for, give us this day our daily bread (Matthew 6:11), and the reason is not stinginess. Daily supply keeps a person coming back to God, which is the point.

As locusts leap. The prayer is answered in advance: when God lifts himself up, the nations scatter, and the plunder they took is stripped from them as locusts strip a field (vv. 3–4).

The stability of your times. Two phrases to keep. The stability of your times: God does not remove the upheaval but is the steady thing within it. And the fear of the LORD is Zion’s treasure: after all the treasuries emptied to buy alliances, the real wealth is named, reverent trust in the LORD, and it is not kept in a vault.

verseByVerse.quote: Behold, their heroes cry in the streets; the envoys of peace weep bitterly. The highways lie waste; the traveler ceases. Covenants are broken; cities are despised; there is no regard for man. The land mourns and languishes; Lebanon is confounded and withers away; Sharon is like a desert, and Bashan and Carmel shake off their leaves. "Now I will arise," says the LORD, "now I will lift myself up; now I will be exalted. You conceive chaff; you give birth to stubble; your breath is a fire that will consume you. And the peoples will be as if burned to lime, like thorns cut down, that are burned in the fire." Hear, you who are far off, what I have done; and you who are near, acknowledge my might.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When every human support has failed and the land lies stripped, God himself rises, and the schemes of the nations burn up like straw.

The envoys of peace weep bitterly. The diplomats are crying in public: men whose profession is composure, who negotiated the treaties Judah staked everything on, weeping in the street.

Covenants are broken. Isaiah measures the collapse not by casualties but by empty highways. Every journey depends on agreements honoured by people you will never meet, so when covenants are broken, no one travels. Many think Isaiah has a particular betrayal in mind. Hezekiah paid Sennacherib a huge tribute to call off the invasion, stripping the gold from the temple doors, and the Assyrian took it and sent his army to Jerusalem anyway (2 Kings 18:14–17).

There is no regard for man. The lowest point: not for this man or that class of men, but human life itself counts for nothing.

Lebanon is confounded and withers away. Then come the four places anybody would list as the beauty of the land, Lebanon with its cedars, Sharon, Bashan and Carmel. Isaiah takes the reader round them one by one and shows each of them dying.

Now I will arise. Into that God speaks, and says now three times. Everything so far has been waiting: for the destroyer to be destroyed, for God every morning, envoys weeping while nothing happens. The threefold now ends the waiting, and the three verbs (arise, lift myself up, be exalted) picture someone getting to his feet.

You conceive chaff. The enemy’s plans deliver nothing but straw, and their own breath is the fire that consumes them (vv. 11–12): evil carries the seeds of its own destruction.

Uncertain wording. The word translated heroes (v. 7) is rare and obscure; suggestions include “valiant ones” and “messengers”, and some connect it with Ariel (29:1). The parallel line makes the picture clear: the people Judah relied on are in tears.

Textual note. Where the standard Hebrew text reads cities are despised (v. 8), one of the oldest Hebrew copies reads “witnesses”, a difference of one similar-looking letter. It would fit the broken covenants, which were sworn before witnesses; the sense is not affected.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 14–16 — Who Can Dwell with the Consuming Fire?
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: When God rises, the people who should be afraid are those living nearest to him without being changed by him. Sinners in Zion tremble and ask, “Who among us can dwell with the consuming fire?” (v. 14). The answer is a portrait, not a ritual: someone who walks and speaks uprightly, despises gain made from oppression, refuses the bribe, and will not listen to plans for bloodshed or feast his eyes on evil (v. 15). Such a person lives safely in the fire’s presence, with a rock for his fortress and bread and water that do not fail (v. 16). The portrait is the fruit of grace, and only Christ fits it whole.
verseByVerse.theology: The answer that follows (v. 15) is not a ladder by which sinners climb to God but a portrait of those he has already made his own.
verseByVerse.examples: Most of the answer in verse 15 is about money. Godliness here is measured not by religious intensity but by what a person will refuse to be paid for.

verseByVerse.quote: The sinners in Zion are afraid; trembling has seized the godless: "Who among us can dwell with the consuming fire? Who among us can dwell with everlasting burnings?" He who walks righteously and speaks uprightly, who despises the gain of oppressions, who shakes his hands, lest they hold a bribe, who stops his ears from hearing of bloodshed and shuts his eyes from looking on evil, he will dwell on the heights; his place of defense will be the fortresses of rocks; his bread will be given him; his water will be sure.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God’s presence among his people is a consuming fire, safe only for those whose lives he has made upright; that exposes every sinner, and sends us to the one man who fits the portrait.

Who among us can dwell with the consuming fire? The people asking are in Zion: not pagans but insiders, who kept the festivals of chapter 29. And the fire is not hell. Coming after God’s rising in verse 10, the consuming fire is God himself, in the middle of the city, permanently. Jerusalem treated his presence as its guarantee of safety, but living next door to a consuming fire is good news for one kind of person only.

He who walks righteously. The answer is a portrait, every line concrete and much of it about money. Despises the gain of oppressions: not merely refuses it but finds it contemptible. Shakes his hands, lest they hold a bribe: a man opening his fingers and shaking them out, which implies a bribe was there to be taken. Stopping the ears from hearing of bloodshed means declining to be in the room where violence is planned, which usually costs a man his place in the room; shutting the eyes is the refusal to be a spectator of evil.

His bread will be given him. This is someone whose integrity has cost him. The reward is not riches but a high place, a rock, and bread and water that do not fail: safety and provision, the two things money was supposed to guarantee, given by God’s hand instead.

If only the upright can dwell with the consuming fire, how can any sinner? The portrait of verse 15 describes those whom God has made his own; it is the fruit of grace, not its price. Sinners dwell with the holy God only through the Servant who bore their iniquities (53:5–6) and the Judge who is also their Saviour (v. 22). Only one man has ever fitted the portrait whole, and those who are in him stand before the fire clothed in his righteousness (2 Corinthians 5:21).

Not left to willpower. The open hands of verse 15 are not left to willpower. The holy presence that terrifies the godless comes to those made clean as the Spirit, who grows integrity in them day by day (Galatians 5:22–23): the daily strength verse 2 asks for.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 17–24 — The King in His Beauty
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The end of the road is a sight and a city: the King in his beauty, and a Zion that can never be moved. Eyes that refused to look on evil will see the king and a land stretching far away (v. 17). The officials of the occupation, counting people, tribute and towers, become a memory, and the foreign tongue is gone (vv. 18–19). Zion is a tent whose stakes are never pulled up, and the LORD himself is its broad river, where no enemy ship can sail (vv. 20–21). For the LORD is judge, lawgiver and king, and he will save (v. 22). Even the lame share the spoil, and no one is sick, because all are forgiven (vv. 23–24).
verseByVerse.theology: Verse 22 is the answer to thirty-three chapters of failed leadership: the offices men could not fill are held by God himself.
verseByVerse.examples: For anyone living with long illness, verse 24 is a promise about the end, not a verdict on the present: the cure, when it comes, will go to the root.

verseByVerse.quote: Your eyes will behold the king in his beauty; they will see a land that stretches afar. Your heart will muse on the terror: "Where is he who counted, where is he who weighed the tribute? Where is he who counted the towers?" You will see no more the insolent people, the people of an obscure speech that you cannot comprehend, stammering in a tongue that you cannot understand. Behold Zion, the city of our appointed feasts! Your eyes will see Jerusalem, an untroubled habitation, an immovable tent, whose stakes will never be plucked up, nor will any of its cords be broken.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The reward at the end of the road is not only safety but a sight: the King in his beauty, ruling a city whose oppressors are only a memory.

Your eyes will behold the king in his beauty. After the fire and the trembling comes the goal of the whole chapter. The reward is a sight, and it is a person. The man of verse 15 shut his eyes from looking on evil; here his eyes are opened onto the king. He refused one sight for the sake of a better one, and now he has it. And a land that stretches afar gives back the horizon after a siege in which the world had shrunk to the inside of a wall.

Where is he who counted? Three questions name the machinery of occupation: the men who counted the population for the levy, weighed the tribute, and counted the towers to find where the walls were weak. Not soldiers but administrators with lists, and one day the heart will muse on them only as a memory, because the men themselves will be gone. The foreign speech of the invaders (v. 19) is gone from the streets too; in 28:11 that speech was God’s judgment on people who mocked plain teaching as baby talk.

An immovable tent. Zion, the city of our appointed feasts, is a tent that never moves, a deliberate contradiction: tents are the most temporary structures there are, and this one has stakes that are never pulled up. The permanence God gives does not have to be made of stone.

Which king? Some link him with the righteous king of 32:1; others see the LORD himself, since verse 22 says the LORD is our king. With the Gospels open we need not choose: the King whose beauty the redeemed will see is the Son of David who is also God, in whose face the glory of God shines (2 Corinthians 4:6), and we shall see him as he is (1 John 3:2).

Won’t heaven be dull? It is a real fear, and an old one. Huckleberry Finn, told by Miss Watson that in the good place a body would go around all day with a harp and sing for ever, decided he would rather be wherever Tom Sawyer was going. Many quietly agree: an eternity of looking at anything sounds like a very long afternoon in a gallery. But notice what bores us. It is never beauty itself; it is a limited beauty seen too often. The best things in this life, a face we love, a piece of music, a sunset, leave us wanting more, not less, and they always end. Isaiah promises a sight that does not run out: the king in his beauty, a living Person whose goodness can be explored for ever and never exhausted. “In your presence there is fullness of joy; at your right hand are pleasures forevermore” (Psalm 16:11). And the face we shall see is not a stranger’s. It is the face of the King whose appearance was once so marred, beyond human semblance (52:14), for us.

verseByVerse.quote: But there the LORD in majesty will be for us a place of broad rivers and streams, where no galley with oars can go, nor majestic ship can pass. For the LORD is our judge; the LORD is our lawgiver; the LORD is our king; he will save us. Your cords hang loose; they cannot hold the mast firm in its place or keep the sail spread out. Then prey and spoil in abundance will be divided; even the lame will take the prey. And no inhabitant will say, "I am sick"; the people who dwell there will be forgiven their iniquity.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The LORD himself will be everything Zion lacked: its river, its judge, lawgiver and king, and the one who heals because he first forgives.

A place of broad rivers and streams. Jerusalem’s great weakness was that it had no river. Nineveh had the Tigris, Babylon the Euphrates, Thebes the Nile; Zion had a spring and a tunnel. Isaiah says God himself will be its broad rivers, with one qualification that turns the picture inside out: no galley with oars can go on them. A river lets ships come up, which is both its advantage and its danger. This one has the benefit without the danger.

The LORD is our judge. Each of the three offices in verse 22 has been a scene of failure in this book. The judge: courts that loved bribes and never heard the widow (1:23; 5:23). The lawgiver: the legislators who decreed oppression (10:1). The king: Ahaz emptying the temple to buy Assyria’s help while refusing a sign from God. Judah tried to fill these offices with men and failed in every one. Here one person holds all three, and the sentence ends not with a fourth title but with a consequence: he will save us. The New Testament gives all three to Jesus, judge of the world (Acts 17:31) and King of kings (Revelation 19:16), who came to save.

Even the lame will take the prey. Verse 23 turns the ship picture round, most likely on Zion herself: a vessel with slack rigging, its mast unsteady and its sail unable to spread, in no state to win anything, and yet the spoil is divided. Even the lame get a share, people who could not have fought. The spoils go to those who contributed nothing to the victory, which is how every victory in this book works: God wins and his people receive.

Forgiven their iniquity. The last verse takes away the two things wrong with a human being, sickness and guilt, and the order matters. Nobody says I am sick, and the reason is not medical: the people are forgiven their iniquity. The healing of the body follows the pardon, not the other way round. Jesus showed the same order when a paralysed man was let down through a roof: first Son, your sins are forgiven, and then the command to rise and walk, so that they might know that the Son of Man has authority on earth to forgive sins (Mark 2:5–11).

What it does not mean. This does not mean every illness is punishment for a particular sin; Jesus denied that of the man born blind (John 9:2–3). It means the final cure goes to the root. Believers who are ill now are no less forgiven; they wait for that day, and meanwhile thank God for doctors and medicine.

Where the chapter ends. The chapter that began with a destroyer still standing ends with a city where nobody is ill and nobody is guilty, and verse 24 says both in a single sentence.

Uncertain wording. Whose ship verse 23 describes is uncertain. Most take the loose rigging as Zion’s own, helpless yet given the spoil; others as the enemy’s ship, disabled and stripped. Either way, the victory owes nothing to seamanship.

33.theology:
Be our arm every morning. The community answers the last woe with prayer rather than policy, asking for strength on the daily terms of the manna and of the Lord’s Prayer.

Who can dwell with the consuming fire? The question is asked by people in Zion, not by pagans, and the fire is not hell: it is God’s own presence, which the city had assumed was its guarantee of safety. Living next door to a consuming fire is good news only for a particular kind of person, and verse 15 draws him: concrete, and mostly about money. It is not religious attainment but integrity that costs income, the fruit of grace in those God has made his own.

Three offices, one holder. God is judge, lawgiver and king, and the chapter ends with sickness and guilt removed in one sentence, the pardon first.

34.subtitle: Judgment on the Nations
34.intro:
Where we are. Chapters 34 and 35 close the prophecies of Isaiah’s first half, before the history of chapters 36 to 39, and they are a pair: a land turned to burning pitch, then a desert in bloom. After the woes on Jerusalem (chapters 28 to 33), Isaiah widens the view to all the nations, and names one of them, Edom, as the example.

The message. God will judge the whole world that has set itself against him and his people, and his judgment will be exact, total and final. Edom, Israel’s brother nation and long its enemy, becomes the picture of what rebellion comes to in the end: a kingdom unmade back into chaos and left to owls and jackals. Nothing in it is out of control. It happens because the LORD has spoken, and his word will not fail in the smallest detail.

Why it was said. Judah was small, surrounded by nations that had raided and despised it, and tempted to think that wrongs done to God’s people simply stand (see the introduction). Isaiah tells them that God keeps a day of recompense “for the cause of Zion” (v. 8), and that his word can be trusted down to the last bird.

How the chapter makes its case. Summons and sentence (vv. 1–4): the nations and the earth are called to hear, the slain lie unburied, and the heavens roll up like a scroll. The sword on Edom (vv. 5–8): God’s judgment is pictured as a great sacrifice at Bozrah, on a day of vengeance for Zion. The unmaking (vv. 9–15): streams become pitch, smoke rises for ever, the builder’s line is stretched over chaos and emptiness, and the land is handed to wild creatures. The book (vv. 16–17): readers are told to look it up, for not one creature will be missing; God has allotted the ruins to them as he once allotted Canaan to Israel.

Where it leads. The chapter leads to Christ chiefly through the character of God it shows and the need it exposes: a holy God does not overlook cruelty, and the wrath described here is real. Reading the matching promise in Nazareth, Jesus stopped before “the day of vengeance of our God” (61:2; Luke 4:18–19), because he came first to bear that wrath on the cross, not to bring it; he will come again as judge (Revelation 19:11–16). Even Edom is not beyond his reach. Amos foresaw “the remnant of Edom” among the nations called by God’s name, and James saw that fulfilled as Gentiles came to Christ (Amos 9:11–12; Acts 15:16–17).

For us. Do not skip this chapter. It tells us that wrongs done to God’s people are recorded and will be answered, so we need not avenge ourselves (Romans 12:19). And it shows us what Christ bore and what we are saved from, which makes the joy of chapter 35, and of the cross, greater, not less.

keyVerse.quote: “Seek and read from the book of the LORD: not one of these shall be missing; none shall be without her mate. For the mouth of the LORD has commanded, and his Spirit has gathered them.”
keyVerse.note: Even the desolation is governed by God’s written word, carried out to the last detail. This is not chaos but ordered judgment: the God who spoke creation into being speaks desolation over a land that refused him, and invites anyone to check. If his word holds for owls in a wasteland, it holds for every promise he has made, beginning with the next chapter’s.

34.reflection:
Chapter 34 is one of the hardest passages in Isaiah to read. Why do you think God put it in Scripture, and placed it immediately before the joy of chapter 35? What do we lose if we skip the Bible’s descriptions of judgment?

Edom is judged “for the cause of Zion” (v. 8), for wrongs done to God’s people. How does knowing that God keeps a “year of recompense” free us from taking revenge ourselves (Romans 12:19), and how should it shape the way we pray about injustice?

In Nazareth Jesus stopped reading before “the day of vengeance of our God” (Isaiah 61:2; Luke 4:19). What does it mean for you that he came first to bear judgment rather than to bring it?

Verses 16–17 invite readers to check that not one detail of God’s word fails, down to the nesting birds. How does the precision of God’s word strengthen your confidence in his promises?

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–8 — The Skies Rolled Up Like a Scroll
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God summons the whole world to hear its sentence, and names Edom as the example. The nations and the earth itself are called to listen (v. 1), for the LORD is angry with all the nations and has devoted them to destruction, and their slain lie unburied (vv. 2–3). The judgment reaches the sky: the heavens roll up like a scroll and the stars fall like leaves (v. 4). Then the sword comes down on Edom, pictured as a great sacrifice at Bozrah, one of its chief cities (vv. 5–7). The reason is stated plainly: the LORD has a day of vengeance, a year of recompense for the cause of Zion (v. 8).
verseByVerse.theology: The summons runs from the nations to the earth to the sky: nothing created stands outside the reach of its Creator's verdict.
verseByVerse.examples: Jesus himself speaks of stars falling from heaven at his coming (Matthew 24:29), and John takes verse 4 almost whole for the sixth seal. When the New Testament needs language for the last day, it keeps reaching into this chapter.

verseByVerse.quote: Draw near, O nations, to hear, and give attention, O peoples! Let the earth hear, and all that fills it; the world, and all that comes from it. For the LORD is enraged against all the nations, and furious against all their host; he has devoted them to destruction, has given them over for slaughter. Their slain shall be cast out, and the stench of their corpses shall rise; the mountains shall flow with their blood. All the host of heaven shall rot away, and the skies roll up like a scroll. All their host shall fall, as leaves fall from the vine, like leaves falling from the fig tree.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God calls the whole world to hear its sentence: his judgment will reach every nation and the heavens themselves, and it will be as real and final as death.

Draw near, O nations, to hear. The widest summons in the book so far: not one nation, as in chapters 13 to 23, but everybody, and then the earth itself, which was called as a witness in 1:2.

The stench of their corpses shall rise. Verse 3 describes the aftermath without flinching: bodies unburied, the stench going up, the mountains flowing with blood. Scripture does not pretend that judgment is clean.

The skies roll up like a scroll. Then the judgment leaves the ground, in images from everyday life. The skies roll up like a scroll at the end of a reading: not something breaking but something put away because it is done. And the stars come down the way leaves fall from the vine or the fig tree in autumn: suddenly and all at once, and then the branches are bare. Isaiah is not forecasting astronomy. He is saying that a creation turned against its Maker can be taken down as easily as it was put up, and by the same word.

All the host of heaven. The host of heaven were the stars, which the nations, and at times Judah itself, worshipped as powers (Deuteronomy 4:19; 2 Kings 21:3). When they fall, the gods the nations trusted fall with them.

John saw it. At the opening of the sixth seal the sky vanished like a scroll that is being rolled up, and the stars fell to earth as the fig tree sheds its winter fruit when shaken by a gale (Revelation 6:13–14).

verseByVerse.quote: For my sword has drunk its fill in the heavens; behold, it descends for judgment upon Edom, upon the people I have devoted to destruction. The LORD has a sword; it is sated with blood; it is gorged with fat, with the blood of lambs and goats, with the fat of the kidneys of rams. For the LORD has a sacrifice in Bozrah, a great slaughter in the land of Edom. Wild oxen shall fall with them, and young steers with the mighty bulls. Their land shall drink its fill of blood, and their soil shall be gorged with fat. For the LORD has a day of vengeance, a year of recompense for the cause of Zion.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God’s sword falls on Edom, his people’s nearest kin and long their enemy, as a solemn act of justice settling the wrongs done to Zion.

Upon Edom. Out of all the nations, one is named, and not arbitrarily. Edom was Esau’s people, Israel’s nearest relative, and across the Old Testament the standing example of family hostility that never healed. Edom had raided Judah in Ahaz’s day (2 Chronicles 28:17), and when Jerusalem fell in 586 BC, more than a century after Isaiah, Edom stood by and cheered (Obadiah 11–14; Psalm 137:7). So Edom stands here for what Babylon stands for in chapter 13: a real country, and the representative of every nation that sets itself against God and his people.

The LORD has a sacrifice in Bozrah. The vocabulary is sacrificial rather than military: lambs and goats, the fat of rams’ kidneys, a sacrifice at Bozrah. The point of the picture is that this is not a massacre out of control but, like a sacrifice, a solemn act carried out by God at a place and time he appointed.

For the cause of Zion. The reason is stated plainly. This is not free-floating anger but the settlement of a case, a recompense owed to people who were wronged and could do nothing about it. Everything Edom did to its brother was recorded, down to the cheering when Jerusalem burned, and this verse is the court date.

How can a loving God speak like this? Devoted to destruction (v. 5) translates herem, the word for something handed over wholly to God, here for judgment. It is no licence for anyone to make war in God’s name; the sword in this chapter is God’s alone, the sentence of the Judge of all the earth on cruelty that has run its course.

The day Jesus did not read. The chapter also shows what Christ saves from. In Nazareth Jesus read the parallel promise and stopped short of the day of vengeance of our God (61:2; Luke 4:19), because he came first to bear wrath, not to bring it, and his cross is the only shelter from the day this chapter describes. Yet even Edom is not shut out: Amos foresaw the remnant of Edom among the nations gathered to David’s restored house, and James saw that fulfilled as Gentiles turned to Christ (Amos 9:11–12; Acts 15:16–17).

If you have been wronged. If you have been on the wrong end of something never put right, there is a year of recompense. Its date is fixed, in God’s diary and not in ours, and that frees you to leave vengeance to him (Romans 12:19). That is no reason to stay silent about abuse or crime now: God also gives the authorities to punish wrongdoing (Romans 13:4).
verseByVerse.note: Bozrah was a chief city of Edom. “Devoted to destruction” means set apart to the LORD for destruction (ESV note).

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Edom is unmade, and God’s word governs even its ruins. Its streams become pitch and its soil sulphur, burning night and day, its smoke going up for ever (vv. 9–10). God stretches over it the builder’s line and plumb line, but what he measures out is chaos and emptiness, and no nobles are left to call it a kingdom (vv. 11–12). Thorns grow in its fortresses, and wild creatures move in, nesting and raising their young (vv. 13–15). Finally readers are told to look it up in the book of the LORD: not one creature will be missing, because his mouth commanded it, his Spirit gathered them, and his hand allotted them the land for ever (vv. 16–17).
verseByVerse.theology: The precision is the frightening part: Edom is not wrecked in a rage but measured out, line by line, back into emptiness.
verseByVerse.examples: The word of God that numbers the desert birds is the same word that promises mercy in the next chapter. If he keeps it for owls, he will keep it for his people.

verseByVerse.quote: And the streams of Edom shall be turned into pitch, and her soil into sulfur; her land shall become burning pitch. Night and day it shall not be quenched; its smoke shall go up forever. From generation to generation it shall lie waste; none shall pass through it forever and ever. But the hawk and the porcupine shall possess it, the owl and the raven shall dwell in it. He shall stretch the line of confusion over it, and the plumb line of emptiness. Its nobles—there is no one there to call it a kingdom, and all its princes shall be nothing. Thorns shall grow over its strongholds, nettles and thistles in its fortresses. It shall be the haunt of jackals, an abode for ostriches. And wild animals shall meet with hyenas; the wild goat shall cry to his fellow; indeed, there the night bird settles and finds for herself a resting place. There the owl nests and lays and hatches and gathers her young in her shadow; indeed, there the hawks are gathered, each one with her mate.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God unmakes Edom with a builder’s care, turning a proud kingdom back into the formless emptiness before creation and handing it over to wild creatures.

Her soil into sulfur. Every reader would have known the picture: sulphur, burning, smoke going up from a plain. What happened to Sodom in one morning (Genesis 19:24–28) happens to Edom permanently.

Its smoke shall go up forever. This is the strong language of permanent ruin, used of Sodom (Jude 7) and fulfilled in Edom’s long desolation. Revelation takes the image up for the final judgment (Revelation 14:11; 19:3).

The line of confusion. The two tools in verse 11 are a builder’s: the measuring line and the plumb line, used to lay out a wall straight and upright. What they measure out is tohu and bohu (here confusion and emptiness), the Hebrew words for “without form and void” in the second verse of the Bible, before God said, “Let there be light.” God comes to Edom with building tools and carefully measures out chaos: he unmakes what he made, with precision, which is far more frightening than destruction in a rage. Nothing here is out of control.

There is no one there to call it a kingdom. Of the nation’s nobles nothing is left but a name for the place: No Kingdom There. Thorns and nettles grow in its fortresses, and the animals move in. The last detail is the quiet one: the night bird is not scavenging but settling, finding a resting place. What was a kingdom has become somewhere comfortable for owls, and they have no idea anything was ever there.

Uncertain wording. Several creatures in verses 11 to 15 are rare words, and hawk, porcupine and owl are reasonable guesses. The night bird (v. 14) translates lilith, which later Jewish legend made a night demon (some older versions have “night hag”), and the wild goat could mean a goat-demon (“satyr”). In a list of desert creatures, animals are more likely; either way, the kingdom has been given over to the wild and the eerie.

verseByVerse.quote: Seek and read from the book of the LORD: Not one of these shall be missing; none shall be without her mate. For the mouth of the LORD has commanded, and his Spirit has gathered them. He has cast the lot for them; his hand has portioned it out to them with the line; they shall possess it forever; from generation to generation they shall dwell in it.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God’s word governs even the ruins: every creature he named will be there, because what he says, he does.

Seek and read from the book of the LORD. The chapter ends with an instruction unlike anything else in it: go and look it up, and see whether a single one of the creatures turns out to be absent.

Not one of these shall be missing. The small claim matters. Told that God rules history, a reader may remain unconvinced, because history is too large to check; whether one night bird is missing her mate a person could go and verify. If God’s word reaches the nesting arrangements of desert birds, nothing is too small for it to govern.

His Spirit has gathered them. The mouth of the LORD commands and his Spirit gathers: the same partnership of word and Spirit that made the world (Genesis 1:2–3; Psalm 33:6) now settles its smallest creatures in their place.

He has cast the lot for them. The last verse uses the vocabulary of the conquest under Joshua, when Canaan was divided by lot and measured with a line as an inheritance (Joshua 14:2). God casts lots for the jackals and portions out the ruins to the ostriches, and they hold it permanently.

Nothing beneath his attention. It is the bleakest possible ending, and strangely tender. The care God took over the boundaries of Judah’s tribes he takes over nesting territory in a wasteland nobody will visit, because nothing is beneath his attention, and he keeps everything he says. Jesus drew the comfort out for his disciples: of two sparrows sold for a penny, not one of them will fall to the ground apart from your Father (Matthew 10:29).

Uncertain wording. What the book of the LORD is cannot be settled. Most take it as this prophecy itself, written down so that later readers could compare it with events (compare 30:8); others think of a wider collection of God’s written words.

34.theology:
The sky put away. Verse 4 is not an astronomical forecast. Its images are domestic, a scroll rolled up and leaves falling, and they say that a created world turned against its Maker can be taken down as easily as it was put up.

De-creation done with a plumb line. God unmakes Edom carefully, measuring it back into the “without form and void” of Genesis 1:2. Nothing here is done in a rage or out of control.

Go and check. The chapter argues from the tiny to the enormous: nobody can check all of history, but anyone could check whether an owl has her mate. And the care God took over tribal boundaries he takes over nesting territory in a wasteland nobody will visit.

35.subtitle: The Highway of Holiness
35.intro:
Where we are. Chapter 35 is the bright partner of chapter 34 and the last word before the history of chapters 36 to 39. Where Edom became burning pitch and a haunt of jackals, the desert now blossoms, and the words of the two chapters are matched item for item. It is also a foretaste of chapters 40 to 66, with their highway home through the wilderness.

The message. When God comes, everything that sin and judgment have spoiled will be made new: the desert blooms, the weak are strengthened, the blind see, the lame leap, and the redeemed walk home to Zion on a road they cannot lose, crowned with everlasting joy. The courage the chapter calls for rests not on our strength but on one fact: “Behold, your God will come.”

Why it was said. Judah faced the Assyrian invasion that the next chapters describe, and later generations would sit in exile in Babylon (see the introduction). Tired, frightened people needed to know that the story does not end in the wasteland of chapter 34, and that the God who judges also comes to save.

How the chapter makes its case. The desert rejoices (vv. 1–2): the glory of Lebanon, Carmel and Sharon is given to it, and God’s people see the glory of the LORD. The weak are strengthened (vv. 3–4): those who can are to steady the feeble and tell the anxious that God is coming to save. Bodies and land are made whole (vv. 5–7): blind eyes and deaf ears open, the lame leap, the mute sing, and water breaks out in the desert. The road home (vv. 8–10): the Way of Holiness, safe from lions and walked by the redeemed, ends in Zion with singing as sorrow and sighing flee away.

Where it leads. Here the line to Christ is direct promise. When John the Baptist asked from prison whether Jesus was the one who was to come, Jesus answered with this chapter’s list: the blind see, the lame walk, the deaf hear (Matthew 11:4–5). The God who “will come and save you” came in person, and his healings were the first flowers in the desert. He gave his life “as a ransom for many” (Mark 10:45), making the ransomed of verse 10, and he is himself the way to the Father (John 14:6). The full bloom waits for the new creation, where God wipes away every tear (Revelation 21:4).

For us. Strengthen someone’s weak hands this week, and tell them what Isaiah gives you to say: your God will come. And when sorrow seems to be chasing you, remember how the chase ends: the ransomed are walking home, and it is sorrow and sighing that will flee.

keyVerse.quote: “And a highway shall be there, and it shall be called the Way of Holiness; the unclean shall not pass over it. It shall belong to those who walk on the way; even if they are fools, they shall not go astray. No lion shall be there, nor shall any ravenous beast come up on it; they shall not be found there, but the redeemed shall walk there.”
keyVerse.note: The Way of Holiness is the image John picks up for the New Jerusalem: nothing unclean will enter it (Rev. 21:27). But Isaiah adds what John implies: the travellers are not people who were already pure. They are the redeemed, the ransomed, even the simple. Holiness here is not the entry requirement for the road but the nature of the road itself. You travel it because you have been ransomed, not because you are already holy.

35.theology:
Chapter 34 from the other side. The two chapters are one landscape seen from opposite directions, and the place with nothing receives the beauty of the places that had everything.

Comfort delivered by hand. The strong are told to strengthen the weak, and what they are to say points not to their own strength but to someone coming: behold, your God will come. Jesus answered John the Baptist by reporting that this chapter had begun (Matt. 11:4-5).

A road fools cannot wander off. God does not raise the entry requirements for people who get lost; he builds a road they cannot leave. And the prophecies of the book’s first half end with a reversal: sorrow, the long pursuer, is now the one running away.
35.reflection:
Chapter 35 is set right beside the desolation of chapter 34. How does reading the judgment first change the way the promise of verses 1–2 sounds? Where in your life or church do you long to see a wilderness blossom?

Verses 3–4 tell those who are able to strengthen the weak and to say, “Be strong; fear not!” Who around you has weak hands or an anxious heart, and what would it look like to stand beside them this week?

Jesus answered John the Baptist’s doubt by pointing to what was happening, in the words of verses 5–6 (Matthew 11:4–5). Why was that a better answer than a simple “yes”, and how does it help us when we doubt?

The Way of Holiness is safe even for fools (v. 8), and its travellers are “the redeemed” and “the ransomed of the LORD” (vv. 9–10). How does it change the Christian life to know that you walk this road because you have been ransomed, not because you are already good at walking it?
35.text: <sup>1</sup>The wilderness and the dry land shall be glad; the desert shall rejoice and blossom like the crocus;<sup>2</sup>it shall blossom abundantly and rejoice with joy and singing. The glory of Lebanon shall be given to it, the majesty of Carmel and Sharon. They shall see the glory of the LORD, the majesty of our God.<sup>3</sup>Strengthen the weak hands, and make firm the feeble knees.<sup>4</sup>Say to those who have an anxious heart, "Be strong; fear not! Behold, your God will come with vengeance, with the recompense of God. He will come and save you."<sup>5</sup>Then the eyes of the blind shall be opened, and the ears of the deaf unstopped;<sup>6</sup>then shall the lame man leap like a deer, and the tongue of the mute sing for joy. For waters break forth in the wilderness, and streams in the desert;<sup>7</sup>the burning sand shall become a pool, and the thirsty ground springs of water; in the haunt of jackals, where they lie down, the grass shall become reeds and rushes.<sup>8</sup>And a highway shall be there, and it shall be called the Way of Holiness; the unclean shall not pass over it. It shall belong to those who walk on the way; even if they are fools, they shall not go astray.<sup>9</sup>No lion shall be there, nor shall any ravenous beast come up on it; they shall not be found there, but the redeemed shall walk there.<sup>10</sup>And the ransomed of the LORD shall return and come to Zion with singing; everlasting joy shall be upon their heads; they shall obtain gladness and joy, and sorrow and sighing shall flee away.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–7 — The Desert Puts on Sharon
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: When God comes, the land that judgment ruined blossoms and broken people are made whole. The desert that became pitch and sulphur in chapter 34 rejoices and blossoms like the crocus (v. 1), and is given the glory of Lebanon, Carmel and Sharon, though the true sight is the glory of the LORD himself (v. 2). Those who can are told to steady weak hands and feeble knees and to tell the anxious, “Be strong; fear not!”, because their God will come to save (vv. 3–4). Then blind eyes and deaf ears open, the lame leap like deer and the mute sing, while water breaks out in the desert and the jackals’ haunt turns to marsh (vv. 5–7).
verseByVerse.theology: Isaiah wrote the two chapters side by side so that the same reader would meet both, and the grace of this one is measured by the desolation of the last.
verseByVerse.examples: The command of verses 3 and 4 is given to those who are not currently frightened. If you are steady today, someone near you is not, and you have been told what to say.

verseByVerse.quote: The wilderness and the dry land shall be glad; the desert shall rejoice and blossom like the crocus; it shall blossom abundantly and rejoice with joy and singing. The glory of Lebanon shall be given to it, the majesty of Carmel and Sharon. They shall see the glory of the LORD, the majesty of our God. Strengthen the weak hands, and make firm the feeble knees. Say to those who have an anxious heart, "Be strong; fear not! Behold, your God will come with vengeance, with the recompense of God. He will come and save you."
verseByVerse.commentary:
When God comes, the desert left by judgment will blossom, and the weak and anxious are to be strengthened with that news: your God is coming to save you.

The wilderness and the dry land shall be glad. Isaiah set this chapter beside chapter 34 on purpose. There the streams turned to pitch and the land became a haunt of jackals; here the desert blossoms and sings: the same landscape seen from opposite sides.

The glory of Lebanon shall be given to it. Lebanon, Carmel and Sharon, the cedar forests, the wooded headland and the flowering coastal plain, are three of the four that withered in 33:9. Their beauty is not simply handed back to them; it is given to the desert. The place with nothing gets the beauty of the places that had everything, which is how grace works everywhere in this book. Yet the blossoming desert is not the climax: they shall see the glory of the LORD, the majesty of our God. The flowers are the setting; the sight is God himself.

Weak hands and feeble knees. Then the scene moves to people, and the descriptions are of exhaustion rather than wickedness: weak hands, knees that will not hold, and an anxious heart, literally a hurried one, racing.

Strengthen the weak hands. The instruction is addressed not to the weak but to whoever is standing near them: strengthen the weak hands, say to the anxious heart. The comfort is delivered by hand, through other people. And what they are told to say is not “you will manage” but Behold, your God will come. Courage rests not on what the weak have but on who is coming. He comes with vengeance (34:8): the arrival that ends the oppressor’s power sets the oppressed free.

Behold, your God. Set that beside the Gospels. These things happen when your God comes, and verses 5 and 6 are the list Jesus sent back to John the Baptist. He was not claiming to be one more prophet with a gift for healing; he was telling John whose arrival the healings announced.

How do I strengthen weak hands? Hebrews takes up these very words for a tired church: lift your drooping hands and strengthen your weak knees (Hebrews 12:12). Notice who is flagging. The friend who has stopped coming on Sundays, the carer three years into a parent’s dementia, the colleague who has gone quiet since the bad news: weakness rarely announces itself. Go and stand beside them. Hands are strengthened by hands: a visit, a meal, an offer to sit with the parent for an afternoon. Say less, and say the true thing. Not “it will all work out”, which you cannot promise, but what Isaiah gives you to say: your God will come, and he will save. Read a psalm with them, or pray briefly, out loud. Keep at it. Encourage the fainthearted, help the weak, be patient with them all (1 Thessalonians 5:14); feeble knees take more than one visit. And remember who did this for you first. Christ came to the weak and the anxious, and of him it was written, a bruised reed he will not break (Isaiah 42:3). His strength is what you are passing on.

When is this fulfilled? In stages: the return from exile was a beginning; Jesus pointed to his own healing of the blind and lame as the sign that the promised day had come (Matthew 11:4–5); and its fullness comes in the new creation, when the redeemed will be whole.

Where Christians differ. Dispensational and other premillennial Christians place much of this chapter in a future thousand-year reign of Christ on earth; others read it as begun at his first coming. All agree that he is the one who brings it.

This commentary’s view. The promise began at Christ’s first coming and will be completed in the new creation (the amillennial view), because Jesus himself says it began with him. Faithful Christians differ here.

Uncertain wording. The flower of verse 1 is uncertain: crocus is a good guess, older translations have “rose”, and others suggest a narcissus. Either way, something bright springs up where nothing grew.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the eyes of the blind shall be opened, and the ears of the deaf unstopped; then shall the lame man leap like a deer, and the tongue of the mute sing for joy. For waters break forth in the wilderness, and streams in the desert; the burning sand shall become a pool, and the thirsty ground springs of water; in the haunt of jackals, where they lie down, the grass shall become reeds and rushes.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God’s coming makes broken bodies more than whole and turns the desert into wetland, and Jesus pointed to these very signs to show who he was.

The eyes of the blind shall be opened. Sight is the first item on Isaiah’s list, and it is what chapter 6 said had been taken from the nation (6:9–10). The blind receiving sight is among the commonest miracles in the ministry of Jesus.

The lame man leap like a deer. The reversals are not modest. The lame man does not merely walk; he will leap like a deer. The mute does not merely speak; his tongue sings. God does not restore people to just about working; he gives far more than they lost.

The burning sand shall become a pool. If the word means the shimmering mirage a thirsty traveller walks toward and never reaches (see below), a cruel illusion becomes real water. God often does the same with human longing: what we ached for and could never reach, he gives in the end. And the jackals of 34:13 lie down where they always did, except that the ground under them has turned to marsh.

Go and tell John. Centuries later John the Baptist, in prison and no longer sure, sent to ask Jesus whether he was the one who was to come. Jesus said: “Go and tell John what you hear and see: the blind receive their sight and the lame walk, lepers are cleansed and the deaf hear” (Matthew 11:4–5). He answered a question about who he was by listing the signs of this chapter and letting John draw the conclusion.

What it does not mean. It does not promise that every sick or disabled believer will be healed now if only they have enough faith. Jesus’ healings were signs that the kingdom had come; the full cure waits for the resurrection, when the body is raised in power (1 Corinthians 15:42–44). God still heals in answer to prayer, but not always, and he also heals through doctors and medicine: using them is no failure of faith.

Uncertain wording. The word translated burning sand (sharab) is rare. It may mean the parched, burning ground itself, or the mirage that shimmers over it, as a related Arabic word does. Both make good sense; the mirage gives the sharper picture.
verseByVerse.note: Reeds and rushes grow only where water stands all year: the desert has become wetland.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 8–10 — A Road for People Who Get Lost
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God builds his people a road home that even the weak and foolish cannot lose. A highway runs through the renewed land, called the Way of Holiness: the unclean do not travel it, yet it belongs to those who walk it, and even fools will not go astray (v. 8). No lion or ravenous beast is found on it; the redeemed walk there in safety (v. 9). And it ends where every journey in the book is heading: the ransomed of the LORD come to Zion singing, crowned with everlasting joy, while sorrow and sighing flee away (v. 10).
verseByVerse.theology: Holiness here is a road rather than an achievement, laid down by God for people who could never have found their own way.
verseByVerse.examples: John hears the promise of verse 10 at the end of Scripture, where God wipes away every tear and mourning is no more (Rev. 21:4). For anyone whom sorrow has chased a long way, this is where the chase ends.

verseByVerse.quote: And a highway shall be there, and it shall be called the Way of Holiness; the unclean shall not pass over it. It shall belong to those who walk on the way; even if they are fools, they shall not go astray. No lion shall be there, nor shall any ravenous beast come up on it; they shall not be found there, but the redeemed shall walk there. And the ransomed of the LORD shall return and come to Zion with singing; everlasting joy shall be upon their heads; they shall obtain gladness and joy, and sorrow and sighing shall flee away.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God builds a road home for his ransomed people that is holy, safe and impossible to lose, and it ends in Zion with everlasting joy.

A highway shall be there. This image will dominate the second half of the book: a road through the wilderness, the one the voice of chapter 40 calls for (40:3), which the Gospels hear in John the Baptist. What this chapter adds is the road’s name and what kind of road it is.

The Way of Holiness. The name would ordinarily suggest a route for the qualified, and the unclean shall not pass over it. Yet the description says even if they are fools, they shall not go astray. It takes no skill to follow and has no turning to miss: a simple person who keeps walking arrives. Everything this book has said about Israel is that they get lost: they could not tell good from evil, could not read a sealed book, could not see or hear. So God does not raise the entry requirements. He builds a road they cannot wander off, and makes the travellers fit for it.

No lion shall be there. Predators do not have to be driven off the road: they are simply not found there. The travellers are the redeemed, and verse 10 calls them the ransomed of the LORD: they are on the road because a price was paid for them, not because they earned a place. The New Testament names the price. The Son of Man came “to give his life as a ransom for many” (Mark 10:45), and he calls himself the way (John 14:6).

Sorrow and sighing shall flee away. The last verse before the history of chapters 36 to 39 ends in a flight. The ransomed obtain gladness and joy, a verb for running someone down and catching them, and sorrow and sighing flee away. For thirty-five chapters sorrow has chased this nation, through vineyards and sieges, drunken priests, empty highways and a city sitting in the dust. Here the direction reverses: grief is running, and joy is in their hands.

Everlasting joy shall be upon their heads. It is the last thing anyone in this book wears on his head. Chapter 3 stripped away the finery; chapter 28 had a fading garland on a drunkard. This crown does not wilt.

No more tears. The book has already promised that God will wipe away tears from all faces (25:8), and John hears it once more at the very end: neither shall there be mourning, nor crying, nor pain anymore, for the former things have passed away (Revelation 21:4).

Uncertain wording. The middle of verse 8 is compressed in Hebrew, literally and it (or he) for them, walking the way. Most translations, like the ESV, take it to mean the road belongs to those who walk it; some take “he” as the LORD, walking the road with his people.

36.subtitle: Sennacherib’s Threat
36.intro:
Where we are. Chapters 36 to 39 change from poetry to narrative and closely match 2 Kings 18 to 20. They stand between the two halves of the book: chapters 36 and 37 bring the Assyrian crisis that the first half has been preaching into to its head, and chapters 38 and 39 point ahead to Babylon. Chapter 36 is the challenge; chapter 37 is God’s answer.

The message. The question the whole book has been asking, “What are you trusting?”, is now shouted at Jerusalem by its enemy. The Rabshakeh’s speech gets almost everything right, that Egypt is useless and Judah helpless, and one thing fatally wrong: he thinks the LORD is one more local god. Faith is tested here not by a demand to deny that God exists but by a demand to stop trusting him in this situation, and the right answer is silence before the enemy and prayer before God.

Why it was said. In 701 BC Sennacherib had taken Judah’s fortified cities and surrounded Jerusalem (see the introduction). Isaiah records the crisis so that every later generation, including the exiles who would one day face Babylon, would see what happens when a king of David’s line trusts the LORD rather than the great powers.

How the chapter makes its case. The setting (vv. 1–3): every fortified city has fallen, and the Rabshakeh stands at the very spot where Ahaz once refused God’s sign (7:3). The case against trust (vv. 4–10): Egypt is a broken reed, Hezekiah has offended his own God, Judah cannot even find riders, and the LORD himself sent Assyria. The appeal over the leaders’ heads (vv. 11–17): refusing to speak Aramaic, he tells the men on the wall to surrender, offering them their own vine and fig tree until the day of deportation. The fatal comparison (vv. 18–22): no god has saved its land, so neither will the LORD; the city answers not a word, and the officials bring the speech to Hezekiah with their clothes torn.

Where it leads. The chapter leads to Christ by pattern. Hezekiah, the son of David, has his trust in God mocked in public, holds his tongue, and waits for God to answer. At the cross the Son of David heard the same taunt, “He trusts in God; let God deliver him now” (Matthew 27:43), and answered not a word; God’s answer was the resurrection. And the Rabshakeh’s error, putting the LORD on a list with the gods of the nations, is answered for ever in Christ, to whom God has given the name above every name (Philippians 2:9).

For us. Many voices still ask, “On what do you rest this trust of yours?”, and some of what they say about our weak supports may even be true. Do not argue on the tempter’s terms and do not panic; take the words, as Hezekiah’s officials did, to the God who has pledged himself to his people.

keyVerse.quote: “Do not let Hezekiah make you trust in the LORD by saying, ‘The LORD will surely deliver us. This city will not be given into the hand of the king of Assyria.’”
keyVerse.note: The Rabshakeh knows what he is attacking: not Egypt as a military ally, but trust in the LORD. He knows this is the specific ground of Jerusalem’s resistance. His entire speech is designed to make that trust seem irrational. This is how every temptation aimed at faith works: it does not ask you to deny God exists; it asks you to stop trusting him in this specific situation.

36.reflection:
The Rabshakeh asks, “On what do you rest this trust of yours?” (v. 4). If someone asked you that today, what would an honest answer be, and are there any “broken reeds” you are leaning on?

Much of the Rabshakeh’s speech was true: Egypt was unreliable and Judah was weak. Why are half-truths often more dangerous to faith than plain lies, and where have you met arguments like his?

He turned Hezekiah’s faithful reform into an accusation (v. 7) and offered Israel’s own hope, each man under his vine and fig tree, on Assyria’s terms (vv. 16–17). How does the enemy of our souls still use these tactics?

The people on the wall said nothing, because the king had commanded it (v. 21), and Jesus too was silent under mockery (Matthew 27:43). When is silence the right answer to an attack on faith, and what should follow it?

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–22 — The Same Patch of Ground
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The trust Isaiah has preached is now put to the test, as Assyria’s spokesman tries to talk Jerusalem out of trusting the LORD. Sennacherib has taken every fortified city in Judah and sends the Rabshakeh to Jerusalem (vv. 1–3). His speech is brilliant: Egypt is a broken reed, Hezekiah has offended his own God by removing the altars, Judah cannot even find riders for two thousand horses, and the LORD himself sent Assyria (vv. 4–10). Asked to speak Aramaic, he turns to the men on the wall in their own language, offers surrender on terms borrowed from Israel’s own hope, and puts the LORD on a list with the gods of Hamath and Sepharvaim (vv. 11–20). The city answers not a word (vv. 21–22).
verseByVerse.theology: The frightening thing about the speech is how much of it is true. The Rabshakeh has read the situation correctly, and the one thing he gets wrong is the only thing that matters.
verseByVerse.examples: Every believer meets some version of this speech: an argument against trusting God built mostly from true facts. The answer is not to deny the facts but to see the one fact the argument leaves out.

verseByVerse.quote: In the fourteenth year of King Hezekiah, Sennacherib king of Assyria came up against all the fortified cities of Judah and took them. And the king of Assyria sent the Rabshakeh from Lachish to King Hezekiah at Jerusalem, with a great army. And he stood by the conduit of the upper pool on the highway to the Washer's Field. And there came out to him Eliakim the son of Hilkiah, who was over the household, and Shebna the secretary, and Joah the son of Asaph, the recorder.
verseByVerse.commentary:
With Judah’s cities fallen and an Assyrian army at the gates, the crisis the book has been preaching into comes to its head, at the very spot where an earlier king refused to trust God.

In the fourteenth year of King Hezekiah. The book changes from poetry to prose, because everything argued from chapter 7 onwards is about to be tested in a single crisis, under Hezekiah.

All the fortified cities of Judah. The situation is desperate. All the fortified cities have fallen; Assyrian records boast of forty-six walled towns taken in this campaign. Only the capital is left.

The conduit of the upper pool. Isaiah has been waiting twenty-nine chapters to name the place where the Rabshakeh stands. At 7:3 God sent Isaiah to meet Ahaz at the end of the conduit of the upper pool on the highway to the Washer’s Field: the same conduit, the same pool, the same patch of ground outside the wall. There a king of Judah was offered a sign as deep as Sheol (the grave) or as high as heaven, refused it, and bought Assyrian protection with temple silver. Here, at that exact spot, Assyria has arrived to collect, and a different king is about to do something different with what he is handed.

Eliakim and Shebna. Two of the officials are from chapter 22. Shebna, who was cutting himself a grand tomb while the city was threatened, has been demoted from steward to secretary; Eliakim, on whom God said he would hang the key of the house of David, is over the household. The prophecy of 22:15–22 has already come true, and the three men walking out are the proof.

What the Assyrian records say. Sennacherib’s annals add that he shut Hezekiah up in Jerusalem, and his reliefs of the siege of Lachish survive in the British Museum. Isaiah leaves out the tribute Hezekiah paid to buy Sennacherib off (2 Kings 18:14–16), because his subject is the trust that came after it. The date is a known puzzle: 2 Kings 18:10 puts the fall of Samaria (722 BC) in Hezekiah’s sixth year, which would make his fourteenth year about 714, not 701. Many think Hezekiah first reigned alongside his father, with the years counted from different starting points; others suspect a copying slip in one number. It is not settled, and it is a question of how the years were counted, not of whether the siege happened.

Uncertain wording. Rabshakeh is a title, not a name. It is usually explained from an Assyrian title meaning something like “chief cupbearer”, though by this time it marked one of the king’s highest officials, so some translations render it “field commander”.
verseByVerse.note: Chapters 36–39 largely repeat 2 Kings 18–20. Sennacherib’s campaign came in 701 BC.

verseByVerse.quote: And the Rabshakeh said to them, "Say to Hezekiah, 'Thus says the great king, the king of Assyria: On what do you rest this trust of yours? Do you think that mere words are strategy and power for war? In whom do you now trust, that you have rebelled against me? Behold, you are trusting in Egypt, that broken reed of a staff, which will pierce the hand of any man who leans on it. Such is Pharaoh king of Egypt to all who trust in him. But if you say to me, "We trust in the LORD our God," is it not he whose high places and altars Hezekiah has removed, saying to Judah and to Jerusalem, "You shall worship before this altar"? Come now, make a wager with my master the king of Assyria: I will give you two thousand horses, if you are able on your part to set riders on them. How then can you repulse a single captain among the least of my master's servants, when you trust in Egypt for chariots and for horsemen? Moreover, is it without the LORD that I have come up against this land to destroy it? The LORD said to me, "Go up against this land and destroy it."'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Rabshakeh attacks Jerusalem’s trust with a speech that mixes truth and lies: he is right about Egypt, wrong about Hezekiah’s reforms, and half right that God sent him.

On what do you rest this trust of yours? The speech opens with the question the whole book has been asking Judah, and the Rabshakeh is a better theologian than most of Jerusalem’s officials, which is what makes him dangerous. His jibe about mere words is aimed at a nation whose defence consists of a prophet’s sentences.

That broken reed of a staff. He is right about Egypt. A river reed looks like a walking stick and will take no weight; lean on it and it splinters into your palm. Isaiah has been saying so for six chapters: Egypt is “Rahab who sits still” (30:7), and “The Egyptians are man, and not God” (31:3). The Assyrian is quoting the substance of God’s own prophet back at God’s own city.

Whose high places and altars Hezekiah has removed. The second move is cleverer, and false. Hezekiah had torn down the local shrines (the high places), the most obedient thing he ever did, and the Rabshakeh presents it as an offence against the very God being trusted. It is the standing tactic of Satan the accuser, who produces obedience as evidence of guilt.

Two thousand horses. The horses are an insult: he will supply the cavalry if Judah can find two thousand men who can ride, which everyone knows they cannot.

The LORD said to me. The boldest move is the claim that God sent him, and in a sense God had: chapter 10 called Assyria the rod of his anger. The Rabshakeh has stumbled onto something true and is using it as a weapon, and he does not know what chapter 10 said next: the axe that boasts against the one who swings it is judged (10:15).
verseByVerse.note: “Rabshakeh” is an Assyrian title, not a name.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Eliakim, Shebna, and Joah said to the Rabshakeh, "Please speak to your servants in Aramaic, for we understand it. Do not speak to us in the language of Judah within the hearing of the people who are on the wall." But the Rabshakeh said, "Has my master sent me to speak these words to your master and to you, and not to the men sitting on the wall, who are doomed with you to eat their own dung and drink their own urine?" Then the Rabshakeh stood and called out in a loud voice in the language of Judah: "Hear the words of the great king, the king of Assyria! Thus says the king: 'Do not let Hezekiah deceive you, for he will not be able to deliver you. Do not let Hezekiah make you trust in the LORD by saying, "The LORD will surely deliver us. This city will not be given into the hand of the king of Assyria." Do not listen to Hezekiah. For thus says the king of Assyria: Make your peace with me and come out to me. Then each one of you will eat of his own vine, and each one of his own fig tree, and each one of you will drink the water of his own cistern, until I come and take you away to a land like your own land, a land of grain and wine, a land of bread and vineyards.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Refusing to keep the talks private, the Rabshakeh goes over the leaders’ heads to the people, attacking their trust in the LORD and offering them Israel’s own hope on Assyria’s terms.

Please speak to your servants in Aramaic. The officials’ request is transparent: soldiers and civilians are listening on the wall, and morale is the only asset the city has left. Aramaic was the diplomatic language of the region; they are asking him to keep this between professionals.

The men sitting on the wall. He refuses, because the men on the wall are exactly who he came for. He has not come to negotiate with the government but to turn the people against it, and he describes the starvation of a siege in the hearing of the very people who would suffer it.

Do not let Hezekiah make you trust in the LORD. So an Assyrian officer, fluent in the language of Judah, stands where a prophet once stood and shouts theology at a wall. What he attacks is not the existence of God, who he claims sent him, but trust, by name, twice, driving a wedge between the people and the king who is telling them to trust.

Israel’s hope on Assyria’s terms. Then the cruellest thing in the speech, because it is borrowed from the Bible: every man under his own vine and fig tree, Scripture’s standard picture of the peace God promised (1 Kings 4:25; Micah 4:4). He offers Israel’s own hope on Assyria’s terms, and the small print follows: until I come and take you away to a land like your own land. That is deportation, described as an estate agent describes a house. Temptation still offers God’s good gifts without God, and hides the cost in the small print.

verseByVerse.quote: Beware lest Hezekiah mislead you by saying, "The LORD will deliver us." Has any of the gods of the nations delivered his land out of the hand of the king of Assyria? Where are the gods of Hamath and Arpad? Where are the gods of Sepharvaim? Have they delivered Samaria out of my hand? Who among all the gods of these lands have delivered their lands out of my hand, that the LORD should deliver Jerusalem out of my hand?'" But they were silent and answered him not a word, for the king's command was, "Do not answer him." Then Eliakim the son of Hilkiah, who was over the household, and Shebna the secretary, and Joah the son of Asaph, the recorder, came to Hezekiah with their clothes torn, and told him the words of the Rabshakeh.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Rabshakeh’s one fatal error is to count the LORD among the gods of the nations, and Jerusalem answers him not with argument but with silence, taking his words to the king and so to God.

Where are the gods of Hamath and Arpad? Now the argument from evidence, the strongest thing he has said. He names cities and asks where their gods are, and every answer is: gone. His record is unbroken and factual.

That the LORD should deliver Jerusalem. Then the sentence that undoes him: he puts the LORD on the list. Everything up to this point was accurate: Egypt is a reed, the record is unbroken, the situation is hopeless. The one error in the speech is what he takes the LORD to be. He has filed the God of Israel among the gods of Hamath and Sepharvaim, the mistake chapter 10 said he would make and be judged for. It is the mistake the first half of this book was written to prevent, and chapter 40 will spend thirty-one verses on it: To whom then will you compare me? (40:25) The Rabshakeh has answered that question out loud, in Hebrew, at the top of his voice, and wrongly.

But they were silent. The city’s reply is disciplined silence: listening to its faith ridiculed in its own language by a man with most of the facts on his side, and ordered to say nothing. That is not weakness or indifference. Some arguments cannot be won by answering back, and the right response is to take them to God. The officials come to Hezekiah with their clothes torn in grief, and the next chapter shows the king taking the words to the LORD.

Let God deliver him now. The same taunt was later thrown at the Son of David himself. As he hung on the cross the chief priests said, He trusts in God; let God deliver him now (Matthew 27:43), and he answered not a word. God’s answer to Hezekiah came in a night; his answer to that taunt came on the third day, and it is why anyone may trust him still.

One god further. The Rabshakeh’s argument has a modern cousin. You already disbelieve in Zeus, Thor and the gods of Hamath, the sceptic says; I simply go one god further. It rests on the same assumption as the speech under the walls: that the LORD is one more item in the category, a local deity with better publicity. Hezekiah’s prayer in the next chapter gives the answer. The gods of the nations were destroyed, for they were no gods, but the work of men’s hands, wood and stone (37:19). The difference between them and the LORD is not one of size but of kind, the difference between a statue and the sculptor. The prophets mocked made gods long before the sceptics did. The real question is whether there is a Maker who is on nobody’s list, and the answer this story gives is a night, an angel and a lifted siege, and centuries later an empty tomb outside the same walls.

Uncertain wording. Hamath and Arpad were well-known cities of Syria that Assyria had conquered; where Sepharvaim lay is not known, though 2 Kings 17:24 names it among the places whose people Assyria resettled in Samaria. The point does not depend on it: every name on the list was a god who failed.

36.theology:
The same patch of ground. The Rabshakeh stands on the very spot where Isaiah met Ahaz at 7:3. Two kings of Judah, one address, two answers: Ahaz bought Assyria with temple silver; Hezekiah takes what he is handed into the house of the LORD. Isaiah built his book around that piece of ground, and this chapter completes the comparison.

A speech that is mostly true. Egypt is a broken reed, and no nation’s god has stopped Assyria. The cleverest move is to present Hezekiah’s most obedient act as an offence against God, which is what Satan the accuser always does.

The one error, and the silence. The Rabshakeh puts the LORD on a list of gods, the mistake chapter 40 will spend thirty-one verses correcting, and the city replies with disciplined silence.

37.subtitle: Hezekiah’s Prayer and the Angel
37.intro:
Where we are. Chapter 36 left Jerusalem surrounded, its people silent on the wall, and the Rabshakeh’s boast hanging in the air: no god has ever saved a nation from the king of Assyria. Chapter 37 gives God’s answer, the climax of the Assyrian crisis Isaiah has been addressing since chapter 7.

The message. The living God hears when his name is mocked, and he answers the prayer of a helpless people by defending his own honour. Sennacherib thought he was the author of his conquests, but he was only carrying out what God planned long ago. Jerusalem is spared not because of its walls or even its king’s faith, but for God’s own sake and for his promise to David.

Why it was said. In 701 BC Judah’s fortified cities had fallen and Jerusalem stood alone (see the introduction). Every visible argument was on Assyria’s side. Later generations, facing Babylon and other empires, would need to know whether the God of Zion could be trusted against the great powers.

How the chapter makes its case. Hezekiah goes into the temple and sends to Isaiah, and God answers: do not be afraid (vv. 1–7). A sharper letter claims that God himself is a deceiver (vv. 8–13). Hezekiah spreads it before the LORD and prays that all the kingdoms of the earth may know that he alone is God (vv. 14–20). Isaiah’s reply taunts the emperor: whom have you mocked? I planned it all, and I will put my hook in your nose (vv. 21–29). The remnant will take root again (vv. 30–32), and the city will not see one arrow (vv. 33–35). In one night the angel of the LORD strikes the camp, and Sennacherib goes home to die in the temple of his own god (vv. 36–38).

Where it leads. Chiefly by covenant: the city is defended “for the sake of my servant David” (v. 35), and that promise is kept in Jesus, to whom God gives “the throne of his father David” (Luke 1:32). Also by pattern: a son of David at the end of his strength cries to God while an enemy mocks. The true Son of David was mocked in the same way, “He trusts in God; let God deliver him now” (Matthew 27:43), and God answered not by sparing him death but by raising him from it, defeating an enemy far greater than Assyria.

For us. When the letter arrives, the diagnosis, the final demand, the voice that says God cannot be trusted, we can do what Hezekiah did: spread it before the LORD and ask him to act for the honour of his name. We pray through the Son of David who was not spared, and his victory means that no enemy of God’s people has the last word.

keyVerse.quote: “So now, O LORD our God, save us from his hand, that all the kingdoms of the earth may know that you alone are the LORD.”
keyVerse.note: The motive of this prayer, that the world should know who God is, runs all the way from here to the Lord’s Prayer: “hallowed be your name.” Hezekiah does not pray primarily for his own comfort or survival but that the nations may see that the LORD alone is God. He asks for what God himself intends, which is why it is answered so spectacularly.

37.reflection:
Hezekiah went first to the house of the LORD and to God’s prophet (vv. 1–2), where Ahaz had gone to inspect the water supply. When trouble comes, where do you instinctively go first, and why?

Hezekiah “spread it before the LORD” (v. 14). What letter, worry or accusation are you carrying at the moment, and what would it look like to lay it out before God rather than argue with it or hide it?

Hezekiah asked for rescue “that all the kingdoms of the earth may know that you alone are the LORD” (v. 20). How might praying for God’s name to be known change the way you pray about your own needs?

God defended the city “for my own sake and for the sake of my servant David” (v. 35). How does it help, on a bad day, to know that God keeps us for Christ’s sake and not because of our record?
