verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–20 — He Spread It Before the LORD
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: When the enemy mocks God, the right answer is not argument but prayer. Hezekiah tears his clothes, goes into the house of the LORD and sends to Isaiah with a picture of utter exhaustion: children at the point of birth and no strength to deliver them (vv. 1–4). Isaiah replies at once: do not be afraid, for the insult was against God, and Sennacherib will hear a rumour, go home and fall by the sword (vv. 5–7). A second letter goes further, claiming that God himself is deceiving Hezekiah (vv. 8–13). Hezekiah spreads it before the LORD (v. 14) and prays: you alone are God; hear and see; save us, so that all the kingdoms of the earth may know it (vv. 15–20).
verseByVerse.theology: The prayer is a model, and its shape is the thing to learn. It says who God is before it makes a single request: you are enthroned above the cherubim, you alone are God of all the kingdoms of the earth, you made heaven and earth. Then Hezekiah concedes the Assyrian's evidence entirely. The other gods did fall, and he says why: they were no gods. He does not dispute the Rabshakeh’s facts; he explains them differently. When the petition comes it is not "save us because we deserve it" but save us from his hand, that all the kingdoms of the earth may know that you alone are the LORD. The ground of the request is God's reputation, not Judah's need or merit, which is the safest ground any prayer can stand on.
verseByVerse.examples: Verse 14 is a model for anyone holding a letter, a diagnosis, a message they cannot answer: take it, unedited, to the God who has already bound himself to you by covenant, and spread it out where he can read it.

verseByVerse.quote: As soon as King Hezekiah heard it, he tore his clothes and covered himself with sackcloth and went into the house of the LORD. And he sent Eliakim, who was over the household, and Shebna the secretary, and the senior priests, covered with sackcloth, to the prophet Isaiah the son of Amoz. They said to him, "Thus says Hezekiah, 'This day is a day of distress, of rebuke, and of disgrace; children have come to the point of birth, and there is no strength to bring them forth. It may be that the LORD your God will hear the words of the Rabshakeh, whom his master the king of Assyria has sent to mock the living God, and will rebuke the words that the LORD your God has heard; therefore lift up your prayer for the remnant that is left.'" When the servants of King Hezekiah came to Isaiah, Isaiah said to them, "Say to your master, 'Thus says the LORD: Do not be afraid because of the words that you have heard, with which the young men of the king of Assyria have reviled me. Behold, I will put a spirit in him, so that he shall hear a rumor and return to his own land, and I will make him fall by the sword in his own land.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Hezekiah turns to God’s house and God’s prophet, and God answers at once: do not be afraid, for the insult was against me.

Into the house of the LORD. The contrast with chapter 7 needs no comment. Ahaz, facing a smaller threat at the same spot (7:3; 36:2), inspected the water supply and sent to Assyria for help. Hezekiah, facing Assyria itself, puts on sackcloth, goes into the temple, and sends for the prophet; Ahaz had a prophet come to him unasked and refused what he offered. Hezekiah’s first steps are open to any believer at the end of his strength: into God’s presence, and to God’s word.

Children have come to the point of birth. An exact image of helplessness: a labour at full term that has stopped. The child is there, the moment has come, and the strength is not. It is not despair, which has given up, but the misery of reaching the last stage with nothing left for it.

Do not be afraid. The reply comes immediately, and it says whose insult it was: the words that have reviled me. God takes the mockery personally and lifts it off Hezekiah, the first relief in the chapter.

He shall hear a rumor and return. Verse 7 announces the whole deliverance before anything has happened: a rumour, a withdrawal, and a death in his own land. Every part comes true by the end of the chapter (vv. 9, 37–38).

verseByVerse.quote: The Rabshakeh returned, and found the king of Assyria fighting against Libnah, for he had heard that the king had left Lachish. Now the king heard concerning Tirhakah king of Cush, "He has set out to fight against you." And when he heard it, he sent messengers to Hezekiah, saying, "Thus shall you speak to Hezekiah king of Judah: 'Do not let your God in whom you trust deceive you by promising that Jerusalem will not be given into the hand of the king of Assyria. Behold, you have heard what the kings of Assyria have done to all lands, devoting them to destruction. And shall you be delivered? Have the gods of the nations delivered them, the nations that my fathers destroyed, Gozan, Haran, Rezeph, and the people of Eden who were in Telassar? Where is the king of Hamath, the king of Arpad, the king of the city of Sepharvaim, the king of Hena, or the king of Ivvah?'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Sennacherib answers with a letter that goes further than before: it calls God himself a deceiver.

Fighting against Libnah. Sennacherib has finished with Lachish, Judah’s second city, whose siege he later had carved on the walls of his palace at Nineveh, and moved on to Libnah nearby. Jerusalem is being left till last.

He sent messengers to Hezekiah. The rumour of verse 7 arrives on schedule, an Egyptian-Cushite army on the move, and Sennacherib responds not by breaking off the campaign but with a letter, more threatening than the first speech because it is written and personal.

Do not let your God in whom you trust deceive you. The Rabshakeh said Hezekiah was deceiving the people (36:14); the letter says God is deceiving Hezekiah. It is the serpent’s old question (Genesis 3:1–5), aimed not at the walls but at trust in what God has said.

Have the gods of the nations delivered them? The list of conquered places and their kings (vv. 12–13) makes an argument that by every visible measure was true: no god had ever stopped Assyria. Why should the God of Judah be different? Sennacherib had never yet met the living God.
verseByVerse.note: Cush is probably Nubia (ESV note). Tirhakah (Taharqa) led the army in 701 BC but became king only about 690; the account gives him the title he later held.

verseByVerse.quote: Hezekiah received the letter from the hand of the messengers, and read it; and Hezekiah went up to the house of the LORD, and spread it before the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Hezekiah lays the threat itself open before God, without a word. Verse 14 is the hinge of the chapter.

Spread it before the LORD. He takes the actual sheet with the blasphemy on it, carries it up the hill and opens it out flat in front of God. He does not summarise it, soften the parts about God being a liar, or compose a reply. He puts it where it can be read, and steps back.

What the silence was for. In chapter 36 the order was do not answer him, and the city said nothing. This is what the silence was for. Some accusations should not be argued with; they should be carried to God and laid out before him.

Your letter. The diagnosis, the final demand, the message that says your God has let you down: through Jesus our high priest we may bring them all and “with confidence draw near to the throne of grace” (Hebrews 4:16).

verseByVerse.quote: And Hezekiah prayed to the LORD: "O LORD of hosts, God of Israel, enthroned above the cherubim, you are the God, you alone, of all the kingdoms of the earth; you have made the heavens and the earth. Incline your ear, O LORD, and hear; open your eyes, O LORD, and see; and hear all the words of Sennacherib, which he has sent to mock the living God. Truly, O LORD, the kings of Assyria have laid waste all the nations and their lands, and have cast their gods into the fire. For they were no gods, but the work of men's hands, wood and stone. Therefore they were destroyed. So now, O LORD our God, save us from his hand, that all the kingdoms of the earth may know that you alone are the LORD."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Hezekiah’s prayer rests everything on who God is, and asks for rescue so that the world will know that the LORD alone is God.

Enthroned above the cherubim. The prayer is addressed to the LORD of hosts enthroned above the cherubim over the ark, while the most powerful king on earth sits in a tent outside the walls. Its shape, first who God is and then a request resting on God’s name, is set out in the section note above.

Incline your ear, O LORD, and hear. Hezekiah asks God to hear and see “all the words of Sennacherib, which he has sent to mock the living God” (v. 17). The living God is the point of contrast. The gods Assyria burned were “the work of men’s hands, wood and stone” (v. 19), with ears that do not hear and eyes that do not see (Psalm 115:4–7). The prayer asks the living God to do what they could not.

Truly, O LORD. Hezekiah does not pretend the threat is smaller than it is: Assyria really has laid waste the nations (v. 18). Faith does not deny the facts; it sets them before a greater fact.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 21–38 — By the Way He Came
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Because Hezekiah prayed, God answers, and the boaster is undone exactly as foretold. Isaiah’s reply is a taunt-song, Assyria’s own form turned back on her, with Zion as a young girl tossing her head at a retreating emperor (vv. 21–22). The real question is whom he has mocked: the Holy One of Israel (vv. 23–25). God planned long ago what Sennacherib thought he had achieved, knows his every movement, and will lead him home with a hook in his nose (vv. 26–29). The remnant will take root again (vv. 30–32), and not one arrow will touch the city, defended for David’s sake (vv. 33–35). The outcome takes three sentences: one night, one angel, and a death in the temple of a useless god (vv. 36–38).
verseByVerse.theology: Verses 26-27 are the centre of the chapter and the answer to the boast of chapter 36. Assyria thought it was writing history, but it was carrying out a plan God settled long ago: every conquest she took credit for was already on his list. In 10:15 Assyria was the axe that cannot boast against the one who swings it; here the axe is told so to its face.
verseByVerse.examples: The sign in verses 30-32 is remarkable for what it is not. It is not a display of power, not fire from heaven, but a farming calendar. An occupied country cannot plant, so for two years they will eat what grows of itself; in the third year they sow, reap and plant vineyards. God's sign that the crisis is over is the resumption of ordinary life, which is what deliverance actually looks like from inside a household.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Isaiah the son of Amoz sent to Hezekiah, saying, "Thus says the LORD, the God of Israel: Because you have prayed to me concerning Sennacherib king of Assyria, this is the word that the LORD has spoken concerning him: "'She despises you, she scorns you— the virgin daughter of Zion; she wags her head behind you— the daughter of Jerusalem.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Because Hezekiah prayed, God answers with a mocking song over the emperor, sung by the city he thought he had cornered.

Because you have prayed to me. The chapter attributes what follows to a man with a letter spread out in a temple. God had already promised the outcome (v. 7), yet he ordains the means as well as the end, and prayer was one of them.

The virgin daughter of Zion. A taunt-song, the mocking song of a victor, which Assyria sang over everyone it conquered, is turned back on her. The picture is deliberately humiliating: not an army but a young girl, untaken, standing behind a retreating emperor and shaking her head at him.

verseByVerse.quote: "'Whom have you mocked and reviled? Against whom have you raised your voice and lifted your eyes to the heights? Against the Holy One of Israel! By your servants you have mocked the Lord, and you have said, With my many chariots I have gone up the heights of the mountains, to the far recesses of Lebanon, to cut down its tallest cedars, its choicest cypresses, to come to its remotest height, its most fruitful forest. I dug wells and drank waters, to dry up with the sole of my foot all the streams of Egypt.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Sennacherib’s real mistake was not military but theological: he did not know whom he was mocking.

Against the Holy One of Israel! The question the confrontation turns on (v. 23) is not what he has done but whom he has done it to, the one thing the Rabshakeh never stopped to ask. The answer rings out at the end of the verse in Isaiah’s own name for God (6:3).

By your servants you have mocked the Lord. Sennacherib spoke through the Rabshakeh and his letter (chapter 36; vv. 9–13), and God holds the king answerable for what his servants said. The boast (vv. 24–25) is the language of Assyrian royal inscriptions: chariots driven up the mountains, the tallest cedars of Lebanon cut down for the king’s buildings, wells dug in foreign land.

With the sole of my foot. The emperor at his most absurd: he dried up the rivers of Egypt with the sole of his foot, by walking through them. Every “I” in the boast is answered in the next verse by God’s “I”.

verseByVerse.quote: "'Have you not heard that I determined it long ago? I planned from days of old what now I bring to pass, that you should make fortified cities crash into heaps of ruins, while their inhabitants, shorn of strength, are dismayed and confounded, and have become like plants of the field and like tender grass, like grass on the housetops, blighted before it is grown. "'I know your sitting down and your going out and coming in, and your raging against me. Because you have raged against me and your complacency has come to my ears, I will put my hook in your nose and my bit in your mouth, and I will turn you back on the way by which you came.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
God tells the emperor that his conquests were God’s plan, that his every movement is known, and that he will be led home like a captive.

I determined it long ago. The emperor who thought he had planned his campaigns was only bringing to pass what God planned from days of old (v. 26), the axe of 10:15 boasting over the one who swings it. That does not excuse him: verse 29 still judges his rage.

Like plants of the field. The cities fell not because Assyria was great but because God left their people “shorn of strength” (v. 27), like grass on a housetop, which withers before it grows (Psalm 129:6). And God knows the king through and through: his sitting down, his going out and coming in, and his raging (v. 28; compare Psalm 139:1–3).

My hook in your nose. Assyrian monuments show captives led by ropes fastened to rings through their lips. God applies the empire’s trademark cruelty to the empire, and the destination is not a prison but home, back on the way by which you came, the same road in reverse.

On a leash they cannot see. The powers that rage against God’s people serve a plan they did not write (Psalm 2:1–4). The early church prayed exactly this when Herod and Pilate had done to Jesus only what God’s plan had predestined (Acts 4:25–28).

verseByVerse.quote: "And this shall be the sign for you: this year you shall eat what grows of itself, and in the second year what springs from that. Then in the third year sow and reap, and plant vineyards, and eat their fruit. And the surviving remnant of the house of Judah shall again take root downward and bear fruit upward. For out of Jerusalem shall go a remnant, and out of Mount Zion a band of survivors. The zeal of the LORD of hosts will do this.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God gives Hezekiah a sign that the land will recover and the remnant will grow again, guaranteed by his own zeal.

This shall be the sign for you. Two years of eating what grows of itself, then sowing, reaping and planting vineyards (v. 30). It is not what anyone would have asked for, and it is exactly right: planting a vineyard is the most confident act in farming, because vines take years to bear and nobody plants them expecting to leave.

Take root downward and bear fruit upward. Sennacherib boasted in his annals of taking forty-six of Judah’s walled towns, and the countryside was stripped. The survivors are a plant cut back almost to nothing: roots first, then fruit (v. 31), a small people from whom God will grow his people again, as the holy seed in the stump promised (6:13). From that stump would come the shoot of Jesse (11:1).

The zeal of the LORD of hosts will do this. The guarantee is the sentence that closed the promise of the child in 9:7. Not Hezekiah’s faith, not the walls, not the Egyptian army marching up from the south: his zeal.

verseByVerse.quote: "Therefore thus says the LORD concerning the king of Assyria: He shall not come into this city or shoot an arrow there or come before it with a shield or cast up a siege mound against it. By the way that he came, by the same he shall return, and he shall not come into this city, declares the LORD. For I will defend this city to save it, for my own sake and for the sake of my servant David."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The city will not see a single arrow, because God defends it for his own sake and for his promise to David.

He shall not come into this city. Not one arrow, shield or siege mound (v. 33). A siege mound was the ramp an army built to bring its battering rams up to a wall; the remains of the Assyrian ramp at Lachish can still be seen. At Jerusalem none was ever built (v. 34).

For the sake of my servant David. Not Judah’s merit, but God’s honour and a promise made to David three centuries earlier, that his son would sit on his throne for ever (2 Samuel 7:12–16). That promise runs on to the angel’s words to Mary (Luke 1:32). The city was kept that night because the Son of David had still to come to it, and believers are kept on the same ground: not their record but God’s covenant with the true David.

Then why did Jerusalem fall to Babylon? This was no promise that the city could never fall. After the sins of Manasseh, God gave it up (2 Kings 23:26–27), as chapter 39 foresees. What could not fail was the promise to David, and the line survived the exile to reach Christ.

verseByVerse.quote: And the angel of the LORD went out and struck down 185,000 in the camp of the Assyrians. And when people arose early in the morning, behold, these were all dead bodies. Then Sennacherib king of Assyria departed and returned home and lived at Nineveh. And as he was worshiping in the house of Nisroch his god, Adrammelech and Sharezer, his sons, struck him down with the sword. And after they escaped into the land of Ararat, Esarhaddon his son reigned in his place.
verseByVerse.commentary:
In one night God destroys the army without a Judean sword, and the emperor who mocked him dies in the temple of his own god.

The angel of the LORD went out. There is no battle in these two sentences. No Judean sword is drawn, as 31:8 promised: the Assyrian shall fall by a sword, not of man. Scripture names only the angel; some think his instrument was a sudden plague, as in David’s day (2 Samuel 24:15–16). Either way God did it, overnight, without Judah.

When people arose early in the morning. The timing is the sentence from 17:14, written years earlier: at evening time, behold, terror! Before morning, they are no more.

Struck him down with the sword. The last verse completes the word of verse 7: a rumour, a return, and a death by the sword in his own land. The narrative compresses time: the murder came about twenty years later, in 681 BC, and Babylonian records confirm that Sennacherib was killed by a son.

In the house of Nisroch his god. The man who asked what god had ever delivered anybody was killed by his own sons while worshipping in the temple of his own god. The God he had put on a list with Hamath and Sepharvaim never sent a soldier: only an angel, once, at night.

Did this happen? Sennacherib’s annals boast that he shut Hezekiah up “like a bird in a cage” but never claim to have taken Jerusalem, and royal annals rarely record defeats. The siege lifted, Sennacherib never returned, and Herodotus preserves an Egyptian story of a sudden disaster striking an Assyrian army. The account is best read as plain history.

The greater victory. God won the greater battle the same way. At the cross Christ alone disarmed the rulers and authorities (Colossians 2:15); his people, like Jerusalem that morning, wake to find the victory already won.

Uncertain wording. The Hebrew word for thousand can in some passages mean a clan or military unit, and some take it so here, which would make the number far smaller. Nothing in the passage requires it, and 185,000 remains the likeliest reading.

37.theology:
He spread it before the LORD. Hezekiah answers blasphemy not with argument but with prayer, and the prayer does not ask God to notice Judah's virtue; it asks him to defend the honour of his own name before all the kingdoms of the earth.

Three earlier promises land here. 31:8 said Assyria would fall by a sword, not of man; 17:14 said it would be gone before morning; and 7:3 put a king of Judah at the same conduit where 36:2 put the Rabshakeh. Verse 35 gives the deepest reason: the city is defended for the sake of my servant David, because the promise of a Son of David on the throne for ever was still to be kept, as it is in Jesus (Luke 1:32–33).

Prayer from a people already his. Hezekiah does not bargain or plead his record; he prays as one of the people the LORD has already made his own, to the God who promised David a house. That is the believer's ground still. We pray badly and trust fitfully, but Christ's perfect trust and obedience stand for us, and the Spirit himself helps us in our weakness when we do not know what to pray (Romans 8:26).

38.subtitle: Hezekiah’s Illness and Recovery
38.intro:
Where we are. “In those days” (v. 1) takes us back before the deliverance of chapter 37: Hezekiah fell ill while Assyria still threatened, for verse 6 promises the city’s rescue. Chapters 38 and 39 are placed after the great deliverance to turn the book from Assyria towards Babylon.

The message. God holds every life in his hand, and he hears the prayers and sees the tears of those who cry to him. He gives Hezekiah fifteen more years, but the song Hezekiah writes afterwards finds something greater than added years: a God who in love has cast all his sins behind his back. Life is a gift to be lived humbly and in praise, and its deepest need is pardon.

Why it was said. Hezekiah was the king through whom God had promised to keep Jerusalem, and Manasseh, his heir, was not yet born (compare 2 Kings 21:1). The illness threatened the king, the city and, as it seemed, David’s line (see the introduction). The chapter also prepares for chapter 39, where the healed king’s pride opens the door to Babylon.

How the chapter makes its case. The sentence and the prayer (vv. 1–3): Isaiah tells Hezekiah to set his house in order, and the king turns to the wall and weeps. The answer (vv. 4–8): God has heard and seen, adds fifteen years and the city’s deliverance, and makes the shadow go back ten steps on the dial of Ahaz. The song (vv. 9–20): Hezekiah remembers the terror of being cut off in mid-life (vv. 9–14), sees that the bitterness was for his good and that God has cast his sins behind his back (vv. 15–17), and resolves to praise God among the living (vv. 18–20). A footnote records the fig poultice and the king’s request for a sign (vv. 21–22).

Where it leads. By pattern, and by the need it exposes. Another son of David “offered up prayers and supplications, with loud cries and tears, to him who was able to save him from death, and he was heard” (Hebrews 5:7). Hezekiah was heard by being spared death for a while; Christ was heard by passing through death and rising, never to die again. Hezekiah’s fifteen years ran out, but Christ gives a life that death cannot end (John 11:25–26). And the pardon Hezekiah praised rests on the cross, where the LORD laid our iniquity on his Servant (53:6).

For us. We may bring illness, fear and the unfinished half of a life to God, with tears if need be, for he sees them. He does not always answer with more years, but he never refuses pardon to those who ask, and every year he gives is for walking humbly and praising him among the living.

keyVerse.quote: “It was for my welfare that I had great bitterness; but in love you have delivered my life from the pit of destruction, for you have cast all my sins behind your back.”
keyVerse.note: Hezekiah could call his bitterness good only looking back, and the reason is in the rest of the verse. He puts forgiveness at the centre of his thanks: not the healing, nor the miracle of the shadow, but “you have cast all my sins behind your back”. What he most needed was not years but pardon, and the pattern is the cross, where the deepest suffering carried the deepest love.

38.reflection:
Hezekiah turned his face to the wall and wept as he prayed, and God said, “I have seen your tears” (v. 5). What difference does it make to know that God sees our tears and not only hears our words?

God does not always heal in answer to prayer (2 Corinthians 12:7–9), and Hezekiah’s healing came with a fig poultice (v. 21). How can we pray boldly for healing, use medicine gladly, and trust God whatever the answer?

Hezekiah could say “it was for my welfare that I had great bitterness” only afterwards (v. 17). Why is this a sentence for the sufferer to say rather than for others to say to him? Is there a hard season you can now see God used for good?

Of all he received, Hezekiah gave thanks above all that God had cast all his sins behind his back (v. 17). What are you still carrying that Christ has already dealt with?

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God hears the prayer and sees the tears of a dying man, and gives him time back. Isaiah brings a sentence with no comfort in it: set your house in order, for you shall die (v. 1). Hezekiah turns his face to the wall, asks God to remember his faithfulness, and weeps bitterly (vv. 2–3). The word returns at once: God has heard and seen, and he adds fifteen years, with the city’s deliverance from Assyria attached (vv. 4–6). The sign fits the gift: the shadow on the dial of Ahaz goes back ten steps, time running backwards where the king can see it (vv. 7–8).
verseByVerse.theology: The prayer is not resignation but protest. Hezekiah does not accept the verdict quietly; he argues from his record and weeps bitterly. Modern readers sometimes find that unspiritual, but Scripture contains a good deal of this kind of praying and does not disapprove of it: the answer here comes so fast that Isaiah is sent back before he can leave the middle court (2 Kings 20:4).
verseByVerse.examples: The sign is chosen with some irony. Ahaz is the king who stood at the conduit and was offered any sign at all, as deep as Sheol or as high as heaven, and said he would not ask (7:11-12). What Ahaz would not ask for, his son is given on a structure bearing his father's name.

verseByVerse.quote: In those days Hezekiah became sick and was at the point of death. And Isaiah the prophet the son of Amoz came to him, and said to him, "Thus says the LORD: Set your house in order, for you shall die, you shall not recover." Then Hezekiah turned his face to the wall and prayed to the LORD, and said, "Please, O LORD, remember how I have walked before you in faithfulness and with a whole heart, and have done what is good in your sight." And Hezekiah wept bitterly.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Told he will die, Hezekiah takes the sentence straight to God in tears, asking him to remember a servant who has been loyal to him.

Set your house in order. The message has no comfort in it. Not you are seriously ill but the instruction given to a man with days rather than years: settle your affairs.

Hezekiah turned his face to the wall. The detail is exact and human: it is what a person does when he does not want to be watched. This prayer happens not in the temple, as in the previous chapter, but with his face to the plaster.

With a whole heart. Hezekiah does not claim to be sinless. “A whole heart” means undivided loyalty, and his record bears it out: he removed the high places, broke up the bronze serpent Israel had begun to worship, and trusted the LORD as no king of Judah after him did (2 Kings 18:3–6). He is not paying for healing with his merits; he asks God to remember a covenant servant.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the word of the LORD came to Isaiah: "Go and say to Hezekiah, Thus says the LORD, the God of David your father: I have heard your prayer; I have seen your tears. Behold, I will add fifteen years to your life. I will deliver you and this city out of the hand of the king of Assyria, and will defend this city.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God answers at once: he has heard the prayer and seen the tears, and he gives fifteen more years together with the city’s rescue.

I have seen your tears. God names two things: I have heard your prayer; I have seen your tears. The tears are mentioned separately, as something else God noticed. The crying told him something the words did not.

The God of David your father. God answers in the name that carries his promise to David’s house, the promise for whose sake he would defend the city (see the note on 37:33–35). The king is healed, and the city saved, as David’s son and David’s city.

Did Hezekiah’s prayer change God’s mind? “You shall die” was the true verdict on the illness, given as a word that drew out the prayer God meant to answer, as with Nineveh (Jonah 3:4, 10). God’s purpose did not change; he ordained the prayer as the means of the healing (James 5:16).

What it does not mean. Not that every prayer for healing will be answered with more years. God heals in answer to prayer, but not always, and Paul prayed three times and was given grace instead of relief (2 Corinthians 12:7–9). The tears are seen either way.

verseByVerse.quote: "This shall be the sign to you from the LORD, that the LORD will do this thing that he has promised: Behold, I will make the shadow cast by the declining sun on the dial of Ahaz turn back ten steps." So the sun turned back on the dial the ten steps by which it had declined.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God confirms his promise with a sign that fits it: the shadow that measures time goes backwards.

The dial of Ahaz. Ahaz refused a sign from God (7:10–12); his son is given one, on a structure his father built.

Ten steps back. Hezekiah has been given back time, fifteen years he did not expect, and the shadow that marks the hours goes back up the steps, time running backwards where he could see it.

Uncertain wording. The word translated dial is literally “steps”, the same word as the steps the shadow crossed. It may have been a sundial, or a stairway whose steps the shadow climbed through the day. How the shadow went back Scripture does not say; it says only that God did it.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 9–22 — I Walked Slowly All My Years
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Looking back, Hezekiah finds that God’s greatest gift was not more years but pardon. His song is unusually honest about facing death: life cut off in the middle, his tent pulled down, his cloth cut from the loom, his prayers reduced to bird noises (vv. 9–14). Then the turn: God has done it, the king will walk slowly all his years, and the bitterness proves to have been for his good, for in love God has delivered him and cast all his sins behind his back (vv. 15–17). The living are the ones who can praise, so he will praise with music in God’s house all his days (vv. 18–20). A closing footnote records the fig poultice and the king’s request for a sign (vv. 21–22).
verseByVerse.theology: The song moves from lament to praise without skipping the lament. Hezekiah does not call death a friend, or his fear a failure of faith; he calls it the pit and Sheol (the realm of the dead), the end of seeing the LORD in the land of the living. Death is an enemy here, and the praise at the end is reached through the bitterness, not round it.
verseByVerse.examples: The point of the extra years is named at the end (v. 19). Not achievement, not more reign, but a father telling his children what God is like. It is the last thing the song says about the fifteen years, and it is the best use anyone has found for extra time.

verseByVerse.quote: A writing of Hezekiah king of Judah, after he had been sick and had recovered from his sickness: I said, In the middle of my days I must depart; I am consigned to the gates of Sheol for the rest of my years. I said, I shall not see the LORD, the LORD in the land of the living; I shall look on man no more among the inhabitants of the world. My dwelling is plucked up and removed from me like a shepherd's tent; like a weaver I have rolled up my life; he cuts me off from the loom; from day to night you bring me to an end; I calmed myself until morning; like a lion he breaks all my bones; from day to night you bring me to an end. Like a swallow or a crane I chirp; I moan like a dove. My eyes are weary with looking upward. O Lord, I am oppressed; be my pledge of safety!
verseByVerse.commentary:
Hezekiah’s song begins by telling the truth about facing death: the shock of being cut off in mid-life, and prayer worn down to groaning.

A writing of Hezekiah. Hezekiah’s own composition, written afterwards, and its value is that it does not tidy up what the experience was like.

In the middle of my days. He was about thirty-nine (compare 2 Kings 18:2). That grief has its own shape: not the end of a long life but the interruption of one, with the second half simply cancelled.

I shall not see the LORD. Of the two losses in verse 11 he names God first, and only then human company. That order tells you a great deal about the man.

Like a shepherd’s tent. Both images in verse 12 are of something taken down before it looks finished. A shepherd’s tent is pulled up in the morning, pegs out, poles down, and there is no sign anyone lived there. A weaver rolls his cloth as he works, and then the thread is cut at the loom, and whatever was going to be woven will never exist. Anyone facing an early death recognises both.

Like a lion he breaks all my bones. Hezekiah does not hide that he felt God as the one doing it. Honest lament keeps talking to God even when God feels like the enemy.

Like a swallow or a crane I chirp. Verse 14 gives the sound of it: not eloquence but bird noises, the small involuntary sounds a person makes when there are no sentences left. My eyes are weary with looking upward: he has prayed so long that looking up has become physically tiring.

Be my pledge of safety! The phrase is the language of standing surety for another, as Judah told his father, “I will be a pledge of his safety” for Benjamin (Genesis 43:9). Hezekiah asks God himself to stand for him. That prayer is answered in full in Jesus, “the guarantor of a better covenant” (Hebrews 7:22).

Uncertain wording. In verse 13 the verb rendered I calmed myself is uncertain; other translations have “I waited patiently” or “I cried out”. Either way it is a sleepless night.
verseByVerse.note: Hezekiah’s psalm is found only here.

verseByVerse.quote: What shall I say? For he has spoken to me, and he himself has done it. I walk slowly all my years because of the bitterness of my soul. O Lord, by these things men live, and in all these is the life of my spirit. Oh restore me to health and make me live! Behold, it was for my welfare that I had great bitterness; but in love you have delivered my life from the pit of destruction, for you have cast all my sins behind your back.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Looking back, Hezekiah sees that the bitterness was for his good, and that God’s greatest gift was the pardon of his sins.

I walk slowly all my years. Verse 15 is easy to read past. Hezekiah has his fifteen years, and what he says about them is that he will walk slowly all my years. He does not describe himself as restored to what he was. A man who has been that close does not walk at the old pace, and he does not call the change damage. It is what the experience left in him.

By these things men live. The sense of verse 16 is probably that the things God does, his word and even his discipline, are what people live by: in all these is the life of my spirit. The illness was not outside God’s care; it was one of the ways he gave life.

It was for my welfare that I had great bitterness. A verdict he could only reach afterwards. It would have been intolerable from anybody else at the time. Nobody should say this sentence to a suffering person; it belongs in the mouth of the one who suffered, looking back, and nowhere else.

You have cast all my sins behind your back. Then the pardon, the finest image in the song. God casts all his sins behind his back, the one direction in which a person does not look: not forgiven and kept on file, but put where they cannot be seen from the throne. Hezekiah brings no record now, only mercy received; it was love that delivered him. How a holy God can do this the book will show: he lays the iniquity of us all on his Servant (53:6).

Uncertain wording. The Hebrew of verses 15 and 16 is difficult. For I walk slowly the KJV has I shall go softly all my years, and others have walk humbly; all describe a man who now walks more carefully before God. Verse 16 is harder still, and translations of it differ widely.

verseByVerse.quote: For Sheol does not thank you; death does not praise you; those who go down to the pit do not hope for your faithfulness. The living, the living, he thanks you, as I do this day; the father makes known to the children your faithfulness. The LORD will save me, and we will play my music on stringed instruments all the days of our lives, at the house of the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Because the living can praise God, Hezekiah gives his added years to thanksgiving and to handing God’s faithfulness on to his children.

Death does not praise you. Hezekiah’s understanding of death is limited: in verse 18 he speaks as if praise stops at the grave. The fuller answer is at 26:19, where the dead live and their bodies rise, and it is not complete until Jesus’ empty tomb outside this same city. What he has is the strong Old Testament conviction that praise belongs to the living, and he doubles the word: the living, the living.

The father makes known to the children your faithfulness. The added years are for passing on what God has done. Yet the son born in those years, Manasseh, undid his father’s reforms (2 Kings 21:1–3): handing on the faith is a duty, not a guarantee.

At the house of the LORD. The song ends in the temple (v. 20). Hezekiah’s private prayer by the wall becomes public praise with others, in the house where he once spread out Sennacherib’s letter (37:14).

verseByVerse.quote: Now Isaiah had said, "Let them take a cake of figs and apply it to the boil, that he may recover." Hezekiah also had said, "What is the sign that I shall go up to the house of the LORD?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
God’s healing came through an ordinary remedy, and what the king wanted from health was to go up to God’s house again.

A cake of figs. God adds fifteen years by sovereign decree and the prophet sends for a fig plaster, and the narrative sees no tension between them. Using medicine is no failure of faith: God commonly heals through means, and the believer who prays and takes the treatment is doing what Hezekiah did.

Why these verses come last. In 2 Kings 20:7–8 they stand in the middle of the story, before the sign is given, but here they follow it, so the song is left uninterrupted. Hezekiah’s question shows what he wanted most from recovery: to go up to the house of the LORD.

38.theology:
Prayer as protest. Hezekiah does not receive the death sentence quietly, and God saw the tears as well as hearing the words. Not every prayer for healing is answered with more years, and Scripture does not promise that it will be; Paul prayed three times and was given grace instead of relief (2 Corinthians 12:7–9). The tears are seen either way.

A reprieve that points past itself. The song is honest about the bitterness and ends in thanks for a pardon in which God puts a man's sins where they cannot be seen from the throne. But Hezekiah was given fifteen years and then died. Christ gives a life that death cannot end, because he has gone through death himself (John 11:25–26).

39.subtitle: The Shadow of Babylon
39.intro:
Where we are. This is the last chapter of the story section (chapters 36–39) and of the first half of the book. Hezekiah has been rescued from Assyria and raised from his deathbed (chapters 37–38); now friendly envoys arrive from Babylon.

The message. The great danger after a great deliverance is not the enemy at the gate but the pride that wants to be admired. Flattered by Babylon, Hezekiah shows off everything God has given him, and God announces that everything, and some of his own sons, will be carried to Babylon. And the best king Judah had had for generations turns out to care for no future beyond his own days: Judah needs a better Son of David than Hezekiah.

Why it was said. In Hezekiah’s day Babylon was a lesser power looking for allies against Assyria (see the introduction), and nobody could have guessed that it would destroy Jerusalem in 586 BC. The chapter explains the exile before it happens: it was not an accident of politics but the word of the LORD. And it opens the way for chapters 40 to 66, written to the exiles.

How the chapter makes its case. The visit (vv. 1–2): envoys bring letters and a present, and Hezekiah welcomes them gladly and shows them everything, his armoury included. The questions (vv. 3–4): Isaiah arrives unasked and asks who they were and what they saw, and Hezekiah answers without embarrassment: from Babylon, and everything. The sentence (vv. 5–7): everything will be carried to Babylon, and some of his sons will be eunuchs in its palace. The response (v. 8): the king calls the word good, thinking there will be peace in his days.

Where it leads. By the need it exposes. Even the best of David’s sons was proud and short-sighted, and the book now turns to a Servant who does the opposite of verse 8: he looks past his own days, pours out his life, and “shall see his offspring” (53:10). Where Hezekiah accepted loss for his children to keep his own peace, Christ bore the loss himself so that his children might have peace. Even the sons made eunuchs are not beyond his reach: God promises eunuchs who hold fast his covenant “a name better than sons and daughters” (56:5), and in Acts a eunuch reading Isaiah 53 is baptised into Christ (Acts 8:27–38).

For us. Every blessing God gives is a gift to thank him for, not a treasure to show off, and the moments of success are the ones in which we most need to pray. Real faith cares about the generations after us, because it belongs to a Saviour who gave up his days for people not yet born.

keyVerse.quote: “Then Hezekiah said to Isaiah, ‘The word of the LORD that you have spoken is good.’ For he thought, ‘There will be peace and security in my days.’”
keyVerse.note: The contrast with chapter 37’s prayer is stark. There, Hezekiah interceded for others and future generations; here, he accepts judgment on his descendants with private relief. The chapter stands as a warning about the way personal comfort can corrupt what began as genuine faith. Hezekiah did not lose his faith; he shrank it to his own comfort and his own lifetime.

39.reflection:
Hezekiah took Sennacherib’s threatening letter straight to God (37:14), but handled Babylon’s friendly letter by himself (vv. 1–2). Why are success and flattery often more dangerous to our faith than threats?

Hezekiah showed the envoys “all that was found in his storehouses” (v. 2). What do you most like to be admired for, and how does remembering that every good thing is a gift (1 Corinthians 4:7) change the way you hold it?

Hezekiah was relieved that “there will be peace and security in my days” (v. 8). Where are we, as individuals, churches or a society, tempted to leave the cost of our choices to the next generation?

Christ gave up his own days so that people not yet born might have peace (53:10). Whose future could you serve this year, even at some cost to your own comfort?
39.text: <sup>1</sup>At that time Merodach-baladan the son of Baladan, king of Babylon, sent envoys with letters and a present to Hezekiah, for he heard that he had been sick and had recovered.<sup>2</sup>And Hezekiah welcomed them gladly. And he showed them his treasure house, the silver, the gold, the spices, the precious oil, his whole armory, all that was found in his storehouses. There was nothing in his house or in all his realm that Hezekiah did not show them.<sup>3</sup>Then Isaiah the prophet came to King Hezekiah, and said to him, "What did these men say? And from where did they come to you?" Hezekiah said, "They have come to me from a far country, from Babylon."<sup>4</sup>He said, "What have they seen in your house?" Hezekiah answered, "They have seen all that is in my house. There is nothing in my storehouses that I did not show them."<sup>5</sup>Then Isaiah said to Hezekiah, "Hear the word of the LORD of hosts:<sup>6</sup>Behold, the days are coming, when all that is in your house, and that which your fathers have stored up till this day, shall be carried to Babylon. Nothing shall be left, says the LORD.<sup>7</sup>And some of your own sons, who will come from you, whom you will father, shall be taken away, and they shall be eunuchs in the palace of the king of Babylon."<sup>8</sup>Then Hezekiah said to Isaiah, "The word of the LORD that you have spoken is good." For he thought, "There will be peace and security in my days."

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–8 — The Door That Was Left Open
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: A good king falls to the oldest temptation, the wish to be admired, and his pride opens the door to the empire that will carry his people away. Merodach-baladan of Babylon sends letters and a present to congratulate Hezekiah on his recovery (v. 1). Hezekiah welcomes the envoys gladly and shows them everything he has, his armoury included (v. 2). Isaiah comes unasked with two questions: where were they from, and what did they see? Babylon, and everything (vv. 3–4). The oracle matches the act: all of it will be carried to Babylon, and some of his own sons will be eunuchs in that palace (vv. 5–7). Hezekiah calls the word good, relieved that there will be peace in his own days (v. 8).
verseByVerse.theology: Babylon was a minor power at this date and Assyria was the enemy; the visit looked like a diplomatic opportunity and was in fact the test. Hezekiah, who in the book's order took Sennacherib's letter into the temple two chapters ago, takes this delegation on a tour and never once asks God about it. The man who prayed brilliantly under threat did not think to pray under flattery.
verseByVerse.examples: The test came straight after the rescue from death, and it came not as a threat but as flattery: letters, a present, congratulations from a foreign king to a man just raised from his sickbed. Danger dressed as admiration is harder to recognise than danger dressed as an army, and Hezekiah, who knew exactly what to do with the second, did not see the first.

verseByVerse.quote: At that time Merodach-baladan the son of Baladan, king of Babylon, sent envoys with letters and a present to Hezekiah, for he heard that he had been sick and had recovered. And Hezekiah welcomed them gladly. And he showed them his treasure house, the silver, the gold, the spices, the precious oil, his whole armory, all that was found in his storehouses. There was nothing in his house or in all his realm that Hezekiah did not show them. Then Isaiah the prophet came to King Hezekiah, and said to him, "What did these men say? And from where did they come to you?" Hezekiah said, "They have come to me from a far country, from Babylon." He said, "What have they seen in your house?" Hezekiah answered, "They have seen all that is in my house. There is nothing in my storehouses that I did not show them."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Flattered by a foreign king, Hezekiah shows Babylon everything he has without asking God, and does not see that anything is wrong.

At that time. The timing is everything. Hezekiah has been raised from his deathbed and promised the city’s deliverance (38:6), and a delegation arrives from Babylon, at this date a second-rank power wanting allies against Assyria, with letters, a gift and congratulations. Merodach-baladan held Babylon briefly around 703 BC and was gathering allies, so the visit probably came before the siege. Isaiah tells it last because it leads into the exile in Babylon, where chapter 40 begins.

Sent envoys with letters and a present. It looks like a diplomatic opportunity. It is the test, as the Chronicler says: “God left him to himself, in order to test him and to know all that was in his heart” (2 Chronicles 32:31).

Hezekiah welcomed them gladly. The key word in verse 2 is gladly. Somebody important had noticed him, and a foreign king was sending presents.

He showed them his treasure house. Isaiah lists the stops of the tour the way an inventory is read out, ending with the armoury: his military capacity, shown to a foreign power.

What he did not do. He does not send for Isaiah or go up to the house of the LORD, as he did with Sennacherib’s letter (37:14). A hostile letter drove him to prayer; a friendly one he handles entirely by himself. The prophet arrives without being sent for, and that shows what was missing.

What have they seen in your house? Isaiah’s last question is the one that matters, and it is precise: not what they said but what they saw. Hezekiah answers it fully and without embarrassment. He does not appear to know anything is wrong, and that is the most sobering thing in the chapter.

Flattery is more dangerous than threat. Success, recovery and praise are the moments we are least likely to pray, and most likely to display what God has given as though it were our own. “What do you have that you did not receive?” (1 Corinthians 4:7).
verseByVerse.note: Merodach-baladan was a Babylonian rebel king seeking allies against Assyria.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Isaiah said to Hezekiah, "Hear the word of the LORD of hosts: Behold, the days are coming, when all that is in your house, and that which your fathers have stored up till this day, shall be carried to Babylon. Nothing shall be left, says the LORD. And some of your own sons, who will come from you, whom you will father, shall be taken away, and they shall be eunuchs in the palace of the king of Babylon." Then Hezekiah said to Isaiah, "The word of the LORD that you have spoken is good." For he thought, "There will be peace and security in my days."
verseByVerse.commentary:
God announces that everything Hezekiah showed off, and some of his own sons, will be carried to Babylon, and the king is relieved that it will not happen in his lifetime.

Nothing shall be left. The judgment matches the act exactly, as judgment usually does in this book. He showed them everything; everything will go. He left nothing unshown; nothing shall be left.

Shall be carried to Babylon. The destination is the point. Not Assyria, the enemy just broken, but Babylon, the friendly delegation with the presents. The men admiring the silver were the advance party. More than a century later Nebuchadnezzar carried off the treasures of the temple and the palace (2 Kings 24:13).

They shall be eunuchs. Then the second half, and it is far worse: not only the treasure but the sons, and not as princes but as eunuchs, castrated servants in a foreign court. Young men of the royal family and the nobility were later placed under the chief of Nebuchadnezzar’s eunuchs (Daniel 1:3). A man who has just been given fifteen extra years is told what will happen to the children born in them.

The word of the LORD that you have spoken is good. The first half of verse 8 sounds like piety. Then the narrator tells us what he was thinking, and it is not defiance but relief, and the days in question are the fifteen he was given as a gift when he wept at the wall. He is not raging against the sentence; he is comfortable with it, because the cost falls on people he will not meet. A man who begged for his own life accepts the mutilation of his descendants as good news, because it will not happen in his time.

The idol of my own lifetime. Hezekiah’s relief sounds shocking until we notice how ordinary it is. Economists call the habit discounting the future: giving less weight to a cost the further off it falls. Whole societies run on it. We borrow against our grandchildren, spend the soil and the seas, and leave the bill to people we will never meet, while thinking of ourselves as decent. The idol of comfort shrinks the circle of people we care about until it is no wider than our own days. Isaiah’s book answers it with another King. Fourteen chapters on, a Servant pours out his life and dies childless, and yet he shall see his offspring; he shall prolong his days (53:10). Hezekiah accepted his descendants’ ruin to keep his own peace. Jesus gave up his peace, and his days, to secure a future for people not yet born.

A kinder reading. Some readers take Hezekiah more kindly, as humbly accepting mercy in his own day, as Josiah later would (2 Kings 22:19–20). But the narrator’s aside, for he thought, puts the weight on relief.

Where the first half ends. Isaiah closes the first half of his book here, deliberately: not on the angel, nor on the shadow going back up the steps, but on a good king whose concern reaches no further than his own lifetime. That is why chapter 40 must say what it says. Everything from here on is written for the exiles in Babylon, the exile this chapter announces, and the first word spoken to them is comfort.
verseByVerse.note: Fulfilled when Babylon carried off Jerusalem's treasures and royal family a little over a century later, in 597 BC (2 Kings 24:12–15).

39.theology: Peace in my days. The last sentence of the first half of the book is the most uncomfortable in it: a good king, at the end of a good life, whose concern turns out to reach no further than his own lifetime. Hezekiah was the best king Judah had had for generations, and still not the Son of David the people needed. The second half of the book shows a Servant who does the opposite of verse 8: he looks past his own days, pours out his life, and shall see his offspring (53:10). Where Hezekiah accepted loss for his children to keep his own peace, the Servant bears the loss himself so that his children may have peace.

40.subtitle: Comfort, Comfort My People
40.intro:
Where we are. Chapter 39 ended with everything in Hezekiah’s house bound for Babylon and a king content with peace in his own days. Chapter 40 opens the second half of the book, speaking ahead to the exiles in Babylon (see the introduction), and its first word is comfort.

The message. Your God has not finished with you, and he is far greater than what you fear. To a people who think their sin has cut them off for ever and that God has lost track of them, the LORD says two things: your guilt has been dealt with, and I am coming to you myself, the God beside whom every empire is a drop from a bucket. So do not give up: wait for him, and he will carry you.

Why it was said. The exiles had lost their land, their temple and their king, and they drew two conclusions: God had rejected them for their sins, and Babylon’s power and gods were simply bigger. Their complaint is in verse 27: “My way is hidden from the LORD, and my right is disregarded by my God.” The whole chapter answers that sentence.

How the chapter makes its case. First pardon (vv. 1–2): the sentence is served, so comfort, not condemnation, is God’s last word. Then presence (vv. 3–11): a road is built for God himself; all flesh withers, but his word stands; and the one who comes with might gathers the lambs in his arms. Then size (vv. 12–26): oceans, nations, idols, rulers and stars are set beside him until Babylon shrinks to its real size. Only then does God answer the complaint (vv. 27–31): the God who never grows weary gives power to the faint who wait for him.

Where it leads. By direct promise. All four Gospels say the voice of verse 3 was John the Baptist, and the LORD who came along the road he prepared was Jesus. In him the glory of the LORD was revealed (v. 5; John 1:14); the word that stands for ever is the gospel preached to us (1 Peter 1:25); and “Behold your God!” (v. 9) comes true in the Shepherd who lays down his life for the sheep (John 10:11). The pardon of verse 2 rests finally on the Servant of chapter 53, on whom the LORD laid the iniquity of us all.

For us. When guilt says God is done with you, or life says he has forgotten you, this chapter answers both: you are pardoned, and he is great enough and near enough to carry you. Strength for the long walk is not found by trying harder but by waiting on him.

keyVerse.quote: “But they who wait for the LORD shall renew their strength; they shall mount up with wings like eagles; they shall run and not be weary; they shall walk and not faint.”
keyVerse.note: The word wait (qavah) is related to the word for a cord: not passive waiting but hope that holds on to God as to a rope. The renewal is not our natural energy coming back but strength given by God. This is the great promise of the second half of Isaiah: what human strength cannot keep up, God’s grace renews.

40.theology:
The incomparability of God. Everything in chapters 40 to 55 rests on the claim made here: the God who speaks is not the largest item in a list of powerful things but the one on whom everything that exists depends. That is why the chapter comforts: only an infinite God can offer an infinite comfort, so the tenderness of verses 1 and 2 and the cosmic scale of verses 12 to 26 are not two subjects but one argument.

The road built for the LORD. Verse 3 prepares a way for Yahweh, and all four Gospels assign that road-building to John the Baptist, whose road was walked by Jesus of Nazareth (Matt. 3:3; Mark 1:3; Luke 3:4-6; John 1:23). The New Testament does not argue that Jesus is the LORD who comes; it assumes it.

Grace to the empty-handed. The chapter’s last section shows in small how grace always works. Nothing is earned. The faint receive what the strong could not keep. For the Christian that strength is God's own Spirit living in us, as Paul prays that believers be strengthened with power through his Spirit in your inner being (Ephesians 3:16).
40.reflection:
God’s first word to his guilty people is “Comfort”, because her “iniquity is pardoned” (vv. 1–2). Why does it matter that Christian comfort rests on a settled account rather than on how we feel, and what difference does that make when guilt returns?

“The grass withers, the flower fades, but the word of our God will stand forever” (v. 8). What are you tempted to lean on that is grass, and how could you build more of your life on what God has said?

The God who measures the waters “in the hollow of his hand” (v. 12) is the shepherd who will “gather the lambs in his arms” (v. 11). Which do you find harder to believe, his greatness or his gentleness, and why?

Israel said, “My way is hidden from the LORD” (v. 27). When have you felt that, and what would waiting for the LORD (v. 31) look like in the weariness you are carrying this week?
