verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–11 — Comfort, and the Road for God to Come On
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God’s first word to a people under judgment is comfort, and he means it: the punishment is over, and God himself is coming to bring them home. Verses 1 and 2 give the ground: a sentence served and guilt pardoned. Verses 3 to 5 promise that nothing will stand in his way, and that all flesh will see his glory. Verses 6 to 8 say why the promise can be trusted: it rests not on frail people, who wither like grass, but on God’s word, which stands for ever. Verses 9 to 11 show what kind of God is coming, strong enough to rule and gentle enough to carry the lambs.
verseByVerse.theology: The comfort of this section is not encouragement but the announcement that the debt has been settled, which is why it can be commanded rather than merely hoped. It rests on two things only: what God has said (v. 8) and who God is (v. 9).
verseByVerse.examples: The herald's message in verse 9 is still the shortest summary of Christian proclamation available. Not a programme, not a technique, not even the benefits first: Behold your God.

verseByVerse.quote: Comfort, comfort my people, says your God. Speak tenderly to Jerusalem, and cry to her that her warfare is ended, that her iniquity is pardoned, that she has received from the LORD's hand double for all her sins.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God’s first word to his guilty, exiled people is comfort: the punishment is over, their sin is pardoned, and he is still their God.

Comfort, comfort my people. Thirty-nine chapters of indictment stop here. The last thing said was that everything in Hezekiah’s house would be carried to Babylon; the first word after it is comfort, said twice, for doubling is how Hebrew shouts. The command is plural: God is commissioning a company of heralds.

Two possessives restored. My people. Your God. Through the first half of the book they have mostly been “this people”, what you call a nation addressed at arm’s length. The relationship is spoken back into place before anything is explained.

Speak tenderly to Jerusalem. Literally “speak to the heart”, the phrase for winning a heart back: Joseph used it to reassure the brothers who had sold him (Genesis 50:21), and God will speak tenderly to his unfaithful wife when he takes her into the wilderness to win her back (Hosea 2:14). God is not merely informing his people that the punishment is over. He is wooing them.

What is cried to her. Three things. Her warfare (or “hardship”), a term of hard service with a fixed end, is over. Her iniquity is pardoned. And she has received double for all her sins: the sentence has been served in full, with nothing left to be collected later.

A settled account. That is why comfort can be commanded here rather than merely offered. Christian comfort has never been a mood worked up in the face of trouble; it is the proper response to a settled account. If the debt is paid, cheer is not optimism but accuracy. The exile was discipline; the Servant of chapter 53, on whom the LORD laid the iniquity of us all (53:6), is how the guilt itself comes to be settled.

Who wrote these chapters? Many scholars hold that chapters 40 to 66 come from a later prophet, or prophets, speaking to the exiles around 540 BC, because they address that situation so directly and name Cyrus (44:28). This commentary holds the traditional view that they are Isaiah’s, written ahead of time: the Gospels introduce verse 3 as the words of Isaiah the prophet (Matthew 3:3; Luke 3:4), John quotes both halves of the book under his name (John 12:38–41), and these chapters rest their case on God announcing events before they happen (41:21–23). The question is still debated among believing scholars (see the introduction), and the comfort of the chapter does not hang on it.

Uncertain wording. The sense of double is debated. Some take it as twice over, an acknowledgment of how heavy the exile had been; others as the full equivalent, the matching counterpart of the debt. Either way the point is that the sentence is complete, not that God was unjust.
verseByVerse.note: Chapters 40–66 speak comfort to God’s people beyond the coming exile.

verseByVerse.quote: A voice cries: "In the wilderness prepare the way of the LORD; make straight in the desert a highway for our God. Every valley shall be lifted up, and every mountain and hill be made low; the uneven ground shall become level, and the rough places a plain. And the glory of the LORD shall be revealed, and all flesh shall see it together, for the mouth of the LORD has spoken."
verseByVerse.commentary:
God is coming to his people himself, nothing will stand in his way, and when he arrives everyone will see his glory.

Prepare the way of the LORD. The picture is a road gang. When an eastern king travelled, men went ahead to make the route passable, filling holes and levelling the surface, because the road had to be ready before the king would come. Isaiah puts that royal practice in the desert between Babylon and home, and the king being announced is God.

Every mountain and hill be made low. Nothing is left in the way, not even the mountains, the obstacles that cannot ordinarily be moved. Verse 5 is the point of the roadworks: not a rumour of God, nor a report brought back by specialists, but the glory itself, in the open, seen by everybody at once.

A voice cries. All four Gospels quote this verse about one man. Matthew, Mark and Luke apply it to John the Baptist (Matthew 3:3; Mark 1:3; Luke 3:4–6), and when the delegation from Jerusalem asked John who he was, he refused every title offered and answered with this verse: “I am the voice of one crying out in the wilderness, ‘Make straight the way of the Lord’” (John 1:23). The Gospels follow the Greek translation, which joins in the wilderness to the voice; the Hebrew joins it to the road. Either way John stood in the wilderness and prepared the road.

A highway for our God. Isaiah says the road is being built for the LORD, the covenant name, the God whose glory fills the earth. John built his road, and then Jesus of Nazareth walked up it. The Gospel writers do not argue this; they simply take a sentence about the coming of God and hand it to a carpenter’s son, and expect the reader to notice.

All flesh shall see it together. What the road-builders were told to expect, John saw: “We have seen his glory, glory as of the only Son from the Father” (John 1:14). What came along the finished road was a man they could touch.

The road today. John’s road-building was a call to repent (Luke 3:3–6). The valleys and mountains that still need levelling are in the heart: pride brought low, and the despairing lifted up, so that Christ may be welcomed.
verseByVerse.note: The Gospels quote the Greek Old Testament, which joins in the wilderness to the voice; the Hebrew joins it to the road. Both are true of John, who cried out in the wilderness so that a way would be ready there.

verseByVerse.quote: A voice says, "Cry!" And I said, "What shall I cry?" All flesh is grass, and all its beauty is like the flower of the field. The grass withers, the flower fades when the breath of the LORD blows on it; surely the people are grass.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Before the comfort is preached, the herald must say the plain truth: human life and glory are as short-lived as wild grass.

What shall I cry? The herald is willing and does not know the message. The answer is not the one he expects: before the comfort can be preached, something has to be said about the people being comforted.

All flesh is grass. The image is exact. After the rains the hills go green with wildflowers; then the east wind comes off the desert, hot and dry, and in a day or two the whole hillside is brown. Isaiah does not say all flesh is weak but grass, and what goes first is the beauty: strength, looks, competence, the years when everything works. Read the obituaries of the people who ran the world eighty years ago. The withering is not a threat hanging over human glory; it is its ordinary weather.

When the breath of the LORD blows on it. Who does the withering? Not time or bad luck but the breath of the LORD, on a schedule that belongs to God. That is a harder thought than mortality in the abstract, and a better one, because a wind that is God’s breath is not a random wind.

Who is really pretending? The poet Philip Larkin, waking at four in the morning in his poem “Aubade” (1977), dismissed religion as “That vast moth-eaten musical brocade / Created to pretend we never die.” It is one of the most serious modern charges against faith: that it is a consolation for people who cannot face the facts. But no secular writer has put mortality more bluntly than Isaiah. It is our own culture that pretends, with the creams and the procedures and the quiet removal of the dying from public view. The prophet will not let us look away. His hope does not deny the withering; it stands outside it, in a word that does not wither (v. 8), and finally in one body that went into the grave and came out, the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep (1 Corinthians 15:20). Christianity does not ask you to pretend you will not die. It points you to the one who has already been through death and back.

Textual note. Some ancient manuscripts and translations read And I said, which the ESV follows; the standard Hebrew text reads and he said (so the KJV). The sense is the same: the herald asks what he is to cry.
verseByVerse.note: “And I said” follows the Dead Sea Scroll and ancient versions (ESV note).

verseByVerse.quote: The grass withers, the flower fades, but the word of our God will stand forever.
verseByVerse.commentary:
One thing does not wither, what God has said, and so his comfort stands on his word, not on us. The whole chapter rests on this sentence: one thing in the picture is not grass.

What the comfort stands on. If the pardon of verses 1 and 2 were built on national recovery, a change of imperial policy or the exiles finding new resolve, it would go the way of grass. It is built on something God said, and what God has said outlasts the people he said it to, the empire that overheard it, and the language it was first spoken in.

Not a feeling. That is a specific kind of security. It is not the promise that the believer will feel certain; feelings are grass, and they were in the list. It is the promise that the thing believed does not depend on the believer to hold it up.

Peter’s application. Peter quotes these verses in full to Christians scattered and under pressure, and then adds: “And this word is the good news that was preached to you” (1 Peter 1:24–25). The word that never withers is not an idea floating above history. It was the gospel, in a room, out of somebody’s mouth, and it is the one thing in your life that is not grass.

verseByVerse.quote: Go on up to a high mountain, O Zion, herald of good news; lift up your voice with strength, O Jerusalem, herald of good news; lift it up, fear not; say to the cities of Judah, "Behold your God!" Behold, the Lord GOD comes with might, and his arm rules for him; behold, his reward is with him, and his recompense before him. He will tend his flock like a shepherd; he will gather the lambs in his arms; he will carry them in his bosom, and gently lead those that are with young.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Zion is to shout the good news that God himself is coming, as a conqueror strong enough to rule and a shepherd gentle enough to carry the lambs.

O Zion, herald of good news. The city that has spent thirty-nine chapters being preached at is handed the message. Zion is sent up a hill so the sound will carry, told twice to lift her voice and once not to be afraid, which suggests that a recently disgraced people with good news is inclined to say it quietly.

Behold your God! The message is three words long. Not “behold your deliverance”, though that is coming, but Behold your God. Everything the exiles wanted followed from that, and Isaiah will not let the gift be announced ahead of the giver.

His arm rules for him. Then two pictures of the God being pointed at. Verse 10 is a conqueror coming home, the spoils carried before the column, an image meant to terrify God’s enemies. Verse 11 is a shepherd.

Gently lead those that are with young. The most practical clause in the chapter. A flock moves at the speed of its slowest member, and a shepherd who drives it at the pace of the strongest will kill the pregnant ewes. Jacob said so to Esau: if the flocks are driven hard for one day, all of them will die (Genesis 33:13–14). God sets the pace of his people by the weakest one among them.

He will tend his flock like a shepherd. Two images and one God. The arm that cannot be resisted is the arm that carries lambs; the might that comes with recompense is the tenderness that slows down for a pregnant animal. This is what almighty power looks like when it belongs to a shepherd, and it is the same one who said centuries later that he was the good shepherd and would lay down his life for the sheep (John 10:11).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 12–26 — To Whom Then Will You Compare Me?
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Babylon looked like the biggest thing in the world, so God makes the room bigger: whatever has filled your horizon is small beside the God who made it, so fear him and not it. The oceans in his palm and nobody to advise him (vv. 12–14) mean no power can outwit him. The nations as a drop from a bucket (vv. 15–17) mean the empire that holds you is nothing to him. The idol that must be kept from falling over (vv. 18–20) shows what Babylon’s gods really are. Princes blown away like stubble (vv. 21–24) and stars called out by name (vv. 25–26) mean that rulers, and the very heavens Babylon worshipped, answer to him.
verseByVerse.theology: This is the doctrine later theology calls aseity: God exists of himself, depending on nothing, taught by nobody. The attack on idols is exact rather than sneering. The nations and their gods are not God's rivals but his creation, and apart from him nothing stands by itself.
verseByVerse.examples: These verses are best read slowly by anyone whose horizon has shrunk to the size of one fear. Their method is not to argue the fear away but to make the room bigger.

verseByVerse.quote: Who has measured the waters in the hollow of his hand and marked off the heavens with a span, enclosed the dust of the earth in a measure and weighed the mountains in scales and the hills in a balance? Who has measured the Spirit of the LORD, or what man shows him his counsel? Whom did he consult, and who made him understand? Who taught him the path of justice, and taught him knowledge, and showed him the way of understanding?
verseByVerse.commentary:
God is not merely bigger than creation but on another scale altogether, and he has never needed anyone’s advice.

Measured the waters in the hollow of his hand. Four measurements, and the units are the point: every ocean in a cupped palm, the sky measured with a span (about nine inches), the dust in a grain scoop, the mountains on the kitchen scales. These are not images of a very large God but of a God not on the same scale at all, who handles the whole created order with the casual gestures of a merchant checking a quantity.

Whom did he consult? The questions turn from power to wisdom, and every one expects the answer “nobody”. God has never taken advice, never had a teacher, never been shown something he had not considered. Paul quotes verse 13 at the end of eleven chapters of argument (Romans 11:34) and again in 1 Corinthians 2:16, both times where the right response to God is to stop talking.

For the exiles. This was intensely practical. Babylon was full of professional advisers, astrologers and diviners whose trade was telling a king what was coming. The God directing the history that had swept the exiles into that city had consulted none of them, and did not need to.

verseByVerse.quote: Behold, the nations are like a drop from a bucket, and are accounted as the dust on the scales; behold, he takes up the coastlands like fine dust. Lebanon would not suffice for fuel, nor are its beasts enough for a burnt offering. All the nations are as nothing before him, they are accounted by him as less than nothing and emptiness.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The nations that terrify God’s people are, before him, a drop on a bucket’s rim: no rival at all.

Like a drop from a bucket. The images are precisely chosen: not a bucket but the single bead of water on its rim that nobody counts; not a load of dust but the film on the pan of a balance that does not move the needle.

Lebanon would not suffice for fuel. Lebanon meant the great cedar forests, the timber kings sent for when they wanted a temple. Burn the whole forest, put every animal in it on the altar, and you still have not made an offering big enough for this God.

Less than nothing and emptiness. The last word of verse 17, emptiness, is tohu, the word used of the formless earth in the second verse of the Bible, before anything had been shaped. Not a rival to be reckoned with, but nothing at all.

Resetting the scale. For people living inside the Babylonian empire, Babylon is the entire horizon: its army, its gods, the daily weight of it. Isaiah is resetting the scale, because a captive’s real problem is usually not that he has too high a view of God but that he has an accurate view of his captor and nothing to set beside it.

verseByVerse.quote: To whom then will you liken God, or what likeness compare with him? An idol! A craftsman casts it, and a goldsmith overlays it with gold and casts for it silver chains. He who is too impoverished for an offering chooses wood that will not rot; he seeks out a skillful craftsman to set up an idol that will not move.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Nothing can be compared with God, least of all an idol whose makers’ highest hope is that it will not fall over.

To whom then will you liken God? The question of verse 18 is the one chapters 40 to 48 turn on. The making of an idol is followed like a work order: somebody casts it, somebody gilds it, somebody chains it, and verse 20 goes down the market to the customer who cannot afford gold. After the timber selection and the hiring of a specialist, the one requirement that matters is that the finished god will not move. Not that it will act, or hear, or save: that it will not fall over.

An idol that will not move. Two verses ago the nations were dust on a balance. Here their gods are objects that have to be steadied. They are not God’s rivals; they are objects in his world.

Foolish before wicked. The error is foolish before it is wicked: treating a made thing as though it were the Maker. That reaches further than carved wood. Anything that gets a person’s ultimate trust while remaining something he built, a portfolio, a reputation, a career, will need propping up, and the propping gives it away. Ask what in your life you spend most effort keeping upright. The God of this chapter needs no propping; he carries his people (46:4).

verseByVerse.quote: Do you not know? Do you not hear? Has it not been told you from the beginning? Have you not understood from the foundations of the earth? It is he who sits above the circle of the earth, and its inhabitants are like grasshoppers; who stretches out the heavens like a curtain, and spreads them like a tent to dwell in;
verseByVerse.commentary:
God’s greatness has been plain since creation: he sits enthroned above the world he spread out like a tent, and its people are small before him.

Do you not know? The four questions of verse 21 offer no new information. Isaiah charges his hearers with forgetting what has been in plain view since the world began, the same argument Paul makes about the whole human race: what can be known about God is plain, and the problem is not lack of evidence but its suppression (Romans 1:18–20). Nobody in this chapter is short of evidence. They are short of attention.

He who sits above the circle of the earth. He sits above: not one of the forces operating inside the system but above it, seated, the posture of a king who is not worried.

Spreads them like a tent to dwell in. The picture is domestic: anyone in that world had watched a tent go up in an afternoon. That is what God did with the sky, one unhurried gesture, and every human being who has ever lived has lived inside it.

Its inhabitants are like grasshoppers. Not contempt but scale. An insect on the floor of a very large tent is not worthless (it is alive, fed, provided for); it is simply very small in a very big room. The verse does not ask the reader to despise himself, only to stop imagining that the room is the size of his own concerns.

Does “the circle of the earth” mean Isaiah knew the earth was a sphere? The word means a circle or vault, most likely the horizon or the dome of the sky seen from above. It does not teach a flat earth, nor does it claim a globe; it is poetry about God enthroned above all.

verseByVerse.quote: who brings princes to nothing, and makes the rulers of the earth as emptiness. Scarcely are they planted, scarcely sown, scarcely has their stem taken root in the earth, when he blows on them, and they wither, and the tempest carries them off like stubble.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The rulers who seem permanent are seedlings that God blows away with a breath.

Who brings princes to nothing. Isaiah applies the scale to what an exile could not stop thinking about: power. Not power in general but princes, people who could decide where a family would live and whether it would live.

Scarcely are they planted. Three times scarcely: the dynasties that seemed permanent are seedlings. God does not send an army against them. He blows on them, the smallest gesture in the chapter, and the same one as verse 7, where the breath of the LORD blows on the grass. What happens to a wildflower in the desert wind is what happens to an empire; the difference is size, not kind.

Where that empire is now. Nebuchadnezzar was the most powerful man alive when these words were read by people he had deported. What is left of his empire now stands in museum cases. That is not a claim that politics is unimportant; the exiles’ suffering was real, and God takes a whole book to say so. It is a comfort about proportion. A believer frightened of a government is frightened of stubble in a wind, and the wind belongs to his Father.

verseByVerse.quote: To whom then will you compare me, that I should be like him? says the Holy One. Lift up your eyes on high and see: who created these? He who brings out their host by number, calling them all by name; by the greatness of his might and because he is strong in power, not one is missing.
verseByVerse.commentary:
No one compares with the Holy One, who calls out every star by name and never loses one.

Says the Holy One. The question returns in God’s own voice, with the title that runs through the whole book. The claim is not that God wins the comparison but that no comparison is possible. He is not the best of a kind; there is no one else of his kind.

The religion of the night sky. Babylon was the great civilisation of the night sky. Its astronomers kept star records over centuries, its priests read the heavens for omens, and its gods were largely the lights themselves. To an exile, looking up meant looking at the religion of the people who owned him.

Lift up your eyes on high and see. Isaiah tells him to look up anyway, and changes what he sees. The lights are not gods and not fates but a host, an army, which God brings out as a commander parades a regiment, by number, calling each by name. The Babylonians catalogued the stars. God named them, and they answer to him.

Not one is missing. He takes the roll every night and it is always complete: countless suns, each known by a name he gave it, and the whole procession no strain to him. Hold that phrase, because the next verse is about people who believe God has lost track of them.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Here the whole chapter lands. God’s people feel forgotten, and the answer is not a pep talk but God himself: he never tires, never loses track of them, and gives his own strength to those who have none left, if they will wait for him. Verse 27 voices the complaint of the worn-down believer. Verse 28 answers it with who God is: everlasting, tireless, with understanding no one can search out. Verses 29 and 30 show that even the strongest human beings run out. Verse 31 promises new strength to those who look to him, not only for the rare days of soaring but for the long ordinary walk.
verseByVerse.theology: Verse 28 does not tell the people they are wrong to feel forgotten; it tells them who it is they think has forgotten them. The promise of verse 31 is not that the faithful will never run out. It is that there is a place to bring what has run out and have strength renewed.
verseByVerse.examples: Most Christian lives are lived in the third clause of verse 31, the plodding faithfulness of an ordinary week, and it is the one the verse ends on.

verseByVerse.quote: Why do you say, O Jacob, and speak, O Israel, "My way is hidden from the LORD, and my right is disregarded by my God"? Have you not known? Have you not heard? The LORD is the everlasting God, the Creator of the ends of the earth. He does not faint or grow weary; his understanding is unsearchable.
verseByVerse.commentary:
To a people who feel forgotten, God answers not by arguing with their feelings but by showing them himself: everlasting, tireless, and understanding beyond all searching.

My way is hidden from the LORD. This is the sentence the whole chapter has been walking toward, and it is not unbelief. It says two ordinary things: “he cannot see where I am”, and “he is not doing anything about what has been done to me”. My way. My right. It is the believer’s complaint, and the possessives are the ache in it. Anyone who has prayed for years about the same thing knows it: not rebellion but being worn down, the doctrine all in place and the sense that any of it applies to you quietly drained away.

His understanding is unsearchable. God does not answer the feeling. He answers with himself, and the attributes are chosen. To people who feel overlooked: his understanding is unsearchable; there is no corner of your situation he has not thought all the way through. To people worn out with waiting: he does not faint or grow weary; the very thing that has happened to you has never once happened to him.

A bigger God. That is not evasion but the only real cure. A believer who feels forgotten does not need to be told his feelings are wrong; he needs a bigger God than the one he has been carrying around, because the small god of his imagination could lose track of him. The everlasting God, who has just taken the roll call of the stars, could not.

Too small to matter? Modern people feel verse 27 in a way Isaiah’s hearers could not, because we know the numbers: our sun is one of perhaps a hundred billion stars in our galaxy, and our galaxy one of countless others. Surely, many conclude, the idea that its Maker knows my name is a fond human vanity. But Isaiah does not shrink the universe to make room for us; he makes it larger still, and then says its Maker calls every star by name and loses none (v. 26). Size is no argument against being known, if the knower is great enough. The modern worry assumes that attention is scarce, as ours is. Isaiah’s God has no such limit. And the Christian story makes the point unforgettable: the Maker of the galaxies did not keep his distance from the speck. He was born on it, and died on it for people who thought he had forgotten them.

verseByVerse.quote: He gives power to the faint, and to him who has no might he increases strength. Even youths shall faint and be weary, and young men shall fall exhausted;
verseByVerse.commentary:
God gives his strength to those who have none, while even the strongest human beings run out.

He gives power to the faint. God works with two categories we would not choose: the faint, already running on empty, and the one with no might at all, which means not little strength but none. This is where the last twenty verses have been going. The God who does not grow weary distributes strength, and he distributes it downward, to the people who have none.

Young men shall fall exhausted. Isaiah takes the best specimen available and puts him on the ground: young men at their peak, whose bodies have not yet started sending the bills, shall fall exhausted, not in a graceful decline but with legs that simply go.

No human reserve is enough. He is not being gloomy but closing an exit. As long as we believe some level of human vigour would be sufficient, we will keep trying to reach it and half-praying about the shortfall. Isaiah shows the highest human number failing and leaves only one place for strength to come from. That is a strange relief. Much of the exhaustion Christians carry is not from serving God but from the effort of appearing to have enough. Verse 30 says the strongest person you know does not have enough either, so that verse 31 has somewhere to land.

verseByVerse.quote: but they who wait for the LORD shall renew their strength; they shall mount up with wings like eagles; they shall run and not be weary; they shall walk and not faint.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Those who look to the LORD in hope are given new strength, not only for the rare days of soaring but for the long ordinary walk.

They who wait for the LORD shall renew their strength. Both verbs repay attention. Wait is expectant waiting, looking toward someone in hope, the opposite of passive. Renew is a word also used for exchange, as of a worn-out garment for a new one, not a top-up from a reserve.

Renewal, not topping up. That distinction decides how a person prays on a bad week. Topping up asks God to make a depleted resource go further, which keeps the depleted resource at the centre. Renewal starts from the emptiness itself, brought and handed over. The first is a request for endurance; the second is closer to what the whole Bible means by faith.

They shall walk and not faint. Then three clauses in an order that is wrong on purpose: mount up, run, walk. Every instinct builds the other way, with the eagles at the summit. Isaiah is describing not a crescendo but a life. Days that feel like flight are rare gifts; seasons of running bring visible progress; but most of a Christian life is walking: the same obedience, the same prayers, the same job, on an ordinary day, with nothing to show anybody. That is the hardest to sustain, and the promise to walk and not faint is the one most needed. It is not a call to grit; the strength is his, given by his Spirit to those who keep looking to him.

How do I wait for the LORD? Waiting here is a direction, not a pause, and it can be practised on an ordinary week. Bring the emptiness itself. When the strength has gone, say so to him in plain words before trying to manufacture more: “pour out your heart before him” (Psalm 62:8). Hold on to a word. Take one promise (this verse will do) and carry it into the day: “I wait for the LORD, my soul waits, and in his word I hope” (Psalm 130:5). At two in the morning, when the mind starts on the list again, go back to the sentence instead of the list. Keep walking. Do the next plain duty, the shift, the school run, the hospital visit, without waiting to feel like an eagle first. Look at the one who waited for you. Jesus waited on his Father through Gethsemane and the cross, and was heard (Hebrews 5:7); risen, he is now the giver of the strength, so we run “looking to Jesus, the founder and perfecter of our faith” (Hebrews 12:2). Waiting is not proving that you are patient enough. It is leaning, again tomorrow, on someone who does not grow weary.

Where the chapter comes to rest. So the chapter that opened with heralds told to comfort a beaten people comes to rest here. He does not faint or grow weary. He gives power to the faint and never runs low himself, because what he hands out is not a portion of a supply but an overflow of who he is. Grass withers, princes go like stubble, the stars answer to the names he gave them, and the everlasting God stoops to the ones with no might left and trades them his own strength for their emptiness.

41.subtitle: Fear Not, I Am with You
41.intro:
Where we are. Chapter 40 opened the second half of the book with comfort for exiles who thought God had forgotten them, and ended with weary people promised new strength (40:31). Chapter 41 begins the great courtroom scenes of chapters 41 to 48, in which the LORD summons the nations and their gods to trial.

The message. The LORD alone runs history and alone can say what is coming; the idols can do neither, because there is nobody there. So his small, frightened people, a “worm” in their own eyes, need not fear: the God who stirred up the conqueror is the God who holds their hand and has made himself their Redeemer.

Why it was said. The chapter speaks ahead to the exiles in Babylon, a beaten people surrounded by the gods of a victorious empire, who wondered whether the LORD had dropped them (see the introduction). A conqueror from the east was about to shake the world, and everyone would be asking whose hand was behind him.

How the chapter makes its case. The court is called (vv. 1–7): who raised up the conqueror from the east? The LORD answers, “I am he,” while the terrified nations nail together new gods. Then God turns to Israel (vv. 8–20): chosen and not cast off, told three times not to fear, held by his right hand, given the Holy One as Redeemer, turned from a worm into a threshing sledge, and promised rivers in the desert. Last, the idols are cross-examined (vv. 21–29): explain the past, announce the future, do anything at all. They are silent, and the LORD alone announced the conqueror and sends Jerusalem a herald of good news.

Where it leads. The line to Christ runs mainly through the character of God revealed in him, and partly through promise. The first, and with the last (v. 4) is the title the risen Jesus takes when he lays his right hand on a terrified apostle and says, “Fear not” (Revelation 1:17). The Redeemer who takes the place of nearest relative became our kinsman in the flesh, going lower than the worm Jacob (Psalm 22:6) to buy us back. The herald of good news (v. 27) runs on to the gospel (52:7; Romans 10:15), and the God who promised water to the thirsty stood up at a feast and said, “If anyone thirsts, let him come to me and drink” (John 7:37).

For us. Our fears usually wait for a change of circumstances; this chapter offers God himself instead. Anything we lean on that has to be nailed down to stay upright will fail us, but the hand that holds ours in Christ will not open.

keyVerse.quote: “Fear not, for I am with you; be not dismayed, for I am your God; I will strengthen you, I will help you, I will uphold you with my righteous right hand.”
keyVerse.note: The command “fear not” rings through Isaiah 40–55. It does not scold honest fear but turns the eyes: you are looking at the wrong thing. The cure for fear is not courage but the presence of God: I am with you is the reason, not an afterthought.

41.reflection:
God answers his people’s fear not by promising that circumstances will change but with two facts about himself: “I am with you” and “I am your God” (v. 10). Finish the sentence “My fear would lift if…”. How is what God offers in this verse different, and why is it both harder and better?

The nations encourage one another and nail their new god down so that it cannot topple (vv. 6–7), while the LORD says, “I, the LORD your God, hold your right hand” (v. 13). What in your life needs constant propping up, and what would it mean to be held rather than to do the holding?

God calls Israel “you worm Jacob” and in the same breath says, “your Redeemer is the Holy One of Israel” (v. 14). How is this different from both self-contempt and the self-esteem our culture recommends? How does Christ, who went lower than any of us (Psalm 22:6), make it true for you?

The idols are tested by whether they can tell the future and do anything about it (vv. 22–23). What do the people around you rely on for security, and how does it fare under Isaiah’s two questions?

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–7 — The Court Is Called to Order
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The LORD claims the coming conqueror as his own work, and the nations answer by making new gods. God convenes a court and summons the coastlands, the ends of the earth, to come near and speak (v. 1). His opening question is who stirred up the conqueror from the east, whose campaign sweeps all before it (vv. 2–3), and he answers it himself: “I, the LORD, the first, and with the last; I am he” (v. 4). The nations see the evidence and tremble, but instead of turning to him they cheer one another on in the workshop and fasten a new idol down with nails so that it cannot fall over (vv. 5–7).
verseByVerse.theology: The courtroom question in this chapter is never whether history is turbulent. Both sides agree that it is. The question is who is causing it, and the trial turns on one piece of evidence only: whether anyone announced it in advance.
verseByVerse.examples: Verse 7 is a sharp picture of man-made religion: men steadying each other, then steadying their god with nails. Three verses later the LORD says the opposite to his people: I will uphold you. Every idol eventually asks to be carried, and the difference between the two religions in this chapter is who holds up whom.

verseByVerse.quote: Listen to me in silence, O coastlands; let the peoples renew their strength; let them approach, then let them speak; let us together draw near for judgment. Who stirred up one from the east whom victory meets at every step? He gives up nations before him, so that he tramples kings underfoot; he makes them like dust with his sword, like driven stubble with his bow. He pursues them and passes on safely, by paths his feet have not trod. Who has performed and done this, calling the generations from the beginning? I, the LORD, the first, and with the last; I am he. The coastlands have seen and are afraid; the ends of the earth tremble; they have drawn near and come. Everyone helps his neighbor and says to his brother, "Be strong!" The craftsman strengthens the goldsmith, and he who smooths with the hammer him who strikes the anvil, saying of the soldering, "It is good"; and they strengthen it with nails so that it cannot be moved.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God summons the world to court and claims the coming conqueror as his work, while the nations make gods that must be nailed down to stand.

Listen to me in silence, O coastlands. A court is convened. The summons goes to the coastlands, the far edge of the known world, and the first instruction is silence. Then comes a phrase that anyone who has just read chapter 40 will catch: let the peoples renew their strength. That is the promise of 40:31, offered here to the other side: bring whatever strength you can raise.

Whom victory meets at every step. The evidence entered is a conqueror, Cyrus of Persia, though Isaiah keeps the name back until 44:28. His campaign never stalls: kings underfoot, armies turned to dust and stubble, and a general moving so fast through country he has never seen that his feet hardly touch it.

I, the LORD, the first, and with the last. God answers his own question (v. 4), and his title is the whole argument in a line: he was there before the first generation was called and will be there when the last is finished.

Everyone helps his neighbor. The nations see the evidence, tremble, and go down to the workshop: an exact picture of frightened religion, everybody busy and encouraging, the metalworker assuring the goldsmith that the soldering is good. And the god is finished by being nailed down, because otherwise it falls over. Keep that nail in mind (see the note on vv. 11–13).

The first and the last, in person. On Patmos the risen Christ takes this title as his own, laying his right hand on a terrified apostle: “Fear not, I am the first and the last” (Revelation 1:17). The Lord of history and the friend of the frightened are one person.

Uncertain wording. Verse 2 is compressed: word for word, righteousness calls him to its foot. The word may mean victory, as the ESV takes it, or that the conqueror is summoned to serve God’s righteous purpose. Either way his success is God’s doing, not his own.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 8–20 — Fear Not, I Am with You
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Turning from the frightened nations to his frightened people, God tells Israel that they need not fear, because he is with them. They are his servant, chosen and not cast off, the offspring of Abraham his friend (vv. 8–9), and he will strengthen, help and uphold them (v. 10). Their enemies will one day be looked for and not found, because the LORD holds their right hand (vv. 11–13). The worm Jacob has the Holy One as Redeemer and becomes a threshing sledge that turns mountains to chaff (vv. 14–16). And the poor and thirsty are promised rivers on bare hills and forests in the desert, so that all will know that the LORD has done it (vv. 17–20).
verseByVerse.theology: Fear is treated here as a matter of what we are looking at, not of how brave we are. The commands of verse 10 rest entirely on who God is, not on how things look, and they are spoken to a people he had already chosen and not cast off.
verseByVerse.examples: The title Redeemer in verse 14 is the one Job reached for when he had nothing else left (Job 19:25): when every other relative has failed, God himself stands up as next of kin.

verseByVerse.quote: But you, Israel, my servant, Jacob, whom I have chosen, the offspring of Abraham, my friend; you whom I took from the ends of the earth, and called from its farthest corners, saying to you, "You are my servant, I have chosen you and not cast you off"; fear not, for I am with you; be not dismayed, for I am your God; I will strengthen you, I will help you, I will uphold you with my righteous right hand.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God tells his exiles they are still his chosen servant, and gives them the cure for fear: not better circumstances but himself, with them and holding them up.

But you, Israel, my servant. The address turns, and the turn is audible: but you. Three names are laid down in a row, and none of them is something Israel achieved. Servant is a task God assigned. Chosen is something done to a person, not by him. And Abraham is called my friend, a staggering word to use of a man, kept by Israel long afterwards (2 Chronicles 20:7) and picked up by James when he wants to say what faith finally amounts to (James 2:23).

I have chosen you and not cast you off. Notice which fear verse 9 answers. It is not “will I be rescued?” but “have I been dropped?” People in exile do not usually doubt that God is strong; they doubt that they are still his. So the sentence God puts in their ears ends: I have chosen you and not cast you off.

Fear not, for I am with you. Verse 10 gives two commands, each with its reason, and then three promises. Neither reason has anything to do with the situation. Nothing says that Babylon is weaker than it looks or the exile shorter than it feels. The reasons are two facts about God: I am with you, I am your God.

I will uphold you with my righteous right hand. The three verbs move outward: strengthen (something put into you), help (something done alongside you), uphold (something that carries you when the first two have run out). And the hand is righteous: a grip that will not let go, and will not do anything shabby to keep hold of you.

A test for your own fears. Name your fear and finish the sentence: my fear would lift if… The honest answer is nearly always a change of circumstances: the scan comes back clear, the money arrives. This verse offers God himself instead, as enough.

What this looks like. Answer the fear with the reasons. Say them over, aloud if need be: he is with me; he is my God. Neither depends on the scan or the bank balance. Trust while afraid. David did not pretend to be brave: “When I am afraid, I put my trust in you” (Psalm 56:3). Fear is the occasion for trusting, not proof that you have failed to. Take the next step held. Make the phone call, open the letter, walk into the meeting, knowing whose right hand is underneath you. Reason from the cross. The God who says I am with you came to be with us in the flesh, and was forsaken on the cross so that those who trust him never will be. If he did that, the rest follows: “He who did not spare his own Son but gave him up for us all, how will he not also with him graciously give us all things?” (Romans 8:32). The fear may not leave at once, but you are not facing it alone.

May a Christian claim this promise? It was spoken to Israel, but it rests on God’s character and covenant, and those who belong to Christ are Abraham’s offspring (Galatians 3:29). Hebrews applies the same promise to believers: I will never leave you nor forsake you (Hebrews 13:5).
verseByVerse.note: Abraham is called God’s friend, as again in James.

verseByVerse.quote: Behold, all who are incensed against you shall be put to shame and confounded; those who strive against you shall be as nothing and shall perish. You shall seek those who contend with you, but you shall not find them; those who war against you shall be as nothing at all. For I, the LORD your God, hold your right hand; it is I who say to you, "Fear not, I am the one who helps you."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The enemies who loom so large will one day be gone without trace, because the LORD holds his people’s hand.

You shall seek those who contend with you. Verse 12 promises not that the enemy will be beaten in front of you, but that one day you will go looking for him and not find him. Anyone afraid of a person for years knows how much room that person takes up: in the diary, in the stomach, in the last thought before sleep. A day is coming when the search party goes out for that figure and comes back empty. Not smaller, but gone.

How the story ends. This is not a promise that the pressure lifts by next week: Babylon did not vanish the year after these words were written. It is a statement about how the story ends, as when Paul names the last enemy to be destroyed without pretending it has been destroyed yet (1 Corinthians 15:26).

I, the LORD your God, hold your right hand. Now the nail from verse 7 comes back. There, men held their god upright; here, God holds the man. The picture is a hand taken at a kerb. A small child crossing a road does grip back, and the grip is real, but it is not what keeps him safe; what keeps him safe is that the hand around his is not going to open. Everything in this chapter that looks like religion comes down to which hand is doing the holding.

What it does not mean. Trusting God with a person you fear does not mean staying where that person can harm you. If someone is threatening or hurting you, getting to safety, telling someone you trust and calling the police are not failures of faith.

verseByVerse.quote: Fear not, you worm Jacob, you men of Israel! I am the one who helps you, declares the LORD; your Redeemer is the Holy One of Israel. Behold, I make of you a threshing sledge, new, sharp, and having teeth; you shall thresh the mountains and crush them, and you shall make the hills like chaff; you shall winnow them, and the wind shall carry them away, and the tempest shall scatter them. And you shall rejoice in the LORD; in the Holy One of Israel you shall glory.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God agrees that his people are as weak as a worm, names himself their Redeemer, and turns what was trodden on into a sledge that threshes mountains.

Fear not, you worm Jacob. The tenderest promise in the chapter is fastened to the most humiliating name in it. A worm is what lies underfoot: no defence, no speed, no dignity, something a man steps on without breaking stride. God does not flatter his people out of their fear. He agrees with their estimate of themselves and tells them not to be afraid anyway, which is a far better comfort than being told they were stronger than they thought.

Your Redeemer is the Holy One of Israel. Then comes a word that will run through the rest of Isaiah: Redeemer, a family term rather than a religious one. The redeemer (go’el) was the nearest relative, the man bound to buy back the land you had lost, pay the debt you could not pay, and stand up for you when nobody else would. Boaz is one for Ruth. The title Holy One of Israel goes back to the “Holy, holy, holy” Isaiah heard in the temple (6:3), when he thought he would die. That holiness owed this people nothing and could have stayed at an infinite distance. Instead it came near, took the family name of Redeemer, and accepted the obligations that go with it. He did not have to become their kinsman; he chose to.

A threshing sledge, new, sharp, and having teeth. A threshing sledge was a heavy board studded underneath with stone or iron teeth, dragged over cut grain until the husks broke off. So the worm gets teeth. What was trodden on does the threshing, and the mountains go through it like chaff and blow away. The mountains are probably the powers that loomed over Israel and blocked her way, like the mountains in the road of 40:4. And the passage ends not with Israel admiring her new teeth but with her glory in someone else: you shall rejoice in the LORD; in the Holy One of Israel you shall glory (v. 16).

Lower than the worm. The same word appears at the bottom of the psalmist’s abandonment: I am a worm and not a man (Psalm 22:6), in the psalm whose opening cry Jesus prayed from the cross. The Redeemer did not stoop to the worm from a safe height. The Son of God became our kinsman in flesh and blood (Hebrews 2:14–15) and went as low as the people he came to buy back.

A worm with a kinsman. Few words grate on modern ears like worm. We are taught that the cure for most troubles is to think better of ourselves, and there is something kind in that, because many have been crushed by contempt. But a self-image built on affirmation must be propped up daily, like the gods of verse 7 nailed down so they will not topple; one failure and it falls over. Isaiah offers neither self-contempt nor self-esteem. He tells Israel the truth about her weakness and, in the same breath, who has taken responsibility for her. That is the Christian’s position too: you are not enough, and you are loved by one who was more than enough for you, which frees you from having to think about yourself so much.

Uncertain wording. The word translated men in you men of Israel is a rare one. The ESV gives its usual meaning; some translations, reading it differently to match worm, have “you insect Israel”. Either way the line pictures Israel as small and weak.

verseByVerse.quote: When the poor and needy seek water, and there is none, and their tongue is parched with thirst, I the LORD will answer them; I the God of Israel will not forsake them. I will open rivers on the bare heights, and fountains in the midst of the valleys. I will make the wilderness a pool of water, and the dry land springs of water. I will put in the wilderness the cedar, the acacia, the myrtle, and the olive. I will set in the desert the cypress, the plane and the pine together, that they may see and know, may consider and understand together, that the hand of the LORD has done this, the Holy One of Israel has created it.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God promises the thirsty far more than they ask, rivers on hilltops and forests in the desert, so that all will see that he did it.

When the poor and needy seek water. The scene shrinks from empires to a dry mouth: thirst at the stage where speech begins to fail. And the answer does not quite match the request: they seek water, and God says he will answer them. He promises himself to the people before he promises the water.

I will open rivers on the bare heights. This is deliberately the wrong place for water. Hilltops are where water runs off; springs belong in valleys. God names the ridgelines first, as though to say that the shortage was never about geography.

The cedar, the acacia, the myrtle, and the olive. Seven trees are planted in a desert, and not one of them is a survival crop. Cedar is timber for temples, myrtle is scent, olive is oil and light and food. A thirsty man asked for a cup and is given a forest with shade in it. God’s answers in this book regularly give more than was asked.

That they may see and know. Verse 20 gives the reason for all of it: that the giver be recognised. Four verbs of noticing are stacked up, because a gift can be received while the giver is missed. The desert is watered so that somebody will say who did it.

No more thirst. On the last day of the Feast of Tabernacles Jesus stood up and cried, “If anyone thirsts, let him come to me and drink” (John 7:37): the God who promised to answer the thirsty came to be the water. And Revelation keeps both halves of this passage: no more thirst, and the Lamb guiding his people to springs of living water (Revelation 7:16–17).

Uncertain wording. Several trees in verse 19 cannot be identified with certainty; older versions have the pine and the box tree for the ESV’s plane and pine. The picture is clear: fine trees where nothing grew.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 21–29 — The Silence in the Dock
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The idols are put on the stand and found to be nothing. The LORD, the King of Jacob, invites them to explain the past or announce the future (vv. 21–23), and when nothing comes he lowers the bar to anything at all: do good, or do harm. Their silence is the verdict: they are nothing, and whoever chooses them is an abomination (v. 24). Then God sets out his own evidence. He stirred up the conqueror from the north and the east, he alone announced it beforehand, and he gives Jerusalem a herald of good news (vv. 25–27). When he looks for a counsellor among the gods there is none; their images are empty wind (vv. 28–29).
verseByVerse.theology: An idol is not exposed by argument here but by silence. The gods of the nations are not refuted; they are asked a question and nothing happens, and the nothing is the whole case. Isaiah's verdict is not that they are weak but that they are not there.

verseByVerse.quote: Set forth your case, says the LORD; bring your proofs, says the King of Jacob. Let them bring them, and tell us what is to happen. Tell us the former things, what they are, that we may consider them, that we may know their outcome; or declare to us the things to come. Tell us what is to come hereafter, that we may know that you are gods; do good, or do harm, that we may be dismayed and terrified. Behold, you are nothing, and your work is less than nothing; an abomination is he who chooses you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Challenged to explain the past, announce the future or do anything at all, the idols are silent, and the silence is the verdict: they are nothing.

Set forth your case, says the LORD. The hearing resumes and the gods of the nations are called to the stand. The examination is fair and the questions are open: explain the past, or announce the future. Either will do.

Do good, or do harm. When nothing comes, the bar drops until it is lying on the floor: anything at all. Frighten us, if that is all you have. God is no longer asking these gods to be good; he is asking them to be there.

The silence of the gods. The room stays quiet, and the silence is the entire case. Isaiah does not argue that the idols are weaker than the LORD, but something simpler: there is nobody in there (compare 1 Corinthians 8:4).

Your work is less than nothing. Nothing would be bad enough; less than nothing means the account goes negative. Whatever is served in God’s place charges a fee for services it never renders. And the last line turns to the worshipper: an abomination is he who chooses you, for “those who make them become like them” (Psalm 115:8).

If idols are nothing, why does the Bible take them so seriously? The image is nothing, but the turning from God is real, and so is the darkness that uses it: Paul also warns that pagan sacrifices are offered to demons (1 Corinthians 10:19–20). The god is empty; the damage is not.

A test for this week. Put Isaiah’s two questions to whatever your peace depends on: can it tell you one true thing about tomorrow, and can it do one thing about tomorrow? A career, a portfolio, a person’s approval all fail both. The God who “has spoken to us by his Son” (Hebrews 1:2) passes both, and invites the anxious to rest their weight on him.

verseByVerse.quote: I stirred up one from the north, and he has come, from the rising of the sun, and he shall call upon my name; he shall trample on rulers as on mortar, as the potter treads clay. Who declared it from the beginning, that we might know, and beforehand, that we might say, "He is right"? There was none who declared it, none who proclaimed, none who heard your words. I was the first to say to Zion, "Behold, here they are!" and I give to Jerusalem a herald of good news. But when I look, there is no one; among these there is no counselor who, when I ask, gives an answer. Behold, they are all a delusion; their works are nothing; their metal images are empty wind.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God alone raised up the conqueror and announced it beforehand, and he sends Jerusalem good news, while the gods’ bench stays empty.

I stirred up one from the north. North and east in one sentence is not a slip. Cyrus came out of Persia, east of Babylon, but his conquests also took in the lands to the north, and Isaiah is describing a campaign, not giving a compass bearing.

He shall trample on rulers as on mortar. The point is in the first word: I stirred him up (as in v. 2). The most powerful man of the sixth century BC is someone God set in motion, and treading rulers like a potter’s clay is work God assigns.

He shall call upon my name. This does not mean that Cyrus became a worshipper of the LORD; 45:4 says plainly that he did not know him. But his decree freeing the exiles speaks in the LORD’s name: “The LORD, the God of heaven, has given me all the kingdoms of the earth” (Ezra 1:2).

There was none who declared it. Three times verse 26 says none. No other voice put this on record beforehand, and that is the evidence the trial has been driving at: anyone can explain a thing once it has happened.

A herald of good news. A runner appears in the courtroom (v. 27), carrying the Old Testament word for gospel, as in 40:9. Isaiah will send him over the hills again with beautiful feet at 52:7, where Paul finds him and puts him at the centre of Christian preaching (Romans 10:15). News that the exile was over previewed the news that ends a far deeper exile.

Their metal images are empty wind. Nobody rises to advise or answer, and the verdict on everything the nations nailed down in verse 7 is short: empty wind.

The only voice in the room. One voice has spoken in this room from the beginning. He called the generations before anyone could hear him, moved an emperor across a continent without consulting him, and stooped to a worm and called himself its kinsman. The court adjourns with the LORD still on his feet, and the earth has nothing to say back.

Uncertain wording. Verse 27 opens abruptly in Hebrew, roughly First to Zion, behold, behold them; the ESV supplies to say. The likely meaning is that the LORD was the first, and only, one to announce Zion’s deliverance.
verseByVerse.note: The one from the north and east is Cyrus.

41.theology:
The credential God stakes everything on. Chapters 41–48 are a trial, and the LORD chooses the ground he will be judged on: not power, which the nations could claim too, but prediction. He names a conqueror before that conqueror arrives, and points to the record afterwards. It is the same logic Jesus uses in the upper room: I have told you before it takes place, so that when it does take place you may believe (John 14:29). God secures faith by putting his word on record in advance and then keeping it.

Fear not is not a rebuke. The command comes three times, never with a reason drawn from the circumstances. Courage here is not worked up from within; it comes from looking at him.

The worm and the Redeemer. The Holy One, who owed this people nothing, took on himself the duty of a nearest relative, and came down, in the end, to where the redeemed were lying (Psalm 22:6).

42.subtitle: The First Servant Song
42.intro:
Where we are. Chapter 41 put the nations’ gods on trial and found them empty, and called Israel God’s chosen servant. Chapter 42 opens with the first of four Servant Songs (vv. 1–9; the others are 49:1–6; 50:4–9; 52:13–53:12), and then turns back to the servant Israel, who turns out to be blind.

The message. God has a Servant who will do what Israel never did. Filled with God’s Spirit, he will set the whole world right, not by force but so gently that he will not break a bruised reed, and he will not give up until the work is done. The world will sing about it, and God, silent so long, is about to act. But the servant people are blind and deaf, and their need is the very thing the true Servant comes to meet.

Why it was said. The exiles in Babylon (see the introduction) felt crushed and forgotten, and wondered where God had been. They also needed to face why they were there: not because Babylon’s gods were stronger, but because the LORD had handed them over for their sin (vv. 24–25).

How the chapter makes its case. The Servant is introduced (vv. 1–9): chosen, upheld, given the Spirit, gentle with the bruised, made a covenant for the people and a light for the nations, sent to open blind eyes and free prisoners, all announced beforehand by the God who gives his glory to no other. The world answers with a new song (vv. 10–12), and God goes out like a warrior and cries out like a woman in labour after his long silence, leading the blind home while idol worshippers are turned back (vv. 13–17). Then the hard turn (vv. 18–25): Israel, the LORD’s servant, is blind, deaf and plundered, burned by judgment and still not understanding.

Where it leads. Here the line to Christ is direct promise. The Father’s words at Jesus’ baptism echo verse 1 (Matthew 3:17), and Matthew quotes verses 1–4 to explain Jesus’ quiet, healing ministry (Matthew 12:17–21). Jesus is the covenant in person (Luke 22:20) and the light for the nations (Luke 2:32), and he opened blind eyes and set captives free. And the gap between the faithful Servant of verse 1 and the blind servant of verse 19 is closed only at the cross, where the one bears the sins of the other (53:5–6).

For us. If you feel like a bruised reed or a wick almost out, this Servant will not throw you away. And if you have seen many things and kept none of them (v. 20), the answer is not more effort but coming to the one who opens blind eyes.

keyVerse.quote: “Behold my servant, whom I uphold, my chosen, in whom my soul delights; I have put my Spirit upon him; he will bring forth justice to the nations.”
keyVerse.note: God’s introduction of his Servant is echoed at Jesus’ baptism, when the Spirit comes down on him and the Father’s voice speaks of the beloved Son with whom he is well pleased (Matthew 3:16–17). The verse holds the whole song in small: the Father’s delight, the Spirit’s anointing, and a mission of justice that reaches the nations. It tells us what the mission will look like before it begins.

42.reflection:
The Servant will not break a bruised reed or quench a faintly burning wick (v. 3). When have you felt like either? How does it help to know how he treats such people, and who near you needs the same gentleness this week?

The Servant brings justice to the nations without crying aloud in the street (v. 2). Where are you tempted to put things right by pressure, volume or force? What would his way look like there?

God says, “For a long time I have held my peace” (v. 14). How does this help with prayers that seem to meet only silence? What does it suggest about what God is doing while he waits?

Israel “sees many things, but does not observe them” (v. 20). What is the last thing you knew God was saying to you, and what has happened to it?
