Who is blind as my dedicated one, or blind as the servant of the LORD?<sup>20</sup>He sees many things, but does not observe them; his ears are open, but he does not hear.<sup>21</sup>The LORD was pleased, for his righteousness' sake, to magnify his law and make it glorious.<sup>22</sup>But this is a people plundered and looted; they are all of them trapped in holes and hidden in prisons; they have become plunder with none to rescue, spoil with none to say, "Restore!"<sup>23</sup>Who among you will give ear to this, will attend and listen for the time to come?<sup>24</sup>Who gave up Jacob to the looter, and Israel to the plunderers? Was it not the LORD, against whom we have sinned, in whose ways they would not walk, and whose law they would not obey?<sup>25</sup>So he poured on him the heat of his anger and the might of battle; it set him on fire all around, but he did not understand; it burned him up, but he did not take it to heart.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God introduces his Servant, who will set the world right by a method no one expects. The credentials come first: upheld, chosen, delighted in, given God’s Spirit, sent with justice for the nations (v. 1). Then the method: no shouting in the street (v. 2), no breaking of bruised reeds or snuffing of faint wicks, and no growing faint himself until the work is done (vv. 3–4). The Creator of heaven and earth commissions him as a covenant for the people and a light for the nations, to open blind eyes and bring prisoners out of the dark (vv. 5–7). The song closes with God refusing to share his glory and announcing new things before they spring up (vv. 8–9).
verseByVerse.theology: The song sets out a Messiah whose power does not force or bully. Justice is repeated three times, but brought by a man who does not raise his voice. Verse 8 then says, without arguing it, who this servant must be (see the note on vv. 8-9).
verseByVerse.examples: Matthew quotes verses 1 to 4 in full, his longest quotation of the Old Testament, to explain why Jesus healed crowds and then told them not to make him known (Matt. 12:18-21), and verse 7's three tasks are the shape of Jesus' public ministry. The bruised reed and the smouldering wick have comforted more frightened Christians than almost any other line in the prophets.

verseByVerse.quote: Behold my servant, whom I uphold, my chosen, in whom my soul delights; I have put my Spirit upon him; he will bring forth justice to the nations.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God presents his Servant with delight, gives him his Spirit and sends him to set the world right: words the Father spoke again over Jesus.

In whom my soul delights. The introduction is all affection before it is any description of the work. Whom I uphold: the hand is under him. My chosen: the choice is settled. In whom my soul delights: not the language of an employer about a competent worker but of a father about a son.

I have put my Spirit upon him. This one line holds a Father who delights, a Spirit who is put upon the servant, and the servant himself. The Old Testament does not explain how God is three; it simply describes the scene, and there are three in it.

He will bring forth justice to the nations. Justice (mishpat) runs three times through the first four verses. It does not mean punishment but the setting right of things, everything at last as it should be. And its reach is the nations, from the first verse of the first song.

At the Jordan. Seven centuries later the voice from heaven says over a man standing in a river, “This is my beloved Son, with whom I am well pleased” (Matthew 3:17). Before Jesus has preached or healed anybody, the Father says the sentence Isaiah wrote down, and the Spirit descends, exactly as the verse says.

Who is the servant? Israel is called God’s servant (41:8). But this servant is faithful where Israel is blind and deaf (42:18–19), he brings justice to the nations quietly and gently, and he is himself a covenant for the people (v. 6). Matthew quotes these verses of Jesus (Matthew 12:17–21).

Where Christians differ. Many medieval Jewish commentators, and some modern scholars, read this servant as Israel, whose quiet faithfulness will one day bring the nations God’s justice; others think of the prophet, or of Cyrus (45:1). Yet the ancient Aramaic paraphrase, the Targum, names the servant here as the Messiah, so the messianic reading has deep Jewish roots.

This commentary’s view. The readings need not be rivals: the servant gathers up Israel’s calling in one person, who fulfils what the nation was called to be, and Matthew identifies him as Jesus (Matthew 12:17–21).
verseByVerse.note: The first of four “Servant Songs” (42:1–4; 49:1–6; 50:4–9; 52:13–53:12), fulfilled in Jesus.

verseByVerse.quote: He will not cry aloud or lift up his voice, or make it heard in the street;
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Servant will set the world right without shouting, campaigning or making a name for himself.

He will not cry aloud. Here is the surprise of the song. Every other programme for setting the world right runs on volume: a platform, a crowd, a slogan and an enemy. This one refuses all of it. The street was the public square, where causes were argued and reputations made, and he will bring justice to the nations without raising his voice there.

Why Jesus kept quiet. Matthew used this to explain something in Jesus that would otherwise look strange: he heals everyone who comes, then orders them not to make him known, and Matthew quotes the whole song (Matthew 12:15–21). His quietness was neither modesty nor tactics. It was the shape of the mission, written down centuries in advance.

Did Jesus never raise his voice? He did (John 7:37), and he drove the traders from the temple. The point is not volume but method: he did not promote himself or force his way to power, and he went to the cross rather than call down angels.

In everyday life. When we want something put right, the instinct is pressure: a louder argument, a sharper post, a confrontation that settles it. The servant’s way is the opposite, and it worked: nothing has changed the world as much, yet almost nothing began more quietly.

verseByVerse.quote: a bruised reed he will not break, and a faintly burning wick he will not quench; he will faithfully bring forth justice. He will not grow faint or be discouraged till he has established justice in the earth; and the coastlands wait for his law.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Servant will not throw away damaged and spent people, and he himself will not be crushed or give up until the earth is set right.

A bruised reed he will not break. Both pictures are of things you throw away. A split reed will not sound a note, so a shepherd snaps it and cuts another; a wick burned down gives smoke instead of light, so you pinch it out. Neither act is cruel; it is what a sensible person does with something that no longer works. The servant will not do it. And the two objects are chosen with terrible accuracy, because they are what damaged people are like: not dead, but not working, producing smoke and no note at all. It is one thing to believe God is patient with sinners. It is harder to believe he has any use for someone who has stopped working.

He will not grow faint or be discouraged. In verse 4 the ESV’s footnote shows what the English hides: discouraged may be rendered “bruised”. The reed was bruised and the wick faintly burning; the servant will not grow faint or be bruised, and in Hebrew these are the same two words. Isaiah describes the servant and the people he rescues in one vocabulary: he will not break the crushed, and he will not be crushed; he will not quench the faint, and he will not grow faint. Carrying the smouldering and the splintered, he does not himself give way.

When you are the difficult person. That answers the fear of anyone who has been the difficult person in somebody’s life: that patience is a limited supply you are drawing down, and that one day the person carrying you will reach the end of it and be right to. The verse says the supply does not run out and the carrier does not wear through.

The coastlands wait for his law. His law means his teaching: the far edge of the world stands on tiptoe for a man who will not discard the useless. Matthew, quoting the Greek Old Testament, renders the line and in his name the Gentiles will hope (Matthew 12:21); to wait for someone’s teaching is to hope in him, so the sense is the same.

Sparta’s scoreboard and ours. The ancient world was clear about what to do with people who did not work. The Greek writer Plutarch records that in Sparta a newborn judged weak or misshapen by the elders was left in a ravine below Mount Taygetus. Rome exposed unwanted infants as a matter of course, and some early Christians became known for taking them in. We are rightly horrified, but we have kept more of that scoreboard than we admit: a modern society quietly ranks people by output, and the old, the disabled and the depressed are tempted to wonder whether they are only a burden. The servant overturns the scoreboard. He does not merely tolerate the bruised reed; he refuses to break it, because its worth never depended on its usefulness. And he could promise that because, three songs later, he would himself be crushed (53:5), bruised so that the bruised would never be thrown away.

If you feel like a burden. If the thought that others would be better off without you has settled in, tell someone you trust today, and if you are in danger, call the emergency services now. That is no lack of faith.

verseByVerse.quote: Thus says God, the LORD, who created the heavens and stretched them out, who spread out the earth and what comes from it, who gives breath to the people on it and spirit to those who walk in it: "I am the LORD; I have called you in righteousness; I will take you by the hand and keep you; I will give you as a covenant for the people, a light for the nations,
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Creator takes his Servant by the hand and makes him, in person, God’s covenant with his people and the light of the nations.

Who created the heavens and stretched them out. The one giving the commission has cosmic credentials: he made sky and ground, and every person breathes air he supplied. Then the same God takes one man by the hand, a gesture almost parental.

A covenant for the people. The first of two titles should stop the reader. The servant is not given the covenant, or sent to explain it, or made a minister of it. He is the covenant: the bond between God and his people is a person rather than a document. At the Last Supper Jesus held up a cup and said that the new covenant was in his blood (Luke 22:20): a man speaking of himself as the covenant.

A light for the nations. The second title reaches straight past Israel. It is the phrase old Simeon sings over the baby Jesus in the temple courts (Luke 2:32), and the one Paul and Barnabas quote when a synagogue turns them out and they go to the Gentiles instead (Acts 13:47).

Uncertain wording. It is debated whether the people in a covenant for the people means Israel (compare 49:8) or humanity, as the same word does in verse 5. Either way the Servant is himself the covenant, and his light reaches beyond Israel.

verseByVerse.quote: to open the eyes that are blind, to bring out the prisoners from the dungeon, from the prison those who sit in darkness.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Servant gives sight, freedom and light to people who cannot help themselves, as Jesus did.

To open the eyes that are blind. The job description is concrete: sight, freedom, light. Read the Gospels with those three in hand and the ministry of Jesus stops looking like an assortment of kindnesses and starts looking like a man working through a list. He opened blind eyes, again and again, and he opened the eyes of people who could see perfectly well but could not see who he was. He announced liberty to captives, and told the synagogue in Nazareth, reading the parallel passage from chapter 61, that this Scripture was fulfilled in their hearing (Luke 4:18–21).

To bring out the prisoners from the dungeon. The dungeon is a pit prison, a hole with the door overhead, where a man is not punished for a term but simply kept, with no daylight and no reason to expect the door to open today. That is where the servant walks: into a hole where somebody sits because nobody has ever come. And the last phrase names the posture: those who sit in darkness, which is what people do when they have stopped expecting anything to change; that is exactly where the light was sent.

verseByVerse.quote: I am the LORD; that is my name; my glory I give to no other, nor my praise to carved idols. Behold, the former things have come to pass, and new things I now declare; before they spring forth I tell you of them."
verseByVerse.commentary:
God gives his glory to no other and announces his work in advance; yet he gives everything to his Servant, who must therefore share that glory.

My glory I give to no other. The song ends where the whole of chapters 40 to 48 stands: God will not share. Not a sliver of glory goes anywhere else, least of all to carved idols, the manufactured gods of chapter 40 that had to be kept from falling over.

What God gives the servant. Set that sentence beside the verses before it. God has put his Spirit on this servant, called him in righteousness, taken him by the hand, made him the covenant in person, the light of the nations, the opener of blind eyes and the bringer of justice to the earth. If God gives his glory to no other, and has given all that to the servant, then the servant does not count as an “other”: he shares the glory that belongs to God alone. Isaiah does not argue it; he lays the two side by side and declines to separate them, which is how the Old Testament often does its deepest work.

Before they spring forth I tell you of them. Verse 9 states the argument these chapters keep making: the LORD announces beforehand and then brings it about. And spring forth is a gardening word, a shoot breaking the soil. The new thing is already growing underground while it is being announced; by the time anybody sees it, it will have been growing a long time.

That is my name. The capital letters in LORD stand for God’s own name, Yahweh, which he explained to Moses as “I AM WHO I AM” (Exodus 3:14). These chapters keep repeating it: “I am the LORD, and there is no other” (45:5); “that you may know and believe me and understand that I am he” (43:10). A name means someone to be known and trusted, not a force to be kept on side. The night before he died, Jesus took up these words, with the argument of verse 9 attached: “I am telling you this now, before it takes place, that when it does take place you may believe that I am he” (John 13:19). The name that gives its glory to no other is the name Jesus answers to. So when you pray in his name, you are calling on the LORD himself, made known in a man you can trust. See Lord.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 10–17 — A New Song, and the God Who Has Kept Quiet
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The Servant’s mission sets the whole world singing, and the silent God goes into action. The far ends of the earth are called to sing a new song: sea and coastlands, desert towns, the tents of Kedar and the rock of Sela (vv. 10–12). Then come two pictures that seem impossible to hold together: the LORD as a warrior shouting his battle cry (v. 13), and as a woman in labour who has held back as long as she can (v. 14). He levels the landscape to lead the blind home by roads they do not know, and promises not to forsake them, while those who trust idols are turned back in shame (vv. 15–17).
verseByVerse.theology: Verse 14 matters most in the section, because it answers the question the exiles were actually asking: where has God been? The two images of verses 13 and 14 belong together: a warrior's cry and a woman's cry are both the sound of something held back finally being released.
verseByVerse.examples: Anyone who has waited years for God to act on something has felt the silence of verse 14 from the inside and drawn the natural conclusion from it. This verse denies the conclusion without denying the experience.

verseByVerse.quote: Sing to the LORD a new song, his praise from the end of the earth, you who go down to the sea, and all that fills it, the coastlands and their inhabitants. Let the desert and its cities lift up their voice, the villages that Kedar inhabits; let the habitants of Sela sing for joy, let them shout from the top of the mountains. Let them give glory to the LORD, and declare his praise in the coastlands.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The whole world, even its wildest corners, is called to sing a new song: the Servant’s light has reached the nations.

His praise from the end of the earth. The song about the servant is answered by a song from the world, and the geography is the whole point: the sea, the far coastlands, the desert, the goat-hair tents of Kedar out on the steppe, the rock city of Sela in old enemy territory, and the mountain tops, where people shout because sound carries. Isaiah lists places with no share in Israel’s worship and puts a hymn in every one. The mission of verse 6 has borne fruit inside the poetry: the light went to the nations, and the nations sang back.

Sing to the LORD a new song. In Scripture a new song is the song of people who have just seen God act, and it sounds finally around the throne, sung to a Lamb who was slain and ransomed people for God from every tribe and language and people and nation (Revelation 5:9): the same music heard from a different distance.

Declare his praise in the coastlands. Praise turns outward in verse 12. The redeemed do not sing privately; the song itself carries the report to people who have not heard it, which is why worship and mission have never really been two separate departments of the church’s life.
verseByVerse.note: Kedar and Sela were in the Arabian desert and Edom.

verseByVerse.quote: The LORD goes out like a mighty man, like a man of war he stirs up his zeal; he cries out, he shouts aloud, he shows himself mighty against his foes.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The same God whose Servant is gentle with the bruised goes out like a warrior against everything that destroys his people.

The LORD goes out like a mighty man. Eleven verses ago the servant would not raise his voice. Now God himself is shouting the battle cry. There is no contradiction: the servant’s quietness was never weakness in God but a chosen method for a particular work. The God who will not snap a bruised reed goes out like a soldier against what is destroying the people the reed belongs to.

Gentleness and ferocity. Any parent understands the pairing without having it explained. The gentleness shown to a frightened child and the ferocity shown to whatever frightened him are not two temperaments. They are one love, meeting two different objects.

He stirs up his zeal. His zeal is the burning commitment a person feels about something that belongs to them. God is not reluctantly discharging a duty of justice; he is angry at what is destroying his people.

verseByVerse.quote: For a long time I have held my peace; I have kept still and restrained myself; now I will cry out like a woman in labor; I will gasp and pant.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God’s long silence was restraint, not absence, and now, like a woman in labour, he will bring forth what he held back.

For a long time I have held my peace. This sentence answers the question the exiles were actually asking: not whether God is able, but where he has been. The answer is not “I was not there.” The silence that felt from underneath like absence was self-control, a decision held at cost, for reasons that belonged to God and were never explained to the people doing the waiting.

Like a woman in labor. Then he reaches for the one experience that joins a long silence to an irresistible release: a woman in labour, past the point where anything can be held in. The Lord of hosts describes himself so, and does not soften it.

The fullness of time. Israel would know a longer silence, the centuries between the last prophet and Christ. Then, “when the fullness of time had come, God sent forth his Son” (Galatians 4:4).

When prayer meets silence. If you have prayed for years and heard nothing back, this verse is God’s own account of such silence: not neglect, but restraint, and restraint has an end built into it. What comes at the end is not an explanation but a birth, something alive that could not have arrived any sooner.

verseByVerse.quote: I will lay waste mountains and hills, and dry up all their vegetation; I will turn the rivers into islands, and dry up the pools. And I will lead the blind in a way that they do not know, in paths that they have not known I will guide them. I will turn the darkness before them into light, the rough places into level ground. These are the things I do, and I do not forsake them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God clears the ground to lead blind people home by roads they do not know, and he will not let go of them.

I will lay waste mountains and hills. The landscape is dismantled, and for a verse it reads like sheer destruction. Then the reason arrives and changes the colour of everything before it: the ground is being cleared for people who cannot see where they are going.

I will lead the blind. Two things deserve slowing down. First, the blind are not outsiders: verse 19 will say the blind man is God’s own servant. Their blindness is their own fault, and he flattens mountains for them anyway, which is grace. Second, in a way that they do not know is not an apology for the route but part of the plan. A blind man on a road he knows can still tell himself he is managing; on an unfamiliar road he has nothing but the hand he is holding. God does not usually cure the blindness first and then hand over directions. He takes the hand and starts walking, and not knowing the road is what turns the walk into trust.

I do not forsake them. Then a flat promise dropped into the cosmic engineering. Out of all of it, the sentence he wants remembered is that he does not let go of people’s hands.

verseByVerse.quote: They are turned back and utterly put to shame, who trust in carved idols, who say to metal images, "You are our gods."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Those who trust idols end up going backwards, and are shamed when their gods are seen for what they are.

They are turned back. The chapter keeps its two roads apart. One set of people is being led home by a God they cannot see; the other trusts objects they can see very well, and goes backwards. Turned back is not struck down but reversed: they set out somewhere and end up further from it than when they started, which is the characteristic motion of trusting something that cannot move.

Utterly put to shame. The shame is not God being vindictive. Shame is what happens when a thing is finally seen for what it is, in public, by everybody including its owner. A man who has given his life to an object that cannot act does not need to be punished in order to be humiliated by it; he only needs to see it clearly on a day when he badly needs it to do something.

What everyone trusts. The question of the chapter is not whether a person will trust, since everybody trusts something, but whether the thing trusted has hands that can act.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 18–25 — Who Is Blind but My Servant?
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The chapter turns sharply: the servant who should open blind eyes is blind himself. The deaf and blind are summoned to listen, and then God asks who is blind but his own servant, his messenger, his dedicated one (vv. 18–19). Israel sees many things but takes none of them to heart (v. 20). God meant his law to be glorious, yet his people lie plundered and trapped, with no one to say, “Restore!” (vv. 21–22). Who handed them over? The LORD himself, because they sinned and would not walk in his ways; and even in the fire of his anger they did not understand (vv. 23–25).
verseByVerse.theology: This is the theological problem the servant songs exist to solve. Israel is God's servant and Israel cannot do the work: the people appointed to open eyes are the people who cannot see, and verse 25 rules out the hope that suffering by itself will teach them.
verseByVerse.examples: Paul spends three chapters of Romans on Israel's blindness and refuses to explain it away (Rom. 9-11). The honest response to verse 25 is not to point to somebody else as the man in it, but to see ourselves there.

verseByVerse.quote: Hear, you deaf, and look, you blind, that you may see! Who is blind but my servant, or deaf as my messenger whom I send? Who is blind as my dedicated one, or blind as the servant of the LORD?
verseByVerse.commentary:
The servant people sent to open blind eyes are themselves blind, so the Servant of verse 1 cannot simply be Israel.

The servant who is blind. After seventeen verses admiring the servant, the reader sees the same title land on the nation as an accusation. The people meant to be a light (v. 6) and to open blind eyes (v. 7) turn out to be the blind man in the story.

Blind as the servant of the LORD? Isaiah stacks up four titles in one verse: my servant, my messenger whom I send, my dedicated one, the servant of the LORD. Every one is an honour, and every one is used as an indictment. The closer the relationship, the worse the blindness looks.

Two servants. This is the hinge of all the servant material. One servant will not break a bruised reed; the other cannot see and has to be led home. They cannot be the same servant, and by chapter 53 it will be plain that one of them is dying for the other.

Uncertain wording. The word for my dedicated one is rare and its sense uncertain; the ESV notes the one at peace with me, others suggest my covenant partner. Each points to someone close to God, which makes the blindness worse.

verseByVerse.quote: He sees many things, but does not observe them; his ears are open, but he does not hear.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Israel’s trouble was not ignorance but inattention: they had seen and heard a great deal and kept none of it.

He sees many things, but does not observe them. A precise and uncomfortable diagnosis. The eyes work and the ears are open, which makes it worse. These were people with the law, the prophets, the temple and the exodus behind them; the problem was never a shortage of what God had shown them but a failure to pay attention. He sees many things and could pass an examination on the covenant. He simply does not observe: does not keep, guard or do anything with what he has plainly seen.

A danger for good readers. A person can read this chapter, be genuinely moved by the bruised reed, and put the book down unchanged. Seeing many things and observing none is the particular danger of the well-taught.

What to ask yourself. So the question is not whether you have heard enough but what happened to the last thing you knew was meant for you. The answer to that failure is not more resolve but the Servant of verse 7, who opens blind eyes and does not snap the bruised reed of a dull hearer who comes back to him.

verseByVerse.quote: The LORD was pleased, for his righteousness' sake, to magnify his law and make it glorious. But this is a people plundered and looted; they are all of them trapped in holes and hidden in prisons; they have become plunder with none to rescue, spoil with none to say, "Restore!"
verseByVerse.commentary:
God meant his law to make his people glorious, but they lie plundered and helpless, and the gap shows that more law cannot save them.

To magnify his law and make it glorious. Verse 21 is the intention, and it is entirely good. God gave the law to display his own righteousness, and meant it to be magnificent: a whole nation living visibly well before a watching world, so that anyone could look at Israel and work out what God was like.

A people plundered and looted. Beside it, without transition, is what actually happened: plundered, trapped in holes, hiding down cisterns while soldiers went through the villages. The last detail is the loneliest in the chapter: not one voice anywhere saying Restore!

Not a little short. The measure of Israel’s failure is the distance between those two verses: not falling a little short of a standard, but the complete reverse. The people who were to be the glory of the law are being carried off in pieces by their neighbours.

Why more law cannot help. It also explains why the answer, when it comes, cannot be more law. The law was glorious, the law was given, and this is the result. Something else has to happen, which is what the servant is for, and why chapter 53 will speak of iniquity laid on somebody rather than met by better behaviour.

verseByVerse.quote: Who among you will give ear to this, will attend and listen for the time to come? Who gave up Jacob to the looter, and Israel to the plunderers? Was it not the LORD, against whom we have sinned, in whose ways they would not walk, and whose law they would not obey? So he poured on him the heat of his anger and the might of battle; it set him on fire all around, but he did not understand; it burned him up, but he did not take it to heart.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The LORD handed his people over for their sin, and even in the fire they did not learn, which leaves the Servant as the only way out.

Who gave up Jacob to the looter? Isaiah asks who did this to Israel, and the answer is not Assyria, not Babylon, and not bad luck. It was the LORD. The armies and their cruelty were real, and they will answer for it, but behind all of it stood God, handing his own people over.

Against whom we have sinned. That is a hard thing to say, and Isaiah says it in the first person: against whom we have sinned. He does not stand outside the sentence he pronounces. It is the same instinct as chapter 6, where he confessed his own unclean lips before adding that he lived among a people of unclean lips.

He did not take it to heart. The chapter ends on a picture that is hard to shake off: a man standing inside a fire and not noticing it. The judgment fell, the cities went, the people were carried away, and the thing it was sent to teach was not learned.

The only door left. If neither revelation nor catastrophe opened their eyes, nothing human will. The chapter that began with a servant who opens blind eyes ends with a people blind and burned, and the only door left is the one the servant came through. Eleven chapters later the LORD’s hand falls again, this time on the Servant: “it was the will of the LORD to crush him” (53:10), so that people who never took it to heart could be healed.

What it does not mean. This was the covenant curse Moses had warned of (Deuteronomy 28). It does not mean every hardship in a believer’s life is God’s anger: Jesus refused that reading of suffering (Luke 13:1–5; John 9:1–3), and for those in Christ the anger has been borne.

42.theology:
Two servants, and why there must be. Nothing in the chapter suggests that more effort or a better generation would close the gap between the servant of verse 1 and the servant of verse 19. What is required is a servant who does what Israel could not, which is where the songs are going: to a Servant wounded for the transgressions of the blind servant (53:5), whom Philip names as Jesus on the desert road (Acts 8:32–35). That is the gospel for every reader who sees much and observes little: Christ did not merely show the way; he walked it perfectly in our place, and his obedience is counted as ours (Romans 5:19). Our failures to see are met first with mercy, and then with the Spirit he puts on his people, who opens blind eyes still.

Power that refuses coercion. Justice is promised three times in four verses and established without volume. The servant will not break the bruised reed, and he himself will not be bruised: carrying the broken does not break him.

43.subtitle: I Have Called You by Name
43.intro:
Where we are. Chapter 42 ended with Israel blind, deaf, plundered and burned by God’s anger, and still not understanding. Chapter 43 begins, astonishingly, with But now, and with some of the tenderest words in the Bible.

The message. God’s people belong to him because he made them, redeemed them and called them by name, and nothing can undo that: not deep water, not fire, not the price he must pay. They are his witnesses that he alone is God and Saviour, and he is about to do a new thing greater than the exodus. And he blots out their sins, not because they deserve it, but for his own sake.

Why it was said. The exiles (see the introduction) were scattered, had neglected God’s worship and wearied him with their sins, and had every reason to think he was finished with them. This chapter says he is not.

How the chapter makes its case. God claims his people (vv. 1–7): created, redeemed, named, his own; he will go with them through water and fire, pay any price for them, and order the four winds to give them back. The court reopens (vv. 8–13): the nations have no witnesses, but blind Israel is God’s witness that besides him there is no saviour. He will bring Babylon down and, as he once opened the sea, make a way in the wilderness and rivers in the desert (vv. 14–21). Last comes the charge (vv. 22–28): they did not call on him but burdened him with their sins, and yet he blots out their transgressions for his own sake, even while judgment runs its course.

Where it leads. The line to Christ runs through promise and through the character of God revealed in him. The ransom of verses 3–4 points to the Son of Man who came “to give his life as a ransom for many” (Mark 10:45). Because there is no saviour besides the LORD (v. 11), the apostles’ confession of Jesus as “our great God and Savior” (Titus 2:13) is either blasphemy or the plain truth. The new exodus of verses 18–21 comes through his death and resurrection, and the God who blots out sin for his own sake does it justly at the cross, where the record of our debt was nailed (Colossians 2:14).

For us. If you belong to Christ, you are named, redeemed and his, and you will cross no river alone. And when your worship has been thin and your sins heavy, the way back is not to make up the shortfall but to come to the God who says, “I, I am he who blots out your transgressions.”

keyVerse.quote: “Fear not, for I have redeemed you; I have called you by name, you are mine.”
keyVerse.note: Three basic declarations: redeemed, named, owned. Each one fully answers a different fear: the fear of condemnation (redeemed), the fear of being unknown (named), the fear of abandonment (mine). The chapter builds everything else on these three. Knowing you are named and owned is what makes it possible to walk through waters and fire without being overwhelmed.

43.reflection:
God says, “I have called you by name, you are mine” (v. 1). Which of the three, redeemed, named or owned, do you most need to hear today, and why?

Verse 2 promises not a way round the waters and the fire but God’s presence in them. In your own hard place, what have you been praying for: a detour, or his company? How have you seen him keep this promise?

God calls his people his witnesses (v. 10). What have you seen God do that you could tell someone this week, and how might telling it strengthen your own faith?

God blots out sins “for my own sake” (v. 25). Why is forgiveness that rests on God rather than on us more secure, and how does the cross show that it was never cheap?

I give Egypt as your ransom, Cush and Seba in exchange for you.<sup>4</sup>Because you are precious in my eyes, and honored, and I love you, I give men in return for you, peoples in exchange for your life.<sup>5</sup>Fear not, for I am with you; I will bring your offspring from the east, and from the west I will gather you.<sup>6</sup>I will say to the north, Give up, and to the south, Do not withhold; bring my sons from afar and my daughters from the end of the earth,<sup>7</sup>everyone who is called by my name, whom I created for my glory, whom I formed and made."<sup>8</sup>Bring out the people who are blind, yet have eyes, who are deaf, yet have ears!<sup>9</sup>All the nations gather together, and the peoples assemble. Who among them can declare this, and show us the former things? Let them bring their witnesses to prove them right, and let them hear and say, It is true.<sup>10</sup>"You are my witnesses," declares the LORD, "and my servant whom I have chosen, that you may know and believe me and understand that I am he. Before me no god was formed, nor shall there be any after me.<sup>11</sup>I, I am the LORD, and besides me there is no savior.<sup>12</sup>I declared and saved and proclaimed, when there was no strange god among you; and you are my witnesses," declares the LORD, "and I am God.<sup>13</sup>Also henceforth I am he; there is none who can deliver from my hand; I work, and who can turn it back?"<sup>14</sup>Thus says the LORD, your Redeemer, the Holy One of Israel: "For your sake I send to Babylon and bring them all down as fugitives, even the Chaldeans, in the ships in which they rejoice.<sup>15</sup>I am the LORD, your Holy One, the Creator of Israel, your King."<sup>16</sup>Thus says the LORD, who makes a way in the sea, a path in the mighty waters,<sup>17</sup>who brings forth chariot and horse, army and warrior; they lie down, they cannot rise, they are extinguished, quenched like a wick:<sup>18</sup>"Remember not the former things, nor consider the things of old.<sup>19</sup>Behold, I am doing a new thing; now it springs forth, do you not perceive it? I will make a way in the wilderness and rivers in the desert.<sup>20</sup>The wild beasts will honor me, the jackals and the ostriches, for I give water in the wilderness, rivers in the desert, to give drink to my chosen people,<sup>21</sup>the people whom I formed for myself that they might declare my praise.<sup>22</sup>"Yet you did not call upon me, O Jacob; but you have been weary of me, O Israel!<sup>23</sup>You have not brought me your sheep for burnt offerings, or honored me with your sacrifices. I have not burdened you with offerings, or wearied you with frankincense.<sup>24</sup>You have not bought me sweet cane with money, or satisfied me with the fat of your sacrifices. But you have burdened me with your sins; you have wearied me with your iniquities.<sup>25</sup>"I, I am he who blots out your transgressions for my own sake, and I will not remember your sins.<sup>26</sup>Put me in remembrance; let us argue together; set forth your case, that you may be proved right.<sup>27</sup>Your first father sinned, and your mediators transgressed against me.<sup>28</sup>Therefore I will profane the princes of the sanctuary, and deliver Jacob to utter destruction and Israel to reviling.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Straight after the judgment that closed chapter 42, God turns with “But now” and claims his people as his own. He created and formed them, redeemed them and called them by name: “you are mine” (v. 1). So he sends them through waters and fire, not round them, promising that neither will destroy them and that he will be with them (v. 2). He names the price he will pay, whole nations as their ransom, and the reason: they are precious in his eyes and he loves them (vv. 3–4). Then he commands north, south, east and west to give back his scattered sons and daughters, created for his glory (vv. 5–7).
verseByVerse.theology: Everything in this section is said before anything is asked. Who God is to his people (Creator, Redeemer, the one who calls them by name) comes first, and every promise that follows, through the water, through the fire and home from the ends of the earth, rests on that and on nothing they have done.
verseByVerse.examples: Verse 4 is the verse to read to someone who believes they matter to God only as long as they are useful to him. The reason God gives for paying the price is not usefulness at all, but love.

verseByVerse.quote: But now thus says the LORD, he who created you, O Jacob, he who formed you, O Israel: "Fear not, for I have redeemed you; I have called you by name, you are mine. When you pass through the waters, I will be with you; and through the rivers, they shall not overwhelm you; when you walk through fire you shall not be burned, and the flame shall not consume you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God claims his ruined people as his own and promises to go with them through water and fire, not around it.

But now thus says the LORD. Two words carry this chapter, and they are the first two. Chapter 42 finished with Israel robbed, trapped in holes, given up to the plunderer, with nobody saying “Restore!” But now. No repentance is recorded in between. The change of tone is entirely God’s doing.

He who created you, O Jacob. Then four statements, none of them earned. Created and formed are potter’s words, used of a nation as though it were a body being shaped. Redeemed is the family word from 41:14: the redeemer was the nearest relative, who paid what you could not to buy you back. And then two clauses that go deeper than any of them: called by name, and mine.

I have called you by name. Many believe that God saves in general and quietly doubt that he knows which one they are. Exile breeds that fear: you become one of a column of prisoners, a number in a ledger. Against it, God does not merely say he has saved the nation. He says, “I have called you by name.” The Good Shepherd does the same: “he calls his own sheep by name and leads them out” (John 10:3).

When you pass through the waters. Verse 2 does not promise a bridge, a detour or a lower water level. The word is through, three times. What is promised is a limit and a companion: the water will not close over your head, the fire will not finish you, and you will not be in either alone. Three men found out how literally God means it when they were thrown into a furnace and a fourth figure was seen walking with them in the flames (Daniel 3:25; see Shadrach, Meshach and Abednego).

What it does not mean. It does not promise that no believer will ever drown or burn; martyrs have (Hebrews 11:36–38). It promises that the waters will not have the last word, and that God will be with his people in them.

What you pray for. What have you been praying for in the hard thing you carry? Nearly always the detour. This verse offers something better and harder: not an exemption from the river, but company in it and a guarantee about the far bank.

verseByVerse.quote: For I am the LORD your God, the Holy One of Israel, your Savior. I give Egypt as your ransom, Cush and Seba in exchange for you. Because you are precious in my eyes, and honored, and I love you, I give men in return for you, peoples in exchange for your life.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God values his people so highly that he will pay whole nations for them, and in the end he paid with his own Son.

I give Egypt as your ransom. God begins to talk about price. Ransom and exchange are the vocabulary of a slave market, and the sums named are entire countries. Egypt, Cush and Seba are the wealth of the Nile from the delta to the far south, and God speaks of them the way a man might speak of emptying his account for one person.

Precious in my eyes, and honored. Then he says why, and the reason is not usefulness: precious, honored, I love you, said of a nation last seen being plundered. The middle word is the strangest: not pitied, but honored. This is easily sentimentalised. It does not say Israel deserved it; the last chapter and the end of this one say the opposite. Their worth is given to them by God, not found in them. A thing is precious because somebody prices it that way, and God has set the price of this people at the wealth of three empires.

A ransom for many. That turns out not to be the final figure. The language of exchange runs on through Scripture until it reaches a Son of Man who came to give his life as a ransom for many (Mark 10:45), and a sentence Paul writes with this chapter’s language of price in his head: “He who did not spare his own Son but gave him up for us all” (Romans 8:32). In the end God did not spend Egypt, Cush and Seba. He spent his Son, and the price tells the truth about the value as no adjective could.

Who decides what you are worth? The modern self is told to answer that question alone. Earlier ages handed people an identity: a family name, a trade, a place in a village and a church. We are expected to make our own, by achievement, appearance and a curated self that others will notice. It sounds like freedom, and in part it is. But a self you construct is a self you must keep defending, and every verdict, the exam result, the promotion, the number of people who liked what you posted, starts to feel like a verdict on whether you count at all. Isaiah’s answer is that worth is never self-made. We all take it from someone’s eyes; the only question is whose. You are precious in my eyes is spoken by the one whose opinion cannot be reversed, because it was settled with a price. Whoever knows that can hold the other verdicts more lightly, the good ones as well as the bad.

Is God trading other peoples’ lives for Israel’s? The verse pictures a price, not a slave sale. Many think it looks ahead to Persia, which let Judah go and later conquered Egypt (525 BC), as though Cyrus’s empire were paid with the Nile for releasing Israel. Nor are those nations thrown away: Isaiah promises that Egypt itself will be called my people (19:25), and the wealth of Cush comes to Zion with a confession on its lips (45:14).
verseByVerse.note: Cush is probably Nubia, south of Egypt.

verseByVerse.quote: Fear not, for I am with you; I will bring your offspring from the east, and from the west I will gather you. I will say to the north, Give up, and to the south, Do not withhold; bring my sons from afar and my daughters from the end of the earth, everyone who is called by my name, whom I created for my glory, whom I formed and made."
verseByVerse.commentary:
God orders the ends of the earth to hand back his scattered children, daughters as well as sons, because he made them for his glory.

I will say to the north, Give up. The four directions are addressed as though they were jailers. North and south are told to hand over what they are holding: give up, do not withhold. Nobody is negotiating. The scattering was the judgment of chapter 42; the gathering is God collecting his own.

My daughters from the end of the earth. The daughters are named. In a world where a genealogy could run for pages without a woman in it, the sons come from afar and the daughters from the end of the earth, and the daughters are given the longer distance.

Whom I created for my glory. Verse 7 gives the reason for the gathering, and it is not that the exiles were homesick. It is glory. That can sound cold until you see what it rules out: if a people exists for God’s glory, their return is as secure as his reputation, and it does not depend on their usefulness or their behaviour on the road home.

Still being gathered. John reaches for this promise when he explains what the death of Jesus was for: “not for the nation only, but also to gather into one the children of God who are scattered abroad” (John 11:52). The compass points are still being emptied, and John’s last sight of this crowd has them from every nation, tribe, people and language (Revelation 7:9), with no one left behind in any direction.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God reopens his court and calls his own people as witnesses that he alone is God and Saviour. Blind and deaf Israel is brought in (v. 8), and the nations, who cannot foretell anything, are challenged to produce witnesses (v. 9). God’s witnesses are his chosen servant, who know that there is no god before or after him and no saviour besides him, and that no one can turn back his hand (vv. 10–13). For their sake he will bring proud Babylon down (vv. 14–15), as he once made a way through the sea and snuffed out Pharaoh’s army (vv. 16–17). Now he is doing a new thing: a way in the wilderness and rivers in the desert for the people he formed to praise him (vv. 18–21).
verseByVerse.theology: What Israel is required to testify to is not doctrine she worked out but events she lived through, and in telling what happened, the witness comes to believe it more firmly herself.
verseByVerse.examples: Every believer has a former thing, a conversion or an answered prayer that he tells and retells. Verse 18 does not take it away; it forbids him to make it the limit of what he expects.

verseByVerse.quote: Bring out the people who are blind, yet have eyes, who are deaf, yet have ears! All the nations gather together, and the peoples assemble. Who among them can declare this, and show us the former things? Let them bring their witnesses to prove them right, and let them hear and say, It is true. "You are my witnesses," declares the LORD, "and my servant whom I have chosen, that you may know and believe me and understand that I am he. Before me no god was formed, nor shall there be any after me. I, I am the LORD, and besides me there is no savior. I declared and saved and proclaimed, when there was no strange god among you; and you are my witnesses," declares the LORD, "and I am God. Also henceforth I am he; there is none who can deliver from my hand; I work, and who can turn it back?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
In God’s court the nations have no witnesses, but his own people, blind as they are, are called to testify that he alone is God and that there is no saviour besides him.

Bring out the people who are blind, yet have eyes. The courtroom of chapter 41 reopens, and the first people brought in are the blind and the deaf. That is not the nations. It is what God called Israel at the end of chapter 42: his own servant, with working eyes and ears and nothing coming through them.

You are my witnesses. Here is the surprise of the chapter: God’s case against every idol rests on the testimony of the blind man in the dock. He is chosen not for his eyesight but because he was there, at the sea and at Sinai, and a witness is needed for what he saw, not for what he understands.

That you may know and believe me. The reason runs both ways: the testimony is for God’s sake in the world and for the witness’s own sake. Something happens to a person who is made to say aloud what God has done; saying it is part of how belief grows. Any Christian who has stammered out the story of his own conversion and found his faith steadier at the end of it has met verse 10.

Before me no god was formed. Three claims stand at the centre of the testimony: none before, none after, none besides. And the last clause is the one to take to bed: who can turn it back? Not who would like to, but who can.

Besides me there is no savior. If there is no saviour besides the LORD, then the apostles’ habit of calling Jesus our great God and Savior (Titus 2:13) is either blasphemy or the plainest confession of who he is. They knew this verse, and they chose the second.

The commission to witness. Jesus hands this verse’s job description to a small group of men who had understood almost nothing until very recently, and gives the power with the commission: you will receive power when the Holy Spirit has come upon you, and you will be my witnesses (Acts 1:8).

verseByVerse.quote: Thus says the LORD, your Redeemer, the Holy One of Israel: "For your sake I send to Babylon and bring them all down as fugitives, even the Chaldeans, in the ships in which they rejoice. I am the LORD, your Holy One, the Creator of Israel, your King." Thus says the LORD, who makes a way in the sea, a path in the mighty waters, who brings forth chariot and horse, army and warrior; they lie down, they cannot rise, they are extinguished, quenched like a wick:
verseByVerse.commentary:
For his people’s sake God will bring proud Babylon down, and the God who once snuffed out Pharaoh’s army like a wick can certainly open the way home.

In the ships in which they rejoice. The empire’s own pleasure boats become the transport for its refugees. Babylon was a river city and its ships were a matter of civic pride; God says the day is coming when the people who cheered them will be going downstream in them, running.

For your sake. In the middle of it stand three words: for your sake. Whole imperial histories turn over, and God tells a small displaced people that the reason is them.

Who makes a way in the sea. Then the exodus, told in a breath: the greatest army of its age, Pharaoh’s chariots and horses, lies down, cannot rise, and goes out like a wick pinched between finger and thumb. No battle is described, no struggle worth recording, just a small hiss and the smell of smoke. The same God who opened that sea has just said he will open a way home from Babylon. The argument is not that God is able in principle but that it has already happened once, at a real place, to a real army, and there are people alive who tell their children about it.

Uncertain wording. Verse 14 is hard Hebrew. The word the ESV renders fugitives can also mean bars, as of a gate or prison, and in the ships in which they rejoice is literally something like in the ships their shout; some translations take it that the Chaldeans’ shouting will be turned to lament. The general sense is plain: proud Babylon will be brought down, and her people will flee.

verseByVerse.quote: "Remember not the former things, nor consider the things of old. Behold, I am doing a new thing; now it springs forth, do you not perceive it? I will make a way in the wilderness and rivers in the desert. The wild beasts will honor me, the jackals and the ostriches, for I give water in the wilderness, rivers in the desert, to give drink to my chosen people, the people whom I formed for myself that they might declare my praise.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God tells his people not to let the old exodus set the limit of their hopes, because he is already doing a new and greater thing.

Remember not the former things. Two verses after rehearsing the exodus, God says stop remembering. The apparent contradiction is the point. He is not asking them to forget the sea; he has just used it as evidence. He is telling them not to let the best thing God has done become the biggest thing they expect him to do. That danger wears a devout face. A man can hold his conversion, or a rescue thirty years ago, so tightly that it becomes a ceiling: God was great, once. Isaiah says the former things are the floor, not the limit.

Do you not perceive it? There is a rebuke folded into the question. The new thing is not off in the future; it is already springing up, and it goes unnoticed because everyone is still facing the other way.

The jackals and the ostriches. These inherited the ruins in chapter 34, shorthand for a place where nothing lives. Here they are given a drink, and they honour the one who gives it. Even the scavengers get water in this new thing.

That they might declare my praise. The chain closes in verse 21: formed for himself, so that praise would exist. God takes a desert nobody crosses and a nation nobody wants, and out of the two he makes a river, a road, and a song about himself.

The new thing. The return from Babylon was the first instalment. The greater new exodus came in Christ, whose death Luke calls his departure, in Greek his exodus (Luke 9:31), and it ends where the Bible ends, with the one on the throne saying, “Behold, I am making all things new” (Revelation 21:5).

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God presents his charge, and then, astonishingly, a pardon. Israel did not call on him or bring him their offerings, though he never made worship a burden; instead they burdened him with their sins and wearied him with their iniquities (vv. 22–24). Into that, with no repentance recorded, comes the promise that he blots out their transgressions for his own sake and will not remember their sins (v. 25). He invites them to argue their case if they can, but from their first father to their mediators they have all sinned (vv. 26–27), and so judgment must still fall on the nation (v. 28).
verseByVerse.theology: The ground of the pardon is stated and it is not repentance, merit, or even pity: for my own sake. God forgives because of who he is, which is the only foundation that cannot be undermined by the person standing on it.

verseByVerse.quote: "Yet you did not call upon me, O Jacob; but you have been weary of me, O Israel! You have not brought me your sheep for burnt offerings, or honored me with your sacrifices. I have not burdened you with offerings, or wearied you with frankincense. You have not bought me sweet cane with money, or satisfied me with the fat of your sacrifices. But you have burdened me with your sins; you have wearied me with your iniquities.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Israel had neglected God’s worship, though he never made it heavy, and loaded him with their sins instead.

Yet you did not call upon me, O Jacob. After all that tenderness, the bill is presented, and the charge is not that the worship was badly done but that it was not done at all. Whatever was happening in the temple, God says he was not receiving it.

I have not burdened you with offerings. Most striking is what he adds in his own defence: the requirements were never heavy. God answers the ancient complaint that religion is exhausting by pointing out that he did not make it so. Even the sweet cane of verse 24, a fragrant reed brought from a distant land and bought at a price (Exodus 30:23; Jeremiah 6:20), is mentioned as something he had not demanded.

You have burdened me with your sins. Then the two verbs change direction. God had not burdened them; they had burdened him. He had not wearied them; they had wearied him. The load was real all along, but it was on God’s back, not theirs.

Two kinds of weariness. Set this beside 40:28, where the everlasting God does not faint or grow weary. Both are true. His strength never runs down; his heart can be worn by the people he loves, which is not weakness but the cost of caring about them at all.

An easy yoke. Centuries later the God who says here that he never made worship heavy invites a crowd of exhausted religious people to come to him for rest, because his yoke is easy and his burden is light (Matthew 11:28–30). And the sins that wearied him he finally carried himself.

verseByVerse.quote: "I, I am he who blots out your transgressions for my own sake, and I will not remember your sins. Put me in remembrance; let us argue together; set forth your case, that you may be proved right. Your first father sinned, and your mediators transgressed against me. Therefore I will profane the princes of the sanctuary, and deliver Jacob to utter destruction and Israel to reviling.
verseByVerse.commentary:
In the middle of the charge sheet God promises to wipe out his people’s sins for his own sake, though from their first father on they deserve judgment, and the judgment of exile will still come.

Pardon without confession. Verse 25 follows three verses of indictment with no confession in between. God interrupts his own charge sheet to announce a pardon. The order matters: pardon comes first, and the call to return follows from it: “return to me, for I have redeemed you” (44:22).

I, I am he who blots out your transgressions. The doubled I, I is emphatic, as though nobody else were in the running for the job. Blotting out is ink sponged off a scroll; the record is not filed away but removed. And I will not remember is not divine forgetfulness. It is a promise about what will never be raised again, the way a cancelled debt will not be mentioned at the next meeting (Jeremiah 31:34; Hebrews 8:12).

For my own sake. Then the ground of it: not because they repented, not because they were worth it, not because the sins were minor. If forgiveness rested on anything in them, it could be lost by something in them. Resting on God’s own name, it cannot.

Let us argue together. With irony, God invites them to make their case, if they have one. The first father sinned; the mediators, whose job was to stand in the gap, transgressed. There is no clean generation to appeal to and no clean priest to send in.

Deliver Jacob to utter destruction. So the chapter that began with you are mine ends in profaned princes and reviling, and it is honest to say so. Utter destruction translates herem, the ban: the word used at the conquest for something devoted wholly to God by destruction. Israel, once told to put Canaan’s idolatry under the ban, finds her own idolatry has put her under it, which shows how seriously God takes the sin he is forgiving. The debt is cancelled while the consequences are still being lived through.

The question the chapter leaves. How a holy God blots out sin for his own sake and remains just is the question this chapter raises and does not answer. The answer is given on a hill outside Jerusalem, where the record of debt that stood against us was cancelled and nailed to the cross (Colossians 2:14). The blotting was never cheap: free to those who receive it, but not to the one who paid. So a believer who has failed at the very worship this passage describes is not sent away to make up the shortfall. He is sent back to the God who blots out, and to the confession God has promised to meet with mercy (1 John 1:9).

Uncertain wording. The first father of verse 27 is not named. Most likely it is Jacob, the father of the nation (compare Hosea 12:2–4); some think of Abraham, or of Adam. The mediators are probably Israel’s priests and prophets, who also sinned.

43.theology:
Grace with no bridge in front of it. Twice this chapter puts mercy immediately after guilt with nothing in between: But now after the spoiler, and verse 25 after the charge sheet. This is not a denial that repentance matters but a statement about what causes it: the pardon comes first and the turning follows, which is Paul’s order when he says God’s kindness is meant to lead us to repentance (Rom. 2:4).

For my own sake. A pardon granted on account of merit can be revoked when the merit fails; a pardon granted on account of God’s character can only fail if his character does. At the cross Christ bore the sins of a people who had not brought him even a sheep, and his perfect offering stands in place of all they withheld.

44.subtitle: I Have Blotted Out Your Transgressions
44.intro:
Where we are. Chapter 43 ended with God blotting out Israel’s sins for his own sake while judgment still fell. Chapter 44 opens again with But now, and brings the courtroom of chapters 40 to 48 to a first climax: the sharpest exposure of idolatry in the Bible, and the naming of Cyrus.

The message. The LORD alone is God, the first and the last, and the gods people make are pieces of firewood; to trust them is to feed on ashes. But the true God has not forgotten his people. He will pour out his Spirit on their children, he has blotted out their sins like a morning mist, and he will bring them home and rebuild Jerusalem through a king he names long before that king is born.

Why it was said. In Babylon the exiles lived among splendid images carried in procession, and it was easy to think the winners’ gods must be real (see the introduction). They needed to see idols for what they are, and to hear that their own idolatry was blotted out.

How the chapter makes its case. Promise (vv. 1–5): God calls his people Jeshurun and promises his Spirit on their offspring, until outsiders write “The LORD’s” on their hands. Courtroom (vv. 6–8): the first and the last challenges any rival to foretell the future. Satire (vv. 9–20): a craftsman cooks his dinner over half a log and bows down to the rest, never asking whether there is a lie in his right hand. Redemption (vv. 21–23): the LORD has not forgotten Israel and has blotted out their sins, and all creation is called to sing. Proof (vv. 24–28): the Creator who makes fools of diviners names Cyrus as his shepherd, through whom Jerusalem and the temple will be rebuilt.

Where it leads. The line to Christ runs through promise and pattern. The Spirit promised for the offspring was poured out by the risen Christ at Pentecost (Acts 2:33). I am the first and I am the last is the title the risen Jesus claims (Revelation 22:13). Against gods carved in the figure of a man, the true God took the form of a man (Philippians 2:7), and sins blotted out like a cloud were taken away at the cross. And Cyrus, the pagan shepherd who freed captives, foreshadows the Good Shepherd who lays down his life for the sheep (John 10:11).

For us. Put the chapter’s question to whatever you are quietly counting on: is there a lie in my right hand? Then come home, not to earn a pardon but because one has been given: “return to me, for I have redeemed you” (v. 22).

keyVerse.quote: “I have blotted out your transgressions like a cloud and your sins like mist; return to me, for I have redeemed you.”
keyVerse.note: The picture is precisely chosen: a cloud disappears without leaving a trace. God does not file Israel’s sins for later reference; he makes them as though they had never been. The reason for returning is not fear of punishment, since the sins are gone, but gratitude: for I have redeemed you. The command rests on what God has already done.

44.reflection:
God promises to pour his Spirit on his people’s offspring like water on thirsty ground (v. 3). Where do you feel dry, and which of the next generation are you praying for? How does Pentecost (Acts 2:33) encourage that prayer?

The carpenter cooks his dinner over half a log and bows down to the other half (vv. 15–17). What do people around you treat as both everyday comfort and final security? What would it mean to ask of the thing you most count on, “Is there not a lie in my right hand?” (v. 20)

God says, “return to me, for I have redeemed you” (v. 22), not “so that I may redeem you”. How does that order change the way you come back to God after you have wandered?

God names Cyrus, a pagan king, as his shepherd who will fulfil all his purpose (v. 28). How does it help to know that God can work through rulers who do not know him, and how should that shape the way you think about the news?
