Let him proclaim it. Let him declare and set it before me, since I appointed an ancient people. Let them declare what is to come, and what will happen.<sup>8</sup>Fear not, nor be afraid; have I not told you from of old and declared it? And you are my witnesses! Is there a God besides me? There is no Rock; I know not any."<sup>9</sup>All who fashion idols are nothing, and the things they delight in do not profit. Their witnesses neither see nor know, that they may be put to shame.<sup>10</sup>Who fashions a god or casts an idol that is profitable for nothing?<sup>11</sup>Behold, all his companions shall be put to shame, and the craftsmen are only human. Let them all assemble, let them stand forth. They shall be terrified; they shall be put to shame together.<sup>12</sup>The ironsmith takes a cutting tool and works it over the coals. He fashions it with hammers and works it with his strong arm. He becomes hungry, and his strength fails; he drinks no water and is faint.<sup>13</sup>The carpenter stretches a line; he marks it out with a pencil. He shapes it with planes and marks it with a compass. He shapes it into the figure of a man, with the beauty of a man, to dwell in a house.<sup>14</sup>He cuts down cedars, or he chooses a cypress tree or an oak and lets it grow strong among the trees of the forest. He plants a cedar and the rain nourishes it.<sup>15</sup>Then it becomes fuel for a man. He takes a part of it and warms himself; he kindles a fire and bakes bread. Also he makes a god and worships it; he makes it an idol and falls down before it.<sup>16</sup>Half of it he burns in the fire. Over the half he eats meat; he roasts it and is satisfied. Also he warms himself and says, "Aha, I am warm, I have seen the fire!"<sup>17</sup>And the rest of it he makes into a god, his idol, and falls down to it and worships it. He prays to it and says, "Deliver me, for you are my god!"<sup>18</sup>They know not, nor do they discern, for he has shut their eyes, so that they cannot see, and their hearts, so that they cannot understand.<sup>19</sup>No one considers, nor is there knowledge or discernment to say, "Half of it I burned in the fire; I also baked bread on its coals; I roasted meat and have eaten. And shall I make the rest of it an abomination? Shall I fall down before a block of wood?"<sup>20</sup>He feeds on ashes; a deluded heart has led him astray, and he cannot deliver himself or say, "Is there not a lie in my right hand?"<sup>21</sup>Remember these things, O Jacob, and Israel, for you are my servant; I formed you; you are my servant; O Israel, you will not be forgotten by me.<sup>22</sup>I have blotted out your transgressions like a cloud and your sins like mist; return to me, for I have redeemed you.<sup>23</sup>Sing, O heavens, for the LORD has done it; shout, O depths of the earth; break forth into singing, O mountains, O forest, and every tree in it! For the LORD has redeemed Jacob, and will be glorified in Israel.<sup>24</sup>Thus says the LORD, your Redeemer, who formed you from the womb: "I am the LORD, who made all things, who alone stretched out the heavens, who spread out the earth by myself,<sup>25</sup>who frustrates the signs of liars and makes fools of diviners, who turns wise men back and makes their knowledge foolish,<sup>26</sup>who confirms the word of his servant and fulfills the counsel of his messengers, who says of Jerusalem, 'She shall be inhabited,' and of the cities of Judah, 'They shall be built, and I will raise up their ruins';<sup>27</sup>who says to the deep, 'Be dry; I will dry up your rivers';<sup>28</sup>who says of Cyrus, 'He is my shepherd, and he shall fulfill all my purpose'; saying of Jerusalem, 'She shall be built,' and of the temple, 'Your foundation shall be laid.'"

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God promises to renew his weary people by pouring out his Spirit, and reminds them that he alone is God. He calls them by Moses’ affectionate name for Israel, Jeshurun, and tells them not to fear (vv. 1–2). As water revives thirsty ground, his Spirit will come on their children, who will spring up like willows by streams (vv. 3–4), and outsiders will gladly claim the LORD and Israel as their own (v. 5). Then the courtroom again: the King and Redeemer, the first and the last, challenges any rival to announce the future as he has done, and calls Israel to witness that there is no other God and no other Rock (vv. 6–8).
verseByVerse.theology: The section moves from water to witness. The God who pours out his Spirit on the thirsty (v. 3) is the only God there is (v. 6), and the people he waters are the ones who stand in the witness box to say so (v. 8).
verseByVerse.examples: The Spirit is promised to the offspring rather than to the generation being addressed. A people who could see no future beyond their own captivity are told that the thing God is pouring out will land on their grandchildren, which is a particular kind of comfort and a hard one to receive.

verseByVerse.quote: "But now hear, O Jacob my servant, Israel whom I have chosen! Thus says the LORD who made you, who formed you from the womb and will help you: Fear not, O Jacob my servant, Jeshurun whom I have chosen. For I will pour water on the thirsty land, and streams on the dry ground; I will pour my Spirit upon your offspring, and my blessing on your descendants. They shall spring up among the grass like willows by flowing streams. This one will say, 'I am the LORD's,' another will call on the name of Jacob, and another will write on his hand, 'The LORD's,' and name himself by the name of Israel."
verseByVerse.commentary:
God will pour out his Spirit on his people’s children like water on dry ground, until even outsiders gladly take his name.

Jeshurun whom I have chosen. Jeshurun is a nickname, probably meaning upright one, and Moses used it three times in his last songs, once of a people who grew fat and kicked (Deuteronomy 32:15). God uses the family pet name of a nation that is in chains for its idolatry.

I will pour water on the thirsty land. The two halves of verse 3 are one sentence, and the second explains the first: what water does to cracked ground, the Spirit does to a family. Willows are not a rugged plant; they grow where there is plenty of water and nowhere else, so the picture is of a generation whose greenness depends entirely on what is running past their roots.

I will pour my Spirit upon your offspring. The promise is made to the offspring, not to the men hearing it. Centuries later Peter stands up in Jerusalem and explains the wind and the tongues as the Spirit poured out on all flesh. He quotes Joel rather than Isaiah (Acts 2:16–17), but it is the same promise, and the one who has poured it out is the risen Christ (Acts 2:33).

Another will write on his hand. Verse 5 shows what happens when the water lands. People who were never born into this family start claiming it, and one writes the owner’s name on his own hand, the way a household slave was marked. He is not embarrassed to be owned; he is signing up for it. Five chapters later God says that he has engraved his people on the palms of his own hands (49:16). The writing goes both ways, and his was there first.
verseByVerse.note: Jeshurun is a poetic name for Israel.

verseByVerse.quote: Thus says the LORD, the King of Israel and his Redeemer, the LORD of hosts: "I am the first and I am the last; besides me there is no god. Who is like me? Let him proclaim it. Let him declare and set it before me, since I appointed an ancient people. Let them declare what is to come, and what will happen. Fear not, nor be afraid; have I not told you from of old and declared it? And you are my witnesses! Is there a God besides me? There is no Rock; I know not any."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The LORD is the first and the last, the only God and the only Rock, and his record of foretelling proves it.

The King of Israel and his Redeemer. Three titles are stacked before the claim: King, Redeemer, LORD of hosts. He rules them, he is the relative bound to buy them back, and he commands the armies of heaven. Then the claim itself, I am the first and I am the last, which the risen Christ takes on his own lips at the beginning and the end of Revelation (Revelation 1:17; 22:13).

Who is like me? The challenge is the one from chapter 41, on the same terms. Anybody may enter; the test is prediction, the one credential that cannot be faked after the fact.

There is no Rock; I know not any. The most understated sentence in the chapter. God could have thundered his claim; instead he files the report a truthful witness would file: I know not any. And consider who is speaking: the one who counts the stars and names them and has been present at everything that has ever happened. When he says he has not come across another God, there is nowhere he has not looked.

The Rock. Rock is Moses’ title for God in the song that names Israel Jeshurun (Deuteronomy 32:4, 15), and Paul, thinking of the water in the wilderness, says, “the Rock was Christ” (1 Corinthians 10:4).

Uncertain wording. In verse 7 the ESV’s since I appointed an ancient people follows the traditional Hebrew; others, dividing the words differently, read something like who has announced from of old the things to come? Either way the challenge stands: show a record of foretelling.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 9–20 — Half of It He Burns in the Fire
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Isaiah exposes idolatry simply by describing how an idol is made. Its makers and its witnesses are nothing and will be put to shame (vv. 9–11). The ironsmith works until he is faint with hunger; the carpenter measures and planes a block into the figure of a man (vv. 12–13). The tree was planted by a man and grown by God’s rain, and half of it warms the craftsman and cooks his dinner while he bows down to the other half and prays, “Deliver me” (vv. 14–17). Why can he not see it? His eyes are shut and a deluded heart leads him astray, so that he feeds on ashes and cannot ask whether he holds a lie in his right hand (vv. 18–20).
verseByVerse.theology: Verse 13 quietly reverses the first chapter of the Bible. There, God makes man in his own image; here, man makes a god in his, with the beauty of a man, to live in a house like a lodger.
verseByVerse.examples: The modern equivalent of the carved log is not a wooden figure. It is something good that we use for ordinary comfort and at the same time trust to save us, held by somebody far too intelligent to be worshipping wood.

verseByVerse.quote: All who fashion idols are nothing, and the things they delight in do not profit. Their witnesses neither see nor know, that they may be put to shame. Who fashions a god or casts an idol that is profitable for nothing? Behold, all his companions shall be put to shame, and the craftsmen are only human. Let them all assemble, let them stand forth. They shall be terrified; they shall be put to shame together. The ironsmith takes a cutting tool and works it over the coals. He fashions it with hammers and works it with his strong arm. He becomes hungry, and his strength fails; he drinks no water and is faint. The carpenter stretches a line; he marks it out with a pencil. He shapes it with planes and marks it with a compass. He shapes it into the figure of a man, with the beauty of a man, to dwell in a house.
verseByVerse.commentary:
An idol is only as strong as the tired craftsman who made it in his own image.

Their witnesses neither see nor know. The court is still sitting, and the idols are allowed witnesses of their own. The trouble is that these are the men who did the carving, and Isaiah’s verdict on them is the verdict he has just passed on their gods: they neither see nor know.

He becomes hungry, and his strength fails. The strong arm gives out. Halfway through beating a god into shape the man needs his lunch, and the deity has to wait while its maker recovers.

The carpenter stretches a line. The tools are laid out one by one, and the craftsmanship is real. The finished piece is beautiful, and that is the danger: the better the work, the more convincing the lie.

The figure of a man. The phrase turns the Bible’s first chapter upside down: God made man in his image, and here man makes a god in his. Every idol ever made has been a self-portrait, which is why idols never say anything their makers did not already believe, and can never rescue them from themselves.

verseByVerse.quote: He cuts down cedars, or he chooses a cypress tree or an oak and lets it grow strong among the trees of the forest. He plants a cedar and the rain nourishes it. Then it becomes fuel for a man. He takes a part of it and warms himself; he kindles a fire and bakes bread. Also he makes a god and worships it; he makes it an idol and falls down before it. Half of it he burns in the fire. Over the half he eats meat; he roasts it and is satisfied. Also he warms himself and says, "Aha, I am warm, I have seen the fire!" And the rest of it he makes into a god, his idol, and falls down to it and worships it. He prays to it and says, "Deliver me, for you are my god!"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The same log that cooks a man’s dinner becomes the god he begs to save him, and the absurdity is the point.

He plants a cedar and the rain nourishes it. Isaiah goes back past the workshop to the seedling. The man planted the tree; God sent the rain that grew it. Before a tool is picked up, the raw material of the idol has been supplied by the God it will be used to replace.

Half of it he burns in the fire. This is one of the great passages of satire in Scripture, and there is not a joke in it. Isaiah simply sets the facts side by side: the same log, the same afternoon, the same man. He cooks his dinner over one end of it and kneels down in front of the other.

Deliver me, for you are my god! Set the two quoted sentences side by side: Aha, I am warm, and an hour later, Deliver me. The first is honest and the second desperate, and the wood cannot tell the difference.

Not a failure of intelligence. What makes the passage uncomfortable rather than merely funny is that the man is not stupid. He is a skilled tradesman doing careful work. Idolatry has never been a failure of intelligence.

verseByVerse.quote: They know not, nor do they discern, for he has shut their eyes, so that they cannot see, and their hearts, so that they cannot understand. No one considers, nor is there knowledge or discernment to say, "Half of it I burned in the fire; I also baked bread on its coals; I roasted meat and have eaten. And shall I make the rest of it an abomination? Shall I fall down before a block of wood?" He feeds on ashes; a deluded heart has led him astray, and he cannot deliver himself or say, "Is there not a lie in my right hand?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Shut eyes and a deluded heart keep the idolater feeding on ashes, never asking whether he holds a lie.

He has shut their eyes. Isaiah’s explanation is not the one a modern reader expects. He does not say the idolater lacks education. He says the eyes have been shut, probably by God (the Hebrew leaves the subject unnamed): the same closing of eyes, as a judgment, pronounced over Isaiah’s own hearers in the temple (6:9–10). Persistent refusal to see eventually becomes an inability to see, and Scripture is willing to say that God himself confirms a man in what he chose.

Half of it I burned in the fire. Verse 19 gives the exact question the man cannot ask himself, and it is not complicated. He has all the information; he handled both halves of the log. What is missing is the ability to put the two facts side by side.

He feeds on ashes. This is the picture to keep: a man sitting down to a meal of what is left when the fire has gone out, and rising from the table as hungry as he sat down.

Is there not a lie in my right hand? Here is the test the passage hands over. Not “Do I own an idol?”, which everybody answers correctly, but the question this man never asks. Take the thing you are quietly counting on, the savings, the reputation, the person whose approval settles you, and ask whether it has ever once fed you back. Seeing it is itself a mercy, and the next verses tell the one who sees it where to go.

The god made in our image. The modern reader smiles at the carpenter and his log, and then, if he is honest, stops smiling. We do not carve wood; we carve ideas. Ask many people today what God is like and you will meet a god who shares their politics, approves their choices and dislikes the people they dislike: the figure of a man (v. 13), and usually the man is the speaker. The novelist and philosopher Iris Murdoch, who did not believe in a personal God, named the great enemy of the moral life “the fat relentless ego”, and that ego is the most skilful carpenter there is. It can make a god out of anything, religion included, and its god will always say what it wanted to hear. Isaiah’s cure is not a better idol but the God who cannot be made.

The gospel turns this chapter inside out. Here a man shapes wood into the figure of a man and calls it god. In Christ the true God took the form of a man himself (Philippians 2:7–8), was nailed to wood, and gives himself as bread, not ashes, to those who will stop feeding on what they have made (John 6:35).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 21–28 — Blotted Out Like a Cloud, and a Pagan Called My Shepherd
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The chapter turns from the idol makers to the God who made Israel and has not forgotten them. He has blotted out their sins like a cloud and calls them to return because he has already redeemed them (vv. 21–22), and heaven, earth, mountains and forest are summoned to sing (v. 23). Then one long sentence sets out who this Redeemer is: the Creator who alone stretched out the heavens, who frustrates diviners and fulfils his servants’ words, who promises that Jerusalem and the towns of Judah will be rebuilt, and who names Cyrus as his shepherd, under whom the city will be built and the temple’s foundation laid (vv. 24–28).
verseByVerse.theology: The order of verse 22 is the order of the gospel. The blotting out is announced as already done, and the command to return follows it. Nobody here is being asked to come back in order to be forgiven; they are being asked to come back because they have been.
verseByVerse.examples: Shepherd is the royal title of David, and God hands it to a Persian who does not know him (45:4 will say so plainly). The point is not that Cyrus was secretly godly but that God was using him.

verseByVerse.quote: Remember these things, O Jacob, and Israel, for you are my servant; I formed you; you are my servant; O Israel, you will not be forgotten by me. I have blotted out your transgressions like a cloud and your sins like mist; return to me, for I have redeemed you. Sing, O heavens, for the LORD has done it; shout, O depths of the earth; break forth into singing, O mountains, O forest, and every tree in it! For the LORD has redeemed Jacob, and will be glorified in Israel.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God has not forgotten his people: he has wiped away their sins like mist, calls them home because he has redeemed them, and sets creation singing.

You are my servant. It is said twice in one verse, as though God were answering the fear that they had been dismissed from his service. Then the last clause meets the deepest fear of a small nation in a big empire: not that God is unable, but that he has moved on. You will not be forgotten by me.

I have blotted out your transgressions like a cloud. The image is chosen with care. A stain has to be scrubbed and often leaves a shadow. A cloud does not: the sun comes up, the mist lifts off the field, and by mid-morning there is no sign that anything was ever there. That is what God says he has done with the record of a nation’s idolatry, and he did it at a cost the cross would one day show (Colossians 2:14).

Return to me, for I have redeemed you. Notice the order: not “return to me so that I may redeem you”, but return to me, for I have redeemed you. The homecoming is not the price of the pardon but the response to it. It is the gospel order everywhere: “We love because he first loved us” (1 John 4:19).

Sing, O heavens, for the LORD has done it. The summons goes to the sky, the depths, the hills and every tree in the forest. A few verses ago those trees were being carved into gods that could not speak. Now the timber has found its voice, and it sings not about itself but about the LORD who has redeemed Jacob: no mouth on earth is equal to the news.

verseByVerse.quote: Thus says the LORD, your Redeemer, who formed you from the womb: "I am the LORD, who made all things, who alone stretched out the heavens, who spread out the earth by myself, who frustrates the signs of liars and makes fools of diviners, who turns wise men back and makes their knowledge foolish, who confirms the word of his servant and fulfills the counsel of his messengers, who says of Jerusalem, 'She shall be inhabited,' and of the cities of Judah, 'They shall be built, and I will raise up their ruins'; who says to the deep, 'Be dry; I will dry up your rivers'; who says of Cyrus, 'He is my shepherd, and he shall fulfill all my purpose'; saying of Jerusalem, 'She shall be built,' and of the temple, 'Your foundation shall be laid.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Creator who overturns the diviners names Cyrus, long before his birth, as the shepherd under whom Jerusalem and its temple will be rebuilt.

Who alone stretched out the heavens. A single sentence runs from here to the end of the chapter, hung on a string of clauses that each begin who. It starts at creation, with two words that will matter in a moment: alone, and by myself. Nobody assisted.

Makes fools of diviners. Babylon was the world capital of divination, where the state employed men to read livers and stars. God makes fools of them and confirms the word of his servants: two kinds of prediction, and only one comes true.

He is my shepherd. Then the name. Cyrus is a Persian who will not be born for well over a century, and God speaks of him as a man speaks of an employee: he shall fulfill all my purpose. The title is the shocking part. Shepherd is David’s word, the word for Israel’s king, and it is handed to a foreigner who does not know the God handing it to him (45:4). Two uncomfortable consequences follow. God is free to keep his promises through people who have no interest in him. And the empires, which small nations must simply survive like the weather, are in this book only God’s staff, doing his work.

She shall be built. The God who stretched out the heavens alone bends over the ruins of a provincial city and says She shall be built, and over a burnt-out temple and says Your foundation shall be laid, and moves an unborn emperor into position to do it. Nothing is too large for him to hold and nothing too small for him to bother with, and it is the same hand in both.

A better Shepherd. Cyrus was the LORD’s shepherd for a season, a pagan who freed captives and ordered a temple rebuilt (Ezra 1:1–4) without knowing whom he served. He is a pattern of the greater Shepherd who lays down his life for the sheep (John 10:11) and raised the true temple, his own body (John 2:19–21).

Where Christians differ. Could Isaiah name Cyrus a century and a half before he took Babylon? Most modern scholars assign chapters 40–55 to an unnamed prophet of the exile, around 550–540 BC, because of the name, because these chapters address exiles already in Babylon with Jerusalem in ruins, and because their style differs from chapters 1–39. Some who hold Scripture to be wholly true agree, believing that God inspired a later prophet in Isaiah’s line. Many conservative scholars answer that Isaiah of Jerusalem (about 740–700 BC) looked ahead by the Spirit. These chapters rest God’s case on announcing events beforehand (41:22–23; 46:10); Scripture names Josiah centuries ahead (1 Kings 13:2); the Great Isaiah Scroll from Qumran, the oldest complete copy, presents the book as one; and the New Testament quotes both halves under Isaiah’s name (John 12:38–41). To rule prediction out at the start would settle the question before looking at it.

This commentary’s view. This commentary takes the traditional view (see the introduction), while granting that the debate is not closed among those who hold Scripture to be wholly true. On either view the point stands: the LORD named Cyrus and his work before Babylon fell, and then did it.
verseByVerse.note: Isaiah names Cyrus some 150 years before he conquered Babylon in 539 BC.

44.theology:
The way back. Nobody in this chapter is asked to come home in order to be forgiven; they are asked to come home because they have been. For idolaters still, the way back is not to reform first and then approach, but to return to the Redeemer who has already blotted the record, whose Spirit, poured out as verse 3 promised, makes new hearts that write the LORD’s on their hands.

A pagan called my shepherd. God’s purposes are not confined to people who intend to serve them, which is the logic Peter uses about Herod and Pilate doing whatever God’s hand had predestined to take place (Acts 4:27-28). And prophecy of this kind is the credential these chapters keep staking everything on: anyone can explain history afterwards, and only God writes the name down first.

45.subtitle: The Creator’s Sovereign Freedom
45.intro:
Where we are. Chapter 44 ended by naming the conqueror: Cyrus, who will say of Jerusalem, “She shall be built” (44:28). Chapter 45 now speaks to him directly, and it brings the courtroom scenes of chapters 41 to 48 to their widest point.

The message. The LORD alone made light and darkness, peace and disaster, so he is free to use anyone he chooses, even a Persian king who does not know him, to set his people free. No one has the right to argue with the Potter about his methods. And the God who rules history this way is not a tribal deity: he opens his arms to every nation on earth, “Turn to me and be saved” (v. 22), and swears that every knee will one day bow to him.

Why it was said. The exiles in Babylon (see the introduction) would find it hard to believe, and some would resent, that their rescue could come through an idol-worshipping emperor. Surrounded by Babylon’s gods, they needed to hear that one God stands behind everything and has spoken openly to them.

How the chapter makes its case. The commission (vv. 1–8): God calls Cyrus his anointed and goes ahead of him, so that all may know “there is none besides me”; he claims light and darkness alike, and calls righteousness down like rain. The objection answered (vv. 9–13): woe to the pot that argues with the potter; the Maker of heaven has raised Cyrus to build his city and free his exiles for nothing. The invitation (vv. 14–25): foreigners confess that God is in Israel; the God who hides himself has never spoken in secret; the nations are invited to turn and be saved, and God swears that every knee shall bow and his people be justified.

Where it leads. In two ways, honestly distinguished. Cyrus is a pattern, and only a pattern: an anointed deliverer who frees captives without knowing the God who sent him, pointing to the Anointed who knows the Father and frees his people from sin and death (Luke 4:18). And verses 22 to 25 are promise. Paul hears the oath of verse 23 fulfilled at the name of Jesus, before whom every knee will bow (Philippians 2:10–11), and the last verse holds the word his gospel turns on: in the LORD the guilty are justified, declared right by God’s verdict, because Christ has done what they could not (Romans 3:26).

For us. No circumstance, ruler or disaster lies outside the hand of the God who loves us, so we can stop arguing with the Potter and trust him with what we cannot see round. And the door he opens is as wide as the earth: anyone, anywhere, can turn and look to Christ today, and be saved.

keyVerse.quote: “Turn to me and be saved, all the ends of the earth! For I am God, and there is no other.”
keyVerse.note: Nothing is required of the one turning except the turn itself. The reach, all the ends of the earth, is not a prediction that everyone will be saved but an offer open to everyone. The chapter that began with an uncircumcised Persian king ends with an invitation to every nation.

45.reflection:
God used Cyrus, a king who did not know him, to set his people free (vv. 1–4). Where have you seen God work through unlikely or unbelieving people? How does this change the way you think about the leaders and powers of our day?

“I make well-being and create calamity” (v. 7). Why is it, in the end, more comforting to know that disaster is not outside God’s control than to believe he had nothing to do with it? How do we hold this together with real grief, as Job did?

The pot complains, “Your work has no handles” (v. 9). What about your own life, temperament or circumstances are you most tempted to argue with God about? What is the difference between that complaint and the honest lament of the Psalms?

“Turn to me and be saved, all the ends of the earth!” (v. 22). How would you explain to a friend what it means to turn to God, and how does this verse answer the charge that Christianity is narrow and arrogant?

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–8 — My Anointed, Who Does Not Know Me
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God names a pagan king as his chosen instrument, so that the whole world may learn there is no other God. He calls Cyrus “his anointed”, takes him by the hand and promises to go ahead of him, breaking gates and handing over hidden treasure (vv. 1–3). Twice he adds that Cyrus does not know him (vv. 4–5): the king is used, not converted. The purpose runs two ways, for the sake of Jacob and so that people from east to west may know the LORD (vv. 4, 6). Verse 7 makes the widest claim of all, that light and darkness, peace and calamity, lie in one hand, and verse 8 answers it with a call for righteousness to rain down and salvation to spring up.
verseByVerse.theology: Cyrus is given the title of anointed and told twice that he does not know the God who names him. God is not limited to willing instruments, which is the logic Peter later applies to Herod and Pilate (Acts 4:27-28). And standing in a useful place in God's plan is not the same thing as knowing God.
verseByVerse.examples: Verse 8 is a prayer for weather. Righteousness is to come down like rain and salvation to sprout up out of the opened ground, which many Christians have heard as the shape of what happened when heaven sent down a Son and he was born of a woman.

verseByVerse.quote: Thus says the LORD to his anointed, to Cyrus, whose right hand I have grasped, to subdue nations before him and to loose the belts of kings, to open doors before him that gates may not be closed: "I will go before you and level the exalted places, I will break in pieces the doors of bronze and cut through the bars of iron, I will give you the treasures of darkness and the hoards in secret places, that you may know that it is I, the LORD, the God of Israel, who call you by your name. For the sake of my servant Jacob, and Israel my chosen, I call you by your name, I name you, though you do not know me.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God takes a Persian king by the hand and opens the world’s gates for him, for the sake of his captive people, though Cyrus does not know him.

Thus says the LORD to his anointed. The word translated anointed is mashiach, messiah: the word for kings and priests set apart by oil poured over the head, used here of a Persian who worships other gods. No other foreigner in Scripture is given the title: Cyrus is set apart for a task, not made one of God’s people.

Whose right hand I have grasped. In Babylon a king’s right to rule was expressed by taking his god by the hand in procession. Isaiah reverses the grip: God takes hold of Cyrus, and the loosing of the belts of kings pictures men disarmed before he arrives. The Cyrus Cylinder, the king’s own clay inscription found in Babylon, claims that Marduk took him by the hand and called him by name. Isaiah says it was the LORD, and said so before Babylon fell; the decree that sent the exiles home in 538 BC bears Cyrus’s name (Ezra 1:1–4).

The treasures of darkness. The bullion of conquered cities, stored in vaults where no light gets in. God offers a general the wealth of the world and gives the reason in the same breath: that you may know. The plunder is meant to end in a recognition.

Though you do not know me. An empire changes hands for the sake of a small captive people nobody thought important, and God attaches a qualification to his commissioning, repeated in the next verse: though you do not know me. Cyrus is not a secret believer, but a man used, by name, by a God he could not have identified. God does not need the powerful to believe in him to bend them to his people’s good.

A greater Anointed. The title is lent, not kept. Cyrus frees one nation from one empire and dies like any king. Many Christians have seen in him a faint outline of the greater Anointed, who said the Spirit had anointed him to proclaim liberty to the captives (Luke 4:18), who knows the Father perfectly, and who frees his people from sin and death.

Uncertain wording. The word behind the exalted places (v. 2) is rare and its meaning uncertain, perhaps swellings or rough ground; some ancient copies read “mountains”. Either way, every obstacle is flattened.
verseByVerse.note: Cyrus is called the LORD’s “anointed”: the only foreign king given that title.

verseByVerse.quote: I am the LORD, and there is no other, besides me there is no God; I equip you, though you do not know me, that people may know, from the rising of the sun and from the west, that there is none besides me; I am the LORD, and there is no other. I form light and create darkness; I make well-being and create calamity; I am the LORD, who does all these things. "Shower, O heavens, from above, and let the clouds rain down righteousness; let the earth open, that salvation and righteousness may bear fruit; let the earth cause them both to sprout; I the LORD have created it.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Cyrus is raised so that the whole world may learn there is one God, Lord of light and darkness alike, who rains righteousness down from heaven.

From the rising of the sun and from the west. The commissioning of Cyrus is evidence, shown from east to west (v. 6), so that people who never heard of Judah will hear that something was announced in advance and then happened.

I make well-being and create calamity. Verse 7 is the hardest sentence in the chapter. It does not say God authors moral evil; the New Testament states plainly that he tempts no one (James 1:13). Calamity means disaster and trouble: the famine, the invasion, the loss. What the verse refuses is a tidy universe run by two rival powers, a good one for the light and an evil one for the dark. Everything, including the day everything went wrong, is under one hand.

The better comfort. That sounds severe until you try the alternative. A calamity God had nothing to do with is one he cannot use, time, end or redeem. Job knew which was the better comfort when he asked whether we should receive good from God and not evil (Job 2:10), and he asked it sitting in ashes.

Shower, O heavens, from above. After the hardest verse, the loveliest: righteousness is not manufactured on the ground; it falls out of the sky like rain, soaks in, and comes up green.

An Advent verse. Isaiah’s own horizon is the righteousness and salvation of the return. The church has long sung this verse at Advent all the same, and fairly: righteousness did come down from heaven and was born on earth, and Christ is that righteousness in person (1 Corinthians 1:30).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 9–13 — Woe to the Pot That Argues with the Potter
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The creature has no standing to put his Maker in the dock, least of all over how he chooses to save. The chapter has provoked an objection, that God should not rescue his people through a pagan, and two woes answer it. The first sets the objector in a workshop, a pot among pots finding fault with its own making (v. 9); the second in a delivery room, demanding to know what is being born (v. 10). Then God answers the substance: he made the earth, man and the heavens, and he may do what he wills with the work of his hands (vv. 11–12). He has raised Cyrus, who will build his city and free his exiles, and take no payment for it (v. 13).
verseByVerse.theology: The woes do not forbid questions. This book is full of God explaining himself, and the Psalms are full of honest lament. What they forbid is a way of questioning that has misunderstood who is being made: the creature putting its Maker in the dock.
verseByVerse.examples: The last clause of verse 13 is easy to skim. Cyrus releases the exiles not for price or reward. The most valuable thing in the chapter, the exiles’ freedom, costs them nothing.

verseByVerse.quote: "Woe to him who strives with him who formed him, a pot among earthen pots! Does the clay say to him who forms it, 'What are you making?' or 'Your work has no handles'? Woe to him who says to a father, 'What are you begetting?' or to a woman, 'With what are you in labor?'" Thus says the LORD, the Holy One of Israel, and the one who formed him: "Ask me of things to come; will you command me concerning my children and the work of my hands? I made the earth and created man on it; it was my hands that stretched out the heavens, and I commanded all their host. I have stirred him up in righteousness, and I will make all his ways level; he shall build my city and set my exiles free, not for price or reward," says the LORD of hosts.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The creature has no right to put his Maker in the dock: God may save his people however he chooses, even through a pagan king.

Woe to him who strives with him who formed him. Somebody has objected that God should not save his people through an uncircumcised foreigner. God’s answer puts the objector in a pottery, not as a critic outside the workshop but as one of the pots, and his complaint is a complaint about his own manufacture. Your work has no handles is the detail to keep: the pot is saying it should have been made differently.

With what are you in labor? The second woe moves from the workshop to the delivery room, and it is deliberately grotesque: a man standing over a woman in labour, demanding to know what she intends to produce. There is a way of questioning that has misunderstood who is doing the making.

Ask me of things to come. God answers as Creator (vv. 11–12): the hands that stretched out the heavens shaped Israel, and the creature does not give the Maker orders about his children.

Not for price or reward. Then he simply restates the plan (v. 13). The exiles go home for nothing, because their release was never a deal between them and the empire; it is God’s doing.

Paul and the potter. Paul takes up the potter in Romans 9:20–21 for God’s sovereign mercy in choosing whom he will: “Will what is molded say to its molder, ‘Why have you made me like this?’” In Isaiah the complaint is about God’s way of saving Israel; in both, the creature has no standing to put his Maker on trial.

Where quarrels with God live. Most quarrels with God live not in arguments about providence but in a settled objection to one’s own design: the temperament, the family, the limitation that will not lift. This does not forbid honest lament, which the Psalms are full of: the lamenter brings his pain to God; the pot tells God he got it wrong.

Uncertain wording. The Hebrew behind Your work has no handles (v. 9) is compressed, word for word your work, no hands to him. It may mean the pot has no handles, or that the potter has no hands, no skill. Either way the clay is finding fault with its maker.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 14–25 — Turn to Me and Be Saved
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The God who rules all nations opens his arms to all of them. Foreigners come to Israel confessing that God is with her and there is no other (v. 14), and the prophet breaks in with the startling confession that God hides himself, yet saves his people for ever (vv. 15–17). The Creator made the earth to be lived in and never told anyone to seek him in vain (vv. 18–19). The survivors of the nations are summoned to court once more, and their idols cannot save (vv. 20–21). Then the summons becomes an invitation: turn to me and be saved, all the ends of the earth (v. 22). God swears that every knee shall bow, and promises that in the LORD all his people shall be justified (vv. 23–25).
verseByVerse.theology: The hiddenness and the clarity are both true and they are not in tension. God does not explain himself on demand, and he has never left the world without a word it could act on. What he hides is his timing and his method; what he has published is his character and his summons.
verseByVerse.examples: Verse 23 is the sentence God swears by himself. Paul quotes it twice, and in Philippians 2:10-11 he puts it under the name of Jesus. The knee that Isaiah says will bow to the LORD alone bows, Paul says, to a crucified carpenter, and no apology is offered for the transfer, because none is needed.

verseByVerse.quote: Thus says the LORD: "The wealth of Egypt and the merchandise of Cush, and the Sabeans, men of stature, shall come over to you and be yours; they shall follow you; they shall come over in chains and bow down to you. They will plead with you, saying: 'Surely God is in you, and there is no other, no god besides him.'" Truly, you are a God who hides himself, O God of Israel, the Savior. All of them are put to shame and confounded; the makers of idols go in confusion together. But Israel is saved by the LORD with everlasting salvation; you shall not be put to shame or confounded to all eternity.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Foreigners will confess that the only God is with his people, and the prophet confesses that this God hides himself, yet saves for ever.

Surely God is in you. What the foreigners bring in the end is not tribute but a confession, Surely God is in you, and there is no other: the sentence the whole book has been arguing for, from people who were not raised on it. The chains are probably not Israel’s revenge but a picture of willing surrender: these foreigners come over and follow of their own accord. Paul hears the same confession when an outsider walks into a Christian gathering and declares “that God is really among you” (1 Corinthians 14:25).

Truly, you are a God who hides himself. Verse 15 is one of the most surprising interruptions in Scripture. It is not an unbeliever’s complaint but is said in worship, by people who have just watched God act; anyone who has walked with God for long knows it. He is not vague; he is hidden, which is different. A vague God has no clear edges. A hidden God has edges you cannot see round, and the frustration of that is the frustration of dealing with someone real.

Everlasting salvation. Set against the hiddenness is something with no time limit at all: everlasting salvation, and to all eternity (v. 17). God may keep his methods to himself. He has not kept the outcome to himself.

Why doesn’t God make himself obvious? A fair question: if God exists and wants to be known, why not write his name across the sky? Blaise Pascal, who quoted this very verse, argued that God has given light enough for those who want to see him and obscurity enough for those who do not, so that he is found by the seeking heart rather than forced on the unwilling mind. A God who simply overwhelmed every doubt would have subjects, not children: nobody would be won, only overpowered. The deepest hiding came later, and it was the opposite of absence. God came in person, hidden in a carpenter, a criminal’s cross and a borrowed grave, close enough to touch and easy to walk past. He is hidden the way a father kneeling to a child’s height is hidden: not far away, but lower than we were looking.

verseByVerse.quote: For thus says the LORD, who created the heavens (he is God!), who formed the earth and made it (he established it; he did not create it empty, he formed it to be inhabited!): "I am the LORD, and there is no other. I did not speak in secret, in a land of darkness; I did not say to the offspring of Jacob, 'Seek me in vain.' I the LORD speak the truth; I declare what is right. "Assemble yourselves and come; draw near together, you survivors of the nations! They have no knowledge who carry about their wooden idols, and keep on praying to a god that cannot save. Declare and present your case; let them take counsel together! Who told this long ago? Who declared it of old? Was it not I, the LORD? And there is no other god besides me, a righteous God and a Savior; there is none besides me.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Creator who made the earth to be lived in has spoken openly, and he alone is a righteous God and a Saviour.

He did not create it empty. The word behind empty is tohu, the formless waste of Genesis 1:2. The earth was made to be lived in, so every settled house and occupied city is nearer the purpose of creation than the ruins Isaiah’s readers were looking at.

I did not speak in secret. Four verses after the confession that God hides himself comes the denial that he has ever been secretive, and both stand. Hold on to the middle of verse 19 through a dry season: God never said to Jacob’s offspring, “Seek me in vain.” Whatever else is uncertain, the search itself has not been set up to fail.

Who carry about their wooden idols. The picture of verse 20 is a procession of refugees carrying their gods on their backs, which is exactly where chapter 46 will open. The contrast is set up here and paid off there: gods that must be carried, and a God who carries.

A righteous God and a Savior. A righteous judge condemns the guilty; a saviour rescues them. Isaiah does not yet say how one God can be both, but the Servant chapters will (53:11), and Paul says it outright: God put forward his Son “so that he might be just and the justifier of the one who has faith in Jesus” (Romans 3:26).

verseByVerse.quote: "Turn to me and be saved, all the ends of the earth! For I am God, and there is no other. By myself I have sworn; from my mouth has gone out in righteousness a word that shall not return: 'To me every knee shall bow, every tongue shall swear allegiance.' "Only in the LORD, it shall be said of me, are righteousness and strength; to him shall come and be ashamed all who were incensed against him. In the LORD all the offspring of Israel shall be justified and shall glory."
verseByVerse.commentary:
God invites every nation to turn to him and be saved, and swears that every knee will bow and that in him his people will be justified.

Turn to me and be saved. Everything narrows to one command asking the smallest possible action. The Hebrew word for turn is about facing: turn round, look this way. Nothing is required in the hand or the record, no qualification, no journey. A man on the far rim of the world is told to change the direction he is facing.

All the ends of the earth! The chapter that began with an uncircumcised Persian called God’s anointed ends by throwing the door open to every outsider at the ends of the earth who will look.

By myself I have sworn. There is no higher name to swear by, so God swears by himself. What he guarantees is universal: not that everyone will be saved, but that everyone will bow. The knee bends either in worship or in surrender, and both are covered by the oath.

To me every knee shall bow. Paul quotes this verse in Romans 14:11, and elsewhere does something that should stop the reader cold. Isaiah’s God, who insists there is no other, is the one Paul has in view when he writes that at the name of Jesus every knee will bow and every tongue confess that Jesus Christ is Lord (Philippians 2:10–11), and he does not pause to justify the move. He did not think he was transferring the honour of God to somebody else.

All the offspring of Israel shall be justified. The last verse holds the word Paul will build a letter on. Justified: declared in the right, by a verdict rather than by an achievement, because another has done what we could not. The oath was sworn by God on his own name, and the name he chose to make it good by was the name of his Son.

How do I turn to him? The smallness of the act is the good news, and it can be done today. Stop looking to yourself. Turning is first a turning away: from the record you hope is good enough, the feelings you are waiting for, whatever else you have been facing for rescue. Look at the one God sets before you. John the Baptist pointed and said, “Behold, the Lamb of God, who takes away the sin of the world!” (John 1:29). Faith is that look: not a work offered but a gift received. Say it to him. Tell him you have nothing to bring and are coming anyway; the promise is “whoever comes to me I will never cast out” (John 6:37). Keep facing him. The Christian life is the same turn made again, the morning after a failure as on the first day. Charles Spurgeon, aged fifteen, sheltering from a snowstorm in a small Colchester chapel in 1850, heard a lay preacher take this very verse and tell him, in effect, to look. He looked, and spent the rest of his life telling others it was that simple.

Isn’t it arrogant to say there is only one way? To many it sounds like the root of religious violence; surely the humble view is that all religions are paths up the same mountain. But that view is itself a confident claim about God, that he can be reached by any road and has said nothing definite himself, and it quietly excludes every faith that thinks otherwise. Everybody draws a line somewhere; the question is what lies inside it and how you get in. Here Isaiah is startling. The claim could hardly be narrower: I am God, and there is no other. The invitation could hardly be wider: all the ends of the earth, and the only condition is to turn and look. Many ways up the mountain are open in theory and closed in practice, for they are only for those good enough to climb. The gospel is narrow in its claim and wide in its door, because the God at the top came down the mountain for those who could not climb.

Uncertain wording. The Hebrew of it shall be said of me (v. 24) is compressed and the speaker unclear: perhaps what people will say of God, perhaps a voice saying, he has said to me. The point is not in doubt: righteousness and strength are in the LORD alone.
verseByVerse.note: The Greek Old Testament reads “every tongue shall confess to God” (ESV note). Paul applies these words to Jesus.

45.theology:
Light and darkness, well-being and calamity. Verse 7 denies that the universe is run by two rival powers. Amos asks whether disaster comes to a city unless the LORD has done it (Amos 3:6). The doctrine is severe, and it is the only version in which a catastrophe can be timed, limited and redeemed. It does not make the loss less real or grief less right: Job tore his robe and fell on the ground before he blessed the name of the LORD (Job 1:20-21).

From Cyrus to the ends of the earth. The chapter that began with a pagan called anointed ends with all the ends of the earth invited to turn and be saved, and every knee bowing to the God who swore it by his own name.

46.subtitle: Bel Bows Down
46.intro:
Where we are. Chapter 45 ended with the whole world invited to turn to the LORD and be saved. Chapter 46 turns to the gods those nations had been looking to, and shows the gods of Babylon on the day their city falls.

The message. There are only two kinds of god: the kind you have to carry, and the God who carries you. Babylon’s gods are loaded onto weary animals and go into captivity, unable to save even themselves. The LORD has carried his people from before they were born and will carry them to old age, and he alone tells the end from the beginning, so his purpose will stand and his salvation will not be late.

Why it was said. The exiles lived under the shadow of Babylon’s gods (see the introduction), whose great processions looked like proof of their power, and many were tempted to think the LORD was finished. Some were not merely discouraged but stubborn, slow to believe that he could or would act for them.

How the chapter makes its case. The gods carried away (vv. 1–2): Bel and Nebo, Babylon’s chief gods, bow and stoop as cargo on pack animals. The God who carries (vv. 3–4): Israel has been carried by the LORD from the womb and will be carried to grey hairs. The god you pay for (vv. 5–7): gold weighed, a goldsmith hired, a god that cannot move or answer. The God who declares the end (vv. 8–11): remember, transgressors; he alone foretells and fulfils, and calls a bird of prey from the east. The God who comes near (vv. 12–13): to the stubborn of heart he brings his righteousness near, and his salvation will not delay.

Where it leads. Through the character of God revealed in Christ, and through promise. The God who carries his people is the Good Shepherd who puts the lost sheep on his shoulders (Luke 15:5), and whose shoulders bore a cross on which he “bore our sins in his body” (1 Peter 2:24). And the righteousness brought near to the stubborn is the righteousness of faith Paul preaches: “The word is near you” (Romans 10:8), because God came near himself, in the flesh.

For us. Whatever we have to keep propping up, paying for and defending will one day be a burden, not a help. The God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ has carried us since before we could say his name, and he will not set us down when we are old, weak or dependent; we can stop carrying ourselves and let him carry us.

keyVerse.quote: “Even to your old age I am he, and to gray hairs I will carry you. I have made, and I will bear; I will carry and will save.”
keyVerse.note: The contrast with Bel and Nebo is precise: they were carried into exile; God carries his people to salvation. The idol is the god you must transport; the LORD is the God who transports you. The whole of life, from womb to grey hairs, is held in arms that have never grown tired.

46.reflection:
Bel and Nebo had to be carried, and in the end they could not save even themselves (vv. 1–2). What in your life, or in our culture, needs constant upkeep, money and defending to stay upright? What does it give you in return?

God says he has carried his people “from the womb” and will carry them “to gray hairs” (vv. 3–4). At what stage of life do you most easily forget that you are being carried, and why?

Many people fear above all becoming a burden in old age or illness. How does this chapter, and the Christ who carried our sins, change the way we think about dependence and dignity, our own and other people’s?

God tells the stubborn of heart, “I bring near my righteousness” (v. 13), rather than ordering them to close the distance. How is that good news for someone who feels far from God today?

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–7 — The Gods That Have to Be Carried
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Gods that must be carried are a burden, not a help; the true God carries his people. Babylon’s two great gods, Bel and Nebo, are shown roped onto tired pack animals, bowing and stooping, unable to save the load or themselves (vv. 1–2). Against that picture God sets his own record with Israel: carried from before birth, and promised to be carried to grey hairs (vv. 3–4). Then comes the challenge, to whom will you liken me (v. 5), and the economics of idolatry: gold poured out, silver weighed, a goldsmith hired, and a god that must be lifted into place and can neither move nor answer when someone in trouble cries to it (vv. 6–7).
verseByVerse.theology: The whole chapter turns on one question: who carries whom? Every other religion in the ancient world required its god to be transported. Israel's God does the transporting, and the difference is not a matter of degree.
verseByVerse.examples: Verse 4 is worth reading aloud at the bedside of someone who can no longer do anything for anybody and fears that she has become a burden. The God who carries her has not changed, and his arms were never relying on her strength.

verseByVerse.quote: Bel bows down; Nebo stoops; their idols are on beasts and livestock; these things you carry are borne as burdens on weary beasts. They stoop; they bow down together; they cannot save the burden, but themselves go into captivity.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Babylon’s mighty gods end up as cargo on weary animals, unable to save the load or themselves. A god that has to be carried away cannot carry anyone.

Bel bows down; Nebo stoops. Bel is Marduk, the chief god of Babylon; Nebo is his son, the god of wisdom and writing. Their names are in the names of the men who ran the empire, Nebuchadnezzar and Belshazzar, the way Christian families once named children after saints. Bows down and stoops are worship words: the gods are made to do to the invader exactly what their worshippers used to do to them.

Their idols are on beasts and livestock. Once a year those two images were carried through the city in the great procession, gold in the sun, the whole population in the streets. Isaiah shows the same statues on the move again, and the second procession is nothing like the first: they are lashed to the backs of pack animals in a refugee column, and even the animals are weary.

They cannot save the burden. Then the sentence that finishes them. The god cannot rescue even the cart it is tied to, but themselves go into captivity. A god that has to be hauled away as cargo is no god at all.

What history shows. History did not stage this as a single scene. When Cyrus took Babylon in 539 BC he honoured Marduk rather than carting him off, and only decades later, after a revolt, is Xerxes said to have removed the great statue. Isaiah paints a tableau of the gods’ helplessness, and history bore it out in its own time: they did not save their city, and they have had no worshippers for many centuries.
verseByVerse.note: Bel (Marduk) and Nebo (Nabu) were the chief gods of Babylon, carried as burdens, while the LORD carries his people.

verseByVerse.quote: "Listen to me, O house of Jacob, all the remnant of the house of Israel, who have been borne by me from before your birth, carried from the womb; even to your old age I am he, and to gray hairs I will carry you. I have made, and I will bear; I will carry and will save.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The LORD has carried his people since before they were born, and he promises to carry them through old age to the end.

Borne by me from before your birth. The picture is exactly reversed. Babylon’s gods are freight; Israel’s God is the carrier, and nobody has ever had to lift him onto anything. The carrying is dated from before your birth, before there was anyone there to be grateful.

Even to your old age I am he. And it runs forward a long way. Most promises in Scripture are addressed to people in danger; this one is addressed to people getting old. That is a rarer comfort and a more searching one. There is a stage of life where nothing dramatic happens and something is quietly lost each year: the strength, the names, the friends. It is a slow subtraction, and it is when a person is most likely to feel he has become a burden.

To gray hairs I will carry you. To that fear God says: I carried you before you could walk, and I will carry you when you cannot. There are four verbs, made, bear, carry, save, and in every one God does the acting.

The same shoulders. Jesus told of a shepherd who finds a lost sheep and does not drive it home: he puts it on his shoulders and walks the whole way back rejoicing (Luke 15:5). The same shoulders later carried a cross out of the city, and on it he “bore our sins in his body” (1 Peter 2:24). From the womb to the grey hairs, and from Bethlehem to Calvary, it is the same load-bearing God, and he has never once set his people down.

The fear of becoming a burden. Our culture largely defines dignity as independence: managing your own affairs, paying your own way, needing nobody. It is a fine ideal for a strong forty-year-old, but it turns cruel at the end of life, when the hands shake and someone else must do the buttons, because by its measure the person being helped has lost not only strength but worth. That is why so many old people say that above all they do not want to be a burden. Isaiah sets a different measure. Dependence is not a fall from human dignity but the human condition from the start: we were carried from the womb (v. 3) and have never stopped being carried. The only question is who does the carrying, and whether he resents it. The God of verse 4 does not, and in Christ he carried far more than our frailty. To need him is not to lose your dignity; it is to discover where it always came from.

verseByVerse.quote: "To whom will you liken me and make me equal, and compare me, that we may be alike? Those who lavish gold from the purse, and weigh out silver in the scales, hire a goldsmith, and he makes it into a god; then they fall down and worship! They lift it to their shoulders, they carry it, they set it in its place, and it stands there; it cannot move from its place. If one cries to it, it does not answer or save him from his trouble.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Nothing can be compared to God, least of all a god that people pay for, carry into place, and cry to in vain.

Those who lavish gold from the purse. The question of verse 5 is answered with an invoice. Gold is poured out, silver weighed in the scales, a craftsman engaged at an agreed rate: a god commissioned like a piece of furniture. Then, without a break in the sentence, the customers kneel down in front of what they have paid for.

They lift it to their shoulders. Every verb belongs to the worshippers. They lift, they carry, they set it down. All the god does is stand where it was put, and it never moves because it cannot.

If one cries to it, it does not answer. Then the moment that matters, not the buying or the carving but the crying out: somebody in real trouble is on his knees in front of it, and it does not answer.

Which way the carrying runs. Here is the useful test, since few readers of this commentary own a statue. Take whatever you would turn to first if the worst news came this afternoon, and ask which way the carrying runs. Do you maintain it, fund it, defend it and keep it upright, or does it carry you? The God of verse 4 asks for no such upkeep; he offers to carry the one who turns to him.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The God who declares the end from the beginning will carry out his purpose, and he brings his salvation near to people who do not deserve it. The tone hardens into a summons: remember, you transgressors (v. 8). What they are to remember is what makes God God: he alone tells the end from the beginning, and his counsel will stand (vv. 9–10). The proof is close at hand, a bird of prey called from the east, the man of his counsel (v. 11). The chapter ends by telling the stubborn of heart, who are far from righteousness, that God is bringing his righteousness near himself, and that his salvation will not be late (vv. 12–13).
verseByVerse.theology: The section moves from memory to promise. The forgetful are told to remember who God is (vv. 8-11), and the stubborn are told what he is bringing to them (vv. 12-13).
verseByVerse.examples: Verse 8 treats forgetting as a moral condition, but verse 13 shows that the cure is not a better memory. It is a God who comes near to the forgetful anyway.

verseByVerse.quote: "Remember this and stand firm, recall it to mind, you transgressors, remember the former things of old; for I am God, and there is no other; I am God, and there is none like me, declaring the end from the beginning and from ancient times things not yet done, saying, 'My counsel shall stand, and I will accomplish all my purpose,' calling a bird of prey from the east, the man of my counsel from a far country. I have spoken, and I will bring it to pass; I have purposed, and I will do it.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God alone declares the end from the beginning, so his purpose will certainly stand, and his forgetful people are called to remember it and stand firm.

Remember this and stand firm. Three commands to remember in two verses, addressed to transgressors. Their problem is not that they were never told but that they have forgotten, and Isaiah treats forgetting as a moral condition rather than a mental lapse.

Declaring the end from the beginning. This is as close to a definition of God as the Old Testament comes, and it defines him by what he can say about the future. Everything the last six chapters have argued sits inside that clause: a god you have to carry cannot tell you about tomorrow, and a God who tells you about tomorrow before it arrives is not the sort of thing you carry.

My counsel shall stand. God says his counsel, his plan, will stand. He does not say he will try. There is no clause anywhere in these chapters about God’s purposes being frustrated and rescheduled.

Calling a bird of prey from the east. Cyrus was called God’s shepherd in 44:28. Here he is a bird of prey: swift, sudden, and coming for something. He is the man of my counsel because he carries out God’s plan, though nobody asked his opinion of it.

How do I remember? If forgetting is a moral condition, remembering is something God gives us ways to practise, and it is what makes a person stand firm. Rehearse his works on purpose. The psalmist does it as a decision, not a mood: “I will remember the deeds of the LORD” (Psalm 77:11). Keep a simple record of prayers answered and help given, and read it on the day you are tempted to think he has never done anything. Count the benefits by name. “Bless the LORD, O my soul, and forget not all his benefits” (Psalm 103:2); the next verses name them, and forgiveness comes first. Come to the Table. Jesus gave his church a meal for the same reason Isaiah gave Israel this verse: “Do this in remembrance of me” (Luke 22:19). The Supper is God’s answer to our short memory, a broken body and poured-out blood set again and again before forgetful people. Tell it to someone younger. A child’s question about why you pray is an invitation to rehearse what God has done. Underneath all of it: “Remember Jesus Christ, risen from the dead” (2 Timothy 2:8). What steadies us is not the strength of our memory but that he does not forget us.

Uncertain wording. The verb translated stand firm (v. 8) occurs only here in the Old Testament, and its meaning is uncertain. It may come from a word for a man, “show yourselves men”, or mean “be firm” or “take courage”. The ESV’s stand firm fits the call to remember well.

verseByVerse.quote: "Listen to me, you stubborn of heart, you who are far from righteousness: I bring near my righteousness; it is not far off, and my salvation will not delay; I will put salvation in Zion, for Israel my glory."
verseByVerse.commentary:
To stubborn people far from righteousness, God does not say “come near” but “I bring near my righteousness”, and he promises his salvation will not be late.

I bring near my righteousness. Look at what does not happen in these two verses. God addresses people who are stubborn and far from being right with him, and the obvious next line, a command to close the distance, never comes. Instead God moves: I bring near my righteousness; it is not far off. The gap between the stubborn heart and the righteousness it lacks is closed from God’s side, exactly as the carrying in verse 4 was. Everything in this chapter that actually works is done by God.

Paul’s echo. Paul has this kind of sentence in mind when he insists that the righteousness of faith does not ask who will go up to heaven to fetch it down, but says, “The word is near you” (Romans 10:6–8). Nobody is being asked to climb.

My salvation will not delay. The promise comes with a schedule attached: not that salvation will arrive eventually, but that it is not late now. Every year the exiles spent waiting was inside the timetable rather than outside it.

Righteousness in a body. Righteousness came near in the end, and it came near in a body. The gods of Babylon had to be lifted onto shoulders and set in their places, and they never once crossed the room to anybody. The God of Israel crossed everything there is to cross, was carried in a womb, walked out to the far country himself, and brought his righteousness to the stubborn of heart in his own two hands.

46.theology:
Which way the carrying runs. The chapter is built on one reversal, stated in pictures rather than propositions: gods that must be carried, and a God who carries his people from the womb to grey hairs. That is the practical difference between an idol and God.

Righteousness brought near. The stubborn of heart are told to remember (v. 8), and they are not told to close the distance themselves (vv. 12-13). God closes it. What they lacked he brings, and in the end he brought it in his Son, whose obedience is counted to those who could never have reached it (Romans 5:19). That is why the call to remember and stand firm is not a threat to the forgetful but an invitation back to a salvation that will not delay.

47.subtitle: The Fall of Babylon
47.intro:
Where we are. Chapter 46 showed Babylon’s gods carried off as cargo. Chapter 47 turns from the gods to the city herself, in a taunt song sung over Babylon while she still looked invincible.

The message. Pride that takes God’s place will be brought down in a day. Babylon, the proud queen of the nations, showed God’s people no mercy and said of herself what only God can say: “I am, and there is no one besides me.” So she will sit in the dust as a slave, and none of her wisdom, charms or astrologers can save her, because her real need, a covering for her guilt, was the one thing she could not buy.

Why it was said. The exiles lived under the most powerful and learned city on earth (see the introduction), whose rule looked permanent. They needed to know that Babylon’s days were numbered, and that the God who had handed them over in judgment had not forgotten how they were treated.

How the chapter makes its case. The queen dethroned (vv. 1–4): told to grind at the millstones and wade the rivers like a captive, while her victims’ Redeemer is named. The charge (vv. 5–7): God gave his people into her hand, and she showed them no mercy, loading the aged heaviest, sure she would be mistress for ever. The boast reversed (vv. 8–9): she claimed God’s own words, and the two losses she said would never come will come in one day. Her defences fail (vv. 10–15): she felt secure because no one saw; a disaster comes that she cannot charm away or atone for, her astrologers burn like stubble, and there is no one to save her.

Where it leads. By the character of God revealed in Christ, and by the need it exposes. In the middle of the taunt, God’s people call him “our Redeemer” (v. 4), the kinsman who buys back what his family has lost, and the Son became our kinsman in the flesh to buy us back with his own blood. And the disaster Babylon could not atone for (v. 11) names the need every proud heart shares, which only the Servant meets when he is “pierced for our transgressions” (53:5). The pattern runs on to the end: John hears the last Babylon boasting, “I sit as a queen,” before she too falls in one day (Revelation 18:7–8).

For us. Every claim to be self-sufficient and answerable to no one is a counterfeit of God, whether made by an empire, an economy or a single heart, and it ends in the dust. But the Redeemer who humbles the proud also sees the overlooked, and has given freely the one thing no wealth or wisdom could buy, the covering of our guilt.

keyVerse.quote: “I am, and there is no one besides me; I shall not sit as a widow or know the loss of children.”
keyVerse.note: Babylon takes for herself the language God uses of his own uniqueness (45:5–6). The claim is both audacious and suicidal: to speak what belongs only to God is to stand where only God can stand. The next verse reverses it exactly: both things she said would never happen will happen in a single day.

47.reflection:
Babylon said, “I shall be mistress forever” (v. 7), and the assumption that her power would last made her cruel. Where are we tempted to treat others carelessly because we assume our position, health or comfort is secure?

“I am, and there is no one besides me” (v. 8) is God’s own language. Where do you see nations, systems or individuals today claiming self-sufficiency and answering to no one? Where might the same claim hide, more quietly, in your own heart?

Babylon felt secure because she said, “No one sees me” (v. 10). How does it change your life to know that God sees everything, both as a warning and, through Christ, as a comfort?

Babylon could not charm away, atone for or predict her disaster (v. 11). What do people today rely on to manage guilt and an uncertain future, and how does Christ’s atonement answer that need?
