verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–9 — Come Down and Sit in the Dust
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The proud queen of the nations will be brought down to the dust, because she showed no mercy and claimed for herself what belongs to God alone. Babylon, still standing, is addressed as a pampered queen and told to come down, grind at the millstones like the lowest slave and wade the rivers with the captives (vv. 1–3). Verse 4 breaks in with the name of Israel’s Redeemer. Then comes the charge: God handed his people over, and Babylon showed them no mercy, loading even the aged (vv. 5–6), sure she would be mistress for ever (v. 7). She said of herself what only God can say, “I am, and there is no one besides me”, and widowhood and loss of children arrive in a single day (vv. 8–9).
verseByVerse.theology: The crux of the chapter is in verse 6. Babylon was genuinely the instrument of God's anger and is genuinely guilty, and both halves are stated in one breath. Being used by God is no defence, because the cruelty was hers: God never told her to show no mercy.
verseByVerse.examples: Babylon's boast in verse 8 outlives every particular empire that says it, and it is spoken in smaller ways by every heart that thinks its own position permanent.

verseByVerse.quote: Come down and sit in the dust, O virgin daughter of Babylon; sit on the ground without a throne, O daughter of the Chaldeans! For you shall no more be called tender and delicate. Take the millstones and grind flour, put off your veil, strip off your robe, uncover your legs, pass through the rivers. Your nakedness shall be uncovered, and your disgrace shall be seen. I will take vengeance, and I will spare no one. Our Redeemer—the LORD of hosts is his name— is the Holy One of Israel.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The pampered queen of the nations is ordered off her throne to do a slave’s work and walk with the captives, and in the middle of the taunt God’s people name their Redeemer.

O virgin daughter of Babylon. Babylon is called a virgin because she thought herself untouchable, and tender and delicate because she had never had to do anything hard. The titles are read out the way a court reads a defendant’s titles before they are taken away, and she is sent to sit in the dust, the place of mourning and ruin.

Take the millstones and grind flour. Each instruction strips off a layer of status. Grinding flour at a hand millstone was the work of the lowest slave woman in a household, hours of it every day. The veil that marked a lady comes off, and she fords the river on foot with the deportation column.

Babylon’s own measure. This is meant to be hard to read. It is exactly what Babylon’s own columns of prisoners had looked like for a century, and Isaiah shows the queen walking in them. The woman is a city, not a person, and the shame is the shame Babylon had dealt out to others, returned to her. It is never a licence for anyone to humiliate another; vengeance belongs to God alone (Romans 12:19).

Our Redeemer. Verse 4 does not belong to the taunt at all. Another voice cuts in, and what it says about God is not he is strong or he is just but our Redeemer, the family word for the kinsman who buys back what his relatives have lost. Empires rise and fall, and Isaiah gives them a verse or two apiece. The one line in the chapter not about Babylon is about the Holy One of Israel, spoken in the plural by people who have nothing left except a relative who owns everything. That Relative took our flesh and bought us back with his own blood (1 Peter 1:18–19).

verseByVerse.quote: Sit in silence, and go into darkness, O daughter of the Chaldeans; for you shall no more be called the mistress of kingdoms. I was angry with my people; I profaned my heritage; I gave them into your hand; you showed them no mercy; on the aged you made your yoke exceedingly heavy. You said, "I shall be mistress forever," so that you did not lay these things to heart or remember their end.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God handed his people to Babylon in judgment, but she is condemned for the merciless way she treated them, because she assumed her power would never end.

Sit in silence, and go into darkness. Silence and darkness are what is left when a great city stops being great. Isaiah does not describe the ruins; he describes the quiet.

I gave them into your hand. Verse 6 is the hinge of the chapter, and it holds two things at once: the deportation was God’s doing, and Babylon is condemned for how she handled what she was handed.

You showed them no mercy. The commission did not include cruelty. Then the detail that makes the charge specific: the aged. Of all the prisoners, those who could carry least were loaded heaviest. Read that beside the chapter before it, where God carries his people to grey hairs and will not set them down (46:4). Here an empire takes the same grey-haired people and adds to their weight. Two ways of dealing with the old, one chapter apart, and only one of them survives to the end of the book.

I shall be mistress forever. The sin named in verse 7 is not brutality but the assumption underneath it. Believing you will always hold the position you now hold is what makes cruelty feel safe. Nobody who has thought seriously about how his own power ends treats the weak the way Babylon did.

verseByVerse.quote: Now therefore hear this, you lover of pleasures, who sit securely, who say in your heart, "I am, and there is no one besides me; I shall not sit as a widow or know the loss of children": These two things shall come to you in a moment, in one day; the loss of children and widowhood shall come upon you in full measure, in spite of your many sorceries and the great power of your enchantments.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Babylon claims God’s own words for herself, and the two losses she said she would never know will come together in a single day.

I am, and there is no one besides me. This is not Babylonian court flattery. It is God’s own self-description, sounded again and again in chapter 45, now recited by a city about herself. That is what the chapter means by pride, and it is more than arrogance. It is a counterfeit: a human power applying to itself the words that belong to God alone, as if it had no equal and answered to no one.

In a moment, in one day. The second half of the boast names her two unthinkable losses, widowhood and the loss of children, the ancient world’s two pictures of a woman with no future and no protector. Both arrive together. God does not argue with the boast; he names the day it will end. Babylon was in fact taken in a single night in 539 BC, with hardly a fight (Daniel 5:30 sets Belshazzar’s death on the night of his feast), though her slow decay as a city took centuries more. The one day is the day her boast ended.

Still being said. The same sentence is still being said. John, writing of the last Babylon of all, hears a city say in her heart that she sits as a queen, is no widow, and will never see mourning, and then hears that her plagues will come “in a single day” (Revelation 18:7–8).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 10–15 — Let Your Astrologers Stand Up and Save You
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Nothing Babylon trusted for her security can save her from the judgment of God. She felt safe in her wickedness, sure that no one saw, and her famous wisdom led her astray (v. 10). Against that come three troubles matched to her specialities: an evil she cannot charm away, a disaster she cannot atone for, a ruin she cannot foresee (v. 11). Her enchanters and astrologers, who mapped the heavens and forecast each new moon, are invited with cold irony to try (vv. 12–13). The answer is a bonfire in which they are the fuel and nobody gets warm (v. 14), and the chapter ends with her business partners scattering and no one to save her (v. 15).
verseByVerse.theology: Babylon's security rested on what she knew and on the belief that no one saw her (v. 10). The section takes both apart: what she knew could not save her, and she had been seen all along.

verseByVerse.quote: You felt secure in your wickedness; you said, "No one sees me"; your wisdom and your knowledge led you astray, and you said in your heart, "I am, and there is no one besides me." But evil shall come upon you, which you will not know how to charm away; disaster shall fall upon you, for which you will not be able to atone; and ruin shall come upon you suddenly, of which you know nothing.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Babylon felt safe because she thought no one saw her, but a disaster is coming that none of her learning can charm away, atone for or foresee.

You felt secure in your wickedness. The security came from two things. The first is the belief that nobody was watching, which makes wickedness feel safe rather than merely profitable. The second is stranger: her wisdom and knowledge led her astray. Babylon was the most learned city on earth, and Isaiah says her learning misled her.

Which you will not know how to charm away. Three troubles are named, each matched to a Babylonian speciality that fails. She had charms, and this cannot be charmed. She had rituals of appeasement, and this cannot be atoned for. She had astronomers, and this one is not on the charts.

For which you will not be able to atone. The middle clause is the deepest. Babylon could buy grain, armies, allies and information; the one thing not for sale anywhere in the empire was the covering of guilt. The word belongs to the temple’s vocabulary of atonement, used of sacrificial blood and the mercy seat, and that need is the one the whole Bible is written to meet. Six chapters later the covering is provided by a man wounded for transgressions that were not his (53:5). What Babylon could not purchase at any price was given away.

What would you do if no one could see? In Plato’s Republic a shepherd, Gyges, finds a ring that makes him invisible and promptly uses it to seduce a queen, kill a king and take his throne, and Glaucon argues that anyone would do the same: we are just only because we are watched. The modern world has handed out something like that ring. Behind a screen name or a closed door, real character comes out, and much of it says what Babylon said: No one sees me. Isaiah does not answer by installing more cameras. He says someone does see, and always has, and for Babylon that is terror. But Scripture shows the other face of being seen. A runaway slave woman in the desert, invisible to everyone who mattered, called the LORD a God of seeing (Genesis 16:13). The gaze that unmasks the proud also finds the overlooked. And at the cross the one who sees everything looked at the worst we had hidden and paid for it, so that we need no ring and no screen to hide behind.

Uncertain wording. The word behind charm away in verse 11 is uncertain. It may mean to drive off by magic, which suits the sorceries of verses 9 and 12, or come from the word for dawn, so that she will not know where the evil dawns from. Either way, none of her arts can stop it.

verseByVerse.quote: Stand fast in your enchantments and your many sorceries, with which you have labored from your youth; perhaps you may be able to succeed; perhaps you may inspire terror. You are wearied with your many counsels; let them stand forth and save you, those who divide the heavens, who gaze at the stars, who at the new moons make known what shall come upon you. Behold, they are like stubble; the fire consumes them; they cannot deliver themselves from the power of the flame. No coal for warming oneself is this, no fire to sit before! Such to you are those with whom you have labored, who have done business with you from your youth; they wander about, each in his own direction; there is no one to save you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God invites Babylon to try her sorceries and astrologers, knowing they will burn like straw and leave her with no one to save her.

Perhaps you may be able to succeed. The tone is not rage but something colder. God tells her to go ahead and use everything she has. Perhaps, he says, twice: the voice of a man watching somebody try a key that will not turn.

Those who divide the heavens. The astrologers are described fairly. Babylonian sky-watching was serious work, with records kept for centuries and forecasts at each new moon, the best predictive science of its day. Chapters 41 to 48 have asked one question of it: did anyone tell you Cyrus was coming? She is also wearied with your many counsels: managing the machinery of security had become exhausting in itself.

No coal for warming oneself is this. The image turns savage and then oddly domestic. The wise men go up like dry straw, and Isaiah adds an aside: you could not even warm your hands at this. In chapter 44 the idolater at least got a hot meal out of half his log. Here the fire consumes and gives nothing back.

There is no one to save you. The last sentence is flat and final. It is true of Babylon. It is not true of everyone. Four chapters earlier the same voice said that besides him there is no savior (43:11), and the whole point of the trial in these chapters is that a Saviour exists, has said so out loud in advance, and is at that moment arranging a homecoming for prisoners who had nothing to bring him.

Uncertain wording. The exact sense of those who divide the heavens (v. 13), a rare expression, is uncertain: perhaps those who mark the sky into sections to read it. Either way they are star-gazers claiming to know the future.

47.theology:
An instrument can still be guilty. God’s sovereignty over an event does not transfer the moral responsibility for it to him, and being used by God is no defence in his court.

Why the chapter is not the last word. The tragedy of Babylon is not that no rescuer existed. It is that she had said aloud that she needed none. Anyone who catches himself making her boast has a way out that she never took: to confess his need to the Redeemer of verse 4.

48.subtitle: Refined in the Furnace of Affliction
48.intro:
Where we are. Chapter 48 closes the first movement of chapters 40 to 55, the long trial in which the LORD has put the idols in the dock and named Cyrus as his instrument. Babylon’s gods and Babylon herself have fallen (chapters 46–47); now God turns to his own people.

The message. God’s people are obstinate, religious in words but not in truth, rebels from birth, and yet God keeps them and rescues them for the sake of his own name. He told them everything in advance so that they could not credit their idols or themselves; he grieves over the peace they could have had; and he commands them to leave Babylon, singing that the LORD has redeemed his servant Jacob.

Why it was said. The exiles (see the introduction) were not only oppressed but hard-hearted. Many had settled into Babylon and kept the language of faith without its reality. They needed to hear both why they did not deserve rescue and why it was certain.

How the chapter makes its case. The obstinate kept (vv. 1–11): a people who swear by the LORD but not in truth were told the former things long before, so that they could not credit an idol, and new things now, so that they could not say they knew; God restrains his anger for his own name’s sake. The lament (vv. 12–19): the first and the last has called Cyrus; a voice says the Lord GOD has sent him with his Spirit; and God grieves that if only they had listened, their peace would have been like a river. The exodus (vv. 20–22): go out from Babylon, shout that the LORD has redeemed Jacob, remember the water from the rock, but there is no peace for the wicked.

Where it leads. First, by the need it exposes: Israel’s ear was never opened (v. 8), and two chapters later a Servant says, “The Lord GOD has opened my ear, and I was not rebellious” (50:5). Where Israel would not listen, Christ listened perfectly, and his obedience is counted to all who trust him. By promise: the one sent by the Lord GOD with his Spirit (v. 16) stood up at Nazareth and read that the Spirit was upon him (Luke 4:18–21). By pattern: the rock split in the desert was, Paul says, Christ (1 Corinthians 10:4).

For us. God does not keep us because we are easy to keep but for the sake of his name, which is why his hold on us is safe. Yet his grief over lost peace is real: the way to river-like peace is to listen to him, and the way back for those who have not is the Redeemer who still teaches and leads. Leave whatever Babylon you have settled in, and tell others what he has done.

keyVerse.quote: “Oh that you had paid attention to my commandments! Then your peace would have been like a river, and your righteousness like the waves of the sea.”
keyVerse.note: The “oh that” is God himself grieving over the peace his people did not take hold of. River-peace is deep and continuous: not a burst of feeling but a sustained, flowing peace, there in the dry months as well as the wet. It was always on offer, and listening was always the channel; the lament is an invitation dressed as regret.

48.reflection:
Israel swore by the LORD’s name “but not in truth or right” (v. 1). How can the language of faith carry on when the reality has gone? What signs of that do you need to watch for in yourself or your church?

God says he refines and keeps his people “for my own sake” (v. 11), for the honour of his name. Why is that a stronger comfort than being kept because we deserve it?

“Oh that you had paid attention to my commandments! Then your peace would have been like a river” (v. 18). What do you learn about God’s commandments from this grief? Where might you be missing peace because you have not been listening?

The exiles were told to leave a comfortable Babylon and shout to the end of the earth that “The LORD has redeemed his servant Jacob!” (v. 20). What settled comforts make it hard for you to follow Christ wholeheartedly, and who needs to hear from you what he has done?
48.text: <sup>1</sup>Hear this, O house of Jacob, who are called by the name of Israel, and who came from the waters of Judah, who swear by the name of the LORD and confess the God of Israel, but not in truth or right.<sup>2</sup>For they call themselves after the holy city, and stay themselves on the God of Israel; the LORD of hosts is his name.<sup>3</sup>"The former things I declared of old; they went out from my mouth, and I announced them; then suddenly I did them, and they came to pass.<sup>4</sup>Because I know that you are obstinate, and your neck is an iron sinew and your forehead brass,<sup>5</sup>I declared them to you from of old, before they came to pass I announced them to you, lest you should say, 'My idol did them, my carved image and my metal image commanded them.'<sup>6</sup>"You have heard; now see all this; and will you not declare it? From this time forth I announce to you new things, hidden things that you have not known.<sup>7</sup>They are created now, not long ago; before today you have never heard of them, lest you should say, 'Behold, I knew them.'<sup>8</sup>You have never heard, you have never known, from of old your ear has not been opened. For I knew that you would surely deal treacherously, and that from before birth you were called a rebel.<sup>9</sup>"For my name's sake I defer my anger; for the sake of my praise I restrain it for you, that I may not cut you off.<sup>10</sup>Behold, I have refined you, but not as silver; I have tried you in the furnace of affliction.<sup>11</sup>For my own sake, for my own sake, I do it, for how should my name be profaned? My glory I will not give to another.<sup>12</sup>"Listen to me, O Jacob, and Israel, whom I called! I am he; I am the first, and I am the last.<sup>13</sup>My hand laid the foundation of the earth, and my right hand spread out the heavens; when I call to them, they stand forth together.<sup>14</sup>"Assemble, all of you, and listen! Who among them has declared these things? The LORD loves him; he shall perform his purpose on Babylon, and his arm shall be against the Chaldeans.<sup>15</sup>I, even I, have spoken and called him; I have brought him, and he will prosper in his way.<sup>16</sup>Draw near to me, hear this: from the beginning I have not spoken in secret, from the time it came to be I have been there." And now the Lord GOD has sent me, and his Spirit.<sup>17</sup>Thus says the LORD, your Redeemer, the Holy One of Israel: "I am the LORD your God, who teaches you to profit, who leads you in the way you should go.<sup>18</sup>Oh that you had paid attention to my commandments! Then your peace would have been like a river, and your righteousness like the waves of the sea;<sup>19</sup>your offspring would have been like the sand, and your descendants like its grains; their name would never be cut off or destroyed from before me."<sup>20</sup>Go out from Babylon, flee from Chaldea, declare this with a shout of joy, proclaim it, send it out to the end of the earth; say, "The LORD has redeemed his servant Jacob!"<sup>21</sup>They did not thirst when he led them through the deserts; he made water flow for them from the rock; he split the rock and the water gushed out.<sup>22</sup>"There is no peace," says the LORD, "for the wicked."

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God keeps his stubborn people for the sake of his own name, not because of anything in them. A very religious people is described, with the right name, oath, confession and city, and then six words undo it: not in truth or right (vv. 1–2). God explains why he announced the former things so far in advance: he knew their iron necks, and would not let them credit an idol (vv. 3–5). Now he announces new things, so that they cannot claim they knew all along, for they have been rebels from birth (vv. 6–8). The reason they still exist lies in him alone: for his name’s sake he restrains his anger and refines them in the furnace of affliction, and will not give his glory to another (vv. 9–11).
verseByVerse.theology: God's reason for keeping this people is given plainly, and it is not their improvement. Everything in verses 9-11 rests on his name, his honour, so nothing the people do can cancel it.
verseByVerse.examples: It is possible to say every right word in church, to sing the creeds and lean on the name of the LORD, and for none of it to be in truth or right (v. 1). The chapter does not say this to drive the reader to despair but to the God who keeps such people anyway.

verseByVerse.quote: Hear this, O house of Jacob, who are called by the name of Israel, and who came from the waters of Judah, who swear by the name of the LORD and confess the God of Israel, but not in truth or right. For they call themselves after the holy city, and stay themselves on the God of Israel; the LORD of hosts is his name. "The former things I declared of old; they went out from my mouth, and I announced them; then suddenly I did them, and they came to pass. Because I know that you are obstinate, and your neck is an iron sinew and your forehead brass, I declared them to you from of old, before they came to pass I announced them to you, lest you should say, 'My idol did them, my carved image and my metal image commanded them.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
God’s people use all the right religious words without truth, so God announced events long in advance to leave their iron necks no excuse.

But not in truth or right. Without the last clause, verses 1–2 describe model believers: the covenant name, the oath, the confession, the holy city. Then six words undo it: but not in truth or right. Isaiah is not describing pagans but the religious, whose vocabulary is correct while the reality behind it is missing. Jesus said the same, quoting this book (Matthew 15:8; Isaiah 29:13).

Your neck is an iron sinew and your forehead brass. The diagnosis is given as anatomy. An iron sinew in the neck will not turn when someone calls; a brass forehead cannot blush. Stubbornness is treated not as a view a person holds but as something that has happened to him.

I declared them to you from of old. What God does about the iron neck is remarkable. He does not remove the stubbornness first; he works around it. The prophecies were issued long in advance so that this people could not credit the outcome to a carved image. God closed the door on the excuse before anyone reached it.

Uncertain wording. Who came from the waters of Judah (v. 1) is unusual: perhaps Judah pictured as a spring, or, with a small change to one Hebrew word, from the loins of Judah. Either way it names their proud descent.

verseByVerse.quote: "You have heard; now see all this; and will you not declare it? From this time forth I announce to you new things, hidden things that you have not known. They are created now, not long ago; before today you have never heard of them, lest you should say, 'Behold, I knew them.' You have never heard, you have never known, from of old your ear has not been opened. For I knew that you would surely deal treacherously, and that from before birth you were called a rebel.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God announces new things so that his people cannot claim they knew them all along, for they have been rebels from birth.

They are created now, not long ago. The second excuse is closed the same way. Old prophecies stopped them crediting the idols; brand-new ones stop them claiming they had worked it out themselves. God knows both faces of the heart, the one that gives the credit elsewhere and the one that takes it, and leaves room for neither.

From before birth you were called a rebel. The last clause goes furthest: not that they became rebels under pressure, but that the name applied before they were born. This is what the church later called original sin: we do not become sinners by our first wrong choice; we are born turned away from God (Psalm 51:5). If the rebellion is that old, nothing that follows is a reward for a promising start. And in the middle: your ear has not been opened. Two chapters on, a Servant says that the Lord GOD opened his ear, and that he was not rebellious (50:5).

verseByVerse.quote: "For my name's sake I defer my anger; for the sake of my praise I restrain it for you, that I may not cut you off. Behold, I have refined you, but not as silver; I have tried you in the furnace of affliction. For my own sake, for my own sake, I do it, for how should my name be profaned? My glory I will not give to another.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God holds back his anger and keeps his people through the furnace for his own name’s sake, the safest ground they could have.

For my name’s sake I defer my anger. Anger is deferred and restrained: both words imply something real held back, not something never felt. The reason the nation still exists has nothing to do with the nation.

I have refined you, but not as silver. Silver refining is taken to completion, until the dross is off and the metal is pure. God says the exile was not that. Either the fire was restrained, because full refining would have consumed them, or little pure metal came out; the text allows both. What it does not allow is the sentimental reading in which suffering automatically improves people. Yet the furnace is still God’s: nothing enters it unpermitted and nothing leaves before his purpose is served, as Peter tells scattered Christians whose tested faith is more precious than gold refined by fire (1 Peter 1:7).

For my own sake, for my own sake, I do it. He says it twice, as though he expected to be misheard: not for your sake, for mine. That sounds cold until it is examined; then it turns out to be the one ground solid enough to hold a person who knows his own record. A rescue undertaken because the rescued were worth it can be reconsidered when they prove they were not. A rescue undertaken for the sake of God’s own name can fail only if he stops caring what his name is worth. He has staked his reputation on keeping people who have given him no reason to keep them, and that is exactly what makes them safe.

Textual note. In verse 10 the standard Hebrew text reads chosen; some early manuscripts read tried, which the ESV follows. The words differ by one letter, and both fit.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 12–19 — If Only You Had Paid Attention
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The almighty God who called his people grieves over the peace they lost by not listening. He reminds them who is speaking: the first and the last, whose hands laid the earth and spread the heavens, at whose call they stand to attention (vv. 12–13). He loves and has called the conqueror who will carry out his purpose on Babylon (vv. 14–15), and verse 16 ends with an unexpected voice, sent by the Lord GOD and his Spirit. Then argument gives way to grief. The Redeemer who teaches and leads mourns what might have been: peace like a river, righteousness like the waves of the sea, and descendants beyond counting (vv. 17–19).
verseByVerse.theology: The voice that calls the heavens to attention in verse 13 is the voice that grieves in verse 18. Verse 18 is a lament rather than a threat: God is not warning them what they will lose; he is mourning what they did not take.
verseByVerse.examples: The end of verse 16 is one of the Old Testament's genuine puzzles. Isaiah does not resolve it and should not be forced to; the New Testament does, and reading it back here is legitimate, as long as we remember that the New Testament’s light came later.

verseByVerse.quote: "Listen to me, O Jacob, and Israel, whom I called! I am he; I am the first, and I am the last. My hand laid the foundation of the earth, and my right hand spread out the heavens; when I call to them, they stand forth together. "Assemble, all of you, and listen! Who among them has declared these things? The LORD loves him; he shall perform his purpose on Babylon, and his arm shall be against the Chaldeans. I, even I, have spoken and called him; I have brought him, and he will prosper in his way. Draw near to me, hear this: from the beginning I have not spoken in secret, from the time it came to be I have been there." And now the Lord GOD has sent me, and his Spirit.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The first and the last, who commands heaven and earth, has called the conqueror against Babylon, and a voice speaks, sent by the Lord GOD and his Spirit.

My hand laid the foundation of the earth. One hand sets the footings of the earth, the other stretches the sky like a tent; then he calls, and heaven and earth stand forth together, the way a room of soldiers comes to attention when the officer speaks. The universe is not merely made; it is on parade, and the one who commands it is the one calling Jacob.

The LORD loves him. Cyrus is described one last time with a word not used of him before: loved. A Persian who does not know God is spoken of with affection, a further enlargement of what chapters 44 and 45 said about whom God may use.

The Lord GOD has sent me, and his Spirit. At the end of verse 16 a voice that has been speaking as God, the first and the last, says that the Lord GOD has sent him, together with his Spirit. Many think the prophet, or the Servant, breaks in here, but the Hebrew marks no change of speaker. If the speaker is the same, someone who has been talking as God is also sent by God and accompanied by God’s Spirit. It would be dishonest to pretend Isaiah’s first readers had a doctrine of the Trinity to file it under. But when the sent one stood up in the synagogue at Nazareth, he read from this book, “The Spirit of the Lord GOD is upon me, because the LORD has anointed me” (61:1), and told the room it had just come true (Luke 4:18–21). The hint in verse 16 is small; at Nazareth the sent one stood there in person.

Uncertain wording. The grammar of the last line allows the Spirit to be either sender or sent: the King James Version reads the Lord GOD, and his Spirit, hath sent me. Either way the Lord GOD, the sent one and the Spirit stand in one sentence.

verseByVerse.quote: Thus says the LORD, your Redeemer, the Holy One of Israel: "I am the LORD your God, who teaches you to profit, who leads you in the way you should go. Oh that you had paid attention to my commandments! Then your peace would have been like a river, and your righteousness like the waves of the sea; your offspring would have been like the sand, and your descendants like its grains; their name would never be cut off or destroyed from before me."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Redeemer who teaches and leads grieves over the lasting peace his people would have had if they had listened.

Who teaches you to profit. The commandments come from the one who first calls himself your Redeemer and the LORD your God: grace comes before law, as at Sinai, where rescue came first and commandments second. Two verbs describe what he has been doing all along, teaching and leading. This is not thunder on a mountain but a parent walking a child to school.

Oh that you had paid attention to my commandments! Then God grieves out loud, and the lament shows what the commandments were for: not a ladder to his favour but the shape of the peace he wanted to give. A river is not a cloudburst; it is continuous, there in August as well as March. The waves of the sea are the one thing on earth that has never once failed to come in: righteousness with the reliability of a tide. Descendants as many as the sand, promised to Abraham, were within reach, and the people did not take hold of the promise.

The same grief at Jerusalem. The sound of this verse is heard again on a hillside overlooking Jerusalem, where a man who knew this book better than anyone looked at the city and wept: “Would that you, even you, had known on this day the things that make for peace!” (Luke 19:42). The form of the sentence is the same, and so is the grief. And the one who wept is the Servant whose ear was opened (50:5), who paid attention where Israel did not. For the reader who hears this lament over his own wasted years, the way back is the same Redeemer, and the teaching and leading now come by his Spirit within (Ezekiel 36:27).

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Because the LORD has redeemed his people, they are to leave Babylon and tell the whole world. The command everything has been building towards is a marching order: go out, flee, and shout it to the end of the earth, with a song of one line, the LORD has redeemed his servant Jacob (v. 20). The first exodus is offered as the guarantee of the second: he led his people through the deserts and split the rock so that they did not thirst (v. 21). Then verse 22 stops the celebration with a warning that the offer of peace can be refused: there is no peace for the wicked.
verseByVerse.theology: The last verse is not tacked on. The gate out of Babylon is open, and walking through it is the whole of what is required; those who prefer to stay are not covered by a promise made to those who leave.

verseByVerse.quote: Go out from Babylon, flee from Chaldea, declare this with a shout of joy, proclaim it, send it out to the end of the earth; say, "The LORD has redeemed his servant Jacob!" They did not thirst when he led them through the deserts; he made water flow for them from the rock; he split the rock and the water gushed out. "There is no peace," says the LORD, "for the wicked."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Redeemed by the LORD, his people are to leave Babylon and tell the whole earth, trusting the God of the first exodus; but there is no peace for those who refuse.

Go out from Babylon, flee from Chaldea. After eight chapters of argument come five commands: go, flee, declare, proclaim, send. Only the first two are about leaving; the rest are about telling everyone. And the order matters: they are told to go because the LORD has redeemed them. The departure does not earn the redemption; it answers it.

What leaving cost. These people had been in Babylon long enough to own houses in it. Going out meant leaving a settled life for a ruined city nearly nine hundred miles away, on the strength of a sentence, and some of them did not go.

He split the rock and the water gushed out. The evidence for the second journey is the first: the desert was survivable once, when Moses struck the rock and a nation drank. Paul says of that rock a sentence no one saw coming: “the Rock was Christ” (1 Corinthians 10:4). Struck, opened, and pouring out what a dying people needed, in a place where there was no other source.

The hard last line. The chapter ends on purpose with a hard line: there is no peace for those who refuse the rescue and would rather stay in Babylon. The same sentence closes chapter 57 (57:21), and the book ends on a similar warning (66:24), so it works as a refrain dividing chapters 40 to 66 into three movements, each ending with the reminder that the offer of peace can be refused.

The trial closes. The trial that began in chapter 41 closes here. Every idol has been asked to speak and has not, and the verdict is a set of prison gates standing open. The LORD has redeemed his servant Jacob, and the redemption was announced, dated, financed and carried out by the one who had been saying from the beginning that there was no other.

48.theology:
For my own sake, twice. The chapter gives the reason this people survive, and it is not their repentance, their usefulness, or their promise, but God’s care for his own name (v. 11). Stated coldly it sounds like divine self-interest; examined, it is the only foundation strong enough for someone who knows his own record.

Refined, but not as silver. Verse 10 refuses the comfortable doctrine that suffering automatically improves people, in a chapter that has just called this people iron-necked and brass-faced. What remains true is that the furnace is God’s, and he governs what it does.

A rebel from before birth. Verse 8 teaches original sin, that we are sinners from birth, without the technical vocabulary, and it settles what the rest of the chapter can mean: nothing that follows is a reward for a promising start. Israel’s ear was not opened; two chapters later the Servant says the Lord GOD opened his (50:5). What Israel could not do, the Servant does in her place.

Sent, with his Spirit. The last clause of verse 16 names the Lord GOD, a sent one and the Spirit together, and Isaiah leaves it standing. It would be wrong to claim his first hearers held a doctrine of the Trinity; it would be equally wrong to pretend the verse does not distinguish the three.

49.subtitle: The Second Servant Song
49.intro:
Where we are. Chapters 40 to 48 put the idols on trial and named Cyrus as the one who would free the exiles; chapter 48 ended with the cry to go out from Babylon. Chapter 49 turns from Cyrus to the servant, who speaks for himself in the second Servant Song, and from Babylon to Zion, the ruined mother.

The message. God’s rescue is bigger than anyone dared hope, and it rests on a love that cannot forget. The servant who feels he has laboured for nothing is told that bringing Israel home is too small a task: he will be a light for the nations. And Zion, who says the LORD has forgotten her, is told that a nursing mother may forget her child, but God has engraved her on the palms of his hands.

Why it was said. The exiles had been told that release was coming (see the introduction), yet they still felt forgotten: their city was rubble, their numbers few, their captors strong. The chapter answers the discouraged worker and the discouraged people with the same God.

How the chapter makes its case. The servant speaks (vv. 1–7): called from the womb and hidden like an arrow, named Israel yet sent to bring Israel back, he confesses that his labour seems vain, and God answers by enlarging his mission to the end of the earth and promising that kings will bow to the despised one. God sets the timetable (vv. 8–13): a day of salvation, prisoners freed, a road through the mountains, and creation singing because the LORD has comforted his people. Then Zion objects (vv. 14–26): God answers with a mother, a pair of engraved hands, a city too small for its children, kings carrying her sons home, and a promise that even the tyrant’s prey will be taken back.

Where it leads. This chapter leads to Christ by direct promise. The servant who bears Israel’s name and restores Israel is the one Simeon held in the temple and called “a light for revelation to the Gentiles” (Luke 2:32), and Paul and Barnabas took verse 6 as their commission to the nations (Acts 13:47). Paul announces that the day of salvation of verse 8 has come (2 Corinthians 6:2). And the God who engraves his people on his palms is revealed in the risen Christ, who held out his wounded hands to a doubting disciple (John 20:27).

For us. If your faithful work looks wasted, do what the servant did: leave your case with the LORD, who honours you and has larger purposes than you can see. And if you feel forgotten, look at the hands of Jesus. Those who wait for him will not be put to shame (v. 23).

keyVerse.quote: “Can a woman forget her nursing child, that she should have no compassion on the son of her womb? Even these may forget, yet I will not forget you. Behold, I have engraved you on the palms of my hands.”
keyVerse.note: The argument moves from the most reliable human attachment, a mother to her nursing infant, to something more reliable still. God does not merely match a mother’s love; he concedes that hers can fail and puts his own beyond it. The engraved palms point forward to the wounds in the hands of Christ, the lasting bodily record of what it cost to keep the promise.

49.reflection:
The servant says, “I have labored in vain,” yet leaves his right with the LORD (v. 4), and God answers by enlarging his mission rather than explaining the failure (v. 6). Where have you been tempted to judge your faithfulness by visible results? What would it look like to leave the verdict with God?

Paul and Barnabas took verse 6 as their own commission (Acts 13:47). What does it mean for your church that salvation is meant to reach “to the end of the earth”, and where is the “too light a thing” in your own ambitions for God’s work?

Zion says, “The LORD has forsaken me; my Lord has forgotten me” (v. 14), straight after creation is told to sing, and God answers without a word of rebuke. What does that teach you about bringing your own fears and complaints to God, and about how to answer a friend who feels forgotten?

God says, “I have engraved you on the palms of my hands” (v. 16). How do the wounds in the hands of the risen Christ (John 20:27) make that promise more certain to you?
