The LORD called me from the womb, from the body of my mother he named my name.<sup>2</sup>He made my mouth like a sharp sword; in the shadow of his hand he hid me; he made me a polished arrow; in his quiver he hid me away.<sup>3</sup>And he said to me, "You are my servant, Israel, in whom I will be glorified."<sup>4</sup>But I said, "I have labored in vain; I have spent my strength for nothing and vanity; yet surely my right is with the LORD, and my recompense with my God."<sup>5</sup>And now the LORD says, he who formed me from the womb to be his servant, to bring Jacob back to him; and that Israel might be gathered to him— for I am honored in the eyes of the LORD, and my God has become my strength—<sup>6</sup>he says: "It is too light a thing that you should be my servant to raise up the tribes of Jacob and to bring back the preserved of Israel; I will make you as a light for the nations, that my salvation may reach to the end of the earth."<sup>7</sup>Thus says the LORD, the Redeemer of Israel and his Holy One, to one deeply despised, abhorred by the nation, the servant of rulers: "Kings shall see and arise; princes, and they shall prostrate themselves; because of the LORD, who is faithful, the Holy One of Israel, who has chosen you."<sup>8</sup>Thus says the LORD: "In a time of favor I have answered you; in a day of salvation I have helped you; I will keep you and give you as a covenant to the people, to establish the land, to apportion the desolate heritages,<sup>9</sup>saying to the prisoners, 'Come out,' to those who are in darkness, 'Appear.' They shall feed along the ways; on all bare heights shall be their pasture;<sup>10</sup>they shall not hunger or thirst, neither scorching wind nor sun shall strike them, for he who has pity on them will lead them, and by springs of water will guide them.<sup>11</sup>And I will make all my mountains a road, and my highways shall be raised up.<sup>12</sup>Behold, these shall come from afar, and behold, these from the north and from the west, and these from the land of Syene."<sup>13</sup>Sing for joy, O heavens, and exult, O earth; break forth, O mountains, into singing! For the LORD has comforted his people and will have compassion on his afflicted.<sup>14</sup>But Zion said, "The LORD has forsaken me; my Lord has forgotten me."<sup>15</sup>"Can a woman forget her nursing child, that she should have no compassion on the son of her womb? Even these may forget, yet I will not forget you.<sup>16</sup>Behold, I have engraved you on the palms of my hands; your walls are continually before me.<sup>17</sup>Your builders make haste; your destroyers and those who laid you waste go out from you.<sup>18</sup>Lift up your eyes around and see; they all gather, they come to you. As I live, declares the LORD, you shall put them all on as an ornament; you shall bind them on as a bride does.<sup>19</sup>"Surely your waste and your desolate places and your devastated land— surely now you will be too narrow for your inhabitants, and those who swallowed you up will be far away.<sup>20</sup>The children of your bereavement will yet say in your ears: 'The place is too narrow for me; make room for me to dwell in.'<sup>21</sup>Then you will say in your heart: 'Who has borne me these? I was bereaved and barren, exiled and put away, but who has brought up these? Behold, I was left alone; from where have these come?'"<sup>22</sup>Thus says the Lord GOD: "Behold, I will lift up my hand to the nations, and raise my signal to the peoples; and they shall bring your sons in their arms, and your daughters shall be carried on their shoulders.<sup>23</sup>Kings shall be your foster fathers, and their queens your nursing mothers. With their faces to the ground they shall bow down to you, and lick the dust of your feet. Then you will know that I am the LORD; those who wait for me shall not be put to shame."<sup>24</sup>Can the prey be taken from the mighty, or the captives of a tyrant be rescued?<sup>25</sup>For thus says the LORD: "Even the captives of the mighty shall be taken, and the prey of the tyrant be rescued, for I will contend with those who contend with you, and I will save your children.<sup>26</sup>I will make your oppressors eat their own flesh, and they shall be drunk with their own blood as with wine. Then all flesh shall know that I am the LORD your Savior, and your Redeemer, the Mighty One of Jacob."

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–7 — Called from the Womb, and Sent Further Than He Knew
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The servant tells the far-off nations that God called him before birth, prepared him in hiding, and sends him further than he could have imagined. Formed in the womb and hidden like a sword in the hand or an arrow in a quiver (vv. 1–2), he bears the name Israel (v. 3), yet he confesses that his work seems to have come to nothing and leaves his case with God (v. 4). God answers not by consoling him but by enlarging his commission: restoring Israel is too small, so he will be a light for the nations to the end of the earth (vv. 5–6). The one despised and abhorred will have kings rise and princes bow, because the LORD is faithful (v. 7).
verseByVerse.theology: The song presses the question of who the servant is (see verse 3). Verse 4 adds something the first song did not: this servant experiences the work as failure from the inside, and holds on by entrusting the verdict to God rather than by seeing results.
verseByVerse.examples: Verse 4 has kept more discouraged ministers, parents and missionaries at their posts than almost any other sentence in the prophets.

verseByVerse.quote: Listen to me, O coastlands, and give attention, you peoples from afar. The LORD called me from the womb, from the body of my mother he named my name. He made my mouth like a sharp sword; in the shadow of his hand he hid me; he made me a polished arrow; in his quiver he hid me away.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The servant tells the distant nations that God called him before birth and has kept him hidden, ready like a sharpened weapon, for the moment he is needed.

Listen to me, O coastlands. The servant speaks for himself for the first time, and not to Jerusalem: to the coastlands and distant peoples, the far edge of the map, places that had never heard of the covenant. The song is addressed outward from its opening word.

The LORD called me from the womb. His vocation is older than he is. Jeremiah was told the same (Jer. 1:5), and Paul said it of himself (Gal. 1:15), but both echo a pattern that belongs most fully to one man, whose name was given by an angel to his mother before he was conceived (Luke 1:31).

He made my mouth like a sharp sword. Two weapons, and both are the mouth: the word is the sword and the word is the arrow. The New Testament keeps the image: the word of God sharper than any two-edged sword (Heb. 4:12), and the risen Christ with a sharp two-edged sword coming from his mouth (Rev. 1:16).

In his quiver he hid me away. Both weapons are hidden: a sword in the shadow of a hand, an arrow shut in a quiver. Isaiah spends half the verse on concealment, and it is not failure; it is what you do with a weapon you intend to use. A polished arrow is polished in the dark and kept in the dark until it is wanted.

Hidden, not shelved. That is the honest description of nearly every life God is preparing for something. Jesus’ thirty years in a carpenter’s shop were the shadow of the hand. From the inside it does not feel like being sharpened; it feels like being shelved. But a weapon hidden in God’s hand has not been put aside.
verseByVerse.note: The second Servant Song (vv. 1–6).

verseByVerse.quote: And he said to me, "You are my servant, Israel, in whom I will be glorified."
verseByVerse.commentary:
God gives the servant the name of the nation, Israel, because he will be everything Israel was called to be, and God will show his glory in him.

You are my servant, Israel. Yet two sentences later the same servant is formed to bring Jacob back to him (v. 5). He cannot simply be the nation, because he has a mission to the nation; he cannot simply be a private individual, because he bears the nation’s name.

Who is the servant? Readers have answered in different ways: the nation, a faithful remnant, the prophet himself. The answer the whole book moves toward is fuller. Israel was called to be God’s son, servant and light, and failed at all three (ch. 42). So one comes who is everything Israel was meant to be, carrying the name and keeping the calling, and then does for Israel what Israel could not do for itself.

Why this matters. Everything the New Testament says about being in Christ rests on this. A believer is saved not by becoming a better Israelite but by being joined to the one who wears the name and kept the covenant, so that what is true of him becomes true of those joined to him.

In whom I will be glorified. God’s first purpose is to show his glory in this person, and rescuing his people is how he shows it.

verseByVerse.quote: But I said, "I have labored in vain; I have spent my strength for nothing and vanity; yet surely my right is with the LORD, and my recompense with my God."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The servant honestly confesses that his work seems wasted, and leaves the verdict with God.

I have labored in vain. The chosen servant, in the middle of his own song, says that the work has come to nothing. Not that it was hard or slow: in vain, empty, nothing in the hand at the end of the day.

The faithful worker’s view. Anyone who has taught the same child the same thing for eleven years, or prayed for a marriage that got worse, or preached faithfully in a place that emptied, knows that sentence. It is not unbelief. It is what a faithful worker honestly sees.

Yet surely my right is with the LORD. Then the turn, which is the whole art of persevering. He does not talk himself out of the assessment or invent a hidden fruitfulness. He moves the verdict to a different court. My right, my case, is with the LORD: lodged with someone who holds it, and it will be given. The believer who copies him does it not by gritting his teeth but by resting on the same faithful God.

The tyranny of impact. Our age wants every life to make a measurable difference. But when the worth of a life is read off its visible results, most faithful lives look like failures: the carer whose patient never improves, the teacher whose pupils forget her, the parent whose child walks away. By that measure Jesus’ own life ended in disaster, with a handful of followers who had all run. The servant’s release is ours too (see the note on Ecclesiastes 2:24–26). Faithfulness is not the same as visible fruit, and only God can see which seeds are in the ground. The servant who said I have labored in vain became a light for the nations. The measure of a life is not what can be counted at its end but whose hands it was placed in.

verseByVerse.quote: And now the LORD says, he who formed me from the womb to be his servant, to bring Jacob back to him; and that Israel might be gathered to him— for I am honored in the eyes of the LORD, and my God has become my strength— he says: "It is too light a thing that you should be my servant to raise up the tribes of Jacob and to bring back the preserved of Israel; I will make you as a light for the nations, that my salvation may reach to the end of the earth."
verseByVerse.commentary:
God answers the discouraged servant by telling him he is honoured and that restoring Israel is too small a task: he will bring God’s salvation to the end of the earth.

I am honored in the eyes of the LORD. Before the commission is enlarged, the servant is told what he already is. The man who has just said he laboured for nothing is honoured in the only eyes that finally assess anything. That does not deny what he has been through; it tells him whose verdict counts.

It is too light a thing. God does not say the labour was fruitful after all or explain the apparent failure. He says the job is too small. Restoring a whole nation from exile, the very thing the servant believes he has failed at, is too light a thing, a load not worth his strength. So it is enlarged. Not Israel only, but the nations; not only the return, but salvation to the end of the earth.

God’s answer to futility. That is God’s characteristic answer to the sense of futility, worth remembering by anyone ready to give something up: he rarely shrinks the assignment to fit our discouragement. Paul and Barnabas, opposed in the synagogue at Pisidian Antioch, took this verse as theirs and turned to the Gentiles with it in their mouths (Acts 13:47). What was said to Christ became the marching orders of the church sent out in his name.

That my salvation may reach to the end of the earth. The reach is total: not many nations, not most, but the end of the earth. In a book for a small people pinned between empires it was the most implausible sentence available, and it has been fulfilled in front of everybody for two thousand years. Simeon, holding a forty-day-old child in the temple, took this verse’s words for him: “a light for revelation to the Gentiles” (Luke 2:32).

How Jewish readers take it. Because verse 3 calls the servant Israel, Jewish interpreters usually read the passage of the nation, or of the prophet speaking for it, and treasure verse 6 as Israel’s calling to bring knowledge of the one God to the end of the earth. Christians can gladly affirm that calling; the church’s mission begins in Israel’s Scriptures. This commentary reads the servant as the one who carries Israel’s name and also restores Israel (v. 5), as noted at verse 3: Simeon saw that light in the infant Jesus (Luke 2:32), and Paul carried it to the Gentiles (Acts 13:47).

verseByVerse.quote: Thus says the LORD, the Redeemer of Israel and his Holy One, to one deeply despised, abhorred by the nation, the servant of rulers: "Kings shall see and arise; princes, and they shall prostrate themselves; because of the LORD, who is faithful, the Holy One of Israel, who has chosen you."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The servant despised by his own people and at the mercy of rulers will one day have kings bow before him, because God is faithful and has chosen him.

One deeply despised. Three descriptions, each worse than the last: deeply despised; abhorred by the nation, his own people; the servant of rulers, at the disposal of whoever holds power. Every one came true. He came to his own and they did not receive him, and in one morning he was passed between the Jewish council, the Roman governor Pilate and Herod.

Kings shall see and arise. The reversal is in the same sentence. The kind of men before whom he stood as a prisoner will rise and then go down on their faces. They see; nothing has to be argued to them. What overturns their judgment is the sight of him.

Because of the LORD, who is faithful. The reversal does not rest on the servant earning his way back up or on public opinion coming round. God is faithful and God chose him, and those two facts are enough.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 8–13 — The Day of Salvation and the Road Home
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God answers the servant with a day of salvation, and it becomes a homecoming for captives from every direction. In a time of favour God has heard him and made him a covenant for the people, to resettle the ruined land and tell prisoners to come out (vv. 8–9). The road home through the desert is safe, because the one who has pity on them leads them, and the mountains themselves become the highway (vv. 10–11). They come from far away, from north and west and the far south (v. 12), and heaven, earth and mountains are called to sing, because the LORD has comforted his people (v. 13).
verseByVerse.theology: The comfort does not depend on conditions improving. It rests on a day God has fixed and on a servant who is himself the covenant: in him God binds himself to his people.
verseByVerse.examples: The road home in Isaiah 49 and the arrival in Revelation 7 are the same journey (Rev. 7:16-17), and the church walks it between the two: Paul tells the Corinthians that the day of salvation has already dawned (2 Cor. 6:2).

verseByVerse.quote: Thus says the LORD: "In a time of favor I have answered you; in a day of salvation I have helped you; I will keep you and give you as a covenant to the people, to establish the land, to apportion the desolate heritages, saying to the prisoners, 'Come out,' to those who are in darkness, 'Appear.' They shall feed along the ways; on all bare heights shall be their pasture;
verseByVerse.commentary:
God has answered the servant in a day of salvation, made him the covenant for his people, and sends him to set captives free and bring them home.

In a time of favor I have answered you. The servant left his right with the LORD (v. 4), and here is the answer, with a time attached, spoken as already done though nothing can yet be seen. Paul quotes it and adds, “now is the day of salvation” (2 Cor. 6:2): the time of favour has begun, and his readers are living in it.

A covenant to the people. The title from the first song returns: he does not merely deliver the covenant, he is it (42:6). The work attached is oddly practical, parcelling out ruined inheritances like a surveyor after a war. Salvation in Isaiah ends with people back on their own ground.

Freedom by command. One short command to the prisoners, Come out, with no ransom named at the door, no conditions read out and no interview. It is the same voice that would one day stand outside a tomb in Bethany and call Lazarus out (John 11:43). That authority is why the gospel is an announcement of freedom, not a bargain to be negotiated.

verseByVerse.quote: they shall not hunger or thirst, neither scorching wind nor sun shall strike them, for he who has pity on them will lead them, and by springs of water will guide them. And I will make all my mountains a road, and my highways shall be raised up.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The road home is safe because the God who pities his people leads them himself, and he turns the very mountains into a highway.

He who has pity on them will lead them. The road home runs through desert, and Isaiah names four things that kill people on it, hunger, thirst, wind and sun, and rules out all four. The reason is a person, and the word for his pity is the word for a mother’s compassion that verse 15 will use. What gets them across is not their supplies but the character of the one walking in front.

The end of the journey. At the end of the Bible the promise returns almost word for word, said of a crowd from every nation that no one could number, whom the Lamb will shepherd to springs of living water (Rev. 7:16–17). John is not borrowing a nice phrase; he is reporting the arrival of this journey.

I will make all my mountains a road. The mountains are not gone round; they become the road. That is not a general rule about adversity, but it is exactly what God did with the cross, the worst thing that ever happened, and anyone who has looked back at a hard year and found it was the road has tasted this verse.

verseByVerse.quote: Behold, these shall come from afar, and behold, these from the north and from the west, and these from the land of Syene." Sing for joy, O heavens, and exult, O earth; break forth, O mountains, into singing! For the LORD has comforted his people and will have compassion on his afflicted.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God’s people will stream home from every direction, and all creation is called to sing because the LORD has comforted his afflicted.

These shall come from afar. Twice behold, as though the prophet stood on a rise pointing at different horizons as the columns appear: from far away, from the north and the west, and from Syene, Aswan, on the southern frontier of Egypt, the far end of the known world in that direction.

Bigger than the return. What is described is bigger than the return from Babylon, and deliberately so. The exiles came home from one direction; this is a homecoming from every direction there is. The New Testament describes the final gathering the same way: people from east and west and north and south reclining at table in the kingdom of God (Luke 13:29).

Sing for joy, O heavens. When the subject is too large for human voices, Isaiah tells the sky, the ground and the hills to make the noise. And the reason given is not the scale of the rescue or the defeat of the enemy but one word, comforted, and one more: he will have compassion on his afflicted. The universe is called to sing because God has been tender with hurt people, and that tells you a great deal about the God being sung to.

Uncertain wording. The traditional Hebrew text reads the land of Sinim, a name found nowhere else; older readers sometimes guessed China. Some ancient copies, and most modern translations including the ESV, read Syene, the city at Egypt’s southern border, which fits the list of far-off directions well. Either way the point is the farthest reaches.
verseByVerse.note: “Syene” (Aswan, in southern Egypt) follows a Dead Sea Scroll; the Masoretic Text reads “Sinim” (ESV note).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 14–26 — The Mother Who Cannot Forget
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God answers Zion’s fear that she has been forgotten, not with rebuke but with promises she can see and feel. A nursing mother may forget her child, yet God will not, and he has engraved Zion on the palms of his hands (vv. 14–16). Builders hurry in as destroyers leave, and the bereaved city will be bewildered to find herself crowded with children (vv. 17–21). The nations will carry her sons and daughters home, kings serving as foster fathers, so that she knows that those who wait for the LORD will not be put to shame (vv. 22–23). Even the prey of a tyrant will be taken back, because God himself will contend for his people (vv. 24–26).
verseByVerse.theology: God’s faithfulness is more than a kind feeling. It is a commitment that cost him something: her name is engraved, not written. What is cut into a hand cannot be removed without injury. Zion's fear is not answered by an argument that she is lovable; it is answered by a mark on God.
verseByVerse.examples: Verse 15 is one of the places Scripture reaches for a mother rather than a father to say what God is like, at the exact point where the reader most needs it.

verseByVerse.quote: But Zion said, "The LORD has forsaken me; my Lord has forgotten me."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Even surrounded by songs of God’s comfort, Zion says that God has forsaken and forgotten her, and God takes the complaint seriously enough to answer it.

But Zion said. The heavens, the earth and the mountains have just been told to sing, and in the very next sentence one voice cuts across all of it and says that God has gone.

How faith actually works. Isaiah places it there deliberately, and the placement is a kindness. It is one of the most accurate things in Scripture about how faith works. It is possible to know that God is good, to be surrounded by people singing that he is good, and to be unable to feel that any of it applies to you. Praise and despair stand in neighbouring verses because in real lives they come minutes apart.

My Lord has forgotten me. Read the two verbs. Forsaken: he has left. Forgotten: worse, he did not even leave on purpose; I simply went out of his mind. The second does the real damage, because it does not even grant her the dignity of being rejected.

No word of reproach. Now watch what God does not do. He does not rebuke her or correct her theology, though it is wrong. He does not point out that he has just spent thirteen verses promising the opposite. There is not a word of reproach in the answer that follows. God takes the complaint seriously enough to answer it, and that is the first thing anyone in that condition needs to know about him.

verseByVerse.quote: "Can a woman forget her nursing child, that she should have no compassion on the son of her womb? Even these may forget, yet I will not forget you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God’s love for his people is more faithful than the strongest human love there is, a nursing mother’s for her baby.

A mother and her infant. The answer to feeling forgotten is a question about a mother, and God picks the strongest attachment in human experience. Not a mother and a grown son, but a nursing mother and the infant at her breast: a bond that is physical as well as emotional, where her own body will remind her if she forgets and the child’s life depends hour by hour on her attention.

Even these may forget. The expected answer is no, and God does not give it. He concedes the point. Sometimes she does forget: through illness, poverty, the collapse of a mind, the thousand ways human beings fail at the things they would die for. God says so plainly rather than building his comfort on a sentimental picture of motherhood that would fall apart the moment someone’s own mother came to mind.

Past the highest love. He takes the highest human love, grants that it can fail, and puts himself past it; the argument is stronger for the concession. And note where God is willing to be found. He does not reach for a king, a general or a judge to say what his commitment is like. He reaches for a woman feeding a baby, and then says he is more constant than she is.

verseByVerse.quote: Behold, I have engraved you on the palms of my hands; your walls are continually before me.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God answers the fear of being forgotten by holding out his hands: he has cut his people’s name into his own palms and keeps their future always before him.

I have engraved you. God’s final answer is not an argument but a gesture: he holds out his hands. Not written but engraved, cut in. Writing can be washed off a hand at the end of a day; this is a mark made by a blade, which does not come off because the hand has been altered to carry it. God has done something permanent to himself to make forgetting impossible.

On the palms of my hands. Not on a wall in heaven, not in a book or on a list, but on the palms: the working surface of a hand. Every act of God in history is done by hands with his people’s names cut into them. He cannot lift a finger without the names moving.

Your walls are continually before me. She is looking at rubble; God says her walls are always in his sight. He is not looking at the ruin but at the finished city, and has been all along.

The marks in his hands. Centuries later a man will stand in a locked room and hold out his hands to someone who cannot believe he is there, and the marks in them will settle it (John 20:27). The New Testament does not quote this verse there, but many Christians have heard it in that room: the palms of Isaiah 49 became more literal than anyone in exile could have guessed. He has our names cut into his hands, and the cutting was done on the cross.

verseByVerse.quote: Your builders make haste; your destroyers and those who laid you waste go out from you. Lift up your eyes around and see; they all gather, they come to you. As I live, declares the LORD, you shall put them all on as an ornament; you shall bind them on as a bride does.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The ruin is already giving way to rebuilding, and Zion’s returning children will be her bridal ornaments; God swears it by his own life.

Your builders make haste. The two crews pass each other in the gate: the destroyers are still leaving as the masons hurry in. She is looking at a ruin, and he describes a building site. That is not optimism about the rubble; it is a future made certain and reported as present, which is how prophets speak.

Lift up your eyes around and see. Zion has been looking down, at the stones and at herself. She is told to look at the horizon, where people are already coming.

As I live, declares the LORD. Then the oath: God swearing by his own existence, the strongest undertaking there is, since there is nothing greater to swear by. The pledge that her children are coming home is secured on the fact that God is alive.

You shall bind them on as a bride does. The image is unexpectedly warm. The returning exiles are not counted as a population or a workforce but as jewellery, put on as a bride puts on her ornaments on her wedding morning, for delight. The woman who thought she was forgotten is being dressed.

Uncertain wording. The Hebrew letters behind your builders can also be read your sons, as older translations have it. The ESV’s reading pairs builders with destroyers; the other anticipates the children of verses 20 to 22. Both say the same thing: the ruin is being reversed.

verseByVerse.quote: "Surely your waste and your desolate places and your devastated land— surely now you will be too narrow for your inhabitants, and those who swallowed you up will be far away. The children of your bereavement will yet say in your ears: 'The place is too narrow for me; make room for me to dwell in.' Then you will say in your heart: 'Who has borne me these? I was bereaved and barren, exiled and put away, but who has brought up these? Behold, I was left alone; from where have these come?'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The empty, bereaved city will be so crowded with children that she will be astonished, unable to explain where they have come from.

Too narrow for your inhabitants. The reversal is pressed until it becomes almost funny: the city’s complaint has been emptiness, and it will be overcrowding, the sound of a household outgrowing its house.

Who has borne me these? Her question is the sound of grace arriving in a quantity nobody asked for. She is not grateful yet; she is bewildered. She counts the children and cannot make the arithmetic work, because she knows exactly what she had, which was nothing, and here is a crowd calling her mother.

Bereaved and barren, exiled and put away. Read the four terms slowly. She had lost children, could have no more, had been removed from her land, and had been sent away like a divorced wife. There was no natural road from that condition to this one, so she is right to be astonished. Anyone who has been given more than his life had any capacity to produce will recognise it. The New Testament hears the same note when Paul applies Isaiah’s barren woman to the church born of promise (Galatians 4:27, quoting 54:1).

verseByVerse.quote: Thus says the Lord GOD: "Behold, I will lift up my hand to the nations, and raise my signal to the peoples; and they shall bring your sons in their arms, and your daughters shall be carried on their shoulders. Kings shall be your foster fathers, and their queens your nursing mothers. With their faces to the ground they shall bow down to you, and lick the dust of your feet. Then you will know that I am the LORD; those who wait for me shall not be put to shame."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The nations that carried Israel away will carry her children home with tender care, kings will acknowledge Zion’s God, and those who wait for the LORD will never be put to shame.

They shall bring your sons in their arms. The answer to from where have these come? is that the nations are bringing them. The empires that carried Israel away will carry Israel’s children back, and the detail is domestic rather than political: sons in the arms, daughters on the shoulders, the way an adult carries a tired child the last mile.

Kings shall be your foster fathers. The powers that treated her as a resource become her household staff, and not distant patrons but foster fathers and nursing mothers, the people who get up in the night. Isaiah keeps choosing images of physical care rather than political triumph, because tender care is the point.

With their faces to the ground. Bowing and licking the dust of your feet is the vassal’s posture of homage in the ancient Near East, the way subject kings were shown prostrate before an Assyrian overlord (compare Psalm 72:9). It describes kings acknowledging that God is with this people, which is why the next line is then you will know that I am the LORD.

Those who wait for me shall not be put to shame. This is the line to hold. Waiting is what Zion has been doing badly and complaining about, and God does not promise it will be short. He promises what it will not end in. Shame is the particular fear of everyone who has staked a life on God and watched nothing happen: not that God will punish them, but that they will look foolish, that the whole thing will turn out to have been a misplaced confidence held in public. This sentence closes that fear. Nobody who waited will be embarrassed at the end.

Where Christians differ. Dispensational readers expect Gentile rulers to serve a restored national Israel in a coming age, and take kings as foster fathers and queens as nursing mothers in that way.

This commentary’s view. Zion is the people of God, gathered in Christ from the nations, because the New Testament applies Zion’s promises to the church (Galatians 4:26; Hebrews 12:22), and the homage of kings is the nations bowing to Christ and serving his church (60:3; Rev. 21:24). Faithful Christians differ over Israel’s future, and many who read this verse of the church still expect a great turning of Jewish people to Christ (Romans 11:25–26).

verseByVerse.quote: Can the prey be taken from the mighty, or the captives of a tyrant be rescued? For thus says the LORD: "Even the captives of the mighty shall be taken, and the prey of the tyrant be rescued, for I will contend with those who contend with you, and I will save your children. I will make your oppressors eat their own flesh, and they shall be drunk with their own blood as with wine. Then all flesh shall know that I am the LORD your Savior, and your Redeemer, the Mighty One of Jacob."
verseByVerse.commentary:
No tyrant is strong enough to keep God’s people captive, because God himself will fight for them and rescue their children, and all flesh will know that he is their Saviour.

The last objection. Zion raises the practical one. Everything promised has assumed that the people can be got back. But predators do not give up their prey, and tyrants do not release the men they hold. Anyone who has watched an addiction, a regime or a death hold onto somebody has asked it.

I will contend with those who contend with you. God does not soften the question. He agrees that nobody takes prey from the strong, then says that this is precisely what he will do, and in person. Not send help, not raise up a deliverer: he steps into the dispute himself and makes his people’s opponents his own. Jesus used the same picture of himself: no one can plunder a strong man’s house unless he first binds the strong man (Mark 3:27).

Violence turned back. Verse 26 is deliberately hard to read: the oppressors made to eat their own flesh and drink their own blood as wine. It is the Old Testament’s way of saying that violence turns back on the violent; the machinery they built to consume others finishes by consuming them.

The Mighty One of Jacob. The chapter began with a servant who thought he had laboured for nothing, and it ends with all flesh knowing who God is. Between those points nothing changed except that God kept going. He is the Redeemer, the near kinsman with the right to buy his relatives out of slavery, and the Mighty One of Jacob, the title Jacob himself used when he blessed his sons (Gen. 49:24). And the hands that pay the price have the names cut into them.

Textual note. In verse 24 the traditional Hebrew text reads the captives of a righteous one; some ancient copies and versions read a tyrant, matching verse 25, and the ESV follows them. The question is the same either way: can a lawful or powerful captor be made to let go?

49.theology:
The servant who is Israel and is sent to Israel. Verse 3 calls him Israel; verse 5 sends him to bring Jacob back. He is the true Israel, wearing the name and keeping the covenant, and everything the New Testament means by being in Christ rests on this: a believer is saved by being joined to the one who kept it all.

Futility answered by enlargement. The servant’s confession in verse 4 is an honest report, not unbelief, and God’s reply neither disputes it nor shrinks the assignment. It doubles it. This is the standing pattern of God’s dealing with discouraged servants.

Assurance with a body. Zion’s fear in verse 14 is answered in three movements: a comparison she can feel (v. 15), a mark she can look at (v. 16), and a promise about waiting (v. 23). The middle one is the ground of the other two: God has marked his own hands so that he cannot forget her.

54.subtitle: Sing, O Barren One
54.intro:
Where we are. Chapter 53 left the servant cut off out of the land of the living, childless, and yet promised that “he shall see his offspring” (53:10). Chapter 54 follows at once with a childless woman told to sing. What the servant suffered for, his people now inherit.

The message. God takes back the people he had set aside, not grudgingly but as a husband reclaiming the wife of his youth. His anger lasted a moment; his love is everlasting, sworn with an oath as sure as his promise after the flood. He will rebuild his people as a city of jewels, teach all their children himself, and see that no weapon raised against them finally succeeds.

Why it was said. Zion lay in ruins, emptied of her people, and the exiles feared that the covenant itself was over, that God, like a husband who had walked out, was gone for good (49:14; see the introduction). The chapter answers that fear.

How the chapter makes its case. A barren woman is told to sing and to enlarge her tent (vv. 1–3). Her Maker is her husband, and he calls her back (vv. 4–6). The desertion was a brief moment; the compassion is everlasting (vv. 7–8), sworn like the oath to Noah and firmer than the mountains (vv. 9–10). Then the ruined city is rebuilt in precious stones, with all its children taught by the LORD (vv. 11–13), and its people are established in righteousness, safe from every weapon (vv. 14–17).

Where it leads. The chapter leads to Christ by promise and covenant, and its placing is the argument: the barren woman’s children are the servant’s offspring, and the covenant of peace rests on “the chastisement that brought us peace” (53:5). Paul applies verse 1 to the church, the children of promise gathered from every nation (Gal. 4:26–28); Jesus quotes verse 13 to explain why anyone comes to him (John 6:45); and John sees the bride of the Lamb as a city with foundations of precious stones (Rev. 21:9–21). The husband who will not let his people go is Christ, who loved the church and gave himself up for her (Eph. 5:25).

For us. If God seems absent, this chapter does not tell you to pretend; it sets the moment inside everlasting love. If you are ashamed of your past, your Redeemer will not bring it up again. And because he means to fill his house, make room, in your plans, your church and your prayers, for the children still to come.

keyVerse.quote: “For the mountains may depart and the hills be removed, but my steadfast love shall not depart from you, and my covenant of peace shall not be removed, says the LORD, who has compassion on you.”
keyVerse.note: The stability of the mountains is the benchmark for everything we think permanent, and God sets his love above it: mountains will move before his love departs. This answers the shadow of chapter 39 and every experience of God’s seeming absence. The absence was a moment; the love is permanent, and the covenant of peace was sealed by the servant who bore the chastisement that brought us peace (53:5).

54.reflection:
The chapter tells a barren woman to “enlarge the place of your tent” before any children have come (vv. 1–2). What would it look like for your church, or your household, to make room now for people God has not yet brought?

God calls the exile a “brief moment” set against “everlasting love” (vv. 7–8), without pretending it did not hurt. How does that help you think about a season when God seemed absent, whether your own or a friend’s?

God says that “the mountains may depart” before his steadfast love will (v. 10). How does the cross, where the servant bore “the chastisement that brought us peace” (53:5), make that covenant of peace certain for you?

Verse 17 promises that “no weapon that is fashioned against you shall succeed,” yet verse 16 says God made the smith. How is this different from a promise of an easy life, and how should it shape the way you face opposition?
54.text: <sup>1</sup>"Sing, O barren one, who did not bear; break forth into singing and cry aloud, you who have not been in labor! For the children of the desolate one will be more than the children of her who is married," says the LORD.<sup>2</sup>"Enlarge the place of your tent, and let the curtains of your habitations be stretched out; do not hold back; lengthen your cords and strengthen your stakes.<sup>3</sup>For you will spread abroad to the right and to the left, and your offspring will possess the nations and will people the desolate cities.<sup>4</sup>"Fear not, for you will not be ashamed; be not confounded, for you will not be disgraced; for you will forget the shame of your youth, and the reproach of your widowhood you will remember no more.<sup>5</sup>For your Maker is your husband, the LORD of hosts is his name; and the Holy One of Israel is your Redeemer, the God of the whole earth he is called.<sup>6</sup>For the LORD has called you like a wife deserted and grieved in spirit, like a wife of youth when she is cast off, says your God.<sup>7</sup>For a brief moment I deserted you, but with great compassion I will gather you.<sup>8</sup>In overflowing anger for a moment I hid my face from you, but with everlasting love I will have compassion on you," says the LORD, your Redeemer.<sup>9</sup>"This is like the days of Noah to me: as I swore that the waters of Noah should no more go over the earth, so I have sworn that I will not be angry with you, and will not rebuke you.<sup>10</sup>For the mountains may depart and the hills be removed, but my steadfast love shall not depart from you, and my covenant of peace shall not be removed," says the LORD, who has compassion on you.<sup>11</sup>"O afflicted one, storm-tossed and not comforted, behold, I will set your stones in antimony, and lay your foundations with sapphires.<sup>12</sup>I will make your pinnacles of agate, your gates of carbuncles, and all your wall of precious stones.<sup>13</sup>All your children shall be taught by the LORD, and great shall be the peace of your children.<sup>14</sup>In righteousness you shall be established; you shall be far from oppression, for you shall not fear; and from terror, for it shall not come near you.<sup>15</sup>If anyone stirs up strife, it is not from me; whoever stirs up strife with you shall fall because of you.<sup>16</sup>Behold, I have created the smith who blows the fire of coals and produces a weapon for its purpose. I have also created the ravager to destroy;<sup>17</sup>no weapon that is fashioned against you shall succeed, and you shall refute every tongue that rises against you in judgment. This is the heritage of the servants of the LORD and their vindication from me, declares the LORD."

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Because the servant has borne sin and been promised offspring, God’s desolate people are called to sing. A childless woman is told to break into song and to enlarge her tent for a family she does not yet have (vv. 1–3). Her shame and widowhood are cancelled, because her Maker is her husband and the Holy One of Israel her Redeemer (vv. 4–6). The desertion was real but brief, set against great compassion and everlasting love (vv. 7–8), and God binds himself with an oath like the one he swore to Noah, firmer than the mountains (vv. 9–10). The section moves from a broken home to an unbreakable covenant.
verseByVerse.theology: Chapter 54 is what chapter 53 produced: the Servant has just been cut off with no offspring, and the first thing that follows is a barren woman told to sing.
verseByVerse.examples: The chapter moves from a tent (v. 2) to a city (vv. 11-12). God's people begin as a household enlarged by faith and end as a city built of jewels.

verseByVerse.quote: "Sing, O barren one, who did not bear; break forth into singing and cry aloud, you who have not been in labor! For the children of the desolate one will be more than the children of her who is married," says the LORD. "Enlarge the place of your tent, and let the curtains of your habitations be stretched out; do not hold back; lengthen your cords and strengthen your stakes. For you will spread abroad to the right and to the left, and your offspring will possess the nations and will people the desolate cities.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Because of the servant’s work, desolate Zion, pictured as a childless woman, is told to sing and to make room for a family larger than she can imagine.

Sing, O barren one. The command is cruel until you notice where it stands. A woman who cannot have children is told to sing, straight after a man was cut off out of the land of the living, with no children, and promised that he would see his offspring anyway (53:8, 10). Chapter 54 is what chapter 53 produced.

Who did not bear. Childlessness in that world was public, often assumed to be a verdict, and left a woman without protection in old age. Isaiah takes the person with the least reason to sing and gives her the solo. For the first readers the woman is Zion herself, Jerusalem emptied by Babylon, her children killed or carried off, sitting like a widow with no one left (49:20–21; Lam. 1:1). And Israel’s story had begun with such a woman: Sarah was barren (Gen. 11:30), and Isaiah has just told the exiles to look to Abraham their father and to Sarah who bore them (51:2).

The children of the desolate one. Paul quotes this verse and says the barren woman stands for the people of God’s promise, whose children are born not by natural descent but through what God promised (Gal. 4:26–28). Everyone who has come to Christ from outside the family is one of the children being counted here.

Enlarge the place of your tent. Then the instructions get practical, and wonderfully premature: more canvas, longer ropes, deeper pegs, all for a woman who has not yet had one child. That is what faith looks like in ordinary hands: not a feeling about the future but arrangements made for it, extra chairs put out for people who have not arrived, on the strength of what God has said. William Carey’s sermon on these verses in 1792 helped to launch the modern missionary movement.

What it does not promise. To anyone reading this beside an empty nursery: the verse does not promise that every childless believer will bear children, and it does not hint that childlessness is a judgment. It promises a family God is building in Christ, where no one of his is without a household, and where many a childless saint has more sons and daughters in the faith than she can count (Mark 10:29–30).

verseByVerse.quote: "Fear not, for you will not be ashamed; be not confounded, for you will not be disgraced; for you will forget the shame of your youth, and the reproach of your widowhood you will remember no more. For your Maker is your husband, the LORD of hosts is his name; and the Holy One of Israel is your Redeemer, the God of the whole earth he is called. For the LORD has called you like a wife deserted and grieved in spirit, like a wife of youth when she is cast off, says your God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God’s people need fear shame no longer, because the Creator himself is their husband and Redeemer, and he calls the deserted wife back to himself.

The shame of your youth. Two griefs are named, at the two ends of a life. The shame of her youth is what went wrong early, the thing done or suffered before she knew better; the reproach of her widowhood is the loss that came late and left her exposed and pitied. God says both will be forgotten, which is more than being forgiven for them: forgiven means the account is settled; forgotten means the subject stops coming up.

Your Maker is your husband. Six titles in one verse, and the first is the one nobody would have dared write. Isaiah has spent fifty chapters insisting on the distance between the Holy One and everybody else, and here that same God takes the most intimate and binding relationship a human being can enter and says it is his. Hosea had used the same picture of God winning back his unfaithful people (Hos. 2:16–20).

Like a wife deserted and grieved in spirit. Not a bride at her wedding but a woman who was left: deserted, grieved in spirit, cast off when she was young. He does not call her back as though nothing had happened. He calls her by exactly what has happened to her, and calls her anyway.

Who the wife is. The wife is God’s covenant people, as the church is the bride Christ loved and gave himself up for (Eph. 5:25–27), so the verse is first a word to the whole people. But it is rich comfort for the single, widowed or abandoned believer: no one in Christ is unloved or unprotected, for the Maker of the universe has bound himself to them.

verseByVerse.quote: For a brief moment I deserted you, but with great compassion I will gather you. In overflowing anger for a moment I hid my face from you, but with everlasting love I will have compassion on you," says the LORD, your Redeemer.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God’s anger and absence were real but brief; his compassion and love are everlasting.

For a brief moment I deserted you. The two halves of each sentence are not the same size, and that is the whole point: a brief moment against great compassion, a moment of hidden face against everlasting love.

In overflowing anger for a moment I hid my face. Nothing is denied. The desertion was real; the anger was real and is called overflowing; the face was genuinely hidden. God does not tell them they imagined it, and any comfort that requires a sufferer to pretend nothing happened is not this one. What he does is put it in proportion. The exile ran for the better part of seventy years, Jeremiah’s figure (Jer. 25:11), long enough for a generation to be born and buried inside it, and God calls it a moment: not minimising those years, but showing what they are measured against.

With everlasting love. Many believers pass through a season in which God seems to have gone quiet, and the fear underneath is that the quiet is the truth and the promises were the exception. This verse says the opposite: the silence is the brief moment; the love is everlasting. At the cross the Son himself cried out under the hidden face of God (Matt. 27:46), so that for those who belong to him the hiding is never the last word.

Paul’s arithmetic. Paul learned to count this way. Beaten, shipwrecked and imprisoned, he calls the whole of it this light momentary affliction, preparing an eternal weight of glory beyond all comparison (2 Cor. 4:17). Nothing in that sentence denies that the whip hurt.

What it does not mean. This is no picture of a husband’s temper to be copied or endured: God’s anger was just, and his return costs him everything. No wife should read here a reason to stay under a man’s cruelty; anyone being abused should seek safety at once.

verseByVerse.quote: "This is like the days of Noah to me: as I swore that the waters of Noah should no more go over the earth, so I have sworn that I will not be angry with you, and will not rebuke you. For the mountains may depart and the hills be removed, but my steadfast love shall not depart from you, and my covenant of peace shall not be removed," says the LORD, who has compassion on you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God has bound his love to his people by an oath as sure as his promise after the flood, firmer than the mountains themselves.

This is like the days of Noah to me. God reaches for one of the oldest covenant oaths in the Bible. He had sworn once before that a particular judgment would never be repeated, and tied the oath to something visible in the sky, the rainbow (Gen. 9:13–15). The waters have not come back for as long as anybody has been counting, and God says his love for this people rests on an oath of the same kind.

For the mountains may depart. The mountains are what people mean when they say something is immovable: not built, not maintained, simply there before anyone arrived and there after they have gone. Isaiah says they will walk off before the love does.

My steadfast love… my covenant of peace. Steadfast love is covenant loyalty, the settled commitment of one who has bound himself by promise; the covenant of peace guarantees not merely an end of hostilities but wholeness restored. That peace was bought by the servant, on whom was “the chastisement that brought us peace” (53:5). The Holy One of Israel has fixed his loyalty to a people who broke every term of the arrangement, and staked his own oath on never withdrawing it. The hills are the temporary things in that sentence.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God turns from the restored wife to the rebuilt city, and promises it beauty, teaching and safety. He names her condition first, afflicted, storm-tossed and not comforted, and then promises foundations of sapphires and gates and walls of precious stones (vv. 11–12). Better than the stones, all her children will be taught by the LORD and know great peace (v. 13). Established in righteousness, she need not fear (v. 14): attacks will come, but God made the smith who makes the weapons, and none will finally succeed (vv. 15–17). This is the heritage of the servants of the LORD, the offspring of the one Servant.
verseByVerse.theology: The promise in verse 17 is precisely limited and should be read as it stands: the conflict is not removed; the outcome is guaranteed.
verseByVerse.examples: No weapon that is fashioned against you shall succeed is regularly quoted as a promise of a quiet life, and the verse before it forbids that reading: God says he created the smith who makes the weapon.

verseByVerse.quote: "O afflicted one, storm-tossed and not comforted, behold, I will set your stones in antimony, and lay your foundations with sapphires. I will make your pinnacles of agate, your gates of carbuncles, and all your wall of precious stones. All your children shall be taught by the LORD, and great shall be the peace of your children.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God promises to rebuild his battered people as a city of precious stones and, better still, to teach all its children himself, so that their peace will be great.

O afflicted one, storm-tossed and not comforted. Before he promises anything, God names her condition, and the hardest phrase is not comforted. This part of Isaiah began with comfort at chapter 40, and fourteen chapters later God says the comfort has not yet reached her. He is honest about his own timetable before he adds to it.

I will set your stones in antimony. The rebuilding is described by a jeweller. Antimony was the dark paste women used around the eyes, here the setting that makes a stone stand out; then sapphire, agate, carbuncle, every stone precious. And the jewels go not into the treasury but into the foundations, which nobody sees, and the gates, which everybody walks through. John sees the same city, the bride of the Lamb, with foundations adorned with every kind of jewel and gates of pearl (Rev. 21:9–21).

All your children shall be taught by the LORD. The best promise in the passage has nothing to do with stone: every child taught by God himself, not at second hand. Jesus quotes it when he explains why anyone comes to him at all: it is written in the Prophets, ‘And they will all be taught by God’ (John 6:45). That teaching is now the work of the Spirit, given to every believer to lead them into the truth (John 16:13).

Uncertain wording. Several of these stones cannot be identified with certainty. Antimony renders a word for eye paint, used here of the setting or mortar; the words for agate and carbuncles are rare (other translations give rubies and sparkling jewels); and pinnacles is literally suns, perhaps battlements that catch the light. The picture is clear even where the stones are not: a city of dazzling, costly beauty.

verseByVerse.quote: In righteousness you shall be established; you shall be far from oppression, for you shall not fear; and from terror, for it shall not come near you. If anyone stirs up strife, it is not from me; whoever stirs up strife with you shall fall because of you. Behold, I have created the smith who blows the fire of coals and produces a weapon for its purpose. I have also created the ravager to destroy; no weapon that is fashioned against you shall succeed, and you shall refute every tongue that rises against you in judgment. This is the heritage of the servants of the LORD and their vindication from me, declares the LORD."
verseByVerse.commentary:
God’s people stand secure on his righteousness: attacks will come, but none will finally succeed, because God rules even the makers of weapons and he himself vindicates his servants.

In righteousness you shall be established. The foundation is righteousness, and being established on it is what puts fear at a distance. Isaiah is not promising a city that cannot be attacked; he is describing a people no longer ruled by the fear of attack.

I have created the smith. God does not claim the weapons do not exist. He says he made the blacksmith. The forge, the blade and the man who will carry it are all under the rule of the God who made the promise.

No weapon that is fashioned against you shall succeed. Weapons will be fashioned and tongues will rise. What is guaranteed is the outcome, which is why Paul can list sword, famine, nakedness and danger and still say that in all these things we are more than conquerors (Rom. 8:35–37). He does not say the sword misses.

The heritage of the servants of the LORD. Through chapters 42 to 53 there has been one Servant, cut off with no descendants of his own. Here there is a household of servants with a heritage, the portion allotted to a family and handed down within it. The barren woman is singing, the tent is being enlarged, and the children counted into it are the offspring the Servant was promised he would see. He had none, and now he has these.

How can God say that strife against Zion is not from me (v. 15) and then say he created the ravager (v. 16)? Both are true at different levels. Nothing happens outside his hand, but he has not commissioned this attack, as he once commissioned Babylon, and he will not let it stand. The sovereignty that made the smith guarantees that the smith’s work will fail.

Uncertain wording. Verse 15 is difficult Hebrew. The verb rendered stirs up strife usually means to stay as a stranger, and a similar verb means to attack, so the line has been read in different ways, including as a word about strangers who come to live among God’s people. The ESV’s reading suits the surrounding talk of weapons and attack best, and the promise of verse 17 does not depend on it.

54.theology:
Chapter 54 is what chapter 53 produced. The order is the argument. A man is cut off with no descendants, and the next thing said is sing, O barren one. One Servant died childless; a household of servants inherits a heritage (v. 17).

A moment, and everlasting love. Verses 7-8 do not deny the desertion, the overflowing anger, or the hidden face; they put them in proportion. Some seventy years of exile are called a moment, not to minimise them but to show what they are measured against.

An oath the sky keeps proving. God grounds the promise in the days of Noah (v. 9), the one covenant any reader can check for himself, since no second flood has come, and then says that the mountains will go before his steadfast love does (v. 10).

What verse 17 actually promises. Weapons will be made and tongues will rise. What is guaranteed is the verdict, not the absence of the attack.

55.subtitle: Come, Everyone Who Thirsts
55.intro:
Where we are. Chapter 53 told how the servant bore the sins of many; chapter 54 sang of the people restored by his work. Chapter 55 closes the central part of the book (chapters 40 to 55) by throwing the doors open: everyone who is thirsty is invited to come and receive it all for nothing.

The message. God offers life, pardon and an everlasting covenant, free, to anyone who will come, and his word guarantees that the offer will not fail. The only cost is to stop paying elsewhere and come; the only danger is delay. And his thoughts about pardon are as far above ours as the heavens are above the earth.

Why it was said. The exiles were being called home (see the introduction), but some had settled comfortably in Babylon, some thought themselves too sinful to be received, and all had watched David’s throne fall. God answers each: the feast is free, the pardon is abundant, and the promise to David has not lapsed.

How the chapter makes its case. First the invitation: come, buy without money, and stop spending on what does not satisfy (vv. 1–2). Then the covenant behind it: the sure love promised to David, given to the people, who will draw nations they never knew (vv. 3–5). Then urgency and pardon: seek him while he may be found, forsake your way and your thoughts, and he will abundantly pardon, because his thoughts are higher than ours (vv. 6–9). Then the guarantee: his word, like rain, does not return empty (vv. 10–11). Last, the outcome: a people going out in joy and a creation where thorns give way to cypress (vv. 12–13).

Where it leads. This is direct promise, and the stallholder has a face. Jesus stood up at the feast in Jerusalem and cried out, “If anyone thirsts, let him come to me and drink” (John 7:37). The sure love for David is kept in the risen Son of David (Acts 13:34). The pardon is abundant because the servant has already borne the iniquity of us all (53:6). And the word that never returns empty became flesh and did not go back to the Father until his work was finished (John 1:14; 19:30). The Bible ends with the same invitation (Rev. 22:17).

For us. Come with empty hands; that is the only way anyone comes. If you think your sins too many, read verses 7 to 9 again: they were written for you. And keep speaking God’s word, to your children, your friends, your church: it does not come back empty.

keyVerse.quote: “So shall my word be that goes out from my mouth; it shall not return to me empty, but it shall accomplish that which I purpose, and shall succeed in the thing for which I sent it.”
keyVerse.note: This is Isaiah’s doctrine of the word: it does not depend on human response. It goes, it works, and it comes back with the harvest of its purpose. Chapters 40 to 55 have been one long word from God, comfort, promise, prediction and invitation, and this verse stands at their end as the guarantee of everything spoken. Its fullest form is the Word made flesh, who did not return to the Father until he could say, “It is finished” (John 19:30).

55.reflection:
Verse 1 invites the one “who has no money” to “come, buy and eat.” Why do people find a free offer of grace harder to accept than one they could pay for, and where do you still try to pay?

“Why do you spend your money for that which is not bread?” (v. 2). What do you keep going back to that has never once satisfied you, and what would it mean to bring that thirst to Christ instead?

Verses 8–9 are about pardon: God “will abundantly pardon” (v. 7). How does reading them that way change the way you think about your own sins, or about someone you find it hard to forgive?

God says his word “shall not return to me empty” (v. 11). Where have you been discouraged that the word seems to bear no fruit, in your family, your church or your own heart, and how does this promise help you keep going?

Come, buy wine and milk without money and without price.<sup>2</sup>Why do you spend your money for that which is not bread, and your labor for that which does not satisfy? Listen diligently to me, and eat what is good, and delight yourselves in rich food.<sup>3</sup>Incline your ear, and come to me; hear, that your soul may live; and I will make with you an everlasting covenant, my steadfast, sure love for David.<sup>4</sup>Behold, I made him a witness to the peoples, a leader and commander for the peoples.<sup>5</sup>Behold, you shall call a nation that you do not know, and a nation that did not know you shall run to you, because of the LORD your God, and of the Holy One of Israel, for he has glorified you.<sup>6</sup>"Seek the LORD while he may be found; call upon him while he is near;<sup>7</sup>let the wicked forsake his way, and the unrighteous man his thoughts; let him return to the LORD, that he may have compassion on him, and to our God, for he will abundantly pardon.<sup>8</sup>For my thoughts are not your thoughts, neither are your ways my ways, declares the LORD.<sup>9</sup>For as the heavens are higher than the earth, so are my ways higher than your ways and my thoughts than your thoughts.<sup>10</sup>"For as the rain and the snow come down from heaven and do not return there but water the earth, making it bring forth and sprout, giving seed to the sower and bread to the eater,<sup>11</sup>so shall my word be that goes out from my mouth; it shall not return to me empty, but it shall accomplish that which I purpose, and shall succeed in the thing for which I sent it.<sup>12</sup>"For you shall go out in joy and be led forth in peace; the mountains and the hills before you shall break forth into singing, and all the trees of the field shall clap their hands.<sup>13</sup>Instead of the thorn shall come up the cypress; instead of the brier shall come up the myrtle; and it shall make a name for the LORD, an everlasting sign that shall not be cut off."

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–5 — Come and Buy Without Money
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God throws open a free feast and turns it into an everlasting covenant. Like a trader at a market stall, he calls everyone thirsty and everyone with no money to come and receive water, wine and milk without price (v. 1), and asks why they spend themselves on what never satisfies (v. 2). Those who listen will live, because God makes with them an everlasting covenant, his steadfast, sure love for David (v. 3). David was a witness to the peoples (v. 4); now his people will call nations they never knew, who will run to them because of what the LORD has done (v. 5).
verseByVerse.theology: Verse 3 shows that the offer is no passing kindness but a binding covenant: what is handed to ordinary thirsty people is the sure mercies promised to David. Grace costs the receiver nothing because it cost the giver everything.
verseByVerse.examples: Verse 2 is a question worth putting to a diary and a bank statement rather than only to a conscience: what is currently being paid for that has never once satisfied?

verseByVerse.quote: "Come, everyone who thirsts, come to the waters; and he who has no money, come, buy and eat! Come, buy wine and milk without money and without price. Why do you spend your money for that which is not bread, and your labor for that which does not satisfy? Listen diligently to me, and eat what is good, and delight yourselves in rich food.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God freely offers all that truly satisfies to anyone who is thirsty and has nothing to pay, and asks why we keep spending ourselves on what never satisfies.

Come, everyone who thirsts. The voice is a stallholder’s. The Hebrew opens with hoy, the syllable that began the six woes of chapter 5, now a street trader’s shout: Ho, over here!

He who has no money, come, buy. Only two qualifications: thirst, and having no money, which is a disqualification everywhere else in the world. Isaiah keeps the word buy and removes the price. Something is genuinely received, and nothing whatever is contributed. The only people who go hungry at this stall are the ones who insist on paying.

Wine and milk. Water, without which you die; milk, the staple that builds; and wine, which nobody needs and which exists for gladness. God does not stock the stall with bare necessities; he puts the celebration out beside the survival rations.

Why do you spend your money for that which is not bread? The question is diagnostic. Not why do you sin? but why do you keep paying for things that have never once fed you? God describes a wasted life as bad economics: real money and effort spent on what has a proven record of not working. For the exiles it probably had a sharp edge. Many had done what Jeremiah told them, building houses and planting gardens in Babylon (Jer. 29:5), and some had done well enough that going home to a ruined Jerusalem looked like a poor trade. The tragedy of verse 2 is not ignorance about what satisfies. It is going back to the same stall when the free one is open.

The stallholder has a face. Jesus stood at the feast in Jerusalem crying that anyone who thirsts should come to him and drink (John 7:37), and the last page of the Bible repeats the call: let the one who is thirsty come, and take the water of life without price (Rev. 22:17). The water he gives was paid for by his own thirst on the cross (John 19:28).

The economy of never enough. Verse 2 could be carved over the door of any shopping centre. Our economy runs on a steady supply of mild dissatisfaction: the phone is fine until the new one is announced, the kitchen was lovely until we saw a better one. Psychologists call what follows the hedonic treadmill: we adjust to each new pleasure so quickly that it stops pleasing, and we need the next one simply to feel as we did before. God does not tell us to want less, as the moralist would, or to grab more, as the market would. He says the appetite is real and has been aimed at the wrong stall. The thirst is not the enemy; it is evidence of what we were made for, and only a fountain can answer it. Christ does not sell satisfaction at a discount. He gives himself, and a person who has him can enjoy the good things on every other stall without needing them to save him.

verseByVerse.quote: Incline your ear, and come to me; hear, that your soul may live; and I will make with you an everlasting covenant, my steadfast, sure love for David. Behold, I made him a witness to the peoples, a leader and commander for the peoples.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Listening to God brings life, because he gives ordinary people the everlasting covenant he made with David, kept and widened in David’s greater Son.

Incline your ear, and come to me. Three commands, all about listening: tilt the head, come, hear. And the result is life: hear, that your soul may live. Life comes through hearing, which is what Paul means when he says that faith comes from hearing (Rom. 10:17).

An everlasting covenant. The free meal turns out to be a covenant, and not a new one: the promise to David of a son, a throne and a kingdom that would not end (2 Sam. 7:12–16). And it is offered not to a dynasty but to the penniless crowd at the stall. The word attached is sure, from the root behind amen: a promise that will bear a person’s whole weight. The exiles’ last king was a captive in Babylon (2 Kgs 25:27–30), and the throne looked finished; God says the promise has not lapsed but widened.

My steadfast, sure love for David. Paul quoted this line in the synagogue at Pisidian Antioch to explain the empty tomb: God raised Jesus, and this is what was meant by “I will give you the holy and sure blessings of David” (Acts 13:34). A promise of an everlasting kingdom could not be kept by a king who stayed dead; it is kept in a Son of David who rose.

A witness to the peoples. David was made a witness to the peoples: not a private blessing but a public exhibit, through whom the nations were meant to learn about God. The role is handed on in the next verse.

Uncertain wording. The phrase behind my steadfast, sure love for David is literally the faithful mercies of David. Most take it, as the ESV does, as the covenant love God promised to David; some read it as David’s own faithful deeds, or as mercies shown through him. The covenant language around it favours the ESV, and Paul’s use of it in Acts 13:34 reads it the same way.

verseByVerse.quote: Behold, you shall call a nation that you do not know, and a nation that did not know you shall run to you, because of the LORD your God, and of the Holy One of Israel, for he has glorified you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
What David was to the nations, God’s restored people will be: nations they never knew will come running, drawn by what the LORD has done for them.

You shall call a nation that you do not know. The witness to the peoples is now a whole community, and the traffic runs both ways: they will call nations they have never heard of, and nations who have never heard of them will come running.

Shall run to you. The verb matters. Not walk, not consider, not be persuaded: run. Isaiah pictures the nations this way throughout the book, flowing to the mountain of the LORD in chapter 2 and coming with their gifts in chapter 60, and the picture always has the same energy. Nobody is being dragged. Paul and Barnabas took up the same promise when the Gentiles of Antioch rejoiced to hear the gospel (Acts 13:47–48).

Because of the LORD your God. The reason is given twice, so that no one mistakes the attraction: because of the LORD your God, and of the Holy One of Israel, for he has glorified you. They are not running toward Israel’s culture or record or virtue. They are running because something has visibly happened to these people, and it is the LORD who has done it.

The shape of witness. That is the honest shape of Christian witness, and it removes a great deal of anxiety about technique. The church is not asked to be impressive. It is asked to be a people to whom God has plainly done something, and the running starts when that becomes visible.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 6–11 — Seek Him While He May Be Found
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The free invitation comes with a time limit and an astonishing promise. Seek the LORD while he may be found (v. 6); let the wicked forsake both his way and his thoughts and return, for God will abundantly pardon (v. 7). Verses 8 and 9 defend that pardon: God’s thoughts about forgiveness are as far above ours as the heavens are above the earth. Verses 10 and 11 guarantee it: as rain and snow do not go back until they have watered the earth, God’s word will not return empty but will accomplish what he purposes. The whole section presses the reader to come now, and to believe the welcome.
verseByVerse.theology: Verse 7 is the heart of the section, and the weight falls on the pardon rather than on the forsaking. Verses 8 to 11 exist to defend it.
verseByVerse.examples: Verse 7 has been the turning-point for many who thought they had gone too far: the one thing asked is returning, and what waits is pardon in abundance.

verseByVerse.quote: "Seek the LORD while he may be found; call upon him while he is near; let the wicked forsake his way, and the unrighteous man his thoughts; let him return to the LORD, that he may have compassion on him, and to our God, for he will abundantly pardon.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now is the time to turn to God, leaving both sinful ways and sinful thinking, because he will pardon abundantly all who return.

Seek the LORD while he may be found. Two little words hold the urgency of the chapter: while, and while. The free invitation has a time limit, and Isaiah gives no way of calculating it, which makes delay a bad bet rather than a manageable risk. But the verse is first an announcement: right now he may be found and is near. The door is open, and God himself says so.

Let the wicked forsake his way, and the unrighteous man his thoughts. Two things are forsaken, and the second is harder. The way is what a man does. The thoughts are what he privately believes: what he can get away with, what he is owed, what God is like. Repentance goes past behaviour into the reasoning that produced it, which is why it is never a feat of willpower but the work of God’s word and Spirit in the one who returns (Ezek. 36:26–27).

For he will abundantly pardon. The promise carries the weight of the verse: literally, he will multiply to pardon. Not reluctantly, not within limits, but pardon and pardon again, past the point where any accountant would have closed the account. It is not the reward for a repentance done well enough; it is what the returning sinner runs to, and it is abundant because the servant of chapter 53 has already borne the iniquity of us all (53:6). Everything in the next two verses defends this clause against our instinct to disbelieve it.

How do I seek the LORD? Not by waiting to feel close to him, but by going where he has promised to be found. Open his word. He is found where he speaks: start with one of the Gospels, a chapter a day, asking what it shows you of him. Call on him. Say it plainly, even in one sentence on the drive to work: I want to know you; show me your Son. Everyone who calls on the name of the Lord will be saved (Rom. 10:13). Name what you are forsaking. Seeking and forsaking go together in this verse: tell him the habit, the grudge or the private reasoning you have been protecting, and let it go. Do it today. The verse says while, so do not wait until after the exams, the wedding or the retirement. Go where his people are. Join them on Sunday and ask someone to read the Bible with you. And you will find that the seeking was never only yours. In the parable, while the son was still a long way off, his father saw him and felt compassion, and ran and embraced him (Luke 15:20). Christ came to seek before we sought.

Can a person truly seek God and be turned away? No. Jesus promises that whoever comes to him he will never cast out (John 6:37). The limit is death, or the day of Christ’s return, or a heart grown hard by long putting off; the danger lies in the delaying, never in the coming.

verseByVerse.quote: For my thoughts are not your thoughts, neither are your ways my ways, declares the LORD. For as the heavens are higher than the earth, so are my ways higher than your ways and my thoughts than your thoughts.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God’s readiness to forgive is as far beyond our ideas of forgiveness as the heavens are above the earth.

For my thoughts are not your thoughts. Look at the word that opens verse 8: for. It ties these verses to what has just been said, that God will abundantly pardon. Their subject is not first the mystery of suffering but forgiveness.

Neither are your ways my ways. Read in context, they say that your thoughts about pardon are not God’s thoughts about pardon. Your calculation of what can be forgiven, how often, after how long, at what cost, and whether a person who has done that can really be received: every one of those calculations is made at ground level, and his are made at the height of the sky.

As the heavens are higher than the earth. In this passage the gap between heaven and earth is not first a measure of how much God knows that we do not. It is a measure of how much more willing he is to forgive than we would ever be. The cross is where the distance shows: God showed his love in that while we were still sinners, Christ died for us (Rom. 5:8).

A rescue, not a rebuke. The reason a returning sinner cannot believe the offer is that he has assessed his case correctly by human arithmetic. He knows what he did, and what he would think of somebody else who did it. Isaiah’s answer is not that the offence is smaller than he thinks. It is that the mercy runs on a different scale, and the most he can imagine being forgiven comes nowhere near its limit.
