What it does not mean. These verses are usually quoted to someone in bewildering trouble, to say that God’s providence is beyond our understanding. That is true, and Scripture teaches it elsewhere (Rom. 11:33), but it is not what this paragraph is about, and used only that way it loses its best comfort.

verseByVerse.quote: "For as the rain and the snow come down from heaven and do not return there but water the earth, making it bring forth and sprout, giving seed to the sower and bread to the eater, so shall my word be that goes out from my mouth; it shall not return to me empty, but it shall accomplish that which I purpose, and shall succeed in the thing for which I sent it.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God’s word never fails: like rain that waters the earth before it returns, it always accomplishes what he sends it to do.

As the rain and the snow come down from heaven. The picture is a complete circuit. Water falls, soaks in, and does not go back up as it came: it goes back up having been through a wheat field. The crop becomes seed for next year and bread on a table this year. Nothing is wasted and nothing comes back unchanged.

So shall my word be. God’s word is that kind of rain. It is not information issued in the hope of a response; it is a messenger sent to do a task, and the task gets done. That is the guarantee under the whole of chapters 40 to 55, every promise of comfort, every announcement about the servant, every invitation in this chapter, and it is why Isaiah can speak of a future restoration in the past tense. It is also why the apostles could preach Christ in hostile cities with confidence: the gospel is this word, at work in those who believe (1 Thess. 2:13).

It shall accomplish that which I purpose. Read the promise precisely, because it is often misused. It does not say the word accomplishes what we purposed by it, but what God purposed. A parent who has said true things to a son for fifteen years and seen nothing is not holding a failed promise; he is holding rain that has gone into ground he cannot see into, on a schedule never shown to him. Rain does not ask permission, and it never fails to water; but it does not always fall where or when the farmer expected.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 12–13 — Out in Joy, and the Thorns Gone
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The chapter ends with what the word achieves: a people going out in joy and a world being mended. The exiles go out in joy and are led in peace, while the mountains sing and the trees clap their hands (v. 12). Where thorn and brier grew, the marks of the curse on the ground (Gen. 3:18), cypress and myrtle come up instead, an everlasting sign that makes a name for the LORD (v. 13). The return from Babylon is the first step of a renewal that ends in a new creation, where the curse is gone for good.
verseByVerse.theology: Salvation in verse 13 is not the rescue of souls out of a ruined world but the mending of the world they were made for: the thorns of the curse (Gen. 3:18) are not merely cleared; good trees grow in their place.
verseByVerse.examples: Psalm 98 sings the same scene: let the rivers clap their hands; let the hills sing for joy together before the LORD, for he comes to judge the earth (Ps. 98:8-9).

verseByVerse.quote: "For you shall go out in joy and be led forth in peace; the mountains and the hills before you shall break forth into singing, and all the trees of the field shall clap their hands.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God’s people will go out of exile in joy and peace, and the whole creation will celebrate their rescue.

Go out in joy and be led forth in peace. Two verbs describe the people. They go out, walking out of exile on their own feet, and they are led forth, as a flock or a child is led. They walk and they are walked, which is a fair account of how a Christian actually gets anywhere: his real steps, God’s leading hand.

The trees of the field shall clap their hands. The hills sing and the trees applaud, and Scripture treats that as more than poetry. Paul says the creation waits with eager longing, groans, and will be set free from its bondage to decay when the children of God are revealed (Rom. 8:19–22). The singing is a creation that has groaned since Genesis 3 hearing that what it waited for has begun.

verseByVerse.quote: Instead of the thorn shall come up the cypress; instead of the brier shall come up the myrtle; and it shall make a name for the LORD, an everlasting sign that shall not be cut off."
verseByVerse.commentary:
God will reverse the curse on the ground, and the renewed world itself will be a lasting monument to his name.

Instead of the thorn. Two plants out, two plants in, and the first pair is not random. Thorns and briers are what the ground was told to produce when it was cursed: “thorns and thistles it shall bring forth for you” (Gen. 3:18). Isaiah reaches back to the third chapter of the Bible for the thing being reversed.

Shall come up the cypress. The thorns are not merely weeded. They are replaced: where the thorn was, a cypress comes up, and the soil that produced the curse now produces timber and fragrance. This is not the tidying of a ruined world but the mending of it. The one who wore a crown of thorns (John 19:2) bore the curse to remove it (Gal. 3:13).

Not escape, but mending. This is the difference between the Christian hope and a vague hope of going somewhere better. Isaiah does not promise escape from a thorny world. He promises that the thorns themselves will be gone from the actual ground, and the last chapters of the Bible say the same: no more curse, and the leaves of the tree for the healing of the nations (Rev. 22:2–3).

An everlasting sign that shall not be cut off. The chapter that opened by calling to a crowd of penniless people closes with a permanent monument, and the monument is a landscape. The evidence that God did this will not be a text or a memory. It will be the world itself, growing the right things at last, with his name on it for ever.

55.theology:
Free, and therefore real. Verse 1 keeps the word buy and removes the price: something is genuinely received and nothing is contributed. Verse 3 raises the offer from a meal to an everlasting covenant, kept in the resurrection of the Son of David.

Verses 8-9 are about pardon. They are almost always quoted to someone bewildered by providence, but the word that opens verse 8 is for, attaching them to the promise that God will abundantly pardon. Read that way the passage stops being a rebuke to curiosity and becomes the answer to the returning sinner’s strongest objection, which is that he knows exactly how much there is to forgive.

The word as agent. Verse 11 makes God’s word a messenger sent to do a task, not merely information: it goes, it works, it comes back having done what it was sent for. Its last and fullest form is the Word who came down from heaven and did not go back until he could say, “It is finished” (John 19:30; see 1:14).

56.subtitle: My House Shall Be a House of Prayer for All Peoples
56.intro:
Where we are. Chapter 55 closed the central part of the book with a free invitation to everyone who thirsts. Chapter 56 opens the last part (chapters 56 to 66), which speaks to the community back from exile (see the introduction), small, struggling and still waiting for the glory God had promised.

The message. God’s house is open to everyone who joins himself to the LORD and holds fast his covenant, including those the old order kept out, and while his salvation is on its way his people are to live in justice and righteousness. But leaders who sleep at their post and feed themselves stand under his judgment.

Why it was said. The returned community was anxious about who belonged, and would later separate foreigners from Israel (Neh. 13:1–3). Foreigners who had come to trust Israel’s God, and eunuchs, among them perhaps men of David’s own line made eunuchs in Babylon’s palace, as Isaiah had told Hezekiah (39:7), had reason to wonder whether they had any place. And the people’s leaders were failing them.

How the chapter makes its case. First the call for the meantime: keep justice, because salvation is near, and keep the Sabbath (vv. 1–2). Then the eunuch who calls himself a dry tree is given an everlasting name in God’s house, better than sons and daughters (vv. 3–5), and the foreigner who loves the LORD is brought to his holy mountain and his altar, in a house of prayer for all peoples, with more still to be gathered (vv. 6–8). Last, the sudden contrast: blind watchmen, silent guard dogs and greedy shepherds, drinking as if tomorrow will be the same (vv. 9–12).

Where it leads. The chapter leads to Christ by promise and by contrast. Jesus quoted verse 7 as he cleared the temple’s outer court (Mark 11:17). An Ethiopian eunuch reading Isaiah met the servant who was cut off childless and yet sees his offspring, and was baptised (Acts 8:27–39). Jesus spoke of other sheep he must bring (John 10:16), and through him Gentiles are no longer strangers but members of the household of God (Eph. 2:19). And against the shepherds who each turn to their own gain stands the good shepherd who lays down his life for the sheep (John 10:11).

For us. No one who comes to Christ is a dry tree or an outsider in God’s house, whatever their past, their background or their circumstances, and churches must not rebuild walls he has taken down. And those who lead must keep watch and speak, for the flock’s sake, not their own.

keyVerse.quote: “For my house shall be called a house of prayer for all peoples.”
keyVerse.note: This is the text Jesus quoted when he cleared the temple (Mark 11:17). God’s house was always meant for all peoples, not for Israel alone. The trading he drove out was not incidental: it filled the outer court, the space where outsiders could come to pray, so to clear it was to act out Isaiah 56.

56.reflection:
The foreigner feared, “The LORD will surely separate me from his people,” and the eunuch said, “Behold, I am a dry tree” (v. 3). What private verdicts do people pass on themselves that keep them from believing they belong in God’s house, and how does this chapter answer them?

God gives the eunuch “a name better than sons and daughters” (v. 5). How should that shape the way your church values and includes single, widowed and childless believers?

Jesus quoted “my house shall be called a house of prayer for all peoples” (v. 7) as he cleared the temple. What in our churches might crowd out the outsider, and what would it take to clear the floor?

The watchmen of verses 10–11 saw no danger worth speaking of and turned each to his own gain. Where are you tempted to keep quiet when love requires you to speak, and how does Christ the good shepherd (John 10:11) give you both a pattern and a remedy?
56.text: <sup>1</sup>Thus says the LORD: "Keep justice, and do righteousness, for soon my salvation will come, and my righteousness be revealed.<sup>2</sup>Blessed is the man who does this, and the son of man who holds it fast, who keeps the Sabbath, not profaning it, and keeps his hand from doing any evil."<sup>3</sup>Let not the foreigner who has joined himself to the LORD say, "The LORD will surely separate me from his people"; and let not the eunuch say, "Behold, I am a dry tree."<sup>4</sup>For thus says the LORD: "To the eunuchs who keep my Sabbaths, who choose the things that please me and hold fast my covenant,<sup>5</sup>I will give in my house and within my walls a monument and a name better than sons and daughters; I will give them an everlasting name that shall not be cut off.<sup>6</sup>"And the foreigners who join themselves to the LORD, to minister to him, to love the name of the LORD, and to be his servants, everyone who keeps the Sabbath and does not profane it, and holds fast my covenant—<sup>7</sup>these I will bring to my holy mountain, and make them joyful in my house of prayer; their burnt offerings and their sacrifices will be accepted on my altar; for my house shall be called a house of prayer for all peoples."<sup>8</sup>The Lord GOD, who gathers the outcasts of Israel, declares, "I will gather yet others to him besides those already gathered."<sup>9</sup>All you beasts of the field, come to devour— all you beasts in the forest.<sup>10</sup>His watchmen are blind; they are all without knowledge; they are all silent dogs; they cannot bark, dreaming, lying down, loving to slumber.<sup>11</sup>The dogs have a mighty appetite; they never have enough. But they are shepherds who have no understanding; they have all turned to their own way, each to his own gain, one and all.<sup>12</sup>"Come," they say, "let me get wine; let us fill ourselves with strong drink; and tomorrow will be like this day, great beyond measure."

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–8 — The House of Prayer for All Peoples
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God’s salvation is near, and his house will be open to all who hold fast his covenant, however they were once excluded. The last part of the book opens with instructions for the meantime: keep justice, for salvation is coming, and keep the Sabbath (vv. 1–2). Then two men who thought they had no place are answered, the foreigner who fears separation and the eunuch who calls himself a dry tree (v. 3). The eunuch receives a name better than sons and daughters (vv. 4–5); the foreigner, a joyful place at God’s altar in a house of prayer for all peoples (vv. 6–7). And God has more to gather still (v. 8).
verseByVerse.theology: Both men are excluded by something they cannot change, ancestry or a mutilated body. Isaiah does not soften the exclusion; he announces that God is overriding it, because they hold fast to his covenant, not because of their birth.
verseByVerse.examples: Many believers who are single, childless or far from family have found in verses 4-5 the assurance that they are not a dry tree in God's house: what he gives them there cannot be cut off.

verseByVerse.quote: Thus says the LORD: "Keep justice, and do righteousness, for soon my salvation will come, and my righteousness be revealed. Blessed is the man who does this, and the son of man who holds it fast, who keeps the Sabbath, not profaning it, and keeps his hand from doing any evil."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Because God’s salvation is about to arrive, his people are to live now in justice and righteousness, and the one who does so is blessed.

Keep justice, and do righteousness. The last part of Isaiah begins with housekeeping. Sixteen chapters of the highest promises in the Old Testament have been delivered; now come instructions for the interval between the announcement and the arrival.

For soon my salvation will come. The order of the sentence matters: keep justice for my salvation is coming. The behaviour does not earn the salvation; it is the fitting way to wait for something already guaranteed, like tidying a house before a guest who is definitely on the road. And the same word sits at both ends of the verse: do righteousness, for my righteousness will be revealed. God’s saving righteousness comes first, and his people’s is the answer to it.

Blessed is the man who does this. The waiting people never keep it perfectly. The one whose salvation is coming kept justice and righteousness without a lapse in their place (53:9, 11), and those who belong to him now walk in it by his Spirit (Rom. 8:4), returning to his pardon when they fail (55:7).

Who keeps the Sabbath, not profaning it. Of all the commandments, the Sabbath is singled out in every promise in this chapter. It needs no temple, land, priest or family tree. It is the one part of the law an exile in a foreign city could keep in full, and, as the next verses show, the one a man with the wrong ancestry or the wrong body could keep as completely as anybody else.

verseByVerse.quote: Let not the foreigner who has joined himself to the LORD say, "The LORD will surely separate me from his people"; and let not the eunuch say, "Behold, I am a dry tree." For thus says the LORD: "To the eunuchs who keep my Sabbaths, who choose the things that please me and hold fast my covenant, I will give in my house and within my walls a monument and a name better than sons and daughters; I will give them an everlasting name that shall not be cut off.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God tells the foreigner and the eunuch, who feared they had no place among his people, that if they hold fast his covenant he will give them a lasting name in his house, better than children.

Two private verdicts. Both sentences are things people said about themselves, and God answers the verdict two kinds of men had passed on their own standing. The foreigner’s fear had a basis: the law kept certain nations out of the assembly (Deut. 23:3–8), and in Nehemiah’s day the returned community would read that law aloud and separate foreigners from Israel (Neh. 13:1–3).

Behold, I am a dry tree. The eunuch’s verdict is the more desolate. In a world without written records for ordinary people, children were the only remembrance available; a man without them simply ended. And the law barred him from the assembly of the LORD (Deut. 23:1).

A monument and a name. God does not tell him his fear is imaginary. He gives him something instead. The word rendered monument is literally a hand, as the ESV footnote says, a memorial set up inside God’s own house in place of the children he will never have, and better because it cannot be cut off. Sons die. Names carved into God’s house do not.

The Ethiopian eunuch. Centuries later an Ethiopian court official, a eunuch, was riding home from Jerusalem reading this very scroll. Before the journey was over he was baptised and went on his way rejoicing (Acts 8:27–39). One of the first outsiders brought into the church in Acts was a man Isaiah 56 had gone out of its way to name.

Is God contradicting his own law? No. The barrier of Deuteronomy belonged to an order that was meant to pass, a picture of the wholeness God requires, and Acts 8 shows it passing through Christ, the servant whose story the eunuch was reading: cut off out of the land of the living (53:8; Acts 8:32–33), and yet promised that he would see his offspring (53:10). The man who feared he would leave no children met the one who died childless and gained a countless family. The Sabbath named in these promises was the sign of belonging to the covenant then; now the door for every outsider is faith in Christ, our rest (Heb. 4:9–10).

Is a life without sex or children a smaller life? Our culture rarely says so outright, but it often assumes it. Romance and sexual fulfilment are treated as so central to being human that a single person is quietly pitied, and someone who stays celibate for conscience’ sake is suspected of repression. Ancient Israel had its own version: a man without children was a dry tree. The eunuch carried both griefs, no marriage and no heir, and God does not answer him by finding him a family. He gives him a name better than sons and daughters. That means the deepest human fulfilment is found not in sex or offspring, good gifts as they are, but in belonging to God, and so it is open to everyone. Jesus never married and had no children, and he was the most fully human person who has ever lived. He spoke of some who have made themselves eunuchs for the sake of the kingdom of heaven (Matt. 19:12), and no single believer in his household is half a person.
verseByVerse.note: Eunuchs had been excluded from the assembly; here they are welcomed.

verseByVerse.quote: "And the foreigners who join themselves to the LORD, to minister to him, to love the name of the LORD, and to be his servants, everyone who keeps the Sabbath and does not profane it, and holds fast my covenant— these I will bring to my holy mountain, and make them joyful in my house of prayer; their burnt offerings and their sacrifices will be accepted on my altar; for my house shall be called a house of prayer for all peoples." The Lord GOD, who gathers the outcasts of Israel, declares, "I will gather yet others to him besides those already gathered."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Foreigners who give themselves to the LORD will be welcomed into his house and its worship, because he means it to be a house of prayer for all peoples, and he will gather still more.

The foreigners who join themselves to the LORD. Every verb describing these foreigners is a verb of attachment: join, minister, love, serve, hold fast. Nothing is said about where they were born, and they receive what an Israelite thought was his by birth: the holy mountain, the altar, an accepted sacrifice.

A house of prayer for all peoples. Jesus quoted this sentence as he overturned the tables (Mark 11:17), and Mark alone keeps the words for all the nations. The temple’s outermost court was the only place a Gentile could stand and pray, and it had been filled with livestock pens and currency stalls. He was clearing the floor of the room Isaiah had promised to the nations.

I will gather yet others. The gathering is left open: more are coming who are not on Israel’s list at all. Jesus says it in his own words: I have other sheep that are not of this fold. I must bring them also (John 10:16). So Paul can tell Gentile believers that they are no longer strangers and aliens but members of the household of God (Eph. 2:19).

Where Christians differ. Will literal sacrifices return? Many dispensationalists read promises like verse 7 of a rebuilt temple with memorial sacrifices.

This commentary’s view. Isaiah describes new-covenant worship in the language of the temple he knew. The New Testament never expects renewed sacrifice: the sacrifices are fulfilled in Christ, once for all (Heb. 10:12), and his people now offer a sacrifice of praise (Heb. 13:15) and themselves (Rom. 12:1). The house of prayer for all peoples is God’s people gathered in Christ from every nation.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The open house has failing guards, and God exposes them. Wild beasts are called to devour (v. 9), because Israel’s watchmen are blind and its guard dogs silent, too fond of sleep to warn anyone (v. 10). They are greedy shepherds without understanding, each turned to his own gain (v. 11), and they close the chapter with a drinking song, sure that tomorrow will be like today (v. 12). The contrast is deliberate: God welcomes outsiders while the insiders paid to keep watch neglect the flock. The passage runs on into chapter 57, and it makes the reader long for a shepherd who will lay down his life for the sheep.
verseByVerse.theology: The placing is deliberate and savage. God has just thrown his house open to foreigners and eunuchs, and the men employed to keep watch over that house are asleep on the job with their mouths full. The outsiders are being let in past leaders who never noticed the door was unlocked.

verseByVerse.quote: All you beasts of the field, come to devour— all you beasts in the forest. His watchmen are blind; they are all without knowledge; they are all silent dogs; they cannot bark, dreaming, lying down, loving to slumber. The dogs have a mighty appetite; they never have enough. But they are shepherds who have no understanding; they have all turned to their own way, each to his own gain, one and all. "Come," they say, "let me get wine; let us fill ourselves with strong drink; and tomorrow will be like this day, great beyond measure."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Israel’s leaders, set to guard God’s people, are blind, silent, lazy and greedy, so the flock lies open to its enemies.

All you beasts of the field, come to devour. The tone drops without warning. Wild animals are invited in, a picture of hostile nations let loose on a flock nobody is guarding.

His watchmen are blind. The two jobs that protect a settlement are the man on the wall and the dog in the yard, and both have failed: the watchman cannot see and the dog will not bark. A guard dog does not have to be brave. It has to make a noise. Isaiah’s dog hears the footsteps, opens one eye, and goes back to sleep, which is what happens when a leader sees the danger perfectly well and has decided that speaking up would cost him too much.

The dogs have a mighty appetite. Their appetite shows what is wrong. These men are extremely energetic about themselves; what has gone is any sense that the flock was the point. Then they are called shepherds, and they have all turned to their own way, the very words used of the straying sheep in 53:6, while one and all leaves nobody out of the charge.

Tomorrow will be like this day. The drinking song’s last line is Babylon’s assumption in chapter 47, that things go on as they are, only more so (47:7). The men paid to keep God’s house sleep at the gate with a drink in their hands.

The good shepherd. Against shepherds who each turn to their own gain stands the one who said, “I am the good shepherd. The good shepherd lays down his life for the sheep” (John 10:11). Where they fed themselves, he fed the flock with his own life.

For leaders, and for churches. Pastors and elders are watchmen, and love sometimes requires them to bark, to warn of real danger even when it costs them. Churches should pray for leaders who will speak, and choose them for faithfulness, not appetite.

Uncertain wording. The word rendered dreaming occurs only here in the Bible. It may mean dozing, panting or raving; the ESV takes it as half asleep, which fits lying down, loving to slumber.

56.theology:
Two men who could not qualify. Deuteronomy had barred the eunuch, and foreigners of certain nations, from the assembly (Deut. 23:1-8), and Isaiah does not pretend otherwise. His welcome to them is one of the plainest statements in the book that the household of God will be composed of people who joined it rather than people who were born into it.

Why the Sabbath, every time. The Sabbath is attached to every promise in this chapter (vv. 2, 4, 6), which can look like earning favour by rule-keeping until the situation is considered: God names the one command that the excluded were able to obey.

The Sabbath for Christians. This commentary holds that the Sabbath is fulfilled in Christ, who is our rest (Heb. 4:9-10), and that the Lord’s Day is a gift: Christians gladly set Sunday apart for worship and rest out of joy, not as a law with rules about work. Many godly Christians, with the Westminster Confession and the 1689 London Baptist Confession, hold instead that the fourth commandment carries over to the Lord’s Day as the Christian Sabbath. Faithful believers differ here, and neither side may bind the other’s conscience (Rom. 14:5).

A name, and a house. The eunuch is given a name that will not be cut off (v. 5), and the foreigner a place at the altar (v. 7). When Jesus cleared the temple’s outer court, he was clearing the floor of the room this chapter gave to the nations.

57.subtitle: The High and Holy One Who Dwells with the Contrite
57.intro:
Where we are. Chapter 56 opened the last part of the book by throwing God’s house open to outsiders, then turned on Israel’s leaders as blind watchmen (56:9–12). Chapter 57 shows what that neglect has produced: good people dying unnoticed, and a people giving themselves to every god but their own.

The message. The idols you run after will wear you out and leave you with a handful of stones; the God you have deserted is the only refuge that holds. And this God, who is high above everything and whose name is Holy, has chosen to live with the crushed and the contrite, to revive them. He has seen all their ways, and still he says, “I will heal him.”

Why it was said. The sins named here are those of Jerusalem under Ahaz and Manasseh, the very sins that brought the exile (see the introduction). Whether first heard in those dark years or read by the small community that came home, the chapter warned God’s people not to drift back into them, and told the broken among them that the holy God had not abandoned them.

How the chapter makes its case. First a short lament: the righteous perish and no one cares, though God has taken them into peace (vv. 1–2). Then a fierce indictment: sorcery, sexual rites, child sacrifice and a search for security pursued to exhaustion, with idols a breath will carry away (vv. 3–13). Then the turn: the High and Holy One gives his two addresses, heaven and the contrite heart; he will heal, and speaks peace to far and near, while the wicked toss like a restless sea (vv. 14–21).

Where it leads. The chapter leads to Christ chiefly by revealing God’s character, and then by promise. The God who is “high and lifted up” yet lives with the lowly came down in person when the Word became flesh and dwelt among us (John 1:14), and the Servant whose wounds heal (53:5) is how God can say of a guilty man, “I have seen his ways, but I will heal him.” Paul hears verse 19 fulfilled at the cross, where Christ made peace and then “came and preached peace to you who were far off and peace to those who were near” (Ephesians 2:17).

For us. Every idol still asks for more than it gives, and our tiredness is often the proof. Stop holding up your collection, and bring God what he actually asks for, a contrite heart; he has promised to live there. The peace that the restless world cannot find is offered freely in Christ, to the far as well as the near.

keyVerse.quote: “For thus says the One who is high and lifted up, who inhabits eternity, whose name is Holy: I dwell in the high and holy place, and also with him who is of a contrite and lowly spirit.”
keyVerse.note: This verse holds together what seem to be opposites: the infinite God and the broken person. The way to have God live with you is not religious achievement but contrition, and Jesus’ first beatitude, “Blessed are the poor in spirit” (Matthew 5:3), is this verse in the New Testament. In Christ the High and Holy One came to live among the lowly in person, so that the throne and the broken heart are the same address.

57.reflection:
The chapter opens with the complaint that “the righteous man perishes, and no one lays it to heart” (v. 1). Why do you think the godly so often die unnoticed, and how does it comfort you that God says they “enter into peace” (v. 2)?

Ancient idols demanded children, and verse 10 describes people worn out by their idols yet never saying “It is hopeless.” What modern gods ask to be paid in the people we love, or keep us going long after they have stopped giving anything back?

God lives “in the high and holy place, and also with him who is of a contrite and lowly spirit” (v. 15). What is the difference between being contrite and simply feeling bad, and why does God choose to live with the one rather than the impressive?

“I have seen his ways, but I will heal him” (v. 18). How does the cross make that “but” possible, and where do you need to believe it about yourself or someone you love?
57.text: <sup>1</sup>The righteous man perishes, and no one lays it to heart; devout men are taken away, while no one understands. For the righteous man is taken away from calamity;<sup>2</sup>he enters into peace; they rest in their beds who walk in their uprightness.<sup>3</sup>But you, draw near, sons of the sorceress, offspring of the adulterer and the loose woman.<sup>4</sup>Whom are you mocking? Against whom do you open your mouth wide and stick out your tongue? Are you not children of transgression, the offspring of deceit,<sup>5</sup>you who burn with lust among the oaks, under every green tree, who slaughter your children in the valleys, under the clefts of the rocks?<sup>6</sup>Among the smooth stones of the valley is your portion; they, they, are your lot; to them you have poured out a drink offering, you have brought a grain offering. Shall I relent for these things?<sup>7</sup>On a high and lofty mountain you have set your bed, and there you went up to offer sacrifice.<sup>8</sup>Behind the door and the doorpost you have set up your memorial; for, deserting me, you have uncovered your bed, you have gone up to it, you have made it wide; and you have made a covenant for yourself with them, you have loved their bed, you have looked on nakedness.<sup>9</sup>You journeyed to the king with oil and multiplied your perfumes; you sent your envoys far off, and sent down even to Sheol.<sup>10</sup>You were wearied with the length of your way, but you did not say, "It is hopeless"; you found new life for your strength, and so you were not faint.<sup>11</sup>Whom did you dread and fear, so that you lied, and did not remember me, did not lay it to heart? Have I not held my peace, even for a long time, and you do not fear me?<sup>12</sup>I will declare your righteousness and your deeds, but they will not profit you.<sup>13</sup>When you cry out, let your collection of idols deliver you! The wind will carry them all off, a breath will take them away. But he who takes refuge in me shall possess the land and shall inherit my holy mountain.<sup>14</sup>And it shall be said, "Build up, build up, prepare the way, remove every obstruction from my people's way."<sup>15</sup>For thus says the One who is high and lifted up, who inhabits eternity, whose name is Holy: "I dwell in the high and holy place, and also with him who is of a contrite and lowly spirit, to revive the spirit of the lowly, and to revive the heart of the contrite.<sup>16</sup>For I will not contend forever, nor will I always be angry; for the spirit would grow faint before me, and the breath of life that I made.<sup>17</sup>Because of the iniquity of his unjust gain I was angry, I struck him; I hid my face and was angry, but he went on backsliding in the way of his own heart.<sup>18</sup>I have seen his ways, but I will heal him; I will lead him and restore comfort to him and his mourners,<sup>19</sup>creating the fruit of the lips. Peace, peace, to the far and to the near," says the LORD, "and I will heal him.<sup>20</sup>But the wicked are like the tossing sea; for it cannot be quiet, and its waters toss up mire and dirt.<sup>21</sup>There is no peace," says my God, "for the wicked."

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–2 — Nobody Notices When the Good Die
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The death of good people should make a community stop and think, and it does not; but God sees what the mourners miss. The complaint is not that the righteous die but that no one lays it to heart: devout people are taken away and nobody understands what it means (v. 1). Isaiah then gives the reading no one at the graveside had reached for. The righteous man is taken away from the calamity that is coming, he enters into peace, and those who walked uprightly rest in their beds (vv. 1–2). Death is still a loss, but for the godly it is not the last word.
verseByVerse.theology: The comfort is severe and honest: it does not say the death was not a loss, but that God may have been getting a godly man out before something worse arrived.

verseByVerse.quote: The righteous man perishes, and no one lays it to heart; devout men are taken away, while no one understands. For the righteous man is taken away from calamity; he enters into peace; they rest in their beds who walk in their uprightness.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Good people are dying and no one stops to think about it; yet God has taken them out of the coming disaster into peace and rest.

No one lays it to heart. The chapter opens at a graveside, and the grievance is the silence. Isaiah does not say the righteous were persecuted, only that no one noticed or asked what their loss meant.

Taken away from calamity. Then he offers a reading that nobody at the grave would have reached for. Something was coming, and the righteous man was got out first, as Josiah was gathered to his grave in peace before the disaster fell on Jerusalem (2 Kings 22:20). It is a hard comfort, not a sentimental one: the loss is still a loss, but where the timing of a death looks like the cruellest accident, God may be doing something the mourners cannot see.

They rest in their beds. A bed, not a battlefield: it is the grave seen from God’s side, a picture of rest, not of unconsciousness: to depart is “to depart and be with Christ, for that is far better” (Philippians 1:23), and those who die in the Lord rest from their labours (Revelation 14:13). Death remains an enemy and grief is right, but for anyone who has buried a godly parent or friend while the world went on without noticing, this is Isaiah’s comfort: the death was seen, and the one who died is safe.

What it does not mean. Not that every early death is a rescue we can explain, nor that death is something to reach for. If you find yourself longing to die, tell someone you trust today, a pastor, a biblical counsellor or your doctor, and if you are in danger, call emergency services now.

Uncertain wording. Taken away from calamity could also mean “taken away by the evil”, swept off in the wickedness of the times. The rescue reading fits the peace and rest of verse 2 best, and most translations take it so.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Israel has given herself to every god but the LORD, and the gods have worn her out and will not save her. The indictment is unsparing: mocking faces and lust under the trees, children killed in the valleys, and a portion of smooth stones (vv. 3–6); a bed set up on the mountains, a pagan token where God’s word should hang, and envoys sent as far as the grave (vv. 7–9). The saddest line follows: wearied by the way, yet never saying it is hopeless (v. 10). Fear of others has pushed out the fear of God, and the idols will blow away in a breath; only the one who takes refuge in the LORD will inherit his holy mountain (vv. 11–13).
verseByVerse.theology: Verse 10 is the diagnosis to keep: the strength to keep going gets mistaken for proof that the idols are working.
verseByVerse.examples: Verse 6 turns on a Hebrew pun: the smooth stones and the portion, a family's allotted inheritance, sound almost alike.

verseByVerse.quote: But you, draw near, sons of the sorceress, offspring of the adulterer and the loose woman. Whom are you mocking? Against whom do you open your mouth wide and stick out your tongue? Are you not children of transgression, the offspring of deceit, you who burn with lust among the oaks, under every green tree, who slaughter your children in the valleys, under the clefts of the rocks? Among the smooth stones of the valley is your portion; they, they, are your lot; to them you have poured out a drink offering, you have brought a grain offering. Shall I relent for these things?
verseByVerse.commentary:
God summons the idolaters to court and names what they have done: mockery, sexual rites, child sacrifice and offerings poured out to stones.

Whom are you mocking? The elegy ends and the prosecution begins in street language: children of a sorceress and an adulterer, because their religion has been magic and their worship unfaithfulness. Someone in the crowd has been pulling faces at the prophet, and God describes the wide mouth and the stuck-out tongue before the sin, because the contempt is part of the evidence.

Who slaughter your children in the valleys. Two practices are named in one breath, and the second must be stated plainly. The fertility shrines stood under the green trees; the child sacrifice happened in the valleys, in Jerusalem in the Valley of Hinnom, whose name became Gehenna, the New Testament’s word for hell. Kings records it under Ahaz and Manasseh, who burned their sons as offerings (2 Kings 16:3; 21:6). These were the same people who kept the festivals: an offering in the morning and a child burned in the evening, and no sense of contradiction. They are set out so the people would know what had brought the exile, and not drift back into it.

Among the smooth stones of the valley is your portion. Smooth and portion sound alike in Hebrew, and a portion was a family’s share of the land God gave. So God says of the stones of the streambed: here is your inheritance, then. A handful of pebbles out of a dry valley, and you are pouring out wine to them. Shall I relent for these things? expects the answer no.

What our idols still ask of our children. Verse 5 seems a horror from another world, but ancient parents did not give their children to Molech out of simple cruelty; the god promised what they most wanted, rain, harvest, victory and safety, and the gods of security always ask a great deal. Ours are better mannered, and they still take children. A career can claim a father’s evenings for twenty years. A parent’s ambition can turn a child into a project, loved for his results. Sooner or later every idol asks to be paid in the people we love most. God reverses the transaction: he does not take our children to secure our future; he gave his own Son to secure theirs (Romans 8:32). And the Son who was given took the little children in his arms and blessed them (Mark 10:16).

Uncertain wording. The smooth stones of the valley are probably stream stones set up as objects of worship. Some scholars suggest the Hebrew means “the dead of the valley”, pointing to rites for the dead. Either way they chose something lifeless as their inheritance.

verseByVerse.quote: On a high and lofty mountain you have set your bed, and there you went up to offer sacrifice. Behind the door and the doorpost you have set up your memorial; for, deserting me, you have uncovered your bed, you have gone up to it, you have made it wide; and you have made a covenant for yourself with them, you have loved their bed, you have looked on nakedness. You journeyed to the king with oil and multiplied your perfumes; you sent your envoys far off, and sent down even to Sheol. You were wearied with the length of your way, but you did not say, "It is hopeless"; you found new life for your strength, and so you were not faint.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Israel has acted like an unfaithful wife, giving herself to other gods and buying protection from foreign kings, and she has worn herself out without ever admitting it was hopeless.

On a high and lofty mountain you have set your bed. The imagery is deliberately marital and deliberately shocking, because that is the relationship being betrayed. The bed is the hilltop shrine, and verse 8 piles up the picture of a wife who has opened her bed to strangers and made a covenant with them.

Behind the door and the doorpost. The detail is exact: the pagan token stands where an Israelite household wrote the words of God (Deuteronomy 6:9). The charm has been put in the place where the Scripture was supposed to be.

You journeyed to the king with oil. The picture widens from religion to foreign policy: gifts prepared, ambassadors dispatched, alliances bought. The search for security ran so far that it reached Sheol, the realm of the dead, and found nothing there either.

You were wearied with the length of your way. They were exhausted, and kept finding just enough strength to keep going. That is how a person stays in something that is destroying him: not by believing it works, but by never quite running out of energy long enough to notice that it does not. The stamina to survive the tiredness is mistaken for proof that the thing still pays. Anyone who has watched a friend keep a habit, an ambition or a relationship alive years after it stopped giving anything back has seen verse 10 lived out. The words Israel would not say, It is hopeless, are where rescue begins: Jesus calls “all who labor and are heavy laden” (Matthew 11:28).

Uncertain wording. The memorial was some pagan token; exactly what is unknown. You have looked on nakedness is literally “you have seen a hand”, probably a sexual euphemism, though “hand” can also mean a monument (1 Samuel 15:12). King is melek, possibly a pun on Molech, and journeyed may mean “lavished”. New life for your strength is literally “the life of your hand”, an idiom for renewed vigour. The overall sense is clear.

verseByVerse.quote: Whom did you dread and fear, so that you lied, and did not remember me, did not lay it to heart? Have I not held my peace, even for a long time, and you do not fear me? I will declare your righteousness and your deeds, but they will not profit you. When you cry out, let your collection of idols deliver you! The wind will carry them all off, a breath will take them away. But he who takes refuge in me shall possess the land and shall inherit my holy mountain.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Fear of others pushed God out of their minds; neither their idols nor their own deeds will save them, but whoever takes refuge in the LORD will inherit his holy mountain.

Whom did you dread and fear? The question is a diagnosis. Somebody frightened them into lying, and the fear of that person pushed God out of mind. Fear of man and forgetfulness of God arrive together, exactly as 51:12–13 said.

Have I not held my peace? God asks whether his long silence is why they stopped taking him seriously. His patience was read not as mercy but as absence (compare 2 Peter 3:9).

Let your collection of idols deliver you! God will set out their “righteousness” in full, bitterly ironic, and it will not help them. So, at the moment of crisis, let them call the gods they have been paying for. It will not take an army to scatter this collection; a breeze will do it. The gods people build their lives around weigh less than the air moving through a doorway.

He who takes refuge in me shall possess the land. Set that against verse 6. Their portion was a handful of stones from a dry riverbed; the portion of the one who simply takes shelter in God is the land itself and the mountain where God lives. The only thing required to hold it is to stop trying to hold anything else. Jesus promised the meek the same inheritance (Matthew 5:5).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 14–21 — The High and Holy Place, and the Crushed Heart
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The holy God who lives above all things also lives with the crushed, and he comes to heal the very people he has had to strike. A road is to be cleared of every obstruction (v. 14). Then one of the great sentences of the Old Testament: the One who inhabits eternity keeps two addresses, the high and holy place and the contrite and lowly spirit (v. 15). He will not be angry for ever, for his creatures would faint (v. 16); he struck and it did not change them (v. 17), but he will heal, lead and comfort (v. 18). Peace goes out to the far and the near (v. 19), while the wicked are a sea that cannot rest (vv. 20–21).
verseByVerse.theology: Verse 15 is not a puzzle to be admired but a promise to be used. God truly dwells far above us, for he inhabits eternity, and he truly dwells with the crushed and lowly too.
verseByVerse.examples: Verse 17 is candid about the failure of discipline on its own; what breaks the deadlock in verse 18 is not a heavier blow but healing offered to the same unchanged man.

verseByVerse.quote: And it shall be said, "Build up, build up, prepare the way, remove every obstruction from my people's way." For thus says the One who is high and lifted up, who inhabits eternity, whose name is Holy: "I dwell in the high and holy place, and also with him who is of a contrite and lowly spirit, to revive the spirit of the lowly, and to revive the heart of the contrite. For I will not contend forever, nor will I always be angry; for the spirit would grow faint before me, and the breath of life that I made.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The holy God, who lives above all things, also lives with the crushed and humble in order to revive them, and he limits his anger because his creatures could not survive it.

Build up, build up, prepare the way. The road-building command of chapter 40 returns, and the obstacles have changed. Here the obstructions lie in the way of my people, and everything the chapter has just described must be cleared: the beds on the hills, the charm behind the door, the pocketful of stones.

The One who is high and lifted up. These are the titles Isaiah first heard when he saw the Lord on a throne and thought he was going to die (6:1–5).

I dwell in the high and holy place. Then God gives his address, and there are two. One is the high and holy place, as anyone would expect. The other is a person. Contrite means crushed: not modest, but broken, the way ground is broken before anything is planted in it. And he comes there not to inspect but to revive. So the qualification for having God live with you is not achievement, not a record, not even recovery. It is being crushed enough to have run out of alternatives: “a broken and contrite heart, O God, you will not despise” (Psalm 51:17). Jesus opened the Sermon on the Mount with this verse in six words: “Blessed are the poor in spirit” (Matthew 5:3).

The two addresses meet in Christ. In Christ the high and the lowly met in one person. The eternal Word took flesh and dwelt among us (John 1:14), and he promises that he and the Father will come and make their home with the one who loves him (John 14:23). The God of the high place has never been ashamed of the low one.

I will not contend forever. God gives the reason he limits his anger, and it is not that the anger was unjustified. It is that we would not survive it. In the middle of a chapter about child sacrifice and adultery, he remembers how fragile his creatures are, because he made them.

What it does not mean. Contrition is not a mood worked up to earn God’s presence, nor permanent self-loathing; the crushed heart is where God begins, not where he leaves us.

verseByVerse.quote: Because of the iniquity of his unjust gain I was angry, I struck him; I hid my face and was angry, but he went on backsliding in the way of his own heart. I have seen his ways, but I will heal him; I will lead him and restore comfort to him and his mourners, creating the fruit of the lips. Peace, peace, to the far and to the near," says the LORD, "and I will heal him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Punishment did not change his people, but God has seen all their ways and will heal them anyway, giving comfort, praise and peace to near and far.

I was angry, I struck him. God describes the failure of discipline on its own. Because of greed he was angry, he struck, he hid his face, and the man carried on exactly as before. Punishment alone did not produce repentance. Anyone who has tried to change someone by making things unpleasant enough knows the ending of verse 17.

I have seen his ways, but I will heal him. Everything turns on but. God has seen the full record, none of it excused, and the sentence does not go where justice would lead us to expect. Not “therefore I will strike him”, but I will heal him. This is the way back for anyone the chapter has exposed: not a better record brought to God, but the healing the Servant’s wounds have already bought (53:5). What punishment could not do, grace does.

Restore comfort to him and his mourners. The verbs are patient ones: heal, lead, restore comfort. And the comfort reaches past the man to his mourners, who had been grieving over what he had become: a promise to every parent or spouse who has wept over a wandering one.

Creating the fruit of the lips. This fruit is praise (Hebrews 13:15), and God says he creates it: even the thanks is his own work. The doubled peace means complete peace. Paul applies the clause to a church of Jews and Gentiles in the same room: Christ “came and preached peace to you who were far off and peace to those who were near” (Ephesians 2:17). He had first made that peace by his cross (Ephesians 2:14–16), so no one is too far away for it to reach.

verseByVerse.quote: But the wicked are like the tossing sea; for it cannot be quiet, and its waters toss up mire and dirt. There is no peace," says my God, "for the wicked."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Those who refuse God can never be at rest: like the sea, their restlessness churns up their own filth, and there is no peace for them.

The wicked are like the tossing sea. Isaiah does not say the sea will not be quiet; he says it cannot. Restlessness is a condition, not an imposed penalty: a rough sea churns up mire and dirt that was already lying on the bottom. Set it beside verse 2, where the righteous rest in their beds. The chapter has two endings, and the difference is stillness.

No peace for the wicked. The line also closed chapter 48, and here, as there, it marks the end of a section of the book. Peace is a Person’s gift, and it cannot be had while running from him. It is offered to the far and the near; the only one left without it is the one who will not come.

He went there anyway. The One who is high and lifted up, whose name is Holy, keeps a second address in a crushed heart. He could have stayed in the first. Nothing required the eternal God to take a room in the wreckage of people who had put a charm where his word should have hung, and he went there anyway, and called it dwelling. In Jesus he came in person, and stilled a sea that could not be quiet with the words, “Peace! Be still!” (Mark 4:39).

57.theology:
The exhaustion that proves nothing to the exhausted. Verse 10 is the chapter’s sharpest diagnosis. These people are not enjoying their idolatry; it has worn them out, and they refuse to treat the tiredness as evidence that their idols are failing them.

Two addresses. The One who is high and lifted up, whose name is Holy, lives in the high and holy place and also with the contrite and lowly (v. 15). The qualification for God’s presence is not achievement or recovery but having run out of alternatives.

Discipline that failed, and the word that turned it. Punishment on its own does not produce repentance (v. 17). What breaks the deadlock is one small word in verse 18. Justice would have written therefore. Grace writes but.

Peace, and its absence. Peace goes out to the far and the near (v. 19); the wicked are a sea that cannot be still, and the mire it throws up was already lying on its own bed: their unrest comes from within (vv. 20-21).

58.subtitle: The Fast That God Chooses
58.intro:
Where we are. Chapter 57 ended with peace offered to the far and the near, and no peace for the wicked. Chapter 58 turns from open idolatry to something closer to home: a devout people who fast, pray and seek God every day, and cannot understand why he does not seem to notice.

The message. Religion that leaves your neighbour hungry and your workers driven is not what God asked for, however sincere it feels. The fast God chooses is a life opened to others: chains loosed, bread shared, the homeless brought in. To people who live like that, and who delight in his holy day rather than in their own pleasure, he promises light in the darkness, his own presence, and a life like a watered garden.

Why it was said. After the exile the people kept fasts of mourning and longed for the promised restoration, which seemed slow in coming (see the introduction). They concluded that God was not paying attention. Isaiah answers that the delay lay in their own lives, where worship and exploitation had settled down side by side.

How the chapter makes its case. The prophet must shout, because the sin hides under real devotion (vv. 1–2). The people’s complaint is quoted, and God answers by showing what filled their fast days: their own business, driven workers, quarrels and fists (vv. 3–5). Then he defines the fast he chooses, in a cluster of verbs aimed at other people’s good (vv. 6–7). Promises follow, each introduced by then: light like the dawn, healing, God answering “Here I am”, a watered garden and ruins rebuilt (vv. 8–12). The chapter ends with the Sabbath, which tests the same heart from another side (vv. 13–14).

Where it leads. The chapter leads to Christ first by exposing a need: no one has kept this fast as God means it. Jesus did. At Nazareth he took a phrase of verse 6, “to set at liberty those who are oppressed”, into his reading of 61:1 (Luke 4:18), and he went on to loose bonds no one else could undo and to carry the yoke himself. He is also the rest the Sabbath pointed to (Matthew 11:28; Hebrews 4:9–10). His obedience is counted to those who trust him, and his Spirit makes them generous.

For us. Ask the people you live and work with whether your religion makes you kinder. Then open your hand, starting at your own table, as one who has been fed by Christ, and keep the Lord’s Day as a delight, not a duty. The promise still stands: the one who pours himself out for others finds the Lord saying, “Here I am.”

keyVerse.quote: “If you pour yourself out for the hungry and satisfy the desire of the afflicted, then shall your light rise in the darkness and your gloom be as the noonday.”
keyVerse.note: The light rising in darkness is the fruit of self-giving, not self-improvement. The one who pours himself out, giving what he himself needs rather than what he can spare, finds that the light which rises is not his own but the LORD’s. Christ, who poured himself out for us, is the source of that light and the pattern of that giving.

58.reflection:
The people “seek me daily and delight to know my ways” (v. 2), yet God rejects their fasting. How can genuine religious habits sit alongside the exploitation of others without our noticing? Ask yourself the question this chapter raises: would the people who live and work with you say your faith makes you kinder?

Read the list of verbs in verses 6–7. Which of them comes closest to home for you, and why do you think God ends with “not to hide yourself from your own flesh”?

Jesus took words from verse 6 into his sermon at Nazareth (Luke 4:18). How does his life fulfil “the fast that I choose”, and how does his keeping of it free us to obey rather than burden us?

God asks his people to “call the Sabbath a delight” (v. 13). What would it look like for you to make the Lord’s Day a gladness rather than either a rule or just another day?
58.text: <sup>1</sup>"Cry aloud; do not hold back; lift up your voice like a trumpet; declare to my people their transgression, to the house of Jacob their sins.<sup>2</sup>Yet they seek me daily and delight to know my ways, as if they were a nation that did righteousness and did not forsake the judgment of their God; they ask of me righteous judgments; they delight to draw near to God.<sup>3</sup>'Why have we fasted, and you see it not? Why have we humbled ourselves, and you take no knowledge of it?' Behold, in the day of your fast you seek your own pleasure, and oppress all your workers.<sup>4</sup>Behold, you fast only to quarrel and to fight and to hit with a wicked fist. Fasting like yours this day will not make your voice to be heard on high.<sup>5</sup>Is such the fast that I choose, a day for a person to humble himself? Is it to bow down his head like a reed, and to spread sackcloth and ashes under him? Will you call this a fast, and a day acceptable to the LORD?<sup>6</sup>"Is not this the fast that I choose: to loose the bonds of wickedness, to undo the straps of the yoke, to let the oppressed go free, and to break every yoke?<sup>7</sup>Is it not to share your bread with the hungry and bring the homeless poor into your house; when you see the naked, to cover him, and not to hide yourself from your own flesh?<sup>8</sup>Then shall your light break forth like the dawn, and your healing shall spring up speedily; your righteousness shall go before you; the glory of the LORD shall be your rear guard.<sup>9</sup>Then you shall call, and the LORD will answer; you shall cry, and he will say, 'Here I am.' If you take away the yoke from your midst, the pointing of the finger, and speaking wickedness,<sup>10</sup>if you pour yourself out for the hungry and satisfy the desire of the afflicted, then shall your light rise in the darkness and your gloom be as the noonday.<sup>11</sup>And the LORD will guide you continually and satisfy your desire in scorched places and make your bones strong; and you shall be like a watered garden, like a spring of water, whose waters do not fail.<sup>12</sup>And your ancient ruins shall be rebuilt; you shall raise up the foundations of many generations; you shall be called the repairer of the breach, the restorer of streets to dwell in.<sup>13</sup>"If you turn back your foot from the Sabbath, from doing your pleasure on my holy day, and call the Sabbath a delight and the holy day of the LORD honorable; if you honor it, not going your own ways, or seeking your own pleasure, or talking idly;<sup>14</sup>then you shall take delight in the LORD, and I will make you ride on the heights of the earth; I will feed you with the heritage of Jacob your father, for the mouth of the LORD has spoken."

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–7 — Why Have We Fasted, and You See It Not?
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Devotion that ignores injustice is not what God asked for, however sincere it feels. The prophet is told to shout at a people who seek God daily and delight to draw near to him (vv. 1–2), but who complain that he ignores their fasting (v. 3). God names what filled their fast days: their own business, workers oppressed, quarrels and blows, and heads bowed like a reed that straightens as soon as the wind drops (vv. 3–5). Then he says what he meant by a fast: chains loosed and yokes broken, bread shared with the hungry, the homeless brought indoors, the naked clothed, and no hiding from one’s own family (vv. 6–7).
verseByVerse.theology: God does not accuse these sincere people of hypocrisy in the ordinary sense. He tells them what their religion had become: a technique for getting something.
verseByVerse.examples: Verse 7 keeps moving the neighbour closer, until the last clause shuts the final exit: your own relatives, usually the hardest people to be generous to.

verseByVerse.quote: "Cry aloud; do not hold back; lift up your voice like a trumpet; declare to my people their transgression, to the house of Jacob their sins. Yet they seek me daily and delight to know my ways, as if they were a nation that did righteousness and did not forsake the judgment of their God; they ask of me righteous judgments; they delight to draw near to God. 'Why have we fasted, and you see it not? Why have we humbled ourselves, and you take no knowledge of it?' Behold, in the day of your fast you seek your own pleasure, and oppress all your workers.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God tells the prophet to shout at a devout people whose religion is real in form but hollow in life, because their fasting has become a way of putting God in their debt while they exploit others.

Lift up your voice like a trumpet. The volume is set before the message is given. A trumpet is what you sound when a city has to hear something whether it wants to or not.

Yet they seek me daily. Then the shock. The people about to be denounced are the observant ones. They seek God daily, enjoy learning his ways, ask for his rulings and like being near him. If this congregation existed today it would be the one with the well-attended prayer meeting. The words as if carry the whole indictment: the behaviour is entirely consistent with a nation doing righteousness. It is just not one.

Why have we fasted, and you see it not? Their complaint is one most religious people have made privately: I have done my part and nothing has come back. It treats the fast as a payment that puts God in their debt. The law of Moses commanded only one fast a year, on the Day of Atonement, when Israel was to afflict themselves (Leviticus 16:29); after Jerusalem fell, the people added fasts of mourning for the city, and when they later asked Zechariah whether to keep them, they received much the same answer as this (Zechariah 7:3–10).

And oppress all your workers. God answers by pointing to what else they did that day. While they fasted, business continued and the workforce was driven as hard as ever. The religion and the exploitation filled the same day, and nobody in the house saw a connection.

Faith in a sealed compartment. Modern life has a place for religion, and the place is private: faith is fine so long as it stays in the home, the heart and the weekend, and does not interfere with business or the office. Many believers have quietly accepted the arrangement, because it asks for an hour on Sunday and leaves the rest of the week alone. The people of verse 3 had found the ancient version: their fast in one compartment and their wage bill in another. God tears the partition down. The God who hears your prayers also reads your payroll. That sounds like a burden until you see the alternative: a God who cares about one hour a week is too small to be worth worshipping, and too small to help you in the other hundred and sixty-seven. The Lord who would not be confined to the temple worked in a carpenter’s shop, and every part of a Christian’s life belongs to him, because every part of it was bought (1 Corinthians 6:20).

Uncertain wording. The word translated workers is rare. ESV takes it as labourers driven hard; older versions read “you exact all your labours”, that is, you demand everything owed to you. Either way the point is the same: on the day they humbled themselves before God, they pressed others hard.

verseByVerse.quote: Behold, you fast only to quarrel and to fight and to hit with a wicked fist. Fasting like yours this day will not make your voice to be heard on high. Is such the fast that I choose, a day for a person to humble himself? Is it to bow down his head like a reed, and to spread sackcloth and ashes under him? Will you call this a fast, and a day acceptable to the LORD? "Is not this the fast that I choose: to loose the bonds of wickedness, to undo the straps of the yoke, to let the oppressed go free, and to break every yoke? Is it not to share your bread with the hungry and bring the homeless poor into your house; when you see the naked, to cover him, and not to hide yourself from your own flesh?
verseByVerse.commentary:
A fast that makes people quarrelsome and leaves others in chains is worthless to God; the fast he chooses sets people free, feeds the hungry, shelters the homeless and does not turn away from family.

You fast only to quarrel and to fight. Hunger makes people irritable, and Isaiah has noticed: the fast was producing arguments and blows. The devotional exercise was making them worse to live with. Any spiritual discipline can be put to that test, and rarely is: ask the people who share your house whether your religion improves you.

To bow down his head like a reed. A reed bends when the wind blows and straightens the moment it stops. The bowed head and the sackcloth and ashes look perfect and change nothing.

Is not this the fast that I choose? A cluster of verbs, every one aimed at another person’s good. Fasting had been about what a man does to himself; God redefines it as what he does about somebody else’s burden. Bondage appears four times in one verse, because a yoke makes a person carry more than he can and keeps him bent while he does it. The yoke is probably meant literally as well: Israelites forced into service for unpaid debts, whom the law said must go free (Deuteronomy 15:12), and whom Jerusalem in Jeremiah’s day once released and then took back (Jeremiah 34:8–11).

Share your bread with the hungry. Then the demands close in. Not send bread, but share your bread, the loaf already on your table. Bring the homeless poor into your house. Cover the naked man. And not to hide yourself from your own flesh: the relative whose calls are not returned, the brother whose trouble is his own fault. God ends the list closest to home, where it costs most.

The fast the Son kept. When Jesus read from Isaiah at Nazareth, Luke records that he wove a phrase of verse 6, to set at liberty those who are oppressed, into the words of 61:1 (Luke 4:18). The fast God chose is what the Son came to do: he loosed the bonds no one else could undo, and broke the yoke by carrying the weight himself. No reader of this list has kept it as he did; his keeping of it is counted to those who trust him (Philippians 3:9), and the Spirit he gives makes generosity grow in people who were once tight-fisted (Galatians 5:22).

What this looks like. Begin at your own table. Invite the lonely neighbour, the student far from home or the newly widowed man to an ordinary Sunday lunch; the verse says your bread, not a donation passed on. Look at whom you employ. Ask whether the cleaner, the builder or the junior colleague is paid fairly and on time. Budget for it. Set a sum aside for the poor before the month starts, so that a need is met from a plan and not only from a mood. Make the phone call. Ring the relative you have been avoiding and ask what would help. The motive is grace: “though he was rich, yet for your sake he became poor, so that you by his poverty might become rich” (2 Corinthians 8:9). We share our bread as people who have been fed.

Does this mean fasting itself is wrong? No. Jesus assumed his disciples would fast, and told them to do it without show (Matthew 6:16–18; 9:15). Isaiah does not abolish the fast; he tests it by what it does to the people around the one who keeps it.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 8–14 — Then Shall Your Light Rise
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: A life poured out for others is met by God’s light, presence and provision. The promises follow the word then: light breaking like the dawn, quick healing, righteousness going before and the glory of the LORD guarding the rear, and God answering his people’s cry with “Here I am” (vv. 8–9). The condition is repeated, to remove the yoke, the pointing finger and malicious speech, and to pour oneself out for the hungry, with guidance, strength, a watered garden and ruins rebuilt to follow (vv. 9–12). The chapter closes with the Sabbath called a delight, and delight in the LORD himself (vv. 13–14).
verseByVerse.theology: The promises that follow then are not wages. They describe what happens to a life that stops being organised around itself, and their source is the LORD who guides and satisfies (v. 11).
verseByVerse.examples: The servant's answer has become the master's: Here I am (v. 9) is what Isaiah said when God called him, and now God says it to anyone who cries for help.

verseByVerse.quote: Then shall your light break forth like the dawn, and your healing shall spring up speedily; your righteousness shall go before you; the glory of the LORD shall be your rear guard. Then you shall call, and the LORD will answer; you shall cry, and he will say, 'Here I am.' If you take away the yoke from your midst, the pointing of the finger, and speaking wickedness,
verseByVerse.commentary:
When God’s people live for others, his light, healing and protection surround them, and he answers their cry at once with “Here I am.”

Then shall your light break forth like the dawn. The word then does a great deal of work. What follows is not a reward negotiated for good behaviour; it is what happens when a life stops being organised around itself. The light breaks the way dawn arrives: not switched on, but already coming, and unstoppable once it starts. Jesus said the same of his disciples: let your light shine before others, so that they may see your good works and give glory to your Father (Matthew 5:16).

The glory of the LORD shall be your rear guard. Righteousness in front and God’s glory bringing up the rear is the marching order of the exodus, when the pillar of cloud moved round to stand between Israel and the pursuing army (Exodus 14:19–20). A rear guard protects against what comes from behind, which is where a person’s past is, and God takes that position himself.

You shall call, and the LORD will answer. In chapter 6 God asked whom he should send, and a young man in the temple said, Here I am. Now, as at 52:6, the words have changed mouths: the servant’s answer has become the master’s. God says them to ordinary people who have done nothing more impressive than shout for help. Not “I will look into it”, but the shortest sentence available: I am here. Whatever else this chapter demands, it ends the fear of praying into an empty room.

verseByVerse.quote: if you pour yourself out for the hungry and satisfy the desire of the afflicted, then shall your light rise in the darkness and your gloom be as the noonday. And the LORD will guide you continually and satisfy your desire in scorched places and make your bones strong; and you shall be like a watered garden, like a spring of water, whose waters do not fail. And your ancient ruins shall be rebuilt; you shall raise up the foundations of many generations; you shall be called the repairer of the breach, the restorer of streets to dwell in.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Those who give themselves to meet others’ needs will find their own darkness lifting, God guiding and refreshing them, and broken places rebuilt through them.

If you take away the yoke from your midst. The condition is repeated with two additions: the pointing of the finger, the gesture of contempt and accusation, and speaking wickedness. A community can share bread and still sneer and slander; God wants both ended.

If you pour yourself out for the hungry. The Hebrew is literally offer your soul, a word that can also mean appetite: the giver hands over what he was hungry for himself, not the surplus at the end of the month.

Then shall your light rise in the darkness. The person who empties himself for the hungry is told that his own darkness will lift. This is not a technique for curing gloom, and nobody in a dark season should hear it as a demand to earn the light. But a life turned outward is turned towards the God who is light, and the way out of gloom often runs through meeting somebody else’s need. Christ poured himself out, and he has become a spring that does not run dry (John 4:14).

Satisfy your desire in scorched places. Nothing here promises easier circumstances. The satisfaction comes in scorched places, not instead of them; a watered garden in a drought is a garden with a source somewhere else.

The repairer of the breach. The last promise is a pair of unglamorous titles. A breach is the hole in a city wall that everything comes through; a street fit to live in is the plainest measure of whether a community works. God does not offer these people fame. He offers them the name of the person who fixed the hole.

verseByVerse.quote: "If you turn back your foot from the Sabbath, from doing your pleasure on my holy day, and call the Sabbath a delight and the holy day of the LORD honorable; if you honor it, not going your own ways, or seeking your own pleasure, or talking idly; then you shall take delight in the LORD, and I will make you ride on the heights of the earth; I will feed you with the heritage of Jacob your father, for the mouth of the LORD has spoken."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Keeping God’s holy day with delight, rather than using it for our own pleasure and business, tests the same heart as the true fast, and leads to delight in the LORD himself.

From the fast to the Sabbath. A chapter about feeding the hungry ends with a day off, and the two belong together. Seeking your own pleasure already appeared in verse 3, on the fast day: the same self-seeking, on a different day. To turn back your foot is to stop trampling the day with ordinary business.

Call the Sabbath a delight. The instruction is less about what may be done between Friday evening and Saturday evening than about calling the day a delight. God is not asking for a grim observance; he asks that the day when his people produce nothing should be the day they like best.

What stopping confesses. To down tools for a whole day is to say out loud that the world will keep turning without your effort, and that the supply does not depend on you. It is the same confession made by the man who gives his loaf away in verse 7. One says it by resting, the other by giving, and neither is open to a person who believes he is holding everything up.

Then you shall take delight in the LORD. Delight in the day turns into delight in God himself, which was the point of the day all along. Riding on the heights is Moses’ picture of a people carried over the high ground and fed on the produce of the land (Deuteronomy 32:13), and the final line settles whether it will happen: the mouth of the LORD has spoken.

The day that says you are not a machine. Our devices never close and our work comes home in our pockets. The Sabbath was a strange gift in the ancient world, and it is stranger still in ours. The Jewish writer Abraham Joshua Heschel called it a palace in time: other peoples made holy places of stone, and Israel was given a holy day that no army could knock down or carry into exile. The inability to stop is rarely just busyness; often it is fear: if I stop producing, who am I? The day answers by making you stop, and letting you find that the world is still turning, God is still there, and you are still loved.

Rest on a finished work. For a Christian that rest stands on a finished work. On the cross Jesus said, “It is finished” (John 19:30), and whoever believes it can put down the tools without guilt, because the one work that had to be done has been done. Nothing in this chapter was earned: the bread was his before it was shared, the day was his before it was kept, and the light that rises in the darkness was never the giver’s own.

How do I call the day a delight? The New Testament carries over the gift of rest and the gathering of God’s people rather than the details of Israel’s calendar (see below), so the question is how to make the Lord’s Day a gladness rather than a rule. Plan it the night before. Shop, finish the emails and set out what the children need, so the morning is not a scramble. Put worship first. Gather with the church, “not neglecting to meet together” (Hebrews 10:25), and let the rest of the day grow around that. Stop producing. Close the laptop and leave the work phone in a drawer. Fill it with good things. A long meal, a walk, a visit to someone housebound, an unhurried hour with a book or a psalm. And hold it as a gift, not a test: “The Sabbath was made for man, not man for the Sabbath” (Mark 2:27), and Jesus offers the deeper rest the day points to: “Come to me, all who labor and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest” (Matthew 11:28).

Where Christians differ: does the Sabbath still bind Christians? It was the sign of the covenant at Sinai (Exodus 31:13). Many godly Christians, with the Westminster Confession and the 1689 London Baptist Confession, hold that the Lord’s Day is the Christian Sabbath, kept under the fourth commandment; Seventh-day Adventists keep Saturday. Others note that the New Testament calls Sabbaths “a shadow of the things to come, but the substance belongs to Christ” (Colossians 2:16–17).

This commentary’s view: the Sabbath is fulfilled in Christ, our rest (Hebrews 4:9–10), so no day binds the conscience (Romans 14:5), while the Lord’s Day remains a gift that Christians gladly set apart for worship and rest. Faithful believers differ here. What abides is the heart Isaiah describes: delight in the LORD above our own pleasure, and glad gathering with his people.

58.theology:
Sincere religion aimed at the wrong thing. The people denounced in this chapter seek God daily and delight to draw near (v. 2), and their complaint is genuine. What God exposes is what the fast was for: it had become a payment for which they expected a return, which is why its failure to deliver was the only thing they noticed about it.

The fast that was chosen. Verses 6-7 replace a show of humility with eight actions, every one of them aimed at a person’s good, and the neighbour gets closer with each. This is the principle Jesus puts at the centre of the last judgment, where the hungry fed and the naked clothed turn out to have been himself (Matt. 25:31-46).

Light rising out of what was given away. The promises of verses 8-12 are not payment; the light that rises is the LORD’s, and the rear guard is his glory.
