Why the Sabbath closes a chapter about the poor. The phrase seeking your own pleasure appears both on the fast day (v. 3) and on the holy day (v. 13), which is the clue that these are one subject: resting and giving both confess that our provision comes from God and not from our own effort.

59.subtitle: Your Iniquities Have Separated You
59.intro:
Where we are. Chapter 58 promised light and answered prayer to a people whose religion was hollow. Chapter 59 takes up the question behind their complaint: if God is able to save and willing to hear, why has the promised salvation not come?

The message. The problem is not that God’s arm is too short or his ear too dull; our sins have built a wall between us and him. That wall cannot be taken down from our side, because no one is righteous enough even to plead for the rest. So God comes himself. His own arm brings salvation, he arms himself with righteousness, and a Redeemer comes to Zion for those who turn from sin, with the promise that his Spirit and his word will never leave them.

Why it was said. The returned exiles had heard the great promises of chapters 40–55, yet life among the ruins looked nothing like them (see the introduction). They were tempted to conclude that God could not or would not keep his word. Isaiah tells them the truth about themselves and the better truth about God.

How the chapter makes its case. First the diagnosis: God is able, but iniquity has made a separation (vv. 1–2), and the evidence is everywhere, in violence, lies and corrupt courts, in schemes as deadly as adders’ eggs and as useless as spiders’ webs, in feet that do not know the way of peace (vv. 3–8). Then the people speak for themselves, confessing that they grope like the blind at noon, that their sins testify against them, and that truth has stumbled in the public square (vv. 9–15). Finally God acts: seeing no one to intercede, he arms himself, repays his enemies and sends a Redeemer to Zion with an everlasting covenant of Spirit and word (vv. 15–21).

Where it leads. The chapter leads to Christ in two ways. It exposes the need: Paul uses verses 7–8 to prove that all, Jew and Gentile, are under sin (Romans 3:15–17). And it gives a direct promise: the arm of the LORD who saves alone is the Servant of 53:1, who “makes intercession for the transgressors” (53:12), and Paul quotes verse 20 of the Deliverer who takes away his people’s sins (Romans 11:26–27). The armour God wears here is the armour he later gives his people (Ephesians 6:14–17).

For us. When God seems far away, the first question is not whether he is able but what stands between us. Confess your sins honestly, saying “we” and not only “they”. Then look to the Redeemer who came through the wall from the other side, and trust his Spirit and word to keep you and your children.

keyVerse.quote: “Behold, the LORD’s hand is not shortened, that it cannot save, or his ear dull, that it cannot hear; but your iniquities have made a separation between you and your God.”
keyVerse.note: These two verses diagnose the human condition precisely: the problem is never God’s ability or willingness, but always the sin that makes the gap. The rest of the chapter shows that God does not wait for the gap to be bridged from our side; he crosses it himself, dressed for battle, as Redeemer. In Christ the arm that was never too short reached all the way.

59.reflection:
Verse 1 answers two suspicions people have when prayer seems unanswered: that God cannot help, or that he is not listening. Which of these do you find yourself thinking, and how does verse 2 change the question?

In verses 9–15 the people stop saying “they” and start saying “we”. Why is it so much easier to describe the sins of others than to confess our own? What would honest confession look like for you, or for your church?

“He saw that there was no man, and wondered that there was no one to intercede; then his own arm brought him salvation” (v. 16). How does this verse point to Jesus, and what does it say about our ability to save ourselves?

Paul gives believers the same armour God wears here (Ephesians 6:14–17). What difference does it make that the righteousness and salvation we put on were first won by Christ? And how does the promise of verse 21 encourage you to pray for your children and grandchildren?

Their works are works of iniquity, and deeds of violence are in their hands.<sup>7</sup>Their feet run to evil, and they are swift to shed innocent blood; their thoughts are thoughts of iniquity; desolation and destruction are in their highways.<sup>8</sup>The way of peace they do not know, and there is no justice in their paths; they have made their roads crooked; no one who treads on them knows peace.<sup>9</sup>Therefore justice is far from us, and righteousness does not overtake us; we hope for light, and behold, darkness, and for brightness, but we walk in gloom.<sup>10</sup>We grope for the wall like the blind; we grope like those who have no eyes; we stumble at noon as in the twilight, among those in full vigor we are like dead men.<sup>11</sup>We all growl like bears; we moan and moan like doves; we hope for justice, but there is none; for salvation, but it is far from us.<sup>12</sup>For our transgressions are multiplied before you, and our sins testify against us; for our transgressions are with us, and we know our iniquities:<sup>13</sup>transgressing, and denying the LORD, and turning back from following our God, speaking oppression and revolt, conceiving and uttering from the heart lying words.<sup>14</sup>Justice is turned back, and righteousness stands far away; for truth has stumbled in the public squares, and uprightness cannot enter.<sup>15</sup>Truth is lacking, and he who departs from evil makes himself a prey. The LORD saw it, and it displeased him that there was no justice.<sup>16</sup>He saw that there was no man, and wondered that there was no one to intercede; then his own arm brought him salvation, and his righteousness upheld him.<sup>17</sup>He put on righteousness as a breastplate, and a helmet of salvation on his head; he put on garments of vengeance for clothing, and wrapped himself in zeal as a cloak.<sup>18</sup>According to their deeds, so will he repay, wrath to his adversaries, repayment to his enemies; to the coastlands he will render repayment.<sup>19</sup>So they shall fear the name of the LORD from the west, and his glory from the rising of the sun; for he will come like a rushing stream, which the wind of the LORD drives.<sup>20</sup>"And a Redeemer will come to Zion, to those in Jacob who turn from transgression," declares the LORD.<sup>21</sup>"And as for me, this is my covenant with them," says the LORD: "My Spirit that is upon you, and my words that I have put in your mouth, shall not depart out of your mouth, or out of the mouth of your offspring, or out of the mouth of your children's offspring," says the LORD, "from this time forth and forevermore."

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–8 — Not a Short Hand but a Wall
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God is fully able to save and to hear; what stands between him and his people is their sin. The chapter clears God of two suspicions people rarely voice, a hand too short and an ear too dull (v. 1), and locates the problem: iniquities have made a separation and hidden his face (v. 2). The evidence follows: hands stained with blood, lying lips and courts where no one pleads honestly (vv. 3–4); schemes like adders’ eggs that kill and spiders’ webs that clothe no one (vv. 5–6); feet that run to evil and roads so crooked that no one on them knows peace (vv. 7–8).
verseByVerse.theology: The whole diagnosis turns on the difference between distance and obstruction. God has not moved and has not gone deaf. Something has been built between him and us, and we built it.
verseByVerse.examples: The two pictures in verses 5-6 are about wasted skill. These people are not idle. They are busy making things that are either lethal or useless.

verseByVerse.quote: Behold, the LORD's hand is not shortened, that it cannot save, or his ear dull, that it cannot hear; but your iniquities have made a separation between you and your God, and your sins have hidden his face from you so that he does not hear. For your hands are defiled with blood and your fingers with iniquity; your lips have spoken lies; your tongue mutters wickedness. No one enters suit justly; no one goes to law honestly; they rely on empty pleas, they speak lies, they conceive mischief and give birth to iniquity.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God is able to save and ready to hear; it is our sins that have built a wall between us and him, and the evidence of them is everywhere.

The LORD’s hand is not shortened. Two suspicions are answered before they are spoken. When prayer goes unanswered the mind offers two explanations: God cannot do anything, or God is not listening. Isaiah names both, a short arm and a dull ear, and rules both out. The great promises of chapters 40 to 55 had been given, and life among the ruins still looked nothing like them, so the question was whether God could not or would not keep his word (compare 50:2).

Your iniquities have made a separation. The important word is separation. Something has been built, and it was built from our side, not God’s. That is the pastoral value of the verse and its sting: it refuses to let a person conclude that heaven is indifferent, and it refuses to let him conclude that nothing is wrong. The wall is real, and it stands on our sins (compare Psalm 66:18).

If God is there, why is he so hard to find? It is one of the commonest reasons people give for not believing: if God wanted to be known, surely he would make himself plain. Verse 2 does not deny the hiddenness; it locates it. Pascal argued that God has given light enough for those who want to see and darkness enough for those who would rather not, so that he is found by those who seek him with all their heart. A God who overwhelmed us with proof would get our compliance without our love. So when he did come out of hiding, he came not in a blaze across the sky but as a man within reach, who could be touched, ignored or nailed to a beam. The wall was real, and he came through it from the other side (v. 20).

Your hands are defiled with blood. The catalogue moves over the body, hands, fingers, lips and tongue, and then into the courts, which met at the city gate and were the one place an ordinary person could go for protection. Everybody is bringing a lawsuit, and nobody an honest one.

They conceive mischief and give birth to iniquity. The last phrase is a picture of birth: mischief conceived and iniquity delivered. These are not accidents. Something was carried, on purpose, for as long as it took (compare James 1:15).

verseByVerse.quote: They hatch adders' eggs; they weave the spider's web; he who eats their eggs dies, and from one that is crushed a viper is hatched. Their webs will not serve as clothing; men will not cover themselves with what they make. Their works are works of iniquity, and deeds of violence are in their hands. Their feet run to evil, and they are swift to shed innocent blood; their thoughts are thoughts of iniquity; desolation and destruction are in their highways. The way of peace they do not know, and there is no justice in their paths; they have made their roads crooked; no one who treads on them knows peace.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The schemes of the wicked are deadly to others and useless to themselves, and their whole way of life leads away from peace.

They hatch adders’ eggs. Two pictures, both of effort that produces nothing anyone can use. The eggs are the deadlier image, and the detail in the middle is exact: crushing one does not make it safe; it only lets the viper out early. Some evils cannot be neutralised by force; handling them roughly brings forward the moment they bite.

They weave the spider’s web. The web is the sadder one. Spider silk is a genuine marvel, spun with real skill, and Isaiah’s verdict is domestic and devastating: you cannot make a shirt out of it. A lifetime of clever, delicate work, and nobody is any warmer.

Their feet run to evil. Paul lifts verses 7–8 almost word for word into Romans, where he strings passages together to prove that Jew and Gentile alike are under sin: “in their paths are ruin and misery, and the way of peace they have not known” (Romans 3:15–17). He agrees with Isaiah’s diagnosis and extends it to the whole human race. The roads are crooked, and everyone who walks them loses his peace.

In everyday life. Put the question to your own week. Of the things you are spinning, how many would cover anybody? The answer is not more spinning but the Redeemer of verse 20, who is himself our peace (Ephesians 2:14), and whose Spirit (v. 21) produces work that really does other people good.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 9–15 — We Grope for the Wall Like the Blind
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The people stop blaming others and confess their own sin. From verse 9 the speakers say “we”. Justice and light are far away, and they grope for the wall like the blind, stumbling at noon (vv. 9–10). They growl like bears in anger and moan like doves in grief, hoping for salvation that does not come (v. 11). Then the confession becomes specific: our transgressions are many and our sins testify against us, rebellion against the LORD and lies spoken from the heart (vv. 12–13). The result is a society where justice is turned back, truth stumbles in the public square, and the man who turns from evil becomes prey (vv. 14–15).
verseByVerse.theology: This is the turning point of the chapter, and it is a change of pronoun: only after the speakers say we and include themselves in the charge does God act (v. 16).

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore justice is far from us, and righteousness does not overtake us; we hope for light, and behold, darkness, and for brightness, but we walk in gloom. We grope for the wall like the blind; we grope like those who have no eyes; we stumble at noon as in the twilight, among those in full vigor we are like dead men. We all growl like bears; we moan and moan like doves; we hope for justice, but there is none; for salvation, but it is far from us. For our transgressions are multiplied before you, and our sins testify against us; for our transgressions are with us, and we know our iniquities: transgressing, and denying the LORD, and turning back from following our God, speaking oppression and revolt, conceiving and uttering from the heart lying words. Justice is turned back, and righteousness stands far away; for truth has stumbled in the public squares, and uprightness cannot enter. Truth is lacking, and he who departs from evil makes himself a prey. The LORD saw it, and it displeased him that there was no justice.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The people confess as one that they are lost in darkness because of their own sins, and that truth and justice have collapsed among them, so that whoever turns from evil becomes a target.

Now it is we. Everything up to verse 9 has been you and they, and a reader can hear eight verses of that without being implicated. From here it is we. Ezra and Daniel prayed the same way, owning sins they had not personally committed (Ezra 9:6; Daniel 9:5).

We grope for the wall like the blind. The wall of verse 2 returns, and now they are feeling along it with their hands, like men who know the room and cannot find the door. Stumbling at noon is worse than stumbling at night: the light is at its best and they still cannot see.

We all growl like bears. The bear is the anger, low and dangerous; the dove is the grief, going on and on. They usually come from the same people, often on the same day.

Our sins testify against us. The confession of verses 12–13 is unhurried and names particular sins instead of speaking vaguely: rebellion, denying the LORD, oppression, lies conceived in the heart. Honest confession always does; and “if we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins” (1 John 1:9).

Truth has stumbled in the public squares. Verse 14 sums up a society coming apart: truth has fallen over in the market square in front of everybody and is left lying there, and honesty is refused entry at the gate. The last line describes the cost of decency when everything else has gone. The man who walks away from a dishonest arrangement is not admired; he becomes a target. Anyone who has declined to sign something at work and then watched the room reorganise itself around him knows this verse from the inside.

After truth. In 2016 Oxford Dictionaries chose “post-truth” as its word of the year, for a public life in which feelings and loyalties count for more than facts. Isaiah points deeper than technology or politicians. Truth stumbles in the square when people no longer think they will answer to anyone for what they say. If there is no God, truth becomes whatever the loudest voice can make stick. The gospel puts a face on the reality that does not bend to our preferences. When the Truth stood in a public court in Jerusalem, Pilate asked, “What is truth?” (John 18:38), and the crowd chose the lie. Jesus let himself be condemned by false witnesses, so that people who have loved lies could be forgiven and made people of the truth.

Uncertain wording. In verse 10 the word ESV renders among those in full vigor occurs only here. Most take it as “among the robust”; older versions have “in desolate places”. The sense of the line is clear either way: they are like dead men while still alive.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 16–21 — His Own Arm Brought Him Salvation
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: When no one can save, God saves by his own arm and comes as Redeemer. The LORD sees that there is no justice and no one to intercede, and wonders at it; so his own arm brings salvation (vv. 15–16). He arms himself with righteousness, salvation, vengeance and zeal, and repays his enemies to the ends of the earth (vv. 17–18). His name will be feared from west to east, for he comes like a rushing stream driven by his wind (v. 19). Then the promise the chapter has climbed towards: a Redeemer will come to Zion for those who turn from sin (v. 20), with a covenant that his Spirit and words will never leave his people or their children (v. 21).
verseByVerse.theology: Paul hands this armour to the church at Ephesus (Eph. 6:14-17), and the order is the thing to remember: God wore it first, into a battle nobody else would fight.
verseByVerse.examples: In Israel a kinsman-redeemer bought back the land or the freedom a relative had lost and could never recover himself (Lev. 25:25, 47-49). Verse 20 gives God himself that part to play for his people.

verseByVerse.quote: He saw that there was no man, and wondered that there was no one to intercede; then his own arm brought him salvation, and his righteousness upheld him. He put on righteousness as a breastplate, and a helmet of salvation on his head; he put on garments of vengeance for clothing, and wrapped himself in zeal as a cloak. According to their deeds, so will he repay, wrath to his adversaries, repayment to his enemies; to the coastlands he will render repayment.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Finding no one to stand in the gap, God saves by his own arm, clothing himself with righteousness and salvation and coming to judge his enemies.

Wondered that there was no one to intercede. God looks for one honest advocate to stand in the gap and plead, finds none, and wondered. It is a startling word to use of God: the vacancy was so complete that it was remarkable.

His own arm brought him salvation. The logic of the whole Bible in one sentence: there is no man, so God does it himself. No committee, no coalition, no faithful few found at the last minute.

The arm of the LORD. Isaiah has already said who that arm is. “To whom has the arm of the LORD been revealed?” he asked of the Servant who was pierced for our transgressions (53:1, 5), and John applies the question to Jesus (John 12:37–38). The word for intercede is the one used of that Servant, who “makes intercession for the transgressors” (53:12). There was no man to stand in the gap, so God became one.

He put on righteousness as a breastplate. Then God arms himself. The breastplate covers the vital organs and the helmet the head, and they are made not of metal but of character: righteousness and salvation, the two things this world had run out of. Over them go garments of vengeance and a cloak of zeal. God’s salvation and his judgment are one campaign: he repays his enemies according to their deeds, as far as the coastlands. The same Christ who saves will come again to judge (Acts 17:31).

Before the armour of God. Every Christian taught to put on the armour of God should read this verse first, for Paul takes the breastplate and helmet from here (Ephesians 6:14, 17; 1 Thessalonians 5:8). It is not equipment for a battle believers must win. It is the uniform of the one who went out alone and won it. The righteousness the people lacked in verses 3–15 was supplied by the one who wore it, and it is counted to those who trust him.

verseByVerse.quote: So they shall fear the name of the LORD from the west, and his glory from the rising of the sun; for he will come like a rushing stream, which the wind of the LORD drives. "And a Redeemer will come to Zion, to those in Jacob who turn from transgression," declares the LORD. "And as for me, this is my covenant with them," says the LORD: "My Spirit that is upon you, and my words that I have put in your mouth, shall not depart out of your mouth, or out of the mouth of your offspring, or out of the mouth of your children's offspring," says the LORD, "from this time forth and forevermore."
verseByVerse.commentary:
God will come with irresistible power, and a Redeemer will come to Zion for those who turn from sin, with an everlasting covenant that his Spirit and his words will never leave his people.

He will come like a rushing stream. God is feared from one horizon to the other, and his arrival is described as weather: a flash flood in a dry country, water filling a wadi (a dry riverbed) that was a footpath an hour earlier, moving too fast to argue with.

A Redeemer will come to Zion. This is the sentence the chapter has been building towards since verse 2. The separation was made from the human side, and it is crossed from the other side. Redeemer means what it has meant since chapter 41: the near relative who pays what his family cannot.

Paul’s use of it. Paul quotes it as the guarantee of Israel’s future (Romans 11:26). His wording follows the Greek Old Testament (the Septuagint, the translation most of his readers used), which has the Redeemer come from Zion and banish ungodliness from Jacob; the Hebrew has him come to Zion, for those who turn. Together they say that his people turn, and that their turning is his gift.

My Spirit that is upon you. The chapter opened with a wall that shut God out and closes with God moving in to stay. The Spirit and the words are promised to remain not for a lifetime but through a child and a grandchild and beyond the last name anyone present could have listed: a promise parents may plead for their children (Acts 2:39). The Spirit who rests on God’s people is the one who produces the truth and justice the chapter found missing.

The whole chapter in Christ. The one who looked for a man and found nobody did not lower the requirement or wait for a better generation. He put on the breastplate himself, went out alone, came to Zion as its kinsman, and then moved into the very space the sin had occupied. The hand was never too short. It reached the whole way.

Where Christians differ: when Paul ties this verse to the day when “all Israel will be saved” (Romans 11:26), what does he mean? Calvin read “all Israel” as the whole church; others take it as the elect Jews of every age; dispensationalists add a separate national plan for Israel.

This commentary’s view: held with humility, Romans 11 most naturally looks for a future turning of many Jewish people to Christ, within the one people of God, and faithful Reformed Christians have held each of the other views. Isaiah’s own words limit the promise to those in Jacob who turn from transgression: it comes by repentance and faith.

Uncertain wording. Verse 19 can be read two ways. ESV has God coming like a rushing stream, which the wind of the LORD drives. The older rendering, familiar from the King James Version, reads, “When the enemy shall come in like a flood, the Spirit of the LORD shall lift up a standard against him.” The Hebrew word can mean “enemy” or “narrow” (a pent-up stream), and the verb “drive” or “raise a banner”. Most modern translations follow ESV, which fits the picture of God himself coming in power.

59.theology:
Not distance but obstruction. What exists is a separation built out of iniquity (v. 2). That is a harder diagnosis than divine indifference and a far more hopeful one, because a wall can be dealt with and an absent God cannot. Everything from verse 16 onwards is God dealing with it.

The pronoun that changes everything. Verses 1-8 can be read at a safe distance; from verse 9 it is we, and nothing in the chapter moves until then. Confessing together, saying we, is not a literary device here; it is the doorway to what follows, because God has promised mercy to those who confess (Psalm 32:5).

He saw that there was no man. God searches for one intercessor and finds none, and the vacancy is filled the only way it could be: his own arm brought him salvation (v. 16). Where no one could stand in the gap, God stood there himself, in the Servant who bore the sin of many and made intercession for the transgressors (53:12).

From a wall to God living with his people. The crossing is made from God’s side, not by a people who have first cleared the obstruction away (v. 20). The final verse then fills the space the sin had occupied: the Spirit and the words of God, staying with his people from now on and forever.

60.subtitle: Arise, Shine
60.intro:
Where we are. Chapter 59 ended with the Redeemer coming to Zion and God’s Spirit resting on his people for ever. Chapter 60 shows what happens next: the dark, ruined city is lit by the glory of the LORD, and the whole world comes to her. With chapters 61 and 62 it forms the bright centre of the book’s last section.

The message. God’s light has dawned on his people, so they are to rise and shine, though darkness still covers the earth. The nations will be drawn to that light, bringing home Zion’s scattered children and their wealth to honour God. The city once forsaken will become beautiful, safe and righteous, with walls called Salvation and gates called Praise, and in the end it will need no sun, because the LORD himself will be its everlasting light.

Why it was said. The returned exiles were few, poor and surrounded by contempt, living in a city with broken walls and no one passing through (see the introduction). They needed to know that their smallness was not the end of the story, and that God would yet make his people the joy of the earth.

How the chapter makes its case. The call to arise rests on a fact: your light has come. Nations and kings come to the brightness, sons and daughters come home, and caravans and ships bring gold, frankincense and flocks for God’s altar (vv. 1–9). Then everything is reversed: foreigners rebuild the walls, the gates stand open day and night, Lebanon’s timber adorns the sanctuary, and the children of oppressors bow, so that Zion knows the LORD as Saviour and Redeemer (vv. 10–16). Finally every material is upgraded, violence ends, the sun and moon give way to God’s own light, and the people are all righteous, God’s own planting (vv. 17–22).

Where it leads. The chapter leads to Christ by direct promise, fulfilled in two stages. When he was born, the first Gentiles came to the light with gold and frankincense (Matthew 2:11), and Simeon called him “a light for revelation to the Gentiles” (Luke 2:32). Since then the nations have been streaming in through the gospel. And John takes up the chapter for the new Jerusalem, whose gates are never shut and which needs no sun, “for the glory of God gives it light, and its lamp is the Lamb” (Revelation 21:23).

For us. The church’s light is borrowed: we shine only by facing Christ, so arise and let his glory be seen in you, especially in dark places. If you feel small and overlooked, remember that God makes the least one a clan, in his own time.

keyVerse.quote: “Arise, shine, for your light has come, and the glory of the LORD has risen upon you.”
keyVerse.note: The two commands, arise and shine, follow a statement of fact: your light has come. Rising and shining respond to what God has done; they do not earn his presence. Paul echoes the language: “Awake, O sleeper, and arise from the dead, and Christ will shine on you” (Ephesians 5:14). The light that has come is Christ himself, the glory of the LORD in a human face.

60.reflection:
“Arise, shine, for your light has come” (v. 1). Why does it matter that the command comes after the fact? How does this order free you from trying to produce your own light?

The nations come not because Zion is impressive but because “the LORD will arise upon you” (v. 2). What does this mean for how a church, or a Christian, attracts others to Christ today?

Gates that are “open continually” (v. 11) and walls called “Salvation” (v. 18) describe a city with nothing left to fear. Which of these promises do you most long to see, and how does Revelation 21 show where they are heading?

“The least one shall become a clan … in its time I will hasten it” (v. 22). Where do you feel small, slow or overlooked in your work for God, and how does this promise encourage you to keep going?

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God’s glory has dawned on his people, and the nations are drawn to it. Two commands open the chapter, and both rest on something already done: arise, shine, for your light has come (v. 1). Verse 2 is honest that darkness still covers the earth, but the LORD rises on one place and is seen there. Nations and kings travel towards the brightness (v. 3), scattered sons and daughters come home (v. 4), and the wealth of sea and land is turned towards Zion: caravans bring gold, frankincense and the praises of the LORD (vv. 5–6), flocks come for God’s altar (v. 7), and ships fly home like doves, carrying her children back for the sake of the LORD who has made her beautiful (vv. 8–9).
verseByVerse.theology: The light is not Zion's. She is told to shine because the glory of the LORD has risen upon her, and everything the nations come for is his light, not hers.
verseByVerse.examples: The doves of verse 8 are birds flying home. The nations are not wandering into a strange city; they are coming to the place they were always meant to land.

verseByVerse.quote: Arise, shine, for your light has come, and the glory of the LORD has risen upon you. For behold, darkness shall cover the earth, and thick darkness the peoples; but the LORD will arise upon you, and his glory will be seen upon you. And nations shall come to your light, and kings to the brightness of your rising.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God’s light has already dawned on his people, so they are to rise and shine; though darkness covers the earth, the nations will come to the light God has put on them.

Arise, shine, for your light has come. Two commands, and both come after the fact. Zion is not told to generate light so that God will come; she is told to get up because he already has. The whole Christian life follows that order: first what God has done, then what we are to do.

Darkness shall cover the earth. Verse 2 does not promise that the darkness lifts. The picture is of a covered earth with one lit place in it, and the light is not the city’s own doing: the verb is the one used of the sun coming up, which no one has ever had to help. That is a relief for anyone who has felt responsible for producing light of his own. Zion is like the moon: all its brightness comes from the sun it is facing.

Nations shall come to your light. What draws the world is not how good Zion is but the light God has shone on her. Nobody in this chapter is persuaded by an argument; they see something and start walking. The arrival of the nations has been promised since Abraham was told that all the families of the earth would be blessed through him (Genesis 12:3).

The light has a name. Jesus said, “I am the light of the world” (John 8:12), and the old man Simeon, holding him, called him “a light for revelation to the Gentiles” (Luke 2:32). The church shines only as it faces him: God “has shone in our hearts to give the light of the knowledge of the glory of God in the face of Jesus Christ” (2 Corinthians 4:6).

Where Christians differ: is this chapter fulfilled in the church or in a future Israel? Premillennial and dispensational readers see a literal Jerusalem restored in a future earthly kingdom, with the nations serving Israel.

This commentary’s view: Revelation takes this chapter up for the new Jerusalem: “By its light will the nations walk”, and it needs no sun, for the Lamb is its lamp (Revelation 21:23–26). Zion is the people of God, and the nations streaming in are the fruit of Christ’s mission, now and in the new creation, where Jew and Gentile walk in one light. Faithful Christians differ on Israel’s future, but the New Testament itself carries these images into the new Jerusalem.

verseByVerse.quote: Lift up your eyes all around, and see; they all gather together, they come to you; your sons shall come from afar, and your daughters shall be carried on the hip. Then you shall see and be radiant; your heart shall thrill and exult, because the abundance of the sea shall be turned to you, the wealth of the nations shall come to you. A multitude of camels shall cover you, the young camels of Midian and Ephah; all those from Sheba shall come. They shall bring gold and frankincense, and shall bring good news, the praises of the LORD. All the flocks of Kedar shall be gathered to you; the rams of Nebaioth shall minister to you; they shall come up with acceptance on my altar, and I will beautify my beautiful house. Who are these that fly like a cloud, and like doves to their windows? For the coastlands shall hope for me, the ships of Tarshish first, to bring your children from afar, their silver and gold with them, for the name of the LORD your God, and for the Holy One of Israel, because he has made you beautiful.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Zion’s scattered children come home and the wealth of the nations flows to her, as peoples who had been strangers and enemies come to worship the LORD who has made her beautiful.

Lift up your eyes all around, and see. The command is to look up, which is what a person stops doing when things have gone badly. The first thing on the horizon is not an army but a family: sons walking, daughters small enough to be carried on somebody’s hip.

Your heart shall thrill and exult. Thrill is a heart that trembles: not satisfaction but the shock of seeing what you had stopped expecting.

They shall bring gold and frankincense. Then the caravan from the south, carried by peoples long Israel’s enemies or strangers. Midian and Ephah descended from Abraham through Keturah (Genesis 25:1–4), Kedar and Nebaioth (v. 7) from Abraham through Ishmael (Genesis 25:13), and Sheba was the incense kingdom of south Arabia whose queen once brought gold and spices to Solomon (1 Kings 10:1–2): Abraham’s scattered families are coming to worship. And what the camels carry is not only cargo: they bring good news, the praises of the LORD, arriving already singing about the God they have come to see. Their rams are accepted on God’s altar, outsiders welcomed into worship, as 56:7 promised.

Gold and frankincense in Bethlehem. Some seven hundred years later, the first Gentiles on record to come looking for the king of the Jews arrived with gold and frankincense in their luggage (Matthew 2:11). The direction of travel is the one Isaiah describes, and it has not stopped.

Who are these that fly like a cloud? The last picture is sails on the horizon, white and fast like doves heading home to their nesting holes. The ships of Tarshish, the great ocean-going traders, carry Zion’s children home. And the final clause settles whose city this is: the beauty that has drawn half the world is something God did to her, because he has made you beautiful.
verseByVerse.note: Midian, Ephah and Sheba were in Arabia; Kedar and Nebaioth were desert tribes.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 10–16 — Gates That Are Never Shut
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Everything that was done to Zion is reversed, so that she will know the LORD as her Saviour and Redeemer. Foreigners rebuild the walls and kings serve, for God who struck in wrath now shows mercy (v. 10). The gates stay open day and night to receive the wealth of the nations, while those who refuse will perish (vv. 11–12). Lebanon’s timber beautifies the sanctuary (v. 13); the children of oppressors come bowing and call her the City of the LORD (v. 14). The forsaken city becomes a joy from age to age, fed by nations and kings (vv. 15–16). The point of it all: you shall know that I, the LORD, am your Saviour and your Redeemer (v. 16).
verseByVerse.theology: Verse 15 names what had actually been wrong, and it is not only the ruins. No one passing through: the city had become a place nobody had any reason to visit. The promise answers the emptiness rather than the rubble.
verseByVerse.examples: Verse 12 is a hard sentence and should not be skated over: the nation that will not serve shall perish. A door that is never shut is an invitation to everyone, so the only way left to be outside is to refuse to come in.

verseByVerse.quote: Foreigners shall build up your walls, and their kings shall minister to you; for in my wrath I struck you, but in my favor I have had mercy on you. Your gates shall be open continually; day and night they shall not be shut, that people may bring to you the wealth of the nations, with their kings led in procession. For the nation and kingdom that will not serve you shall perish; those nations shall be utterly laid waste. The glory of Lebanon shall come to you, the cypress, the plane, and the pine, to beautify the place of my sanctuary, and I will make the place of my feet glorious. The sons of those who afflicted you shall come bending low to you, and all who despised you shall bow down at your feet; they shall call you the City of the LORD, the Zion of the Holy One of Israel. Whereas you have been forsaken and hated, with no one passing through, I will make you majestic forever, a joy from age to age. You shall suck the milk of nations; you shall nurse at the breast of kings; and you shall know that I, the LORD, am your Savior and your Redeemer, the Mighty One of Jacob.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God reverses Zion’s humiliation: her enemies rebuild and honour her, her gates stand open without fear, and she will know by experience that the LORD is her Saviour and Redeemer.

Foreigners shall build up your walls. The men who broke the walls are back with trowels. God does not pretend about how the walls came down: in my wrath I struck you. The same hand is named in both halves of verse 10, and the mercy is not an apology for the wrath but its answer.

Your gates shall be open continually. An ancient city shut its gates every sunset; to leave them open was suicide. A permanently open gate says there is nothing left outside to fear. Verse 12 does not contradict it. The only nations left outside are those who refuse the King, and they perish; as John says of the same city, “nothing unclean will ever enter it” (Revelation 21:27).

The glory of Lebanon shall come to you. The trees are the three named in 41:19, when God planted them in a desert; now they are timber for his sanctuary, as the cedars of Lebanon once were for Solomon’s temple. God furnishes his own house out of a forest he grew for the purpose.

The sons of those who afflicted you. The oppressors’ children come bending low and call her the City of the LORD. The bowing honours the God who lives there, not the city’s pride. Jesus turned the promise round: to a small, despised church in Philadelphia he promised that those who claimed to be the true Israel would “come and bow down before your feet” (Revelation 3:9). Zion’s promises belong to all who are in Christ.

Forsaken and hated. The phrase to hold in verse 15 is with no one passing through. Jerusalem had stopped being on anybody’s way anywhere, the condition of many people as well as cities; now it will be sought out, a joy from age to age. And the purpose is stated: you shall know that I, the LORD, am your Savior and your Redeemer. Everything is given so that God’s people will know him.

Uncertain wording. The trees of verse 13 cannot be identified with certainty, and translations vary; the point is that the finest timber is brought to honour God’s house.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 17–22 — Your Walls Salvation, Your Gates Praise
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God will make his people’s city perfect, lit by his own presence and filled with people he has made righteous. Every material is exchanged for a better one, and the city’s rulers become peace and righteousness (v. 17). Violence is no longer heard, and the defences are renamed Salvation and Praise (v. 18). Sun and moon are retired, because the LORD is the everlasting light and the days of mourning are over (vv. 19–20). The people are all righteous, planted by God for his glory (v. 21), and the chapter ends with a promise about growth and timing: the least will become a mighty nation, and God will hasten it in its time (v. 22).
verseByVerse.theology: John takes verse 19 into the last chapter of the Bible almost unchanged (Rev. 21:23). What Isaiah could only say negatively, no sun, no moon, John is able to say with a name: the city’s lamp is the Lamb.
verseByVerse.examples: The final clause holds two things that look opposed. In its time is patience: there is a date and it is not being brought forward on demand. I will hasten it is urgency: nothing is drifting. God is neither early nor late, and he is not idle in the meantime.

verseByVerse.quote: Instead of bronze I will bring gold, and instead of iron I will bring silver; instead of wood, bronze, instead of stones, iron. I will make your overseers peace and your taskmasters righteousness. Violence shall no more be heard in your land, devastation or destruction within your borders; you shall call your walls Salvation, and your gates Praise. The sun shall be no more your light by day, nor for brightness shall the moon give you light; but the LORD will be your everlasting light, and your God will be your glory. Your sun shall no more go down, nor your moon withdraw itself; for the LORD will be your everlasting light, and your days of mourning shall be ended.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God will replace everything poor with something better, end violence for ever, and be himself the everlasting light of his people, so that their mourning is over.

Instead of bronze I will bring gold. Four exchanges, each moving up a grade. Anyone rebuilding after a disaster expects to make do with less; God says everything will be better than what was lost.

I will make your overseers peace. Then the improvement reaches the rulers. Taskmasters is what Exodus calls the men who drove the Hebrew labour gangs in Egypt (Exodus 5:6). Under the new arrangement the overseer is Peace and the taskmaster is Righteousness: nobody is pushed any more.

Violence shall no more be heard in your land. Violence is not merely stopped; it is not heard: not on the news, not in the next street. What keeps the city safe is no longer stone but God’s saving power, and its gates are called Praise.

The LORD will be your everlasting light. The two lamps that have lit every day and night since the fourth day of creation are retired, not because they failed but because they have been outshone. What replaces them is not a brighter object but a Person, and Isaiah draws the consequence: the end of sunset. There is no night to get through, and your days of mourning shall be ended.

The light that never sets. John sees this fulfilled: the city “has no need of sun or moon to shine on it, for the glory of God gives it light, and its lamp is the Lamb” (Revelation 21:23; 22:5). The one whose life was put out on the cross on a Friday afternoon is the light that will never set again. For every believer who mourns tonight, this morning is coming.

verseByVerse.quote: Your people shall all be righteous; they shall possess the land forever, the branch of my planting, the work of my hands, that I might be glorified. The least one shall become a clan, and the smallest one a mighty nation; I am the LORD; in its time I will hasten it.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God will make all his people righteous, as his own planting for his glory, and he will grow the smallest remnant into a great nation at exactly the right time.

Your people shall all be righteous. Every promise so far has been about surroundings. This one is about the people, and it had to come: a perfect city full of the same population would be the old problem inside better walls.

The branch of my planting. Three descriptions, and none of them is an achievement. They are a branch God planted, the work of his hands, and the reason is stated without embarrassment: that I might be glorified. Their righteousness is his work in them, as Paul says of believers now: “we are his workmanship, created in Christ Jesus for good works” (Ephesians 2:10).

The least one shall become a clan. The last verse is for people counting how few they are, and its first readers were a small remnant. God has done it before with Abraham and Sarah (51:2), and the church began as a hundred and twenty in an upstairs room (Acts 1:15). In its time I will hasten it: God will not be late, and he will not be hurried.

Looking back on the chapter. The light rose over one ruined city on a dark earth, and the glory that lit it was borrowed from the beginning. God grew the forest that furnished his own house, made the city beautiful and then received the beauty back as praise, and set the day of it himself. And when the sun is finally taken out of the sky, it will be because it is no longer needed.

60.theology:
Commands resting on a fact. Arise, shine is a command, and the reason attached to it is not a duty but an event: for your light has come, and the glory of the LORD has risen upon you (v. 1). Zion is not asked to generate anything. Paul’s call to the sleeping seems to echo it: Awake, O sleeper, and arise from the dead, and Christ will shine on you (Eph. 5:14).

The darkness is not said to lift. Verse 2 is honest about the world it is describing and promises light in one place rather than the removal of the dark. That is how the nations find their way in: they see something lit and start walking (v. 3). The attraction is never Zion’s excellence, and verse 9 says so in as many words: because he has made you beautiful.

Gates that are never shut. Gates left open day and night (v. 11) say that there is nothing left outside to shut them against. Even the hard sentence of verse 12 is the other side of that invitation: no one is shut out except those who refuse to come.

Sun and moon retired. The two lights that have governed day and night since the fourth day are outshone by a Person, the LORD himself, and with them the days of mourning are over (vv. 19-20).

61.subtitle: The Year of the LORD’s Favor
61.intro:
Where we are. Chapters 60 to 62 are the bright centre of the book’s last section. Chapter 60 has just shown the light dawning on Zion and the nations streaming to it; now, at the heart of that vision, one person steps forward and speaks of himself, the one anointed to bring it about.

The message. God sends an anointed deliverer, filled with his Spirit, to the poor, the brokenhearted, the captives and the mourners, to announce a Jubilee that never ends. His work is exchange, not repair: a headdress for ashes, gladness for mourning, a double portion for shame, and at last a robe of righteousness for people who could never have made one. The God who loves justice guarantees it as surely as sown seed comes up.

Why it was said. Isaiah speaks ahead to those who would come home from exile to ruined cities, poverty and disappointment, still waiting for the glory God had promised (see the introduction). They were mourners sitting in ashes; this chapter tells them who is coming for them and what he will do.

How the chapter makes its case. The anointed one announces his commission: good news, healing, liberty, the year of the LORD’s favour, and comfort for mourners, who are given three exchanges and turned into oaks (vv. 1–3). The comforted then rebuild ancient ruins and receive their true calling as priests of the LORD, with a double portion in place of shame, all grounded in God’s love of justice and his everlasting covenant (vv. 4–9). The chapter ends with the song of one clothed in salvation and righteousness, and a promise that God will make righteousness sprout before the nations (vv. 10–11).

Where it leads. This is direct promise, and Jesus claimed it himself. At Nazareth he read verse 1 and the first half of verse 2, stopped before the day of vengeance, and said, “Today this Scripture has been fulfilled in your hearing” (Luke 4:21). He is the Anointed One, the Messiah, on whom the Spirit came at his baptism. His first coming brought the year of favour; the day of vengeance waits for his return. And the robe of righteousness in verse 10 is what he gives, by faith, to people who could never weave it.

For us. We live in the gap Jesus left in the middle of verse 2, while the offer of favour is still open. Bring him your ashes and your shame, because he deals in exchanges. Then pick up tools: in this chapter the comforted become builders and priests for others.

keyVerse.quote: “The Spirit of the Lord GOD is upon me, because the LORD has anointed me to bring good news to the poor; he has sent me to bind up the brokenhearted, to proclaim liberty to the captives.”
keyVerse.note: Jesus read this verse in the synagogue at Nazareth and said it was fulfilled that day in their hearing (Luke 4:21): one of the plainest places where he names himself the Messiah. He was not admiring an ideal but announcing that it had arrived in him. The whole chapter flows from this commission, and the good news it proclaims in the Spirit’s power is the mission he has handed on to his church.

61.theology:
Jubilee, and one sentence with two comings in it. The year of the LORD’s favour is the Jubilee of Leviticus 25 arriving and not ending: no failure permanent, no debt uncancelled. At Nazareth Jesus stopped reading just before the day of vengeance (Luke 4:19-20). The present age lies between the favour he announced and the vengeance still to come, which is why there is still time to hear this.

Exchange, not improvement. Ashes become a headdress (v. 3) and shame becomes the firstborn’s double portion (v. 7), and the singer of verse 10 is clothed from outside, which is the Old Testament’s own picture of a righteousness that is worn rather than achieved.

Justice as the guarantee. Verse 8 keeps all of this from sentimentality. The recompense is promised because I the LORD love justice; I hate robbery and wrong, so restoration is not God going soft but God being true to himself.
61.reflection:
Read verses 1–3 slowly. Who are the people the anointed one is sent to? Which description comes closest to where you are, or have been, and what does he promise to do for that person?

Jesus stopped reading before “the day of vengeance of our God” (Luke 4:19–20; Isaiah 61:2). What does it mean to live in the year of the LORD’s favour while the day of reckoning still waits, and how should that shape the urgency and the tone of our witness?

Verse 3 promises exchanges, not repairs, and verse 7 a double portion instead of shame. Why is it often harder to believe God has removed our shame than that he has forgiven our sin? How does the robe of righteousness in verse 10 answer that?

The comforted become builders of old ruins and priests of the LORD (vv. 4–6). What ruins, in your family, church or neighbourhood, might God be asking you to help rebuild, and whom could you stand before God for in prayer this week?

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–3 — The Spirit Is Upon Me
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God’s anointed one is sent to the lowest and saddest, and he does not patch them up but exchanges their mourning for joy. An unnamed speaker says the Spirit of the Lord GOD is upon him because the LORD has anointed him (v. 1). His commission has five parts, each aimed downward: good news to the poor, healing for the brokenhearted, liberty for captives, the year of the LORD’s favour with the day of vengeance, and comfort for all who mourn (vv. 1–2). Verse 3 spells out the comfort as three exchanges, a headdress for ashes, oil for mourning, praise for a faint spirit, and the mourners end up as oaks of righteousness, planted by the LORD for his glory.
verseByVerse.theology: Christians have long heard Father, Son and Spirit together in the first line: the Lord GOD anoints, the Spirit rests, and the anointed one is sent. The commission that follows could be carried out only by one so equipped.
verseByVerse.examples: From Nazareth on, the commission reads like a description of Jesus' ministry, and when John the Baptist asked from prison whether he was the one, Jesus answered from this list: the blind see and the poor have good news preached to them (Luke 7:22).

verseByVerse.quote: The Spirit of the Lord GOD is upon me, because the LORD has anointed me to bring good news to the poor; he has sent me to bind up the brokenhearted, to proclaim liberty to the captives, and the opening of the prison to those who are bound;
verseByVerse.commentary:
One anointed by the LORD and filled with his Spirit is sent with good news to people at the bottom: the poor, the brokenhearted and the captives.

The LORD has anointed me. Somebody speaks and does not say who he is, as in the servant songs, where the LORD also put his Spirit upon his servant (42:1). Anointed is mashach, and the person it produces is a mashiach, a Messiah. Kings were anointed, and priests, and occasionally prophets: oil poured on a man’s head marked him out for a task he had not appointed himself to.

Good news to the poor. Then the commission, four tasks here and a fifth in verse 2, every one aimed at people who are low, and none abstract. The poor are the economically destitute and the socially powerless together, used to being the last to hear anything. They are first on the list.

To bind up the brokenhearted. The verb is a physician’s: bandaging a wound, setting a fracture. The brokenhearted are not told to cheer up; they are handled the way an injury is handled.

Liberty to the captives, and the opening of the prison. Two clauses about doors. Liberty is the word used of the release proclaimed in the Jubilee year (Leviticus 25:10), so verse 2 is already sounding; for exiles it meant going home.

Whose voice is this? Jewish interpreters, Rashi among them, generally take the speaker to be the prophet himself, and the Aramaic Targum opens the verse by naming him. Yet before Jesus, a text among the Dead Sea Scrolls already read this passage of an end-time deliverer who would proclaim the great Jubilee. This commentary hears it as Jesus did when he read it at Nazareth and said it was fulfilled that day (Luke 4:16–21). The Spirit who came on him at his baptism is the anointing this verse describes, and the ministry that followed had exactly this shape: particular people in particular trouble, reached one by one.

Uncertain wording. The opening of the prison translates an unusual doubled Hebrew word used elsewhere of opening the eyes, so the ESV notes that it can be rendered “the opening [of the eyes] to those who are blind”: a man long in the dark brought outside, squinting. The old Greek translation took it that way, and Luke’s account of the reading follows it: “recovering of sight to the blind” (Luke 4:18).
verseByVerse.note: The Greek Old Testament reads “recovery of sight to the blind” (ESV note), as Luke quotes it.

verseByVerse.quote: to proclaim the year of the LORD's favor, and the day of vengeance of our God; to comfort all who mourn;
verseByVerse.commentary:
The anointed one announces God’s great Jubilee, a release with no end, together with the day when God puts every wrong right, and comfort for all who mourn.

The year of the LORD’s favor. Every fiftieth year, under Leviticus 25, a trumpet sounded and the economy was reset: debts cancelled, Israelite slaves released, land sold under pressure returned to its family. Whether Israel ever kept it properly is doubtful. Here a herald announces that the fiftieth year has arrived, with no suggestion that it will end.

And the day of vengeance of our God. In Isaiah the vengeance is God taking up the cause of his wronged people (34:8; 35:4). Notice the proportions, as in 63:4: a year of favour, a day of vengeance. And the last task, to comfort all who mourn, picks up the word that opened this half of the book: “Comfort, comfort my people” (40:1).

At Nazareth. Jesus went into the synagogue at Nazareth on the Sabbath, was handed the scroll of Isaiah, found this place, and read down to the year of the LORD’s favor. Then he rolled up the scroll, sat down, and with every eye fixed on him said: “Today this Scripture has been fulfilled in your hearing” (Luke 4:16–21). He stopped in the middle of a sentence. The next clause was and the day of vengeance of our God, and he did not read it.

Why he stopped. He was not cutting out a part he disliked. Isaiah writes the year of favour and the day of vengeance into one line because from where he stands they are one event. From where we stand there is a gap in the middle of the verse, and we are living in it: the first coming brought the favour; the day of vengeance belongs to the second. Even that day is good news for the wronged, because no cruelty will be left standing; and for anyone who comes to Christ in the gap, the vengeance has already fallen, on him, at the cross.

Living in the gap. The Jubilee has been announced and the reckoning has not come. That is why there is still time to hear it, and why the offer will not stay open for ever (2 Corinthians 6:2).
verseByVerse.note: The Jubilee laws are set out in Leviticus 25:8-55.

verseByVerse.quote: to grant to those who mourn in Zion— to give them a beautiful headdress instead of ashes, the oil of gladness instead of mourning, the garment of praise instead of a faint spirit; that they may be called oaks of righteousness, the planting of the LORD, that he may be glorified.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God does not patch up the grieving; he exchanges their mourning for joy, and turns people sitting in ashes into deep-rooted oaks that display his glory.

Grief that was worn. Three exchanges, each a swap rather than a repair: something taken off and replaced. In that world grief was worn: ashes on the head, no oil on hair or skin, and sackcloth, the coarse dark cloth of a mourner (see mourning customs). God reverses precisely those three, in the order a person would put them on.

A beautiful headdress instead of ashes. The first exchange is a pun no Hebrew reader could miss. The headdress is pe’er; the ashes are ’epher: the same three consonants, shuffled. Beauty and ashes are one letter-order apart.

Oaks of righteousness. Then the outcome, and it is not what the sentence has been setting up. People sitting in ashes do not become comfortable, or even happy. They become oaks: deep-rooted, slow-growing, hard to shift, outlasting the people who planted them. They are the planting of the LORD: their strength is his work, and its purpose is that he may be glorified.

Blessed are those who mourn. The Beatitudes echo this passage: “Blessed are those who mourn, for they shall be comforted” (Matthew 5:4). The poor of verse 1, the mourners and the comfort are arranged into a sermon by the one who said the passage was about him.

The myth of closure. We are often told that grief should end in closure: process the loss and one day shut the door on it. The family therapist Pauline Boss, after decades with people whose loved ones had gone missing or slipped away into dementia, wrote The Myth of Closure, arguing that for many losses the door never shuts, and the healthier hope is to learn to carry them. Isaiah agrees that grief is not a door, and goes further. God does not promise these mourners that they will stop feeling it; he promises an exchange, and roots deep enough to grow through every weather. The Christian hope is not that we will manage our losses better, but that the One anointed to bind up the brokenhearted went down into death himself and came back, so that one day grief will not be closed but answered.
verseByVerse.note: A sound-play: “a beautiful headdress” (pe’er) instead of “ashes” (’epher).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 4–9 — Builders, Priests, and a Double Portion
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The comforted are put to work and lifted to a new dignity, because the LORD loves justice. They rebuild ruins that are generations old (v. 4). Strangers tend their flocks, because their own primary calling is now to be priests of the LORD and ministers of God among the nations (vv. 5–6). In place of shame they receive a double portion, the firstborn’s share, and everlasting joy (v. 7). The ground of it all is God’s character: he loves justice, hates robbery, and makes an everlasting covenant with them (v. 8), so that their descendants are recognised everywhere as people the LORD has blessed (v. 9).
verseByVerse.theology: The double portion of verse 7 is the firstborn son's share of an inheritance (Deut. 21:17), and the priesthood of verse 6 is the calling Peter hands to the church (1 Pet. 2:9).
verseByVerse.examples: A grieving reader need not hear verse 4 as an order to get busy. The building comes after the comfort, not instead of it, and the ruins are old ones that nobody blames him for.

verseByVerse.quote: They shall build up the ancient ruins; they shall raise up the former devastations; they shall repair the ruined cities, the devastations of many generations. Strangers shall stand and tend your flocks; foreigners shall be your plowmen and vinedressers; but you shall be called the priests of the LORD; they shall speak of you as the ministers of our God; you shall eat the wealth of the nations, and in their glory you shall boast.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The comforted are put to work rebuilding what generations of ruin left behind, and are given their true calling: to be priests of the LORD for the nations.

They shall build up the ancient ruins. Comforted people do not first rest or celebrate: they pick up tools. And the ruins are not their own but ancient, the devastations of many generations, wreckage already old when they were born, with no prospect of thanks.

You shall be called the priests of the LORD. Verses 5 and 6 do not say manual work is beneath anybody; they have just been rebuilding cities by hand. They say this people has a different primary occupation. Others tend the flocks because they are priests and ministers of our God, standing between God and the nations, and the nations’ wealth comes to them as offerings came to the priests and Levites, who had no land of their own.

Back to Sinai. That was the original intention. At Sinai God told the people he had just carried out of Egypt that they would be “a kingdom of priests and a holy nation” (Exodus 19:6), a calling the book has shown them failing at again and again. Here it is fulfilled, as a gift, and Peter hands the same words to a church of Jews and Gentiles: “you are a chosen race, a royal priesthood, a holy nation” (1 Peter 2:9).

A priestly occupation. So an ordinary Christian is not someone who enjoys the Jubilee privately, but a person whose real occupation is priestly, whatever is written on his payslip: standing before God for people who are not standing there themselves. The calling comes after the comfort, and the Spirit who anointed the speaker of verse 1 equips his people for it.

Where Christians differ. Dispensational and many premillennial readers take verses 5–9 of a future earthly kingdom in which foreigners serve a restored national Israel in its land.

This commentary’s view. With Peter, this commentary reads the promise as fulfilled in Christ’s one people, Jew and Gentile, made priests to God now (Revelation 1:6) and completed in the new creation. The foreigners are not a servant class: Isaiah promises that the LORD will take some of them “for priests and for Levites” (66:21).

verseByVerse.quote: Instead of your shame there shall be a double portion; instead of dishonor they shall rejoice in their lot; therefore in their land they shall possess a double portion; they shall have everlasting joy. For I the LORD love justice; I hate robbery and wrong; I will faithfully give them their recompense, and I will make an everlasting covenant with them. Their offspring shall be known among the nations, and their descendants in the midst of the peoples; all who see them shall acknowledge them, that they are an offspring the LORD has blessed.
verseByVerse.commentary:
In place of shame God gives his people the firstborn’s double share and everlasting joy, and guarantees it by his own love of justice and an everlasting covenant.

Instead of your shame there shall be a double portion. The firstborn son received twice the share of any other heir (Deuteronomy 21:17; see inheritance and the firstborn). That is what is given here, in place of shame: not a normal share restored, but the firstborn’s inheritance. A disgraced people are not merely readmitted; they are promoted past where they stood before they fell.

For I the LORD love justice. Here is why it is safe to believe. The restoration rests not on God’s softness but on his justice: he loves justice and hates robbery, and his people have been robbed. A God who merely felt sorry for them might change his mind. A God whose own character is offended by what was taken will not rest until it is returned, and an everlasting covenant binds him to it.

All who see them shall acknowledge them. The blessing becomes visible in the next generation without being announced. Nothing is preached in verse 9. Something is simply noticed, by outsiders who were not looking for it.

The firstborn’s share, given away. Christ is the Firstborn (Colossians 1:18), who bore the shame of the cross (Hebrews 12:2) so that people who deserved shame could be “heirs of God and fellow heirs with Christ” (Romans 8:17). The everlasting covenant is the one sealed in his blood (Hebrews 13:20).

Forgiven and un-shamed. Anyone who has lived with a public failure knows why this matters. Being forgiven is one thing; being un-shamed is much harder to believe. The story does not end with the disgrace politely never mentioned again, but with the disgraced holding the eldest son’s portion. And in a wrong that was never put right, hold on to verse 8: the case has not been dropped.

Uncertain wording. As its vowels stand in the traditional Hebrew text, the phrase behind robbery and wrong reads robbery “with a burnt offering”, the sense of the King James Version: God hates worship paid for by theft (compare 1:11–17). The ESV, like the ancient Greek translation, reads the same letters with different vowels, and its reading suits the context of a robbed people better; either way God condemns wrong done to others.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 10–11 — The Garments, and the Garden
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The chapter ends in joy at what God gives and certainty that he will finish it. The speaker exults in the LORD for two garments he did not make, the garments of salvation and the robe of righteousness, worn with the gladness of a bridegroom in his headdress and a bride in her jewels (v. 10). Then a garden answers any doubt: as surely as sown ground sends up its shoots, the Lord GOD will cause righteousness and praise to sprout up before all the nations (v. 11). The ending matches the beginning: the headdress given to mourners in verse 3 is the one the bridegroom wears.
verseByVerse.theology: The righteousness worn in verse 10 is received rather than achieved, the same logic as the servant of chapter 53 bearing iniquities so that many are accounted righteous.
verseByVerse.examples: Mission in this chapter is never a sales campaign. The nations in verses 9 and 11 notice what God has grown before anyone argues them into it.

verseByVerse.quote: I will greatly rejoice in the LORD; my soul shall exult in my God, for he has clothed me with the garments of salvation; he has covered me with the robe of righteousness, as a bridegroom decks himself like a priest with a beautiful headdress, and as a bride adorns herself with her jewels.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The rescued sing for joy, because God has dressed them in salvation and righteousness they could never make, as glad as a bridegroom and bride on their wedding day.

I will greatly rejoice in the LORD. The song at last, and in all of it the singer is the one acted on. He describes not an achievement but what he is wearing, and somebody else dressed him. Whether the voice is the anointed one or Zion answering him, the song belongs to everyone he clothes.

He has clothed me with the garments of salvation. Two garments. Garments of salvation: rescue worn, so that it is the first thing anyone sees. And the robe of righteousness, the phrase that matters most: a covering that makes a person fit to be seen, laid over him from outside. This is the Old Testament’s own picture of what the New Testament calls being counted righteous: not a quality generated inside a man, but a garment fitted over one who could not make it (compare Zechariah 3:4; Philippians 3:9).

As a bridegroom decks himself like a priest. Then two wedding pictures (see weddings): a bridegroom putting on his headdress with the care of a priest robing for the sanctuary, and a bride putting on her jewels. Nobody in either picture is dressed for duty; they are dressed for joy. And it is the same beautiful headdress handed to the mourners in verse 3: the gift to the grieving and the finery of the wedding are one article of clothing.

Woven by one who needed none. Christ was anointed to give a headdress instead of ashes, and as the bridegroom he wears one (Matthew 9:15; Revelation 19:7–8). The garments are his to give because they were his to begin with, and the robe that covers a sinner was woven by the one who needed no covering at all.

verseByVerse.quote: For as the earth brings forth its sprouts, and as a garden causes what is sown in it to sprout up, so the Lord GOD will cause righteousness and praise to sprout up before all the nations.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God will make righteousness and praise spring up before all the nations, as surely as a garden brings up what is sown in it. To the question under the whole chapter, will any of this happen?, the answer is not an argument but a garden.

As the earth brings forth its sprouts. Nobody stands over sown ground wondering whether it will come up. During the delay nothing can be seen, but the delay is not evidence that nothing is happening. Seed does what seed does, and the gardener is not anxious.

Righteousness and praise. Right living and glad worship come up out of the same soil. A world put right and a world at worship are one harvest.

The gardener named. The gardener is the Lord GOD. Righteousness among the nations is not manufactured by the church’s strategy; it is grown, on his timetable, from seed sown long before anybody now living was watching. Jesus told the same parable: the seed sprouts and grows while the sower sleeps (Mark 4:26–29).

Looking back on the chapter. The chapter that opened with a man claiming the Spirit was on him closes with a harvest he plants: the poor given news, the brokenhearted bandaged, prisoners brought blinking into the light, ashes swapped for a headdress, mourners turned into oaks, and the whole earth coming up green before the nations, because the Lord GOD said it would.

62.subtitle: A New Name
62.intro:
Where we are. Chapter 61 announced the Anointed One and his Jubilee and ended with righteousness sprouting before the nations. Chapter 62 stays with the same hope, but asks what to do while it has not yet come up: you pray, and you keep praying.

The message. God will not rest until his people shine, and he wants them not to rest either. The city that was called Forsaken will be renamed My Delight Is in Her, because God rejoices over his people as a bridegroom over his bride. Until that day, watchmen on the walls are to give the LORD no rest in prayer, and the people are to clear the road, because their salvation is coming, and it is a person.

Why it was said. Those who came back from exile found a small, poor city, harvests that were not secure, and promises that seemed slow (see the introduction). It is easy to stop praying when nothing appears to change; this chapter gives them, and us, permission and orders to persist.

How the chapter makes its case. A voice refuses to be silent until Zion’s salvation burns like a torch; she will be a crown in God’s hand, and her old names, Forsaken and Desolate, will give way to My Delight Is in Her and Married, for God rejoices over her like a bridegroom (vv. 1–5). Watchmen are posted to pray without ceasing, and God swears that his people will eat their own harvest in his courts (vv. 6–9). The chapter ends with commands to open the gates and build the highway, for “your salvation comes”, and with four new names, the last of them Sought Out (vv. 10–12).

Where it leads. Here Christ is reached by promise and by the character of God revealed in him. The bridegroom who delights in a ruined bride has a name in the New Testament: Jesus calls himself the bridegroom, and Christ “loved the church and gave himself up for her” (Ephesians 5:25). Matthew takes verse 11, Say to the daughter of Zion, for Jesus riding into Jerusalem, and the risen Christ, who always lives to intercede, is the watchman who never tires. The name Sought Out is what the Son of Man came to make true: “to seek and to save the lost” (Luke 19:10).

For us. Your truest name is not the one your failures gave you, but the one God gives: delighted in, sought out. Live from that verdict rather than the crowd’s. And keep praying for the people and the church you love, without giving up, because he has told you to and has promised to answer.

keyVerse.quote: “For as a young man marries a young woman, so shall your sons marry you, and as the bridegroom rejoices over the bride, so shall your God rejoice over you.”
keyVerse.note: The comparison reaches for the most intense and uncomplicated joy in human experience, a young bridegroom on his wedding day, and applies it to God’s delight in a people who had been called Forsaken. This is not a pretty figure of speech; it is the closest human words can come to what God feels. In Christ the Bridegroom has a name, and his delight in his bride cost him his life.

62.reflection:
Read verse 4. What “old names” do people carry, given by their failures, their circumstances or other people? How does God’s renaming of Zion speak to them, and to you?

Verse 5 says God rejoices over his people as a bridegroom over his bride. Why do many Christians find it easier to believe that God tolerates them than that he delights in them? What difference would it make to live from that delight rather than from the verdict of others?

The watchmen are told to “give him no rest” (vv. 6–7). For whom, or for what, is God calling you to keep praying? What would help you persist when nothing seems to change?

In verse 10 those already inside the city are sent out to clear the road of stones for those still coming home. What stones might make it harder for people to come to Christ through our church, and how could we remove them?
