You who put the LORD in remembrance, take no rest,<sup>7</sup>and give him no rest until he establishes Jerusalem and makes it a praise in the earth.<sup>8</sup>The LORD has sworn by his right hand and by his mighty arm: "I will not again give your grain to be food for your enemies, and foreigners shall not drink your wine for which you have labored;<sup>9</sup>but those who garner it shall eat it and praise the LORD, and those who gather it shall drink it in the courts of my sanctuary."<sup>10</sup>Go through, go through the gates; prepare the way for the people; build up, build up the highway; clear it of stones; lift up a signal over the peoples.<sup>11</sup>Behold, the LORD has proclaimed to the end of the earth: Say to the daughter of Zion, "Behold, your salvation comes; behold, his reward is with him, and his recompense before him."<sup>12</sup>And they shall be called The Holy People, The Redeemed of the LORD; and you shall be called Sought Out, A City Not Forsaken.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God will not rest until his ruined people shine, and he renames them because he delights in them. A voice refuses to keep silent until Zion’s righteousness goes forth as brightness and her salvation like a burning torch, for the nations and kings to see (vv. 1–2). She will be given a new name by the LORD himself, and become a crown of beauty held up in his hand (vv. 2–3). Her old names, Forsaken and Desolate, are replaced by My Delight Is in Her and Married (v. 4). The reason is God’s own joy: as a bridegroom rejoices over his bride, so her God will rejoice over her (v. 5).
verseByVerse.theology: The old names were accurate, and that is what makes the renaming more than encouragement. God does not tell Zion the old names were unfair. He changes the fact and then changes the name.
verseByVerse.examples: Verse 5 is not decorative language. Scripture reaches for the most uncomplicated joy any human being knows and says that this is what God feels about his people. Zephaniah says the same thing with God singing (Zeph. 3:17), and Revelation puts it at the end of history as a wedding supper (Rev. 19:7).

verseByVerse.quote: For Zion's sake I will not keep silent, and for Jerusalem's sake I will not be quiet, until her righteousness goes forth as brightness, and her salvation as a burning torch. The nations shall see your righteousness, and all the kings your glory, and you shall be called by a new name that the mouth of the LORD will give. You shall be a crown of beauty in the hand of the LORD, and a royal diadem in the hand of your God. You shall no more be termed Forsaken, and your land shall no more be termed Desolate, but you shall be called My Delight Is in Her, and your land Married; for the LORD delights in you, and your land shall be married. For as a young man marries a young woman, so shall your sons marry you, and as the bridegroom rejoices over the bride, so shall your God rejoice over you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God will not rest until his people’s salvation shines for all to see; he renames the city once called Forsaken, and delights in her as a bridegroom delights in his bride.

For Zion’s sake I will not keep silent. Who speaks in verse 1 is left open. It may be the prophet, refusing to stop praying; it may be God, refusing to stop working; many hear the Anointed One of chapter 61 still speaking. The ambiguity is instructive: praying and promising are the same determination heard from two sides. And the refusal has an end point: until Zion’s righteousness and salvation can be seen by everyone.

A new name that the mouth of the LORD will give. In the Bible a name given by God marks a new identity: Abram became Abraham, Jacob became Israel. Zion does not choose her new name or earn it. She receives it.

A crown of beauty in the hand of the LORD. The crown is in his hand, not on his head, a detail nobody would invent. A crown worn is a statement about the wearer’s status; a crown held up is something shown to the room. God is not decorated by his people; he displays them.

You shall no more be termed Forsaken. The old names, Forsaken and Desolate, are Azubah and Shemamah in Hebrew, and they were not insults invented by enemies. They were accurate. The new names are Hephzibah, My Delight Is in Her, and Beulah, Married. This is not positive thinking: God really changes her situation, and the new name announces it. Azubah and Hephzibah were both names real women bore (1 Kings 22:42; 2 Kings 21:1).

So shall your God rejoice over you. Then the highest comparison there is: a young man on his wedding day who cannot stop looking at his bride. Not tolerates, not has decided to keep, but rejoices over. The Holy One who filled a temple with smoke and made a prophet cry out that he was lost (6:4–5) looks at a burnt city with weeds in the streets and a defeated handful of survivors, and what rises in him is the delight of a bridegroom (compare Zephaniah 3:17).

The bridegroom’s name. In the New Testament the bridegroom has a name. Jesus calls himself the bridegroom (Mark 2:19–20), and Christ loved the church and gave himself up for her, to present her to himself in splendour (Ephesians 5:25–27). The joy of verse 5 cost the bridegroom his life, and he counted it worth the cost.

The verdict we keep checking. Early in the twentieth century the sociologist Charles Horton Cooley described the looking-glass self: we come to see ourselves largely as we imagine others see us. A century later we carry the looking-glass in our pockets, and it gives us a score every few minutes. The measuring has not made anyone more secure, because the crowd’s verdict is never final. Verse 5 holds up a different mirror. The God who sees everything, the ruin included, looks at his people and rejoices. And this verdict is not a reward for performing well; it was won by the Bridegroom, who gave himself for a bride with nothing to commend her. A person who knows that delight no longer has to win the room. She can walk into it already loved, and so be free to notice somebody else.

Uncertain wording. So shall your sons marry you is an unusual picture: the land’s children restored to it in fruitful union. With different vowels the same Hebrew letters read “your Builder shall marry you”, which would make God the husband, as the second half of the verse does. Either way, Zion is no longer forsaken.
verseByVerse.note: Hephzibah means “my delight is in her”; Beulah means “married.”

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Because God has promised, his people are to pray without letting up until he does what he said. He posts watchmen on Jerusalem’s walls who must never be silent, day or night (v. 6), and tells them to take no rest and give him no rest until he makes Jerusalem a praise in the earth (vv. 6–7). The persistence is his own idea, and he answers it with an oath sworn by his right hand: enemies will never again carry off his people’s grain and wine, and those who harvest it will eat and drink it with praise in the courts of his sanctuary (vv. 8–9).
verseByVerse.theology: Persistent prayer is authorised here in the plainest possible terms. Jesus tells a whole parable to make the same point about not losing heart (Luke 18:1-8).
verseByVerse.examples: The smallest promise in the chapter carries the heaviest oath, sworn by God's right hand and his mighty arm (v. 8). God does not think a farmer's harvest beneath his notice.

verseByVerse.quote: On your walls, O Jerusalem, I have set watchmen; all the day and all the night they shall never be silent. You who put the LORD in remembrance, take no rest, and give him no rest until he establishes Jerusalem and makes it a praise in the earth. The LORD has sworn by his right hand and by his mighty arm: "I will not again give your grain to be food for your enemies, and foreigners shall not drink your wine for which you have labored; but those who garner it shall eat it and praise the LORD, and those who gather it shall drink it in the courts of my sanctuary."
verseByVerse.commentary:
God posts watchmen whose task is to pray without stopping until he fulfils his promise, and he answers with an oath that his people will enjoy the fruit of their labour in his presence.

On your walls, O Jerusalem, I have set watchmen. Chapter 56 had watchmen too, and they were blind, dumb and fond of sleep (56:10). These have one instruction: do not stop making a noise. They are watching not for an enemy on the road but for the fulfilment of a promise, and their job is to keep mentioning it. You who put the LORD in remembrance is a title like that of a royal official whose duty was to remind the king of business.

Give him no rest. Then the startling phrase. Not “be patient”, not “leave it with him”, but keep at him until it is done. Two things make that safe rather than impudent. The watchmen were posted by God himself, so the persistence is his idea, not a device for wearing him down. And what they remind him of is his own word; nobody is inventing a request.

The LORD has sworn by his right hand. The answer to all that praying is an oath about food, and it is not an anticlimax. The particular misery of an occupied country is watching your own harvest loaded onto somebody else’s cart, year after year. It was one of the covenant curses Moses set out, that a nation they had not known would eat the fruit of their ground (Deuteronomy 28:33). The oath reverses it, and restores the feast the law prescribed, when the tithe of grain and wine was eaten with rejoicing before the LORD (Deuteronomy 14:22–26). God swears that the one who reaps will be the one who eats, in the courts of his sanctuary. Among grand promises about nations and kings, this one would have made a farmer weep.

The watchman who never sleeps. You are not the only watchman. The risen Christ “always lives to make intercession” for his people (Hebrews 7:25), so weak, repeated prayers are carried by one who never tires and is never refused. And the meal in God’s courts points on to the table he spreads for his people now and the wedding supper to come (Revelation 19:9).

How do I give him no rest? If there is a person, a family or a church you have no permission to stop praying for, verse 7 says your persistence is obedience, not impatience. But persistence needs a little structure, or it fades by February. Write the names down. The son who has drifted from church, the friend with cancer, your own congregation: a name on paper is harder to forget than a good intention. Pray his promises back to him. The watchmen remind the LORD of what he has said, so pray Isaiah 62 for your church, or Ezekiel 36:26 for the child whose heart seems stone. Fix a time. Tie the prayer to something you already do: the kettle in the morning, the drive to school, the last light off at night. Do not stop when nothing changes. Jesus told them a parable to the effect that they ought always to pray and not lose heart (Luke 18:1). Some of these prayers will take years.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Salvation is on its way, so the road must be made ready and the world told. The commands come doubled, as orders given in a hurry: go through the gates, prepare the way, build the highway, clear it of stones, raise a signal for the peoples (v. 10). The LORD has proclaimed to the end of the earth that Zion’s salvation is coming, and it comes as a person bringing his reward with him (v. 11). The chapter closes with four new names: The Holy People and The Redeemed of the LORD for the people, and Sought Out and A City Not Forsaken for the city (v. 12).
verseByVerse.theology: This is the third time in the book that a road is ordered built (40:3; 57:14; 62:10). The traffic runs both ways: out through the gates to the nations, and home again with the people who were scattered. The stones are cleared not for God, who needs no smooth road, but for the people coming back.
verseByVerse.examples: The last two names answer the first two: Forsaken has become A City Not Forsaken, and Desolate has become Sought Out.

verseByVerse.quote: Go through, go through the gates; prepare the way for the people; build up, build up the highway; clear it of stones; lift up a signal over the peoples. Behold, the LORD has proclaimed to the end of the earth: Say to the daughter of Zion, "Behold, your salvation comes; behold, his reward is with him, and his recompense before him." And they shall be called The Holy People, The Redeemed of the LORD; and you shall be called Sought Out, A City Not Forsaken.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Salvation is coming, and it is a person, so God’s people must throw open the gates, clear the road for those still coming home, and receive the new names he gives them.

Go through, go through the gates. Each command is said twice, as orders are given when there is no time to lose. Chapter 40 built a road for God to come on (40:3); here the gates are thrown open and the stones picked up by hand.

Clear it of stones. Note who does the stone-clearing. Not angels. The people already inside the city are sent out to make the surface passable for those still coming home. The church’s work is still this: to remove whatever makes the way harder for others, and to lift up a signal the nations can see.

Behold, your salvation comes. The announcement has gone out to the end of the earth before Zion herself is told. And what arrives is not a change of circumstances but a person: your salvation comes, with his wages in his hand, like a workman bringing the pay home (40:10). Matthew takes the words Say to the daughter of Zion for Jesus riding into Jerusalem (Matthew 21:5), and the last chapter of the Bible has him saying the same thing: “Behold, I am coming soon, bringing my recompense with me” (Revelation 22:12).

Four new names. Each is a reply. The Holy People and The Redeemed of the LORD say what has been done to them. The other two answer the names of verse 4: Forsaken becomes A City Not Forsaken.

Sought Out. That is the name to remember. It is something done to her, not by her. It records nothing the city achieved, no reform carried through, no case made for herself. It says that somebody came looking. That is the name she will answer to for ever, and it belongs to a people whose whole history in this book is of being found by a God who never stopped searching. Jesus said it of himself: “the Son of Man came to seek and to save the lost” (Luke 19:10).

62.theology:
Renaming that follows re-making. The pattern of verse 4 holds for everything Scripture says about who God’s people are: God first changes them, and then he gives the new name. Nobody in Isaiah is talked out of a true description of themselves; they are rescued out of it.

The joy is God’s. Verse 5 is not chiefly about Zion’s feelings toward God but about his toward her. They are not merely rescued. They are wanted.

Authorised persistence. Because God posted the watchmen himself and they plead his own promise (vv. 6-7), their refusal to give him rest is faith, not impudence. This is the lesson of the parable of the widow and the judge (Luke 18:1-8), and the opposite of the sleeping watchmen of chapter 56.

Sought Out. The decisive last name records only that somebody came looking for her. In a book whose whole argument is that God announces, comes and redeems, that is the right name to end on.

63.subtitle: Who Is This Coming from Edom?
63.intro:
Where we are. Chapter 62 ended with the cry, “Behold, your salvation comes.” Chapter 63 opens with someone coming, but the salvation arrives as a warrior from Edom, his clothes stained red. Then the vision gives way to a long prayer of memory, confession and longing that runs to the end of chapter 64.

The message. God alone will defeat every enemy of his people, and he will do it in justice; no one helps him and no one needs to. And the same God who judges has always suffered with his people: in all their affliction he was afflicted. So the right response, even when his people have rebelled and he seems far away, is to remember his steadfast love, confess honestly, and call on him as Father to look down and act again.

Why it was said. Isaiah writes ahead for a people who would see Jerusalem’s temple burned and their enemies triumphant (see the introduction). They needed to know that God would put the wrong right, and they needed words to pray when they felt like people he had never owned.

How the chapter makes its case. A sentry challenges a figure on the road from Edom; he has trodden the winepress of judgment alone, because no one else could bring salvation (vv. 1–6). Then a prayer begins by recounting the LORD’s steadfast love, his suffering with his people and his carrying them, before confessing that they grieved his Holy Spirit (vv. 7–10). It remembers Moses and the sea and asks where that God is now (vv. 11–14), and ends by pleading with him as Father to look down, return and end the trampling of his sanctuary (vv. 15–19).

Where it leads. The chapter reaches Christ by promise and by the character of God revealed in him. The lone warrior who treads the winepress reappears in Revelation 19 as Christ coming to judge, but this judge first walked out of Jerusalem alone with his own blood on him: no one survives his judgment except through his cross. The God who was afflicted in his people’s affliction took flesh and suffered with us and for us (Hebrews 4:15), and the cry you are our Father is answered when the Son teaches us to pray “Our Father” and gives us his Spirit to say it.

For us. Do not soften God’s judgment, and do not try to carry it out yourself; leave vengeance to him. When God seems absent, do what this prayer does: recount his kindness aloud, confess your sin plainly, and keep calling him Father. He has not stopped feeling for his people, and in Christ he has come down.

keyVerse.quote: “In all their affliction he was afflicted, and the angel of his presence saved them; in his love and in his pity he redeemed them; he lifted them up and carried them all the days of old.”
keyVerse.note: This verse says that God suffered with his people, and that this is why he redeemed them. He was not a distant manager of the exodus but present within it, afflicted in their affliction, and the angel of his presence was his own presence going with them. Hebrews 4:15 brings this to its fullness in Jesus, a high priest “who in every respect has been tempted as we are, yet without sin.” The God who enters our suffering is not a new idea in the New Testament; it is the character of God revealed in the Old.

63.reflection:
The warrior of verses 1–6 treads the winepress “alone”. How does this picture of God’s judgment make you feel? Why might it be good news, and how does knowing that Christ first bore judgment alone at the cross change the way you read it?

The prayer begins, “I will recount the steadfast love of the LORD” (v. 7). Why is remembering a choice? Share one particular mercy of God you could recount when you are struggling.

Verse 9 says, “In all their affliction he was afflicted.” What difference does it make in suffering to know that God feels for his people, and that in Christ he has shared our weakness?

The prayer is raw: it asks where God is and why he lets them wander (vv. 15–17), yet it still says, “You, O LORD, are our Father.” What does this teach us about honest prayer? Is there something you need to bring to God this plainly?

Like a horse in the desert, they did not stumble.<sup>14</sup>Like livestock that go down into the valley, the Spirit of the LORD gave them rest. The stirring of your inner parts and your compassion are held back from me.<sup>16</sup>For you are our Father, though Abraham does not know us, and Israel does not acknowledge us; you, O LORD, are our Father, our Redeemer from of old is your name.<sup>17</sup>O LORD, why do you make us wander from your ways and harden our heart, so that we fear you not? verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–6 — Who Is This Coming from Edom?
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God alone defeats the enemies of his people, and he does it in justice. A sentry sees a splendid figure coming from Edom in crimson garments and asks who he is; the answer is the LORD, speaking in righteousness, mighty to save (v. 1). Asked why his clothes are red, he says he has trodden the winepress alone, and the stains are his enemies’ lifeblood (vv. 2–3). The day of vengeance and the year of redemption have come (v. 4). He looked for help and found none, so his own arm brought salvation (vv. 5–6). The picture is disturbing on purpose: evil will not be left standing.
verseByVerse.theology: The passage is not describing a battle that has been enjoyed. Judgment in Isaiah is never eager; it is what is left when there is no one to intercede, which is exactly what chapter 59 reported: God looked and found no one (59:16).
verseByVerse.examples: John takes this vision and puts it on Christ returning, clothed in a robe dipped in blood, treading the winepress of the wrath of God (Rev. 19:13-15).

verseByVerse.quote: Who is this who comes from Edom, in crimsoned garments from Bozrah, he who is splendid in his apparel, marching in the greatness of his strength? "It is I, speaking in righteousness, mighty to save." Why is your apparel red, and your garments like his who treads in the winepress? "I have trodden the winepress alone, and from the peoples no one was with me; I trod them in my anger and trampled them in my wrath; their lifeblood spattered on my garments, and stained all my apparel. For the day of vengeance was in my heart, and my year of redemption had come. I looked, but there was no one to help; I was appalled, but there was no one to uphold; so my own arm brought me salvation, and my wrath upheld me. I trampled down the peoples in my anger; I made them drunk in my wrath, and I poured out their lifeblood on the earth."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The LORD comes as a lone warrior who has judged his people’s enemies, his garments stained with their blood, because no one else could bring salvation.

Who is this who comes from Edom? A sentry’s challenge from a city wall: who goes there? Edom, descended from Esau, was Israel’s oldest neighbour and oldest grievance, the nation that cheered when Jerusalem fell (Psalm 137:7; Obadiah 10–14). The names fit: Edom sounds like the Hebrew for red, as the ESV notes at Genesis 25:30, and Bozrah, its chief city, like the word for grape harvest. As in chapter 34, Edom stands for every power set against God and his people. The answer, speaking in righteousness, mighty to save, shows that this judgment is no loss of temper: it is justice, and its aim is rescue.

Like his who treads in the winepress. A man who has spent a day in the winepress, ankle deep, comes out spattered to the waist. But here the juice is blood, and it belongs to those being trodden. The image is chosen because a winepress is violent and total, and it should not be softened.

I have trodden the winepress alone. The emphasis falls somewhere unexpected: loneliness. No one was with me (v. 3), there was no one to help (v. 5), and he was appalled that there was nobody. So my own arm brought me salvation, as in 59:16. And the proportions of verse 4 matter, as in 61:2: a day of vengeance, a year of redemption.

The blood is his own. Ten chapters earlier there is another solitary figure whom no one helped, pierced and crushed; in chapter 53 the blood is his own. Revelation shows Christ returning “clothed in a robe dipped in blood” to tread “the winepress of the fury of the wrath of God the Almighty” (Revelation 19:13, 15). The one who will come with his enemies’ lifeblood on him first walked out of Jerusalem to the cross with his own blood on him. His death is the reason anyone will survive his judgment.

What it does not mean. This is no licence for violence in God’s name. The point is that God does this alone, and believers are told to “leave it to the wrath of God” (Romans 12:19). The wronged may rest their case with him, and be free to love their enemies.

Where Christians differ. Many older Christian readers took the red garments as Christ’s own blood shed in his passion; most interpreters today read them as his enemies’ blood at the final judgment.

This commentary’s view. The text says their lifeblood, and Revelation 19 places the scene at Christ’s return, so this is judgment. But the older reading saw something true: the Judge who treads the winepress alone first bore judgment alone.
verseByVerse.note: Bozrah was a chief city of Edom.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 7–14 — I Will Recount the Steadfast Love
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Remembering what God has done is how his people learn to pray in the dark. The vision ends and a prayer begins that runs to the end of chapter 64. It opens by deliberately recounting the LORD’s steadfast love (v. 7) and quoting what he said when he took Israel as his own (v. 8). Verse 9 says what the chapter is best known for: in all their affliction he was afflicted, and he carried them. Then the honest half: they rebelled and grieved his Holy Spirit, and he fought against them (v. 10). Verses 11–14 go back to Moses and the sea, and ask in the present tense, where is he?
verseByVerse.theology: The prayer models something rare: honest memory of God's goodness and honest confession of failure held in the same paragraph, with neither cancelling the other. It refuses cheap despair, which would forget verse 7, and cheap comfort, which would skip verse 10.
verseByVerse.examples: Verse 10 is one of the few places in the Old Testament that speaks of grieving the Holy Spirit. The Spirit is not described here as a force but as someone whose feelings can be hurt by the people he is living among.

verseByVerse.quote: I will recount the steadfast love of the LORD, the praises of the LORD, according to all that the LORD has granted us, and the great goodness to the house of Israel that he has granted them according to his compassion, according to the abundance of his steadfast love. For he said, "Surely they are my people, children who will not deal falsely." And he became their Savior. In all their affliction he was afflicted, and the angel of his presence saved them; in his love and in his pity he redeemed them; he lifted them up and carried them all the days of old. But they rebelled and grieved his Holy Spirit; therefore he turned to be their enemy, and himself fought against them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The prayer begins by choosing to remember God’s steadfast love: he took Israel as his own, suffered in their suffering and carried them, though they rebelled and grieved his Holy Spirit.

I will recount the steadfast love of the LORD. The prayer starts with a decision. Nobody feels grateful automatically in a ruined city; this prayer chooses to go through the record aloud before saying anything about the present.

Surely they are my people. God’s words at the start are heartbreaking to read with Israel’s later history in view. He was not deceived; he knew. He committed himself anyway, and became their Saviour.

In all their affliction he was afflicted. Verse 9 is the summit of the chapter. God was not managing the exodus from a distance; he was inside the suffering, and the slavery hurt him too. The angel of his presence is God’s own presence going with Israel (Exodus 23:20–23; 33:14), the angel of the LORD who speaks and acts as the LORD, most likely the Son before his incarnation. And the carrying is what chapter 46 promised, even to old age (46:3–4).

They rebelled and grieved his Holy Spirit. Then the honest half of the memory. The Spirit is grieved, not merely provoked but hurt, the word Paul uses in Ephesians 4:30. The consequence is stated without flinching: he fought against them. A prayer that left out the confession of verse 10 would have no right to the comfort of verse 9.

The God the Old Testament knew. A God who suffers with his people is not a New Testament idea imported backwards. It is the character of God the Old Testament already knew, and the reason a Christian is not surprised by the incarnation: we have a high priest able to sympathise with our weaknesses, tempted in every way as we are, yet without sin (Hebrews 4:15).

What steadfast love is. Steadfast love (hesed) is not a feeling that comes and goes, but love that has bound itself by a promise and keeps it when the other side does not. We assume, after a run of failure, that his love has worn thin, because ours would. Verse 8 shows its shape: the commitment came first, and the saving flowed from it, not from their record. It went furthest at the cross: “God shows his love for us in that while we were still sinners, Christ died for us” (Romans 5:8). So on a bad day, recount aloud God’s particular mercies to you, beginning with that one. See Steadfast Love.

Textual note. Verse 9 has a well-known variant. The written Hebrew text can be read he was not afflicted, and the Greek Old Testament reads no envoy or angel, but he himself saved them. The ESV and KJV follow the reading the Hebrew scribes wrote in the margin. Every form of the verse says that God himself came to their rescue.

verseByVerse.quote: Then he remembered the days of old, of Moses and his people. Where is he who brought them up out of the sea with the shepherds of his flock? Where is he who put in the midst of them his Holy Spirit, who caused his glorious arm to go at the right hand of Moses, who divided the waters before them to make for himself an everlasting name, who led them through the depths? Like a horse in the desert, they did not stumble. Like livestock that go down into the valley, the Spirit of the LORD gave them rest. So you led your people, to make for yourself a glorious name.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The prayer remembers how God led his people through the sea by Moses and gave them rest by his Spirit, and asks where that God is now.

Where is he? The remembering turns into questions in the present tense: not “where was he”, but where is he. This is the prayer of a generation that has inherited the stories and seen nothing like them.

Like a horse in the desert, they did not stumble. The details are lovingly kept: the arm at Moses’ right hand, the divided water, the Spirit in their midst. A horse on open ground runs. So Isaiah remembers a nation crossing a seabed: not creeping between walls of water but going through at a gallop, and not one of them tripping.

The Spirit of the LORD gave them rest. Then cattle walking down into a sheltered valley at the end of the day, and the word is rest. The exodus is remembered as a homecoming, and both animals are unafraid.

To make for yourself a glorious name. Twice in four verses: God acted to make himself a name. The prayer has noticed that he acts for his own sake (48:11), and it is not offended. It is counting on it.

The greater shepherd. The God who brought them up out of the sea with the shepherds of his flock did it again on a larger scale, when he brought again from the dead our Lord Jesus, “the great shepherd of the sheep” (Hebrews 13:20). The exodus was the pattern; the resurrection is the deliverance it pointed to.

In everyday life. Anyone who has grown up on stories of what God did in an earlier revival, or in a grandparent’s life, and looked round at a church where nothing much seems to be happening, has prayed verse 11. The prayer shows what to do with that ache: remember, and ask.

Uncertain wording. Then he remembered does not say who remembered: the people, which suits the questions that follow, or God. Either way, memory of the exodus becomes the ground of the plea.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 15–19 — Look Down from Heaven and See
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: When God seems far away, his people may plead with him as their Father, honestly and without pretending. Remembering turns into petition: look down from heaven, where are your zeal and your compassion (v. 15)? Verse 16 sets aside any claim based on ancestry and goes straight to God: you are our Father, our Redeemer from of old. Verse 17 asks the hardest question, why God lets them wander and harden their hearts, and pleads with him to return. Verses 18–19 end at the bottom, with the sanctuary trampled and the people looking as if they had never been his.
verseByVerse.theology: Verse 16 is theology under pressure: with no appeal left to Abraham, the prayer rests its whole claim on God as Father.

verseByVerse.quote: Look down from heaven and see, from your holy and beautiful habitation. Where are your zeal and your might? The stirring of your inner parts and your compassion are held back from me. For you are our Father, though Abraham does not know us, and Israel does not acknowledge us; you, O LORD, are our Father, our Redeemer from of old is your name. O LORD, why do you make us wander from your ways and harden our heart, so that we fear you not? Return for the sake of your servants, the tribes of your heritage. Your holy people held possession for a little while; our adversaries have trampled down your sanctuary. We have become like those over whom you have never ruled, like those who are not called by your name.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The prayer pleads with God as Father to look down and act, asks honestly why he has let his people wander, and ends at the bottom, with his sanctuary trampled.

The stirring of your inner parts. The language gets physical: literally the churning of the insides. Hebrew locates compassion in the gut, as English locates it in the heart. The complaint is that God is feeling something and not acting on it.

You are our Father, though Abraham does not know us. Verse 16 cuts off the obvious appeal to ancestry, then goes straight past the fathers to you are our Father. John the Baptist made the same point to a crowd relying on descent from Abraham (Matthew 3:9), and every Gentile Christian since has stood on the ground this verse cleared.

Why do you make us wander from your ways? The hardest question in the chapter is asked without softening. The prayer has already confessed that the hardening was deserved (v. 10); now it lays the mystery before God and asks him to reverse it: Return for the sake of your servants. Scripture does not answer the question here, and it does not rebuke the asking.

Like those who are not called by your name. We look like people who were never yours. The ground of the complaint is the trampled sanctuary of verse 18, almost certainly Solomon’s temple burned by the Babylonians (2 Kings 25:9): a people whose God’s house lay in ruins looked like a people without a God. Yet it is allowed to sound like this, in the Bible, without correction.

Our Father. The cry of verse 16 is answered in the Son. Jesus teaches his disciples to pray “Our Father in heaven” (Matthew 6:9), and God sends “the Spirit of his Son into our hearts, crying, ‘Abba! Father!’” (Galatians 4:6). The Father whose compassion seemed held back “did not spare his own Son” (Romans 8:32).

Honest prayer. Scripture prints this prayer at its most exposed, with no hint that God is offended. He gave his people these words for days when everything seems to count against him.

Don’t you only believe because of where you were born? The objection has some force: most people hold roughly the faith of their parents. But verse 16 got there first. Israel had the best pedigree on earth, and the prayer says it is worth nothing: nobody is a child of God by birth. And the objection cuts both ways: the secular Westerner who thinks every religion an accident of upbringing mostly holds the outlook of his own time and place. Where we were born may explain how we came to a belief; it cannot tell us whether it is true. That is settled by the evidence, above all by looking at Jesus. And the gospel says you become God’s child only by a new birth, not of blood nor of the will of the flesh nor of the will of man, but of God (John 1:13).

Does God harden hearts? Here the hardening is a judgment: God giving over a people who had already rebelled and grieved his Holy Spirit (v. 10), as with Pharaoh, who hardened his own heart (Exodus 8:15) before God confirmed it. God is never the author of sin (James 1:13), yet he is sovereign even over hardening (Romans 9:18). And the prayer shows the way out: ask him to return.

Uncertain wording. Verse 18 is compressed. ESV reads it as a lament that God’s people held the land only briefly; others read it of the enemy possessing the sanctuary for a little while. The sense is clear either way: possession was short and the sanctuary lies trampled. In the Hebrew Bible the line Oh that you would rend the heavens (64:1 in English) ends this verse, so the plea runs on without a break.

63.theology:
Two solitary figures, and whose blood it is. The warrior from Edom treads the winepress alone (vv. 3, 5). Ten chapters earlier there is another solitary sufferer, and the difference is decisive: in chapter 53 the blood is his own.

A day of vengeance, a year of redemption. Isaiah 61 used the same pair, and when Jesus read that passage aloud in Nazareth he stopped before the day of vengeance (Luke 4:19-20). The year of redemption is still running.

In all their affliction he was afflicted. Verse 9 denies that God managed the exodus from a distance, and verse 10 says his Spirit can be grieved. A God who can be afflicted and grieved is not a difficulty to be explained away in this book; he is the reason the incarnation, God coming as a man to suffer with us, is no surprise (Heb. 4:15).

Past the fathers, straight to the Father. Under real pressure the prayer gives up any claim based on ancestry and goes directly to God as Father (v. 16). Relationship to him, not ancestry, is the whole of its hope.

64.subtitle: Oh That You Would Rend the Heavens
64.intro:
Where we are. Chapter 64 completes the long prayer that began at 63:7. The people have remembered God’s steadfast love and confessed their rebellion, and now the prayer reaches its climax and its end. God’s answer follows in chapters 65 and 66.

The message. When God’s people have nothing left to offer, not even their best deeds, they may still cry to him to come down, and cling to who he is: our Father, our potter. The chapter exposes how deep the need goes: even our righteousness is stained, and no one is even reaching for God. But a people with no claim of their own can appeal to the God who made them and owns them, and ask him not to be angry for ever.

Why it was said. Isaiah gives words ahead of time to a people whose cities would lie waste and whose temple would be burned (see the introduction). They needed to know that it is right to pray with nothing in their hands, and that a prayer may end without an answer and still be faith.

How the chapter makes its case. The prayer cries for God to tear open the heavens and come down, as he did at Sinai, because no other God acts for those who wait for him (vv. 1–4). Then comes a total confession: God was angry, we sinned, even our righteous deeds are like a polluted garment, we fade like leaves, and no one calls on your name (vv. 5–7). With nothing to stand on, the prayer turns on But now: you are our Father and our potter, we are all your people; and it ends by laying the ruins of Zion and the burned temple before God with two questions (vv. 8–12).

Where it leads. The chapter leads to Christ by the need it exposes and by the answer God gave. The heavens were torn open at the Jordan, when the Spirit came down on Jesus (Mark 1:10), and the temple curtain was torn at his death (Mark 15:38). The polluted garment of verse 6 can only be replaced by the robe of righteousness of 61:10, which Christ gives. And the cry “you are our Father” is answered when the Son gives us his Spirit to cry “Abba! Father!” (Galatians 4:6).

For us. Stop offering God your best deeds as a reason to accept you; bring him your need and his name. Pray for him to come down in power on his church, confess honestly, and when the answer does not come at once, keep laying it before him: he is the God who acts for those who wait for him.

keyVerse.quote: “But now, O LORD, you are our Father; we are the clay, and you are our potter; we are all the work of your hand.”
keyVerse.note: This is where the whole prayer turns. The potter and clay image has appeared in Isaiah as a warning against human presumption (29:16; 45:9); here it becomes a reason to pray. The fact that God made us, which makes us answerable to him, is also what we appeal to: we have no standing of our own, but we are his clay and his children, and the potter does not discard what his hands have made.

64.reflection:
“Oh that you would rend the heavens and come down” (v. 1). Have you ever longed for God to act like that? How did God answer this cry in Jesus (Mark 1:10; 15:38), and how does that shape what we pray for today?

Verse 6 says that even “all our righteous deeds are like a polluted garment.” Why is this hard for respectable people to accept? How does it prepare us for the robe of righteousness that only Christ gives (61:10)?

With nothing left to offer, the prayer says, “But now, O LORD, you are our Father; we are the clay, and you are our potter” (v. 8). What does it look like to pray after a failure by starting with God’s name rather than our own case?

The chapter ends with questions and no answer (v. 12). How can we keep praying faithfully when heaven seems silent, and what encouragement does God’s reply in 65:1 give?

Behold, you were angry, and we sinned; in our sins we have been a long time, and shall we be saved?<sup>6</sup>We have all become like one who is unclean, and all our righteous deeds are like a polluted garment. We all fade like a leaf, and our iniquities, like the wind, take us away.<sup>7</sup>There is no one who calls upon your name, who rouses himself to take hold of you; for you have hidden your face from us, and have made us melt in the hand of our iniquities.<sup>8</sup>But now, O LORD, you are our Father; we are the clay, and you are our potter; we are all the work of your hand.<sup>9</sup>Be not so terribly angry, O LORD, and remember not iniquity forever. Behold, please look, we are all your people.<sup>10</sup>Your holy cities have become a wilderness; Zion has become a wilderness, Jerusalem a desolation.<sup>11</sup>Our holy and beautiful house, where our fathers praised you, has been burned by fire, and all our pleasant places have become ruins.<sup>12</sup>Will you restrain yourself at these things, O LORD? Will you keep silent, and afflict us so terribly?

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–7 — Oh That You Would Rend the Heavens
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God’s people cry for him to come down in power, and confess that they have nothing to offer him. The prayer asks God to tear open the heavens and come down, so that mountains quake and the nations tremble, as when fire kindles brushwood (vv. 1–2). He did it before, doing awesome things no one expected (v. 3), for no other God acts for those who wait for him (v. 4). Then the confession, and it is total: God was angry and they sinned; even their righteous deeds are like a polluted garment; they fade like leaves blown by the wind of their own iniquities; and no one even calls on his name (vv. 5–7).
verseByVerse.theology: Verse 6 does not confess the obvious failures. It confesses the successes: all our righteous deeds. What is put on the table is not the community's worst record but its best, and the verdict on the best is the same as on the worst.
verseByVerse.examples: For a reader with no strength left, verse 4 may be the kindest line in the chapter: this God acts for those who wait for him, and waiting is something even the exhausted can do.

verseByVerse.quote: Oh that you would rend the heavens and come down, that the mountains might quake at your presence— as when fire kindles brushwood and the fire causes water to boil— to make your name known to your adversaries, and that the nations might tremble at your presence! When you did awesome things that we did not look for, you came down, the mountains quaked at your presence. From of old no one has heard or perceived by the ear, no eye has seen a God besides you, who acts for those who wait for him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God’s people cry for him to tear open the heavens and come down in power, as he did before, because no other God acts for those who wait for him.

Oh that you would rend the heavens and come down. In the Hebrew Bible this cry is the last line of chapter 63, so the verse numbers in this chapter run one behind the Hebrew. The verb is violent: not open the heavens but tear them, the way a man rips his garment when the news is unbearable.

As when fire kindles brushwood. The two images are domestic and instant. Dry brushwood does not smoulder; it goes up. Water on a hot fire boils. Both are fast, and fast is what the community wants and is not getting.

Awesome things that we did not look for. The precedent in verse 3 is Sinai, when the mountain quaked (Exodus 19:18), and the clause in the middle is the honest one: things that we did not look for. When he came down before, it was not what anyone had expected either.

Who acts for those who wait for him. The distinguishing mark in verse 4 is not power; every nation claimed a powerful god. It is that this one acts for those who wait. The gods of the ancient world required their people to act for them; this God works while his people wait. Paul draws loosely on the verse for what God has now revealed in the gospel: what no eye has seen, nor ear heard, nor the heart of man imagined, God has prepared for those who love him (1 Corinthians 2:9).

The heavens torn open. The cry of verse 1 was answered, though not as the prayer imagined. Mark puts a tearing at the beginning and the end of Jesus’ ministry. At the Jordan the heavens were torn open and the Spirit came down on a man standing in the water; at Golgotha the curtain of the temple was torn in two from top to bottom (Mark 1:10; 15:38). The sky was rent. It did not shake a mountain; it opened over a carpenter’s head. And he will come down once more, in glory (1 Thessalonians 4:16).

verseByVerse.quote: You meet him who joyfully works righteousness, those who remember you in your ways. Behold, you were angry, and we sinned; in our sins we have been a long time, and shall we be saved? We have all become like one who is unclean, and all our righteous deeds are like a polluted garment. We all fade like a leaf, and our iniquities, like the wind, take us away. There is no one who calls upon your name, who rouses himself to take hold of you; for you have hidden your face from us, and have made us melt in the hand of our iniquities.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The people confess that their sin goes all the way down: even their best deeds are unclean before God, they are withering under their iniquities, and no one is even praying.

You meet him who joyfully works righteousness. Verse 5 begins with the people God draws near to, and in naming them the nation confesses it is not among them.

You were angry, and we sinned. The order is strange and not a mistake. The prayer is not accusing God of causing the sin. It describes what a long time under God’s displeasure did to a community: things got worse, not better, and hardening under judgment became part of the problem. Then the question, asked aloud and left open: shall we be saved?

All our righteous deeds are like a polluted garment. Verse 6 confesses not their sins, already confessed a line earlier, but all our righteous deeds: the offerings brought, the fasts kept, the good done. The community puts its best on the table and says that beside God’s holiness the best is as unusable as the worst. The comparison is deliberately repellent: a cloth of ritual uncleanness, which no Israelite would carry into a room, let alone into the temple. Older versions have “filthy rags”.

We all fade like a leaf. The most exact image in the chapter. A leaf does not fall because something tore it off. It dries, loses colour, and one ordinary day a breeze takes it, and the wind here is their own iniquity.

There is no one who calls upon your name. The last confession is of prayerlessness, made while praying. Nobody rouses himself, shakes himself awake, to take hold of God; and the honest half of the sentence follows: it is hard to reach for a face that is turned away.

What it does not mean. This is not self-hatred, nor exaggeration for effect. It is the discovery that ruins every attempt at religion and opens the door to the gospel: our righteousness cannot make us acceptable, because even at its best it falls short of God’s holiness. Paul had to lose a lifetime of blameless law-keeping, counting it as rubbish, to “be found in him, not having a righteousness of my own” (Philippians 3:8–9). The polluted garment of verse 6 has only one remedy: the robe of righteousness of 61:10, which God puts on us in Christ.

Are even a Christian’s good works filthy rags? Offered as a ground of acceptance before God, yes: everything we do is stained by sin. But the believer’s works, done by the Spirit and covered by Christ’s righteousness, please God (Ephesians 2:10; Hebrews 13:16), though they earn nothing.

Uncertain wording. Verse 5 is among the hardest lines in Isaiah to translate. The connection in you were angry, and we sinned is simply “and”, so it can also be read “you were angry because we sinned”, as the King James Version does. The end of the verse is very compressed; ESV makes it a question, shall we be saved?, while the King James reads a statement of hope: “in those is continuance, and we shall be saved.” Either way the prayer hangs between deserved anger and the hope of salvation.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: With nothing left of their own, God’s people appeal to who he is. Everything turns on but now: the LORD is their Father and their potter, and they are clay, the work of his hand (v. 8). So they ask him not to be angry for ever or remember their iniquity for ever, and simply to look: we are all your people (v. 9). Then they lay the evidence before him: the holy cities a wilderness, Jerusalem a desolation, and the house where their fathers praised him burned by fire (vv. 10–11). The chapter ends with two questions and no answer: will you restrain yourself, will you keep silent (v. 12)?
verseByVerse.theology: The potter image has been a rebuke twice in this book, at 29:16 and 45:9, where the clay is told it has no business arguing with the one who shaped it. Here the same image becomes a plea. The fact that he made them, which left them no right to argue, is exactly what they now hold on to: a potter does not throw away what his own hands have made.
verseByVerse.examples: Verse 11 is worth reading slowly with anyone whose home or church has known loss. The prayer does not pretend the ruins are not ruins; it names the place where the singing used to be, and it says so to God.

verseByVerse.quote: But now, O LORD, you are our Father; we are the clay, and you are our potter; we are all the work of your hand. Be not so terribly angry, O LORD, and remember not iniquity forever. Behold, please look, we are all your people. Your holy cities have become a wilderness; Zion has become a wilderness, Jerusalem a desolation. Our holy and beautiful house, where our fathers praised you, has been burned by fire, and all our pleasant places have become ruins. Will you restrain yourself at these things, O LORD? Will you keep silent, and afflict us so terribly?
verseByVerse.commentary:
With nothing to stand on, God’s people appeal to who he is, their Father and their potter, ask him not to be angry for ever, and lay their ruins before him with questions only he can answer.

But now, O LORD, you are our Father. Everything turns on but now. There is nothing in the previous three verses to build on, no merit, no leftover good deeds, no promise of improvement, so the prayer reaches instead for two names.

Our Father. The first is bolder than it looks. Israel rarely addressed God as Father in prayer, and here the word comes from people with nothing left to stand on. After shaming a father we tend to come back rehearsing our case and offering to be servants. That is what the son in Jesus’ parable did, and he never finished his speech: “while he was still a long way off, his father saw him and felt compassion, and ran and embraced him and kissed him” (Luke 15:20). Timothy Keller often pointed out that a dignified head of a family in that world did not run; to run he had to hitch up his robes and lose his dignity in the street. This father throws his dignity away to reach his son sooner. That is the Father this prayer was reaching for, and the Son has opened the way to him: “God has sent the Spirit of his Son into our hearts, crying, ‘Abba! Father!’” (Galatians 4:6). So when you pray after a failure, do not open with the speech. Open with the name. See Adoption.

We are the clay, and you are our potter. The second name is the surprising one. Potter and clay have appeared twice already in Isaiah, both times as a rebuke, to shut down an argument (29:16; 45:9). Here the picture is picked up by the people it was used against and turned into a plea. The logic is exact: if we are only clay, we have no right to argue with you; but we are your clay, and no potter throws away what he has shaped himself. The smallness that leaves them no right to object becomes the reason for their appeal.

Remember not iniquity forever. Very little is asked in verse 9. Not that the anger was unjust; the confession has conceded that. Only that it should not be for ever. And the last clause is barely a sentence: behold, please look. The prayer has been reduced to asking God to turn his head.

Where our fathers praised you. That phrase carries the grief of verse 11. It is not the architecture they mourn. The building where the singing happened is a black ruin, and everyone remembers the singing.

Will you keep silent? The prayer ends on two questions and no answer, with the people still on their knees and nothing in their hands. That is a mercy to every believer who has prayed and heard nothing back: such a prayer is still faith.

The answer that comes. The answer does come, and it is not manufactured by the people who prayed. It comes in the first line of the next chapter, and it is more than they asked: “I was ready to be sought by those who did not ask for me; I was ready to be found by those who did not seek me” (65:1). They had confessed that nobody roused himself to take hold of God. God’s reply is that he had been holding out his hands all day long (65:2).

64.theology:
The tearing that was answered. The prayer wanted mountains shaking (v. 1). The heavens were torn open over a man standing in the Jordan, and the temple curtain was torn when he died. It was not the coming the prayer had pictured, and it was the answer.

Confessing the successes. The point of verse 6 is not that good works are worthless but that they can never reach high enough: our righteousness cannot be improved up to the standard of God’s holiness. The righteousness God accepts is the one Christ lived in our place and counts to those who trust him, a righteousness from God that depends on faith (Philippians 3:9). That is why a people who can only confess are not left hopeless.

The potter, turned from rebuke into plea. The picture that once silenced complaint is now the reason for the appeal (v. 8): no potter discards what his own hands have shaped.

A prayer allowed to end unanswered. Not every prayer in the Bible receives its answer before it stops (v. 12), and the ones that do not are not the weaker ones. God’s answer in chapter 65 goes further than the request.

65.subtitle: Behold, I Create New Heavens and a New Earth
65.intro:
Where we are. Chapters 63 and 64 ended with an anguished prayer: rend the heavens and come down, “Will you keep silent, and afflict us so terribly?” (64:12). Chapter 65 is God’s answer, and with chapter 66 it brings the book to its close.

The message. God has never been the silent one. He has held out his hands all day to a people who would not come, and he has been found by people who were not even looking. Now he draws a line, not round Israel but through it: his servants, who answer him, will inherit everything, and those who go their own way will lose everything. And what the servants inherit is not a patched-up Judah but new heavens and a new earth, where weeping, early death, wasted work and the serpent’s harm are gone for ever.

Why it was said. The people waiting for God’s promises were a mixed community, some trusting him, others blending his worship with pagan rites (see the introduction). They needed to hear that God had not gone silent, that belonging to Israel saved no one by itself, and that his future was larger than anything they had asked for.

How the chapter makes its case. God answers the charge of silence: his hands have been out all day while the people filled their days with forbidden worship (vv. 1–7). Then the chapter divides. Like juice in a spoiled bunch of grapes, a remnant is kept for his servants’ sake (vv. 8–10), while those who feed the gods of luck meet the destiny God appoints (vv. 11–12). The two futures are set side by side, and the servants receive a new name under the God of Amen (vv. 13–16). Finally God creates new heavens and a new earth: weeping silenced, infant death ended, the covenant curses reversed, prayer answered before it is spoken, and the wolf grazing beside the lamb (vv. 17–25).

Where it leads. The chapter leads to Christ by direct promise. Paul hears in verses 1 and 2 the gospel going to the Gentiles while Israel refuses (Romans 10:20–21), and those outstretched hands took flesh in Jesus, weeping over Jerusalem and stretched out on a cross. The God of Amen is revealed as “the Amen, the faithful and true witness” (Revelation 3:14). And the new creation described here began when Christ rose (1 Corinthians 15:20; Revelation 21:1–5).

For us. You did not find God; he was holding out his hands before you turned round, and he still is. Do not mistake busy religion for an answer to his call. And hold on to a hope as solid as houses and vineyards: in Christ, your work, your children and your grief all have a future in his renewed world.

keyVerse.quote: “For behold, I create new heavens and a new earth, and the former things shall not be remembered or come into mind.”
keyVerse.note: This is the Old Testament’s great promise of a renewed universe, and Revelation 21:1 takes it up: “Then I saw a new heaven and a new earth, for the first heaven and the first earth had passed away.” The verb is create, the verb of Genesis 1:1: God is not repairing the old order at the edges but renewing the whole of it. The former things will not come to mind, not because they are erased but because joy outshines them, and that new world began on the morning Christ rose.

65.theology:
Grace precedes the search. Paul splits the first two verses between Gentiles and Israel (Rom. 10:20-21), and for both the hands were out before anyone turned round. The sober warning that goes with it is verse 12: “when I called, you did not answer”.

New creation, and why it is physical. Verses 17-25 are the Old Testament’s fullest account of where God’s work of redemption is heading, and everything in it is material: houses, vineyards, work, children, animals, soil. The hope is not escape from the world but its repair, which is why Christian faith has always held to a bodily resurrection and a renewed earth, not merely a soul set free from the body.

The one curse left standing. Verse 25 leaves dust as the serpent’s food (Gen. 3:14), so the evil that began all of it will not have been rehabilitated. It will be defeated, permanently, in a world where everything else has been healed.
65.reflection:
God says he was found by those who did not seek him and held out his hands all day to those who would not come (vv. 1–2). How does it change the way you think about your own conversion, and about people who seem uninterested in God, to know that he takes the first step?

The people of verse 5 used religion to keep others at a distance: “I am too holy for you.” Where are we tempted to do the same, and how did Jesus show a different kind of holiness?

The people set tables for Fortune and Destiny because they feared the future (v. 11). What are our modern ways of trying to control what lies ahead, and what does it look like to trust the Father instead?

Verses 17–25 describe a new creation full of houses, vineyards, work and children. Which promise here speaks most to your own losses or labours, and how does Christ’s resurrection make it more than wishful thinking?
