verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–7 — The Hands Spread Out All Day
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God has never been the silent one: he has held out his hands all day to a people who would not come. He describes himself as ready to be found even by those who never looked for him, calling “Here I am, here I am” and spreading out his hands to a rebellious people (vv. 1–2). Verses 3 to 5 list what they did instead: busy, secret, forbidden worship, ending in the startling claim, “I am too holy for you.” Verses 6 and 7 answer that God has not stopped watching. The record has been written before him, and it will be paid in full.
verseByVerse.theology: Verse 1 is the answer the prayer of chapter 64 did not dare to ask for. They begged God to look at them; he says he has been calling out to them all along.
verseByVerse.examples: The religion of verses 3-5 is busy, ancient and self-assured, and none of it is an answer to the God who has been calling. A full calendar of worship can be one more way of walking the other way.

verseByVerse.quote: I was ready to be sought by those who did not ask for me; I was ready to be found by those who did not seek me. I said, "Here I am, here I am," to a nation that was not called by my name. I spread out my hands all the day to a rebellious people, who walk in a way that is not good, following their own devices;
verseByVerse.commentary:
God is not silent or hard to find: he has been calling “Here I am” and holding out his hands all day, to people who never looked for him and to a people who kept walking away.

I was ready to be sought by those who did not ask for me. Two chapters of desperate prayer have just ended with God apparently silent (64:12). His answer turns the complaint round: he has been findable all along, even by people who were not looking.

Here I am, here I am. These are the words a servant says when his master calls, and Isaiah’s own answer to the voice asking whom to send (6:8). God had promised to say “Here I am” when his people cried to him (58:9). Now he says it first, twice over, to a nation that has not called on his name at all: the master answering like a servant, to a call nobody made.

I spread out my hands all the day. Arms held out, the gesture of someone pleading with another to come. The weight falls on all the day: not once, not only at the crisis, but the whole day long, to people following their own devices the other way.

Who starts the search. Nobody in this chapter starts the search. The hands were out before anyone turned round, and still out at the end of the day, after nobody had. C. S. Lewis, looking back on his conversion in Surprised by Joy, said that talk of man’s search for God struck him as about as apt as talk of the mouse’s search for the cat: he had been keeping out of the way, and he was found. That undoes both the pride of the seeker and the despair of the one who has stopped looking: nobody can boast of tracking God down, and nobody is too indifferent to be reached.

How Paul reads it. Paul quotes these verses at the end of his argument that Israel had heard the message and was without excuse, and splits them: verse 1 of the Gentiles, “I have been found by those who did not seek me”, verse 2 of Israel, “All day long I have held out my hands to a disobedient and contrary people” (Romans 10:20–21). What separates the two groups is not that one tried harder.

The hands in Jesus. The outstretched hands took flesh. Jesus said over the city, “How often would I have gathered your children together as a hen gathers her brood under her wings, and you were not willing!” (Luke 13:34), and in the end his hands were spread out on a cross. The shepherd in his story does not wait for the lost sheep to find its way home; he goes “after the one that is lost, until he finds it” (Luke 15:4).

Uncertain wording. The standard Hebrew text reads a nation that was not called by my name, a people outside Israel, which is how Paul applies it. With different vowels the same letters read a nation that did not call on my name, which could describe Israel itself. Either way the people addressed had no claim on God, and he came to them first.

verseByVerse.quote: a people who provoke me to my face continually, sacrificing in gardens and making offerings on bricks; who sit in tombs, and spend the night in secret places; who eat pig's flesh, and broth of tainted meat is in their vessels; who say, "Keep to yourself, do not come near me, for I am too holy for you." These are a smoke in my nostrils, a fire that burns all the day.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Instead of answering God, the people poured their energy into forbidden, secret religion, and then looked down on others as less holy than themselves.

A people who provoke me to my face continually. Every item in the catalogue is a religious act, and that is what makes it damning. These people have not abandoned worship; they are worshipping energetically in every direction at once.

Sacrificing in gardens and making offerings on bricks. The gardens are the grove shrines of Canaanite fertility worship (1:29). The bricks are most likely an altar of the wrong construction, when the law asked for one of earth or uncut stones (Exodus 20:24–25). The tombs and secret places are for consulting the dead, the one source God had forbidden his people to ask (8:19). The pig’s flesh and tainted broth are the food laws broken deliberately, probably as part of a rite.

I am too holy for you. These same tomb-sitters and garden-worshippers claim to be holier than others and use it to keep people at a distance. Everywhere else in Isaiah, real holiness humbles: when it came near Isaiah, he cried, “Woe is me! For I am lost” (6:5). Holiness used as a fence to keep others out is a reliable sign that a person has not been anywhere near the holy God.

The Holy One who came near. Jesus met the same attitude: “This man receives sinners and eats with them” (Luke 15:2). The only truly holy man who ever lived did the opposite of verse 5. He touched a leper (Mark 1:41) and ate with outcasts, and instead of being defiled by them, his holiness made them clean. Real nearness to God makes a person easier for sinners to approach, not harder.

A smoke in my nostrils. Not the pleasing aroma of an accepted sacrifice but smoke in the face, an irritation that will not clear. And it is there all the day, as in verse 2: he held out his hands all day, and all day this is what came back.

Uncertain wording. Several details are obscure. Bricks may mean brick altars, or incense burned on tiled rooftops (compare Jeremiah 19:13). Secret places is literally guarded or hidden places, perhaps caves or vaults among the graves. Tainted meat is a rare word the law uses for sacrificial meat kept too long (Leviticus 7:18). And I am too holy for you may also be read I would make you holy, as if contact with the initiated passed on a dangerous holiness (compare Ezekiel 44:19). The overall picture is clear: forbidden rites, practised with pride.

verseByVerse.quote: Behold, it is written before me: "I will not keep silent, but I will repay; I will indeed repay into their lap both your iniquities and your fathers' iniquities together, says the LORD; because they made offerings on the mountains and insulted me on the hills, I will measure into their lap payment for their former deeds."
verseByVerse.commentary:
God’s silence was never indifference: every deed has been written down before him, and he will repay it in full.

Behold, it is written before me. The picture is a ledger lying in front of God, an account kept entry by entry over years. The people had concluded from the silence that nothing was being recorded.

I will not keep silent. The prayer of chapter 64 ended, “Will you keep silent?” (64:12), and here is the answer, cutting both ways. Silence gets read as absence or permission, and the inference is always wrong. The silence was a postponement, and meanwhile the writing went on (Romans 2:4–5).

Into their lap. The lap is the fold of a robe gathered at the waist and used as a pocket for grain or coins. The image is commercial: a quantity measured and poured into the fold of the buyer’s own garment (compare Luke 6:38). He gets exactly what he has earned.

Your fathers’ iniquities together. This is not children punished for what their parents did (Ezekiel 18:20). It describes a generation that carried on its fathers’ practices, on the same mountains and hills, and so joined itself to the account.

The record nailed to a cross. No one could face that ledger and survive. The gospel’s answer is not that the record was lost but that it was paid: God forgave us “by canceling the record of debt that stood against us with its legal demands. This he set aside, nailing it to the cross” (Colossians 2:14).

Mercy and judgment together. So far the chapter has an outstretched hand (v. 2) and an open ledger (v. 6), and both belong to the same God. Neither cancels the other, and anyone who thinks he must choose between them has not read on to verse 8.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 8–16 — Two Kinds of People, and a Blessing in the Cluster
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God will not destroy his whole people, but the line between his servants and those who forsake him now runs inside Israel itself. Like a picker who spares a ruined bunch of grapes because there is still juice in it, God keeps a remnant for his servants’ sake and gives them the land, even turning the Valley of Trouble into a place of rest (vv. 8–10). Those who set tables for Fortune and Destiny will meet the destiny God appoints, because they would not answer when he called (vv. 11–12). Four times the two futures are set side by side (vv. 13–14), and the servants receive a new name and live before the God of Amen (vv. 15–16).
verseByVerse.theology: The division running through these verses is not between Israel and the nations but inside the covenant community itself, and it is drawn by how people respond to God, not by who their ancestors were.
verseByVerse.examples: Verse 8 is a comfort for anyone who looks at the church, or at himself, and sees mostly shrivelled fruit. What matters is not how the bunch looks from a distance but what the one holding it can see in it.

verseByVerse.quote: Thus says the LORD: "As the new wine is found in the cluster, and they say, 'Do not destroy it, for there is a blessing in it,' so I will do for my servants' sake, and not destroy them all. I will bring forth offspring from Jacob, and from Judah possessors of my mountains; my chosen shall possess it, and my servants shall dwell there. Sharon shall become a pasture for flocks, and the Valley of Achor a place for herds to lie down, for my people who have sought me.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God will not throw away his whole people: for his servants’ sake he keeps a remnant, like juice in a spoiled bunch of grapes, and gives them a land where even the Valley of Trouble becomes a place of rest.

As the new wine is found in the cluster. Here is why the chapter does not end at verse 7. A picker lifts a bunch that is mostly ruined, shrivelled and not worth the basket space, and is about to throw it down. Then he sees juice in it and says the sentence that saves it: Do not destroy it, for there is a blessing in it.

The remnant pictured. That is the doctrine of the remnant, the few God keeps for himself within an unfaithful people, in a picture anyone can hold. What spares the cluster is not that it is a good one; it plainly is not. It is that the man holding it sees what nobody further off could see. Isaiah once sang of God’s vineyard that yielded only wild grapes (5:1–2); now, inside the failure, God finds wine. Paul found the same in his own day: “a remnant, chosen by grace” (Romans 11:5).

The Valley of Achor. Sharon is the fertile coastal plain in the west, where cattle are no surprise. Achor lies in the east near Jericho, and its name means trouble: it is where Achan was stoned for his theft after Jericho, the nation’s first and most humiliating failure in the land (Joshua 7:24–26). Now herds will lie down there, not because the valley is avoided or forgotten, but because the place called Trouble has nothing left to fear. Hosea says it in one phrase: God will “make the Valley of Achor a door of hope” (Hosea 2:15).

For my servants’ sake. The remnant narrows in the end to one. Isaiah’s Servant is addressed as “my servant, Israel” (49:3), the one faithful Israelite in whom the nation’s calling is kept, and every servant in this chapter is spared for his sake. He is the true vine (John 15:1), and the blessing in the cluster is finally his.

verseByVerse.quote: But you who forsake the LORD, who forget my holy mountain, who set a table for Fortune and fill cups of mixed wine for Destiny, I will destine you to the sword, and all of you shall bow down to the slaughter, because, when I called, you did not answer; when I spoke, you did not listen, but you did what was evil in my eyes and chose what I did not delight in."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Those who forsake the LORD and court the gods of luck will meet the destiny God appoints, because they would not answer when he called.

A table for Fortune. Two gods appear by name: Gad and Meni, Fortune and Destiny, deities of luck, and the worship is a meal laid out to persuade fate to be kind. It is the most understandable idolatry in the chapter. Nobody sets a table for Fortune out of conviction; people do it because the future is unknown and frightening and they want some grip on it. Notice the order: first they forget God’s holy mountain, then they set the table. When the God who holds the future is forgotten, something must be fed to quiet the fear of it.

I will destine you to the sword. There is a pun in the Hebrew: I will destine is maniti, from the same root as Meni. They set a table for Destiny; God says, very well, I will destine you. Fate was never a power that could be bargained with. There is one God who appoints outcomes, and those who lay a table for a rival have not escaped his appointment; they have chosen a worse one.

When I called, you did not answer. The charge is not only idolatry but the failure to answer, and it lands hard in a chapter that opened with God calling Here I am, here I am. He answered before he was asked; they would not answer when they were.

The cure for fear of the future. Every generation has its own version of the meal: horoscopes, lucky charms, anxious hedging against every outcome. The cure is not a firmer grip on the future but trust in the One who holds it. Not one sparrow “will fall to the ground apart from your Father” (Matthew 10:29), so do not be anxious about tomorrow (Matthew 6:34).

Uncertain wording. Gad is known as a god of good fortune from place names (compare Baal-gad, Joshua 11:17). Meni appears nowhere else and is known only from its meaning, something like portion or allotment. How they were worshipped is uncertain; the point of the verse is not.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore thus says the Lord GOD: "Behold, my servants shall eat, but you shall be hungry; behold, my servants shall drink, but you shall be thirsty; behold, my servants shall rejoice, but you shall be put to shame; behold, my servants shall sing for gladness of heart, but you shall cry out for pain of heart and shall wail for breaking of spirit.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God’s servants and those who refuse him face two opposite futures, and he will not let anyone blur the difference.

Behold, my servants shall eat. Four times behold, four contrasts, hammered so that nobody can pretend the outcomes have been blurred. And the terms are physical: not that the servants shall be blessed but that they shall eat. Isaiah deals in what will actually be happening at a table. These are the blessings and curses of Deuteronomy 28 in their final form: the same land, the same God, and two entirely different futures for people who have lived side by side.

Where the line runs. Both groups share ancestry, worship in the same city and read the same law, and the line runs straight between them, drawn by what they did when God called. The servants are not on the right side because their record was cleaner but because they answered the hands held out to them, and those hands are still held out to anyone on the wrong side who turns (v. 2).

Jesus’ blessings and woes. Jesus spoke in the same double rhythm: “Blessed are you who are hungry now, for you shall be satisfied” and “Woe to you who are full now, for you shall be hungry” (Luke 6:21, 25). He promised that many will come from east and west to feast with Abraham in the kingdom (Matthew 8:11). And on the cross he said, “I thirst” (John 19:28): he went without, so that his servants might eat and drink.

verseByVerse.quote: You shall leave your name to my chosen for a curse, and the Lord GOD will put you to death, but his servants he will call by another name, so that he who blesses himself in the land shall bless himself by the God of truth, and he who takes an oath in the land shall swear by the God of truth; because the former troubles are forgotten and are hidden from my eyes.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The rebels leave behind only a name used in curses, but God gives his servants a new name and a life before the God who is utterly true, their old troubles gone even from his sight.

You shall leave your name to my chosen for a curse. Their name survives only as a byword in oaths, of the kind Jeremiah records: “The LORD make you like Zedekiah and Ahab” (Jeremiah 29:22).

His servants he will call by another name. In Scripture a new name is a new beginning: Abram became Abraham, Jacob became Israel, and Zion was promised “a new name that the mouth of the LORD will give” (62:2). To the one who conquers, Christ promises a white stone “with a new name written on the stone” (Revelation 2:17).

The God of truth. Twice in verse 16 God is called the God of truth, and the Hebrew is more striking: elohei amen, the God of Amen, a title found nowhere else in the Old Testament. People will bless themselves and swear by him because nothing he has said has ever failed to hold: in him what is said and what is true have never come apart.

The Amen has a name. At the other end of the Bible a letter comes from “the Amen, the faithful and true witness” (Revelation 3:14), and the title belongs to Jesus Christ. “All the promises of God find their Yes in him” (2 Corinthians 1:20). The God of Amen has kept his word in person.

The former troubles are forgotten. They are not merely forgiven, or put behind the people; they are hidden from God’s eyes, the wound no longer visible to the one who healed it. The clause leads straight into verse 17.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 17–25 — New Heavens and a New Earth
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God’s answer to his people’s sorrow is not a patched-up Judah but a whole new creation, and this is the Old Testament’s fullest picture of it. He creates new heavens and a new earth, and a Jerusalem made to be a joy (vv. 17–18). He rejoices in it himself, and the sound of weeping is never heard there again (v. 19). No infant dies after a few days and no life is cut short (v. 20). The curses of the covenant are reversed one by one: houses lived in, vineyards enjoyed, work not wasted, children not born for disaster (vv. 21–23). Prayer is answered before it is spoken (v. 24), and the wolf and the lamb graze together while the serpent eats dust (v. 25).
verseByVerse.theology: This is the goal towards which God’s whole work of redemption is moving. Revelation 21:1 takes verse 17 almost word for word, and Revelation 21:4 takes verse 19.
verseByVerse.examples: Nothing in verses 21-23 is idle. The world to come in this chapter is not an endless rest from everything human but houses, vineyards and families, safe at last from loss.

verseByVerse.quote: "For behold, I create new heavens and a new earth, and the former things shall not be remembered or come into mind. But be glad and rejoice forever in that which I create; for behold, I create Jerusalem to be a joy, and her people to be a gladness.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God promises not to patch up the old world but to make it new, heavens and earth together, and to create joy itself, so that past sorrows are outshone and no longer come to mind.

I create new heavens and a new earth. The verb is create, bara, the verb of the Bible’s first sentence (Genesis 1:1), used in Hebrew only of God. What he makes is not a tidier version of the present arrangement but the whole frame of things, sky and ground.

The former things shall not be remembered. This does not promise amnesia, or say that what happened to you did not matter: the God speaking keeps a record in verse 6 and counts his people’s tears (Psalm 56:8). It promises that the former things will be outshone. They will not come into mind because something will stand in front of them large enough that the mind does not go back. Jesus used the same picture: a mother after the birth “no longer remembers the anguish, for joy that a human being has been born into the world” (John 16:21).

I create Jerusalem to be a joy. God creates joy, with the same verb as the heavens and the earth. Gladness is not a mood the redeemed will work up once conditions are right; it is something he makes.

Already begun in a garden. John saw this and reported it in almost these words (Revelation 21:1), and Peter adds what will live there: “new heavens and a new earth in which righteousness dwells” (2 Peter 3:13). And the new creation has already begun. On the first day of the week a body came out of a tomb in a garden, the firstfruits of the harvest to come (1 Corinthians 15:20), and “if anyone is in Christ, he is a new creation” (2 Corinthians 5:17). The world of verses 17 to 25 is the risen Christ’s world, spread out to its edges.

Where Christians differ: is the new creation this world renewed, or a replacement? Some read “the heavens will pass away” (2 Peter 3:10) as the end of this creation and its replacement by another, or picture eternity simply as a spiritual heaven.

This commentary’s view: this creation will be renewed and transformed, not discarded. Peter compares the coming fire with the flood, which cleansed the world without abolishing it (2 Peter 3:6–7), and Paul says “the creation itself will be set free from its bondage to corruption” (Romans 8:21). That is why this chapter is full of houses, vineyards and animals rather than clouds.

verseByVerse.quote: I will rejoice in Jerusalem and be glad in my people; no more shall be heard in it the sound of weeping and the cry of distress.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God himself delights in his renewed people, and the sound of weeping will never be heard among them again.

I will rejoice in Jerusalem and be glad in my people. The first half is easy to read past: God is the one enjoying himself here, as a bridegroom rejoices over his bride (62:5). The gladness of the new creation begins with his, and ours flows from it.

No more shall be heard in it the sound of weeping. Isaiah does not say there will be no more sorrow in the abstract; he says a sound will no longer be heard. Anyone who has been in a hospital at night, or a house after a death, knows that sound. It is the most recognisable noise human beings make. Isaiah promises a city where it is never heard again, not because people have learned to bear it quietly, but because nothing is left to cause it.

Every tear wiped away. John makes the promise more intimate still: “He will wipe away every tear from their eyes” (Revelation 21:4; compare Isaiah 25:8). The tears are not merely stopped; they are wiped off a face, by a hand, one person at a time. And the hand belongs to one who knows that sound from the inside: at his friend’s tomb, “Jesus wept” (John 11:35).

verseByVerse.quote: No more shall there be in it an infant who lives but a few days, or an old man who does not fill out his days, for the young man shall die a hundred years old, and the sinner a hundred years old shall be accursed.
verseByVerse.commentary:
In God’s new world no baby dies in infancy and no life is cut short: Isaiah describes the end of death’s cruelty in the strongest terms his hearers could grasp.

An honest difficulty. This is the hardest verse in the chapter. Everything around it describes a world without weeping, and this verse still seems to have people dying in it.

An infant who lives but a few days. Whichever way it is read, the two griefs it removes are the ones that break people: the baby who lives only a few days, and the life cut off with things unfinished. For an ancient reader the most extravagant picture of flourishing was a world where nobody buries a baby and the old die full of years. The numbers are not a ceiling but a way of saying the ceiling is gone, and the New Testament finally says it without figures: “death shall be no more” (Revelation 21:4).

Death abolished. This hope rests on Jesus Christ, “who abolished death and brought life and immortality to light through the gospel” (2 Timothy 1:10). At Nain he stopped a funeral and gave a widow’s only son back to his mother (Luke 7:12–15), a preview of what he will do for the world.

For the bereaved. Isaiah does not tell the bereaved their losses are small. He tells them the losses are going to stop, in the specific terms of the loss rather than general assurances about eternity. For anyone who has stood at the wrong kind of graveside, that is the promise made here.

Where Christians differ: does this verse describe the final state? Some godly readers, especially premillennialists, take the chapter as a long earthly age before the final state, in which death is drastically reduced but not abolished: since people still die here and the sinner is still accursed, they argue, this must be the thousand years of Revelation 20.

This commentary’s view: the passage is plainly describing the new heavens and the new earth (v. 17), and verse 20 is poetry describing an unimaginable condition in the strongest terms an ancient reader had. This amillennial reading is the more likely; faithful Christians who hold the other are brothers in the same hope.

Uncertain wording. The last clause is compressed. The sinner a hundred years old shall be accursed can also be translated the one who falls short of a hundred shall be thought accursed, since the Hebrew word for sinner means one who misses the mark. Either way the clause stresses how long life will be.

verseByVerse.quote: They shall build houses and inhabit them; they shall plant vineyards and eat their fruit. They shall not build and another inhabit; they shall not plant and another eat; for like the days of a tree shall the days of my people be, and my chosen shall long enjoy the work of their hands.
verseByVerse.commentary:
In the new creation the covenant curse is undone: God’s people will live in the houses they build and enjoy the fruit they plant, with lives as long as a tree’s.

They shall build houses and inhabit them. Read these verses against Deuteronomy 28, and they turn out to be a curse undone clause by clause. Among the covenant curses Moses set out was this: “You shall build a house, but you shall not dwell in it. You shall plant a vineyard, but you shall not enjoy its fruit” (Deuteronomy 28:30). Isaiah reverses it, with the same two examples in the same order.

They shall not build and another inhabit. This is the misery of a conquered people, and it is not archaic: to do the work and watch the benefit walk away, as happens in occupied countries, bad companies and families.

Like the days of a tree. The measure is an olive or a cedar, which outlives the people who planted it and the people who buried them. And long enjoy the work of their hands means more than possessing it. Work in the new creation is neither abolished nor drudgery: it is finally worth doing, and the one who did it is still there to sit under it.

Why the curse can be lifted. The curse does not simply lapse. “Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us” (Galatians 3:13). He who had nowhere to lay his head (Matthew 8:20) bore it, so that his people might live in the houses they build.

verseByVerse.quote: They shall not labor in vain or bear children for calamity, for they shall be the offspring of the blessed of the LORD, and their descendants with them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Nothing God’s people do or love will come to nothing, because they belong to him.

They shall not labor in vain. Two futilities that between them cover most of a life. The first is work: the project cancelled after four years, the business that never came right, the years given to something that quietly came to nothing.

Or bear children for calamity. This is the heavier one: what a mother in a besieged city thinks, that the child in her arms is being raised for a disaster she can already see coming. Every parent feels it in a smaller way, looking at the world their children will inherit.

The offspring of the blessed of the LORD. Both are cancelled in one sentence, and the reason is not that circumstances improve but whose these people are. They belong to God, and their descendants with them, and what belongs to him does not come to nothing.

Not in vain, even now. Paul ends his great resurrection chapter by bringing this promise into the present: “in the Lord your labor is not in vain” (1 Corinthians 15:58). Because Christ is risen, work done for him is already safe from futility.

verseByVerse.quote: Before they call I will answer; while they are yet speaking I will hear.
verseByVerse.commentary:
In the new creation the long silence of unanswered prayer will be over: God will answer before his people have finished asking.

Before they call I will answer. Chapter 64 ended with two open questions and no reply (64:12). This verse does not merely promise that prayers will be heard; it removes the gap entirely. The answer is under way before the request is made.

While they are yet speaking I will hear. Anyone who prays knows the other side of this: the sense of talking into a room, the pause after the amen, the wondering whether anything was heard. Isaiah promises a world in which the hearing has happened by the middle of the sentence.

Now and the age to come. This is plainly a promise about the age to come. God does not always answer now before we call; chapters 63 and 64 exist because he did not. The silence belongs to this time of waiting, not to God’s character, and it will end. Even now there is a foretaste: “your Father knows what you need before you ask him” (Matthew 6:8), and through Christ we may “with confidence draw near to the throne of grace” (Hebrews 4:16).

verseByVerse.quote: The wolf and the lamb shall graze together; the lion shall eat straw like the ox, and dust shall be the serpent's food. They shall not hurt or destroy in all my holy mountain," says the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The violence built into the present world will be gone for ever, and the only curse left standing will be the serpent’s: evil itself defeated.

The wolf and the lamb shall graze together. The peace among the animals of chapter 11 (11:6–9) returns as a permanent condition. The wolf is not restrained from eating the lamb; the wolf is grazing, and the lion eating straw is a change in what the lion is. That is the difference between a truce and a new creation: the violence built into the present order is not policed but removed (Romans 8:19–21).

Dust shall be the serpent’s food. In the middle of that sentence one thing is left exactly as it was. The serpent was told, “on your belly you shall go, and dust you shall eat all the days of your life” (Genesis 3:14). Every other curse of that chapter is lifted, death itself at last (Revelation 21:4), but the sentence on the serpent stands. In the world to come the evil that started all of this will not have been rehabilitated, negotiated with or given a second hearing. It will be defeated, permanently and visibly.

The serpent’s head crushed. That defeat was promised on the day of the fall: the woman’s offspring “shall bruise your head, and you shall bruise his heel” (Genesis 3:15). It was won at the cross, and Paul promises its completion: “The God of peace will soon crush Satan under your feet” (Romans 16:20).

They shall not hurt or destroy in all my holy mountain. The chapter’s last line, repeated from 11:9, is God’s whole ambition for his world: no hurting, no destroying, anywhere on his mountain. He said he would create it, and he does not plan what he cannot build.

66.subtitle: This Is the One to Whom I Will Look
66.intro:
Where we are. Isaiah’s last chapter completes God’s answer, begun in chapter 65, to the prayer of chapters 63 and 64. It gathers up the whole book: the holy God, the humble, Zion and her children, the nations, and the final division.

The message. The God who fills heaven and earth cannot be housed or impressed by anything we build, yet he looks with favour on the humble and contrite person who trembles at his word. He will vindicate them, bring his new people to birth at a stroke, comfort them like a mother, and gather worshippers from every nation; and he will judge those who choose their own ways. The book ends with two destinies side by side, and the only safe place to stand is the one in verse 2.

Why it was said. Isaiah looks ahead to a community back from exile, tempted to trust a rebuilt temple and correct ritual, where the faithful were mocked and pushed out by their own brothers (see the introduction). They needed to know what God truly looks for.

How the chapter makes its case. First the house and the heart: no building can contain God, but he looks to the trembling (vv. 1–2); self-willed worship is as vile to him as murder (vv. 3–4); and the cast-out faithful will see their mockers shamed (vv. 5–6). Then the birth and the comfort: Zion bears a nation in a day, and God will finish what he starts (vv. 7–9); her mourners rejoice, and God comforts them like a mother (vv. 10–14). Finally the end of all things: the LORD comes in fire (vv. 15–17), gathers the nations, sends survivors to the far coastlands, takes priests even from foreigners, and receives the worship of all flesh, while the rebels lie dead outside (vv. 18–24).

Where it leads. The chapter leads to Christ by promise and by pattern. The God who will not be housed in a temple came to dwell among us in his Son, the true temple (John 1:14; 2:21). A nation was born in a day at Pentecost; survivors were sent to the nations with the gospel (Romans 15:16); believers from every people became “a royal priesthood” (1 Peter 2:9); and John saw the new heavens and new earth. Jesus quoted the last verse as a warning (Mark 9:48), and bore that judgment himself for all who come to him.

For us. Come to God not with what you have built but trembling at his word, and you will find him already looking at you with favour. If you are mourning or mocked for his name, his comfort is that of a mother. And do not close the book without settling where you stand: in Christ, among the worshippers.

keyVerse.quote: “But this is the one to whom I will look: he who is humble and contrite in spirit and trembles at my word.”
keyVerse.note: The God whose throne is heaven and whose footstool is the earth fixes his gaze on one kind of person: not the impressive or the accomplished, but the humble and contrite who trembles at his word. This is the first beatitude, “Blessed are the poor in spirit” (Matthew 5:3), in Old Testament form, and the conclusion the whole book has been building towards: the question was never what house would satisfy God, but what heart.

66.theology:
God stooping down. Verses 1 and 2 argue from size: the greater God is, the more startling his attention to one broken person who shakes at his word. Stephen quoted them to the Sanhedrin against people who had made an idol of the temple itself (Acts 7:49-50).

Worship, and the self-will underneath it. The four shocking comparisons of verse 3 are not an attack on sacrifice, which God commanded. An offering made by someone set on his own way is no longer worship at all, as the book’s first chapter already said.

Two destinations, unresolved. Verse 23 has all flesh worshipping from one Sabbath to the next; verse 24 has the worshippers going out to look at the dead. Jesus quoted that verse in warning his own disciples (Mark 9:48), which makes it harder to soften rather than easier. Isaiah offers no resolution, since both are real and both permanent, and the only response the chapter has ever asked for is the one in verse 2.
66.reflection:
God says no building can house him, yet he looks to the one who is “humble and contrite in spirit and trembles at my word” (v. 2). What would it look like for you to tremble at God’s word this week, and why is that a place of comfort rather than fear?

Verse 3 says that worship from people who have chosen their own ways is no better than an abomination to God. How can regular church attendance become a way of avoiding God rather than meeting him, and what is the remedy?

God promises to comfort his people “as one whom his mother comforts” (v. 13). How does this picture of God help you in grief or weariness, and who around you needs that kind of comfort from you?

The book ends with all flesh worshipping and with the dead who rebelled (vv. 23–24). How should these two final pictures shape the urgency and the tenderness with which we share the gospel with others?

But this is the one to whom I will look: he who is humble and contrite in spirit and trembles at my word.<sup>3</sup>"He who slaughters an ox is like one who kills a man; he who sacrifices a lamb, like one who breaks a dog's neck; he who presents a grain offering, like one who offers pig's blood; he who makes a memorial offering of frankincense, like one who blesses an idol.
