For their worm shall not die, their fire shall not be quenched, and they shall be an abhorrence to all flesh."

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–6 — The One to Whom I Will Look
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God cannot be housed, but he gladly looks to the humble. The LORD of heaven and earth needs no building from human hands, for he made everything (vv. 1–2a); yet he fixes his gaze on the one who is humble and contrite and trembles at his word (v. 2b). Worship offered by people who have chosen their own way is as abhorrent to him as murder and idolatry, because they did not answer when he called (vv. 3–4). And those who tremble at his word, mocked and cast out by their own brothers, are promised that their persecutors will be put to shame when the LORD acts from his temple (vv. 5–6).
verseByVerse.theology: The movement of verses 1 and 2 is the whole truth of God’s stooping down to us in two sentences: he who fills heaven and earth looks at one small trembling person, and he looks not with mere pity but with favour.
verseByVerse.examples: The whole book has been about an incomparable God, and it turns out the question was never what house would suit him but what heart.

verseByVerse.quote: Thus says the LORD: "Heaven is my throne, and the earth is my footstool; what is the house that you would build for me, and what is the place of my rest? All these things my hand has made, and so all these things came to be, declares the LORD. But this is the one to whom I will look: he who is humble and contrite in spirit and trembles at my word.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The God who fills heaven and earth cannot be housed by anything we build, yet he looks with favour on the humble, broken person who trembles at his word.

Heaven is my throne, and the earth is my footstool. Picture the proportions. If heaven is the chair and the whole earth the low stool under the feet, the being described is off the scale entirely, and the question about a house answers itself: any building anyone could put up is a box on the footstool. All these things my hand has made: any house would be built from his own materials.

What is the house that you would build for me? This is aimed at people with a temple project and a good deal of confidence in it. Isaiah is not against the temple, which God commanded, but against the assumption underneath it, that God can be given an address and that once you know where he lives you have him. Solomon had said the opposite when he dedicated the first temple: “heaven and the highest heaven cannot contain you; how much less this house that I have built!” (1 Kings 8:27).

This is the one to whom I will look. Then the turn, from the whole created order to one person. The verb is a deliberate, favourable gaze. The God whom the universe cannot house looks steadily at a particular person, and Isaiah tells us how to recognise him. He is humble, brought low, not necessarily by choice. He is contrite in spirit, literally struck or broken. And he trembles at my word: when Scripture says something, he feels it and it shakes him. God had already said he dwells “with him who is of a contrite and lowly spirit” (57:15).

Nothing earned. Nothing in the list is an achievement: not learning, not office, not a record of service. Two of the three describe damage. This is the first beatitude in Old Testament clothing, “Blessed are the poor in spirit” (Matthew 5:3), and it is the tax collector at the back of the temple who would not lift his eyes and prayed, “God, be merciful to me, a sinner!” (Luke 18:13).

Trembles at my word. Sixty-six chapters have established that this God is beyond comparison: the throne, the seraphim, the waters in the hollow of his hand, the nations as dust. And what he looks at is a broken person who shakes when he reads. The distance between those two facts is the distance grace has to travel, and he crosses it every time.

The true temple. God did come to dwell on earth, not in a building but in a body: “the Word became flesh and dwelt among us” (John 1:14), and Jesus spoke of “the temple of his body” (John 2:21). He told a Samaritan woman that the Father is seeking worshippers “in spirit and truth” (John 4:23), whatever the place. Stephen quoted these two verses in the last speech of his life, minutes before they picked up stones, against people who had made the building the point (Acts 7:48–50).

verseByVerse.quote: "He who slaughters an ox is like one who kills a man; he who sacrifices a lamb, like one who breaks a dog's neck; he who presents a grain offering, like one who offers pig's blood; he who makes a memorial offering of frankincense, like one who blesses an idol. These have chosen their own ways, and their soul delights in their abominations; I also will choose harsh treatment for them and bring their fears upon them, because when I called, no one answered, when I spoke, they did not listen; but they did what was evil in my eyes and chose that in which I did not delight."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Worship from people set on their own way is not worship at all: God counts their correct sacrifices as no better than murder and idolatry, because they would not listen when he called.

He who slaughters an ox is like one who kills a man. Four pairings, each setting a prescribed act of worship beside something revolting. Killing a man is murder. A dog was an unclean scavenger, and breaking its neck a worthless, contemptible act. Pig’s blood combines the forbidden animal with the forbidden substance. Incense to an idol is plain idolatry.

Not against sacrifice. This is no attack on the sacrificial system: God designed it, and every first item in the four pairs was commanded.

These have chosen their own ways. The explanation is in the second half of the verse: these have chosen their own ways, and their soul delights in their abominations. The offering is identical; the man behind it is not. An offering from someone settled on his own path, who privately enjoys what God hates, is not a weak sacrifice but a different act wearing a sacrifice’s clothes. So God answers in kind: they chose their ways, and I also will choose; he brings on them the very things they feared.

When I called, no one answered. The root is in verse 4, in almost the same words as 65:12. The worship failed where the listening failed. The remedy is not more effort at the altar but the ear God opens: he is the one who called first, and his Spirit still makes people hear.

The willing sacrifice. Jesus took up the same charge against the religious of his day, quoting this book: “This people honors me with their lips, but their heart is far from me” (Matthew 15:8; Isaiah 29:13). And he is the one worshipper whose offering never had this fault. He came saying, “Behold, I have come to do your will, O God” (Hebrews 10:7), and the sacrifice of himself was given with a whole heart.

For regular churchgoers. This is hard reading for anyone who attends church regularly: the question at a service is never only whether the right things are being done. Chapter 1 said the same on the first page of the book (1:11–15), and the charge has not changed in sixty-five chapters.

Uncertain wording. The Hebrew has no word for like: it simply sets the phrases side by side, he who slaughters an ox, one who kills a man. Most translations supply like, so that God counts the sacrifice as equal to the crime. Others read it as describing the same people doing both, offering sacrifices while also committing these acts. Either way, worship from a self-willed heart is no worship.

verseByVerse.quote: Hear the word of the LORD, you who tremble at his word: "Your brothers who hate you and cast you out for my name's sake have said, 'Let the LORD be glorified, that we may see your joy'; but it is they who shall be put to shame. "The sound of an uproar from the city! A sound from the temple! The sound of the LORD, rendering recompense to his enemies!
verseByVerse.commentary:
Those who tremble at God’s word may be mocked and thrown out by their own religious brothers, but God will vindicate them and put their persecutors to shame.

Hear the word of the LORD, you who tremble at his word. The people of verse 2 are now addressed directly. They are being hated and expelled, and not by pagans: by your brothers, inside the covenant community, and for my name’s sake. This is religious persecution of the devout by the religious.

Let the LORD be glorified, that we may see your joy. The mockery is unnervingly modern. It is said in pious language and it means: go on then, let’s see this God of yours do something. It is a sneer built entirely out of orthodox words.

It is they who shall be put to shame. God’s answer is one line. Not an argument, not an explanation of the delay: a statement about how the thing will end.

A sound from the temple! Verse 6 is written as a man hearing something before he can see it: noise from the city, noise from the temple, and then the identification, the sound of the LORD. The vindication the mockers demanded arrives, not as a show put on to satisfy them but as judgment on them.

Cast out with Christ. Jesus warned his disciples about precisely this: “They will put you out of the synagogues. Indeed, the hour is coming when whoever kills you will think he is offering service to God” (John 16:2). He went that way first: “He came to his own, and his own people did not receive him” (John 1:11), and he suffered outside the city gate. So “let us go to him outside the camp and bear the reproach he endured” (Hebrews 13:13).

What it does not mean. Not every rejection is persecution for God’s name. Peter warns believers not to suffer “as a meddler” (1 Peter 4:15), and Christians are sometimes pushed out for their own harshness. The promise is for those who suffer for trembling at God’s word, not for being difficult.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 7–14 — Born in a Day, and Comforted Like a Child
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God will bring his new people to birth suddenly and certainly, and comfort them like a mother. Zion gives birth before her labour begins, a nation born in a day (vv. 7–8), and God will not bring a birth to the point of delivery and then stop (v. 9). Those who love Jerusalem and mourn over her are called to rejoice and to feed at her breast (vv. 10–11). Peace flows to her like a river, her children are carried and played with, and God himself comforts them as a mother comforts her child (vv. 12–13). Their very bones flourish, while the same hand of the LORD turns against his enemies (v. 14).
verseByVerse.theology: Verse 9 is why a Christian can be sure of being kept to the end: God does not begin a work and then abandon it.
verseByVerse.examples: Verse 5 has already named the people this comfort is for: those cast out by their own brothers for God's name's sake.

verseByVerse.quote: "Before she was in labor she gave birth; before her pain came upon her she delivered a son. Who has heard such a thing? Who has seen such things? Shall a land be born in one day? Shall a nation be brought forth in one moment? For as soon as Zion was in labor she brought forth her children. Shall I bring to the point of birth and not cause to bring forth?" says the LORD; "shall I, who cause to bring forth, shut the womb?" says your God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God will bring his new people into being suddenly and certainly: what he begins to bring to birth, he will bring to completion.

Before she was in labor she gave birth. Something impossible is reported flatly: a child arrives with no labour at all.

Who has heard such a thing? Then four questions in a row, to stop the reader treating this as a figure of speech. Nations are not born in a day; they accumulate through generations, wars and slow settlement. That is exactly what God says will happen.

Shall I bring to the point of birth and not cause to bring forth? Verse 9 is the argument the passage rests on, put as a question no one can answer yes to. God does not take a thing to the edge of delivery and then abandon it. The one who starts a birth finishes it, because stopping there would be a cruelty he is not capable of.

Pentecost. Read Acts 2 with this in mind. In the morning there is a room with about a hundred and twenty people in it. By the evening about three thousand have been added (Acts 2:41), from fifteen named regions, and the church exists. Peter preaches one sermon at Pentecost, and a nation is brought forth in a moment.

The same confidence in Paul. Paul says the same to people anxious about their own perseverance: “he who began a good work in you will bring it to completion at the day of Jesus Christ” (Philippians 1:6). The confidence is not in the strength of the thing being born but in the character of the one delivering it.

Where Christians differ: what birth is this? Some see the return from exile. Many Christian Zionists and dispensationalists see the founding of the modern state of Israel in 1948, a land born in one day.

This commentary’s view: the birth is Zion’s children brought forth through the gospel. Paul calls the heavenly city our mother: “the Jerusalem above is free, and she is our mother” (Galatians 4:26), and at Pentecost three thousand were born in a day. Faithful Christians differ over how far modern events fulfil prophecy, but the New Testament points this promise to the church.

verseByVerse.quote: "Rejoice with Jerusalem, and be glad for her, all you who love her; rejoice with her in joy, all you who mourn over her; that you may nurse and be satisfied from her consoling breast; that you may drink deeply with delight from her glorious abundance."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Everyone who loves God’s city and has grieved over it is invited to rejoice and to be fed from her abundance like a nursing child.

All you who mourn over her. Look who is invited: those who love her and, the surprise, those who mourn over her. The mourning was never wasted. Someone who has wept for years over a church, a family or a country is on the guest list precisely because of the weeping.

That you may nurse and be satisfied. The image is startling and meant to be. Jerusalem is a nursing mother, and the mourners are infants at the breast: entirely dependent, taking in what they did nothing to produce, and satisfied, fed until nothing more is wanted. Isaiah could have pictured a fortress or a throne; he chooses the most intimate physical bond human beings have, in which one person is kept alive by another’s body without ever asking for it.

A city that feeds others. The city that was a ruin two chapters ago is now feeding people. Restoration in this book is never merely the end of trouble; the restored city begins to feed others.

Blessed are those who mourn. Jesus made the same promise to the same people: “Blessed are those who mourn, for they shall be comforted” (Matthew 5:4). Those who grieve over the brokenness of God’s people are the ones he will gather to the feast.

Uncertain wording. The word behind glorious abundance is rare and its meaning is uncertain. It may mean abundance or fullness; some take it, in keeping with the image, as the full breast itself. The sense is clear either way: rich, satisfying nourishment.

verseByVerse.quote: For thus says the LORD: "Behold, I will extend peace to her like a river, and the glory of the nations like an overflowing stream; and you shall nurse, you shall be carried upon her hip, and bounced upon her knees. As one whom his mother comforts, so I will comfort you; you shall be comforted in Jerusalem.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God promises his people unending peace and the tender comfort of a mother holding her child, and he gives that comfort himself.

I will extend peace to her like a river. A river does not arrive in bursts and stop; it runs, at volume, in the dry season as well as the wet. What is promised is not a spell of calm but peace that keeps coming.

Bounced upon her knees. Then three things done to a small child: fed, carried on the hip, bounced on the knees. The last is not about need at all. Nobody bounces a baby to keep it alive; it is done for delight, and Isaiah puts it at the end of the sentence as the point the others were leading to.

As one whom his mother comforts, so I will comfort you. Go back to 40:1, where this half of the book began: “Comfort, comfort my people, says your God.” For twenty-six chapters what that would actually mean has been left open, and here is the answer. God takes the plainest experience of comfort anyone has, a child who has come off worst somewhere and is being held by his mother, who says nothing useful and fixes nothing but holds him until it stops, and says: like that. Not I will send you comfort, but I will comfort you, myself, in that manner.

The Most High as a mother. He is not embarrassed by the comparison and does not qualify it. The God whose throne is heaven, who measures the waters in the hollow of his hand and calls the stars by name, describes himself as a mother with a crying child on her shoulder, and that is how the book’s great word, comfort, is finally fulfilled.

The comfort in person. Paul calls God “the Father of mercies and God of all comfort”, and says that “through Christ we share abundantly in comfort too” (2 Corinthians 1:3, 5). The One who longed to gather Jerusalem’s children “as a hen gathers her brood under her wings” (Matthew 23:37) went on to stretch out his arms on a cross for them.

Isn’t the God of the Bible a man’s God? Many modern readers assume that a God called Father and King, in books written mostly by men, is male power projected onto the sky. Verse 13 answers the charge. At the climax of the book, where the word comfort from chapter 40 is finally explained, God compares himself to a mother holding a hurt child. Scripture does the same elsewhere: a woman who cannot forget her nursing child (49:15), a hen gathering her brood. The God of Israel is neither male nor female; he made both in his image (Genesis 1:27), and the tenderness we associate with mothers was his before it was theirs. He still gives himself the name Father, and Christians keep the name he gave, but it was never a claim that God is a man. It tells us that he is the source of our life and that we belong to him.

verseByVerse.quote: You shall see, and your heart shall rejoice; your bones shall flourish like the grass; and the hand of the LORD shall be known to his servants, and he shall show his indignation against his enemies.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God’s comfort will renew his servants to the very bones, while the same hand of the LORD is turned against his enemies.

Your bones shall flourish like the grass. Bones in Scripture stand for the deepest physical self; the psalms speak of bones wasting away, out of joint, burning. Isaiah promises the spring flush after rain, happening at the level of the skeleton. It is recovery in the part of a person that recovers last. Anyone who has come out of a long grief knows that the mind agrees things are better some time before the body does. Here the body agrees.

The hand of the LORD shall be known to his servants. The second half of the verse holds two things together without apology: one hand, two effects. The same intervention that greens the bones of the servants is the one his enemies meet. The kindness of verse 13 is not a softer God than the fire of verse 15; it is the same God, and what he is like to you depends on which side of his hand you are standing.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 15–24 — Fire, the Nations Gathered, and Two Endings
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The book ends with God’s final judgment and the gathering of the nations, and leaves two destinies side by side. The LORD comes in fire to judge all flesh (vv. 15–16) and puts an end to those who purify themselves for pagan rites (v. 17). He gathers all nations to see his glory, sends survivors to far coastlands that have never heard of him, and the nations bring God’s scattered people home as an offering (vv. 18–20). Some are even taken as priests and Levites (v. 21). God’s people will last as long as the new creation, and all flesh will worship him (vv. 22–23). The last verse shows the dead who rebelled (v. 24).
verseByVerse.theology: Verse 21 is one of the most radical inclusions in the Old Testament: offices restricted to one tribe of one nation are opened, most likely, to men from the far nations, and the priestly calling of Israel reaches further than anyone expected.
verseByVerse.examples: The pattern of mission in verses 19 and 20 is the pattern of the church: those who have seen the glory are sent to those who have not.

verseByVerse.quote: "For behold, the LORD will come in fire, and his chariots like the whirlwind, to render his anger in fury, and his rebuke with flames of fire. For by fire will the LORD enter into judgment, and by his sword, with all flesh; and those slain by the LORD shall be many.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The God who comforts his people will come in fire to judge the whole world, and his judgment will be real and terrible.

Straight after the comfort. Two verses after a mother comforting a child, this. Isaiah puts them side by side without a transition, and that is the point: both belong to the same God.

The LORD will come in fire. The imagery is military and at full stretch: fire, chariots like a whirlwind, flames, a sword. And the scope is total: with all flesh. Everyone alive is inside the sentence.

Those slain by the LORD shall be many. It should be read plainly. One strand of Christian thinking treats the wrath of God as an Old Testament embarrassment outgrown by the New. The difficulty is Jesus, who spoke about judgment more than anyone else in Scripture and who quotes the last verse of this very chapter.

Love and wrath. A love that is genuinely committed to what it loves must be against what destroys it, and a God who could look at the wreckage of his world and feel nothing in particular would not be worth worshipping. The fire of verse 15 comes from the same love as the comfort of verse 13.

The Judge who saves. Paul takes up this very picture for Christ’s return, “when the Lord Jesus is revealed from heaven with his mighty angels in flaming fire” (2 Thessalonians 1:7–8). The LORD who comes in fire is Jesus. But he is also the one who took judgment in his own body, so that “there is therefore now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus” (Romans 8:1).

verseByVerse.quote: "Those who sanctify and purify themselves to go into the gardens, following one in the midst, eating pig's flesh and the abomination and mice, shall come to an end together, declares the LORD. "For I know their works and their thoughts, and the time is coming to gather all nations and tongues. And they shall come and shall see my glory,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Those who carefully purify themselves for pagan rites will come to an end, and God will gather all nations to see his glory.

Those who sanctify and purify themselves. The garden cults of chapter 65 come back for their verdict, and the detail Isaiah keeps is the one that stings: these people sanctify and purify themselves before going in. Careful, costly religious effort, spent on rites God never asked for. Verse 3 has already named the problem: the acts look devout, and the choosing behind them is self-will.

All nations and tongues. Then the book opens out further than it ever has: from a handful of people mixing pagan rites into the LORD’s worship in a grove, to all nations and tongues gathered to see the glory of God. The judgment and the ingathering are one event. Verse 17 ends one group; verse 18 gathers the world. The fire that consumes what will not stand and the light that draws the nations are one blaze, seen from two positions.

They shall come and shall see my glory. Everything the book has been about is in that line. Not hear about it: see it. Isaiah had promised that “all flesh shall see it together” (40:5).

The glory in a face. The glory was seen. “We have seen his glory, glory as of the only Son from the Father” (John 1:14), and God now shines in human hearts “to give the light of the knowledge of the glory of God in the face of Jesus Christ” (2 Corinthians 4:6). John saw where the gathering ends: a multitude “from every nation, from all tribes and peoples and languages, standing before the throne and before the Lamb” (Revelation 7:9).

Uncertain wording. Following one in the midst is obscure: perhaps a priest or leader directing the rite from the centre, perhaps an idol standing in the middle of the grove. The opening of verse 18 is also abrupt in Hebrew, and translations supply a word such as know to make a sentence of it. Neither uncertainty affects the meaning of the passage.

verseByVerse.quote: and I will set a sign among them. And from them I will send survivors to the nations, to Tarshish, Pul, and Lud, who draw the bow, to Tubal and Javan, to the coastlands far away, that have not heard my fame or seen my glory. And they shall declare my glory among the nations. And they shall bring all your brothers from all the nations as an offering to the LORD, on horses and in chariots and in litters and on mules and on dromedaries, to my holy mountain Jerusalem, says the LORD, just as the Israelites bring their grain offering in a clean vessel to the house of the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God will send those he has rescued to the far nations that have never heard of him, and the nations will bring God’s scattered people home as an offering.

To Tarshish, Pul, and Lud. Read the names, because they are not decoration. Tarshish is the far west, most likely Spain, the edge of the map. Pul and Lud take in Africa and Asia Minor. Tubal is away to the north, and Javan is Greece. The coastlands far away is Isaiah’s phrase for everywhere he has no name for. The mission is aimed at those who do not know: places that have not heard my fame or seen my glory.

From them I will send survivors. Who does the sending? Survivors. The men and women who came through the fire of verse 16 are the messengers, people whose whole qualification is that they were spared and know it.

On horses and in chariots. Then the traffic reverses. The nations who received the message come back carrying God’s scattered people home on horses, in chariots, on mules and camels, the way a family conveys someone who cannot travel alone.

As an offering to the LORD. And the word for what they carry is offering: the gift is people. Paul, whose whole life was spent doing what verse 19 describes, speaks of his ministry the same way. He is “a minister of Christ Jesus to the Gentiles in the priestly service of the gospel of God, so that the offering of the Gentiles may be acceptable” (Romans 15:16).

Survivors with a message. The risen Jesus sent his disciples out on exactly this pattern: “repentance for the forgiveness of sins should be proclaimed in his name to all nations, beginning from Jerusalem” (Luke 24:47). The first messengers were survivors in the deepest sense, men who had deserted him and been restored.

Uncertain wording. Pul is not otherwise known as a nation; it is probably Put in Africa, as the Greek reads. Lud may be Lydia in Asia Minor or a people in Africa. The sign God sets among them is not described; most likely it is God’s saving act among the survivors, which sends them as messengers to the nations, as the gospel sent the apostles.
verseByVerse.note: Tarshish, Pul (perhaps Put), Lud, Tubal and Javan (Greece) stand for the distant nations to whom God’s glory will be declared.

verseByVerse.quote: And some of them also I will take for priests and for Levites, says the LORD. "For as the new heavens and the new earth that I make shall remain before me, says the LORD, so shall your offspring and your name remain.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God will take even people from the nations to serve him as priests, and his people will last as long as the new creation itself.

I will take for priests and for Levites. In its original setting this is almost unthinkable, for the priesthood was not open. A priest was descended from Aaron, a Levite from Levi, and no devotion could make a man from another tribe eligible (Numbers 18:7). King Uzziah tried, the king in whose death-year Isaiah saw the Lord (6:1), and came out of the temple a leper (2 Chronicles 26:16–21). Now people with no ancestry in Israel will be taken by God not merely into the courtyard but for the office itself (see priests and Levites).

A kingdom of priests. At Sinai God had said Israel would be to him “a kingdom of priests and a holy nation” (Exodus 19:6), and the book has shown how badly that went. Here the promise is kept, and kept wider than the people it was made to. Peter hands the same words to congregations in five Roman provinces: “you are a chosen race, a royal priesthood, a holy nation” (1 Peter 2:9). Through Jesus, the great high priest, Christ has “made us a kingdom, priests to his God and Father” (Revelation 1:6).

What it does not mean. Not that a temple will one day be rebuilt with sacrifices and a restored Levitical order. The New Testament never expects that: the one sacrifice has been offered, and the priesthood promised here is the whole people of God, Jew and Gentile, serving him in Christ.

So shall your offspring and your name remain. The guarantee on all of it is the durability of the new creation: God’s people are given the same lifetime as the remade universe, which is to say no end at all. Peter and John close the Bible’s hope with these same words (2 Peter 3:13; Revelation 21:1), and the one seated on the throne says, “Behold, I am making all things new” (Revelation 21:5).

Uncertain wording. Some of them most likely points back to the nations of verses 19 and 20, which is what makes the verse so startling. Some take it of the scattered Israelites they carry home, which would be less surprising. The flow of the passage favours the first.

verseByVerse.quote: From new moon to new moon, and from Sabbath to Sabbath, all flesh shall come to worship before me, declares the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
In the new creation all humanity will worship God without end, the whole of life given to him.

From new moon to new moon. The new moon and the Sabbath marked out the rhythm of Israel’s calendar, the month and the week. Isaiah stretches them over the new creation: from one to the next, and then the next, without end. This is not an event but a permanent condition, worship filling ordinary life for ever.

All flesh shall come to worship before me. The congregation is all flesh. The book has used the phrase before, and not always comfortably: “All flesh is grass” (40:6); the LORD will enter into judgment “with all flesh” (66:16). Here it has its gladdest sense: everybody who is left, from every nation named in verse 19, worshipping.

To a modern reader. That is a strange prospect to modern readers, who tend to find an hour of worship long enough, and the strangeness measures how little we have seen. In this chapter the worshippers have seen my glory (v. 18), and once anyone has, the difficulty is not sustaining worship but stopping it.

From Isaiah 6 to here. This is where the book has been going since a young man watched creatures with six wings cover their faces and call to one another, “Holy, holy, holy is the LORD of hosts” (6:3). The song they sang over one throne, in one room, in the year a king died, turns out to be the sound of the whole world. John heard it: a multitude from every nation, “standing before the throne and before the Lamb” (Revelation 7:9).

Will the Sabbath and new moons be kept in the new creation? Isaiah speaks in the only categories his hearers had; the point is endless worship from all flesh. The Sabbath and the feasts were “a shadow of the things to come, but the substance belongs to Christ” (Colossians 2:17), and the eternal rest is his.

verseByVerse.quote: "And they shall go out and look on the dead bodies of the men who have rebelled against me. For their worm shall not die, their fire shall not be quenched, and they shall be an abhorrence to all flesh."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The book’s last word is a sober warning: those who rebel against God face a ruin that does not end, set right beside the worship of the redeemed.

Where the book ends. Isaiah does not end where a writer wanting to be liked would end. One verse ago the whole world was worshipping. Now the worshippers go out and look at the dead.

Their worm shall not die. Later tradition attached the picture to the Valley of Hinnom below Jerusalem, where children had once been burned as offerings to Molech (2 Kings 23:10). That valley’s name became Gehenna, and Jesus used it for hell, quoting this verse in warning his own disciples (Mark 9:48).

Their fire shall not be quenched. Two things must be said plainly. First, the language is permanent: nothing suggests the condition ends. Universalism, the idea that everyone will be saved in the end, has to get past this sentence, and Jesus, who quoted it, made it harder rather than easier.

Beside the worship. Second, it is set immediately beside the worship of verse 23, and both are left standing, without resolution or reassurance. (When the chapter is read aloud in the synagogue, Jewish practice repeats verse 23 after verse 24 so that the reading does not end on the dead; the written text ends where it ends.)

So what is the response the book asks for? It asked for it in the second verse of this chapter: this is the one to whom I will look: he who is humble and contrite in spirit and trembles at my word. Not the man who builds God a house, nor the scrupulous worshipper in the garden, nor the brother who casts others out, but the one who is broken, who has stopped defending himself, and who shakes when God speaks, because he has understood who is speaking. That was the answer in chapter 6, when a prophet said I am lost and a coal was brought from the altar, and it is the answer on the last page.

From first page to last. The book began with a God whose people did not know him as well as an ox knows its owner (1:3), and it ends with all flesh before his face. Between those two sentences stands a servant who was despised and rejected, who was pierced for our transgressions, and on whom the LORD laid the iniquity of us all (53:3–6). He is the reason anyone is in verse 23 rather than verse 24, and there is no other reason. Holy, holy, holy is the LORD of hosts; the whole earth is full of his glory.

For the anxious. It must be said just as plainly: the trembling believer who fears he may end here is exactly the one verse 2 says God looks to. No one who flees to Christ will be found in verse 24, because he bore the wrath that verse describes, and he has promised, “whoever comes to me I will never cast out” (John 6:37).

Where Christians differ: does the undying worm and unquenched fire mean eternal conscious punishment? Some evangelicals hold annihilationism and read the verse of corpses consumed by worm and fire, destroyed rather than tormented for ever.

This commentary’s view: Jesus took these words up for hell itself, where “their worm does not die and the fire is not quenched” (Mark 9:48), and he set eternal punishment beside eternal life in the same sentence (Matthew 25:46). With the historic confessions, this commentary holds that the punishment of those who die in rebellion against God is conscious and unending. Some faithful Christians hold the other view, and the question should be weighed with tears rather than heat.
verseByVerse.note: Quoted by Jesus in Mark 9:48.

0.subtitle: Introduction
0.intro:
The message. Isaiah shows us a God who is utterly holy and who saves. The prophet sees the Lord “sitting upon a throne, high and lifted up” (6:1), is undone by his own sin, and is cleansed by a coal from the altar; the whole book tells that story on the scale of a nation and then of the world. God brings down the pride of his people and of every empire, and he will not let them trust in horses, treaties or idols. Yet the same Holy One promises comfort on the far side of judgment: a remnant brought home, a King from David’s line, and a Servant who bears the sins of others, until a new heavens and a new earth are full of his glory. “Though your sins are like scarlet, they shall be as white as snow” (1:18): the whole book shows how a holy God can say that.

Background: the prophet. Isaiah son of Amoz, whose name means the LORD saves, prophesied in Jerusalem under four kings of Judah, Uzziah, Jotham, Ahaz and Hezekiah (1:1), from his call in the year Uzziah died, about 740 BC (6:1), to about 700 BC or a little after. He was sent to meet kings and to answer them (7:3; 37:21; 38:1). His wife was a prophetess, and he gave his sons names that were sermons (7:3; 8:3). His younger contemporary Micah preached the same message in the country towns. Jewish tradition says Isaiah was put to death under Hezekiah’s son Manasseh. The New Testament quotes him more than any other prophet.

When and where: the age of Assyria. Isaiah lived through the rise of Assyria, an empire that swallowed whole nations and scattered their peoples. About 734 BC Syria and the northern kingdom of Israel marched on Jerusalem; Isaiah told King Ahaz, “If you are not firm in faith, you will not be firm at all” (7:9), but Ahaz sent to Assyria for help instead (2 Kings 16:7). In 722 BC Samaria fell, and the northern kingdom was carried away. The godly king Hezekiah was still tempted to lean on Egypt (chapters 30–31). In 701 BC Sennacherib of Assyria took the fortified cities of Judah and surrounded Jerusalem, and in one night the angel of the LORD struck down his army (37:36). Chapters 1–39 are preached into these crises, asking one question: will God’s people trust the Holy One, or the great powers?

Looking ahead: Babylon and the return. At the end of chapter 39 Hezekiah shows his treasures to envoys from Babylon, and Isaiah tells him that everything “shall be carried to Babylon” (39:6). That came true when Nebuchadnezzar destroyed Jerusalem and its temple in 586 BC. Chapters 40–55 speak ahead to the exiles in Babylon, who thought God had given them up. Cyrus of Persia, named as the LORD’s shepherd (44:28; 45:1), took Babylon in 539 BC and let them go home (Ezra 1:1–4). Chapters 56–66 speak to the community returning from exile, still waiting for the glory God had promised.

Who wrote chapters 40–66? Since the late eighteenth century many scholars have assigned chapters 40–55 to an unnamed prophet in Babylon and chapters 56–66 to others after the return, because they address the exiles as present, differ in tone, and name Cyrus long before his time. Some who hold Scripture wholly true agree, or think disciples gathered and extended his words. This commentary’s view is that the whole book comes from Isaiah, chapters 40–66 written ahead of time. John quotes 53:1 and 6:10 side by side, both as Isaiah’s words (John 12:38–41). The title the Holy One of Israel runs through both halves, twelve times in the first and thirteen in the second. Chapter 39 already foresees Babylon. The Great Isaiah Scroll from Qumran, copied more than a century before Christ, presents the book as one (see the Dead Sea Scrolls). And the argument of chapters 40–48 is that God alone declares “the end from the beginning” (46:10). The real question is whether God can name a king before he is born; these chapters answer that this is what marks him out as God (44:24–28).

How to read it. Isaiah is prophecy, almost all of it Hebrew poetry: court cases, a love song that becomes a lawsuit (5:1–7), woes, oracles against nations, taunts and hymns, with a stretch of narrative (chapters 36–39). Prophets often see near and far events together, like mountain ridges seen from a distance, so the fall of Babylon becomes a window on the final day of the LORD (chapter 13), and a child born in Ahaz’s day is a sign that reaches beyond him to Immanuel himself (7:14), as Matthew says. The promises of Zion exalted and the nations streaming to it (2:2–4; chapter 60) this commentary reads, with the New Testament, as being fulfilled now, as Christ reigns and the gospel gathers the nations, and completed in the new creation (65:17).

How the book makes its case. Chapters 1–12 set out Judah’s sin and its coming King: the indictment (chapter 1), the vision of the Holy One (chapter 6), Immanuel (chapter 7), the child with four throne-names (9:6–7) and the shoot from the stump of Jesse (chapter 11), closing in a song (chapter 12). Chapters 13–23 show the LORD ruling every nation, from Babylon to Tyre, even promising that Egypt and Assyria will one day be his people (19:25). Chapters 24–27 widen to the whole earth, judged and renewed, where God “will swallow up death forever” (25:8). Chapters 28–35 condemn the alliance with Egypt and end with the desert in bloom (chapter 35). Chapters 36–39 are the hinge: Jerusalem is rescued from Assyria when Hezekiah prays, and then his pride points to Babylon. Chapters 40–48 comfort the exiles, put the idols on trial and raise up Cyrus. Chapters 49–55 go deeper: Cyrus could bring Israel out of Babylon, but the deeper captivity is sin, and only the Servant can deal with that, by suffering in his people’s place (52:13–53:12); then the invitation goes out: “Come, everyone who thirsts” (55:1). Chapters 56–66 open God’s house to all peoples, mourn the people’s continuing rebellion, and end with new heavens and a new earth.

Where it leads: to Christ. Isaiah points to Christ chiefly by direct promise, and the New Testament says so. Matthew hears 7:14 fulfilled in the virgin birth: “they shall call his name Immanuel” (Matthew 1:23). At Nazareth Jesus read Isaiah 61 and said, “Today this Scripture has been fulfilled in your hearing” (Luke 4:21). When an Ethiopian official asked Philip whom Isaiah 53 was about, “beginning with this Scripture he told him the good news about Jesus” (Acts 8:35), and Peter writes, “By his wounds you have been healed” (1 Peter 2:24). The Servant, distinct from the sinful people he dies for, “was pierced for our transgressions” (53:5), yet “he shall be high and lifted up” (52:13), the words used of the Lord on his throne in 6:1. John draws the line: “Isaiah said these things because he saw his glory and spoke of him” (John 12:41). The Holy One on the throne and the Servant on the cross are the same Lord.

For us. Isaiah humbles us and comforts us from the same source. It will not let us shrink God to a manageable size, or trust in money, strategy or the powers of the day; “in quietness and in trust shall be your strength” (30:15). But it tells guilty people that their warfare is ended and their iniquity pardoned (40:2), weary people that “they who wait for the LORD shall renew their strength” (40:31), and the whole world, “Turn to me and be saved, all the ends of the earth!” (45:22). Read it looking for the Servant, and you will find the King.
